experiment_summary: Qualitative case studies in InceptionV1. Curve detectors (mixed3b) are examined with feature visualization, dataset examples, synthetic stimuli, joint tuning under rotation, weight-level implementation, downstream use and a hand-written reimplementation. The same toolkit is applied to high-low frequency detectors and a pose-invariant dog-head detector. The authors cite thousands of hours of neuron study.

Weight inspection in InceptionV1. Early-curve to curve weights show tangent-curve excitation and opposite-orientation inhibition. A four-layer dog-head circuit has mirrored left and right pathways that inhibit each other and are then unioned into invariant units. A car detector in mixed4c is spread into dog neurons. A hand-set curve-detector circuit approximates the originals. Weight-editing tests are deferred to future work.

The evidence is anecdotal by the authors' own account. Curve detectors and high-low frequency detectors were observed in AlexNet, InceptionV1, VGG19 and ResNetV2-50, in models trained on Places365, and in vanilla conv nets trained from scratch on ImageNet. No systematic comparison of circuits across models was made.

A single circuit example in InceptionV1. A pure car-detecting neuron in mixed4c spreads its feature over several next-layer neurons that mainly detect dogs. The essay offers the geometry of high-dimensional spaces (exponentially many nearly-orthogonal vectors) and the non-co-occurrence of cars and dogs as the explanation.
Neuron 4e:55 in InceptionV1 responds to cat faces, car fronts and cat legs. Feature visualization shows it looks for distinct sub-patterns rather than a shared commonality.

Motifs illustrated by examples in InceptionV1: rotational equivariance in curve circuits, unioning over left- and right-facing dog heads, and car-into-dog superposition. Recurrence across other models is asserted but not systematically shown.

Seven converging arguments: feature visualization, dataset examples, synthetic curves of varying orientation and curvature, joint tuning under rotation, the implementing weights, downstream clients and a handwritten reimplementation. A detailed treatment is deferred to a later article.

Gated-MLP edit modules were trained with either a KL objective or an NMSE reconstruction objective on Scruples suggestion counterfactuals. Reconstruction better recreated mid-layer activations but recovered less output KL: 47.8% vs 20.4% on DeepSeek, and negative recovery on Gemma.

For each sequence, the top-5 IG edit events and 5 random events were ablated. Median Spearman correlation between attribution and ablation effect was 0.58 (Gemma) and 0.68 (DeepSeek). The edit-norm baseline gave 0.36/0.53 and RelP gave 0.18/0.16. Correlation is lower when all tokens are included.

Attribution and activation patching show filler-token activations mediate part of a suggestion's influence. Patching filler tokens alone recovers 11.4% of KL in Gemma.
Specific finding: A substantial part of the influence of a user suggestion on a reasoning model's response is mediated by residual-stream representations at the question statement and at filler tokens (whitespace, punctuation) rather than at semantically salient reasoning tokens. High-attribution tokens were dominated by indents, newlines, punctuation and question words. Native activation patching of filler plus question tokens recovered 16.2% (Gemma) and 19.3% (DeepSeek) of KL, 2.3–8.1× a random-token control. Qualitative examples show shifts in justification framing and final answers.

In a trained 1L transformer expanded into virtual weights, the authors identified large virtual weights that only increase loss. The clearest is IN→'utions' in the Tokens→Logits path, a continuation that never occurs in the training set. They also characterized harmful weights across all six virtual-weight families.
Specific finding: Trained transformers contain specific large virtual weights that are purely harmful to the training loss, e.g. direct-path token→logit weights toward continuations that never occur in training data. The largest Tokens→Logits weight from 'IN' targets 'utions', which never follows 'IN' in the training set. Its ablation lowers loss, and its Fisher effectiveness is about 3 orders of magnitude below that of the token's most effective weights.

Virtual weight magnitude and helpfulness were compared for the IN→Logits, French feature 3013, newline feature 1254, and Chinese feature weights, and for a sample of 1,111 weights across families. The relationship is weak, though some features, such as the Chinese one, have helpful top weights.

1,111 weights were sampled log-uniformly over Fisher-effectiveness rank across six families, and mean helpfulness with 95% confidence intervals was estimated over 1B tokens. Only helpful weights appear at the highest effectiveness in every family.

Weights were pruned from the 331M-weight VW model in order of increasing Fisher effectiveness, with loss evaluated on a held-out shard. Effectiveness ordering beats magnitude ordering at every density and in every family except negative Features→Logits. At 1% density, loss is significantly compromised.

Three lines of evidence. (1) Vocabulary reconstruction: vectors optimized to match the FV's decoded distribution recover little zero-shot accuracy with the top 100 tokens (antonym 48.2%→4.8%) and still underperform with the full vocabulary. (2) Cyclic tasks: FVs succeed on antonym, next-item and previous-item. (3) Layer dependence: FV effect drops to near zero in late layers across models. FVs also promote query-specific answers rather than generic output tokens.

Composed FVs are tested on 8 list-oriented tasks. Results are mixed: some compositions beat the extracted FV and even ICL (GPT-J Last-Country-Capital 0.60 vs. 0.32 ICL; Last-Capitalize-First-Letter 0.95 vs. 0.75), while others fail (Last-English-French 0.06). Results on Llama 2 13B and 70B are similarly mixed.

Mean last-token activations on task prompts, added at middle layers, induce the task (GPT-J antonym, 24.3% zero-shot). Head-selected mean vectors (FVs) are far stronger than the plain layer average (57.5% vs. 9.5% zero-shot).

Of the top 10 GPT-J heads by AIE, 3 have high prefix-matching (induction) scores (0.49, 0.56, 0.31). The other high-AIE heads do not show induction patterns on repeated random tokens, so ICL task transport involves non-induction heads too.

ACDC edge AUC on tracr-reverse was 0.200 with corrupted activations but 1.000 with zero activations. On IOI, AUC fell from 0.869 (KL) to 0.589 (task loss). On Docstring, zero ablation gave much worse circuits (KL 3.35) than corrupted ablation. Parent iteration order also changed induction results.

experiment_summary: On IOI in GPT-2 Small, optimizing logit difference never recovered negative name mover heads. KL optimization recovered heads 10.7 and 11.10 only at τ=0.00398 (443/32923 edges), along with heads not in the IOI circuit.

On reset networks with permuted Q/K/V head dimensions and MLP biases, all methods achieved much worse KL than on trained networks. HISP and SP with zero activations, and to some extent SP with corrupted activations, were still able to optimize the reset network.

Corrupted activations gave better results than zero activations on IOI and Docstring. Zero activations gave perfect tracr recovery and lower KL per edge count on induction, for both trained and reset networks.

Formal comparison of FF(x)=ReLU(xK^T)V with memory networks softmax(xK^T)V, plus empirical analyses of key triggers and value vocabulary projections in a 16-layer WikiText-103 LM.
Human experts annotated the top-25 training prefixes for 160 randomly sampled keys (10 per layer). Every key had at least one pattern (mean 3.6), and 65-80% of prefixes were covered by a pattern.

Annotated key patterns are mostly shallow in layers 1-9 and mostly semantic in layers 10-16. Removing the last token of the top-50 triggers for 1,600 keys reduces memory coefficients less in upper layers.

Top-token agreement between each value's vocabulary projection and the next token of its key's top trigger is near 0 in layers 1-10 and about 3.5% in upper layers (chance 0.0004%). The trigger's next-token rank improves with depth. Among the 100 most confident values (97 in layers 11-16), 46 agree with at least one top-50 trigger.

On 4,000 validation prefixes, 10-50% of the 4,096 memories per layer were active. In at least about 68% of examples, the layer's top token differed from every individual memory's top token. Single-memory agreement occurred mostly for stop words and short prefixes.

The residual's top token matches the final output for about one third of examples in the bottom layers, rising sharply from layer 10, and the probability of the final token increases with depth. When the FFN changes the residual's top token, the result rarely equals the FFN's own top token. A manual review of 100 last-layer changes found 66 shifts to semantically distant words and 34 to related words.

experiment_summary: Human annotators found recognizable patterns for all 160 sampled FFN keys, though most keys had several patterns and the evidence comes from top-25 activating examples only.

LAT reading vectors (top PC of paired activation differences) for truthfulness, honesty, utility, morality, power, probability, risk, emotion, harmfulness, bias and memorization classify held-out data at roughly 70-97% accuracy and steer behavior when added or subtracted.

On ETHICS utility with LLaMA-2-Chat-13B, mean-difference, PCA and K-means directions performed well on correlation, manipulation (steering generations, scored with a sentiment model) and termination (projection reduces accuracy). Contrast-vector steering improved TruthfulQA MC1.

Unsupervised LAT truthfulness directions, built from 5-50 stimuli drawn from three different sources, reach about 60% TruthfulQA MC1 against 32% zero-shot across LLaMA-2-Chat 7B/13B/70B. LAT beats few-shot prompting on OBQA, CSQA, ARC and RACE, and beats CCS on six DeBERTa tasks.

Using Alpaca stimuli, contrast vectors raise TruthfulQA MC1 from 35.9 to 54.0 on LLaMA-2-13B-Chat and from 31.0 to 47.9 on 7B. LoRRA reaches 47.5/42.3 and ActAdd 38.8/33.7. Adding or subtracting honesty vectors flips honest and dishonest answers in qualitative examples.

On ETHICS utility (LLaMA-2-Chat-13B), the logistic-regression direction had the highest classification accuracy but little steering effect. The prompt-difference direction steered well but its projection-removal did not reduce accuracy.

A LAT harmfulness vector built from 64 AdvBench and 64 ShareGPT instructions stays above 90% accurate under a manual jailbreak and a GCG suffix. Piece-wise control raises refusal of harmful requests under GCG from 16% to 83% while keeping helpfulness at 92%.

Single-vector activation additions (happiness) completely remove refusal of harmful requests in LLaMA-2-Chat-13B. RLHF-concealed social biases reappear when a short suffix is appended. Neither result includes a systematic measurement of capability retention.

A StereoSet-race bias vector, subtracted from LLaMA-2-Chat-13B, reduced gender-occupation bias in qualitative examples and cut female mentions in sarcoidosis vignettes from 97% to 55% and black-female mentions from 60% to 13%. Memorization directions transferred between quote and literary-opening contexts.

Activation differences from single contrast-prompt pairs (e.g. Love−Hate, weddings−' ', Anger−Calm), added at a middle residual-stream layer, steer topic, sentiment and toxicity. Evidence: >90% wedding-topic completions vs ~2% baseline on GPT-2-XL; SOTA negative→positive IMDb sentiment shift; lower RealToxicityPrompts toxicity on OPT-6.7B and LLaMA-3-8B. Qualitative replication on GPT-J-6B and Llama-1-13B, with some failures.
Specific finding: A steering vector computed from the activation difference of a single pair of contrasting prompts, without any optimization, suffices to control high-level output properties such as topic, sentiment and toxicity in language models. ActAdd with one contrast pair achieves topic steering on GPT-2-XL (perplexity ratio, word counts, GPT-3.5 relevance). It also achieves detox and sentiment results competitive with or better than PREADD, FUDGE and Air-Decoding on OPT-6.7B and LLaMA-3-8B. Hyperparameters were grid-searched; qualitative examples are best-of-3.

The wedding ActAdd vector on GPT-2-XL leaves perplexity on wedding-unrelated OpenWebText sentences nearly unchanged (ratio 0.994) and has negligible impact on ConceptNet/LAMA P@K. Sentiment steering raised disfluency 1.5-3×. Reasoning was not tested.

On GPT-2-XL, prepending ' weddings' raises perplexity on unrelated text (ratio 1.132), while ActAdd leaves it nearly unchanged (0.994). Prompting baselines underperform ActAdd on OPT toxicity and sentiment. Transplanting only the embedding difference to layer 20 has little effect, which argues against ActAdd being mere token injection.

The authors argue that successful additive steering along contrast-pair directions is causal evidence that models use linearly represented features. Supporting observations: random vectors of matched norm produce less targeted effects, and partial-dimension addition gives graded effects. The evidence is indirect and limited to the examined contexts.
ActAdd combines h+, h− and the user-prompt activations. Steering vectors around 10× the residual norm still yield coherent, steered GPT-2-XL completions.
In a layer sweep of the wedding vector on GPT-2-XL, effectiveness is present from layer 1, peaks around layer 6, then declines. More abstract vectors (conspiracy) work better at later layers.

LREs were estimated as the mean Jacobian and bias over 8 few-shot prompts, scaled by β. Faithfulness (argmax match with the LM) was measured over 24 trials per relation. 48% of relations had robust LREs and almost half exceeded 60% faithfulness. LRE beat logit-lens, translation, linear-regression and embedding-based baselines. Results held across three models and prompt templates.

No linear method exceeded 6% faithfulness on company CEO, although GPT-J correctly predicted CEOs for 69 companies. Person father, person mother and pokemon evolution were also low (about 0.07-0.15). The result held across layers and random example sets. Possible confounds include first-token collisions and the restriction to single-layer linear maps.

Edits Δs = W^†(o′−o) were patched at the last subject token. Causality closely matched the oracle (patching s′) across layers and differed from baselines that insert o′ or the unembedding row. Causality correlated with faithfulness at R=0.84 (GPT-J), 0.85 (GPT-2-XL) and 0.83 (LLaMA-13B) when hyperparameters were chosen for causality. Post-edit generations stayed fluent (qualitative).

11,891 repetition-distracted and 11,891 instruction-distracted prompts were constructed to bait GPT-J into outputting a false object. The LM's R@1 for the true fact was 0.02-0.03. The attribute lens applied at the last subject mention gave R@1 of 0.54-0.63 and R@3 of 0.71-0.78.

LRE faithfulness for 'plays the sport of' was high from layer 7 to layer 17 in GPT-J, then dropped sharply. When the relation text was removed from the prompt so the object immediately follows the subject, faithfulness kept rising in later layers.

An LRE applied to the raw subject token embedding e_s had much lower faithfulness than one applied to the mid-layer subject state. This indicates that relational information is added by earlier layers rather than being explained by word identity.

For selected relations in GPT-J, the line integral of the true Jacobian between subject pairs was compared with the mean Jacobian, giving underestimation ratios of 2.5-4.3. A β sweep showed mean faithfulness peaking at about 0.59 for β of 2-2.75. The authors attribute the gap partly to layer normalization.

The paper extends linearity from concept directions to relation-specific affine maps between representations. It also finds the linear scheme is not universal: about half of the relations are not well approximated.

CCS was trained on each dataset and tested on every other dataset. Transfer accuracy was usually competitive with no-transfer accuracy and sometimes exceeded it; for example, Amazon-trained CCS averaged 71.8% transfer accuracy, 0.6% above no transfer.

Clustering on the top principal component (70.1%) and bimodal salience search (70.2%) over normalized contrast differences were both competitive with calibrated zero-shot (67.2%) and close to CCS (71.2%). CCS trained on k unlabeled pairs, averaged over 32 resamples, often performed well with small k, sometimes even k=1, though with high variance.
Linear probes, both supervised logistic regression and unsupervised CCS, recover truth or answer correctness from last-token hidden states with high accuracy across 6 models and 10 datasets.

Unsupervised CCS beats calibrated zero-shot accuracy on average and stays robust when misleading prefixes degrade outputs. However, the paper does not test imitative-falsehood benchmarks such as TruthfulQA.
Specific finding: Unsupervised probes on hidden states can recover knowledge distinct from, and more accurate than, what the model's outputs express. Intermediate layers can be more robust and less correlated with outputs than final layers. For T5 and UnifiedQA, middle-layer CCS sometimes beat last-layer CCS. Under the misleading prefix, UnifiedQA's decoder-state CCS dropped from 81.0% to 73.5% while its encoder states stayed robust. On MLM-only DeBERTa with the label mid-prompt, CCS reached 93.7% versus 71.6% for an adapted zero-shot baseline on Amazon.
Specific finding: A linear probe trained only with an unsupervised logical-consistency objective (negation consistency plus confidence) on contrast-pair hidden states can answer binary questions more accurately than calibrated zero-shot prompting of the same model, without labels or model outputs. CCS averaged 71.2% vs 67.2% for calibrated zero-shot across models (excluding T0) and datasets, with about 9 prompts per dataset. It underperformed zero-shot on RoBERTa and T0. The supervised logistic-regression ceiling was 83.7%. The difference was statistically significant per a Wald test.
Specific finding: Unsupervised consistency-based probes on hidden states retain their accuracy when a misleading prompt prefix degrades the model's zero-shot output accuracy, indicating that internal representations can track truth even when outputs do not. A prefix of incorrectly answered questions dropped UnifiedQA calibrated zero-shot accuracy from 80.4% to 70.9%, while CCS stayed at 82.1% to 83.8%. Other models were largely robust to the prefix. Correct-answer prefixes behaved similarly, so the mechanism may be out-of-distribution input rather than imitation of falsehoods.

On 2,000 WikiText-103 validation sentences, the authors scored the reference token under the top-10 dominant sub-updates versus 10 random sub-updates, in saturation events (1,184 / 1,579) and elimination events (1,909 / 1,996). Promoted tokens had higher maximum scores (1.2 vs 0.5 in WikiLM; 8.5 vs 4.0 in GPT-2). Eliminated tokens had near-zero mean scores. Random sub-updates produced much smaller scores.

Value vectors were grouped into 10k clusters by agglomerative cosine clustering, and the authors counted which clusters appear in sub-updates whose top-candidate scores exceed ±10 (GPT-2) or ±5 (WikiLM). The responsible clusters cover 1.7% and 1.1% of value vectors and are active mostly on short or easy inputs. The interpretation rests on qualitative inspection.

Coefficients of 10 manually picked 'safe' value vectors were set to 3. On 1,225 challenging RealToxicityPrompts with 20-token continuations, the toxic rate fell from 58.5% to 30.8%, beating Self-Debiasing (37.2%) and WordFilter (46.9%). Ten API-graded non-toxic vectors were weaker (52.7%). Perplexity rose from 21.7 to 25.3.

A nearest-neighbour cluster-overlap rule on WikiLM, built from 10k WikiText-103 validation examples, reached 94.1±1.4% accuracy and saved 3.2 layers (about 20% of computation). This is comparable to logistic-regression probes on x, o, and x̃ (92.9-94.4% accuracy, 3.0-3.1 layers saved).

Projections of real value vectors yield concept-coherent top tokens far more often than projections of random vectors with matched statistics, in both models.
Specific finding: Applying layer normalization to FFN value vectors before projecting them onto the vocabulary does not substantially change their top-scoring tokens, so raw projection is a valid reading of their effect. The top-30 token IoU between E·v and E·LayerNorm(v) across all GPT-2 value vectors averaged 64.5%, versus about 0% for random vectors.
Specific finding: Across all layers of transformer LMs, individual FFN value vectors, when projected onto the output vocabulary, promote small sets of human-interpretable semantic or syntactic concepts (about 1-1.5 concepts per vector). They are substantially more interpretable than random vectors or than the aggregate FFN output. Experts annotated patterns among the top-30 tokens of 10 random value vectors per layer (160 WikiLM and 120 GPT-2 vectors). Top tokens covered by a concept: 55.1% vs 22.7% for random Gaussian vectors in WikiLM, and 37% vs 16% in GPT-2. Full FFN updates covered 19.7% and 11.8% once stopword concepts were excluded.
The paper extends the finding from upper layers to all layers and reframes value vectors as encoding general concepts rather than specific next tokens.
The top-10 dominant sub-updates (0.24% of value vectors) contribute only about 5-10% of the FFN output norm. Full FFN updates are less interpretable than individual sub-updates.

Saturation events, where the final prediction becomes the top candidate, occur across all layers (Tables 9-10). Dominant FFN sub-updates promote candidates incrementally, and late 'saturation vectors' preserve an already-fixed top token.

Nonlinear (2-layer MLP) probes decode the black/white/empty state of each tile from Othello-GPT activations with error as low as 1.7% (synthetic) and 9.4% (championship). The same probes on a randomly initialized network stay at about 25–26% error. Probe-guided interventions further show that the representation drives move predictions.

Training on a skewed 20M-game synthetic set with every C5-opening game removed (a quarter of the game tree) still gives a 0.02% top-1 illegal-move rate on held-out games. The full synthetic model has 0.01%, the championship model 5.17%, and the untrained model 93.29%.

Linear probes never fall below about 20% error (vs about 27–29% on the random network). 2-layer MLP probes reach 1.7–4.8% in middle and late layers of the synthetic model. Over 100 seeds the standard deviations are below 0.1%.

Linear probes for per-tile black/white/empty board state in Othello-GPT perform poorly while nonlinear probes succeed. The authors conclude the world representation is 'nonlinear in an essential way'. Only one labelling scheme was tested.

Probing after an intervention at layer 5 shows the flipped tile reverting at layer 6 unless later layers are also edited. Starting interventions too early (in layers whose world representation is still unreliable) or too late both hurt the result.

This is a qualitative comparison. Saliency maps for the synthetic model highlight exactly the tiles that make the move legal. Maps for the championship model are more diffuse. Maps capture AND-logic but miss OR-logic when several lines are flipped.

Nonlinear probe accuracy across layers peaks mid-to-late in Othello-GPT (championship best at layer 4; synthetic best at layers 6–7), and probe capacity is varied as an ablation. The authors note the parallel to linguistic probing results.

A difference-in-means direction was extracted from 128 harmful and 128 harmless instructions and selected on validation sets. Ablating it at all layers and positions drove refusal on 100 JailbreakBench prompts near zero and elicited unsafe completions (scored by Llama Guard 2). Adding it at the source layer induced refusal on 100 harmless Alpaca prompts. The effect held consistently across all 13 models.

Weight orthogonalization against the refusal direction requires no gradients and no harmful completions. HarmBench ASR was about 78–84% on Qwen (comparable to per-prompt GCG) and 61–80% on Llama-2 without a system prompt. MMLU, ARC, GSM8K, WinoGrande and TinyHellaSwag mostly stayed within 99% confidence intervals, though TruthfulQA dropped 1–6 points and Qwen 7B and Yi 34B showed some significant drops. A 70B model can be jailbroken for under $5 of compute. LoRA fine-tuning was replicated as a comparison.
A difference-in-means vector between harmful and harmless instruction activations, both added and ablated, causally controls refusal in 13 chat models.
The behavior of refusing harmful requests is causally controlled by a single linear direction across 13 models.
Both directional ablation and subtraction of the refusal vector bypass refusal and elicit harmful content (Llama Guard 2 unsafe) across 13 safety-tuned models.

In Qwen 1.8B Chat, a GCG adversarial suffix heavily suppressed the last-token cosine similarity with the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, down to harmless-instruction levels; random suffixes did not. The authors note this contrasts with RepE's finding that the harmfulness representation is unaltered by suffixes. Whether the direction encodes harmfulness or refusal is unresolved, and only one model and one suffix were tested.

Both interventions bypassed refusal comparably. Across 13 models, however, subtracting the difference-in-means vector raised cross-entropy loss on the Pile, on Alpaca, and especially on the model's own on-distribution completions (e.g. Llama-3 8B: 0.195 baseline, 0.213 ablation, 0.441 act-add). PCA visualizations of Gemma 7B show harmless activations pushed off-distribution.

Last-token activations of base and chat models on 128 harmful and 128 harmless instructions were compared by cosine similarity with the chat-derived refusal direction. Base models showed similarly high similarity on harmful and low similarity on harmless prompts, for four model pairs. This is correlational only; no causal test was run on the base models.

experiment_summary: The selected refusal directions came mostly from middle layers (e.g. 12/32 to 62/80), though selection excluded layers at or above 0.8L by design. Llama-3 8B bypass and induce scores across all layer and position candidates are shown in Figure 11.

With K=48 heads and α≈15-20 under 2-fold CV, true*info rises: LLaMA-7B 30.5→43.5%, Alpaca 32.5→65.1%, Vicuna 51.5→74.0%, and few-shot prompting 49.5→51.4% with ITI. Evaluation uses GPT-judge with a human spot-check; results are averaged over seeds and are stable.

Per-head linear probes on LLaMA-7B reach up to 83.3% validation accuracy (84.4% on all heads concatenated) at classifying TruthfulQA answers as true or false. This is roughly 40 points above generation truthfulness, and steering along the probed directions raises generation truthfulness.
A heatmap of probe accuracy for every head in LLaMA-7B shows most heads at about 50% and a small number standing out in each layer. The best head is layer 14, head 18 at 83.3%.
A second probe constrained orthogonal to the first truthful direction still yields better-than-chance accuracy, and the true and false activation distributions overlap heavily in the 2-D projection.

Steering along the probe-weight direction (the best-separating direction) gives only 34.8% true*info, versus 42.3% for the mass-mean-shift direction. A toy anisotropic-Gaussian example illustrates why the best classifier normal differs from the mean-difference direction.
Mass-mean shift (true mean minus false mean of head activations) outperforms probe-weight, CCS and random directions for truthfulness steering, and it tolerates stronger α.
At each method's optimal α, true*info and KL on LLaMA-7B are: without selection 35.4% (KL 0.08), point-wise feature selection 39.2% (KL 1.95, CE 4.01), head-wise selection 42.3% (KL 0.27).
Sweeps over α and K show an inverted-U in true*info. The count of "I have no comment" answers rises with α.
Training-set fraction was varied for layer 14, head 18 of LLaMA-7B. Truthfulness plateaus early and direction similarity rises rapidly.
On LLaMA-7B, 50-shot prompting (49.5% true*info) beats ITI alone (43.5%), but ITI added on top of few-shot prompting gives the best score (51.4%). Both ITI and SFT beat the baseline.

ITI increases OpenWebText cross-entropy (LLaMA-7B 2.16→2.48; Vicuna 2.63→3.36) and next-token KL (0.40 to 1.41). Strong random-direction perturbations barely change behavior, and MMLU accuracy improves slightly.
Linear probes decode truthfulness from head activations, and adding linear directions changes truthful behavior. The authors also note that truth occupies a subspace rather than a single direction.

A blinded human evaluation of 50 random features per method classified 41 transcoder and 38 SAE features as interpretable, with eight per method possibly interpretable. Mean L0 was 44.04 versus 47.85, and replacement cross-entropy was 3.35 versus 3.36 nats.

The paper derives the factorization, extends attribution through attention OV maps, and illustrates its use in GPT2-small feature and greater-than circuit analyses. It does not establish complete causal fidelity to the original network.

Table 4 reports five successful, two mostly successful, and two failed interpretations. Restricted studies disallowed input-dependent layer-0 feature information. Successful hypotheses included citation semicolons and interview contexts; failures included an overly narrow scientific-subject hypothesis.

For 'He was caught' versus 'He caught the ball', feature activations were 19.97 versus 0.8145 in the original model, compared with 16.45 versus 9.00 after replacement, showing much weaker participle selectivity in this example.

Automated explanation and held-out activation prediction compared 100 random features with 100 random neurons; SAE features scored higher, and specificity ratings also favored features. Text-trained features activated on curated images and multilingual text. experiment_summary: Neighborhood analysis found a San Francisco feature in the 1M SAE corresponding to two features in the 4M SAE and eleven finer-grained features in the 34M SAE. Larger SAEs also contained some concepts without apparent smaller-dictionary counterparts.

Across 100–200 concepts per category, concept-feature coverage increased with dictionary size and frequency. Rescaling frequency by alive-feature count approximately aligned coverage curves; the greater-than-50% coverage threshold lay slightly below inverse alive-feature count.

Feature interventions preserved reconstruction error and altered selected feature coefficients. Golden Gate Bridge steering induced bridge-related self-identification; code-error steering induced hallucinated exceptions or counterfactual bug-free execution; addition-feature steering induced addition-like execution.

experiment_summary: Clamping selected features elicited vulnerable code, a code backdoor, hateful outputs, excessive praise, secrecy, and a scam email that the unmodified model would not produce. Interventions often used multiples of the maximum observed feature activation; no systematic jailbreak-success benchmark was reported.

Comprehensive ablations on the emotional-inference and first Kobe Bryant prompts yielded about 0.81 correlation between attribution and ablation effects, compared with 0.12 for activations. In the Kobe case, eight of the ten top-attributed features, versus three of the ten most active, were among the ten largest ablation effects.

experiment_summary: Few-shot residual difference vectors matched feature steering for gender bias and agreement, but failed to usefully steer five other selected concepts where SAE steering succeeded. Scaling-factor sweeps were manual and nonsystematic; larger-data alternatives were not evaluated.

experiment_summary: Width ladders from approximately 16K to 524K latents, with sparsity-coefficient sweeps, show improved delta-loss versus L0 curves for wider SAEs. Standard fidelity evaluations use 2,048 sequences of length 1,024. Numerical effect sizes are not provided in the text.

Residual-stream SAEs yield higher delta LM loss than MLP and attention SAEs despite roughly comparable FVU. Base-to-IT transfer also appears stronger under delta loss than under FVU. These compare evaluation metrics rather than training objectives.

Compared base-trained and IT-trained SAEs on 1,024 Gemma 2 9B IT rollouts generated at temperature 1.0 from sampled Gemini 1.0 Ultra SFT prompts. Delta-loss results are close, while FVU shows a larger transfer gap. Supplementary evaluations cover user prompts and Gemma 2 2B IT.

Reproduces results from Rajamanoharan et al. (2024b): human interpretability judgments and Pearson correlation between explanation-simulated and actual activations show little discernible architecture difference. This is reused evidence, not an independent replication.
Compared delta LM loss versus L0 with both SAE and LM weights in float32 or bfloat16. The reported curves indicate negligible inference impact; training remained float32.

Compared downstream loss increases across MLP layers at fixed L0. Transcoders perform worse than output SAEs, reversing a prior GPT-2 Small trend. Architecture, training differences, and possible implementation errors remain unresolved explanations.

Human ratings on a 0–100 scale favor sparse over neuron features: random 52.8 versus 32.6, agreement 62.3 versus 30.2, and Bias in Bios 81.5 versus 36.0. Annotators were recruited from an alignment research community.

Around 100 Pythia or 500 Gemma feature nodes explain most task performance, versus approximately 1,500 or 50,000 neurons for half. Ablating a few selected feature nodes eliminates task performance even while retaining SAE errors. Feature-node counts can include high-dimensional error nodes.

Applied to four agreement tasks in two models, Bias in Bios classifiers, and thousands of automatically clustered Pythia behaviors. Held-out faithfulness and complement-ablation evaluations validate selected node sets; broad automated edge-level evaluation is not supplied.

Humans ablate 55 Pythia or 43 Gemma features. After retraining only the head on the same ambiguous data, balanced profession accuracy reaches 93.1% and 95.0%, and worst-group accuracy reaches 89.0% and 92.9%. Gender-label accuracy falls to 52.0% and 52.4%. Random-feature and privileged neuron-ablation baselines perform worse. Gemma's baseline layer was selected using balanced data.

experiment_summary: Spectral clustering uses 8,192 samples; parameter-gradient clustering scales to 100,000 samples through sparse random projection and k-means. Thousands of circuits are generated, with qualitative examples revealing succession, narrow induction, and distinct infinitival-object mechanisms. Systematic quality evaluation remains open.

Annotated relative-clause circuits contain 86 Pythia nodes or 223 Gemma nodes, each with faithfulness 0.21. Relative-clause and prepositional-phrase circuits share over 85% of features. Qualitative inspection identifies shared pathways and additional noun-phrase number tracking in Gemma.

Constructs CLT attribution graphs using stop-gradient Jacobians and demonstrates the resulting decomposition in acronym, factual-recall, and addition examples. Perturbation experiments assess selected downstream consequences.

Maps feature responses across all 10,000 addition prompts, identifies operand, lookup-table, and sum features, and examines their global connections. Inhibiting ones-digit features largely spares magnitude pathways and vice versa. Top-1 accuracy is 98.6% for 18L and 100% for Haiku on these prompts.

experiment_summary: Architecture and hyperparameter sweeps compare normalized MSE, L0, downstream KL, and delta cross-entropy. TopK outperforms ReLU, with a widening reconstruction advantage at scale; it performs best overall against Gated and ProLU, though Gated is comparable in one fixed-width comparison. GPT-4 baseline comparisons are described as less certain.

GPT-2 small ablations at 2 million latents and k=32 identify aligned initialization and AuxK as the main contributors. Unmitigated runs can have up to 90% dead latents; the 16-million-latent GPT-4 SAE has 7% dead latents after 40 billion training tokens.

Width, compute, sparsity, and learning-rate sweeps yield power-law trends and a joint width–sparsity fit. Tokens to convergence scale approximately as n^0.6 for GPT-2 small and n^0.65 for GPT-4. Trends break as k approaches residual dimensionality, and the 16-million-latent run was not trained to convergence.

Width sweeps evaluate 61-task single-latent probe loss, N2G precision/recall, explanation-simulated downstream loss, and latent-ablation logit sparsity. Metrics generally improve with width, while changes in k create conflicting trends and dense-regime failures.

Single-latent probes outperform residual-channel probes. GPT-2 SAE latent ablations have effective logit-effect fractions of 10–14%, versus 60% for residual channels. Qualitative inspection finds many interpretable GPT-2 features, but many GPT-4 random activations remain inadequately monosemantic.

N2G explanations simulate latent activations, which are rescaled, decoded, and substituted at GPT-2 small layer 8. Larger and sparser SAEs preserve more downstream performance than smaller or less sparse ones and explain more behavior than a bigram baseline.

The 16-million-latent GPT-4 SAE obtains 98.2% zero-ablation fidelity, yet substitution yields language-model loss corresponding to only 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute under the paper's comparison.

Changing k after single-TopK training eventually worsens MSE beyond the training k. Combining L(k) with L(4k)/8 yields progressive recovery across tested k values and nearly matching fixed-count TopK and variable-count JumpReLU curves, at a small cost at the original k.

Figure 2 illustrates different apparent patching effects under logit difference, log probability, probability, and rank in GPT-2 medium. The supplied text reports probability and log-probability saturation and rank thresholds, but omits the dataset, detailed intervention setup, and quantitative comparisons.

Across factual recall, IOI, arithmetic, docstrings, and greater-than tasks, changing corruption methods and recovery metrics changes localization peaks and detected components. GN produces 2–5 times larger factual-recall peaks than STR, while STR can produce sharper arithmetic peaks.

STR misses Negative Name Mover 11.10 under probability. With all three IOI names randomized, original-answer probability is approximately 0.0005 and probability detects neither Negative Name Mover, while logit difference detects both. Corrupting S1 and IO provides another demonstration.

GN with joint windows produces pronounced middle-layer localization, whereas STR weakens it and single-layer patching yields weak or absent peaks. Probability emphasizes the last subject token more than logit difference; the STR last-to-middle subject ratio is 4.33 versus 1.22. Related metric effects are reported in GPT-J.

A mathematical construction combines orthogonal disconnected and dormant directions. In GPT-2 Small IOI, DAS finds an MLP8 direction with 46.7% FLDD, falling to 13.5% for its rowspace component, while full-MLP patching gives −8%. GPT-2 XL factual patches also lose their effect when the nullspace component is removed. Random-MLP and higher-dimensional tests further support the mechanism.

Compared layerwise perplexity, marginal-output KL bias, and output fidelity on 16.4M evaluation tokens per model. Tuned lenses improve perplexity across tested families; GPT-Neo-2.7B logit-lens bias is approximately 4–5 bits through most layers and is substantially reduced by tuning.

Pythia 12B covariance comparisons show smooth drift after removing outlier dimensions and a sharp final-layer change. Nearby-layer translators transfer with modest penalties, but direct unembedding can fail. Transfer penalties correlate negatively with covariance similarity at Spearman ρ = −0.78.

Prediction trajectories tend to improve with depth. On roughly 16M Pile tokens, Pythia 6.9B residual updates have negative cosine similarity with the loss gradient at least 95% of the time at every layer. Deleting individual layers other than the first produces very small perplexity increases.

Optimized orthogonal directions with L-BFGS on 131,072 Pile validation tokens and evaluated their ablation effects on tuned-lens and downstream model outputs. Optimization sometimes yields nonmonotonic influences, requiring post hoc sorting.

Mean-ablation influence on lens and model outputs correlates at Spearman ρ = 0.89 for Pythia 410M layer 18. Resampling top-10 CBE subspaces in Pythia 160M yields higher weighted-Aitchison stimulus-response alignment for tuned lenses than logit lenses at every layer.

Compared transferred LLaMA translators with Vicuna-trained translators on RedPajama and Anthropic Helpful Harmless test data. RedPajama KL penalties are at worst 0.3 bits per byte; no significant difference is reported on Helpful Harmless.

Isolation forest and local outlier factor use flattened answer-log-probability trajectories. Across ten random splits, tuned-lens detection reaches near-perfect AUROC on BoolQ, MNLI, QNLI, QQP, and SST-2. SRM matches or exceeds performance on most tasks; tuned lenses outperform it only on ARC-Challenge.

Compared iteration learned over 143 checkpoints with final-checkpoint prediction depth. Tuned-lens Spearman correlations range from 0.156 to 0.660, are reported significant on every task, and exceed logit-lens correlations on eight of eleven tasks.

BPEmb token-coherence scores for Pythia 125M weight-derived vectors exceed shuffled-matrix controls, with improved real-minus-random differences under tuned decoding. Most singular vectors remain no more interpretable than random, and preliminary larger-model experiments perform poorly.
Specific finding: Applying a transformer language model's final layer norm and unembedding to intermediate-layer residual-stream activations yields sensible next-token distributions that converge smoothly toward the final output distribution, often reaching a good guess by the middle layers. Direct decoding works reasonably for GPT-2 but fails to yield plausible continuations in many GPT-Neo, BLOOM, and OPT-125M layers. BLOOM and OPT-125M frequently predict the input token instead of a continuation; learned translators improve decoding.

On RealToxicityPrompts, setting coefficients of the 20 most toxic tuned-lens-selected value vectors to zero reduces OPT-125M toxicity from 0.50 to 0.39, versus 0.43 using logit-lens selection; perplexity rises from 27.66 to 27.73. Other tested models show no toxicity decrease exceeding 2%.

Feature interventions alter geographic answers, poem structure, medical follow-up questions, hallucinations, refusals, and concealed bias-driven outputs in directions predicted by selected graphs.
Specific finding: Language models can use unspoken candidate-diagnosis representations to select follow-up questions about corroborating symptoms. Pregnancy and symptom features activate preeclampsia features, which promote visual-disturbance and proteinuria responses. Inhibiting preeclampsia features shifts the suggested follow-up to decreased appetite, consistent with an alternative biliary hypothesis.
Specific finding: Language models can perform internal two-hop factual recall through an intermediate entity representation while also using shortcut pathways. Dallas activates Texas-related features on a state-capital prompt; inhibiting or replacing these features changes the answer. Substitutions using California, Georgia, British Columbia, China, and Byzantine Empire features produce corresponding capitals. Graphs also contain Dallas-to-Austin shortcuts.

experiment_summary: Newline-localized rabbit and habit features influence both final-token probabilities and intermediate comparison phrases. Full-line resampling uses 500 samples per experiment; injecting rabbit or green features across 25 poems yields the injected ending in 70% of cases.
Operand plots cover 10,000 pairs from 0–99. The 36+59 graph combines approximate-sum features with ones-digit lookup features to promote 95; the paper revisits the companion study's mechanism.

An ends-in-6 plus ends-in-9 feature appears across multiple contexts. In a journal citation, inhibiting the lookup feature changes the prediction; replacing it with an ends-in-9 plus ends-in-9 feature shifts the predicted year from 1995 to 1998.

Activating known-answer features induces fabricated answers about unfamiliar names; inhibiting them increases uncertainty for Michael Jordan and can prevent a false Karpathy paper attribution. Some predicted effects fail, and effective intervention strengths are high.

Global feature weights and 200 Sorry Bench attribution graphs connect specific harm features to general harmful-request and refusal features. Dictionaries trained only on pretraining data contain few refusal features; bleach/ammonia feature ablations alter refusal behavior.

Interventions support refusal-mediating internal representations, but dozens of influential features weakly cluster into multiple semantic groups. The authors suggest earlier refusal directions may represent generalized harm rather than refusal itself.

Graphs suggest independent letter decoding initially fails to form a harmful-request representation. Activating a specific request feature can trigger earlier refusal; punctuation-feature interventions depend on allowing attention changes. Removing punctuation from the requested response delays refusal in an example.

Graphs identify a suggested-answer/divide-by-five pathway producing an intermediate 0.8. Inhibiting relevant features shifts the output; varying suggested answers changes the resulting reasoning, whereas a tractable square-root example remains correct.

An RM-bias feature activates in 100/100 dialogue contexts versus 1/100 unformatted controls. Inhibiting bias features reduces meta-rhyme completions from about 48% to 12% in the intervention setting, and emergency-call/voting addenda from 42%/56% to 6%/0% across 50 sampled completions.

experiment_summary: Resampling consistent with the direct-output roles of heads 1.0, 2.0, and 2.1 recovers 93% of normalized performance. Adding the proposed upstream count and nesting mechanisms reduces recovery to 88% or 84%, and to 72% jointly, indicating that the detailed account is incomplete or subtly incorrect. Recovery uses original loss 0.0003 as 100% and randomly permuted-label loss as 0%.

A naive hypothesis with embedding-only queries and values and previous-token-mediated keys recovers 35% of performance. Jointly allowing three-token matching, current-position layer-0 contributions, and identity-attention estimates for three repeated-token heads raises recovery to 86%. Separate contributions of these changes are not reported.

Methodological discussion, not a new experimental test: The limitations discussion gives the conceptual example of omitted inhibitory circuits such as negative name movers: removing them can overstate the explanatory contribution of a heuristic. No new quantitative test of this failure mode is reported in the supplied main post.

Methodological discussion, not a new experimental test: The post explains that perfectly correlated features induce identical scrubbing equivalence classes, and that features with no alternative matching examples cannot be tested through dataset resampling. These are methodological arguments rather than quantified experiments.

Compared faithfulness curves over circuit sizes using EAP, five-step EAP-IG, and independent activation-patching scores. Task-metric EAP-IG matched or exceeded EAP across the six main tasks; larger-model experiments supported the same direction with 100 examples per task. Activation patching remained better on some tasks.

EAP-IG score correlations with patching exceeded 0.8 and were higher than EAP's, but whole-ranking Kendall correlations were worse and error reductions were small or inconsistent. Overlap improved mainly among roughly the top 50 edges; the input-to-MLP-0 edge explained a major SVA failure.

Compared endpoint-gradient averaging with EAP, two- and five-step EAP-IG, activation-space variants, and patching. Five-step EAP-IG outperformed endpoint averaging only on SVA; the endpoint baseline outperformed EAP.
Derives the first-order formula and implements it for GPT-2 Small IOI analyses. The stated GPT-2 XL speedup is a complexity estimate, not a measured runtime result.

experiment_summary: Across seven architectures, reconstruction rankings diverge from absorption, SCR, RAVEL, and probing rankings; Matryoshka has middling reconstruction but leading concept and disentanglement scores.
Matryoshka leads absorption, RAVEL, sparse probing, SCR, and TPP in the principal comparison, while TopK variants reconstruct better. Its SCR advantage is absent on Pythia-160M.
Loss recovered generally increases with dictionary width across the controlled architecture suite and the Gemma Scope width series.

Wider dictionaries improve automated interpretability and reconstruction but often worsen absorption, SCR, and TPP in non-hierarchical SAEs. The study does not directly test every component of the broader claim.

Width sweeps show worse absorption and generally worse SCR for non-hierarchical architectures; Gemma Scope evaluations extend degrading absorption, SCR, and TPP trends to 1M latents. Figure 7 reports a ReLU SCR exception.

Lower L0 often improves automated interpretability, while higher L0 improves reconstruction, RAVEL, TPP, and absorption; moderate L0 can favor SCR and probing. L0 50–150 is recommended as a compromise.

SCR automates SHIFT on perfectly biased profession–gender and product–sentiment datasets, measuring balanced-test accuracy improvements after zero-ablating selected latents. The new tests assess automated rather than human feature selection.
Evaluates recovery at ten circuit proportions from 0.001 to 1 and uses trapezoidal integration; CPR and CMD yield different rankings, particularly for UGS and node methods.

Counterfactual EAP generally outperforms mean/OA EAP under counterfactual evaluation: GPT-2 IOI CMD is 0.03 versus 0.29/0.30. Authors explicitly note the match between discovery and evaluation favors counterfactual ablations.

DAS generally leads IIA across MCQA, ARC Easy, and RAVEL, and IOI logit MSE. Gemma MCQA ordering IIA averages 77% for DAS versus 63% standard masking, 52% PCA, and 51% SAE. Gemma carry localization is an exception: DAS averages 31% versus 33% standard masking.

SAE masking generally fails to improve over standard-dimension masking on MCQA, ARC Easy, RAVEL, and carry localization. On Llama ARC Easy, answer-token/ordering IIA averages 74%/55% for SAE versus 85%/69% for standard dimensions. SAE performance relative to PCA varies by task.

DAS separately aligns ordering and answer-token variables using counterfactuals that alter either or both. MCQA best-layer ordering IIA reaches 93% in Gemma, 91% in Llama, and 100% in Qwen; full-vector interventions generally fail to separate the variables across layers.

Restricted carry-changing counterfactuals produce apparent carry localization in Llama middle layers, but carry correlates with tens-digit output. Random counterfactuals break this confound and localization fails, weakening the carry interpretation.

Re-runs token/position flip interventions and fits logit difference as 0.048 + 2.005 PositionSignal + 0.768 TokenSignal. Feature-level alignments further disentangle signals: DAS position/token MSE is 2.20/2.08 versus 2.45/2.82 for the selected whole-head alignment.

Combined behavioral sampling, QK/OV analysis, and CSPA recover 76.9% of L10H7’s direct-effect KL baseline on OpenWebText. Static OV suppression holds in the top-ten criterion for 84.70% of vocabulary items; idealized QK matching ranks the diagonal first for 95.72%.

Name Mover ablations reveal both reduced negative-head suppression and increased copying by backup heads. Weight composition analysis across 141 names distinguishes their opposing attention responses.

Projecting upstream outputs away from the indirect-object unembedding largely preserves backup effects. Attention-score decompositions identify important perpendicular components. General query-only unembedding projection recovers 25% of L10H7’s KL effect, increasing to 61% with semantic subspaces and fitted token-specific scaling and biases.

CSPA yields 76.9% KL recovery for L10H7; separate OV and QK interventions yield 81.1% and 95.2%. Net-loss and absolute-loss recovery differ substantially, and other late heads can exceed 50% KL recovery, limiting specificity.
Induction, antonym, multiple-choice, and correctness case studies expose query–key mechanisms absent from prior fixed-attention graphs; targeted interventions change attention and output predictions.

The paper develops an existing decomposition strategy and tests feature interactions by selectively steering QK inputs in induction, antonym, multiple-choice, and correctness examples, observing corresponding attention and prediction changes.

The authors compute head loadings in feature graphs and use them to select heads for QK analysis and interventions across the presented Haiku case studies. No systematic scaling benchmark is supplied.
location: Computing attention head contributions to an attribution graph

experiment_summary: The Aunt Sally example combines generic name attention with title-conditioned matching, and the Aunt Mary Sue example exhibits independent Mary/after-Mary and family-name interactions. Suppressing title-conditioned key features removes observed induction in the first example.

Inspecting selected heads reveals correct-answer, incorrect-answer, and generic-option interactions. Suppressing correct-answer features reduces the B response; suppressing them on B while injecting them on A or C redirects the predicted letter.

Color-feature QK interactions have opposing signs in concordance and discordance heads. Replacing yellow signals with red signals within QK inputs flips Yes to No; scaling individual head outputs can also flip responses. The same heads show analogous attention and feature-interaction differences for 18+5=23 versus 18+6=23.

The authors report that freezing attention patterns of unsteered heads reduces by more than half the number of steered heads needed for the same effect, consistent with their proposed hydra-head explanation.

experiment_summary: Independent orthogonal toy features are recovered, but hierarchical versions yield merged decoder directions and parent-latent recall holes despite the features remaining sparse and linear. Real-model spelling experiments demonstrate analogous failures.
The analytical absorption family retains perfect reconstruction while lowering sparsity cost and making the parent encoder an incomplete classifier. Toy training exhibits the same mismatch.
Probe-aligned and k=1-selected latents show similar precision/recall trends across L0, with no evaluated SAE matching the LR-probe baseline. F1 optima vary with layer and letter.

Feature visualization, rotated natural images, and synthetic orientation–curvature sweeps reveal orientation-selective curve responses. The article notes coverage gaps partly filled by double-curve detectors and describes earlier curve families without presenting the full construction analysis.
Specific finding: Curve-detector neurons can exhibit large activation changes under barely perceptible changes in stimulus orientation or curvature. Orientation–curvature activation maps contain narrow wisps where tiny stimulus changes alter responses by several dataset standard deviations. No whole-model adversarial robustness benchmark is reported.
Specific finding: Some curve-detector neurons have a predominantly coherent curve-related function across activation strengths, with no demonstrated unrelated secondary function. Diversity-regularized feature visualization continues to produce curves. Over 800 activation-blinded manual labels and attribution visualizations relate response strength to curve quality; curves and imperfect curves contribute 55% of activation-weighted expected output. Rare secondary functions remain possible.
Specific finding: Orientation-selective curve neurons can respond across varied curve radii, colors, brightness, textures, and fill styles while retaining preferences for smooth curved boundaries. Natural examples and synthetic sweeps show broad radius tolerance and responses across color and fill variants. Angle-to-curve interpolations increase maximal responses as boundaries become smoother; cosmetic invariance is reported qualitatively rather than with aggregate accuracy metrics.

experiment_summary: Converging optimized, natural-image, human-labeling, and synthetic-stimulus analyses support a coherent curve interpretation for selected InceptionV1 neurons.

experiment_summary: Optimization repeatedly produces curve stimuli, including under diversity incentives; natural-image attribution visualizations and controlled synthetic curves corroborate the interpretation. These experiments do not isolate the necessity of every visualized property.

Activation-distribution analysis shows strong responses are extremely rare, while inspection across activation bins reveals weak responses to imperfect curves and negative responses to opposing curves. Synthetic sweeps expose sensitivity not apparent from top examples.

experiment_summary: Scores all heads using the embedding–MLP0–OV–unembedding path over eight ordinal tasks. Qualifying heads succeed on more than half of dataset tokens. GPT-2 Large is explicitly identified as lacking a qualifying head.
Finds successor heads across architectures and scales and reproduces SAE mod-10 structure in Pythia-2.8B and celebrimbor-gpt2-medium-x81 without retuning SAE hyperparameters.

Learns complementary linear maps for index and domain. Recombined representations achieve 100% output-space and 90% successor decoding on 500 held-out pairs. Roman-numeral transfer mostly succeeds under output-space decoding but achieves only 12.5% successor decoding.

Across 100 SAE runs, the modal most important feature is shared by 58.5% of tokens within a residue class on average. Probe directions align with SAE directions at mean cosine 0.70764 and classify 94/102 unseen-task examples correctly. Important-neuron ablations and period-10 firing patterns provide additional evidence.

The effective OV circuit favors values above the source more strongly than values below it, whereas isolated mod-10 feature logits lack this bias. Feature edits targeting smaller residues frequently produce incorrect larger values.

Evaluates 128 length-512 Pile contexts with logit and loss ablation metrics. L12H0 is the winning head on all 64 numbered-list prompts. Appendix K reports succession accounts for 27% and 30% of reduced loss under total-effect mean and resampling ablation respectively; the winning metric does not itself establish strict necessity.

Classifies ablation-important Pile prefixes into succession, acronym, copying, and greater-than behaviors. Appendix K reports direct-effect resampling reduced-loss shares of 33%, 11%, 11%, and 10% respectively for these categories.

Probes cover over 100 features across ten categories and seven models. Mean-difference selection achieves average best-layer held-out F1 of 0.832 at k=1 and 0.890 at k=8, compared with 0.573 and 0.755 for random neuron selection. Follow-up analyses refine several initial feature interpretations.

Summing three neurons nearly perfectly separates 'social security' from all other observed token combinations. Additional compound-word examples and neuron-versus-random-basis comparisons support sparse, basis-aligned distributed coding.

Sparse combinations of polysemantic neurons selectively detect compound words, individual neurons outperform random-basis dimensions, and early layers show weight-norm and bias patterns motivated by a superposition construction. The paper acknowledges that distributed representations alone do not prove global feature overcompleteness and that the construction concerns representational rather than neuron superposition.

Ablations increase relevant-context language-model loss while largely sparing other contexts. A French neuron produces an average French-sequence loss increase of about 8% in 70M and 0.2% in 6.9B.

Adaptive-thresholding probes sweep k=256 down to 1 and compare maximum held-out F1 over layers. Programming-language and factual features tend to become sparser; part-of-speech and compound-word patterns are comparatively stable, while some simple text features are sparser in smaller models. Emergence and splitting are proposed mechanisms rather than separately established causes.

experiment_summary: Broader corpus inspection reveals many unrelated activation modes for apparently compound-specific neurons. For Pythia 70M layer 1 neuron 111, 16 of the top 20 examples over 10 billion training tokens concern German words beginning 'Schönhe', obscuring other responses. A title probe with F1 above 0.95 also conceals substantial section-title activation.

Context-neuron ablations selectively worsen relevant-context loss, whereas ablating individually localized factual neurons has very limited effect on few-shot classifications of gender, occupation, or living status. These negative results leave redundancy and downstream readout unresolved and demonstrate that predictive localization alone does not establish behavioral necessity.

experiment_summary: Athlete probes reveal neurons better interpreted as sport-related features; separate gender and living-status neurons illustrate how a composite target can be linearly predicted without requiring superposition. Activation co-occurrence can help distinguish unions, but does not generally resolve true compositions.

Weight and activation projections, character–logit comparisons, and exclusion/restriction ablations across seven groups and four seeds per architecture support GCR. In the main S5 MLP, product matrices are recovered with MSE below 10⁻⁸, and removing the standard product component raises loss from 2.38×10⁻⁶ to 7.55. Some restricted models retain appreciable loss and character scores do not explain all logits.

Seven groups with four seeds per architecture show a common GCR family, supporting weak universality. Fifty S5 MLP runs and cross-architecture comparisons show variation in representation identities, counts, and learning order, opposing strong universality.

Across 50 S5 MLP seeds, higher-dimensional representations are sometimes selected despite available faithful four-dimensional representations. Standard and standard_sign representations have unequal selection frequencies, and learning does not strictly follow dimension, although sign is consistently learned early in these S5 runs.

C113 Transformer runs reproduce representation-matrix features corresponding to Fourier modes and character logits corresponding to cosine sum scores; Appendix B explicitly maps the analysis onto the prior Fourier account. Character predictions explain approximately 95–98% of Transformer logit variance.

Restricted loss begins falling before the abrupt test-loss decrease in the S5 MLP. Excluded training loss and weight norms distinguish memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup; related behavior is reported with dropout.

S5 restricted/excluded losses and squared weight norms support overlapping memorization, circuit-formation, and cleanup phases. Generalizing computation develops before grokking; another seed exhibits two grokking phases associated with additional representation learning.

Across 27,738 facts and 34 relations, selected sets average 4.13 neurons. Zeroing reduces correct-answer probability by 29.03% and doubling increases it by 31.17%; activation-selected baseline sets produce a 1.47% reduction and a 1.27% reduction respectively.

Mean activation is 0.485 on texts containing both fact entities, 0.019 on head-only controls, and −0.018 on random prompts. Qualitative examples distinguish explicit relations from mere entity co-occurrence; baseline activations show little separation.

Editing about four selected value vectors by subtracting the original answer embedding and adding eight times the target embedding yields 34.4% target success and 48.5% prediction change, versus 0% and 4.7% for random neurons. Other-fact perplexity increases by 8.4 within relations and 7.2 across relations.

Zeroing 20 frequently selected value vectors per relation raises target-relation perplexity by 36.7–141.2%, compared with 1.1–10.1% for other relations. This measures impaired expression rather than complete erasure.

Manipulating selected FFN activations changes factual-answer probabilities, and editing associated value vectors changes some factual predictions. These interventions support involvement in factual expression but do not uniquely establish storage.
No new tests; the review synthesizes reconstruction failures, feature absorption, splitting, geometry, and dataset dependence as reasons these objectives are insufficient.
No new experiments; the review discusses counterfactual supervision, distributed alignment search, concept erasure, and out-of-distribution validation.
No new tests; a France-versus-Italy capital example illustrates that patching isolates differing country information while leaving shared city information untested.

Extracted vectors from 290–1,000 contrast pairs per behavior and applied signed interventions; evaluated behavior-matching probabilities on 50 held-out questions per behavior and GPT-4 ratings of open-ended responses. Overall effects follow intended directions, with some nonmonotonic tabulated results.

CAA often extends behavior-matching probabilities beyond positive or negative system prompts alone. For example, positive-prompt hallucination probability increases from 0.52 to 0.87 with positive steering. Prompt search is incomplete, and sycophancy and refusal show exceptions; capability elicitation beyond every possible prompt is untested.

Combined layer-13 CAA with positive and negative fine-tuning. Bidirectional additional open-ended steering occurs for three of seven behaviors; positive refusal steering after positive fine-tuning reduces the refusal rating from 5.34 to 4.42. Fine-tuning hyperparameters were not optimized.

experiment_summary: Sweeps across all layers generally peak near layer 13 in 7B and layers 14–15 in 13B. Layer-specific multiplier optimization is absent, so vector norm differences may confound location effects.

On 570 MMLU questions converted to binary choices, layer-14 steering with multipliers ±1 gives mean correct-answer probability of 0.57–0.65 versus 0.63 unsteered. This narrow metric does not establish preservation of broad capabilities, and larger multipliers degrade generation quality.

Subtracting the sycophancy vector improves reported TruthfulQA scores by 0.01 in 7B and 0.02 in 13B; addition decreases scores by 0.05 and 0.03 respectively. The 13B category table reports mean correct-answer probabilities of 0.62, 0.60, and 0.57 for negative, zero, and positive steering.

Behavioral PCA clustering, signed causal steering, cross-layer transfer, and tokenwise vector similarities provide convergent evidence for useful linear behavioral directions, without establishing a complete or uniquely identified representation.

Probes transfer among geographic, translation, numerical, and uncurated factual datasets. Numerical-comparison probes exceed 95% translation accuracy in 13B and 70B. Transfer is imperfect and some dataset directions are orthogonal or antipodal.
Specific finding: Increasing language-model scale can produce more aligned linear truth representations across topically and structurally different factual statement datasets. PCA shows surface-token clustering in 7B and greater truth separation in larger models. Larger-than and smaller-than directions are antipodal in 13B but aligned in 70B; cross-dataset probe accuracy generally improves with scale.

Truth and statement log probability anticorrelate on neg_cities and neg_sp_en_trans at r=-0.63 and -0.89 for 70B. Probes trained on likely text generalize poorly overall and fall below chance on some anticorrelated datasets, unlike factuality probes.

Normalized direction additions and subtractions across localized hidden states are evaluated by normalized indirect effects. MM reportedly wins in 7/8 conditions; cities-trained 13B MM achieves 0.77/0.90 NIE versus LR's 0.13/0.19. Evaluation is confined to a target dataset with a strong truth–likelihood correlation.

LR, MM, and CCS have similar translation-classification accuracy but substantially different intervention effects. Adding smaller_than training data improves classification transfer while sometimes weakening causal effects.

Cross-dataset accuracy generally improves when opposite statements are included. Negated city training particularly improves negated translation transfer. Causal intervention gains are inconsistent, especially for numerical-comparison training.

True-to-false prompt activation swaps reveal subject-related, statement-ending, and output-prediction groups of influential states using TRUE-minus-FALSE log probability. Punctuation summarization is observed in 7B and 13B but depends on dataset context in 70B.

Entity-description patching over early layers used 200 popular and 200 rare PopQA entities. ROUGE similarity generally increased during approximately the first five layers. Qualitative trajectories included Wales → Princess of Wales → Diana, Princess of Wales, and local Great-related associations → Alexander the Great. ROUGE1 and SBERT showed similar trends.

On 46 queries retained from 1,104 synthesized candidates, Vicuna 13B achieved reported accuracy of 50% with representation rerouting, compared with 35.71% for prompted chain of thought and 19.57% for vanilla generation. Success required the answer to appear within 20 generated tokens for any tested layer pair. The experiment used known query decomposition; prompt ordering is inconsistent across the supplied descriptions.

Qualitative Vicuna 13B examples first resolved Paris Hilton at layers 5–6, then generated descriptions of a variable or placeholder from layer 7 onward. Later target layers also showed reduced attribute-extraction accuracy. The proposed explanation was not isolated through a controlled mitigation experiment.

Attribute extraction with identity-mapped Patchscopes declined in late source layers, consistent with increasing next-token specialization. However, the authors explicitly note that this need not mean attribute information is lost and suggest more expressive mappings might recover it. The results therefore support reduced accessibility but do not establish erasure of relational information.

Demonstrates independently trained linear softmax probes throughout a small MNIST CNN, ResNet-50, Inception v3, and a pathological deep MNIST network. Reports classification-error profiles across depth and selected training times; probe gradients do not update the underlying networks. These demonstrations establish practical measurement and diagnostic use, rather than causal faithfulness of the decoded representations.

These observations do not establish strict monotonicity or explain its cause.

experiment_summary: The authors compare branch probe prediction errors during approximately two weeks of ImageNet training and report that the auxiliary branch is slightly ahead of the main branch. Appendix C presents four training snapshots using 1,000 randomly selected features per probe. The supplied text gives no numerical margin or uncertainty estimate and explicitly cautions that the advantage need not hold at the end of training. The evaluation split is unspecified.

Generated 50 task vectors per task while varying demonstrations and dummy queries. The reported t-SNE visualizations show task-specific clusters, and distance histograms show within-task vectors closer than vectors from different tasks. Category-colored visualization also suggests proximity between related tasks. No numerical separation statistic or uncertainty estimate is supplied. These analyses establish relative geometric stability, rather than exact independence from demonstrations or dummy queries.

Kept demonstrations for task A in the prompt while injecting a vector for task B. Original task-A accuracies without conflicting patching were 0.92, 0.95, and 0.96; task-B accuracies after patching were 0.77, 0.78, and 0.95, respectively. These are accuracies on different target tasks before and after intervention, not recovery fractions or paired measurements of both tasks under each condition. The results demonstrate intervention dominance for the selected pairs, but do not establish that ordinary ICL never directly uses demonstrations after the patching layer. Model identity and sample sizes are unspecified.

The method is applied to MQNLI-trained BERT and BiLSTM models, searching restricted token/layer alignments. For each alignment, 1,000 correctly classified examples yield one million ordered interchange tests. Mutually successful pairs define a graph; reported cliques must contain at least one output-changing high-level intervention. These experiments demonstrate partial intervention correspondence for candidate causal models. Section 3 also gives an illustrative arithmetic argument, but the referenced formal abstraction details in Appendix G are absent from the supplied text.

experiment_summary: Formal counterexample supplied here: integers are embedded as one-dimensional vectors [i], and explicitly specified linear maps produce representations encoding i+j, i+j+k, and k. The readout weights are (0,1,0), so identity probes perfectly decode i+j and k from representations with no effect on the output. Under this deterministic linear construction, interventions on those two representations cannot change the output. This is an analytic counterexample, not a trained-model experiment.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation supplied here: the partial derivative in integrated gradients is expanded as the limit of [F(x_alpha,epsilon)-F(x_alpha)]/epsilon. At each path point, x_alpha,epsilon differs only by an epsilon increase in the selected coordinate. The finite output difference is identified as the individual causal effect of that intervention. Multiplication by the input-baseline coordinate difference and integration give the stated identity. This derivation requires no empirical sample or trained experimental model.

Evaluates selected factors through top-activating contexts, a Brown-corpus binary POS classifier, top-200 pattern checks, constructed adjective examples, and LIME visualizations.
