experiment_summary: A supervised logistic-regression classifier using factor 30's layer-4 coefficient achieves 97.2% precision, 95.8% recall, and 96.5% F1. Reported baselines achieve 92.7% precision, 95.5% recall, and 94.1% F1 for a perceptron POS tagger, and 97.5% precision, 95.2% recall, and 96.3% F1 for fine-tuned BERT-base. Layerwise plots show little separation at layer 0 and increasing separation at layers 2 and 4. Statistical uncertainty, sample counts, and training/evaluation split details are not supplied, so the small F1 difference from fine-tuned BERT does not establish reliable superiority.
models_studied: ["bert-base-uncased", "BERT-base fine-tuned for POS tagging", "Perceptron POS tagger", "Single-coefficient logistic-regression classifier"]

experiment_summary: Constructs matched tagging and dependency control tasks and evaluates linear, bilinear, and MLP probes on Penn Treebank development data. For ELMo1 tagging, linear and MLP-1 probes have similar linguistic accuracies, 97.2% and 97.3%, but control accuracies of 71.2% and 92.8%. Layer and Proj0 comparisons likewise distinguish representations with similar linguistic accuracy. These tests demonstrate the additional diagnostic information supplied by controls, without independently validating selectivity as a measure of representational faithfulness.
models_studied: ["ELMo, first contextual BiLSTM layer", "ELMo, second contextual BiLSTM layer", "Proj0: untrained BiLSTM over ELMo character-CNN embeddings"]

experiment_summary: The authors train ten probes of each family and manually inspect aggregate confusion matrices. They report that the largest category of MLP improvement concerns adjective–noun distinctions, while linear probes more accurately identify NNP, with MLPs often predicting NNPS for proper nouns ending in -s. Examples illustrate both patterns, but no quantitative category-level effect sizes or statistical tests are supplied. The explanation that MLPs combine spurious plurality and proper-noun cues remains a hypothesis.
location: Section 3.6, 'Errors in Selective and Non-Selective Probes'

experiment_summary: Sparsity-penalty sweeps compare Gated SAEs with baseline SAEs given 50% more dictionary features to compensate for Gated training computation. Evaluation on over one million held-out tokens measures average L0 and loss recovered: 1 minus the reconstruction-induced cross-entropy increase divided by the zero-ablation cross-entropy increase. The reported frontiers improve throughout tested Pythia sites and broadly in Gemma. Appendix B reports a Gemma MLP/residual-site exception, while layer-27 attention has anomalous greater-than-100% loss recovery and does not establish uniform Gated dominance. Appendix D.1.1 reverses the width assignments found in the tables; several Gemma rows also contain impossible negative L0 values.
location: Section 4.1; Figures 1 and 5; Appendix B, Figures 12–13; Appendix D.2, Tables 1–8

experiment_summary: The authors freeze baseline encoder and decoder directions and learn magnitude rescaling and shifting parameters. This resolves the measured shrinkage and modestly improves the L0 versus loss-recovered frontier, but a substantial gap to fully trained Gated SAEs remains. The comparison suggests benefits from learning different directions; it does not independently establish how much comes from encoder versus decoder directions.

The authors discard trained encoders and use gradient pursuit with their decoder dictionaries, sweeping inference-time target L0. Gated dictionaries generally show a small loss-recovery advantage, particularly when compared with baselines trained at low L0. However, the best baseline dictionary, trained at approximately L0 99, is reported as comparable to the best Gated dictionary, trained at approximately L0 20. The gap between ordinary encoding and iterative inference is smaller for Gated SAEs. Gradient pursuit is approximate and supplies no guaranteed optimum or rigorous upper bound.

Five raters assess 150 Pythia features and seven assess 192 Gemma features using No/Maybe/Yes labels scored 0/1/2. Pairing controls model, layer, site, and rater. The pooled one-sided Wilcoxon-Pratt test gives p=.060, estimated Gated-minus-baseline mean .13, and a 90% BCa bootstrap interval [0,.26]. Model-specific tests give p=.15 for Pythia and p=.13 for Gemma. No equivalence or noninferiority test is reported. Appendix H's site breakdown finds an MLP-output advantage of .40, p=.003, interval [.18,.63], while attention and residual differences are inconclusive; these are further analyses of the same study. Gemma attention features were rated separately, compromising site blinding, and rater judgments show subjectivity.
location: Section 4.3; Figure 7; Appendix H.1 and H.3

experiment_summary: An ablation allows the auxiliary gate-reconstruction objective to update decoder parameters. This reduces performance on the L0 versus loss-recovered frontier relative to the proposed stopped-gradient decoder. It supports this training choice in the tested setting without proving that every auxiliary-gradient pathway or architectural component is necessary.

Fully untying the gating and magnitude encoders slightly worsens the observed frontier despite increasing expressive capacity. Removing the learned magnitude rescaling while retaining shared directions also slightly worsens performance. These results favor the tested sharing scheme, but the small effects do not establish universal superiority or necessity.

Formal algebraic derivation supplied in Appendix E. Under positive proportional projection weights, writing z=w_mag·x+b_mag transforms the gate condition into z>theta, where theta=b_mag-rho*b_gate. The output is therefore sigma_theta(z)=1[z>theta]ReLU(z). Input centering is absorbed into the input without loss of generality, and the derivation applies coordinatewise to multiple latents. This is an exact architectural equivalence, not an empirical experiment or a proof of improved feature recovery.

location: Section 1 and footnote 1; Section 7, Limitations; Appendix A

experiment_summary: On 652 CounterFact examples selected for GPT-J's true object appearing within 36 greedily generated tokens, ROME rewrite-score regressions achieve R²=0.947 using categorical edit-layer identity, 0.016 using tracing effects, and 0.948 using both with layer interactions. At layer 6, correlation is −0.13 (p<0.001); most evaluated layers show near-zero correlations. Error-injection regressions for the four editing methods gain only 0.001–0.002 R² from tracing beyond layer identity. Additional tests use GPT2-XL on CounterFact, ROME with GPT-J on ZSRE, and ROME with subject-position MLP-output zeroing on GPT-J/CounterFact. ZSRE layer-only versus tracing-only R² values are 0.795 versus 0.042 for rewrite score; its sample size is not supplied. Alternative metrics, window sizes, and last-subject-token tracing also show limited predictive value. These are regression comparisons, not direct measurements of facts' locations in weights.
location: Sections 4–5; Tables 1 and 3; Appendices B–C; Table 8; Figures 13–16 and 19–22
Section 2, Relating Localization to Editing; Section 6, implications for validating localization

experiment_summary: Figure 10 reports larger tracing effects when more adjacent MLP representations are restored. Figure 11 compares distributions of per-example peak layers across window sizes: smaller windows shift peak concentrations toward the first and last layers. The source attributes much of this shift to boundary clipping, since large windows restore fewer layers when centered near a model boundary. Repeating the editing regressions with windows of five versus ten nonetheless gives nearly identical conclusions about tracing's limited predictive value.
location: Section 3.2; Appendix B, Figures 10–11; Appendix C, Results for Different Tracing Window Sizes; Figure 12

experiment_summary: For each subject, the study samples five pre-edit descriptions from the prompt 's is a ' using multinomial top-k sampling with k=5, then measures their perplexity before and after editing. The essence score is one for no increase and zero for an increase of five or more. Later edits generally perform better on this proxy, counter to trends in the other editing metrics. Including it in the aggregate score flattens the layer trend and shifts preference somewhat toward middle layers. This evaluates preservation of model-generated descriptions, not independently verified preservation of core subject properties.
location: Appendix B, Measuring essence drift; Figures 7–9

experiment_summary: Annotators were blinded to whether displayed groups were selected by neuron activation, random-direction projection, or random sampling. Both annotators identified patterns in 27/33 random-direction groups (82%), 20/25 neuron groups (80%), and 4/29 random sentence groups (14%). Among groups judged meaningful, patterns contained a mean of 6.89, 6.80, and 5.05 sentences respectively. This small annotation study does not establish statistical equivalence between random and coordinate directions.

UMAP visualizations showed dataset clustering, and a linear SVM reportedly distinguished the four datasets with high accuracy. Numerical accuracy and train/test details are unavailable in the supplied text. Across dataset pairs and neurons, 38% of top-ten activation ranges overlapped, showing that different datasets can yield top examples with overlapping projection values. This is a new evaluation consistent with the cited prior work of Aharoni and Goldberg, rather than a reported replication of its protocol.

The authors compared dot-product distributions among top examples with distributions between top examples and their nearest neighbors, using random sentences as an additional baseline. Mean per-sentence locality was 0.026 for meaningful examples and 0.010 for meaningless examples, with overall p=0.0004. Dataset-specific p-values were 0.009, 0.090, 0.064, and 0.014 for QQP, QNLI, Wikipedia, and Books respectively. Neighborhood agreement cannot independently distinguish coherence arising from local concepts from coherence arising from global concepts, as explicitly acknowledged in footnote 2.

The most distant 1% of QQP sentences accounted for 48% of all top activations, and the 20 most distant sentences each maximally activated at least 11 neurons. Separately, the 7,680 top-ten entries contained 4,551 unique sentences. The authors report that the illusion persisted after excluding the most distant 1% and 10%, but provide no quantitative post-exclusion annotation results.

Annotators disagreed about pattern presence for 2/25 neuron groups (8%), 6/33 random-direction groups (18%), and 11/29 random sentence groups (38%). Table 6 also reports differing numbers of patterns found per annotated direction across six annotators; multiple patterns could be recorded for one direction. These observations establish disagreement and descriptive variation, but do not identify which judgments were erroneous or establish how much annotator bias causes the illusion.

Demonstrates the compiler through worked compiled models and illustrated forward passes, including running token fractions and sorting. Reports compiling programs for all tasks described by Weiss et al., after modifying some programs to use supported features. Additional compiled examples appear in Appendix G. No comprehensive correctness benchmark, task denominator, or exhaustive input validation is reported; the examples do not constitute a proof of compiler correctness.
location: Sections 3–4; Figures 2, 4–5; Appendices B–D and G

experiment_summary: The compressed sorting model achieves almost perfect task accuracy while average layer-output cosine similarity remains around 0.8. Layer-output inspection localizes discrepancies to target_pos and suggests replacement of its original one-hot encoding with a numerical encoding. The encoding interpretation is tentative, and Section 5.3 contains an apparent compiled/compressed wording error. Exact accuracy, evaluation denominator, and compressed dimensionality are not specified in the supplied prose.

Formal derivation in Appendix F: negating a direct-attention matrix reverses binary selector preferences with an adjusted BOS logit. Adding two binary direct-attention matrices gives logit 2 precisely where both predicates hold; a BOS offset of 3/2 provides fallback when no conjunction-selected key exists. As temperature tends to zero, selected keys receive uniform attention and unselected keys are suppressed. The derivation also explains why these post-softmax constructions cannot simply be composed to implement arbitrary Boolean formulas. No empirical experiment is involved.
location: Appendix F, constructions preceding Lemma F.1; Appendix D.1

experiment_summary: Formal result: Lemma F.1 derives that uniform attention over a selector union, under the stated separate-subspace and unrestricted-co-occurrence assumptions, requires either a constant predicate or predicates that factor into query-only and key-only conditions. The proof uses equal logits among selected keys and bilinearity constraints. Shared input variables, restricted co-occurrences, and newly constructed product encodings can evade the obstruction. Sufficiency for rank-one predicates is explicitly left open. No empirical experiment is involved.
location: Appendix F, Lemma F.1 and following discussion

experiment_summary: On 10,000 generated prompts using 120 duration-related nouns, probability mass on greater years minus mass on no-greater years averages 81.7% (SD 19.3 percentage points). Mean cutoff sharpness, p(YY+1)−p(YY−1), is 6.0% (SD 7.2 points). Appendix A reports 100% correctness among top-1 continuations and 98.6% among top-5 continuations on the filtered task. These are different metrics from probability difference.

Iterative path patching searches direct and mediated contributions using a reported 490-example subset. On the larger dataset, preserving normal inputs only along circuit paths yields 72.7% probability difference, reported as 89.5% of original performance, and 8% cutoff sharpness. Supplying circuit paths with 01-input while preserving normal inputs elsewhere yields −36.6% probability difference. These interventions establish substantial preservation and disruption relative to this corruption; they are not a formal correctness or minimality proof. The reported recovery percentage is retained as given rather than recomputed from rounded aggregate metrics.

Attention analyses show circuit heads attending to the start-year suffix; vocabulary projections strongly favor that suffix. MLPs 9 and 10 show upper-triangular year-logit patterns, while MLP 11 also favors a limited duration. Direct versus indirect 01-input patching produces reported performance drops of 14% versus 39% for MLP 8, 28% versus 32% for MLP 9, and 56% versus 16% for MLP 10. Appendix B reports that corrupting the attention value paths entirely disrupts circuit performance. These observations support operand transport and differentiated MLP roles without fully specifying the internal algorithm.

Iterative path patching through attention values at the start-year position identifies MLPs 0–3 and heads a0.h5, a0.h3, and a0.h1 as important upstream contributors. An extended circuit, using the identified upstream inputs for both keys and values while allowing all normal inputs to queries, achieves 71.5% probability difference and 10.5% cutoff sharpness. The probability difference is reported as 98.3% of the earlier partial-circuit result, not 98.3% of the unpatched baseline. Query/key corruption also produces a reported 15% performance reduction relative to the partial circuit, indicating that attention selection is not completely invariant.

In GPT-2 small's year-span task, normal-versus-01-input path interventions identify attention-to-MLP and MLP-to-logit dependencies. Joint circuit-preservation and reverse-corruption tests retain most of the measured behavior or disrupt it, respectively. Separate direct and mediated interventions distinguish MLP roles. These are task- and corruption-specific demonstrations of causal localization, without independent ground truth establishing a complete or minimal circuit.

location: Sections 3.1–3.2; Appendix E discusses final-layer-normalization limitations

experiment_summary: The authors compare downstream layer-output projections before and after resample ablation using 15 alternative dataset prompts. Examples show downstream attention contributions increasing after upstream attention ablation. An all-layer analysis over 1,209 contexts separates attention compensation from reduced MLP suppression and finds attention responses relatively more prominent earlier in the network. This is new whole-layer evidence in factual recall, rather than a rerun of the cited GPT-2 Small IOI backup-head experiment.

The model exhibiting increased downstream attention contributions after upstream ablation was trained entirely without dropout, stochastic depth, or layer dropout. This supplies a counterexample to the necessity of those explicit training mechanisms for self-repair. The paper does not perform a controlled comparison of training recipes or identify the mechanism that produces repair.

Comparisons of clean and attention-ablated runs show negative late-MLP contributions to the original top-token logit becoming less negative after upstream attention ablation. In the all-layer analysis over 1,209 contexts, the MLP response is more predictive of compensation around layer 22 and accounts for almost all of the response at layer 23. These measurements support token-logit suppression and its attenuation; memory management and broader recalibration remain interpretations.

The authors compare unembedding contributions with total effects of resample ablation at every attention and MLP layer and measure summed downstream contribution changes. Importance measures disagree across most layers. The regression relating direct contributions and compensation peaks at layer 23 with reported variance explained of 92%; reduced MLP suppression accounts for almost all of the response there. The conclusion reports approximately 70% restoration of token-logit reductions at middle layers where compensation is strongest. Regression slopes below one after layer 13 indicate incomplete average restoration, not that every intervention is incompletely compensated.

Selected attention-ablation examples show increased contribution at downstream attention layer 20 while most other downstream attention contributions remain nearly unchanged. The authors characterize this initial evidence as largely anecdotal and note that compensation might restore missing features, potentially concealing dependencies on the ablated layer.

Formal derivation supplied in Section 3.1: expanding final logits as an additive sum of residual contributions and fixing the final RMSNorm denominator gives DE = centered[(replacement − original) G W_U / sigma] when other contributions are held constant. Centering is linear, so the identity also holds for centered logits. Under the paper's intervention-minus-clean convention, a positive original projection is the negative of its zero-ablation direct effect. The prose following Equation 28 incorrectly identifies these signs; the replacement-minus-original formula follows the displayed derivation.

Formal constructions supplied in Section 3.3: f(x,u) = −x keeps y = 0 before and after knockout, while f(x,u) = 0 when x = u and f(x,u) = u otherwise keeps y = u. For nonzero u, changing x to zero while holding f's output fixed changes y by −u, whereas allowing f to respond produces zero total change. These are analytical examples, not experiments on trained models.

Specific finding: Appropriately chosen donor layer outputs have approximately zero mean direct contribution to the recipient prompt's original maximum-likelihood token, so resampling approximates removal of the original contribution.

location: Section 6, Implications for language modelling research

experiment_summary: Joint all-head interventions were compared with the sum of separate head interventions on Winobias, using the default model-specific filtered development examples. The reported relative discrepancies from the joint effect ranged from 0.7% to 11.3% across GPT-2 variants. Some heads reduced rather than increased the aggregate indirect effect.

Direct and indirect effects approximately summed to the total effect for top GPT-2-small heads and concurrent GPT-2 head interventions; Transformer-XL and XLNet-base showed similar selected-head decompositions. Appendix E compared the two normalized sides of the no-interaction equality across attention heads and Winobias examples, reporting slope 1.04, intercept 0.00, and R² = 0.78. That appendix does not explicitly identify the trained model used for this regression. Its plot excludes one outlier for visualization; the text does not state that the regression excludes it.

Formal result, not an empirical experiment: Appendix E rearranges the assumed equality y1 − y1,z0 = y0,z1 − y0, divides by the common baseline y0, and takes expectations to derive TE = NDE + NIE. Consistency identifies y1 with y1,z1 and y0 with y0,z0. The proof does not establish that arbitrary nonlinear models satisfy the no-interaction assumption.

Four metrics were compared for GPT-2-small on filtered Winobias development, filtered Winogender using Bergsma statistics, and Professions. Additional GPT-2 variants were evaluated on filtered Winobias development with the three alternate metrics. The reported relative localization patterns remained broadly consistent, although alternate metrics showed less absolute sparsity and subtracting minimum effects was sometimes needed to expose relative structure.
location: Section 3.5; Appendix F, Figures 25–30 and Tables 5–6

experiment_summary: Figure 6(b) evaluates top-5% neuron interventions by layer in GPT-2-medium for occupation-to-person edits and the gender-neutral continuation. Effects are lower and more evenly distributed across layers than the binary intervention profiles, with higher embedding-effect variance. Section 5.1 also reports low, relatively consistent “they” probabilities across occupations. These observations do not establish that the models lack a singular-they concept, given the template restriction and singular/plural ambiguity.

location: Sections 3–6; especially Section 4.2 and the discussion in Sections 5–6
Section 3, Latent explanation complexity; Section 6; Appendix H

experiment_summary: Formal derivation supplied in Section 4.1: if x conditional on z has mean Dz and Gaussian covariance Σ, then Wx conditional on z has mean WDz and covariance WΣWᵀ. The illustrative latent distribution is heavy-tailed Lomax. The derivation assumes a linear mixture, Gaussian additive noise, and a fixed linear transformation. It establishes preservation of generative form, including potentially degenerate transformed dictionaries or covariances, rather than feature recovery or an analogous result for nonlinear networks.

Trained L1-regularized ReLU SAEs on inputs and outputs of random two-layer ReLU MLPs with equal input and output dimensions and hidden width four times input width. Synthetic data used 512 ground-truth features in 256 dimensions with approximately five active coefficients, 10K points, and 10 seeds. Word-vector experiments used 400K points and one seed. SAEs trained for 100 epochs with 10% validation data. Explained-variance versus sparsity frontiers improved after random MLP transformation, including for Gaussian controls; synthetic and Gaussian output frontiers were much closer than their input frontiers. Ground-truth output-feature recovery was not measured.
models_studied: ["Randomly initialized two-layer ReLU MLPs", "L1-regularized ReLU sparse autoencoders"]

experiment_summary: Repeated the synthetic-feature recovery setup attributed to Sharkey et al. using 512 ground-truth directions in 256 dimensions, approximately five active coefficients, 10K points, and 10 seeds. Measured mean maximum cosine similarity by taking each ground-truth direction's highest cosine similarity with an SAE decoder direction and averaging over ground-truth directions. A suitable L1-regularization range produced near-perfect recovery when enough latents were available. Recovery was evaluated on inputs, where ground-truth directions were known.

Formal basis supplied here: Section 4 and Appendices A–B derive an expected-loss threshold derivative in terms of pre-activation density and conditional reconstruction effects at the threshold. Appendix C algebraically shows that the pseudo-derivatives in Equations 11–12 yield the batch expression in Equation 15. The compact boundary expression uses H(0)=1/2. The derivation assumes densities and sufficient boundary regularity for differentiating expectations. It does not establish unbiased finite-bandwidth estimates, optimization convergence, or an exact expected-loss gradient for every SAE parameter.

Five blinded human raters supplied 405 Yes/Maybe/No monosemanticity assessments, five feature assessments per SAE, across 81 SAEs selected near mean L0 values of 20, 75, and 150. Raters inspected summary information and examples across the activation spectrum. Gemini Flash generated explanations and simulated activations for 1,000 features per SAE across 154 SAEs. Pearson-correlation distributions showed substantial within-architecture variation, and aggregate plots pooled sparsity levels. Simulation reused explanation-generation sequences with true activation labels withheld during simulation. The automated ranking sentence is incomplete. These tests support broad similarity under the reported proxies, without establishing statistical equivalence or downstream utility.

Estimated feature firing frequencies using 10,000 sequences of length 1,024, excluding special tokens. JumpReLU and TopK had more features exceeding 10% firing frequency than Gated SAEs, with this fraction approaching zero at high sparsity. Fewer than 0.06% of dictionary features exceeded that cutoff even in the highest-L0 reported comparisons. At a 1% cutoff, Gated SAEs could instead have more high-frequency features, especially at higher L0. JumpReLU had similar or fewer high-frequency features than TopK in the reported comparisons.

Measured feature firing frequencies over 10,000 sequences of length 1,024, excluding special tokens. JumpReLU SAEs consistently had few features below the stated dead-feature threshold without resampling or an auxiliary loss. TopK with AuxK also had few dead features. The comparison does not isolate the effects of architecture, initialization, and other training choices.

Compared the original Gated training recipe, which used resampling, with a recipe replacing its L1 penalty by RI-L1 and unfreezing the decoder in the auxiliary loss. The modified recipe achieved a similar sparsity–fidelity trade-off without resampling to avoid dead features. The original-loss layer-20 configuration had approximately 40% dead features despite resampling. Because several recipe details changed together, this does not isolate RI-L1 alone as the cause.
location: Section 5; Appendix D; Figures 2 and 13; Appendix I

experiment_summary: Figure 8 compares training with jax.lax.approx_max_k against exact TopK and reports similar sparsity–fidelity performance. The supplied text provides no numerical approximation errors, timing measurements, or detailed layer/site description for this comparison.

Appendix E reports a TopK training comparison with and without the previously introduced AuxK loss. Figure 8 is described as showing a slight fidelity improvement at matched sparsity when AuxK is included. This tests fidelity rather than separately establishing the broader claim that AuxK and aligned initialization prevent dead latents.

Compared squared reconstruction error plus a linear L0 penalty with squared reconstruction error plus lambda times (L0/target_L0−1)^2, using the same threshold pseudo-derivatives. Figure 9 reports converged active-latent counts close to their targets and similar fidelity–sparsity curves. Exact target errors are not supplied in the text; this does not establish exact per-token sparsity.

Compared rectangle and alternative common KDE kernels, identified in Section 3 as triangular, Gaussian, and Epanechnikov, for threshold pseudo-derivatives. Figure 17 reports little impact on fidelity–sparsity curves and no obvious benefit from higher-order kernels in this setting.

Computed attribution-weighted latent magnitudes and measured exp(entropy)/active-count over 2,048 sequences of length 1,024, excluding special tokens. Figure 16 reports more diffuse relative importance at larger L0 for all architectures, with the trend appearing strongest for TopK. Gated and JumpReLU behaved mostly similarly, except for layer-31 residual-stream SAEs. This is a local gradient-based metric, not a feature-ablation experiment or an established measure of feature quality.
location: Appendix G, Attribution Weighted Effective Sparsity; Figure 16

experiment_summary: Five prediction evaluations improve during reconstruction training in each of three Claude NLAs. The paper reports approximately 0.3–0.4 FVE after warm-start and 0.6–0.8 for evaluated NLAs. Opus Classification improves from 83% to 86%. Models have different training budgets and hyperparameters, so these are independent demonstrations rather than controlled scaling comparisons. Several task definitions and plotted numerical results are unavailable in the supplied text.

experiment_summary: The authors transform explanations and measure reconstruction FVE. Meaning-preserving transformations cause small drops without a widening gap over training. Coherence rewrites and short summaries cause larger drops but also remove information. These tests provide evidence against substantial dependence on the tested forms of hidden textual coding, rather than establishing the absence of steganography.
location: Evaluating NLAs during training: Measuring behavioral properties of NLAs

experiment_summary: Behavioral evaluations across training report steadily declining writing quality and a substantial rate of verifiably false context claims that remains roughly flat, despite improving reconstruction and prediction evaluations. The paper also reports general agreement with SAE features, while noting that NLA claims are often more specific than SAE descriptions. Numerical rates and full evaluation details are not available in the supplied figure text.

experiment_summary: Haiku 4.5 extracts and judges verifiable claims for validity and specificity. Thematic claims are supported more often than specific details, and false claims are usually related to the context. For each text, comparing final-token claims with explanations at the other positions among its last 10 tokens shows that recurring claims are more often true. The judge sometimes miscategorizes claims; sample counts and effect sizes are unavailable.
models_studied: ["Claude Opus 4.6 NLA", "Claude Haiku 4.5 claim extractor and judge"]

experiment_summary: The authors delete individual extracted claims and measure reconstruction MSE changes. True-claim deletions have greater aggregate cost than false-claim deletions; context-related false claims matter more than unrelated ones. Effects are noisy on individual transcripts, making the reconstructor only a weak per-claim verifier. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied.
models_studied: ["Claude Opus 4.6 NLA", "Claude Haiku 4.5 claim extractor and judge"]

experiment_summary: Rabbit-to-mouse explanation edits alter subsequent rhyme endings, with imperfect success and some degeneration. In a toy prompt rewarding even answers to an odd-integer request, reward-to-penalty explanation edits yield steering that increases odd responses more effectively than a random vector. Each reward edit direction averages five explanation rollouts at one prompt token; the procedure is repeated 10 times with fresh rollouts. Nonnumeric responses remain at 0%. The reward setup is sensitive to prompt details and numerics and reportedly cannot be replicated through the public API.
location: Planning in Poetry; Reasoning about Rewards; Appendix: Additional reasoning about rewards case study evidence

experiment_summary: Across selected Russian, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, and Spanish switches, string matching finds references to the eventual language before the switch, while references to other foreign languages remain near zero. In the Russian example, replacing vodka with champagne preserves the switch. Investigators subsequently find malformed training data pairing English-translated prompts with untranslated responses. This corroborates a diagnostic hypothesis but does not establish causation through data removal or retraining.

A transcript is flagged if any of 50 randomly sampled response-token explanations, excluding tool calls, is graded aware. Two authors report 97% agreement with the explanation grader on 186 explanations. Awareness exceeds 5% on 10 of 16 evaluations, seven of those having zero verbalized awareness; 2/50 Claude Code controls are flagged, both discussing evaluation design. Positive and negative steering at strengths ±0.1 shift the metric as predicted on six evaluations. A separate audit sweep shows monotonic suppression on three of nine alignment evaluations, with the other six near floor. Realism edits yield equal or lower values on all 11 tested evaluations, with several differences within noise. Blackmail transcripts expose underdetection relative to verbalized awareness. Opus 4.7 produces and judges realism rewrites; Opus 4.6 is the target throughout.
models_studied: ["Claude Opus 4.6 target and awareness grader", "Claude Opus 4.7 realism rewriter and judge"]

experiment_summary: Agents are compared across conversation, NLA, SAE, and corpus-search configurations. NLAs improve root-cause identification with no training-data search and with full PT+SFT+RL search; generic-data SAEs do not reliably help. With PT-only search, search alone performs well and NLAs provide no benefit. NLAs do not consistently increase behavioral-quirk counts. Opus 4.6 grades reports under a rubric tuned against 22 hand-graded reports, including added credit for internal representations naming reward-model bias. Numerical win rates and run counts are unavailable. Different auditor models and scaffolds preclude direct comparison with prior work.

experiment_summary: On nine generic and quirk-eliciting prompts at the Assistant control token, the midpoint NLA surfaces reward-model-sycophancy terms as training progresses. A later-layer NLA produces no reward-model mentions at its own training layer, while still mentioning specific behavioral biases. Applying that same late-layer NLA to earlier-layer activations produces reward-model terms at a higher rate than the midpoint NLA, but entails distribution shift and reduced coherence. This establishes readout sensitivity rather than absence of the objective from the model.

experiment_summary: QA fine-tuning from four NLA checkpoints outperforms the no-activation-pretraining baseline, but additional NLA RL is not monotonically beneficial and the supervised warm-start sometimes performs better. PastLens pretraining on 16,000–3,000,000 sequences is often competitive and cheaper. Large PastLens initializations sometimes reproduce context instead of answering; a Claude grader estimates this may affect 20% of CoT Hints questions for the two-million-activation model. AO scores shift by approximately ±10% under question rewording, and confident hallucinations limit interpretation.

experiment_summary: Introduces the averaged-Jacobian readout and tests it through intermediate recovery, verbal-report interventions, and methodological ablations. Sonnet 4.5 recipe comparisons vary target layer, attention-gradient treatment, target positions, aggregation, and corpus size. The reported intermediate-recovery and causal-effect evaluations exceed logit- and tuned-lens baselines with as few as ten averaging prompts. These are empirical validations of a construction, not a proof that averaged gradients capture every verbalizable representation.

experiment_summary: Combines report swaps, covert-task modulation, intermediate substitutions, cross-function argument swaps, selective ablations, sparse occupancy measurements, and connectivity analyses. These supply converging evidence for several functional workspace properties in the tested models. They do not establish universal workspace dependence, encapsulated specialist modules, recurrent broadcast, or a criterion for predicting which arbitrary tasks require J-space.

experiment_summary: On 50 prompts, intermediate swaps yield target-appropriate top-1 answers on 54% of Haiku, 70% of Sonnet, and 70% of Opus 4.5 trials. Among successful Sonnet trials, intermediate swaps act a median approximately 17% of normalized model depth earlier than answer swaps. In a separate 90-prompt experiment, J-components containing roughly 10–15% of probe variance succeed on 61%, versus 28% for remainders and 60% for raw J-lens vectors. Clamping relevant J-coordinates reduces remainder success to 6%. Illustrative swaps also redirect an unspoken repeat-versus-switch strategy and a Chinese answer through English-aligned directions.

experiment_summary: In a controlled example, swapping the planned fight J-lens direction for light changes the preceding phrase from coming fight to morning light, demonstrating influence before the final word is emitted. Separately, a 52-item lens comparison searches for intended ending words at the newline before the second line. That readout evaluation measures accessibility rather than independently establishing causal planning on every item.

experiment_summary: The experiential-language score averages three binary Opus 4.6 judgments of felt perspective and sensory vocabulary. J-space ablation reduces scores more than matched-norm perturbation controls on self-reports and imagined human experiences; story quality declines only modestly. Effects occur in Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6. Haiku 4.5 loses coherence before a comparable qualitative change. Controls include random directions, non-J-component shrinking, and several SAE or activation dictionaries. The main prose reports five stream-of-consciousness prompts, while Figure 25 refers to six.

experiment_summary: Centered kernel alignment of J-vector geometry, next-token agreement, readout kurtosis, cross-position autocorrelation, and effective dimensionality identify early, middle, and late regimes. Middle layers exhibit persistent abstract content; final layers converge to immediate output predictions. Boundaries are approximate, partly post hoc, and their apparent sharpness is affected by layer subsampling. Most metrics depend on the lens and cannot distinguish absent content from readout failure.
location: In which layers does the J-space act as a workspace?, Figures 27–28

experiment_summary: Measures activations along each trial's pure-endpoint axis independently of the lens. Initially smooth mixture responses become sharp near normalized depth 38. Transition-width analyses show sharpening over roughly depths 21–42, with J-space components reaching narrower transitions earlier than the non-J complement. At pair-specific mixtures maximally ambiguous on average, later activations become bimodal across prompts, especially in the J-space. This is variation across contexts, not evidence of stochastic switching within a fixed deterministic forward pass.
location: Interpretation of ambiguous inputs solidifies at the workspace onset, Figure 29; Ignition Details, Figures 70–71

experiment_summary: During fixed-sentence copying, two held concepts co-occupy top-ten readouts at a rate of 0.46 versus 0.53 for a shuffled control. A held concept and computed arithmetic answer co-occupy at 0.09 versus 0.29 for the control. Each task can still surface somewhere in the response; computed-answer top-five recovery declines from 95% alone to 72% under dual load. The source does not supply trial counts here.
location: Competition in the workspace during concurrent covert tasks, Figure 73

experiment_summary: Restricts evaluation to items with implied-concept naming probability at least 0.85 and avoidance-condition probability at most 0.15. Early ablation leaves naming largely intact but increases avoidance failures roughly fivefold. Late ablation suppresses concept production under both instructions. A matched-magnitude perturbation targeting another same-category concept produces a substantially smaller avoidance impairment. Results are conditional on the baseline selection criteria.
location: Different J-space requirements for naming a concept and avoiding it, Figure 69

experiment_summary: Ablates artificiality-related token directions selected from top-twenty J-lens appearances across the six prompts, throughout workspace layers and token positions. Verbalized evaluation awareness falls from 71% to 3%; attempted blackmail rises from 0/180 to 13/180 rollouts. Most ablated rollouts still reject blackmail on ethical grounds. The experiment does not isolate every semantic effect of the selected directions or establish rates outside these scenarios.
location: Strategic thinking and evaluation awareness in a blackmail scenario, Figures 35–36

experiment_summary: Compares bereavement (nine prompts), danger (ten), and withheld-answer (seven) suites, finding stronger reaction readouts on user tokens after post-training despite similar responses. Roleplay uses forty characters and twelve drift transcripts. Dispreferred-choice prefills elicit a distinctive BUT signal despite continued justification of the prefill in 88% of cases. Across forty suppression concepts, failure words and damn reach lens top five on 93% and 82% of post-trained trials versus 17% and 30% in the base model. Their causal dependence on actual suppression failure, rather than the instruction, is untested.
location: The J-space acquires the Assistant’s point of view during post-training, Figures 42–46; Assistant-reaction appendix, Figures 80–81

experiment_summary: Fine-tunes only reflection-turn tokens after truncated agentic rollouts. Reflections use twenty sampled constitutional principles during target generation; that scaffolding is stripped from training examples. Evaluation requests no reflection. Across twenty-seven fabrication transcripts and one hundred hidden-directive roleplay scenarios, five responses each, mean dishonesty falls from 0.25 to 0.07 and deception from 0.38 to 0.05. Fabrication grading ranges from admission (0) to presenting fabrication as real (1); deception grading assigns 0 for refusal and disclosure, 0.5 for neither promotion nor disclosure, and 1 for promoting the hidden agenda.
location: Shaping the J-space with Counterfactual Reflection Training, Figures 47–50

experiment_summary: Finds increased ethical-reflection readouts before any output in uninterrupted evaluation contexts. Ablating 176 selected directions on fabrication changes the trained score from 0.07 to 0.22 while baseline remains 0.25. Ablating 63 directions on deception changes the trained score from 0.05 to 0.23 and baseline from 0.38 to 0.48. Tokens are selected separately for each benchmark. No matched arbitrary-token-set control is reported, and the intervention does not establish exclusive mediation by these directions.
location: The implanted J-space contents are causally implicated in reflection training’s effects, Figures 49–50

experiment_summary: Constructs regularized inverse-covariance-weighted mean directions from contexts preceding each word. On 126 multihop prompts with one- to four-token intermediates, template top-ten recovery stays comparatively stable as J-lens recovery degrades. A swap evaluation uses 112 pairs: 53 single-token and 59 multi-token pairs, with a similar length-dependent advantage. Tchaikovsky–Beethoven template swaps redirect nationality answers where first-token J-vectors fail. The Stein's-lemma connection is idealized motivation: the stated real activations are non-Gaussian, continuation probabilities depend on more than the chosen activation, and equivalence to the actual J-lens is not established.
location: Extending the Jacobian lens to multi-token concepts: Template lens, Figures 61–63

experiment_summary: Trains a phrase-to-activation reconstructor, builds roughly 3.4 million phrase vectors, labels one million activations using nonnegative pursuit, and trains then RL-refines an oracle. Nonnegative refitting explains an average 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out on-policy Assistant positions. Nine illustrative prompts show phrase-level readouts at depth 67, with ten four-token phrases per readout; two panels select the highest-FVE result among five decodes. The claim that this approach confabulates less than natural-language autoencoders is conjectured, not tested.
location: Extending the Jacobian lens to multi-token concepts: Oracle lens, Figure 64

experiment_summary:
Equips an Opus 4.6 investigator with top-twenty-five J-lens tokens at normalized depth 71 and compares NLA and SAE tools using ten investigator seeds per claim. A judge awards ten points split between answer correctness and evidence quality. J-lens is comparable to NLA on four of six cases, but lower on reward hacking (4.5 versus 10.0) and language switching (6.0 versus 9.9). Ground truth comes from NLA-assisted human analysis. No text-only investigator baseline is reported, so the experiment demonstrates limited tool utility without isolating improvement over behavioral inspection alone.
Specific finding: J-lens response-start readouts can reveal signatures of trained misaligned dispositions on ordinary prompts that do not explicitly mention those objectives. New readout analyses test four checkpoints from MacDiarmid et al.'s reward-hacking lineage on forty coding prompts: twenty user-code and twenty test-passing requests. Deception-token top-ten counts are strongest at a prefilled I token, already present after synthetic-document fine-tuning, amplified after coding RL, and partially reduced after safety training. Separately, reward and bias appear in top-twenty-five readouts of Marks et al.'s hidden-objective model across neutral, quirk-eliciting, and goal-probing prompts, but not its baseline; logit lens misses both tokens. The organisms' training histories and prior behavioral results come from the cited studies.
Specific finding: A simple J-lens score based on artificiality-related words can track several operational indicators of evaluation awareness. Scores mean lens log-probability of fictional and simulation minus one hundred control words, averaged across workspace layers. Of roughly 94,000 Assistant-start positions, a prior NLA pipeline flags 198. On all 198 flagged positions plus 594 sampled unflagged positions, J-score separation has AUC 0.853. New scoring analyses use shared prior-study transcripts: scores vary monotonically with contrastive steering on six suites; realism edits reduce scores on all eleven suites, significantly on eight; evaluation distributions are also compared with two deployment controls. These are new readout evaluations on existing experimental material, not independent reruns of every intervention.

This is a controlled localization example, not a broad localization benchmark.

experiment_summary: For attention from the second token of gleam to the newline after dream, leading QK attributions pair line-ending sound features, while the leading OV interaction pairs a newline value feature with a newline-output feature. This is a worked attribution analysis; no intervention independently validates the attributed feature pairs or reconstructs the circuit.

Individual examples and QK attributions suggest matching a year prefix 1 with its three-digit suffix, potentially covering 1000–1999. Sweeping the year in a fixed prompt instead finds strong attention only for 1000–1986. The supplied text does not specify a numerical threshold for strong attention or report broader prompt sweeps.

New attributions on sentiment-function and dialogue examples resemble the previously studied multiple-choice selection template: relevance-related key features interact with corresponding query features, followed by OV copying. Features nearly orthogonal in residual space align after key projection, with analogous observations on the query side. Q/K/O PCA forms a continuous cloud. No systematic survey or sufficiently precise behavioral hypothesis is supplied to validate monosemanticity.

In 98% of 185 generated sentences of the form '{five cities} are all cities in {country}', the country token attends more to the foreign city than to any domestic city. Country queries from 'The country {X}' and city keys from 'The city {X} is well known', each mean-subtracted across entities, have mean cosine similarity −0.47 for domestic pairs and +0.01 for foreign pairs. Domestic country/city residual representations instead have mean cosine similarity +0.17. These results characterize a controlled attention pattern and geometry, without fully explaining natural-data behavior or demonstrating downstream task effects.

QK attributions identify a Zambian key feature at the token a interacting with an Ivory Coast query feature. Replacing Ivory Coast with Zambia lowers attention to a from 0.87 to 0.08; Lusaka yields 0.10, while substitutions with the other 51 African countries have median attention 0.27. An earlier head attends from a to chikumbuso, and its OV analysis identifies the Zambian features read by the later head. Input substitutions test location sensitivity, but neither the earlier head nor the attributed features are causally ablated.

experiment_summary: Corrupted-to-clean residual-stream and head-output patching with three name-corruption schemes, using batches of 50 randomized prompts, traces preceding-argument information through heads 1.4 and 2.0 on the definition side and head 1.4 on the docstring side. Answer-token corruption identifies heads 3.0 and 3.6 as important answer-copying heads. Attention patterns are consistent with the proposed pathways. A quick param-token corruption test and attention inspection suggest head 0.2 supplies previous-token information for docstring induction, with lower confidence. experiment_summary: Head 0.4 has approximately constant attention scores and position-dependent BOS attention. Swapping its attention patterns between the two documented-argument destination positions reverses head 1.4's preference between those arguments. Swapping the corresponding positional embeddings barely affects the preference; broader positional-embedding swap variants give similar results. The interventions identify an important positional pathway through head 0.4, while attribution of its signal to causal-mask normalization also relies on inspection of its attention pattern. Experiments and visualizations use batches of 50 prompts.

Corruption patching of head 0.5 at relevant positions changes logit difference by up to 1.1. Replacing its attention pattern throughout the prompt with an identity matrix loses less than 0.1 logit difference, indicating that most of its measured contribution survives when attention is restricted to the current position. The post attributes most of the small remaining loss to its attention at B_doc and K-composition with head 1.4. Experiments use batches of 50 prompts.

experiment_summary: Manipulating head 1.2's attention among BOS, the current argument, and its previous occurrence identifies BOS attention as the performance-relevant variable. Point-to-point resampling composition scores connect head 1.2 to both Argument Movers. Varying its BOS attention changes head 3.0's attention to B_doc, consistent with reducing erroneous copying of that argument. Reported corruption-patching logit-difference changes are small: -0.12 at A_doc or B_doc, +0.05 at A_def or B_def, and -0.20 at C_def. The suppression explanation remains partly interpretive. Experiments use batches of 50 prompts.

experiment_summary: Compared average proportional total effects using 300 sampled prompts per structure. Adjacent agreement effects range approximately from 1,000 to 5,000 across model sizes. DistilGPT-2 and GPT-2 Small attain the highest effects with adverbial distractors, while GPT-2 Medium tends to have the highest effects with attractor phrases except across plural relative clauses. Agreement accuracy is not measured in this experiment; the expected accuracy–margin relationship comes from cited prior accuracy findings.

Compared total effects across structures in the GPT-2 size sweep. The GPT-2 Medium grammaticality analysis additionally contrasts two-adverb separation with an equally long prepositional phrase: adverbs have little effect on grammaticality, while the noun-attractor phrase reduces it. experiment_summary: Separated grammaticality ratios by subject number and, where applicable, attractor number. Figure 4 shows higher ratios for plural subjects in every displayed condition. At fixed subject number, matching attractor number improves grammaticality. A plural-verb default is suggested as an explanation by analogy to cited LSTM work, but is not directly tested here.

Compared coordinate-level natural indirect effects across DistilGPT-2 and four GPT-2 sizes. The authors report lower per-layer maximum effects in larger models and broader peaks across layers. Layerwise averages over the highest-NIE 5% retain similar contours for a given structure across model sizes. No joint-coordinate intervention establishes the proposed increase in distributed causal organization.

Compared pairwise coordinate-overlap percentages with a hand-designed similarity matrix normalized to 0–100, using off-diagonal lower-triangle L1 differences. Best-matching layers were GPT-2 Medium layer 21 of 24, Transformer-XL layer 15 of 18, and XLNet layer 8 of 12, with difference norms 443, 510, and 486 respectively. GPT-2 showed a visually close match; Transformer-XL deviated in attractor-number sensitivity; XLNet was noisier and had less overlap. These are selected-layer descriptive comparisons without a reported statistical null or held-out validation.

experiment_summary: Subject-number-based head effects were inconsistent across structures, with positive and negative effects often approximately canceling; the authors suggest these effects may be noise. Zeroing heads produced more consistent patterns, strongly implicating head 0-10 and showing distributed upper-layer positive effects in most non-adverb structures. Qualitative inspection found that heads 0-10 and 2-8 consistently attended to the second and fifth words, respectively. These results do not establish that attention lacks structural information.

Compared relative-clause total effects and coordinate indirect-effect curves with and without “that.” The authors report little change in indirect-effect magnitudes or contours. Total-effect changes depend on size and structure: across-relative-clause effects generally decrease only slightly, while within-relative-clause effects show size-dependent responses, including stronger preferences without “that” in GPT-2 Medium.

Compared average total effects across architectures in Figure 17. Transformer-XL effects were much smaller, while XLNet and GPT-2 generally had similar magnitudes outside relative-clause cases. The supplied prose gives no numerical effect sizes for this comparison. The proposed explanation involving Transformer-XL's longer effective context is conjectural.

Beam search with width 10 compares maximum formula lengths. Across 512 ResNet-18 units, mean IoU increases from 0.059 at length one, equivalent to the atomic NetDissect baseline, to 0.099 at length ten, a reported 68% increase (p = 2 × 10⁻⁹). NLI IoU also improves with formula length and continues increasing beyond length 30. NLI analysis includes only neurons active on at least 500 of 10,000 validation examples. A separate held-out evaluation of the fitted explanations is not reported.

experiment_summary: Manual inspection classified 88 of 128 randomly sampled units as having meaningful concept combinations and the remaining 40 as firing for at least some unrelated concepts. Among the 88 meaningful units, 50 had lexically coherent abstractions, 28 had perceptually coherent but lexically nonobvious abstractions, and 10 expressed specialization through AND NOT formulas. Inter-annotator reliability is not reported, and the authors acknowledge substantial unexplained behavior.

Logical explanations fitted to the SNLI validation set identify selected units associated with premise-only 'man', hypothesis words such as 'nobody', 'sleeping', and 'sitting', and high lexical overlap. Output connection weights associate some of these units with contradiction. The paper also supplies hand-edited input examples but does not ablate the identified neurons to establish mediation. Some units are poorly explained by the available feature set.

experiment_summary: The paper correlates each neuron's explanation IoU with whole-model accuracy on inputs where its binary activation mask is positive, obtaining Pearson r = 0.31 and p < 10⁻¹³. The correlation increases with maximum formula length. Across analyzed neurons, explanation IoU and whole-model accuracy on activating inputs have Pearson r = −0.60 with p < 10⁻⁸. Shorter maximum formulas capture a stronger anticorrelation. This observational analysis does not establish that the neurons cause the errors or that interpretability generally harms performance.

experiment_summary: Formal construction in Equation 4 applies a first-order Taylor expansion at each clean activation. One reference forward pass supplies replacement activations, one clean forward pass supplies clean activations and the metric, and one backward pass supplies all required gradients. This establishes computation of the approximation, not its accuracy for finite replacements.

Compared exact patch-effect ranks with AtP ranks for attention nodes and highlighted the maximum attention-probability change induced by each replacement. Many pronounced query/key false negatives have large probability changes, consistent with the saturation explanation. Explicit softmax recomputation substantially reduces these errors; the analysis does not establish saturation as the cause of every false negative.

Compared AtP with AtP+QKfix using exact activation-patching rankings and verified-recall costs on IOI-PP, RAND-PP, and the 120-pair IOI distribution across four Pythia sizes. The detailed Pythia-12B CITY-PP rank plot shows correction of many query/key false negatives. Appendix A.2.1 separately derives an efficient key-correction algorithm with quadratic rather than cubic dependence on sequence length.

experiment_summary: Constructs per-node tests of effects exceeding a threshold, combines them through the maximum p-value, and inverts the test. Pythia-12B illustrations compare bounds with known effects outside the top 1,024 AtP* estimates at nominal 90%, 99%, and 99.9% confidence as sampling budgets increase. IOI-PP illustrates detection of a large missed effect; IOI illustrates tightening bounds without a large missed effect. Additional settings appear in Appendix B.3. These examples do not constitute a repeated-sampling coverage study. Section 3.2 and Appendix A.3 give conflicting descriptions of the threshold-search direction.

experiment_summary: Appendix B.4 compares true versus estimated ranks under noising and denoising on IOI. Denoising produces notably worse AtP* ranking behavior; the authors provide no satisfactory explanation or broader evaluation of this difference.

Formal derivation in Appendix C.1 sets the clean norm to one and derives Euclidean approximation errors in the plane spanned by clean and replacement vectors. Frozen-denominator error is the absolute difference between replacement norm and one, hence zero for equal norms. The appendix also identifies regimes where freezing increases error; no language-model experiment tests this modification.

For each evaluated task, expert weights are learned using development items from the other tasks. Macro recall@10 is 54.4%, compared with 55.2% when development data include examples from every task. This tests transfer among the five supplied task types, rather than arbitrary unseen domains. The clusters and expert Jacobians are fitted on unlabelled text in both conditions.

Each expert is evaluated globally, including on activations outside its fitting cluster. Of 52 expert Jacobians with their own fit, 24 outperform the pooled map and 17 score below 2% per-layer recall@10. Learned filtering improves macro recall@10 by 11.7 percentage points relative to pooling. Separately, LRP reduces early-layer gradient-norm growth by up to a factor of five. These measurements provide indirect evidence for the noise account, but do not identify biased noise or curvature as the causal source of the poor readouts. Repeats the naming-versus-avoidance intervention protocol attributed to Gurnee et al., using Qwen3.6-27B and comparing J++, J-, and R-Lens directions. Formal asymptotic derivation in Appendix A.4.1 imposes K*p(delta)<epsilon for K active occurrences. Substituting delta approximately a1*2^-b and p(delta) approximately a2*delta^n yields b > (log2 K - log2 epsilon + log2 a2)/n + log2 a1. Under the additional description-cost interpretation, weighting precision costs by usage motivates an f*log(f) term. This is a conditional approximate derivation, not a quantization experiment or proof that frequency measures computational simplicity in general.

Formal derivation in Appendix B.7 uses independence and rotational invariance to express expected normalized overlap, then approximates trace terms by their expectations. It computes E[tr(M)]=d_head*d_model and E[tr(M^2)]=d_model*d_head*(d_model+d_head+1), giving the stated approximation under concentration. A separate Monte Carlo test generates 1,000 independent matrix pairs at dimensions 128 by 768 and reports mean overlap 0.1427, agreeing with 128/897 at the reported precision. This agreement does not turn the approximation into an exact proof. Data-weighted baselines are obtained numerically.

Equation 9 combines absolute overlap of MLP-up write weights with overlap of causal-importance-weighted activations, normalized to unit diagonal. Layer-0 heatmaps and histograms show most entries below self-interaction, with prominent blocks and stripes. The authors explicitly describe the measure as crude and preliminary and do not test whether these patterns suffice to reconstruct nonlinear computations or predict downstream intervention effects.

experiment_summary: Places-CNN was trained from scratch on 2.4 million scene-labeled images without object supervision. Workers annotated top-activating unit regions, and discovered object segmentations were evaluated using the densely annotated SUN dataset, which contains 8,220 images. Object-labeled units include buildings, lamps, and people. Figure 14 reports Jaccard segmentation index and average precision-recall, but its numerical results are unavailable in the supplied text. The evidence establishes emergence in this network rather than across arbitrary scene-training settings.

The authors slid 11×11 randomized patches with stride three over top-activating images, then recentered and averaged activation-discrepancy maps. At pool5, reported empirical square receptive-field side lengths were 72.0±20.0 pixels for Places-CNN and 70.3±21.6 for ImageNet-CNN, compared with the theoretical 195 pixels. Empirical sizes were also smaller in the other evaluated layers, with the discrepancy increasing substantially at later layers. The supplied text does not specify the selected-image count K or the exact rule converting discrepancy maps into field boundaries.

Using SUN's object annotations, the authors compared pool5 object-unit counts with object occurrence counts and with counts of scene categories for which each object was most informative, as assessed through object-based scene-classification performance. Reported correlations were 0.54 with occurrence frequency and 0.84 with scene-discriminative usefulness. This is an observational association, without an intervention separating training frequency from discriminative usefulness.

Starting from correctly classified images, segments were removed in order of smallest decrease in the correct-category score until classification failed, identifying the remaining classification-preserving representation. With annotated object segments, beds were retained in 87% of bedroom cases, paintings in 81% of art-gallery cases, and bookcases in 96% of bookstore cases. Category-specific sample counts were not supplied. The greedy procedure does not guarantee a globally minimal image, and input dependence does not establish mediation by particular internal units.

The authors thresholded internal activation maps and mapped them to image regions using estimated receptive fields and AMT labels while retaining the network's scene-classification output. Figure 13 demonstrated combined scene predictions and localized internal-unit labels. Figure 14 reported SUN segmentation evaluation using Jaccard index and average precision-recall; numerical values and detailed threshold-selection procedures are unavailable in the supplied text.

The authors grouped pool5 units by their annotated object classes and inspected their top five activating images and activation-based segmentations. They reported 15 building units, six lamp units preferring different lamp types, and nine person units preferring different scales or activities. The specialization evidence is qualitative and based on selected high-activation examples.
Specific finding: Human identification of a common concept across strongly activating image regions provides a useful proxy for the semantic selectivity of a visual-network unit.

Methodological demonstrations pair activation-ranked visual dictionaries with interactive spatial and channel attribution views. They do not measure comprehension or validate the visualizations' semantic accuracy.

The authors measure Euclidean distances between original and transformed feature vectors at layers 1 and 7 and separately track true-class probability. Formal result supplied here: Theorem 4.2 and two proofs in Appendix E derive P*=I−W⁺ΠW, where W=(ΣXX^(1/2))⁺ and Π=(WΣXZ)(WΣXZ)⁺. Theorem 4.3 derives the mean-preserving bias b*=E[X]−P*E[X]. Formal construction supplied here: Appendix H sets P'=αP+(1−α)Q and solves a quadratic for α∈[0,1] when LEACE increases covariance trace, selecting a mixture whose output trace equals the original trace. The feasible zero-cross-covariance matrices form a linear subspace, so mixing preserves the constraint. Convexity of squared distortion and LEACE optimality bound the mixture's distortion by SAL's. Formal derivation: Section 3 identifies the local linear coefficients with the input derivative through a first-order Taylor expansion. At differentiable inputs, coefficient magnitude gives the magnitude of the infinitesimal score change per unit coordinate perturbation. This is a mathematical result, not an empirical measurement.

Formal derivation: convolution backpropagates through the flipped kernel, matching DeconvNet reconstruction; max-pooling routes backward values through forward argmax switches. Ordinary ReLU backpropagation gates by positive forward inputs, while DeconvNet gates by positive backward reconstruction values. These operator identities establish the stated similarities and difference without empirical experiments.

experiment_summary:
For the same CaffeNet output neuron, different cluster-mean initializations generated recognizable alternatives such as interior and exterior theater views or distinct pepper colors and arrangements. Corresponding natural examples demonstrate response diversity omitted by an individual visualization. The evidence establishes selected multifaceted cases rather than comprehensive facet recovery.
Specific finding: Initializing activation maximization from means of clustered natural examples can produce distinct visualizations of different stimuli that activate the same CNN neuron. Clustered image codes using PCA, t-SNE, and k-means with k=10, averaged the 15 images nearest each centroid, and optimized each seed. Presented distinct output-unit facets such as theater interiors/exteriors and differently colored or arranged peppers. Output demonstrations use class-labeled training images; hidden-unit examples use the top 1,000 activating validation images or patches. Evidence consists of qualitative examples rather than measured facet coverage.
Specific finding: Activation maximization initialized from interpolations between two natural images can converge toward an individual response facet rather than a visual hybrid, while sometimes departing from both seeded facets. For a class, formed ten clusters, selected two random images from different clusters, generated eight intermediate linear interpolations, and optimized these seeds and the endpoints. Displayed ostrich and fishing-reel results often resembled one facet rather than a blend, with changed details. Stuffed/cut-pepper seeds instead produced whole peppers, and some fishing-reel seeds converged to a third facet. The explanations involving basin sizes or ignored stuffing remain hypotheses.

Figure S5 examines two units each from fc6 and fc7, alongside two fc8 units. For each unit, it displays four facet reconstructions and four sampled seed-contributing images per facet. Some hidden-unit optimizations repeatedly produced similar turtle/goggle-like, dog/bathtub-like, arch-like, or bird-like images despite different seed categories. Preliminary addition of a high-level-code L2 penalty reportedly did not improve facet separation; supporting data are not shown.

Best accuracies include determiner 94.3% versus 51.7% for the best fixed offset, direct object 86.8% versus 40.0%, and prepositional object 76.3% versus 34.6%. For the listed relations, the best direction is dependent-to-head except for prepositional objects. Best overall individual-head UAS is 34.5 versus 26.3 for right branching. Possessive scoring accepts ’s where the annotation identifies its complement. The table includes the ten most common relations and five additional relations on which heads perform well.

Head 5-4 achieves 65% antecedent-selection accuracy overall, with 64% for pronouns, 73% for proper mentions, and 58% for nominal mentions. Overall baselines achieve 27% for nearest mention, 52% for head matching, and 69% for the rule-based sieve system. The cited neural system's 83% uses non-truncated documents and different mention detection and is only roughly comparable; that neural result is prior work.

Trained supervised probes without updating BERT. Attention-only probing achieves 61 UAS; attention plus GloVe achieves 77 UAS. Baselines achieve 26 for right branching, 58 for distances plus GloVe, and 30 for attention plus GloVe from BERT with pretrained word/positional embeddings and randomly initialized remaining weights. The cited structural probe's 80 UUAS is prior work and is not directly comparable because it uses a single representation layer, undirected trees, and a different training objective.

experiment_summary: Retained heads are characterized using the attention-pattern criteria across pruned models. The 17-of-48-head encoder retains all identified function types. With greater pruning, positional heads can begin tracking syntactic dependencies and individual heads can receive multiple function labels. The authors report that specialized heads are retained until late in pruning.

Table 2 compares fine-tuned pruned models with randomly initialized models having identical head configurations. WMT models with 8/13/15 encoder/decoder/cross-attention heads score 29.06 versus 28.56 BLEU; OpenSubtitles models with 6/9/13 score 32.27 versus 31.84. All seven reported sparse configurations favor initialization from a trained model, with gaps ranging from 0.01 to 0.50 BLEU. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

Gates are applied to all 144 heads, initially 48 of each attention type. On WMT, retaining 14/31/30 encoder/decoder/cross-attention heads yields 29.62 BLEU versus 29.6 for the full model. On OpenSubtitles, retaining 6/9/13 yields 32.27 versus 32.4. Sparsity sweeps show encoder heads removed most readily and generally greater retention of cross-attention; decoder self-attention approaches cross-attention retention on WMT.

Retained decoder heads are counted across sparsity levels, summing adjacent layer pairs to reduce noise. Figure 10 shows lower-layer self-attention retention and higher-layer cross-attention retention for WMT; similar observations are reported for OpenSubtitles. These measurements do not directly isolate language-modeling or source-conditioning computations.

Fifty participants perform six tasks each, covering three classes and two saliency methods for a single model per participant. Tasks show four images with saliency masks and solicit image importance, caption importance, and confidence ratings. The study uses 60 unique images and 120 unique saliency maps. Aggregate identification of the more important concept is reported as 52%, versus 50% binary chance. More than half of evaluated conditions show either no significant perceived difference or preference for the wrong concept. The proportions of correct and incorrect answers rated very confident are similar. No direct human evaluation of TCAV explanations is performed.

An AlexNet classifier trained to distinguish clean from adversarial images using their saliency heatmaps achieved 93.6% accuracy with meaningful-perturbation masks and reportedly outperformed the compared heatmap methods. Figure 10 specifies N_trn = 4,000 and N_val = 1,000, without giving class-specific counts in the supplied text.

For N = 5,000 adversarial images, mask application recovered the clean image's predicted label as top one in 40.64% of cases and the ground-truth label as top one in 37.32%. The clean predicted label reportedly appeared among the top five predictions in 100% of mask-plus-adversarial cases. Broader attack robustness and detailed sample-selection conditions are not established.

Masks optimized to minimize the top five predicted classes' softmax scores, using λ₁ = 10⁻³ and β = 2, yielded localization errors of 44.0%, 43.1%, and 43.2% with value, energy, and mean thresholding. Overall pointing precision was 37.49% for masks, 36.40% for gradients, 32.68% for guided backpropagation, 44.50% for occlusion, and 50.95% for contrastive excitation backpropagation. Blur occlusion and variable-size blur occlusion scored 45.41% and 42.31% overall. Small-object failures were observed qualitatively and attributed to regularization without a controlled ablation.

experiment_summary: The proposed estimator is tested through within-prompt MLP-neuron correction on three models and across-prompt average attention-head-effect correction on two models. Within-prompt MAE improves in all nine model–task settings; average correction strongly improves factual completion but harms Qwen2.5 IOI. Separate claims describe the tested configurations and limitations.

Applying the median residual of magnitude-selected verification measurements raises MAE versus verification alone in eight of nine model–task settings. On Gemma IOI/factual/SVA, relative MAEs are 1.93/0.97/1.80 for verification-plus-shift and 0.83/0.74/0.81 for Guided-AP. Uniform and magnitude-stratified representative pilots perform similarly on Gemma. These controls establish failure of this selected-label shift, rather than failure of residual correction in general.

Formal result supplied in Theorem 1 and Appendix C.1: N times the MAE improvement equals H_U − E_U − C. For a stratified pilot of n labels and 0 < t < 1/2, its median lies within the full residual distribution's central quantile band with probability at least 1 − 2 exp(−2nt²), giving an endpoint-convexity bound on E_U. The appendix extends the identity to unequal runtime-matched measurement counts and acquisition discrepancies. Positive improvement requires the common-shift benefit to exceed the estimation and verification costs.

Formal result supplied in Theorem 2 and Appendix C.2: with probability at least 1 − 2 exp(−2nt²), R(c_hat) ≤ R(0) − Gamma + 2t w(t), where Gamma is the population-median shift's benefit and w(t) is the central quantile width. Thus the correction improves on zero correction when recurring bias outweighs the stated estimation bound. This is not a guarantee for the paper's magnitude-guided calibration acquisition.

Formal result supplied in Proposition 1 and Appendix C.3: selecting the B largest scores leaves at most 2B epsilon more expected summed absolute error than selecting the B largest expected absolute remaining errors. A small signed expected residual can coexist with large expected absolute error, motivating a separate selection model. The result assumes score accuracy rather than proving that the fitted scores attain it.

Formal result supplied in Appendix C.4, Lemma 2: squaring |e_bar − c_bar| < |e_bar| gives c_bar² < 2 c_bar e_bar, equivalent to matching sign and |c_bar| < 2|e_bar|. The appendix also identifies acquisition bias: selected-label means target E[e_i | A_i = 1], which can differ from E[e_i]. No empirical models or measurements are required for this scalar result.

Across-prompt verification sets the signed correction to zero and tests selection alone. Each cell uses 1,600 exact calibration labels acquired by magnitude-guided round robin. At a projected 10,000 prompts and B=16, Guided-AP yields MAE reductions of 12%/−20%/3% on Qwen3 IOI/factual/SVA and −29%/−18%/2% on Qwen2.5; negative reductions indicate harm. At B=128, reductions are 7%/2%/4% and 12%/−2%/3%, respectively. Calibration costs favor verify-more at 100 prompts throughout the grid. Across both exact-label and curvature-probe learners, projected break-even at B=16 ranges from 1,900 to 24,000 prompts where learning pays. Horizons are cost projections, not additional evaluation samples.

experiment_summary: ProbeCal uses 400 calibration HVPs per cell, with no probes on evaluation prompts. Its separate factual average-effect correction has uncorrected-to-corrected MAE ratios of 1.87 and 1.86, approximately 46% reductions, below exact-residual correction. Sketches estimate baseline curvature rather than the full finite-intervention residual; their unbiased diagonal-estimation identity is attributed to prior work, while the paper measures sketch-noise agreement on held-out Qwen3 IOI prompts.
