Replacing the repeated item's response with its baseline response leaves mean correlations of 0.25 and 0.40, reported at p < 0.05. Some context statements show reversed relationships; double negatives are discussed as a possible explanation rather than experimentally isolated.
location: Section 5.1; Tables 2–3; Figures 2–3; footnote 3; Appendix C

experiment_summary: The corpus contains 404 retained description–questionnaire pairs: 199 directed and 205 undirected. After outlier removal, reported BERT/GPT2 correlations are 0.44/0.48 for directed descriptions and 0.40/0.48 for undirected descriptions. Minimum-length conditions of 75 or 100 words yield correlations ranging from 0.39 to 0.48 across model and dataset conditions. Post-filter sample sizes, precise correlation aggregation details, and comparisons with dedicated personality predictors are not supplied.

Both frozen models are assessed with each of 1,119 Reddit descriptions as context. Regressions predict context-induced trait-score changes from lexical features, considering contexts with the stated norm of score change at least one. Selected weights associate friendliness with positive extroversion or agreeableness shifts and lack of motivation with negative conscientiousness shifts. Other highly weighted phrases have unclear trait relevance. Appendix D reports trait-score changes, but no held-out regression accuracy or independent semantic-rating metric is reported.

Section 5.4 summarizes minimum, median, and maximum context-conditioned scores, with Figure 6 explicitly captioned as a BERT comparison. The prose reports nearly 0–100 human percentiles for conscientiousness and emotional stability, contexts below the tenth percentile for all five traits, difficulty attaining high agreeableness, and no major differences in observed ranges among context types. These are source-reported descriptions; exact plotted extrema cannot be checked from the supplied text rendering.

The first-person questionnaire is rewritten with each selected name, producing 20 male-name and 20 female-name score profiles per model. Human-percentile conversions of male/female mean scores are 29/34, 49/68, and 47/56 for BERT agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability; GPT2 values are 16/19, 59/64, and 35/43. These are percentiles of group mean scores, not mean individual percentiles. The authors explicitly describe the sample as insufficient for significant inferences.

Projected residual-space singular vectors through the unembedding and inspected highest-scoring tokens. Human labeling covered 960 GPT-2 Medium MLP-input directions using a subjective approximately 70–80% token-coherence criterion. GPT-3 generation plus verification surveyed the first 30 MLP-input/output directions across three GPT-2 sizes, reporting approximately 70–80% accepted directions when aggregated by singular index. Gaussian random-matrix examples reportedly lacked comparable structure; no quantified null distribution or inter-rater agreement is supplied.
location: Examples — analyzing the OV circuit; MLP in interpretability; Manual Labelling of GPT2-medium W_in; Experiments with automated direction labelling

experiment_summary: Tried zero-shot and few-shot formats, sampling, and a separate verifier, then labeled the first 30 MLP-input/output directions per layer across three GPT-2 models. Qualitative spot checks found useful descriptions, while positive/negative example balance and individual examples substantially changed responses. Verification reduced some invented interpretations but rejected some sensible ones. No held-out labeling accuracy or inter-rater agreement is reported, and automated singular-index trends conflict with manual labels. The text does not unambiguously identify which GPT-3 checkpoint produced the final survey.

Formal derivation supplied in the editing section: expand the exact SVD as a sum of rank-one components and subtract the selected summand. The conclusion follows directly under the stated exact-factorization assumption; it is not an empirical result.
location: Directly editing SVD representations, displayed rank-one decomposition and update equations

experiment_summary: Inspected high-scoring vocabulary tokens for both signs of selected OV singular vectors and identified related or opposing semantic groups. The prose reports common-versus-rare-token contrasts in leading directions and selected semantic contrasts including fire versus ice. No systematic prevalence estimate or independent semantic evaluation is supplied, and the underlying token tables are unavailable in this rendering.

location: Discussion, comparison of weight and activation analysis

experiment_summary: Table 4 compares persona configurations with default ChatGPT. Entity toxicity, reported using maximum-of-five scoring when the model responds, increases from 0.11 without a persona to 0.62 for 'a bad person' and 0.64 for 'a terrible person'; 'a good person' scores 0.06. Heuristic response probability increases from 0.13 to 0.96 for 'a bad person' in the table, although prose reports 0.97. RealToxicityPrompts toxicity increases from 0.09 without a persona to 0.53 for 'a nasty person.' The continuation evaluation uses one generation per persona–prefix pair.

The authors elicit persona Good/Bad probabilities from text-davinci-003 because ChatGPT often refuses the rating request. They report Pearson correlation 0.7, p<0.05, between badness probability and average persona toxicity. The number of personas included in this correlation is not separately specified. No intervention tests whether these assessments cause toxicity.

Table 9 reports category means of 0.22 for races, 0.31 for genders, and 0.33 for sexual orientations. The Figure 3 caption supplies race-specific scores of 0.10 for African and 0.29 for Northern European; the text reports higher scores for male and non-binary targets than female targets. Section 4.4 and the Figure 4 caption describe higher country scores for Europe and the Americas after averaging over selected dictator personas and countries within continents. These are selected-inventory comparisons using maximum-of-five entity scores. No additional values are inferred from the unavailable plots.
location: Section 4.4; Figure 3 caption; Figure 4 caption; Table 9
Section 3.2; Appendix C; illustrative outputs in Appendix E

experiment_summary: Appendix D describes eight string-pattern rules and reports that inspection of 200 responses found all refusals covered and no responding cases incorrectly covered. No confusion matrix or sampling procedure is provided. The resulting probability-of-responding metric measures absence of these refusal patterns rather than toxic compliance directly.

Appendix 8.6 reports disconnection only at the three smallest tested retained-kernel fractions: 1%, 0.5%, and 0.1%, with respective disconnection rates 0.057, 0.298, and 0.807. The subsection does not explicitly state its circuit count. Disconnected circuits were assigned Pearson correlation zero in the main preservation evaluation.

Specific finding: Local vector-contribution scores computed with observed attention weights and normalization factors held fixed provide useful proxies for identifying information routes relevant to a language-model prediction.

Extracted routes for original and contrastive IOI and Greater-than templates and compared head inclusion frequencies with published head-role annotations. The prose reports substantial recurrence of known heads and additional heads with frequencies near one. The supplied text gives no example count or numerical overlap score. This is a new attribution comparison, not a replication of the prior patching experiments.

Compared original Greater-than route frequencies with routes for suffix-01 and suffix-00 prompts. Original-task heads remain attribution-important for 01, whereas labeled Greater-than heads become less important for 00. No new activation-patching intervention was performed in this comparison.

The authors report five-second extraction for 50 IOI examples and compare it with ACDC's previously reported eight-minute single-GPU result. Only the route-extraction timing is reported as produced here; repeated timings and hardware details for that measurement are absent.

Constructed per-position vectors containing source-summed head contributions and FFN importances, then visualized them with t-SNE. The prose reports grouping of function-word categories and subword positions, with greater overlap among content-word categories. Next-token labels come from the dataset rather than model generations. Plot geometry cannot be independently inspected in the supplied rendering.

Averaged local head activation frequencies and FFN importance by depth. Section 4.2 reports greater lower-layer activity and a highly important final FFN. Numerical layerwise values and inferential comparisons are not supplied in the text.

Classified heads using contribution-based positional criteria and compared their activation frequencies within layers. Almost all identified previous-token heads are reported among their layers' most active heads; identified subword-merging heads occur low in the network. Appendix B.2 requires later subwords to place over half their influence on earlier same-word subwords in at least 70% of cases, and first-subword influence to be no more than 0.005% in at least 70% of cases, as printed. No ablation validates behavioral necessity.

Inspected component-importance averages and routes for an outlying punctuation cluster, finding near-zero intermediate attention/FFN scores and routes dominated by residual connections. Appendix D describes subsequent attention distributed between BOS and the first period in an L18H3 example. An abbreviation example shows that the period need not end a sentence. No intervention tests functional equivalence to BOS, actual information removal, or generation errors.

Compared component importances on C4, English/Russian/Italian/Spanish FLORES-200 devtest, CodeParrot code, and addition/subtraction data. The prose reports heads prominent for addition that rank low on C4 and different prominent heads for code, arithmetic, and non-English inputs. Addition/subtraction profiles substantially overlap but include operation-associated differences. Separate language-specific heads were not identified. FFN profiles also differ, including lower final-FFN importance for non-English inputs.

Donor contexts supply entity, attribute, or joint replacements into a target context while other context states remain frozen. Reported capitals answer log probabilities across original and donor queries follow the predicted localized substitutions. Appendix J supplies additional task plots and explicitly reports the biography attribute failure. Evaluations use 100 sampled contexts; the supplied rendering does not expose numerical values from the plots.

The apparent positions of two entity or attribute representations are moved past one another by modifying their RoPE rotations. The text reports little change in capitals answer log probabilities for entities and a gradual attribute-position bias rather than an association reversal. Appendix J supplies additional task plots. Exact plotted effects are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
location: Section 3.2; Figure 4; Appendices C and J

experiment_summary: The identifier account is tested through localized donor substitutions, apparent-position interventions, binding-offset swaps, geometric interventions, and cross-task restoration. Section 5 additionally tests three-pair cyclic binding permutations across models and several tasks in LLaMA-30B. These results support a representational mechanism without identifying the complete construction or retrieval circuit. Appendix B supplies an explicitly informal necessity argument, not a formal proof.
models_studied: ["LLaMA-30B", "LLaMA-13B", "LLaMA-65B", "Pythia family models evaluated in Figure 6", "LLaMA family models evaluated in Figure 6"]
location: Sections 3–5; Figure 6; Appendices B, F, H, I, and J

experiment_summary: Across 100 evaluation contexts, original-association accuracy for the two entity queries is 0.99 and 1.00 without intervention, 0.00 and 0.03 after attribute-side swaps, 0.00 and 0.01 after entity-side swaps, and 0.97 and 0.99 after both swaps. Equal-magnitude random-direction interventions retain accuracies of 0.97–1.00. This provides strong evidence for the specified intervention effect and supports approximate additive binding offsets; it does not establish an exact decomposition of every activation component.

Offsets estimated from three-pair contexts define a two-dimensional intervention plane. In two-pair contexts, subtracting the second pair's offset reduces accuracy to chance. Candidate offsets are then added to both entity-side and attribute-side representations. The text reports approximately 50% accuracy for nearby candidates and recovered discrimination for sufficiently separated tested combinations, including combinations outside the generating IDs' convex hull. Figure 5 values and exact grid ranges are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

For each evaluated model, entity-side and attribute-side mean interventions cyclically permute three bindings. Accuracy is measured against the predicted permutation and averaged over the two cyclic shifts; offsets use 500 estimation samples. The text reports increasing intervention effectiveness with scale, but individual model configurations and numerical scores cannot be recovered from the supplied Figure 6 rendering.
models_studied: ["Pythia family models evaluated in Figure 6", "LLaMA family models evaluated in Figure 6, excluding LLaMA-65B"]

experiment_summary: After subtracting capitals offsets from entity and attribute representations, source-task offsets are added back. Table 2 reports mean median-calibrated accuracies of 0.88 for capitals, 0.87 for parallel, 0.71 for shapes, 0.80 for fruits, and 0.47 for bios, compared with 0.30 for zero offsets and 0.31 for random offsets. Chance among the three relevant answers is approximately 0.33. Corresponding mean log probabilities are −1.01, −1.07, −1.18, −1.21, −1.64, −1.86, and −2.15. Transfer from bios is substantially weaker than from the other tested tasks.

The context binds people to countries, and the question supplies city-to-color associations. Table 3 reports original-answer accuracies of 0.73/0.79 for control, 0.25/0.28 for attribute-side swaps, 0.24/0.26 for entity-side swaps, and 0.71/0.77 for joint swaps. Factorizability and apparent-position tests are also reported in Figures 9–10, but their plotted values are unavailable.

For all six class assignments and both query indices, Table 4 reports control accuracy of 1.00, original-association accuracy of 0.00–0.03 after attribute-side swaps and 0.00–0.01 after entity-side swaps, and 0.99–1.00 after joint swaps. The experimental model follows the paper's default LLaMA-30B convention. Although the appendix opens with a four-statement example, the reported analysis fixes one class and uses two varying bindings.

Source and target option contexts retain sentiment-option text while exchanging labels. A sweep copies suffix activations from source option lines into the target. The text reports that copying the shared 'ative' tokens and following whitespace almost completely transfers the source association, consistent with label information being stored at option-text sites. Exact Figure 8 scores are unavailable. LLaMA-30B could not solve the reversed format, so the intervention experiment uses tulu-13b. Appendix E contains inconsistent label notation, which does not affect the reported suffix-transfer observation.

Compared cross-language topic-vector geometry across layers in all four models. Appendix A.8 reports cosine similarity approximately 0.8 and an increase after incorporating the corresponding language vector. Detailed numerical adjustment effects, aggregation rules, and uncertainty are not supplied; figure captions call the plotted quantity cosine distance while the accompanying prose describes similarity.

Added isotropic Gaussian noise to subject-token embeddings, restored clean hidden states at token–layer sites, and measured recovery of the correct capital's output probability relative to the corrupted run. The authors report similar restoration regions across languages in country–city-pair-averaged traces, including middle-layer subject-position effects and later effects. Entity-resolution and attribute-recollection interpretations are tentative. Fact counts, numerical profile similarities, and complete token-alignment and noise-calibration specifications are not supplied.
location: Section 4.3; Figure 5; Appendices A.1 and A.9; Figures 13–16

experiment_summary: Formed convex interpolations between hidden states from language variants of the same factual query and propagated them through the remaining model. Instructions were added to encourage naming a city rather than describing it. Accuracy was the proportion of queries producing the correct city in either language. The authors report accuracy generally between endpoint-language performances. Exact sample counts, intervention sites, numerical accuracies, and uncertainty are unspecified in the supplied prose. Appendix captions include duplicated comparisons and model misidentifications, limiting attribution of individual unseen plots.

The proposed decomposition h(fact in language) = h(fact content) + h(language) is investigated indirectly through same-fact hidden-state interpolation. Correct-city accuracy generally remains between endpoint accuracies while answer-language propensity changes. The experiments do not independently recover or interchange the proposed components. Equations 4–5 stipulate a hypothesis; their interpolation algebra does not prove that trained models satisfy it.

Table 12 reports explicit-word percentages ranging from 0.00–0.39% for Gemma and 6.25–18.35% for Llama across the five languages; Llama's highest reported value is for Dutch. Aya and Mixtral show different language profiles. The counting denominator, vulgar-term identification procedure, and uncertainty are not clearly specified. Qualitative Llama examples accompany the table; the suggested relationship to language-specific safety tuning is not experimentally isolated.

location: Section 5, Factors affecting interpretability methods; Appendix A.3

experiment_summary: Applied the screening pipeline to four partitioning methods per architecture–dataset setting, comparing every eligible subcluster with 19 size- and layer-matched random groups. Main results comprise 20 lesion conditions and 20 feature-visualization conditions. Numerous conditions exhibit enrichment on the proposed importance and visualization-score proxies, but human understanding and recovered subtask identity are not evaluated.
models_studied: ["Four-hidden-layer width-256 MNIST MLPs", "Three-convolutional-layer MNIST CNNs", "13-convolutional-layer CIFAR-10 VGG-style CNNs", "ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16", "ImageNet-pretrained VGG-19", "ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18"]

experiment_summary: Only two of 20 main class-range conditions show significant Fisher enrichment, both weight-based CIFAR-10 VGG partitions; all 20 corresponding mean effect measures are below one. Only four of 20 optimized-input entropy conditions show significant enrichment: three MNIST MLP partitions and CIFAR-10 VGG activation/layer clustering. These findings contrast with more frequent importance and visualization-score enrichment.
models_studied: ["MNIST MLPs", "MNIST CNNs", "CIFAR-10 VGG-style CNNs", "ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16", "ImageNet-pretrained VGG-19", "ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18"]

experiment_summary: Repeated lesion and visualization analyses at k = 8, 12, and 16. Activation-based visualization-score Fisher statistics remain between 2.34 and 2.73, with mean effect measures between 1.327 and 1.379. Weight/layer lesion importance becomes significant only at k = 16, and some class-range and entropy decisions vary, limiting robustness to broad patterns.

Formal constructive argument in Appendix A.5: give each hidden pair detector two incoming weights of one and bias minus one. Under the stipulated one-hot inputs, exactly the detector for the active pair has ReLU output one. Connect each detector with unit weight to the output indexed by its pair's sum modulo M. The resulting output is the exact one-hot modular sum. No empirical measurement is involved.
location: Appendix A.5, MLPs can Compute Modular Sums

experiment_summary: Formal algebraic result: Equation 5 defines NDF through absolute normalized deviation and clipping; Appendix D derives NDF = 1 − min(|1 − NFS|,1) and connects it to the CMD integrand. Boundedness and symmetry follow for finite scalar scores under a nonzero denominator. This is not an empirical experiment; zero-denominator handling is not supplied.

The source describes EAP-IG circuit-size sweeps for three sampled Marketing queries as fluctuating above one and below zero; Table 1 supplies explicit out-of-range NFS examples. Appendix C.1 reports comparisons for the first 18 Marketing examples, and Appendix C.10 reports widely fluctuating NFS after averaging all 152 Astronomy samples. Table 1 uses probability differences, whereas main discovery experiments use logit differences. NDF's boundedness is imposed by its transformation and does not independently validate mechanistic faithfulness. Figure curves are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
location: Sections 3.3.1 and 4.2; Table 1; Appendices C.1 and C.10

experiment_summary: With 20-step EAP-IG, BoN selects among the original-query candidate and up to nine variant candidates using NDF on the original query. Main comparisons cover 1,000 IOI examples, 500 examples per arithmetic task, 1,172 ARC Challenge questions, and nine MMLU subjects. IOI variants are other dataset queries, arithmetic variants permute operands, and MCQ variants are GPT-4o question-stem paraphrases. The text reports consistently improved frontiers, including larger-model evaluations on IOI, multiplication, and Astronomy. Appendix C.9 also reports paraphrase-based BoN outperforming tested Gaussian-score perturbation, edge-replacement, and random-circuit variants on IOI and Astronomy. Increasing candidate count cannot lower the selected maximum on a nested candidate set, so monotonic gains alone are not independent validation.
location: Sections 5.1–5.2 and 6.1–6.3; Appendices C.3, C.5, and C.9

experiment_summary: Section 6.2 reports that original-query-selected BoN candidates reach approximately 0.6 average NDF with 5,000 edges, versus roughly 200,000 edges, or 51.7%, for single-query EAP-IG. The nine categories are Marketing, Professional Medicine, Astronomy, College Biology, High School Computer Science, Logical Fallacies, Nutrition, International Law, and Management. Appendix C.3 describes approximately 0.6 scores across these categories but labels them NFS, inconsistent with the main text's NDF designation. Exact category-level curves and values are not accessible in this rendering.

Appendix C.4 evaluates complements E minus the selected query-circuit edges and reports uniformly low complement NDF across discovery methods. MMLU and ARC complement scores are described as approximately 0.1–0.2, similar to random-circuit baselines. Low complement scores also occur for unsuccessful candidate circuits, limiting their ability to discriminate high-quality discoveries. This tests collective circuit knockout under the chosen corruption semantics, not individual-edge necessity.

Table A4 reports 9.5 seconds for single-query EAP-IG with 20 integration steps and 132.0 seconds for BoN with nine additional paraphrases. BoN with one and four additional paraphrases takes 25.4 and 66.0 seconds. EAP-IG with 500 and 1,000 steps takes 120.2 and 237.5 seconds; the text reports that increasing integration steps still gives suboptimal discovery. These measurements establish the reported runtime tradeoff, not matched-compute superiority or a general scaling law.

Implements input- and model-dependent activation caches with gradient routing, then trains transformers with selected heads disabled or attention, routing, and output computations supplied. These interventions change convergence speed and loss-curve shape. The reported demonstrations establish the framework's operation in this setting, without a comparative evaluation against other intervention libraries.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only transformer, model dimension 64, eight heads per layer, RoPE and LayerNorm"]

experiment_summary: Most single second-layer head ablations barely affect accuracy. The strongest head alone and all remaining heads without it each achieve approximately 98%, versus 99.99% for the full network. Adding heads in induction-strength order monotonically decreases loss, both with and without the strongest head. Appendix I reports related strength-versus-retained-performance comparisons across five initialization seeds.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformers with eight heads per layer"]

experiment_summary: Eight training conditions each retain one second-layer head throughout training. Each eventually reaches near-perfect training performance, with delayed phase changes relative to the full eight-head network. Two-head follow-ups retaining the strongest head plus another head produce curves closer to full-network training. Cross-seed summaries associate faster isolated learning with greater final induction strength, imperfectly.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformers with one, two, or eight active second-layer heads"]

experiment_summary: With only one second-layer head active and second-layer values preserved, first-layer head-retention interventions identify effective matching paths from head 1 to second-layer head 3, head 2 to heads 1/2/3, and head 5 to heads 1/3. The head-2-to-head-3 matching path achieves approximately 90% accuracy; highlighted paths exceed the 50% contextual-label-guessing baseline. Preserved values retain additional unablated computation.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformer with eight heads per layer"]

experiment_summary: Jointly learned tensor-product factors show a plateau and sharp improvement, whereas learning one factor with the others fixed gives smooth loss decay. In transformers, supplying previous-token attention alone leaves a phase change; supplying additional matching or copying computations changes or removes it. The toy objective's displayed gradients explicitly couple the factors, while transformer interventions support an interaction account without identifying a unique dynamical model of the unmodified network.
models_studied: ["Three-vector tensor-product squared-error learning model", "Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformer with one active second-layer head"]

experiment_summary: For the tensor-product toy, checkpoint cosine alignment and loss with other factors temporarily perfected retain a phase change, while training with those factors fixed produces smooth decay. In transformers, perfecting induction attention at ordinary checkpoints yields an abrupt copy-performance trajectory, whereas maintaining the perfect pattern during training yields smooth copying loss.
models_studied: ["Three-vector tensor-product squared-error learning model", "Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformer"]

experiment_summary: Networks are trained from three initialization seeds. A seed-5 recipient then learns with its post-first-layer residual state replaced by that of each completed donor, allowing gradients only into the second layer. Learning is reported as much faster with the same-seed donor than with different-seed donors. This motivates activation clamps that avoid dependence on a particular trained first-layer parameterization.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformers initialized with seeds 5, 6, and 7"]

experiment_summary: Formal result supplied in Appendix F: assuming each target vector is nonzero, all first and second derivatives vanish at the origin. Perturbing one nonzero target coordinate in each factor, with either matching signs or one reversed sign, gives loss changes with opposite leading terms proportional to epsilon cubed. Arbitrarily close points therefore have both higher and lower loss. Directional derivatives at the origin remain zero; the argument uses finite perturbations rather than nonzero first derivatives.

On the 1,553 of 78,400 training sequences missed by the strongest isolated head, every other isolated head performs below its own overall accuracy. With matching perfected, the strongest head misses only 58 examples; head 1 achieves 86.21% on those examples versus 82.80% overall, but the other listed heads do not exceed their overall accuracy. Label-specific copying errors suggest some complementarity, while two-head training does not reproduce the full emergence ordering. The authors conclude that the combined evidence is inconclusive.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformer", "Two-head training variants retaining the strongest second-layer head"]

experiment_summary: The experiment varies the correct-minus-incorrect label attention of one second-layer head throughout training. Perfect correct-label attention gives smooth copying loss decay; zero induction strength returns phase-change learning through other heads. Exclusive wrong-label attention, corresponding to strength -1, again produces an exponential learning curve. The caption interprets this as copying both labels and subtracting the wrong one; that detailed mechanism is not independently established by a separate intervention in the supplied text.
models_studied: ["Two-layer attention-only Omniglot transformer with one second-layer attention pattern clamped and other heads active"]

experiment_summary: The authors apply an LPIPS nearest-reference decision rule using nine activating reference images to existing human psychophysics queries. Across LPIPS representations from five AlexNet layers, reported AUC reaches 0.71 for earlier ResNet50 layers. Appendix G additionally reports early-layer agreement for CLIP ResNet50 and GoogLeNet, without numerical AUCs in the supplied prose.

K-means with K in {128,256,512} yields higher reported II distributions than neurons and evaluated baselines. The K-means mean is −0.0159 versus −0.0188 for the best tested sparse autoencoder. Autoencoders train on 50,000 activation examples for 200 epochs using Adam at learning rate 0.001, across hidden widths and L1 penalties. The source reports no clear effect of K within this range; it does not provide a held-out evaluation protocol or uncertainty estimates for the mean comparison.
models_studied: ["CIFAR-10-trained ResNet50, layer1", "Shallow L1 sparse autoencoders on ResNet50 activations"]

experiment_summary: The authors vary difficulty by restricting image selection to less extreme activation ranges and compare color, LPIPS, and CIFAR-10 label similarity rules. Cluster features outperform neuron axes across the reported difficulty curves, with the largest gains for color and smaller gains for labels. Exact aggregate effect sizes and uncertainty estimates are absent from the supplied prose.

The authors define synergy as II(a+b) minus max(II(a),II(b)) and evaluate neuron pairs. Most pairings have negative synergy, but positive examples occur. Response correlation has a positive relationship with synergy, while individual II has a negative relationship with maximum attainable synergy. Similar qualitative patterns are reported for both macaque datasets. The two highest-synergy pairs are selected for illustration; exact positive-pair fractions are not supplied.
models_studied: ["CIFAR-10-trained ResNet50, layer1", "Macaque IT responses from Vinken et al. (2023)", "Macaque AM responses from Higgins et al. (2021)"]
location: Section 3.4, Equation 4 and Figure 8; Sections 3.5.1–3.5.2, Figures 9–10

experiment_summary: K-means features are compared with 449 IT sites responding to 1,379 images, including 447 faces and 932 non-face objects, and with 159 AM neurons responding to 2,100 human/monkey face images. Both show higher reported simulated psychophysics performance across difficulty conditions. The grayscale AM dataset uses brightness and LPIPS without labels. Subject 1 fMRI comparisons favor clusters across all reported brain areas, with different semantic-level gains across areas. Numerical gains are not supplied in the prose.
models_studied: ["Macaque IT responses from Vinken et al. (2023)", "Macaque AM responses from Higgins et al. (2021)", "Human visual-cortex fMRI responses from Allen et al. (2022), Subject 1"]

experiment_summary: The authors reanalyze correspondence with 400 β-VAE models using UDR, DCI, and MCC-related comparisons. They recover a positive relationship between model disentanglement and neural alignment for both neurons and clusters, while clusters tend to score higher. For the highest-UDR model, maximum absolute model-unit correlations are strongly associated with simulated psychophysics logits. Numerical effect sizes and detailed uncertainty estimates are absent from the supplied prose.
models_studied: ["Macaque AM responses from Higgins et al. (2021)", "400 previously trained \u03b2-VAE instances"]

experiment_summary: Clusters are transferred by computing target-space centroids from source clustering labels. Best-matching response correlations across subjects are compared using 1,000 images, with higher reported correlations for clusters than voxels. The source dataset contains eight subjects, but the prose does not enumerate all analyzed subject pairings or numerical gains.
models_studied: ["Human visual-cortex fMRI responses from Allen et al. (2022)"]

experiment_summary: Using 88 repeated images from sessions 13 and 14, the authors compare maximum response correlations for units and transferred clusters. Clusters match better across sessions, with V1v and FFA-1 illustrated. Numerical stability estimates, a separate held-out transfer protocol, and replication across additional session pairs are not specified in the supplied prose.
models_studied: ["Human visual-cortex fMRI responses from Allen et al. (2022)"]

experiment_summary: The authors rerun their analysis on an untrained model. A cluster-versus-neuron predictability gap is already present at initialization. Low-level color properties predict responses more readily before training, while category information becomes more predictive after training. Numerical gaps and initialization-seed counts are not reported.

Appendix C computes pairwise LPIPS distances among top examples and visualizes them using t-SNE with perplexity 10. Neuron and feature responses are displayed through exponentiated, z-scored squared distances to one-hot vectors or centroids, with temperature 2. The authors report greater localization for cluster features and a correlation between their average-distance sparsity measure and II for both populations. No numerical correlation is given in the prose.

The authors select maximally separated cluster pairings using the Hungarian algorithm, normalize interpolated directions, and compare II and input-gradient norms along the paths. They report reduced II between centroids and a weak negative association between interpretability and minimum gradient norm, Spearman rho = −0.18. The prose contains inconsistent endpoint labels, and the supplied rendering of the p-value is malformed; neither is used to infer precise endpoint effects.

The authors add Gaussian input noise with standard deviation in [0,0.1] and compare maximum absolute response changes with II and simulated psychophysics logits. Both show weak, reportedly significant associations in the robustness direction. Exact coefficients and sample counts for these noise comparisons are not supplied in the prose.

The authors correlate each neuron's response with the mean response of the other neurons and report a significant negative relationship between this statistic and II. No coefficient or sample count is provided in the prose. The accompanying informal ReLU-quadrant argument contains counting errors and is not treated as a formal derivation.
models_studied: ["CNN neuron population analyzed in Appendix E"]

experiment_summary: Appendix A fits W and b on training activations and evaluates matched test activations. Table 4 reports MSE from 4.252e-14 at layer 1 to 0.02151 at layer 31, alongside activation and shift norms. The listed normalized ratios numerically divide by the shift-norm column rather than the unaligned-activation-norm column named in the heading; normalization conventions are not fully clarified.

Section 4 reports concentrated spectra for SSFT and DPO. SSFT effective rank is one in the first ten layers at the plotted thresholds, rises around layer 20, and returns to one at the final layer; DPO has a different late-layer profile. Formal basis: the n=1 case of Proposition 13 equates quadratic coefficients, giving equality of the Gram matrices of the vertically concatenated weight blocks; Lemma 19 gives a common right-unitary factor. The arbitrary-order proof is not credited here: Lemma 22 applies a positive-semidefinite tensor-root result to cross products that need not be positive semidefinite.

Formal result: Proposition 14 and Appendix A.4 use the isolated-fiber condition near the origin to infer matching kernels of the two linear functionals. They must therefore be proportional, and equal norms restrict the proportionality factor to unit modulus. No training experiment is performed for this result.

Formal result: Appendix A.5 compares mixed input Hessians at zero. Orthonormal first-layer rows and distinct nonzero downstream coefficients make their spectral decompositions unique up to phases. The displayed definition of the weight space is malformed relative to the prose, so the normalization and orthogonality assumptions must be retained explicitly.

Appendix A.6 attempts to bound product errors below half the separation between weight columns. However, the exact convention Wi(g) = ρi(g)† gives Wi(g)Wi(h) = Wi(hg), whereas Equation 6 labels the nearest product gh. The proof changes multiplication order without justification; its block-error aggregation also needs qualification. Opposite-group recovery can still be correct up to isomorphism, as used in the experiments, but does not establish the fixed-label theorem.

Appendix A.7 derives a bound on the component of W perpendicular to W′ and invokes Lemma 23 to obtain Equation 35. Lemma 23 assumes unit vectors, while Proposition 18 and the proof require only equal norms. The supplied derivation therefore does not establish the advertised bound over unrestricted weight norms.

For most-wanted holder, code-prefix AP was 0.90, single-feature AP 0.75, and residual AP 0.95. All predictors shared eligible pairs and accessible-context controls.

Across five model means with equal role and layer weighting, matched AUROC ranged from 0.906–0.913 for residual probes, 0.857–0.881 for reconstruction probes, 0.853–0.878 for top-64 probes, and 0.722–0.782 for individual SAE features. These ranges describe variation across systems, not confidence intervals.

On 1,698 accepted original–edit pairs from 948 source groups, residual paired accuracy was 0.813–0.877 across five model means, versus 0.739–0.784 for reconstruction probes. Reconstruction-minus-residual differences were −4.0 to −12.3 percentage points; all five paired 95% source-group bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Ties received half credit. Summaries equally weighted roles and layers, and uncertainty conditioned on the split, fits, and review decisions.

Residual probes achieved original-over-edit paired accuracy of 0.813–0.877, but their validation-selected thresholds produced edited-negative false-positive rates of 0.684–0.713 and balanced accuracy of 0.610–0.637. Thresholds maximized validation sensitivity minus false-positive rate and were not recalibrated on counterfactual examples. The unchanged-name baseline achieved paired accuracy 0.500 and the code-prefix baseline 0.750.

Across five systems, neutral target renaming reduced residual AUROC by 0.6–1.7 percentage points to 0.878–0.887. On the same pairs, name-baseline AUROC fell from 0.602 to 0.492 and code-prefix AUROC from 0.740 to 0.723. Residual binary decisions still changed for 10.8% of positives and 12.4% of negatives; balanced accuracy fell from 0.830 to 0.809. Pair selection did not consult predictor scores.

Across five model means, residual paired accuracy on reviewed edits was 0.495–0.594 at native identifiers, 0.790–0.915 at statement ends, and 0.856–0.920 at inserted diagnostic identifiers. The statement-end control demonstrates substantial sensitivity at later positions in unmodified code; results do not isolate input insertion from all effects of observation position.

experiment_summary: Reported residual stepper AUROC ranged from 0.682 in JavaScript to 0.972 in Python. Single-feature stepper AUROC was 0.728 for for-loop versus 0.757 for other updates, while frozen-threshold recall was 0.895 versus 0.624. Within Python, recall was 0.904 versus 0.750 on 23 and 30 positives. Implicit and structural walker cohorts largely differed in language, preventing an isolated implementation interpretation.

experiment_summary: Removal suppressed roles in 41/91, 72/109, and 131/187 target–task enrollments for Gemma 2 2B, Gemma 3 4B, and Gemma 3 12B. Only 2/91, 4/109, and 15/187 also passed tests; requiring both outputs to pass left 0, 3, and 13. Removal cohorts contained 32, 32, and 63 unique tasks. Joint change-and-passing rates exceeded matched random-control means by 1.3/1.4/3.7 percentage points for removal and 1.9/1.3/0.9 for addition; all six task-grouped 95% bootstrap intervals included zero. Ten same-layer random SAE features were used per target. Scales were not normalized across models and had unresolved historical provenance; enrollments repeat tasks across features.

The selected Gemma 2 representative additions had nonzero reference-conditioned sufficiency scores of only 0.10–0.19. Among pairs with two clean parses, stepper-associated range-call frequency increased by 20.3 percentage points in Gemma 2 2B across 59 pairs and 9.3 points in Gemma 3 4B across 54 pairs; gatherer-associated augmented assignment increased by 1.9 points across 107 pairs and 2.3 points across 44 pairs. Counts reuse tasks across features, addition combines reference-positive and reference-negative cohorts, and representative selection was not established to precede outcome inspection.
location: Section 5, Table 3; Appendix I; Appendix Q.1

experiment_summary: Ten of eleven completed cells selected zero from doses of 0%, 1%, 3%, and 10% of median calibration residual norm. The correctness constraint allowed no net loss of a passing calibration program. In Gemma 2 2B most-wanted holder, the selected 10% dose induced annotations on 3/5 probe and 4/5 SAE eligible test tasks, versus 1/5 random residual and 0/5 random SAE. Joint induction and passage was 1/5 for probe, SAE, and random residual, and 0/5 for random SAE. Overall test correctness was 4/12 for each target and 3/12 for each control. Llama walker was excluded after a failed zero-dose parity check.

Constrained Yes/No scoring used 9,553 matched development pairs, corresponding to 17,770 distinct role/variable queries. Gemma 3 27B had the highest eight-shot macro accuracy/AP at 72.1%/77.2%; Qwen3 14B reached 68.1%/72.6%. Eight-shot accuracy rose with tested size within each family, but Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B demonstration-gain accuracy intervals included zero and their AP did not improve. On a separate shared 1,100-case free-generation panel, Qwen3.5 9B produced only 6/1,100 valid zero-shot Yes/No beginnings despite 70.1% zero-shot AP under constrained scoring. Eight-shot answer validity was 97.6–100%, while 95.5–100% reached the generation cap.

With trained decoders fixed, 50 FISTA iterations improve ReLU coefficient recovery substantially when dictionary recovery is high. At 3,072 atoms and uniform selection, MCC increases from 0.833 to 0.975 and input R² from 0.659 to 0.885. Gains diminish with inaccurate dictionaries, and reconstruction does not improve in every configuration.

experiment_summary: Each method is trained for five epochs on one million observations per configuration with three seeds. ConSDL achieves generating-direction DCS approximately 0.92–1.00 and coefficient MCC 0.90–1.00 across all 16 configurations. At approximately 12K atoms and Zipf exponent 1.0, DCS is 0.92 and MCC 0.90, exceeding all six reported SAE baselines. Some easier settings have near-ties or a baseline advantage on individual metrics. These are finite empirical results without a new recovery theorem or matched-compute comparison.
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Tables 11–14 and 20; Appendices D.3 and E.1

experiment_summary: The four-by-four width/frequency sweep shows substantial baseline recovery failures across three training seeds. TopK, BatchTopK, Matryoshka, and iSAE use a reported search over sparsity settings. Under uniform selection, TopK generating-direction DCS falls from approximately 0.98 at 3K atoms to 0.18 at 12K atoms. At 3K atoms, increasing the Zipf exponent from 0 to 1 reduces ReLU DCS from approximately 0.98 to 0.33. These results do not establish unavoidable failure of the method families.

Adding refitting to sparse coding raises Pythia reconstruction R² from 0.69 to 0.92, removes approximately 9,767 dead atoms, and increases DCS from 0.29 to 0.84. CLIP R² rises from 0.87 to 0.92, although MCC changes from 0.72 to 0.70. Three seeds are used. Actual mean active counts are 113 versus 108 on Pythia and 116 versus 116 on CLIP.

Adding similarity regularization to refitted sparse coding reduces duplicated-atom counts from 5,564 to approximately 1 on CLIP and from 3,191 to 0 on Pythia, with no dead atoms in the full variants. DCS falls from 0.85 to 0.78 on CLIP and from 0.84 to 0.81 on Pythia. Regularization without refitting leaves approximately 8,652 dead Pythia atoms. Results establish complementary benefits within this tuned recipe rather than universal necessity or uniformly improved raw consistency.

Appendix E.2 reports that deduplication at cosine threshold 0.6 removes 41% of CLIP atoms and 29% of Pythia atoms from the unregularized refitted dictionaries, reducing DCS from 0.85 to 0.78 and from 0.84 to 0.79, respectively. Increasing the threshold removes fewer atoms and returns scores toward their original values. This is an analysis of geometric matching, without an external semantic-coverage measure.

At 16-fold expansion and target L0 approximately 128, ConSDL CLIP AUPRC is 0.52/0.55 for Top-1/Top-5, compared with MP-SAE 0.49/0.57. DINOv2 scores are 0.44/0.50 versus best baseline column means 0.45/0.54. Pythia AUROC is 0.73/0.78 and GPT-2 is 0.74/0.79, while some baselines reach 0.80 at Top-5. Vision means equally weight six datasets; language means cover all 113 tasks. Three seeds are used. Atom selection uses training-set normalized mean activation differences; Top-1 scores use absolute activation and Top-5 uses logistic regression on raw activations.

Median timings use 20 measured iterations after five warmups, with 4,096 Pythia activation tokens or 25,216 CLIP activation tokens per step. At 16-fold expansion and L0=128, Pythia per-token ConSDL training/inference costs are 10.45/8.22 microseconds versus ReLU 0.97/0.14; CLIP costs are 8.77/8.04 versus 0.76/0.14. Sparse coding accounts for approximately 69% of measured ConSDL training time on average. MP-SAE has higher high-sparsity inference cost but lower training cost under the reported timing recipes. These results are implementation-specific.
location: Section 7; Appendix C; Tables 4–5; Table 19 for accuracy-run iteration budgets

experiment_summary: Generated 2,072,000 narratives, totaling 1,000 stories per pole for each of 1,036 pairs across both generators, for approximately $500. Extracted all-layer residual directions from six model variants using story-token means after skipping 50 tokens. Subsequent classification, retrieval, and steering tests evaluate the dictionaries. Appendix B.2 incorrectly attributes the full 1,000-per-pole count to each generator; its generation grid implies 500 per generator.

Vectors using eight stories per pole achieved median held-out AUROC 0.81–0.93 but independent-direction cosine only 0.39–0.47. At 128 stories, AUROC was 0.985–0.997 and cosine 0.91–0.93. Disjoint 500-story-per-pole estimates reached median cosine 0.994–0.995. Learning curves used 25 held-out stories per pole and eight draws. Half-sample estimates retained premise-matched story pairs, whereas the learning curves sampled poles independently.

Across 1,036 pairs, mean raw-versus-paired cosine was 0.972–0.983, versus 0.897–0.923 for raw versus paired-assistant. The latter comparison changes model weights as well as formatting. Within instruction-tuned scaffolds, median format-agreement scores were 0.965, 0.962, and 0.944 for Qwen, Gemma, and Llama. Twenty-five pairs were among the most sensitive 5% in all three families; leading ten displacement PCs explained 71–75% of displacement energy.

Five text statistics predicted middle-layer directional agreement using five-fold out-of-fold ridge predictions, with Spearman correlations 0.674, 0.583, and 0.578 for Qwen, Llama, and Gemma. Sign-reversed word-frequency cosine alone achieved 0.649, 0.593, and 0.593, outperforming embedding-layer ridge predictors on this metric. Regularization was selected using the same out-of-fold criterion, so this is not a nested or prospective validation. Pole-name frequency was essentially uncorrelated with convergence.

Leave-one-group-out tests yielded median AUROC 0.997–0.999 for languages, 0.999–1.000 for genres, and 0.993–0.998 for generators. Matched-size comparisons used 150, 75, and 375 training stories per pole respectively and the same held-out quarter of the target group's stories; median AUROC differences were zero for languages and genres and at most 0.002 for generators. Generator-specific versus other-generator directions had median cosine 0.865–0.873.

Searched deterministic 128,000-item samples from each source, ranking up to 128 candidates per pair and pole using token-cosine tails maximized over middle layers. Across six model–dataset runs, 49.1–54.1% of 264,362–265,183 judged candidates contained a verified target-pole span. Every family covered 1,036/1,036 pairs across sources. Selecting each pair's better-covered source yielded at least 16 accepted examples for 1,025 Qwen, 1,026 Gemma, and 1,030 Llama pairs. No population precision, recall, or random-retrieval comparison is supplied.

Applied a residual offset at every generated response position, including special tokens, with greedy decoding capped at 768 tokens and matched unsteered answers. Separate 0–2 judgments measured target expression, topical relatedness, and fluency. Their per-response harmonic mean reached aggregate maxima of 1.24 for Qwen, 1.27 for Llama, and 1.18 for Gemma. Appendix D reports aggregate improvements relative to baseline, without a numerical per-pair success denominator. All 24 prompts per pair were evaluated; no separate development split selected per-feature operating points.

Compared final-input-token states before and after suffix addition, averaging states across prompts before computing concept cosines. Top shifts included encoded-request compliance and role-play disclosure for Qwen/Gemma, and preference-model gaming and proxy-objective contrasts for Llama. Attacks increased StrongREJECT-threshold ASR in all six model–dataset groups; AdvBench ASR rose to 56.9% for Qwen, 38.1% for Llama, and 9.8% for Gemma. These readout associations do not prove that the attacks implement the named behaviors internally.

Ranked directions at fixed intervention layers 29, 26, and 34 for Qwen, Llama, and Gemma. Added each selected unit direction separately at the final input token, scaled by the recipient state's norm. At +0.5, mean StrongREJECT across five directions on 520 AdvBench prompts fell from 0.527 to 0.079 for Qwen, 0.340 to 0.201 for Llama, and 0.101 to 0.091 for Gemma; three-direction random averages were 0.377, 0.332, and 0.103. On 100 JailbreakBench prompts, selected-direction means fell from 0.474 to 0.105, 0.371 to 0.192, and 0.119 to 0.103. On 100 benign Alpaca prompts with the selected direction sets, safety-refusal rates were zero for Llama/Gemma and 0.6% for Qwen at +0.5. This check measures refusal outcomes rather than answer correctness or broad capabilities.

Tracked 1,036 directions during edit–test episodes on a performance test described as unattainable by general summation in the sandbox and a task with contradictory specification/test requirements. Selected confirmation-bias-related readouts rose on test turns and fell on write turns in Qwen and Llama; fear-associated readouts rose in all three models. Plots align first test calls and omit turns reached by fewer than eight episodes. Readout positions and layers were chosen for the clearest contrast, and later-turn averages contain only surviving episodes.

Compared 571 correct and 127 incorrect traces, including 63 failures that never closed the thinking block or produced a final answer. Standardized token readouts separately by benchmark, divided traces into 50 relative-position intervals, and equally weighted benchmark means. Two displayed uncertainty contrasts showed a late confidence shift mainly in correct traces. A separate full-trace analysis ranked eight outcome gaps within a fixed inventory of 16 CoT features, rather than the whole dictionary: correct traces aligned more with reasoning disclosure and intermediate-result tracking, while incorrect traces aligned more with planning, slow thinking, and admission of not knowing.

Repeated the structure of Sofroniew et al.'s cited Tylenol check and added cough-syrup, ibuprofen, and step-count prompts. Measured final-prompt-token cosine readouts at layers 24, 21, and 28 for Qwen, Llama, and Gemma. Selected two directions by their average low-to-high drug change minus the step change. The source reports increasing drug curves with near-zero step and random-direction responses. Selection and evaluation use the same prompt families; this does not independently establish semantic specificity.

Constructed E(r) from extraction-forward-pass writes without fitting it to judged scores. Predicted versus judged peak layers were 19/19 for Qwen, 15/14 for Llama, and 23/22 for Gemma. Spearman correlations against expression averaged over both poles were 0.93, 0.91, and 0.96. Survival-only and amplification-only controls performed less consistently. These are aggregate comparisons without held-out-model validation or a formal derivation establishing the heuristic. Figure 38's token-norm wording differs from the assistant-token calibration described for the main steering protocol, limiting exact interpretation of the stated dose.

Compared finite-difference directional responses across principal axes, concept and shared-situation directions, marker-word directions, and random vectors. Across measured blocks 6–30, gain-versus-log-variance Spearman correlations were 0.79–0.88 except 0.59 at block 18. At block 10, concept median gain was −0.19 versus −0.34 for random directions. Middle-block concept gains differed by at most 0.004 from principal-axis gains at comparable variance. This intervention measures local block response, rather than whole-model semantic preservation.

Figures 5 and 6 compare month and year submatrices of M*, its matrix absolute value, and its positive and negative spectral components against temporal separation. Captions report agreement with periodized or open exponential kernels and describe variation across positions. No numerical goodness-of-fit statistic is supplied in the text.

Figures 1–3 and 8–12 compare PCA coordinates, Lissajous curves, Gram matrices, and state-level eigenmode maps with kernel predictions. Spectral embeddings are constructed from 2.72 billion Wikipedia tokens. Gemma-2-2B representations are final-prompt-token block outputs; EmbeddingGemma supplies normalized 768-dimensional state representations. Figure 9 additionally treats 365 calendar-date phrases as tokens. Text and captions report broad geometric agreement without numerical cross-model fit scores.

Formal derivation: Proposition 4 and Appendix E.5 express the optimal decoder as projection of coordinate functions onto retained Fourier modes, bound the omitted Fourier tail, and relate the retained frequency radius to rank by lattice-point counting. The resulting asymptotic upper-bound order is r^(-1/D); the result does not measure the held-out performance of a probe fitted from a small training subset.

For each retained PCA rank, 100 random splits are evaluated with ridgeless linear regression. Figure 2 reports trial means and standard deviations and describes an interpolation peak at r=n_train, with n_train=60. Appendix A.1.2 specifies that the scaling illustration concerns underparameterized training error. Figure 13 reports that choosing ridge regularization avoids the held-out peak. Numerical errors and an estimated scaling exponent are not given in the text.

The authors set P_ij=P_iP_j for all month pairs, making their M* block zero, and recompute spectral embeddings. Figure 4 reports retained circular ordering and a centered month Gram matrix resembling the original month statistics. No numerical preservation score is supplied for this main comparison.

Figure 4 uses ten selected seasonal helpers with the month–month block zeroed. Appendix C.1 compares number words one through seventeen, the top 100 seasonal words, and varying numbers H of seasonal or randomly sampled helpers. Captions report correct ordering with seasonal helpers and failure with number helpers. The text reports decreasing Procrustes reconstruction error with H and an approximately 1/sqrt(H) trend for seasonal helpers; numerical values and fitted-exponent uncertainty are unavailable.

experiment_summary: The calendar-year metric yields no clear regular linear relationship with estimated manifold distances, with recent-year separations described as expanded. Replacing year by log(2019−year) yields Chatterjee ξ=0.84 for cosine similarity versus squared metric distance and Pearson correlation 0.99 between estimated manifold distances and revised feature distances. No additional PCA is applied to the SAE-extracted representations.

Weighted graph distances are compared with circular calendar distance min(|x−y|,365−|x−y|), giving reported Pearson correlation 0.97. Cosine similarity is described as inconsistent with the proposed metric at large separations. The prose does not specify the retained PCA dimension or graph K for this test.

experiment_summary: Explanations for all latents of two 32,768-latent SAEs are scored on 100 activating and 100 non-activating sequences each. The mean detection score is 0.72, with reported quartile boundaries of approximately 0.62 and 0.80. Latents shared across more seeds generally score higher, but orphan latents include high-scoring cases. Table 1 deliberately selects illustrative pairs and does not estimate their prevalence.

Training-duration ablations show increasing shared-latent fractions and mean matched cosine similarities with additional training. Numerical duration endpoints and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the prose.

Architecture ablations compare GPT-2 SAEs using TopK, ReLU, and Gated designs. Standard ReLU and Gated SAEs trained with L1 have higher latent overlap; the abstract reports a sparsity-controlled ReLU-versus-TopK comparison. Exact numerical architecture results are unavailable in the supplied text rendering.

The layer sweep reports approximately constant overlap across middle layers and lower overlap in early layers and the final layer. At a common expansion factor of 36, MLP dictionaries have greater overlap than residual-stream dictionaries in SmolLM and GPT-2, but this ordering does not hold in Pythia. Exact configuration-specific values are unavailable in the supplied text rendering.

Most latents receive the same cosine value under Hungarian and maximum-cosine comparisons. The paper reports essentially unchanged sharing fractions at its chosen threshold, and width, active-count, and training-duration sweeps yield similar mean-similarity trends, with maximum-cosine means slightly higher.

Implemented across several SAE architectures, primarily on Gemma-2-2B layers 12 and 19 and a Llama 8B layer 16, with 500M OpenWebText training tokens. Evaluations cover reconstruction, automated explanation classification, sparse probing, and RAVEL. Appendix E compares isotropic and activation-covariance-based random initialization and shows substantial initialization dependence.

experiment_summary: At L0=160, soft-frozen versus fully trained BatchTopK RAVEL scores are 0.728 versus 0.720 at Gemma layer 12, 0.509 versus 0.512 at Gemma layer 19, and 0.519 versus 0.533 at Llama layer 16. JumpReLU values are 0.739 versus 0.722, 0.509 versus 0.511, and 0.521 versus 0.527. Fully frozen variants generally score lower, particularly at Gemma layer 12. Statistical equivalence is not demonstrated.

Formal derivation, not an empirical experiment: Appendix D identifies the attainable directions as a union of spherical caps, applies a union bound, and substitutes Tkocz's cited cap-probability inequality. For n=2304, m=73728, and τ=0.8, the source reports an upper bound of approximately 4.67×10^-316. This establishes exact fixed-target reachability under the stated assumptions, without establishing the stronger interpretation that useful approximate feature alignment or learning is excluded.

The reported JumpReLU run reaches explained variance 0.80 after 5% of training and 0.82 after 10%, versus a final value of 0.86. Decoder initialization cosines are described as remaining high. Figure 11's caption says they concentrate near 1.0, whereas the accompanying prose describes concentration near 0.8 at 10%; the supplied rendering does not resolve this discrepancy. No encoder-movement measurement is supplied.

experiment_summary: The four-backbone reconstruction–stability comparisons favor archetypal methods. For DINOv2 with 2,000 atoms and 90% sparsity, RA-SAE has stability 0.927 and reconstruction R² 89.34%, compared with TopK's 0.542 and 89.52%, and JumpReLU's 0.539 and 89.92%. The reported relaxation sweep improves reconstruction while retaining high stability; numerical curve values are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering.

RA-SAE obtains OOD score 0.060 versus TopK's 0.551 and negative interference 0.012 versus 135.7. Stable rank is 5.89 versus 141.6. These differences coexist with higher maximum pairwise coherence, 0.973 versus 0.728, so the reported structural metrics do not uniformly favor RA-SAE.

At 32,000 atoms and delta=1, RA-SAE versus TopK alignment is 0.5581 versus 0.1684 for ConvNeXt, 0.6213 versus 0.3125 for ResNet, and 0.5014 versus 0.2939 for ViT. The score averages each class-weight direction's best dictionary match and does not require one-to-one matching. These are descriptive table comparisons without reported uncertainty estimates.

Each dataset contains 2,000 training and 2,000 test images. Object scores select a coordinate and a threshold among empirical activation percentiles; the split used for this selection is not specified. Averaged across the twelve datasets, A-SAE accuracies are 0.9482, 0.9631, 0.9602, and 0.9615 for DINOv2, ResNet50, SigLIP, and ViT. RA-SAE scores are 0.9447, 0.9602, 0.9585, and 0.9586; TopK scores are 0.8135, 0.8150, 0.8289, and 0.8328. A-SAE and RA-SAE have the highest model-level averages among the reported methods, but A-SAE is not better than RA-SAE on every individual dataset.

Section 5.4 describes selected learned features and clusters, including a rabbit-class comparison with ordinary TopK features. Captions and prose report separate rabbit ears, body, face, and paws and other localized patterns. The supplied rendering lacks the figure images, preventing independent visual assessment. Suggested connections between shadow features and depth reasoning are speculative.

Formal result, Proposition F.1: row-stochasticity makes each dictionary row a convex combination; ZD=(ZW)A with ZW nonnegative establishes conic containment. Extreme-point coverage preserves the candidate convex hull. The proof's stronger displayed equality between the cone of an arbitrary fixed reconstruction and the entire data cone is not established and is excluded from this claim.

Formal result, Proposition F.2: a triangle-inequality decomposition, ||W||2≤sqrt(k), and ||W-W'||F≤2sqrt(k) yield the stated bound; reversing the decomposition gives the minimum over data norms. The derivation does not constrain how optimization selects W or W' and contains no empirical experiment.

Formal result, Proposition F.3: the supplied matrix-product rank inequality establishes the bound. Row-stochasticity defines the archetypal construction but is unnecessary for this inequality. The preceding column-space explanation is dimensionally misstated; the product-rank argument suffices.

Formal result, Proposition F.4: an observation in the positive-weight support has inner product W_ij with its mixture, while ||D_i||2=sqrt(sum_j W_ij²)≤1. Choosing the largest-weight active observation establishes OOD(D_i)≤1-max_j W_ij. Observations outside that support need not satisfy the displayed inner-product equality, but are unnecessary for the inequality. Some surrounding prose incorrectly calls the OOD bound a lower bound.

On 86,157 WildJailbreak prompts per model, CSFD selected 50 candidates. Ablation validated 47/50 in Gemma-2-2B, 42/50 in Qwen3-8B, 39/50 in Gemma-3-4B-IT, and 50/50 in each of Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.2-1B. Filtering pre-extracted statistics took under one minute for the two primary models; this excludes extraction and ablation costs. The filter starts from features recorded as active somewhere in the dataset.

experiment_summary: Clamping an individual feature to its original activation reinstated refusal in 27/182 Gemma-2-2B counterfactual prompts, or 14.8%. Per-feature reversal rates ranged from 0% to 30%. Suppressor reduction is also reported to restore refusal rarely, without corresponding aggregate counts.

CAP-component probe AUROC was 0.788 on Gemma-2-2B versus 0.668 for all 2,301 recorded raw features, 0.657 for the same 50 candidates’ raw activations, and 0.546 for DIM. Qwen3-8B scores were 0.719, 0.421, and 0.453 for CAP components, all raw features, and DIM. Additional CAP-component scores were 0.940 on Qwen3-1.7B and 0.771 on Llama-3.2-1B. The reported recipe uses L2-regularized logistic regression, five-fold cross-validation, and a 20% test split. Removing or permuting prompt-constant SC inputs left reported AUROC unchanged in three models; SC-only probes scored 0.500. A separate train-only SC estimate is reported to retain the advantage.

experiment_summary: Formal construction in Theorem 3.2 and Appendix A: two k-column subdictionaries span the same subspace, using standard basis vectors and invertible mixtures of two basis vectors. Their continuous coordinate maps give identical reconstructions and different supports whenever the reconstructed component in the modified plane is nonzero. This establishes the stated existential counterexample without requiring the stronger assertion that an arbitrary original encoder must disagree in support whenever its values differ.

Theorem 3.6 supplies an attempted formal derivation under A1–A6, but Lemma A.2 does not justify its central support map. The whole-batch projection bound requires all observations to be near one alternative subspace; the proof applies it to individual alternative supports when each observation is only known to be near its own support. Consequently, the subsequent dictionary and code bounds are not established by this derivation. The empirical experiments neither verify all assumptions nor resolve the gap.

Implemented with full GPT-2 fine-tuning on OpenWebText and rank-400 OLMo-7B LoRA on Dolma. Both reported runs reach sub-one-percent active attention fractions while remaining close to specified cross-entropy targets. Appendix C reports seven and fourteen training days, respectively, on a single H100. These implementations demonstrate feasibility without an optimization guarantee.

Separate 32-fold-expansion CLTs are trained on dense and sparse GPT-2, with reported replacement scores above 80%. Across ten pruned graphs, the sparse model requires on average 16.1-fold fewer key–query pairs and 3.4-fold fewer attention heads to reach 90% cumulative component attribution. The analysis measures conditional mediation compactness rather than unrestricted intervention fidelity.

The authors report that restricting attribution computations to active key–query pairs reduces per-graph analysis time from several hours to several minutes. Exact timings, repeated timing measurements, and a detailed matched-runtime protocol are not supplied.

Selected dense and sparse task heads overlap by approximately 40–50%. Across 300 OpenWebText sequences, nonzero sparse attention entries overlap the corresponding dense head's top-k entries by approximately 5–10%, versus 2–5% for randomly matched heads; k equals the sparse head's nonzero-entry count. Uncertainty estimates and the head-selection k values are not reported.

Five late-layer key–query pairs account for 80% of cumulative absolute component attribution on edges from the 'large' cluster to the 'small' logit, routing from position 5 to position 8 in parallel. Figure 5 describes more than forty heads in the dense comparison at the corresponding threshold. The sparse graph has replacement score 0.82 and 82 features after pruning from 459. Main-text feature analysis associates keys with magnitude/opposition information and queries with bracket-related features, but Figure 16's query labeling complicates that detailed assignment.

Table 2 reports sparse-model BOS attention fractions rounded to 0.00 in layers 5–11, compared with dense-model fractions ranging from 0.57 to 0.74 over those layers. experiment_summary: Computed tokenwise cosine similarities between attention-plus-MLP block contributions and averaged them across approximately 100,000 tokens. Adjacent similarities typically range from −0.3 to −0.15 in Llama 3, OLMo, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen2; the reported pattern is absent in GPT-2 and Phi. Non-adjacent updates are predominantly orthogonal or positively correlated. An empirical different-token baseline for Llama layers 4–19 has mean −0.00375 and standard deviation 0.03267, placing the −0.1 cutoff roughly three standard deviations below its mean. These comparisons establish geometric opposition rather than semantic correction or causality.

experiment_summary: Swept α from −1 to 1 in increments of 0.1 and measured cosine between the original preceding update and the following block's perturbed contribution. Increasing α generally increases opposition approximately linearly; removing the prior contribution can produce positive alignment, especially in early layers. Figures show five sampled curves across layers, without an aggregate effect estimate. The interventions establish direct responsiveness to this perturbation, while extreme settings create counterfactual states and compensatory responses may involve other self-repair mechanisms.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation in Appendix B uses the quadratic-form identity and the spectral theorem to express first-order directional response as a sum of symmetric-Jacobian eigenvalues weighted by squared perturbation projections. A strictly negative or positive first-order quadratic form determines the corresponding sign for sufficiently small perturbations along that direction. For a symmetric-Jacobian eigenvector v, vᵀJv=λ||v||². Thus λ=−1 cancels the perturbation's own-direction component after residual addition, but does not imply Jv=−v: perpendicular components can remain. Near-zero eigenvalues likewise do not establish an unchanged full response. The paper inconsistently calls b a full layer and a contribution; the stated correction interpretation requires the contribution Jacobian.

Computed symmetric-Jacobian eigenpairs and selected fifty directions by largest squared projection of the preceding update; the text reports that these directions account for 15% or more of its projection mass. TLCM pairs show eigenvalue modes near −1 and +0.5, while non-TLCM pairs peak near zero. Approximately 3,000 of 4,096 eigenvalues are reported negative. A separate check on 46 randomly selected TLCM Jacobians reports approximately 5% relative linearization error for small nonzero |α|<0.1 along prior-update perturbations. Pair-selection details are limited, and the results do not establish complete vector erasure at λ=−1 or negligible full response near λ=0.
location: Section 5.2; Figure 4; Appendix D, Figure A4

experiment_summary: Constructs probe-targeted graphs for toxicity, sentiment, reasoning/recall, and truthfulness across layers in two models; reports approximately 10,400 Gemma graphs from 100 prompts per concept. Appendix A.4 describes pruning thresholds using final-logit terminology despite CTA's changed target.

Gradient boosting with 200 estimators and depth three achieves Gemma raw-target Spearman ρ=0.905 and R²=0.835, compared with layer-baseline ρ=0.083 and R²=−0.197; demeaned-target scores are 0.925 and 0.850. A separate bootstrap/permutation table reports observed raw ρ=0.890, 95% CI [0.724, 0.964], and p<0.005 from 200 shuffles. Llama raw-target scores are ρ=0.808 and R²=0.850; its separate bootstrap table reports observed ρ=0.780 and CI [0.368, 0.955]. Llama's demeaned correlation is 0.34 with CI [−0.055, 0.743]. These are supervised accuracy predictors, and grouping by concept–layer does not hold out entire concepts or neighboring depths.

experiment_summary: The paper pools selected predictor-feature presence across the 100-prompt CTA sets and compares it with expected random-feature presence. It reports approximately 6–21-fold enrichment across the two selected target layers, with 8–21-fold enrichment at highest-accuracy layers. This provides descriptive evidence of selected-feature recurrence rather than independent recovery of a canonical causal mechanism. The analysis does not rerun the cited multi-circuit study's test.

Figure 6 is described as showing consecutive-layer Jaccard for one representative prompt per concept. The accompanying text reports stabilization near J=0.9 around layers 8–12 and persistence into later layers. A population-wide overlap distribution with uncertainty is not supplied, and high adjacent-layer overlap also enters the appendix's belief-layer selection criterion.

Appendix B.5 reports mean per-prompt Jaccard across truthfulness/reasoning target-layer pairs. Elevated overlap occurs when both layers are early or both late, but reported peak values remain below 0.07. Mean shared-feature counts remain below approximately 40, while reasoning-exclusive and truthfulness-exclusive counts reach roughly 460 and 250 respectively at final layers. These values are stated in the prose; no unseen heatmap values are inferred, and uncertainty estimates are absent.

Formal derivation: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds a fixed unit direction's inner product with the mean unit readout. Expanding the squared mean norm gives the exact finite-sample pairwise-cosine identity. For independent population draws, pairwise coherence equals the squared norm of the population mean. The normalized mean attains the bound when nonzero; Jensen's inequality supplies the label-average bound.

Formal induction over order and layer: order n−1 supplies exact prefix states through its first n−1 layers, enabling order n to compute the original attention and state through its first n layers. Consequently orders at least L−ell reproduce the complete remaining computation, including its local derivatives wherever defined.

Evaluated 7,961 substitution pairs per layer. Layer-average rank correlations with measured output change are 0.94/0.95 for LexFrame[1], versus at most 0.28 across cosine, Euclidean, principal-subspace, Mahalanobis, geodesic, logit-lens, and Jacobian-lens distances. Projection analyses use 64 leading principal directions and local neighborhoods of 128 states; the text reports little native-readout squared norm in these leading variation directions, without supplying numerical plotted values.

Formal construction and algebraic derivation: the readout is J-transpose times the centered unembedding row, while the writing vector is J+ times s_v. Appendix C.1 gives the canonical-dual identity sum_v s_v w_v-transpose = I under full column rank of W, and the transported uncentered frame identity sum_v s_ell(v)(J-transpose w_v)-transpose = J+J. Without ridge, J+J projects onto the row space of J; regularization changes this projection identity.

experiment_summary: The reported correlation between native-readout/state inner products and centered logits is 0.10 in SmolLM3 and 0.02 in OLMo3. The associated decomposition panel evaluates transported and untransported coefficient readings on 512 positions, finding LexFrame[1] KL 0.16/0.15 nats while layer-state and fixed-map readings remain several nats away even at their best scale. Appendix C.1 identifies the gradient/state pairing as the derivative of the centered logit under state rescaling, rather than its coefficient value.

Composition tests use 64 states per layer, 64 labels, explicit float32 Jacobians, and moves of 0.1 state norm: native-basis edits make the target logit gain most in 0.98/1.00 of cases, versus 0.56/0.79 for native readouts. Runner-up steering searches steps from 0.01 to 1 state norm. LexFrame[1] basis clean-flip rates are 0.71/0.82 versus 0.61/0.64 for its readout, requiring other-token change below 0.1 nats. Native-basis clean-flip rates are 0.73/0.85. Mean other-token change at the first successful flip is 0.11/0.06 nats for the native basis versus 0.22/0.19 for native readouts. Steering basis computation uses 30 LSMR steps with Jacobian products.

On 64 test sequences, completed the actual downstream pass after each write removal. Layer-average correlations for LexFrame[1] coefficient differences are 0.88/0.90 for whole layers, 0.79/0.85 for attention, and 0.88/0.90 for MLPs. Native-Jacobian linear attribution reaches 0.62/0.68, 0.75/0.84, and 0.63/0.71 respectively. Evaluated lens-based coefficient-difference attributions reach at most 0.20. These results support an advantage over the tested first-order estimator, not over untested corrected attribution methods such as AtP*.

Replacing ridge predictions by mean attention increases layer-average KL from 0.16/0.15 to 1.26/0.52 nats; zero replacement gives 0.76/0.47. Readout cosine decreases from 0.89/0.87 to 0.73/0.74 for mean and 0.71/0.74 for zero. Layer-attribution correlation decreases from 0.88/0.90 to 0.67/0.77 and 0.68/0.77 respectively. Three disjoint calibration texts produce KL ranges 0.160–0.163 and 0.146–0.151 nats.
