experiment_summary: Formal result supplied in Appendix A: the Gaussian case follows from the conditional distribution of a bivariate normal. The bounded-noise case follows by expanding the Gaussian density inside the conditional-expectation integrals as the centered noise support shrinks. No empirical models, sample sizes, or reward measurements are involved.

Conditional algebraic derivation supplied in Section 4.3: summing k gains of (d/k)[α − β log(d/k)] gives d[α − β log d + β log k]. This establishes the formula under the stated assumptions without testing iterative RLHF, coefficient stationarity, distance additivity, or the law at very small distances.

Sections 2.1–2.2 give the exact algebraic decomposition hAB = sum_i (hA[:,i])B[i,:] for the replacement, establishing local addressability. Experiments fit and intervene on these units in selected GPT-2 and Qwen projections; GPT-2 also receives all-48-matrix replacement. Fitting uses an approximate alternating ADMM procedure, without a global optimization or uniqueness guarantee.

experiment_summary: Whole-MLP SWD factors both c_fc and c_proj while preserving GELU. Its primary checkpoint has CE delta 0.004003, compared with 0.003456 for TC24k and 0.003522 for reconstruction-VPD. Appendix E explicitly reports more mixed circuit results than for single-matrix replacement: competitive SWD edge costs and often fewer edges for necessity, with standard Transcoders competitive in several sufficiency and selected-unit comparisons. No universal frontier dominance is established.

Factorization uses 4.19M calibration tokens and initially yields held-out CE 3.90. Fixed-support training consumes 16.38M additional token presentations, drawn from 4.19M unique training tokens, and reduces CE to 3.44 without changing 26,770,800 body nonzeros. Separately sparse-pretrained references reach CE about 3.45 after 2.884B presentations with 26,770,920 body nonzeros. Circuit results are broadly comparable on Greater-than and pronouns, while sparse pretraining has near-zero or negative necessity drops on IOI and docstring. Candidate surfaces differ: sparse pretraining prunes only post-GELU MLP channels. The models also differ in GELU implementation, and the body budget excludes embeddings, biases, normalization, and the LM head.

experiment_summary: Holding factor dimensions, solver, and budget schedule fixed, the study replaces the calibration Gram matrix with identity. Calibrated SWD achieves lower held-out CE under aggressive sparsification. This compares parameter reconstruction with predictive performance rather than independently validating mechanistic preservation.

All edits start from the original dense layer-8 c_proj. Unit c205 was selected after screening eight prompt–answer–foil triples and candidate units; its source factorization used 131,072 WikiText-2 calibration tokens. At requested local shift 3, the realized down-versus-left margin increases by 0.215797, with mean final-token KL 4.02375e-5 on seven non-target prompts and mean KL 1.96415e-5 on 504 tokens. Its reported efficacy–locality tradeoff improves over one random-unit control and the tested rank-4 LoRA recipe, while a target-activation-conditioned dense rank-one oracle performs best. The requested local projection shift is not the realized final-model margin change.

For all 768 c_proj units on 2,048 held-out tokens, the 95th-percentile absolute complete-contribution correlation is 0.0049, with an exceptional pair reaching 0.345. For 128 high-energy c_fc units selected from 1,536 candidates and evaluated on 8,192 tokens, all 8,128 unordered pairs receive contextual GELU finite-difference measurements projected through the original output matrix. Normalized interaction ratios have mean 0.093, median 0.089, and maximum 0.221; 2,130 of 8,128 pairs reach at least 0.10. The c_fc inputs come from a sequentially reconstructed model. Low contribution correlation does not establish downstream functional independence.

Greater-than attribution ranks 9,208 valid all-layer c_proj units. The six displayed units fall within the global top-512 prefix. GPT-5.5 assigns tentative labels from each unit's 20 largest-magnitude activation contexts among 2,048 task-independent WikiText-2 tokens. Four displayed units receive quantitative hypotheses; the remaining two receive punctuation/function and species/name hypotheses. Labels were not used for circuit selection, but their semantic accuracy and causal specificity were not independently evaluated.

Selected 4,812 features with wait, hmm, but, or alternatively among their ten most promoted tokens and 811 features with at least 80% of maximal examples at one checked chat-template position. Removing output features reduces wait frequency from 5.5 to 1.5; removing both groups reduces it to 0.5 and mean response length from 7.8k to 3.5k tokens. Adding template or output groups alone to the hybrid gives rates of 0.2 and 1.5, while adding both gives 8.2. Modifying 50,000 random features has smaller reported effects. Specific finding: Removing selected hesitation-output and template adapter features can more than halve reasoning-response lengths while preserving reported accuracy on some benchmarks and reducing it on others. Ablated the 5,623 selected features and evaluated long rollouts. Response lengths drop by more than 50%, including AMC23 from 7.2k to 3.2k tokens. Reported accuracy is unchanged on MATH500, AMC23, and GPQA Diamond; AIME25 accuracy falls from 26% to 20%. Benchmark question/repetition counts are 500×1, 40×10, 198×3, and 30×10 respectively. Added negative selected-feature contributions to the original target and reevaluated the four reasoning benchmarks. The authors report shorter responses and a slight accuracy decrease, with somewhat greater accuracy costs than adapter ablation. Scaling by −1 produces incoherent outputs, prompting use of −0.5. Exact target-intervention accuracy and length values are not tabulated in the supplied text. Distribution shift in encoder inputs is offered as a hypothesis for full-strength failure.

Constructed a relevance-propagation graph for a Wait prediction following a correct answer after approximately 1,100 reasoning tokens. Major contributors are hesitation-output features with few incoming adapter-feature dependencies, template features, and token-embedding paths mediated by retained base computation. Earlier hesitation-token embeddings also contribute. The displayed analysis reports no meaningful attribution from the proposed answer token or verification-associated adapter features. Additional examples are described without a systematic denominator; induction and repurposing of base representations are interpretations of these paths.

experiment_summary: The source supplies an attempted formal proof, rather than an empirical test. Theorem 4.2's intersection argument is conditional on Theorem 4.1. Appendix B.2 asserts that restricting two injective maps to preimages of the common pushforward support gives matching images, which need not follow from equal pushforward measures. Continuity and full support do not by themselves justify this assertion. The general guarantee is therefore not fully established by the supplied proof.

The paper attempts a population reformulation of Aharon et al.'s cited dictionary-uniqueness result. Claims 5.1–5.2 invoke sparse injectivity, a sparsity-preserving linear-map argument, and the intersection theorem. Appendix C.2 asserts, without establishing it, that sparse-domain almost-everywhere equality induces a global invertible linear transition. This attempted derivation is not credited as a completed proof of the full claim.

The paper attempts an adaptation of Comon's ICA result using unit-covariance orthogonality and the cited Darmois theorem. Its proof incorrectly assumes every orthogonal matrix that is not a permutation mixes multiple coordinates. Diagonal sign flips violate that step and preserve independence, unit variance, non-Gaussianity, and equivalence to Lebesgue measure. The supplied argument does not establish the printed claim.

Formal proof in Claim B.1: convolution multiplies characteristic functions, the nowhere-zero noise factor can be cancelled, and uniqueness of characteristic functions identifies the original distribution. The proof supplies a stochastic measure-separating base kernel without empirical experiments.

Conditional formal application in Appendix E, Claim E.1: assuming the finite-mixture measure-separation property explicitly imported from Yakowitz and Spragins, the fixed finite latent space permits only bijective injective transitions, hence label permutations. Appendix B.2.2 explains the reduction to finite-support linear independence but cites its substantive Gaussian-family proof. The evidence credited here is the conditional framework derivation, not a new proof of that imported result.

experiment_summary:
Study 1 numerically compares radial-basis and cosine kernel geometries on two-dimensional Gaussian datasets, reporting high correspondence for one dataset despite different feature maps. Studies 2–4 train VGG-16 classifiers on diagnostic pixels or patches and compare their RDMs with ordinary networks or previously recorded IT responses. Cue-dependent classifiers can attain correspondence comparable to ordinary-network baselines despite chance-level classification after cue removal. These are numerical and controlled training demonstrations, not a formal identification theorem; Study 1's printed RBF formula contains an apparent exponent-sign error.
Specific finding: A CIFAR-10 VGG-16 classifier dependent on category-diagnostic pixels can approach the RSA ceiling of an ordinary classifier when pixel-location distances are fitted to the ordinary classifier's category geometry. Study 2 constructs a target 10×10 category RDM using 100 sampled CIFAR-10 test images per category. Pixel placements are optimized for positive, near-zero, or negative correlation with that target, with ten configurations per condition. ImageNet-pretrained VGG-16 networks are fine-tuned for ten epochs. On modified inputs, the positive condition approaches the reported RSA ceiling, while other arrangements yield lower RSA; all cue-trained conditions classify modified images perfectly but perform around chance without the cue. Evaluation RDMs contain five selected images per category and use 1−Pearson dissimilarity followed by Spearman correlation.
Specific finding: A VGG-16 classifier trained to depend on category-diagnostic patches can match the macaque IT RSA correspondence of an ImageNet-pretrained classifier fine-tuned on unmodified images. Study 3 trains randomly initialized VGG-16 networks on images containing category-specific 5×5 white patches with locations positively correlated, uncorrelated, or negatively correlated with the macaque category RDM. Positively arranged patches yield RSA matching the ordinary-network baseline; other arrangements yield significantly lower RSA. Patch-trained networks perform around chance without patches. The reported training/test counts are 2,432/768, inconsistent with the stated 75%/25% split. Main RSA uses the entire 3,200-image dataset aggregated to category RDMs, so it is not an independent held-out correspondence test. Similar full-image-RDM results are reported in an unavailable supplement.
Specific finding: Category-diagnostic pixels arranged according to a stimulus hierarchy can produce human IT RSA correspondence comparable to that of an ordinary image classifier without optimizing their locations against the human RDM. Study 4 trains VGG-16 classifiers on 818 images with hierarchically or randomly placed diagnostic pixels and evaluates on 92 images. Cue-trained networks start from random initialization; the ordinary baseline is ImageNet-pretrained. Hierarchical placements, averaged over five configurations, yield correspondence with an existing human IT RDM matching the ordinary-network baseline, whereas random placements yield significantly lower correspondence. Cue-trained classifiers perform nearly perfectly with pixels but around chance without them. Numerical RSA coefficients and detailed statistical results are not supplied in the main text.

Formal result produced here: Appendix D.1 uses a Taylor bound on softplus to obtain the cross-entropy limit with O(scale) error and the identity softplus(z)=max(z,0)+log(1+exp(-|z|)) to obtain the positive-deficit limit with O(1/scale) error. These are analytic loss properties, with no experimental models or measurements. Displayed Taylor-remainder and factor inconsistencies do not invalidate the stated asymptotic limits.

Formal derivation produced here: differentiating the softplus objective yields gradient -2 sigmoid(beta_t Delta_t) times the gradient of log current token probability, with Delta_t equal to reference minus current log probability. At reference initialization Delta_t=0, so the multiplier of the cross-entropy gradient is exactly one. No empirical test is required for this identity.

Formal result produced here: Theorem 3 establishes nonnegativity and attainability of zero at the reference parameters. Under full conditional vocabulary support, zero expected positive deficit implies current probability is at least reference probability for every token at relevant contexts; normalization forces equality. This concerns the limiting positive-deficit loss, not a finite-coefficient optimization guarantee, and does not establish that the experimental demonstration datasets satisfy the support assumption.

experiment_summary: RSS reconstructs held-out logit changes with R²=0.579 [0.532,0.621] for Gemma and 0.627 [0.568,0.675] for Llama. Clean-value restoration reverses 72.2% [63.5,80.3] and 71.8% [61.0,80.7] of transformed probe errors, respectively. Size-matched mismatched-setting supports achieve R²=0.438/0.490 and reversal fractions 60.3%/61.1%; global-instability and random supports have R² around 0.01–0.02. These are effects inside a known linear classifier, not demonstrations of model-level safety repair.

At 20% review, RSS residual margin captures 89.2% [81.8,93.5] of Gemma errors and 92.8% [88.0,95.6] of Llama errors; harmful false-negative capture is 87.3% [72.4,94.9] and 94.4% [89.1,97.4]. Full residual-margin capture is 94.1%/91.9% for errors and 90.9%/93.5% for harmful false negatives. Known labels are required to compute signed margins. The point estimates do not establish superior Llama capture over the full readout, and the experiment does not establish an unlabeled deployment-review policy.

Formal result: Theorem 1 and Appendix B.1 bound population excess risk by twice the uniform empirical-risk error plus optimization error. Positive feature-risk separation forces convergence to each population feature orbit; the triangle inequality gives encoder and decoder permutation distances between estimators converging to zero in probability. The argument assumes uniform convergence, vanishing empirical optimization error, and separated identifiable population features. These assumptions are not tested in the language-model experiments.

Formal conditional assignment-stability argument: Corollary 1 and Appendix B.2 state that sufficiently small perturbations preserve a unique positive-margin assignment, so both encoder and decoder assignments select the permutation aligning the runs' shared feature labels. Appendix B.2 presupposes convergence under a common labeling rather than deriving it from the separate distances proved in B.1; the claim is therefore restricted to that explicit premise. No empirical assignment margins or finite-sample bounds are supplied.

Specific finding: COCONUT chains on structured logical tasks can have almost unchanged predictions after deletion, while ProsQA answer information is already readable before latent-slot computation begins. On 300 problems per task, each main COCONUT logical-task cell changed at most three predictions after deleting all six slots. These results do not establish that the chain is unused in the intact computation or that the full answer algorithm has been localized.

Formal derivation: realizability makes the optimal expected KL zero. Class log-probability ratios impose linear inner-product identities, and Lemma 8.3 constructs a rank-n′ visible linear map and orthogonal residual. With a centered learned readout, that residual lies in its nullspace. This supports the conditional formulation stated here; centering of the learned readout is not forced by optimality alone.

Formal derivation under the stated kernel-separation condition: local perturbations require pointwise encoder stationarity. Restricting to the kernel yields an exponential-sum identity. Pairwise distinct exponents force identical readout rows and uniform predictions, which admit a strict loss-decreasing direction. The proof does not fully establish its broader advertised genericity conclusion over all optimized bottlenecks.

Formal proof: exact capacity removes the null residual, and non-negative latent support forces an entrywise non-negative invertible map A. Expected activation energy equals 2C plus non-negative within-row cross terms. A diagonal map attains 2C. Equality forces at most one nonzero per row, and invertibility then forces a positive scaled permutation.

Formal derivation: the rank-n′ visible map satisfies UA = W*. Full column rank of the teacher readout and equality of ranks establish ker(A) = ker(A*), equivalently A = BA* for a left-invertible B. This transfers nullspace-dependent sparse-recovery properties; it does not identify an unknown dictionary from observations.

Formal corollary: because the null-space property depends only on the kernel, equality of learned and teacher measurement kernels transfers that property. Combining this observation with the standard NSP characterization gives the Basis Pursuit guarantee. The experimental dimension bound 2k ≤ n′ does not by itself establish NSP.

Per-token Spearman correlations between predicted per-expert probabilities and router probabilities, averaged over tokens, were 0.258, 0.809, 0.741, 0.413, and 0.817 across the five layers. experiment_summary: Logistic regressions predict unstable-set membership from decoder vectors, with within-seed and transferred F1 reported as close. As the seed count used to estimate recurrence increases, scores saturate near 0.73 at cutoff zero and 0.67 at cutoff 0.1. Exact classifier split sizes and corresponding baseline F1 are not specified.

Form vectors by adding the selected unstable reconstruction contribution back to the SAE residual, cluster them with k-means using the known low-rank atom count, and replace unstable decoder rows with centroids. The text reports improved cosine alignment with low-rank ground truth and little change to the generic block. Freezing the replacement rows and retraining the encoder did not improve EV. Recovery relies on the toy selection conditions and accurate recovery of the other contributions.

Greedily deduplicate source decoder vectors at cosine 0.7, estimate recurrence within each source subset, select the 16,384 highest-recurrence features, and tune for approximately two million tokens. Comparisons include pools from 4, 10, and 96 SAEs. High-recurrence construction becomes dominated by stable features and reaches near-baseline EV; least-probable selection reconstructs substantially worse. The text and caption differ on how closely uniform selection matches baseline EV. Some selected directions shift toward lower recurrence during tuning.

experiment_summary: Sparse Probing Top-1 changes from 0.656 to 0.673 and mean AutoInterp from 0.818 to 0.850. SCR Top-20 changes from 0.269 to 0.258 and TPP Top-20 from 0.107 to 0.090. Repeat SAE training on randomly initialized GPT-2 activations. Across a range of matching thresholds, the random-model stable fraction collapses and instability dominates, while high automated detection scores remain achievable. Numerical detection distributions and the number of independently randomized transformer realizations are not specified in the supplied prose.

Formal derivation in Appendix A.1: conditional on selecting cluster X_l, the escape probability is W(X_l, complement(X_l))/vol(X_l). Averaging uniformly over the k clusters gives n-cut/k. The authors explicitly acknowledge a similar argument in Meilă and Shi (2001). No empirical experiment is involved.

Ten networks per dataset and dropout condition were compared with 320 shuffles each. No network in any of the four conditions was reported significantly clusterable in the two-cluster analysis. At seven clusters, all ten networks in every condition beat all 320 shuffles; four- and ten-cluster results were also mostly or entirely above that all-shuffle threshold. The conclusion concerns the tested cluster counts, not every intermediate or larger count.

On 60,000 random images with random labels, training accuracy remained approximately 10%, and 0/10 networks in each dropout condition beat all 50 shuffles. The prolonged-training experiment likewise reports no excess clusterability. In the 3,000-example memorization setup, all ten no-dropout networks reached 100% training accuracy and beat all 50 shuffles. With dropout, 6/10 beat all shuffles while mean training accuracy was 21.3%. The prolonged experiment is described as removing pruning, although Table A.17 also reports pruned-network statistics.

Five runs per condition show that unpruned small CNNs with L2 regularization beat all 50 shuffles in 5/5 runs on each dataset, while every pruned ordinary small-CNN condition has 0/5 such runs. For CIFAR-10 VGGs, pruning with dropout produces 5/5 networks beating all shuffles, and pruning with dropout plus L2 produces 4/5; other pruned VGG conditions produce 0/5. Absolute cut reductions therefore do not uniformly imply relative-clusterability improvements.

experiment_summary: Across five runs per condition, every MLP halves-diff condition has 5/5 networks beating all 50 shuffles, versus 2/5–4/5 for halves-same. Absolute cuts are lower for MNIST halves-diff but higher for Fashion halves-diff. Small-CNN stack-diff cuts are lower than stack-same cuts, but only 1/5 MNIST and 3/5 Fashion unpruned stack-diff networks beat all shuffles; all pruned stack conditions have 0/5. experiment_summary: Ten runs per condition show unpruned cuts falling from 10.020 to 8.93, with test accuracy changing from 95.7% to 95.9%, but only 1/10 regularized networks beating all 50 shuffles versus 2/10 controls. The regularized unpruned mean cut exceeds its shuffle mean of 8.14. With pruning, cuts fall from 7.11 to 5.51 and the all-shuffle count rises from 4/10 to 7/10, while test accuracy falls from 93.4% to 89.6%. These results do not establish uniformly improved relative clusterability with negligible accuracy cost.

Formal result: Proposition 1 and Appendix D apply the second-order chain rule and identify the softmax cross-entropy Hessian as diag(p) − ppᵀ. This establishes the decomposition and positive semidefiniteness of its Gauss–Newton term. It does not establish that this term dominates, that sharp directions reverse behavior, or that spectra differ across coefficients only by α². For a general population expectation, additional differentiation-under-expectation conditions are needed; smoothness and the source's assertion of bounded loss alone do not establish them.

Formal result: Proposition 2 and Appendix E prove the projection identities, bound local loss change by ||P_S g||sqrt(ε)||v|| + 0.5||H||₂ε||v||² plus a cubic displacement remainder, and bound the cleaned vector's absolute normalized quadratic form by the retained spectral radius. These results concern a fixed local Hessian and nonzero cleaned vector. They do not guarantee a realized reduction by the largest-to-retained eigenvalue ratio, particularly when signed eigenvalue contributions cancel, or bound autoregressive generation.

Using 12 estimation prompts and 40 Lanczos iterations per condition, the paper reports spectral ratios of 50–3,727 across three models, four tasks, and three layers per model–task pair. Reported largest-to-sixteenth absolute eigenvalue ratios range from 1.7 to 12.3, with median 4.0. These latter ratios are spectral-gap statistics, not measured reductions in each CAA vector's realized directional curvature. An iteration sweep on Qwen refusal shows that estimated condition numbers change as additional small eigenvalues are discovered.
location: Section 5.2, Table 1; Appendix F, Table 2; Appendix J

experiment_summary: PCA on 2,000 WikiText-2 forward passes is compared with the top-15 Hessian subspace. Their mean principal-angle cosine is 0.077. Removing the PCA projection gives a reported token margin of −0.021, compared with +0.006 after Hessian sharp removal. Uncertainty estimates and broader matched PCA comparisons are absent.

Regrading the Mistral refusal evaluation with GPT-4o-mini changes baseline refusal from 12% under the heuristic to 52% full refusal under the judge. Judge-rated full refusal is 68% for CAA and 88% after sharp removal; full compliance is 46%, 28%, and 4% for baseline, CAA, and cleaning respectively. The authors report manual inspection confirming missed refusals without the keyword matcher's preferred phrases, but provide no systematic human agreement study.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: Theorem 3.1 proves the exact noiseless joint law by Gaussian conditioning, adapting identities explicitly attributed to prior sparse superposition coding work. Proposition 3.2 and Appendix B.2 derive an exact one-gate chi-square mixture for canonical readouts. These are distributional results, not empirical measurements.

Formal results: Theorems 4.1–4.2 and Appendix C prove E[X]→0 above a fixed multiplicative excess over the canonical ball price and divergence below it. Optimization is a second-order cone program; below its optimized price, every gate-local rule has diverging expected errors. Proofs use Gaussian tails, chi-square concentration, and local Gram-matrix bounds without independence between gate errors.

Formal results: Theorem 5.1 reduces reliability for general families to class Gaussian suprema under fixed representations and d/k→∞. Lemma B.2 supplies an exact rearrangement identity for universal families. Theorem 5.4 and Appendix D use extreme order statistics to prove the box threshold and a simultaneous converse over common representations, without the additional d/k restriction.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: Corollary 5.5 compares box and ball support functions by Cauchy–Schwarz, and Corollary 6.2 computes the conjunction threshold ratios. Appendix I additionally proves that inside the midpoint window, for finite limiting beta≥1, the number of inactive features causing at least one error has a mixed-Poisson limit with infinite-mean intensity. This count is distinguished from the full gate-error count X.
location: Corollaries 5.5 and 6.2; Appendix I; Section M.6

experiment_summary: Formal result: Proposition 5.3 and Appendix D.2 analyze max_i(Z_i+max_{j in C(i)}W_j) using Gaussian tail bounds and a variational exponent. They prove concentration at the stated first-order levels and convergence of expectations. The result requires disjoint partner sets and does not establish a formula for arbitrary sharing hypergraphs.

Formal results: Proposition B.3 proves equal-weight optimality by permutation averaging. Theorem 6.1 and Appendix E.1 show that only classes with t−1 and t active inputs can bind and derive midpoint and optimized thresholds. For pairwise conjunction in the skewed regime, midpoint count/reliability and optimized count/reliability constants are 16/8/4/2 in units of k log m. Appendix K numerically checks the programs for r≤4 and five beta values.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: Corollary 6.3 specializes the threshold-gate result to feature recovery and conjunction and computes the ratio. At m=k⁴, the first-order dimensions are 18k log k for recovery and 50k log k for direct pairwise conjunction. Comparisons with Lasso and L1 minimization use cited prior results, not experiments or recovery proofs produced here.

Formal result: Theorem 7.1 and Appendix F derive the midpoint profile Psi_beta(x)=P(G_A+G_B/beta≤x) and optimized profile sup_y Psi_beta(y)F_+(x−y), where F_+ is the distribution function of −log[omega_1(omega_1+omega_2)] for independent unit exponentials. The quantile-based half-slack bias gives Psi_beta(x/2)F_+(x/2). The optimized dimension window is narrower by 4(1+beta)/(3+beta). Corollary M.3 derives asymptotic target-success sizing rules.

Campaign E3 midpoint AND2 center success frequencies at k=1024,m=k⁴,k¹⁶,k⁶⁴ are 0.295,0.324,0.340 versus profile values 0.298,0.326,0.346. Campaign E1 at m=k⁴ and 1.35 times the optimized quantile center reports 3984/4096,3912/4096,2/4096 successes for half-slack, count-optimal, and midpoint biases on shared draws. In E2 at k=1024,m=k⁴, the four gate types have half-slack success rates at most 3.8% at ratio 0.9 and 82.7%–97.9% at ratio 1.2. At m=k⁶⁴ and 1.5 times the midpoint center, all 4096 E3 draws succeed while separate exact-law quadrature estimates E[X]=2.76×10¹⁹. Wilson intervals are pointwise; zero observed failures does not establish zero failure probability. Appendix K compares reduced sampling with direct dictionary simulations.

experiment_summary: Formal result: Proposition 8.1 and Appendix H.1 prove the upper bound through simultaneous norm and coherence bounds. The lower construction selects k−1 dictionary columns aligned with a fixed pairwise probe and includes one of its queried features. This support depends on the realized dictionary.

Formal result: Theorem 8.2 and Appendix H.2 use independent coordinate-row cumulants, exponential tilting, and a Berry–Esseen bound. They derive log q=−d/(16k)(1+o(1)), an expected-count sufficient width of (16+epsilon)k log(km), and entry-law-dependent second-order corrections. A separate sparse-entry extension requires qk→∞ for entry nonzero probability q. No non-Gaussian reliability experiment is reported.

Formal result: Theorem H.5 bounds wrong reads of an ideal execution and applies a union bound; induction transfers ideal-read correctness to actual execution without conditioning on earlier success. Proposition H.4 separately quantifies output-channel costs under its additional assumptions. Universal pairwise conjunction writes binomial(k,2) active outputs, so output storage can dominate input storage. This is a sufficient composition bound, not a sharp multilayer box law.

Formal results: Propositions H.6–H.7 prove a lower bound by hyperplane sign-pattern counting and an upper construction using the 2k nonleading coefficients of product_{l in S}(y−l)². Integer evaluations vanish exactly on S and are at least one elsewhere, so each pair is read by an affine threshold of the coefficients. Appendix K checks 106658 pair outputs over 2427 finite supports; those checks supplement the construction rather than establish the asymptotic lower bound.

Formal result: Corollary M.1 proves both directions from the exact one-gate law and bounds uniform over the finitely many input classes. Separately, the text illustrates the distinction at k=1024,m=k⁴ and the half-slack quantile center: the quadrature-based expected error fraction is 7.1×10⁻²² while approximately 85% of E1 draws contain an error. The formal equivalence assumes a fixed representation.
location: Corollary M.1; Table M.1; Table L.1

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: Corollary M.2 inverts Theorem 6.1 using continuity, monotonicity, and degree-two homogeneity of the threshold formulas. It proves success and failure on either side of fixed multiplicative deviations in log m. The optimized reliability failure statement covers common representations, while optimized count failure covers gate-local rules. No feature-capacity experiment in learned models is supplied.

Formal derivation: Appendix E.3 constructs a unit-gap Fibonacci-bounded representation for every comparator, then proves coordinatewise Fibonacci lower bounds for alternating chains at a specified margin. Binary positional weights give only an achievable rate and can overstate the hardest comparator's dimension cost by an exponential factor in r. Appendix K checks the constructions on all 1013 nonconstant comparator thresholds of arities 1–9 and 348502 truth-table entries.

Formal result: Proposition M.4 applies Lemma B.2's deterministic rearrangement identity to obtain necessary and sufficient correctness inequalities, retaining the threshold rule's strict versus non-strict boundaries. It derives robustness bounds from the minimum audit slack and a perturbation along a binding probe that breaks a gate. Appendix K checks the identity on 3720 class–direction pairs with maximum discrepancy 1.8×10⁻¹⁵. Fitting and testing the factored mechanism in learned models is proposed future work.

experiment_summary: Formal result: Proposition M.5 derives an exact conditional read law with variance scale sqrt(KH/d) and active centering Z_i−c mean(Z), where c=1−nu/sqrt(K). experiment_summary: Formal derivation in Claim 4.11: decompose input and frequency coordinates along v and its orthogonal complement, factor the Fourier integral, and evaluate the perpendicular Gaussian integral. Formal result: Claim 5.2 rewrites Gaussian-weighted Fourier energy as an expectation of two-point correlations for real integrable, square-integrable functions and positive-definite A. Algorithm 1 implements the resulting estimator, including positive-semidefinite A, using paired function queries. Corollary 5.3 bounds oracle bias and sampling error through concentration of bounded real and imaginary parts. No empirical evaluation is reported.

Formal theorem and proof attempt: Fourier-mass search recovers directions, Fourier interpolation reconstructs bounded responses, and Gaussian smoothing plus derivative learning removes boundedness. Definition 6.4's positive signed separation requirement cannot hold for every ordered pair of distinct directions. Lemma 7.4 also invokes Claim 7.3 on a frequency grid containing low frequencies outside that claim's range. These unresolved written steps limit evidence for the complete theorem. experiment_summary: Applies the diagnostic to candidate and control directions in language models and to known feature axes in a denoising toy. Formal derivation in Equations 10–13: tangent projections eliminate the radial displacement term for the two retained axes. Substituting their single-axis threshold crossings removes weights, activation norm, and threshold level, yielding (sin(alpha)cos(phi)/sin(alpha1))^p + (sin(alpha)sin(phi)/sin(alpha2))^p = 1 under the stipulated response model. This is a conditional algebraic result, not an empirical validation of that model.

Formal algebraic reduction in Equation 14 sets A=sum_i wi fi fi-transpose, giving R(v)=F(v-transpose A v). Nonnegative weights make A positive semidefinite, and its rank is bounded by d. The accompanying broader claim that p>2 is necessary for feature-specific error correction is argued within the proposed response framework rather than established for arbitrary mechanisms.

Compare active versus random initialization subspaces across subspace dimensions; the prose reports that random subspaces degrade all evaluated metrics. experiment_summary: Formal result: Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Appendices A–B derive Tr(Ga Gb)/sqrt(Tr(Ga²)Tr(Gb²)), where Ga = AaᵀAa and Gb = AbᵀAb. The RSA calculation concerns off-diagonal bilinear similarities; the CKA calculation uses convergence of the centered latent sample covariance to identity. These are conditional derivations of encoding dependence, not empirical demonstrations of natural-feature recovery.

Formal result: Theorem 3.3 and Appendix C derive W = Ab Aaᵀ(Aa Aaᵀ)⁻¹, per-target-entry MSE = ||Ab − W Aa||F²/mb, R² = 1 − ||Ab − W Aa||F²/||Ab||F², and corresponding Pearson-correlation expressions. The residual depends on how much of the target projection lies outside the source projection's row space.

Formal derivation: Section 3.1 computes E Tr(Ga Gb) = m²nσ⁴ and E Tr(G²) = mn[(m+n−2)σ⁴+μ4] for independent zero-mean i.i.d. projection entries. For Gaussian entries, μ4 = 3σ⁴, giving the exact ratio of expectations m/(m+n+1). Interpreting that ratio as expected normalized overlap requires concentration, which is not proved here. Section 4.1's m/(m+n−2) restatement omits the fourth-moment contribution.

Simulations use 1,000 features, 16,384 samples, k in {2,4,8,16,32,64}, dimensions from 0.2 to 5 times k log(n/k), and 200 independent projection-pair draws per dimension. Section 4.1 reports close agreement with analytical predictions and increasing alignment with dimension. The nonnegative TopK latent generator is not explicitly centered or whitened, so the simulation protocol does not exactly instantiate the stated theoretical assumptions.

Each system has 1,000 features. Simulations use 8,192 samples, overlap u = lab/sqrt(la lb) from 0.7 to 1.0, and sparsity fractions k/l in {0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2}. The union latent dimension is n = 2l − ul, with the top n·k/l entries retained per sample. Source dimension is fixed at 3k log(l/k), while target dimension ranges from k log(l/k) to three times that scale. The text reports partial-overlap curves exceeding full-overlap CKA at the smallest target dimension; exact crossings and effect sizes are unavailable from the supplied figure rendering.

Tables 1–2 report success rates of 74.0% for JSAE, 39.4% for ActAdd, 22.1% for prompting, 2.9% for norm-matched Gaussian directions, 0% for VL-SAE, and 4.1% for JSAE without alignment. The unaligned and VL-SAE comparisons use different category cohorts. Some success rates are incompatible with the reported similarity-gain distributions: for example, ActAdd's food row reports mean 0.31, SD 0.13, and only 25% above 0.2. These inconsistencies limit confidence in the comparison.

Figure 3's caption and Table 1 identify layer 13 as probe-optimal, while Tables 1–2 report steering success of 74.0% at layer 13 and 79.8% at layer 25, each on 104 valid examples with different category mixtures. This is a reported pipeline-level discrepancy, rather than a controlled general relationship between decodability and controllability. The probe plot itself is unavailable in the supplied text.

Same-category subsets contain 50/52/52/56 examples at layers 7/13/25/30. Reported judge suppression scores range from 5.04 to 5.78 out of ten. All six pairwise Welch tests on SBERT similarity changes are nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction, with minimum corrected p=0.30 and maximum absolute Cohen's d=0.39. Unintervened and random-direction suppression references are absent, so the panel does not establish an absolute suppression effect beyond those controls.

On 1,000 sampled COCO image–caption pairs, reconstruction CE at layers 7/13/25/30 is 2.9422/2.8009/2.3800/2.3329 nats versus clean CE 2.3348. Global-zero-relative recovery is 36.8%/51.5%/95.3%/100.2%; counterfactual-relative recovery is 47.7%/59.9%/96.1%/100.2%. Raw-mean broadcast CE is 3.0639/2.8820/2.3849/2.3326. JSAE improves the first three settings and is slightly worse at layer 30, contrary to the prose's every-layer superiority statement. Near-complete late recovery does not show that captioning depends exclusively on the reconstructed visual summary.

Table 6 reports pooled Pearson r=0.627, Spearman rho=0.677, and 76.4% agreement between similarity gain above 0.2 and judge accuracy above five. Layer-13 agreement is 88.5%, whereas layer-25 agreement is 64.4% and its reported within-layer correlations are nonsignificant. Several correlation p-values are incompatible with the listed correlations and sample sizes. The prose's claim of zero Accuracy>5 successes at layer 30 also conflicts with its reported threshold-agreement figures. These reporting inconsistencies limit confidence in the numerical validation.

experiment_summary: The construction assigns each output a Bernoulli code and routes its participating inputs to that code. Formal conditional composition argument in Appendix C.3: if each module returns the exact encoding of its logical output and that encoding is valid for the next module, induction over stages gives exact composed computation without accumulated approximation error. The source's specific cleanup construction remains insufficiently justified for arbitrary compressed states, so this evidence establishes only the conditional principle.

Among 320 generated stories per GPT model, the lexicon-based detector flags personality terminology in 96.56% of GPT-3.5 stories and 31.87% of GPT-4 stories. Human evaluation subsequently selects one GPT-4 story per personality combination from the filtered pool.

Uninformed individual accuracies are 0.68, 0.51, 0.47, 0.41, and 0.46 for extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness. The paper's 0.50 chance reference describes binary guessing rather than random selection among all three permitted prediction categories.

Figure 3 reports GPT-4 individual accuracy of 0.97 for extraversion, 0.68 for agreeableness, 0.69 for conscientiousness, 0.56 for neuroticism, and 0.59 for openness. In the uninformed condition, GPT-4 mean ratings range from 4.84 to 5.00, including 5.00 with zero reported standard deviation for cohesiveness and personalness. Human means range from 3.70 to 4.32. Formal result: Proposition 13 uses sign switching and the cited correspondence between real ETFs and strongly regular graphs. Assuming two rows violate the stated bound leads to a switched row with an impossible negative-entry count. Remark 14 restates the conclusion as a sign-imbalance bound, and Corollary 15 separately establishes a stronger existence result for a (3,6)-ETF.

Aggregated age responses had mean 27.51 years, SD 5.75, and range 13–75; 66.73% of gender responses were female. The reported age slope was −5.81 years per unit temperature, p<.001. Table 1 shows an overall but nonmonotonic decline in female response proportions. The gender regression is reported as significant, but its stated dependent-variable coding conflicts with its male-odds interpretation, so that coefficient cannot be interpreted unambiguously.

Table 2 reports aggregate means of 3.75, 3.05, 3.51, 3.18, 3.54, and 3.59 for honesty-humility, emotionality, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness. The construction of composite observations from repeated independent item completions is not fully specified.

Section-normalized attention to tests changes by +14.60 percentage points under correct steering and −12.69 under incorrect steering, a 27.29-point difference. Description attention decreases under both interventions, with reductions reported not to exceed eight points. Incorrect steering increases code-initiator attention by 17.54 points. No direct intervention on test-versus-description attention or uncertainty analysis is supplied.

The introduction supplies the layer-15 mIoU comparison, 0.516 versus 0.594. Exact additional plotted values are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Multimodal shares among valid features fall from 0.772 to 0.721, 0.770 to 0.482, 0.681 to 0.404, and 0.656 to 0.549 at layers 5, 10, 15, and 20 respectively. Without either regularizer, cluster-mask mIoU is 0.524 and within-group pairwise active-feature-set IoU is 0.199. Exclusive sparsity alone yields 0.568 and 0.080; group sparsity alone yields 0.522 and 0.211; both yield 0.555 and 0.153. Adding group sparsity to exclusive sparsity partially restores within-group agreement while reducing cluster alignment. Combined regularization does not improve within-group agreement over the unregularized baseline.

The hierarchical pipeline uses Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct for visual-reference descriptions and Qwen3-30B-Instruct for language-reference identification and semantic synthesis. The authors select alpha=0.02 from a stated balancing range of 0.01–0.02. Exact plotted scores, uncertainty, and independently annotated segmentation quality are unavailable.

Formal construction in Theorem 1 and Appendix A.1: positive alignment and nonnegative coefficients imply a positively correlated pair of active dictionary atoms across the disjoint supports. Appending the normalized orthogonal residual of one atom permits rewriting one embedding using a coordinate active in its partner, preserving exact reconstruction and adding at most one nonzero coefficient. Applying the construction to the indexed pairs adds at most one atom per pair. This is an algebraic existence result under the stated assumptions, with no empirical models or training measurements.

experiment_summary: The L1-regularized width sweep and bipolar-noise examples exhibit shared hidden coordinates with n specified features and m≥n hidden dimensions. Section 2.2 also constructs opposite-sign, shared-neuron representations that reconstruct all basis-vector inputs exactly. Formal derivation: after rescaling the common gradient constant and regularization coefficient, coordinate magnitudes obey d|w_k|/dt=(1−||w||₂²)|w_k|−λ while nonzero. For the largest surviving magnitude a_1 and another surviving magnitude a_k, γ_k=1−a_k/a_1 satisfies dγ_k/dt=(λ/a_1)γ_k. This proves relative-gap amplification in the interference-free dynamics, rather than convergence of the interacting network.

Conditional derivation in Appendix B substitutes the norm-balance condition into the L1-norm derivative to obtain −d||w||₁/dt=Θ(λ||w||₁²), yielding ||w(t)||₁ of order 1/(1/√m+λt) before saturation. Section 2.4 tests the prediction numerically without interference using m=100,000, λ=10^-5, and initialization standard deviation 0.9/√m. Figure 7 examines the relative-variance condition. The balance step is approximate, and estimating support size by ||w||₁² is a proxy rather than an identity.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: Appendix A.4 substitutes the confusion-matrix definitions to obtain F1 = 2 IoU/(1 + IoU), a strictly increasing function on [0,1]. Consequently both metrics give the same pair ordering and meta-AUPRC when evaluated with identical binarization. The result does not imply identical outcomes when different binarization hyperparameters are used.

Formal derivation supplied in Section 2.3 and Appendix A.1: the paper combines the cited polarisation correspondence with the equality condition for Cauchy–Schwarz. Complete symmetric coefficient tensors identify the polynomial, and normalized inner product one identifies positive proportionality. This establishes the full-tensor statement without establishing that the proposed deep recursion computes it.

Formal derivation: Equations 15–16 move the finite coefficient sums through the expectation. Appendix A.3 counts Isserlis pairings by the number m of internal pairs on each side, obtaining coefficients binomial(n,2m)^2 times ((2m−1)!!)^2 times (n−2m)!. For symmetric homogeneous tensors this yields the partial-trace expression. The derivation does not establish the appendix's claims of positive definiteness on all tensors or a stricter functional-equivalence relation than complete symmetrisation.

Formal derivation extending the cited Gram-recursion approach: Appendix A.2 derives leaf-to-root contraction and recovery of the coefficient inner product by a final trace, and proves commutation of permutation averaging with a tensor power of one Gram map. Equations 12–14 supply a bilinear implementation. Equation 14 omits the averaging factor required for literal agreement with the projector in Equation 11, so its raw inner-product normalization needs qualification. No measured runtime or general global-Gaussian contraction complexity is supplied.

experiment_summary: For the manual IOI circuit, mean versus resample replacement changes correct/error agreement from 99.5%/15.2% to 91.2%/40.6%; KL-optimal constants yield 99.9%/10.0%. For the manual Docstring circuit, mean versus resample changes agreement from 77.1%/35.8% to 47.2%/38.9%, shrinking the gap largely through lost correct agreement. Table 1 reports conditional bootstrap intervals for the gaps.

Matching retains 805/884 IOI errors and 3,534/3,536 Docstring errors, but only 20/56 subtraction errors. All twelve IOI configurations retain positive matched gaps; the manual mean-ablated circuit has 94.9% correct and 14.8% error agreement. For Llama ARC-Challenge at 2% edges, correct agreement is 80.0% across all correct examples and 46.7% among matched correct examples, compared with 54.9% error agreement. Docstring EAP-IG has negative matched gaps under mean and resample replacement. This observational matching does not identify every cause of the original disparities.

Patching the extension-induced change in the S-Inhibition output contribution attending to S2 into reference-circuit Name Mover queries, with reference keys and values fixed, reproduces the wrong subject on 120/137 newly recovered errors. Substituting object-derived content from corresponding prompts using 'snack', while retaining the attention weights at the substituted outputs, repairs 107/137 cases. Holding S-Inhibition outputs at their original extension values eliminates 68 of those repairs. These selected-error pathway tests do not estimate prevalence across all IOI errors.

The extension restores first-layer heads 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.6, and 0.10 at IO. Patching extension-derived Name Mover keys at IO into the reference reproduces wrong-subject choices on 35/137 newly recovered errors; patching keys only at either subject occurrence or only at remaining positions reproduces none. The text reports reduced IO retrieval by Positive Name Movers and increased IO retrieval by Negative Name Movers, both opposing the correct IO margin. No plotted effect magnitudes are inferred.

experiment_summary: Table 4 reports candidate-bias calibration increasing error agreement from 38.5% to 62.8% and correct agreement from 59.3% to 70.3% on 169 reserved validation questions. Formal derivation in Proposition 3.1 and Appendix A.1 decomposes the objective into ordered multi-output regressions, sums their matrix-multiplication costs, and applies the cited FISTA convergence bound. The reported total is O(M L(L-1)d^2/(2 sqrt(epsilon))), suppressing data-dependent convergence factors. This is a fixed-data optimization-cost analysis, not an empirical experiment, a uniform dimension-dependent convergence guarantee, or a causal-identification theorem.

Adjacent-layer regressions use token-averaged activations from 8,551 CoLA sentences and 32,768 SAE features at each of 12 GPT-2 Small block outputs. Roots and parents are selected for human-interpretable illustration rather than by a fixed global threshold. Replacing 'himself' with 'him' or 'he' reduces the illustrated reflexive-feature token activation from 1.3509 to zero; punctuation substitutions also alter a selected ending-punctuation feature. Reported paths include semantically aligned and explicitly spurious associations. These tests probe feature responses, not the native causal validity of regression edges.

experiment_summary: Figure 4 and Appendix D.5 report CoLA training-set node-ablation faithfulness and completeness comparable to restricted SHIFT, with ideal values of one and zero respectively. The text states that feature-node ablations act in the original LLM. Edge ablations instead zero learned coefficients within a linear surrogate. The supplied rendering provides no numerical curve values, uncertainty estimates, or detailed per-quartile results, and the relationship between the supervised grammaticality readout and native GPT-2 predictions is underspecified.

Table 9 reports training/test accuracy of 99.36%/71.10% at lambda=0 and 95.70%/72.77% at lambda=1e-5. Other tested nonzero penalties yield test accuracies of 72.48%, 70.28%, and 69.14%. The authors select lambda=1e-5 by its highest test accuracy. No repeated-run uncertainty or independent validation of that selection is supplied, and this readout experiment does not test recovery of native circuit structure.

Features ranked by sparse classifier coefficients are manually inspected for gender associations and zeroed. The resulting non-retrained pipelines report balanced profession accuracies of 90.5%, 77.5%, and 81.5% for Pythia-70M, Gemma-2-2B, and Gemma-2-9B, compared with original-predictor scores of 61.9%, 69.6%, and 70.8%. Retraining the edited feature classifier gives 94.2%, 95.1%, and 96.9%. Reported gender-predictability scores are near 50%, although the leakage evaluation procedure is not fully specified. These are pipeline comparisons; a matched untrimmed SAE-classifier ablation is not reported.
Specific finding: Sparse-classifier-based SAE feature ranking and human-guided trimming can attain profession accuracy comparable to SHIFT while requiring substantially less reported computational time in the evaluated Bias-in-Bios configurations. CircuitLasso-retrain reports profession accuracies of 94.2%, 95.1%, and 96.9%, versus SHIFT-retrain's 93.1%, 94.2%, and 96.0%. Corresponding runtimes are 61.9, 72.5, and 125.2 seconds versus 356.3, 476.8, and 1,056.0 seconds. Non-retrained selected-feature counts are 41/55/59 versus SHIFT's 49/65/71, with runtimes of 36.5/47.2/107.4 versus 257.6/371.2/908.4 seconds. Retrained worst-group accuracy is not uniformly higher: 88.7/92.9/91.5 versus 89.0/92.4/90.3. Non-retrained CircuitLasso profession accuracy remains below concept-bottleneck and linear-probing baselines in both Gemma settings. No uncertainty estimates or matched-interface comparison are supplied.

experiment_summary: Formal result: Lemmas 5.2–5.3 construct fixed-control matrices in an independent observable basis and show that Ψ′ = TΨ induces A′ = TAT^(-1) after control averaging. Similarity preserves the eigenvalue multiset. Theorem 5.1 connects the averaged operator to the population regression coefficient under its additional distributional assumptions.

Formal derivation combines Gramian concentration, regression perturbation, and spectral perturbation. The joint-regression remainder is asserted to fit a universal constant without tracking control dimension, control conditioning, or control coefficients; next-state tail control also requires care outside stationarity. The eigenvector resolvent proof needs stricter perturbation margins than its stated boundary condition supplies. These gaps limit the claimed finite-sample certificate despite the provided root-sample perturbation argument.

Formal two-point argument: diagonal matrices differing in one eigenvalue by ε = σ/sqrt(2g1M) remain in the separated class while their expected Gaussian KL divergence is 1/4. Pinsker and a two-point testing reduction give a lower bound of order σ/sqrt(g1M). The text contains an incorrectly directed intermediate mixture-TV statement, but its conditional Pinsker calculation supplies the needed closeness bound.

Formal derivation: partition independent samples into K logarithmic-in-confidence blocks, bound each sample Gramian's mean squared Frobenius error using the fourth moment, and apply the cited geometric-median theorem. Equation 62 yields a root-M rate with a linear N+p prefactor. Passing to operator norm preserves that bound, rather than recovering the earlier dimension dependence.

Formal result: a common orthonormal eigenbasis would unitarily diagonalize A and therefore make A normal. Proposition 8.2 constructs a stable two-dimensional upper-triangular family whose normalized eigenvectors approach one direction while the minor covariance principal direction approaches an orthogonal direction. This establishes possible near-orthogonality, not large misalignment in every non-normal realization or in every fit with the same condition number.

Formal derivation uses mutually annihilating spectral projectors and their sum-to-identity property. Lagrange interpolation establishes the polynomial algebra's isomorphism to one complex coordinate per distinct eigenvalue. The stronger intervention-completeness and foundational-uniqueness conclusions are not established: IC3 does not force the full commutant, since the identity subalgebra already satisfies its stated spanning condition. Native-transformer patching predictions are not tested.

Formal derivation applies the cited classical truncation theorem to the statically weighted realization. G_u ⪯ λmax(G_u)I implies P_eff ⪯ λmax(G_u)P, yielding componentwise Hankel-singular-value domination. The stronger effective-rank strictness count is not justified by transferring an input nullity bound through B and reachability, and Corollary 10.6's sqrt(r_eff/p) improvement is asserted without a sufficient derivation. No native-model reduction experiment is supplied.

At N=32 and mid-depth, maximum matched-distance slopes are −0.286 ± 0.007 for GPT-2 spectral dictionaries, −0.329 ± 0.024 for Gemma, and −0.506 ± 0.031 for Qwen. Qwen's mean and median slopes are −0.375 and −0.338. GPT-2 reaches 399,974 rows and Qwen 106,660. N sweeps span 8–128. Across 30 model–dictionary–dimension cells, 300 rolling-window slopes correlate with relative sample threshold at Spearman ρ=−0.28; the two Qwen series oppose the proposed collapse, and the threshold's universal constant is unknown.

The illustrated GPT-2 layer-6 paired slopes are −0.359 ± 0.018 and −0.368 ± 0.019 over nine admissible grid points, with median robust/plain distance ratio 1.000. Its lifted-state excess kurtosis is 0.19. A Qwen layer-18 lift has excess kurtosis 50.7 and reported robust versus plain slopes −0.349 versus −0.289. The synthetic contaminated-design slopes are reported as −0.286 versus −0.405, so those slopes alone do not substantiate the text's claimed robust-estimator advantage.

At j=8, PCA removal reduces IOI logit difference by 60%, versus 25% for modes; at j=32 the reductions are 67% versus 41%. Random directions never exceed 7%. Top-16 attributing-mode subspaces have median agreement of 0.290 across calibration draws. The fitted full-state readout has median held-out relative reconstruction error 0.231. These results do not establish that spectral identification entails reproducible behavior-selected mode sets.

No head class reaches the alignment target of 0.8. Greedy name-mover selection uses 96 of 128 modes and reaches alignment 0.260 against a random-subspace reference of 0.125. Reported S-inhibition and induction-head alignments are 0.311 and 0.298. The readout's held-out median relative reconstruction error is 0.231.

Across six layers, j values spanning 8–64, 156 cells, and 8,192 prompts, the normalized PCA–Koopman gap falls from 0.48 at depth gap one to 0.12 at gap nine, reported as a 4.1-fold decline using underlying values. The raw ratio changes from 1.69 to 1.05. Repeated behavioral ablations do not establish a reversal, and earlier-layer interventions saturate the behavioral readout.

At N=32 and mid-depth, frequency-selected SAE residuals are 0.636, 0.544, and 0.524 for GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen, versus spectral residuals 0.301, 0.177, and 0.154. The preregistered strict ordering with nonoverlapping interquartile ranges succeeds in 49% of 75 cells, below the 80% target. Median SAE/spectral ratios are 2.05 for frequency selection, 1.70 for uniformly sampled live features, 0.70 for variance, and 0.63 for greedy variance explanation. N spans 8–128. Fixed-dictionary split-half spectral stability favors spectral dictionaries in eight of nine layer settings, with a deep-Qwen construction failure as the exception.

Increasing γ from zero to one lowers the TopK relative prediction residual from 0.438 to 0.333 and split-half spectral distance from 0.0170 to 0.0101, a 41% reduction. Reconstruction FVU rises from 0.222 to 0.255, live-feature fraction falls from 0.77 to 0.58, and cross-seed mean maximum cosine falls from 0.526 to 0.428. All three γ=10 runs fail the alive-feature guard. ReLU shows a 22% spectral-distance improvement without a lower residual at its guard-selected operating point.

The rule declares all 36 cross-family pair–depth comparisons and all nine Pythia seed-replica pair–depth comparisons distinct. The closest replica comparison is 4.64 times its floor. Distance still ranks replicas below cross-family comparisons with AUC 0.75 for the maximum statistic and 0.84 for the Wasserstein summary. Dictionary-mismatch bias is the authors' diagnosis, not independently isolated by these comparisons; they recommend a replica-calibrated null.

Median adjacent-layer spectral distances are 3.22, 11.97, and 6.12 times their split-half floors for GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen. Maximum state–control canonical correlations are 0.82, 0.96, and 0.95, while control-regression R² values are 0.08, 0.22, and 0.16. Replacing controls by residuals after regression on lifted states shifts spectra by 6.8, 9.1, and 5.2 times the floors. Pooled/per-layer held-out residuals are respectively 0.433/0.263, 0.417/0.326, and 0.291/0.244; no ambiguous percentage denominator is needed to report these comparisons.

Adding log||x|| produces largest expanding eigenvalues 1.137, 1.107, and 1.291 for GPT-2, Gemma, and Qwen, compared with measured norm-growth factors 1.111, 1.077, and 1.326. Total norm growth across the analyzed range is reported as 4.3-fold, 1.5-fold, and 4.4-fold, motivating layer-specific marginal distributions.

The attention-write covariance is reported to have tr(G_u)/λmax(G_u)=10.8 in ambient dimension 4,096. This establishes second-moment concentration for that setting. No reduced native-transformer error evaluation is supplied.

At every corresponding layer, the 32,768-feature suite has lower L0, a lower alive fraction, and lower reported loss recovery. Its loss recovery spans 72.4–94.6%, versus 86.7–98.4% for the 8,192-feature suite. Reconstruction MSE is worse in layers 1–5 but better in layer 0. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported.

experiment_summary: Formal counting identity in Theorem H.2: equal-score matches each contribute one unit of relative unnormalized weight, while the auxiliary token contributes total weight V alpha and uniform value, adding alpha to each state count. No Layer-2 MLP is required. Exclusion of other positions is an ideal hard-attention assumption, not a property of finite softmax alone.

Formal proof in Theorem H.9 bounds nonmatch leakage and within-match score dispersion separately. With Delta = beta(1-(2k+2)epsilon), stochastic KL is at most kappa when Delta >= log(4N/((n_c+V alpha)kappa)) and epsilon <= kappa/(16k Delta), for kappa in (0,1]. Deterministic correctness follows from epsilon < 1/(2k+2) and Delta > log(2 sqrt(2)(N-n_c)/n_c). Appendix H.7 gives fixed parameters valid uniformly over resolvable queries by choosing the gap for n_c = 1.

Six model–task configurations, each evaluated over 500,000 coverage-filtered test trajectories, attain reported TF cell accuracy 1.0000 after rounding, AR cell accuracy 0.9999–1.0000, and TF sequence accuracy 0.9989–1.0000. experiment_summary: Trained separate bias-label logistic probes on ambiguous BBQ, StereoSet intrasentence, and filtered multiple-choice CrowS-Pairs. Best-layer bias AUROCs were 0.67–0.75, 0.76–0.95, and 0.82–0.94 respectively. Within biased and anti-biased answer groups, correlations between probe score and answer probability were 0.57–0.80 on disambiguated BBQ across eight models. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct's BBQ probe achieved AUROC 0.57 for disambiguated bias labels versus 0.94 for higher-versus-lower-likelihood biased/anti-biased answers. BBQ-trained probes achieved highest-versus-lowest-option confidence AUROC 0.79–0.95 on disambiguated BBQ, 0.52–0.80 on MMLU, and 0.62–0.88 on OpenBookQA. Transfer was heterogeneous: Llama-base StereoSet and Llama-Instruct CrowS-Pairs probes scored 0.33 and 0.35 on disambiguated BBQ confidence labels. These tests establish likelihood-related signal without proving that confidence exclusively determines the probes.

Evaluated BBQ's abstention-sensitive bias score alongside accuracy and ratios of mean answer probabilities. In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ambiguous accuracy increased from 0.76 to 0.99 and bias score fell from 0.08 to 0.01, while the biased-to-anti-biased mean-probability ratio remained above one, declining from 1.58 to 1.38. Disambiguated bias scores generally changed little across checkpoints despite accuracy losses in several models. The score definition explains why increasing correct ambiguous-context abstention can lower the bias metric without eliminating the conditional preference among substantive answers.

experiment_summary: Constructs 500 retained pairs per primary model, with 300 for fitting and 200 held out. Held-out state replacement and vector interventions demonstrate that these contrasts provide usable internal intervention targets; full-state call recovery ranges from 93.5% to 100% across models. The request–tool crossover uses 100 requests per condition. Review produces 4.0% calls with write_file and 100.0% with submit_review; Write produces 100.0% and 34.0%, respectively.

L24 full-state patching recovers calls on 100% of 200 held-out analysis prompts. Vector addition changes call rate from 0% to 100%, and subtraction from 100% to 0%; mean raw call-logit gap recovery is 1.03 and 1.04. A separate 200-training/300-evaluation neighboring-layer control finds complete bidirectional control at L24 and L25. At L24 its norm-matched random control yields 18.7% calling after analysis-side addition and retains 97.7% calling after execution-side subtraction.

On 200 held-out tasks, full-scaffold mean call probabilities are 0.8486 for neutral requests and 0.0038 for analysis requests. Format-only probabilities are 1.0000 and 0.9952; removing the format gives 6.32e-7 and 8.31e-10. Removing the schema gives 0.9521 and 0.4108, while replacing it with length-matched neutral text gives 0.7311 and 0.1553. A separate 300-task cohort gives call rates of 32.3% for task body only, 86.7% for neutral wording, 0% for analysis wording, and 100% for execution wording with the full scaffold. Empty, greeting, and unrelated inputs are checked once each and yield no top-1 calls.

On 100 equal-length Qwen3-8B pairs, all 18 forward-core nodes appear by 2,000 retained EAP-IG edges, where normalized faithfulness is −0.014. Faithfulness reaches 0.809 at 100,000 edges. ACDC component-output replay yields near-unit mean normalized recovery across four Qwen3 scales, but size-matched random sets already recover 0.9768 for 8B and 0.9554 for 14B. Selected-core removal effects are 0.5975 and 0.4077 at those scales. Component replay and retained-edge replay use different intervention interfaces, limiting direct comparisons of circuit size.

At ViT-L/14 width 6,144, RW MSAE has 82.9% zeros, FVU 0.007, and cosine 0.997; UW has 74.8%, 0.002, and 0.999. experiment_summary: Next-number evaluation on 10,000 synthetic sequences reports MAE 4.2748 and R² 0.9958. These metrics establish prediction performance under the supplied distribution without isolating the contribution of repeated structure.

Layerwise probes trained on 4,500 samples and tested on 500 samples show increasing final-number MAE and decreasing R² after approximately layer 8. The earlier-position control described in the prose cannot causally observe the later final number, limiting its value as a localization control. Figure 3 instead describes shuffled-label controls.

Section 7.4 reports increased counterfactual difference scores and decreased ground-truth difference scores under key swapping, while the original answer remains more probable in the absolute-probability comparison. Whole-key swaps alter key content as well as positional information. Numerical effects and uncertainty are unavailable in readable text. Difference-score equations reference a corrupt baseline despite the clean-run setup, and value-restoration onset differs between the prose and appendix caption.

The proposed algorithm is inferred from delta probes, joint hidden-state/query transfer into flat sequences, token-importance peaks, and key swaps on perfectly predicted examples. These tests are consistent with latent-delta induction but do not directly isolate delta matching, successor retrieval, and addition as a complete natural execution pathway. The key-swap comparison does not cleanly separate delta semantics from positional cues.

The text reports negative changes in shallow DLM configurations and absent or markedly weaker effects in the autoregressive comparisons. Numerical effect sizes and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied in readable text.

Collects 5M held-out Common Pile tokens and evaluates up to 1,000 eligible latents per SAE using gpt-4o-mini. Appendix E reports selected classification accuracies of 1.00, 0.714, 0.929, and 0.286. One maximal-activation context is an explicit placeholder. Aggregate scores, selection representativeness, and independent calibration are absent; selected-window accuracy does not establish exhaustive concept specificity.

Uses five neutral prefixes per feature, 30-token continuations, and 30 diffusion steps. Section 4 specifies all-position steering for Dream and currently masked-position steering for LLaDA. The score is concept improvement plus 0.3 times relative perplexity reduction. At L0=80, selecting the higher-scoring DLM variant within each family–layer cell yields higher scores than the autoregressive comparator in 11 of 12 cells. Dream layer-27 Unmask-SAE scores 0.38 versus Qwen's −0.02; Qwen leads at layer 14. LLaDA's largest listed score is 0.20 at layer 26, rather than its deepest tested layer. Feature counts, selection, scoring implementations, scale m_f, and uncertainty are insufficiently specified. Appendix G describes top-activated-position selectors, which are distinct from the masked-position selector.

Defines the diagnostics and applies them to Dream-7B trajectories under Origin, TopK-margin, and Entropy ordering on 800 GSM8K questions with 128 denoising steps. The text does not specify K_feat or how Equation 18 handles tokens decoded on the final step, for which its denominator vanishes. Appendix H's flip statistic is a count over currently decoded positions, rather than a normalized flip rate.

Reports accuracy of 8% for Origin, 56% for TopK-margin, and 59% for Entropy on the 800-question setting. Black patients constitute 0.69 of sarcoidosis vignettes versus a cited 0.376 population fraction; Asian patients constitute 0.74 of hepatitis B vignettes versus a cited 0.211. experiment_summary: Components are individually patched to obtain importance scores and then restored in descending order into a fully patched model. The sine mean discussion reports little improvement through the first 50 restorations. Exact final component counts are unavailable from the image-only plots, and Section 5 is inconsistent about whether the final restored circuits meet faithfulness thresholds.

For each configuration, ten circuit and ten complement components are sampled and each receives ten probe-training seeds. Probes use balanced 1,000-example datasets with 70/10/20 train/validation/test splits. Sine mean-functional accuracy is 0.94 versus 0.93, p=0.661; some configurations favor complement components. Logarithm mean-functional is 0.96 versus 0.88, p=0.015, and mean-model p=0.029; other reported comparisons do not reach p<0.05. Multiple-comparison correction is not reported, nonsignificance does not establish equivalence, and Appendix H inconsistently describes activation dimensions. Its hidden ReLU architecture does not constitute a linear-decoding test.

Specific finding: Passing prediction-retention, circuit-knockout, and component-removal thresholds provides sufficiently reliable reference circuit membership for interpreting native symbolic-regression operator mechanisms.

Five-fold stratified logistic-regression probes with four tested regularization values achieve AUROC 0.9538–0.9816 across layers. Layer 23 reaches approximately 0.982, with bootstrap 95% CI 0.968–0.993 and accuracy 0.9625. Original-parser output sensitivity is 65/144, or 0.451. Independent evaluation of layer and hyperparameter selection, including nested cross-validation, is not established.

Concept suppression at alpha 0 corrects 17/85 false negatives and disrupts 25/47 true positives. TP-P95 targets correct 19/85 and disrupt 24/47. Random-concept suppression corrects 26/85 and disrupts 29/47. The reported hazard-versus-random McNemar comparison has p=0.84. These strategies reduce the count of detected hazards. Table 5 separately reports 99.92% of concept activations below 0.01 and selected-concept means of 0.053 for true positives versus 0.051 for false negatives; these statistics do not establish why interventions fail.

At layer 27, mean hazard-token ranks are 13,380 for 65 true positives and 16,370 for 79 false negatives. Only 1/65 true positives and 0/79 false negatives have any selected hazard token in the top 100; neither group has a top-50 occurrence. The maximum reported between-group rank effect size is Cohen's d=1.39 at layer 22. This statistic concerns selected vocabulary readouts, rather than direct measurement of full hidden-state separation.

At alpha 1, the intervention corrects 6/79 false negatives and disrupts 6/65 true positives, a net change of zero detections. At alpha 5, it corrects 16/79 and disrupts 5/65, a net gain of 11. Independent intervention evaluation and a matched random-direction comparison are not reported for this arm. Section 2.3 describes sampled baselines but greedy steering, leaving the unsteered comparison procedure insufficiently clear.

At alpha 1, TSV corrects 5/79 misses and disrupts 5/65 detections; the random direction corrects 7/79 and disrupts 7/65. At alpha 10, TSV corrects 19/79 and disrupts 4/65, yielding 15 additional detections and leaving 60/79 original misses. The alpha-10 random control was not completed. At alpha 5, the source reports TSV net +10 versus random net −6, without an exact paired comparison. TSV separates TP from FN representations with reported AUROC 0.814 and has cosine similarity 0.50 to the hazard-versus-benign direction; independent validation of this separation is not described. Intervention selection uses the evaluation corpus, and sampled-baseline versus greedy-steering comparison details are unclear.

For Qwen, refined parsing raises true positives from 65/144 to 105/144 and false positives from 40/256 to 54/256; sensitivity changes from 0.451 to 0.729 and specificity from 0.844 to 0.789. For Steerling, true positives rise from 51/144 to 62/144 and false positives from 78/256 to 85/256. The authors identify missed third-person urgency recommendations as one parser limitation. Full refined-parser rules and an independent response-level validation are not supplied.

Section 4.2 supplies a structural and runtime derivation: each added path runs from a model input to an output, so every retained internal vertex has incoming and outgoing retained connections. Longest-path searches in a topologically ordered DAG take O(|V|+|E|) each. Preprocessing includes topological sorting and O(|E| log |E|) score sorting. This establishes path coverage and the stated computational cost under the DAG assumptions, rather than mechanistic faithfulness or globally minimal circuits.

In an 18,240-edge MinAggGNN, raw weights, EAP, and 20-step EAP-IG recover the reported 10-edge reference circuit; WeightGrad requires 12 edges. On the 300-graph evaluation set, full-model multiplicative loss is 0.0578, retained-circuit loss is 0.0545, and circuit-deletion loss is 21870.6836. Four additional initializations are described as functionally identical, but two corresponding circuit losses are blank. Discovery uses corrupted versions of the test graphs, so this is not an independent held-out discovery evaluation. Joint deletion does not establish individual necessity of every retained edge.

At 50% retention the corresponding values are 11.24°, 11.32°, and 37.72°. The full-CLS high/low-error classifier gives 3.41° and 11.14° at 20% and 50%. The sparse bright-clean latent fires on approximately 14% of events and is ineffective as a standalone ranking score at larger target efficiencies under the reported thresholding procedure. Calibration is approximate in the low-error regime and overconfident at intermediate predicted errors.

experiment_summary: Formal derivation, not an empirical experiment: Section 2.2, Equations 2–3, expands the two projected sums coordinatewise and identifies their coefficients with a third-order tensor. Assumes finite-dimensional compatible linear maps and the stated bias-free architecture. Section 2.3, Equation 4, incorporates a linear output projection.

Formal derivation, not an empirical experiment: Equations 14–15 distribute the tensor contraction over two input components and then arbitrary finite component sums, obtaining Σ_i,j a_i a_j [(W1d_i) ⊙ (W2d_j)]. Only the specified linear input decomposition and bilinear architecture are required; sparsity reduces the number of active terms but is unnecessary for the identity.

Formal derivation, not an empirical experiment: Equations 4–10 substitute the direct-plus-attention residual sum into both bilinear branches and distribute their interaction into four categories. Equation 11 adds direct and attention pathways to form a proposed full-logit expression. The structural decomposition follows from this substitution, but the printed expression lacks W_U on the MLP term and has apparent transpose and token-indexing inconsistencies. The literal displayed full-logit formula is therefore not established as correct.

Iterative node pruning and subsequent edge path patching identify overlapping GPT-2 circuits at an 80% normalized-logit-difference threshold. Heads 0.1, 4.4, 7.11, and 9.1 each have reported removal drops above 20% in all three extracted circuits. Attention comparisons suggest order-sensitive detection by 4.4 and recent-member transport by 7.11; OV diagnostics associate 9.1 with succession. One backward node-pruning sweep in Llama identifies heads 5.25, 16.0, and 20.17 with removal drops of at least 12% across all three tasks. Heads 5.25 and 20.17 show analogous detection and successor diagnostics, while 16.0's function remains unresolved. These are selected datasets without a reported independent discovery-validation split.

experiment_summary: OV diagnostics apply a head's transformation to post-first-MLP states and count expected successor tokens among top-five vocabulary readouts.
