experiment_summary: Appendix L reports MLP-9 removal drops from the full model of 71.33%, 84.10%, and 83.97% for numerals, number words, and months. The described sequence-member-to-successor readout patterns occur in 1,531/1,536 numeral, 1,396/1,536 number-word, and 1,495/1,536 month templated examples. Number-word exceptions include numeral-form answers that become word-form answers later. The main text's greater-than-90% MLP-9 damage assertion is not reconciled with the appendix's full-model values.

The Number Words circuit retains 87.35% of numeral-task logit difference, whereas the Numerals circuit retains 48.41% on number words. The Numerals and Number Words circuits score 113.52% and 103.64% on months, while the Months circuit scores 43.74% on numerals and 32.36% on number words. Own-task scores are 81.01%, 81.11%, and 80.30%. The tested IOI circuit yields negative normalized logit differences on all three tasks. These finite comparisons establish asymmetric intervention-relative retention rather than complete functional interchangeability.

For +2, +3, +10, and +100 sequences, selected-set zero ablations produce 96–100% incorrect completions, compared with random-control means of 7.7%, 28%, 4%, and 8.2%, respectively. Double-digit addition failure is 98–100% versus 32.8%; double-digit subtraction failure is 92–96% versus 20%. Single-digit addition failure ranges from 46% to 92% versus 15.6%, and subtraction from 46% to 74% versus 12.4%. Sequence tests use three input members, compared with four in discovery. Random scores average 50 sampled sets per prompt. The text does not explicitly document an initially-correct selection rule for these 50-prompt cohorts.

Gemma-2 2B used 16k/65k dictionaries and feature-specific scales selected from 30–300 to maximize a task's loss decrease, then applied across tasks. experiment_summary: The authors individually disabled eligible nodes and correlated measured effects with attribution approximations. Agreement was reported as relatively low before layer 6, while non-residual dictionaries became adequate only in the model's final third. Numerical correlations and a quantitative adequacy criterion are not given in the prose. SAE quality, task complexity, and token-category aggregation remain candidate explanations rather than experimentally isolated causes.

For each task, negative steering acted on all arrow tokens in a batch of 16 ICL prompts containing 32 examples each. Scales were searched between 1 and 30; each feature received a scale reducing at least one task's accuracy by 0.1, then that scale was used across tasks. The prose reports substantially lower task specificity and substantial disruption from features lacking task-specific positive effects. Positive steering instead used zero-shot answer loss and a globally selected Gemma-1 scale. Exact heatmap values are unavailable.

The authors repeated embedding extraction, SAE training, concept-based model selection, and evaluation after shuffling values within each ESM-2 weight and bias tensor. They report no qualifying randomized-model SAE features for the tested Swiss-Prot biological concepts, while hundreds showed strong associations with individual amino-acid types.

Claude-3.5 Sonnet generated descriptions from protein metadata and activation examples, then predicted maxima for separate proteins using descriptions and metadata without activation information. The reported median Pearson correlation with measured maxima was 0.72. Correlation between Swiss-Prot association performance and description-prediction performance was 0.11. Methods describe eligibility exclusions without clearly reconciling them with the reported feature count or specifying the layer composition of the sampled panel.

Inspection of selected high-activation proteins lacking expected Swiss-Prot annotations produced one Nudix motif candidate and one peptidase S1 domain candidate with corresponding InterPro evidence. Separate proposed binding-site annotations were not independently validated. No systematic candidate denominator or prospective annotation-accuracy evaluation is supplied.

The framework is implemented using 382,459 training sentences and 1,007 test sentences labeled for voice, tense, sentiment, and domain. Multiple featurizers are evaluated on frozen Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B. Science–positive-sentiment correlations are varied for the principal experiments; past–passive correlations receive supplementary concept-identification evaluation.

The concern that direct training-time suppression would damage legitimate repetition is a motivation rather than a tested suppression outcome.

experiment_summary: Over 2,000 test jets, the reported mean clean-minus-corrupt logit gap is -0.068. Normalized recovery, called direct effect in the paper, is +4.25 for L0H1, +0.71 for L3H3, and negative for the other four selected heads. Negative recovery scores indicate movement away from the clean value under this normalization; they do not independently establish upstream conditionality or classification degradation. L0H1 and L0H2 occupy the same attention layer, so L0H2 is not downstream of L0H1 in that layer.

Analyses over 2,000 test jets per procedure report positive recovery for L0H1 and L3H3 and negative recovery for L0H2, L1H0, L1H1, and L1H3 under both corruptions. Recovery magnitude depends on both numerator and denominator; the paper's attribution of smaller ratios to a smaller absolute denominator is not established by these results.

Over 2,000 test jets, L0H1 attention correlates negatively with log-kT (-0.302), log angular separation (-0.481), and log pair mass squared (-0.429), and positively with log-z (+0.152). Table 11 does not include L1H1, so it does not establish that every proposed relay has this pattern.

Joint-minus-summed-singleton damage is -1.512 for {L0H1,L0H2}, -1.498 for {L1H0,L1H3}, and -1.498 for {L1H1,L1H3}. The pairwise-ablation sample count and uncertainty are not separately specified. The paper interprets negative interactions as redundancy, but these observations do not distinguish redundancy from other nonlinear or mediated interactions.

Section 8.2 reports a +4.44 mean-logit-difference change for log-kT zeroing, described as degradation, and relative L2 attention-profile changes of 0.86–1.44 for four discussed heads. Figure 13 profiles use 10,000 test jets. The same section interprets a positive log-z change of +2.69 as improvement, creating a sign inconsistency that prevents a reliable conclusion about behavioral improvement or degradation from those signs. The caption describes six panels while the prose discusses four heads; no unseen profile values are inferred.

The database contains 1,178,970 activations per GPT-2 site from 2,000 MiniPile sequences, 1,000 IOI prompts, and 1,000 Greater-than prompts. Retrieval usually uses cosine similarity above 0.85, with lower thresholds for selected cases. Manual inventories identify recurring roles but leave two of eleven layer-4 subspaces and four of thirteen layer-9 subspaces without clear interpretations. A repetition-associated subspace sometimes instead groups by current token, and some induction examples are deliberately selected. The supplied captions and prose describe the examples, but the underlying figure images are unavailable in the text rendering.

From 927 RAVEL prize-winner entities, factual-recall and single-token-answer filtering retains 552 for Qwen and 719 for Gemma. Donor conditions replace either both mentions of an entity or only its earlier mention with a made-up name of matching token length. The text and captions report selected subspaces with strong prediction effects in one condition and little effect in the other, whereas native/random/PCA baseline effects tend to correlate across conditions. Figure 5's caption reports that patching Qwen's 256-dimensional subspace 2 from the both-mentions-corrupted donor produces a 100% context-answer rate while the other donor condition leaves its parametric-answer rate near the clean rate. Layers and configurations are selected using preliminary or task-based experiments. Routing interpretations rely on the entity-corruption specificity assumption; detailed circuits remain unknown.

The text reports lower pairwise MI after training and describes the comparisons in Figures 15, 17, and 18. These use KSG estimates also used during training. The rendering supplies descriptions and captions but no readable numerical heatmap values or uncertainty estimates. Reduced estimated pairwise MI is a narrower finding than minimization of total correlation.

This establishes the stated readout identity under exact relational linearity and containment assumptions.

experiment_summary: Formal result: Theorem 14 and Appendix D.1 transport the projected affine query relation through compatible effective embedding and unembedding maps, constructing an affine relation in the other model. The construction also confines the transported input dependence to its effective embedding space. This establishes conditional preservation without proving that natural-language queries satisfy the antecedents.

Formal result: Theorem 15 and Appendix D.2 transfer projected parallelism through the invertible effective-space unembedding map. Appendix B.5 constructs two-dimensional predictors with three token unembeddings sharing a first coordinate; changing the first context coordinate nonlinearly leaves probabilities unchanged because centered unembeddings use only the second coordinate. This is a mathematical construction, not a trained-model experiment.

Formal derivation: Lemma 1 bounds each linear, squared, and cross term on the unit box. Theorem 1 uses preservation of score ordering by softmax to convert negative margin upper bounds into top-1 stability. Formal derivation: Propositions 1–2 and Appendix A.3 optimize linear objectives by allocating available probability mass in objective-coefficient order. The supplied evidence-mass formula establishes the stated minimum. These results require valid input bounds. They do not establish Theorem 2's stronger quantitative separation: its displayed witness has a 0.2 margin improvement, below the asserted E/(S-1)=0.3.

Appendix A.4 explicitly handles positive normalization epsilon through the squared-norm inequality. The resulting width cap applies at LayerNorm outputs, not arbitrary attention, FFN, or residual measurement points.

Formal derivation: Proposition 7 applies the triangle inequality to the map displacement and Jacobian term, bounds each by L_f||delta||2, and uses ||delta||2≤epsilon sqrt(n). This conditional inequality does not validate a smaller sampled remainder, nor establish the claimed ease of computing a valid transformer-stack constant.

experiment_summary: At epsilon=0.0005, Table 1 reports Q1 passes on 1/60 prompts for head 0.1 and 60/60 for head 0.10. At epsilon=0.001, the counts are 0/60 and 57/60. Their conjunction passes on 1/60 and 0/60, respectively. Other selected head pairs and triples have higher joint pass rates. This adds robustness measurements to prior head classifications; pre-LayerNorm enclosure validity remains a limitation of interpreting pass rates as guarantees.

Table 25 reports H5 at epsilon=0.001 with Q1/Q2/Q3 pass rates of 47%/90%/100%, whereas H10 at epsilon=0.002 has 73%/100%/0%. These demonstrate different reported query profiles across the specified head–radius conditions. The main text's statement that ten of twelve heads pass all queries is not established by the displayed four-head table, which also includes substantial failures for H6 and H8.

Figure 2's supplied caption reports that epsilon=0.002 balls saturate the three checks for both heads, whereas paraphrase enclosures yield differing Q1 rates, evidence-mass rates, and entropy widths. For example, reported Q2 rates are 71% for H0 versus 14–71% for H1 across the three sets. Section 4.4 supplies the shared-factor enclosure construction. The comparison changes perturbation-set size and geometry, and does not isolate semantic variation or establish that other verification frameworks cannot accept structured inputs.

Tables 8–10 use five synthetic inputs and 40 head–position queries per layer–radius condition. At layer 2, epsilon=0.005, sequential CPZ passes 12.5% versus 95% with the connector; at layer 3 the rates are 0% versus 85%. The latter exceeds the reported 80% empirical stable fraction, contradicting an unqualified soundness interpretation. Table 10 reports 0% sequential versus 47.9% connector passes at GPT-2 Small layer 1, epsilon=0.001. The synthetic timing comparison reports approximately 45 versus 1,040 seconds per radius over all five inputs and four layers.

experiment_summary: At BERT-tiny layer 1, epsilon=0.002, Table 19 reports 92.5% CPZ, 51.2% CROWN, 3.8% IBP, and 95% MC+PGD stability across 80 queries from five inputs; verification baselines receive the same connector enclosure. At GPT-2 Small layer 1, epsilon=0.001, Table 21 reports 47.9%, 0.2%, 26.9%, and 78.1%, respectively, across 480 queries from five inputs. GPT-2 Medium layer 1 reports 41.1% CPZ versus 90.9% empirical stability across 384 queries from three inputs at epsilon=0.0005. Table 23 adds a GPT-2 Small layer-2 probe with 27.1% CPZ versus 62.5% empirical stability across 96 queries from one input. Baseline and runtime descriptions vary, so these results do not establish general method dominance.

At epsilon=0.002, BERT-tiny checks pass on 95/100 inputs versus 98/100 remaining stable under attack evaluation. GPT-2 checks reportedly pass on 45/50 against clean top-20 candidates but only 20/50 with the vocabulary-tail check, versus 45/50 remaining stable empirically. The 45/50 restricted result is explicitly stated, although the text's attempted derivation from full-vocabulary agreement counts does not by itself establish it. An earlier 1.5 multiplier produced two PGD-confirmed false certificates. After calibration to 2.0, the paper reports no detected output contradictions across 450 input–radius pairs: 100 BERT-tiny and 50 GPT-2 inputs at three radii. These are calibration-linked finite checks. The alpha-CROWN comparison uses a quick-GELU surrogate and a different sample count, so it is not a controlled fidelity or speed comparison.

Twenty independently trained seeds reach at least 99.9% test accuracy. At epsilon=0.05, CPZ-guided and gradient-guided one-head models average 84.5% and 78.5% adversarial accuracy across all 20 seeds; outcomes differ on eight seeds, with CPZ-guided pruning winning all eight. The reported one-sided Wilcoxon p-value is 0.0042. At epsilon=0.02, means are 87.0% and 81.5%, with six differing outcomes. PGD uses 20 restarts and 50 steps. In the selected example both head removals preserve clean accuracy, while targeted PGD flips 18.3% versus 5.0% of the two heads' attention positions at epsilon=0.05. These are empirical attack outcomes, not certified accuracy bounds. Table 3 gives H0 the narrower entropy interval at epsilon=0.02, contrary to the surrounding prose's reversed entropy comparison.

experiment_summary: The paper reports certificate generation and verification for GPT-2 small, TinyLlama's 22-layer stack, and Llama-3.2-3B blocks 0, 5, and 10. Verification checks artifact hashes, recomputed metrics, and policy consistency. On an M-series machine with 24 GB RAM and the MPS backend, the reported TinyLlama five-block stress extraction takes about 30 seconds and full-block replay about 16 seconds at the stated sequence length of 256. Artifacts and verifier code are referenced externally rather than reproduced in the supplied text.

GPT-2's two-prompt baseline reports mean extraction error approximately 2.32e-7 and activation coverage approximately one. TinyLlama's 22-layer full sweep reports coverage approximately 0.945–1.0. Llama-3.2-3B blocks 0, 5, and 10 reportedly exceed activation coverage 0.94 and loss coverage 0.9, with reported total residuals on the order of 1e-2. The extraction procedure attributes residual errors to native-versus-interpreter numerical differences. TinyLlama stress coverage is configuration-sensitive: Section 6.2 reports block-15 mean coverage approximately 0.945 and a single-prompt minimum approximately 0.91, whereas Section 6.6 reports stress coverage approximately 0.955.
Specific finding: A TinyLlama stack assembled entirely from architecture-preserving copied block implementations can match the original model's average perplexity to approximately 6e-5 on a small stress-prompt set. The full-block experiment reports baseline and stitched average perplexities approximately 253.1618 and a stitched-minus-baseline difference approximately -6.0e-5 on the stress prompts. The aggregation formula underlying average perplexity is not specified. Section 6.4 separately evaluates selected-block stitching and reports mean per-layer MAE approximately 0.38, worst-layer MAE approximately 2.03, and maximum residual approximately 2.13; these are not established as measurements from the identical stitching configuration.
Specific finding: A fully stitched copied-block TinyLlama implementation can preserve the baseline model's next-token choices on a small authored semantic probe set. The fully stitched TinyLlama matches the baseline next token on every evaluated semantic prompt, yielding reported baseline-label agreement of 1.0. The number of prompts and numerical human-answer accuracy are not supplied. This evaluates a narrow prediction-agreement measure rather than general semantic correctness.
Specific finding: TinyLlama block implementations copied into an explicit interpreter can retain similar numerical replay errors and coverage when transferred from short technical prompts to a small authored stress set. In the prompt-shift experiment, block 0 mean error changes from 1.69e-3 to 1.76e-3 with coverage remaining 1.0; block 5 changes from 6.57e-3 to 6.07e-3 and coverage from 0.955 to 0.950; block 15 changes from 2.66e-2 to 2.38e-2 and coverage from 0.945 to 0.955. All five probed blocks reportedly retain certification coverage thresholds on both sets. These are two small hand-designed prompt collections, without a general distribution-shift guarantee.

Formal derivation: Theorem 1 and Appendix A apply the triangle inequality and surrogate-block Lipschitzness to obtain d_{i+1} <= L_i d_i + epsilon_i, then unroll the recurrence from d_0 = 0. This establishes the conditional mathematical bound. A separate Lean 4 formalization is reported, but its code is not reproduced in the supplied text.

Section 6.6 reports auto-LiRPA local L2 Lipschitz upper bounds approximately 1.1e3–1.9e3 for selected MLP sublayers on radius-1 L2 balls. Table 1 combines these with analytic attention constants to report hybrid block constants approximately 1.6e5–6.0e5. The paper states that substitution into the composition expression yields a bound many orders of magnitude above the observed maximum residual approximately 2.13, but supplies no numerical global bound. Ball centers, full analytic derivations, and coverage of propagated states are not provided.

Across scales 1.0, 0.5, 0.4, 0.33, 0.25, and 0, the selected reference scale 0.33 increases harmful refusal correctness from 0/12 to 3/12 while retaining approximately 12/12 benign correctness. Complete MLP deletion gives approximately 4/12 harmful correctness and 11/12 benign correctness. The reference scale is selected on the same corpus. Human-label metrics are said to be recorded in an external certificate, but their numerical results are not supplied.

For all reported block-and-scale configurations, benign answer correctness remains approximately 1.0 over 12 prompts and harmful refusal correctness remains 0.0 over 12 prompts under the heuristic classifier. No broader layer, head, or feature-direction search is performed.

Trained for two epochs with embedding and unembedding matrices frozen. The adapted model answered 72% of 50 evaluation questions correctly. The authors additionally report typo-tolerant person and state identification rates of 73.5% and 83.7%; the denominators underlying these percentages are unclear, and Appendix D's tolerance notation is inconsistent.

The authors report unsuccessful prompting attempts with and without in-context examples in Llama 3.3-70B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-32B. Two prompts are supplied, but trial counts and quantitative success criteria are absent. Claude 3.5 Haiku is reported to respond correctly to these prompts, motivating the restriction of the negative finding to the tested open-weight models and settings.

Section 2.3 reports monotonically decreasing mean verification F1 as k increases and a width optimum at 512. Across the six widths, the numbers of coordinates ever activated during training are 32, 54, 120, 170, 211, and 122. Numerical F1 values, uncertainty estimates, and a clear averaging rule for dead coordinates are not supplied in the readable text.

The reported percentage is below 3% during the first 1,000 updates, increases by 19.4 percentage points at 5,000, rises by 17.5 points from 10,000 to 20,000, falls by 31.8 points from 20,000 to 30,000, and rises by 55.9 points from 30,000 to 40,000. It exceeds 99% at step 143,000. These are descriptive fixed-probe measurements; no causal test distinguishes representational reorganization from other explanations.

Physics, Mathematics, Economics, Law, and Philosophy are reported to have nonzero activations from the earliest optimization steps. History, Biology, Chemistry, and Business remain inactive until roughly 10,000 updates and approach saturation around 30,000–60,000. Proposed explanations involving corpus frequency and contextual complexity are not tested.

Section 5 reports early-probe reactivation for SAEs trained at layers 0 and 2, localized responses for layer-10 and layer-15 SAEs, and broader late responses for a layer-30 SAE. Appendix A.2 describes related subject-level disappear-and-return patterns, including History and Business. Probe identity and layer numbering are not described consistently across these passages. No causal intervention or quantitative semantic-preservation test is supplied.

The reported global activation percentage is below 5% for models under 200M and increases by 92.9 percentage points between 160M and 410M to approximately 95%. It peaks at 2.8B, and larger models remain above 98%. Biology, Chemistry, Physics, and Mathematics rise from at most 10% at 160M to at least 90% at 410M. Business follows a more variable trajectory and reaches stable activation of at least 90% above 1B. No independent alignment split or behavioral knowledge test is reported; the unfinished History bullet supplies no usable numerical result.

Against full-pipeline accuracy of 82.3%, Table 3 reports 77.4% without SAE decomposition, 74.8% using the last layer instead of selected layers, 78.2% using only correct-answer features instead of the feature differential, and 79.6% using Verify output as a classifier without Elicit. The source does not fully specify the replacement implementations or report uncertainty.
Specific finding: Filtering candidate SAE directions by correct-answer sensitivity improves reported TruthfulQA accuracy and false positive rate within the specified MechELK pipeline. Removing CKS filtering changes elicitation accuracy from 82.3% to 76.1%, detection rate from 91.4% to 88.2%, FPR from 12.7% to 24.3%, and cosine consistency from 0.89 to 0.74. No ablation uncertainty is supplied. Removing layer selection causes a larger accuracy decline than removing verification, contrary to the accompanying prose.

Table 2 reports MechELK DR/FPR of 91.4%/12.7%, compared with 81.2%/28.4% for direct probing, 83.7%/22.1% for CCS, 79.4%/19.8% for RepE, 85.3%/18.6% for SAE-Probe, and 82.1%/21.3% for activation patching. The direct-probing FPR comparison implies approximately 55.3% relative reduction, contradicting the stated 34%; the CCS comparison implies approximately 42.5%.
Specific finding: The specified answer-conditioned MechELK procedure achieves higher reported candidate-answer accuracy than the evaluated CCS implementation on TruthfulQA, Quirky LM, and the curated DAB. Table 5 reports MechELK/CCS accuracy percentages of 82.3/74.2, 83.1/76.8, and 81.2/67.3 for Llama-3-8B; 86.7/78.5, 87.4/81.2, and 85.9/72.1 for Llama-3-70B; and 80.1/72.1, 81.8/74.3, and 79.6/65.9 for Mistral, ordered as TruthfulQA, Quirky LM, DAB. Equal-weight means calculated from these cells are approximately 83.1% versus 73.6%, a 9.5 percentage-point difference, rather than the headline 84.7% versus 78.5%. Table 1 additionally reports higher MechELK accuracy than all five listed baselines in its six selected cells. Evaluation denominators, complete split accounting, quirky checkpoint construction, and information-matched controls are insufficiently specified.

The text reports mean pairwise cosine consistency of 0.89 for MechELK, 0.68 for CCS, and 0.61 for direct probing. Sampling details, uncertainty, handling of potentially different selected layers, and baseline direction construction are insufficiently specified. The figure's plot is unavailable, so only the textual statistics are extracted.

The supplied purported proof invokes derivative linearity and the implicit function theorem, but does not establish the conclusion. Positive local sensitivity need not overcome competing-answer margins, and intervened output dominance would not imply linear ranking of answer-appended states. Equation 10 also substitutes probability finite differences for exact log-probability derivatives. No valid sufficiency result is established by this derivation.

The proof sketch assumes overlapping verified feature sets and a shared low-dimensional knowledge subspace, then invokes reconstruction error and an angular triangle inequality. It supplies no explicit delta bound, feature-selection stability argument, control of CKS weights or direction norms, or identification across selected layers. The reported paraphrase experiment measures observed cosine similarity without varying reconstruction quality and therefore does not establish the claimed guarantee.

Evaluates fine-tuned versions of released BERT-base checkpoints with selected coordinates removed. Removal of coordinate 218 or both coordinates becomes clearly damaging after approximately 80,000 steps; degradation generally increases until approximately one million steps and then fluctuates. Coordinate 674 alone has a different, smaller effect. Repeating with fixed classification-head initialization preserves the broad pattern, addressing that particular source of variation without isolating every cause of checkpoint differences.

BERT coordinate 381 has especially large MNLI and MLM effects around layers 4–6, coinciding with high frequency correlation. Coordinate 308 has larger late-layer MLM effects despite declining correlation, with a final-layer exception acknowledged. RoBERTa coordinates 588 and 77 exhibit analogous distinctions, but Appendix C describes additional peaks and deviations that prevent treating the profiles as universal classes.

Formal derivation: Equations 10–12 enclose each branch using an affine function of the common input plus a remainder set. Subtracting the common-input affine terms and taking the Minkowski difference of remainder sets encloses every pointwise module–replacement difference. Formal derivation: Appendix C.2.5 bounds the selection threshold by the Kth-largest lower and upper preactivation endpoints. Strict comparisons identify definitely selected and definitely excluded gates. If a gates are definitely selected, exactly K-a uncertain gates are selected. Summing the K-a largest nonnegative upper contribution bounds and K-a smallest nonpositive lower contribution bounds encloses every uncertain decoded contribution. The procedure relaxes joint attainability and therefore can be conservative.

MS-HVP K=5 improves CMD over EAP in six of nine listed settings and worsens it in three; single-step HVP improves CMD in three. Gemma-2-2B MCQA improves from 0.506 to 0.414 with MS-HVP, while Llama-3.1-8B IOI worsens from 0.031 to 0.379. Llama arithmetic EAP-IG CMD is 0.048 versus approximately 0.48 for EAP and HVP variants. These are point estimates without circuit-level uncertainty intervals; some accompanying prose conflicts with the completed table.

location: Section 3.3 after Proposition 2; Conclusion; Appendix E.8

experiment_summary: Table 2 reports HVP and MS-HVP for three Llama-3.1-8B tasks and Gemma-2-9B factual completion. Llama IOI top-five error falls from 19.78% to 8.42% with HVP and 3.54% with MS-HVP. Claimed 2.4–28.7 GPU-hour large-model runs conflict with the approximately 25 GPU-hour total. The approximately 25 GPU-day per-component IG cost is an estimate; all-at-once EAP-IG is separately evaluated at 8B scale in Table 16.
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Table 2; Appendices E.1 and E.8

experiment_summary: Activation and path patching implicate head 11.10 and upstream heads 5.8, 6.1, 6.15, and 7.2. Head 11.10 attends from the predicate position to the second middle-term position with reported mean weight 0.15 ± 0.07. Its static embedding–OV–unembedding matrix has a negative diagonal over 26 letters. Value patching and attention inspection identify nine notable positive and negative mover candidates. The text attributes early middle-term preference to long induction and later correction to suppression and predicate movement. Static analysis omits normalization; head 11.1 versus 11.11 and the path-patching direction descriptions are inconsistent.
location: Sections 3.1–3.3; Figure 3; Appendices C, G, and H

experiment_summary: Cumulative head removal and restoration are evaluated by mean predicate-minus-middle-term logit difference. The text reports recovery to the original symbolic margin when retaining the circuit and degradation when circuit heads are removed. Exact curve values, uncertainty estimates, and a fully consistent consolidated head inventory are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Circuit knockouts reduce performance in both concrete datasets. Retaining the symbolic circuit meets the reported belief-consistent recovery criterion but fails to restore the full-model margin for belief-inconsistent examples. Exact recovery magnitudes are not given in the accessible text.

Replacing the subject and measuring clean-minus-corrupted completion margins yields reported degradation of 0.66 ± 1.27 in the non-symbolic setting and 0.00 ± 0.64 in the symbolic setting. The text does not define the uncertainty notation or provide a targeted statistical comparison. These input-substitution effects do not by themselves identify the responsible internal pathways.

Corruption-based patching and OV analyses are applied across checkpoints, with cross-family suppression heads manually selected. The text reports related GPT-2 patterns, although Small has reversed all-term residual effects. Pythia-70M/160M appear erratic; Pythia-410M/1B and Llama-3.2-1B show compatible patterns. Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B suppression occurs at the final position. Table 3 reports symbolic accuracies of 0.19, 0.00, 0.99, and 0.30 for the four Pythia models, and 1.00 for Llama and both Qwen models. Thus compatible diagnostics are not restricted to high-accuracy checkpoints. No quantitative cross-model mechanism-similarity metric is supplied.

The text reports that patching and OV diagnostic patterns of GPT-2 Medium fine-tuned on argumentative texts are nearly indistinguishable from its pretrained counterpart. No quantitative similarity measure or selective mechanism-preservation test is supplied. Presence of related diagnostics before fine-tuning supports pre-existence, but the comparison does not track mechanism development during pretraining.
models_studied: ["GPT-2 Medium (345M)", "GPT-2 Medium fine-tuned for critical thinking"]

experiment_summary: Scaling layer-1 mlp_out at position 2 raises canonicity smoothly from 0.78 at scale 0 to 0.95 at scale 1, followed by decline at larger scales. Position-1-only scaling has little effect. Layer-0 MLP deletion causes comparable damage, whereas deletion beyond layer 3 leaves canonicity above 0.93. These observations do not establish the paper's stronger interpretation that discrete key-value retrieval is ruled out.

Last-position resid_post patches reach 80% source-canonicity gap closure at layer 2 for two-token splits, layer 5 for first-fragment-different three-token splits, and layer 6 for six-token splits. The two-to-three-token transition therefore adds about three layers, with smaller marginal increases thereafter. Among 4,609 three-token pairs differing only in the middle fragment, the threshold is reached at layer 3.

Replacing intermediate resid_post states in successful runs with failed-run states produces canonicity drops concentrated in 2–3-layer windows that shift approximately one layer later per position. Corresponding positions show similar timing across three-, four-, and five-token words. Joint intermediate-position corruption produces peak drops of 9% for three-token words and 21% for five-token words, relative to uncorrupted canonicity. Joint drops exceed summed singleton drops by factors of 1.4 for four-token and 1.6 for five-token words.

Tables 5–6 report two-token recovery depths of 1–3 for six RoPE checkpoints and 5–10 for five learned-absolute checkpoints. Four-token depths are 5–6 versus 11–17. BLOOM-7B1 reaches the threshold at layers 5, 10, and 17 for two-, three-, and four-token splits. Width, depth, tokenizer, activation, corpus, and parameter-count categories cross the observed regime boundary; no matched positional-encoding intervention is performed.
location: Section 5; Appendices F and H, Tables 5–6

experiment_summary: CLTs trained on five million UniRef50 sequences are evaluated using family-classification and fitness-prediction readouts after replacement and latent selection. Reported test-set F1 and Spearman correlations demonstrate operational task preservation under specified replacement semantics, without independently establishing native mechanism recovery.
location: Sections 2.1–2.2 and 3.1; Appendices A–D and G.1–G.2

experiment_summary: Appendix E.1 reports a large performance gap between sequential replacement supplied with original attention outputs and autonomous full replacement, and reports the best performance for direct CLT reconstruction from original layer inputs. The accessible prose supplies qualitative comparisons but no numerical aggregate gap; unseen figure values are not inferred. The experiment does not isolate a unique mechanism causing the degradation.

The windowed ESM2-35M experiment reduces reported CLT parameters from 207M to 125M and training duration from seven to four days, a reported 1.75-fold speedup. Family circuit performance recovery is 82%, compared with 85% for ordinary CLTs and 68% for PLTs. No uncertainty estimates or matched-resource optimization study is supplied.

Appendix E.1 reports family node overlap of 81% ± 21% for ESM2-8M and 79% ± 15% for ESM2-35M after sampling family sequences. Function-circuit overlap is 96% ± 4% and 97% ± 4%, respectively, with the smallest circuit as reference across folds. These comparisons do not evaluate independently retrained CLT dictionaries or establish semantic equivalence.

Table 1 reports mean, maximum, top-10%, and top-20% CNN scores for seven assays selected for extensive multiple-mutant data. Circuit pipelines exceed CAA and random baselines on every displayed score entry. Direct ProtoMech versus sequential PLT has 19 strict wins, one displayed tie, and eight losses across 28 assay–metric entries; the reported 71% apparently includes the tie. Table 8 favors ProtoMech over original-model-logit selection on 27 of 28 displayed entries. Table 9 favors ProtoMech over two black-box optimization baselines on all four metrics in two selected assays. Evaluators share an architecture and assay data with selection models, and no experimental validation of generated candidates is reported.
location: Section 3.2; Appendices C.2, D.3–D.4, and E.3; Tables 1 and 5–9
Section 2.2; Appendix D, Discovery with Supervised Models; Appendices D.1–D.2

experiment_summary: Introduces penetration and evaluates robustness using 1,000 bootstrap resamples, Procrustes comparisons, and thresholds from 0.90 to 0.99. Appendix F reports core-cohort model-ranking correlations above 0.95 between the default threshold and each alternative threshold. The null calibration contains an arithmetic inconsistency: 0.997±0.003 places 0.95 approximately 15.7, rather than 300, reported standard deviations below the mean. The near-perfect CKA–Procrustes association is reported without fully specifying its aggregation.

Reports overall penetration from 0.036 in Qwen-2.5-1.5B to 0.688 in OLMo-2-7B, with affected layers described as contiguous bands. Fourteen of seventeen models are described as inconsistent with changes restricted to the first and last two to three layers. Cross-checkpoint differences confound architecture, training, and chat templates; the supplied rendering does not expose the heatmap images.
Specific finding: Selected persona and formatting instructions produce greater baseline-relative CKA penetration than selected safety and minimal instructions across a diverse checkpoint panel. Core-cohort mean penetration is 50.3%±19.5% for Persona, 44.5%±14.2% for Format, 26.2%±24.5% for Domain, 7.3%±9.2% for Safety, and 4.9%±9.7% for Minimal. Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon tests report p=0.010 for Persona and Format against Minimal and Safety, and p=1.000 for Safety against Minimal. The latter does not establish equivalence. Persona versus safety penetration is 32.1% versus 4.8% in Qwen-2.5-32B, 81.5% versus 9.1% in LLaMA-3.1-70B, and 33.0% versus 5.1% in Qwen-2.5-72B.
Specific finding: System-prompt penetration can change differently with model size in Qwen and LLaMA-family checkpoint sweeps. Qwen penetration rises from 3.6%, 13.9%, and 17.9% at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B to 18.8%, 19.4%, and 20.1% at 14B, 32B, and 72B. The source reports overlapping intervals at the largest sizes, but uncertainty is variously described as confidence intervals and query-subset standard deviations. The LLaMA-family comparison rises from 35.7% at 3B to 59.4% at Nemotron 8B and 64.2% at 70B. Gemma's reported 2B generational difference, 33.3% to 46.2%, also exceeds the observed Gemma 2 size difference, 46.2% at 2B versus 45.2% at 9B.

Pearson correlations across layers range from 0.987 to 1.000, averaging 0.997, across the fourteen core models. LLaMA-3.1-70B and Qwen-2.5-72B each have reported r=0.998 and p<0.001. These compare two profiles of similarity to baseline, rather than directly testing equality of restrictive and permissive activations or causal pathways.

Sixteen of seventeen models satisfy |delta_low_CKA|>|delta_high_CKA|+0.01; SmolLM2-1.7B is the exception. All three larger models reportedly show affected-set changes above 0.42 and control changes below 0.03. Delta is defined as patched minus original code fraction, but later described as degraded compliance, leaving sign interpretation inconsistent. Selecting five lowest-CKA layers need not select five layers below 0.95. Prompt-condition aggregation and replacement positions are insufficiently specified, and reasoning-augmented models receive longer generation windows.
location: Sections 3.3, 5.5, and 5.9; Appendix B; Section 6, Limitations

experiment_summary: Layerwise logistic regression with C=1.0, 1,000 maximum iterations, and five-fold cross-validation over 1,900 examples reportedly exceeds 85% accuracy at every layer, averaging 97.8%, against stated chance approximately 21%. The source does not specify prompt-disjoint or query-grouped folds, token pooling, or independent instruction-wording evaluation. High aggregate five-way accuracy is not a separately reported safety-category accuracy. Larger-model probing is explicitly deferred.

Reports Spearman rho=0.761, p<0.001 across seventeen checkpoints. Excluding format prompts gives rho=0.645, p=0.032, but that analysis's checkpoint denominator is not specified. OLMo-2-7B has reported response divergence 0.683 and SmolLM2-1.7B 0.493. No prospective prediction on new checkpoints or control for checkpoint-level training differences is presented.

Formal derivation: Proposition 1 and Appendix G expand the CKA numerator and denominator using A=XᵀX and C=EᵀX. Both have identical linear contributions 2⟨A,C⟩, establishing cancellation and quadratic-order local deviation for fixed nonzero X. The paper additionally states 1−CKA(X,X+E)≤2||E||_F²/||XᵀX||_F+O(||E||_F³/||XᵀX||_F^(3/2)); its final bounding steps are abbreviated. The strongest explicit derivation concerns first-order cancellation. No empirical model or sample size is part of this formal result.

Section 5.6 reports within-model Spearman correlations of 0.71–0.95 between middle-layer perturbation Frobenius norm and penetration, with p<0.001. Effective rank, defined by entropy of normalized singular values, has correlations of −0.59 to −0.79, but magnitude-controlled partial correlations are 0.11–0.25 with p>0.30. No controlled perturbation experiment separates these factors. These associations are not a test establishing a monotonic consequence of the theoretical upper bound.

location: Section 6, Implications for safety and Why safety is shallow

experiment_summary: The shared-centroid classical condition has Hungarian distances 0.068 for DinoV2 and 0.112 for Pythia, versus 0.433 and 0.200 for randomly initialized classical TopK and 0.243 and 0.170 for full archetypal TopK. Removing convex-hull enforcement and the residual bound gives identical results to shared-centroid classical TopK because the two implementations perform equivalent unconstrained computations. Comparisons use paired dictionaries without reported uncertainty.

Randomizing archetypal combination weights and relaxation offsets produces initial inter-run distance approximately 0.88. Both classical and archetypal distances decrease, but after 50M tokens mean minimum cosine distance is approximately 0.35 for archetypal TopK versus 0.17 for classical TopK. The source describes slower archetypal stabilization, but supplies no hyperparameter sweep, repeated-pair uncertainty, or asymptotic convergence test.

For DinoV2, full archetypal R² is 0.542, compared with 0.570 for shared-centroid classical TopK and 0.573 for randomly initialized classical TopK. For Pythia, corresponding values are 0.758, 0.914, and 0.937. The constraint-removal implementation matches shared-centroid classical TopK exactly by construction. No uncertainty estimates or hyperparameter sweep are reported.

Mean pairwise centroid cosine similarity changes from 0.362 without centering to 0.002 with centering for Pythia, and from 0.298 to −0.001 for DinoV2. These measurements demonstrate a preprocessing-dependent change in centroid cosine geometry; the broader effect on learned cross-run stability is argued rather than separately quantified through a matched centered-versus-uncentered endpoint table.

The authors report inspecting the public Colab and Overcomplete package and finding no centering or standardization before k-means or during training, whereas the prior paper states that its data matrix was element-wise standardized. This is a reported code audit, not an empirical rerun establishing the provenance of all published stability values.
location: Section 4.2; Appendix B, Fel et al. code audit

experiment_summary: HDBSCAN groups InceptionV1 activations into visually recognizable clusters and GPT2-small token activations from a random Pile test-set sample into lexical and semantic clusters. Hamming-distance clustering of binarized GPT2-small codes also yields interpretable examples, including LaTeX references, decimal points, and time spans. Interpretations come from example inspection. The authors report that most clusters appear monosemantic, without a quantified purity evaluation or an enumerated sample size. Prior code-clustering work is explicitly cited.

The authors fit 64 NMF components to GPT2-small layer-4 activations, compare sample cosine similarities with HDBSCAN code-cluster labels, and inspect high-similarity examples. They report largely monosemantic directions and analogous InceptionV1 examples. Plot ranges are manually restricted, and the illustrated GPT2 comparison omits the smallest clusters. No aggregate coherence metric is supplied; Figures 14–15 have no explanatory captions in the supplied rendering.

Same-class and different-class pairs are compared in trained and untrained InceptionV1 using normalized Hamming-distance/Euclidean-distance ratios. Only the trained network shows lower intra-class density. Figure 18 reports Welch's t(1873.3) = -14.7, p = 3.8e-46, and 99% bootstrap intervals. The difference is described as small and grows toward output layers. Appendix A adds spherical-interpolation analyses, including means over 200 image interpolations; the supplied text does not specify a complete pair-sampling protocol or numerical effect sizes.
models_studied: ["Trained PyTorch InceptionV1/GoogLeNet variant with batch normalization", "Untrained PyTorch InceptionV1/GoogLeNet variant with batch normalization"]

experiment_summary: The authors scale hidden activations in InceptionV1 and report changes in predicted classes, including a cougar image becoming classified as a cheetah. Section 2.1.3 plots class logits under inception3a scaling and describes additional class changes at large magnitudes. No representative transition rate or comprehensive scaling benchmark is supplied.

Scaling hidden activations at inception3a reveals a boundary-density peak between the ordinary activation and the origin, which the authors interpret as partial evidence for an inner semantic-validity bound. However, outward scaling produces numerous class changes in low-density regions, contrary to the broader prediction. No aggregate transition-prediction accuracy or systematic boundary-to-transition correspondence is reported.

The main text reports an inner local-density peak during radial scaling for image-induced and Gaussian-noise activations, with the peak absent in untrained networks. Figure 20 describes inception3a image examples. Appendix B provides the controls, but their plots are unavailable in the supplied rendering. The authors also report unexplained rank-collapse-like behavior in the untrained variant.
models_studied: ["Trained PyTorch InceptionV1/GoogLeNet variant with batch normalization", "Untrained PyTorch InceptionV1/GoogLeNet variant with batch normalization"]

experiment_summary: On the reported 8,617-note corpus, with a 4,334-note subset for models of at least 27B parameters, Section 4.1 reports best-depth single-feature AUC ranges of 0.80–0.92 in Qwen and 0.70–0.90 in Gemma; logistic-probe macro AUC is 0.90–0.93 in ten models. Appendix E separately reports item-split AUCs of 0.8814 for Qwen3-8B-Base and 0.8810 for II-Medical-8B, plus patient-split AUC 0.8772 for Qwen3-8B-Base across 1,997 patients. That table does not clearly identify its readout as the same single-feature metric. Main-text patient-split and appendix item-split descriptions differ, and the listed chapter counts do not reconcile with the corpus total.
location: Section 4.1; Figure 1; Appendices C and E; Table 5

experiment_summary: Across seventeen chapters in five Qwen-family models, the mean number of active selected features out of ten is 10.0 on full notes, 2.0–2.7 on bare diagnosis labels, 0.3–0.6 on adjacent-chapter notes, and 0–0.016 on fifteen short geography, sports, and food sentences. Available chapter-title results range from 1.3 to 2.9. Gemma is described qualitatively as following the same pattern without a numerical table.

A fresh TopK SAE with 65,536 features and K=100, trained on II-Medical-8B layer-24 activations, achieves reported explained variance of 97.4% and 0.11% dead features. Its decoded chapter directions have mean cosine 0.835 with borrowed-parent directions, ranging from 0.784 to 0.865 across all seventeen chapters.

Table 1 reports held-out probability increases of 0.0406–0.0780 in five Qwen-family models and 0.0014–0.0193 in six Gemma-family models, with 5,000-resample bootstrap intervals. Qwen intervals exclude zero; Gemma-3-27B-pt and Gemma-3-27B-it intervals include zero. Reported random-adjusted effects range from −0.003 for MedGemma-4B-it to 0.094 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, with Gemma-3-27B-it approximately zero. Appendix G states that the random-adjusted values for Qwen3-8B-Base, Qwen3.5-9B-Base, and II-Medical-8B use earlier best configurations. Shuffled-label and wrong-chapter control designs are described, negative-dose effects are asserted, and the unembedding comparison reports cosine 0.003 in one Qwen setting, but comprehensive numerical outcomes for those controls are not supplied.

The study tracks seventeen chapter projections in 170 generations per model, ten held-out notes per chapter, with a 2,000-token cap. Base models continue notes and chat models produce clinical assessments. The text reports positive dominance across generated positions and a Qwen3.5-27B effect size near 0.5 from approximately token 100 through token 2,000. II-Medical-8B has a median generation length of 359 tokens and a trace ending near 500; Appendix I describes its opening dominance as near zero. Readout layers are selected with a finite-token-coverage constraint. No additional values are inferred from the unavailable plot images.

Matched-specialty prompts increase chapter accuracy by 2.94–11.18 percentage points over no role. Nine Table 8 sign tests have p<0.01; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base has p=0.087. Matched-versus-counterfactual projection t statistics range from 2.90 to 9.53. Appendix J reports counterfactual accuracy within 0.3 points of baseline in Qwen and approximately two points in Gemma instruct models. On Qwen3-8B-Base, matched versus random-specialty projection differs by 1.3010, whereas random specialty versus baseline differs by −0.0815 with p=0.83. Main-text causal-layer and appendix persona-effect-layer descriptions differ.

Table 9 compares identical notes, layers, and doses. Qwen3-8B-Base layer 25 reaches +0.038 probability change with SAE decoding versus −0.005 raw at dose 30. II-Medical-8B layer 17 reaches +0.073 versus +0.049 at dose 100, while both are +0.001 at dose 3. Qwen3-30B-A3B layer 45 gives +0.009 versus −0.029 at dose 10, with both directions harmful at larger displayed doses. Contrary to the prose, raw Qwen3-8B directions yield small positive changes of +0.002 and +0.003 at doses 3 and 10. Separate held-out selection details and uncertainty for this comparison are not fully specified.

With injection active throughout generation, Table 10 reports accuracy-fraction changes of +0.0111 for Qwen3-8B-Base (p=0.047; 74 changed answers), +0.0234 for Qwen3.5-9B-Base (p=0.001; 136 changed answers), and +0.0123 for Gemma-3-4B-it (p=0.080; 118 changed answers). Each row reports true-direction performance above random above wrong-chapter steering. The combined Fisher p is 0.00046; the individual Gemma result is not statistically significant at 0.05. Relative doses are reported as 0.55–1.77 for the Qwen rows and 0.55 for Gemma. Details of dose selection and generation-to-chapter scoring are limited.

A frozen higher-dominance preference rule is evaluated after three cases are excluded from 41 rated cases based on reported capability-related failures. The remaining 38 cases produce 228 judgments, including 34 ties. Agreement is 55.7% of 194 non-tie judgments (p=0.13), 66.0% of 97 larger-gap judgments (p=0.002), and 76.0% of 50 largest-gap judgments (38/50; p=3.1×10⁻⁴). Raters are a senior orthopedic resident and a junior medical student; three-way inter-rater kappa is 0.43. The reported binomial tests pool repeated judgments from the same cases and raters without a described clustering adjustment. Aligned-versus-unprimed agreement remains near chance.

After exclusions, pooled non-tie judgments favor unprimed over matched-specialty responses 41–23 (reported exact binomial p=0.033), and unprimed over adversarial-specialty responses 50–20 (p=0.0004). Matched versus adversarial preferences are 36–24 (p=0.155). Comments identify invented details, persona authority, specialty intrusion, and calibration problems. These secondary comparisons reuse two raters across the same 38 cases, and no clustering-adjusted analysis is described.

Five-fold stratified logistic-regression probing yields Set B AUROC 0.933 and 0.954 for 1B instruct/base, 0.981 and 0.988 for 8B instruct/base, and 0.987 and 0.989 for 9B instruct/base, versus Set A 0.999–1.000. Differences are 1.1–6.6 AUROC percentage points. The paper reports Welch-test p<0.05 in 12/18 model-by-activation-type comparisons, without a stated multiple-comparison correction or a matched keyword-removal design. Its stated 0.125 chance baseline is appropriate to eight-class accuracy, not standard AUROC.

Binary decoding reaches ceiling earlier and at higher AUROC than eight-class clinical decoding. Table 9 displays within-set residual patching success of 75–87.5% for Set A and 44.6–62.5% for Set B in three models. The text reports 100% success for different-emotion cross-set patches on 17 pairs, versus 75–87.5% for same-emotion patches with eight pairs, at selected peak layers. However, Section 6.1 and Figure 7 define success as movement toward the donor emotion while interpreting it as correct target-emotion categorization regardless of donor identity. This contradiction prevents using the reported patching rates as clear evidence of selective salience transfer. Layer matching between the binary and categorical comparison is also unclear across Figure 4 and the peak-layer tables.
location: Sections 5.3, 6.1, and 9.1; Tables 6 and 9; Figures 4 and 7

experiment_summary: Table 10 reports clinical versus keyword-rich critical attention/FFN counts of 12/14 versus 1/4 in Llama-1B-Instruct and 7/10 versus 2/3 in Llama-1B-base. Clinical counts are at least as large in every displayed model-component comparison, with ties common in larger models. Section 6.2 inconsistently gives 13 clinical critical attention layers for Llama-1B-Instruct before reporting 12 in the table and later prose. Knockouts evaluate categorization, not a separately reported binary affect-detection endpoint.

For clinical stimuli, Table 10 reports critical attention/FFN counts of 12/14 and 7/10 in 1B instruct/base, 1/4 and 0/2 in 8B instruct/base, and 0/0 and 0/2 in 9B instruct/base. Noise replacements are described as yielding the same qualitative pattern with higher counts, but corresponding numerical results are not supplied. These are raw critical-layer counts across networks of different depths.

Base-model Set B categorical AUROC is 0.954 for Llama-3.2-1B, 0.988 for Llama-3-8B, and 0.989 for Gemma-2-9B, with binary AUROC reported as 1.000. Corresponding instruction-tuned categorical scores are 0.933, 0.981, and 0.987. No equivalence test establishes identical representations or capabilities, and no training-trajectory intervention identifies when these representations formed.

Table 6 reports tuned node AUCs of 0.854, 0.821, and 0.945 for IOI, Greater-than, and Docstring; fixed-parameter values are 0.853±0.016, 0.832±0.058, and 0.915±0.014. Tuned co-occurrence-based AUCs are 0.863, 0.963, and 0.974; fixed values are 0.840±0.016, 0.856±0.021, and 0.914±0.020. Tuned values exceed the listed Table 6 baselines, while fixed Docstring values do not. These baselines are attributed to Conmy et al.; Figure 2 uses a different aggregation across metrics, and Section 4.1 reports an ACDC advantage for edge-level Docstring. Appendix B.1 reports identification of reference heads L10H7 and L11H10, the negative name movers, and previous-token head L2H2. SAE training is described as converging on the evaluation set, so this is not a fully independent held-out assessment.
models_studied: ["GPT-2 Small", "Docstring model inconsistently specified: main text says GPT-2 Small; appendices imply a smaller model"]
location: Section 4.1; Figure 2; Appendices B.1, B.3, and F, Table 6

experiment_summary: Appendix E.3 varies SAE-training size separately from the number of prompts used to count codes. Reported near-maximal performance occurs around five to ten SAE-training prompts; increasing training data reduces AUC for IOI and Greater-than in these sweeps. IOI and Docstring also attain near-maximal recovery with small counting sets, while Greater-than requires all 250 positive and 250 negative prompts. The prose refers to ten counting examples, whereas Figure 23 labels counting sizes per class, leaving the exact small-set denominator ambiguous. Numerical plotted AUCs are unavailable.

The selected 40/144 IOI heads achieve mean logit difference 3.62 versus 3.55 for the full model and 4.11 for the 26-head reference. On 100 Greater-than examples, 29/144 heads achieve probability difference 76.54% and cutoff sharpness 5.76%, versus 76.96% and 5.57% for the full model and 71.30% and 5.50% for the nine-head reference. Appendix B.2 supplies the correct Greater-than head counts, unlike the combined main-text table. Excluded heads receive subject-swapped IOI activations or Greater-than activations with start-year suffix 01. Figure 5 and accompanying prose report matching or exceeding the tested EAP configuration across the displayed metrics and thresholds; numerical curves and significance tests are not supplied. Standalone circuit selection maximizes reference-label F1.

Section 4.2 describes broadly stable AUC for IOI and Docstring and some degradation for Greater-than as width and penalty increase. Appendix L reports relatively stable performance for intermediate co-occurrence budgets, with deterioration at extremes. F1-optimal thresholds are similar for IOI and Greater-than but differ substantially for Docstring in Table 7. The main text and Appendix L recommend half the pair budget, while Table 6 specifies a quarter for its fixed-parameter results. Search counts also differ between Section 4.2 and Figure 36's caption. No universal threshold or out-of-task robustness test is supplied.
location: Section 4.2; Appendices F and L, Table 7 and Figures 35–36

experiment_summary: Appendix D.1 compares preceding-century Range negatives, suffix-01 Year negatives, letter-corrupted Random negatives, unrelated text, and randomized Copy prompts, using five SAE seeds per construction. Range negatives give the best reported Greater-than recovery. Appendix D.2 reports reduced IOI node AUC when unrelated Pile negatives are added, with five training runs per point. Exact numerical effect sizes are not available in the supplied figure text.

Section 4 reports typically under 15 seconds for GPT-2 Small and under one minute for GPT-2 XL. Appendix A.4 reports under three seconds and under 45 seconds respectively, and conditionally discusses reducing GPT-2 XL time below ten seconds with ten training prompts. Figure 7 distinguishes ten versus 100 SAE-training prompts and a 200-positive-example counting configuration. All experiments are reported to use one 32-GB Tesla V100. The supplied rendering does not expose the individual timing curves.

Appendix G evaluates reverse, fraction-of-previous-tokens, sort, and sort-by-frequency compiled models. Negative examples zero Q/K/V vectors associated with nonzero weight matrices and add Gaussian noise to vectors associated with zero matrices. Ten sampled positive/negative examples train each SAE; all 500 examples supply code counts. Reported ROC AUC is 1.0 for all four tasks. The corruption explicitly uses activity structure closely tied to the reference labels, limiting what this demonstrates about discovery.
models_studied: ["Tracr reverse transformer", "Tracr fracprev transformer", "Tracr sort transformer", "Tracr sortfreq transformer"]

experiment_summary: Appendix H constructs 25 positive and 25 negative prompts and trains on ten examples. In a pretrained two-layer attention-only model with eight heads per layer, node selection reportedly reaches near-zero clean-to-circuit KL around 12–15 retained heads, with other components zero-ablated. The suite covers Bias in Bios, Amazon Reviews, Europarl, GitHub, and AG News, with 4,000 training and 1,000 test examples per binary task. Table 1 reports top-one test accuracy of 0.7161 for ATM, 0.7698 for TopK, 0.7154 for JumpReLU, and 0.6379 for the standard SAE. No significance assessment establishes that ATM's small numerical advantage over JumpReLU is reliable.

experiment_summary: The authors perturb selected rows and columns of attention projections and FFN.down. In Table 5, perturbing five Bottom dimensions in 7B yields perplexity 64,181.316 versus 6.552 for random dimensions. For 13B with 100,000 localization samples, five Bottom dimensions in Attn.o columns and Attn.k/q/v rows yield perplexity 5,283.898 in Table 7, versus 7.486 for the opposite orientation in Table 6. Controls remain near six in these examples. Section 3.4 additionally reports that perturbing coordinates 2100 and 4743 across layers is especially disruptive in 13B, but the Figure 4 curves are unavailable. These comparisons establish coordinate sensitivity rather than exclusive linguistic function.

Table 8 reports baseline perplexity 5.865. Resetting the L1-N2100 weight to one raises it to 83,224.078; multiplying that weight by ten raises it to 4,363.462. The listed control interventions leave perplexity between 5.858 and 5.866. Section 3.4 reports nonsensical generation from the prefix 'Fudan University is located in' after fourfold amplification of the selected coordinate; the actual Figure 5 outputs are unavailable. The evaluation corpus for Table 8, original parameter value, and repeated-run uncertainty are not specified, so resetting to one cannot be characterized quantitatively as a small perturbation.

The paper evaluates LLaMA-family checkpoints on four examination benchmarks. Chinese-LLaMA-7B and Open-Chinese-LLaMA-7B received 30B and 100B additional Chinese pretraining tokens, respectively; their C-Eval, Gaokao-Bench, and AGI-Eval scores are described as almost matching the original LLaMA-7B despite improved Chinese competence. LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA-13B reportedly outperform Open-Chinese-LLaMA-7B on all four benchmarks, including MMLU. Exact Figure 6 scores are unavailable, the language improvement is asserted rather than quantified here, and checkpoint differences do not isolate effects of data, compute, scale, or evaluation format.

The proposed functional interpretation receives indirect tests through low-drift parameter selection, matched-count perturbations, 30-language perplexity evaluations, and Chinese-training recovery evaluated in Chinese and English. Perturbation and recovery results are consistent with shared linguistic machinery, conditional on the perplexity and functional-specificity assumptions. They also remain compatible with disruption of general computational bottlenecks; no retained-region sufficiency test or selective language-versus-nonlanguage intervention is supplied.

experiment_summary: Humans and GPT-4o rated activation contexts for 500 randomly sampled features. The prose reports over 80% identical ratings, around 15% differing by one or two points, and no differences exceeding two points. This tests agreement about safety relevance rather than mechanistic correctness; exact figure values are unavailable.

GPT-4o rated two equal-sized groups of 100 features. The authors report that contrast-ranked features concentrated near rating five and had higher mean and median relevance than random features. No numerical group averages or test statistics are supplied in readable text. Selected qualitative examples illustrate privacy, refusal, stereotypes, and harmful-content associations.

Table 6 varies five extraction-design choices and includes a direct GPT-4o-mini ranking baseline. At 5% poisoning, selecting 64 features yields Safety/Chat 65.68/92.18 versus the default 32-feature configuration's 71.76/91.34. An 8,192-latent dictionary gives 94.46 Safety at 8% removal versus the table's default 92.86. Direct GPT-4o-mini ranking at 5% poisoning yields 91.89 Safety and 76.82 Chat. Results demonstrate configuration-dependent tradeoffs without repeated-run uncertainty; some default entries conflict with Table 3.
Specific finding: Adapting a general-corpus SAE to safety-domain reward-model activations can strengthen SAFER's low-rate poisoning effects and selected denoising gains. In Table 4, safety-adapted versus pretrained-only SAE selection yielded Safety scores of 83.11 versus 91.08 at 0.5% poisoning and 79.73 versus 88.11 at 1%. At 4% removal, scores were 94.20 versus 90.27. The pretrained-only variant performed better at 8% denoising, and Chat comparisons were mixed. Some denoising entries differ from Table 3.
Specific finding: Training safety-domain SAEs on sentence-final activations can improve SAFER denoising Safety scores relative to all-token training, with setting-dependent advantages and Chat tradeoffs. At 4% removal, sentence-final versus all-token training yielded Safety scores of 94.20 versus 93.11 in 1B and 96.46 versus 95.41 in 3B. Table 5 reports higher Safety for sentence-final training in nine of ten model–ratio cells, with a loss at 3B 8%; all-token training has higher Chat in every 3B cell. Several sentence-final results conflict with Table 3.

Fivefold feature amplification increased chosen-response rewards by an average of 1.04 on 20 randomly sampled safety pairs versus 0.02 on 20 randomly sampled chat pairs. In one randomly selected safety pair, the chosen score increased from 4.72 to 5.94 while the rejected score stayed unchanged. Intervention implementation details, matched perturbation controls, score distributions, and uncertainty are not supplied.

Figure images, UMAP settings, quantitative separation metrics, and detailed training or labeling protocols for the additional Qwen dictionaries are unavailable.

Table 1 reports three-seed results using frozen two-layer MLP probes and 20-fold stratified cross-validation. The baseline interventions remove different types and numbers of directions.

All-layer Geneformer tracing reports L0 responses through L17, including 58 retained targets per source at L17. scGPT L0 responses remain approximately 155–176 targets per downstream layer through L6 before declining to 114 at L11. The comparison does not isolate dimensionality, tokenization, training objective, or competitive computation.

Reported examples include Geneformer L0 DNA Repair removal decreasing an L1 DNA Damage Response coordinate, d=-1.87 with 113 shared annotation terms, and scGPT L0 Protein Catabolism removal decreasing an L1 Chromatin Organization coordinate, d=-8.19 with 161 shared terms. Additional selected examples show proteasome-associated responses across layers. Biological explanations are based on annotation overlap and cited literature rather than selective tests of the proposed molecular mechanisms.

experiment_summary: On the same 200 K562 cells, reported coherence rises from 52.9% with K562-only SAEs to 68.8% with mixed K562/Tabula Sapiens SAEs. The former is 16,507/31,176 doubly annotated edges; the mixed-condition denominator is not supplied. Mixed dictionaries cover only layers 0, 5, 11, and 17, versus all 18 layers for K562-only dictionaries. Matched-layer-pair connectivity increases are reported at two pairs, with an exception at L11→L17.

K562/Multi versus TS/Multi yields mean retained-edge |d|=0.98 versus 0.72 and shared-annotation fractions of 68.8% versus 68.5%, each conditional on doubly annotated retained edges. At L0→L5, reported targets per source fall from 236 to 75. Tabula Sapiens sampling comprises 67 immune, 67 kidney, and 66 lung cells across 88 cell types.

Reported causal-target overlap with PMI targets is 90.6% for L0→L5, 94.8% for L5→L11, and 91.7% for L11→L17. Corresponding PMI target sets contain 4,101, 4,369, and 4,205 of 4,608 coordinates; causal target counts are 1,113, 996, and 881. The PMI graphs come from the companion study; this document performs the target-set comparison.

Among 13,698 unique Geneformer domain pairs and 3,511 scGPT pairs, 1,142 overlap. Across 1,000 reported label permutations, expected overlap is 107.3, giving reported 10.6-fold enrichment and p<0.001. Of the shared pairs, 303 have mean |d|>1 in both models. This domain-label analysis includes 37,088 doubly annotated edges out of 96,892 reported aggregate edges; its annotation denominator differs from the broader database-based coherence analysis.

Against 14,021 reference links, the paper labels 29,864/37,088 annotated response edges, or 80.5%, as absent from known biology and reports 87 candidate domain pairs present in all four conditions. However, highlighted supposedly novel pairs are also reported to share 20, 43, or 22 genes, exceeding the stated three-gene threshold for a known link. No new biological intervention validates these candidates.

Expansion of 47,418 gene-annotated response edges produces 975,369 retained gene pairs using at least two contributing edges or |d|>2. Existing Replogle data permit validation of 282,250 pairs involving 599 of 2,023 knockdown targets. Directional accuracy is 56.4%; magnitude Spearman rho=0.038 despite p<10^-92. Only 36/599 source genes have target enrichment at uncorrected p<0.05. Consensus-derived predictions have 57.3% directional accuracy. This document analyzes prior perturbation measurements rather than conducting new CRISPRi experiments.

Reported median centrality is 14 edges for disease-associated domains versus 3 for other domains, with Mann–Whitney p=1.2×10^-11. Disease-relevant pairs are reported as 3.59-fold more likely to be cross-model consensus pairs, with Fisher p<0.001. Independent disease-label validation and degree-controlled enrichment are not reported.

The paper compares 3,541 multi-tissue-specific pairs with 1,334 shared pairs and reports immune-label OR=3.18, Fisher p<0.001. Of 201 identified immune-specific pairs, 89% are reported absent from K562 circuits. Blood and kidney label enrichments are not statistically significant. These are aggregate condition comparisons rather than interventions distinguishing individual tissues.

Independently trained 32,768-latent, K=32 SAEs on normalized Wikipedia activations from multiple checkpoints. The text reports initial mixed activation, subsequent language specificity, and later coherent mixed activation at layer 14 of the 3.7B model, with representative activating-token examples. Layer and size comparisons describe related but size-dependent trends. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported for these trajectories, and numerical curve values are unavailable in the text rendering.

Compared layerwise mixed-feature proportions and entropy-based coherence across training checkpoints. Additional model-size plots provide supplementary comparisons without numerical layerwise effect sizes in the supplied text.

Compared independently trained fixed-width TopK SAE populations across five LLM-jp sizes. The text reports greater late-training growth of coherent mixed middle-layer features in larger models, with the main discussion contrasting 150M and 3.7B and appendix figures covering intermediate sizes. Numerical scaling coefficients and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied.

Measured average consecutive-token feature-activation spans across layers, checkpoints, and five sizes. The text reports increasing upper-layer spans during training and weaker growth in smaller models. Selected layer-26 examples in the 3.7B model activate over building-material phrases and Japanese address sequences. Implemented masked donor addition at layer 14 of LLM-jp 3.7B, transferring from the fully trained checkpoint into the 10,000-step checkpoint, approximately 40B training tokens. Separately, Table 12 classifies 31.42% of analyzed SPA-VL samples as text-dominant, 42.43% mixed, and 26.15% vision-dominant by visual share among top-k tokens; its checkpoint and sample count are unspecified. The modality distribution does not itself establish why baselines differ.

Table 14 reports preference-objective versus likelihood-objective scores of 47.37% versus 45.29% for Llama TruthfulQA, 59.85% versus 57.02% for Qwen TruthfulQA, 48.35% versus 47.32% for LLaVA SPA-VL, and 58.90% versus 57.19% for Qwen-VL SPA-VL. All likelihood variants exceed their unsteered baselines, but do not outperform every main-table comparator. The likelihood comparator's positive/negative-input description is not fully reconciled with paired responses to a common input.

Table 10 reports 59.85% versus 53.86% on TruthfulQA and 58.90% versus 54.34% on SPA-VL for all-token versus final-prompt-token injection. These match the adjacent Qwen-family headline scores, but the table and associated paragraph do not explicitly identify checkpoints. No significance test is supplied despite the prose describing the improvement as significant.

Table 11 reports all-layer versus best-single-layer scores of 59.85% versus 58.97% on TruthfulQA and 58.90% versus 58.96% on SPA-VL. The descriptive differences are small and favor different variants across the two tasks. No equivalence test, uncertainty estimate, or measured layer-search cost is supplied.

Table 15 reports Qwen MMLU accuracy of 74.29% with normalization versus 70.65% without, compared with 74.58% unsteered. Qwen-VL scores are 58.13% versus 49.96%, compared with 58.64% unsteered. The prose identifies the latter benchmark as MMMU, although the table labels both blocks MMLU. Target-behavior efficacy for the normalized versus unnormalized comparison is not reported here.

Table 7 reports Qwen throughput changing from 0.0299 to 0.0288 tokens/ms and Llama from 0.0263 to 0.0254 tokens/ms, with reported drops of 3.55% and 3.62%. Rounded throughput values do not reproduce the percentages exactly. Appendix A.1 reports approximately 96 seconds for 50-example TruthfulQA vector construction and 302 seconds for SPA-VL construction on an RTX A6000-48G, without identifying the precise checkpoint for each timing. No repeated-timing uncertainty is given.

Compared four methods on layers 3, 7, 11, 17, 21, and 25. ADAPT beats GCG on 70.4% of 486 latents, with reported Wilcoxon p<10^-28. The accompanying text reports mean activation ratios matching or exceeding all baselines at every evaluated layer. Table 1 reports 78.6% wins against EPO and 84.0% against BEAST, but the reciprocal BEAST entry is 12.8%; the discrepancy is unexplained. The sampling description also inconsistently combines four samples per 27 bins with 81 latents per layer. No precise plotted layerwise values are available in the text.
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Table 1; Figures 3–5; Appendix A.1, Table 3

experiment_summary: Three raters, including one author, scored randomly ordered prompts from GCG, GCG with fluency weight 1.0, and ADAPT on a five-point reference-pattern rubric. Krippendorff's alpha was 0.650. The paper reports ADAPT superiority with Wilcoxon statistic 4459.5 and p<10^-8, without giving numerical mean ratings in the text or clearly specifying the comparison and statistical unit underlying that statistic.

The paper reports Pearson r=0.645, p<10^-5, between GCG activation and human interpretability ratings. Raters received reference explanations, maximally activating examples, and likely token completions. The text describes prompts with activation ratios above one as predominantly interpretable but supplies no exact denominator for that observation or full correlation-aggregation details.

At fixed cached trajectory states, generated 64 replacements from the gradient top 1,024 and 64 using model top-p sampling at p=0.95. The text additionally discusses uniformly sampled vocabulary replacements without fully specifying their protocol. Reported improvement counts are dispersed across gradient bins, while summed improvement magnitude is more concentrated in favorable bins. Improving punctuation and formatting replacements also occur at unfavorable gradient ranks. Figure references are inconsistent, and precise distribution values are unavailable in the text.

Initialized three GCG slots with the selected autoregressive prompt and three with the selected random-token prompt. The reported median within-initialization final-activation range was 0.20 times the maximal dataset activation; autoregressive initialization achieved higher best activation in 62% of configurations. These finite outcomes are consistent with trajectory dependence but do not prove local minima. Reproducing latent selection is complicated by a hardness formula that rectifies a quantity defined as negative activation, and by ambiguity about the population used to form hardness quintiles.

Reran GCG on the 50-latent hardness-weighted set with constant weights 0.3, 1.0, 3.0, and 9.0; the text reports that higher penalties hindered activation optimization. In the separate 60-latent human panel, weight 1.0 produced no reported significant rating improvement over unconstrained GCG. Exact activation effect sizes and a statistical test for the rating null result are not supplied in the text. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence.

Applied the previously cited L0.1 joint-activation objective to pairs 823/2738, 1264/154, and 823/154. Table 2 presents three prompts reported to activate both targets, including a prompt containing 'Stark magnet' for MCU and magnet-associated latents. No numerical activations, unsuccessful-pair denominator, or comparative baseline is supplied. The semantic interpretations rely on the authors' reference-pattern assignments.

Demo-R Table B.4 reports mean perplexity increases of 29.99% for attribution and 29.16% for non-overlap, compared with 4.06% for correlation and −0.39% for intersection. Corresponding mean parsed-pair label validity is 92.5%, 93.6%, 95.6%, and 92.4%. Race-Profession source conditions average 73.6% validity. These aggregate results qualify claims of capability preservation; they do not establish the exact quality cost of every successful debiasing condition. Unparsed malformed content is not fully represented by validity among parsed pairs.

location: Section 4, Equations 4–15; Appendices A.2 and B

experiment_summary: Formal algebraic derivation: Equations 17–23 substitute the centered token state, concept-plus-relation weight, and positive radius bias into Equation 16 to obtain the affine-sigmoid predictor in Equation 20. The result is conditional on these identifications and the positive-bias restriction. It is not an empirical experiment or a semantic-preservation theorem.

ProtSAE versus dense linear probing yields Fmax 0.579 versus 0.537, AUC 0.797 versus 0.751, equal rounded Smin of 20.9, and lower AUPR of 0.487 versus 0.522. No uncertainty estimates accompany these aggregate comparisons, and probe training and pooling details are not fully specified.

At reported L0=1,000, ProtSAE versus TopK normalized MSE is 0.115 versus 0.111 for MFO, 0.109 versus 0.104 for BPO, and 0.108 versus 0.104 for CCO. Corresponding zero-ablation-relative loss recovery is 0.955 versus 0.968, 0.980 versus 0.992, and 0.987 versus 0.991. ProtSAE has higher normalized MSE at all twelve corresponding table entries. Replacement-loss recovery includes small gains at low-count MFO settings, a rounded tie at CCO L0=500, and losses elsewhere.

Removing detachment reportedly slightly improves reconstruction fidelity but sharply reduces AUC. Removing ontology penalties or learned rescaling reportedly reduces both AUC and reconstruction fidelity.
