Removing forced activation decreases the fraction of predictor-positive defined coordinates participating in decoding. Evidence is supplied through the textual account of Figure 6; numerical plot values and uncertainty are unavailable.

Mean Pythia-to-Mamba maximum Pearson correlation is 0.74, compared with 0.76 for a different Pythia model seed and 0.81 for independently trained SAEs on the same Pythia. More than 30% of Pythia features exceed 0.95 cross-architecture correlation. Across the stated Pythia feature inventory, 90% of cross-architecture-minus-model-seed differences lie between −0.22 and 0.14; over 60% are described as near zero without a numerical tolerance. Appendix C reports higher correlations for reverse Mamba-to-Pythia matching, without supplying numerical means in the prose.

The paper applies its maximum-Pearson comparison to Pythia MLP neurons and Mamba post-SiLU activations and reports almost no similarity, whereas the SAE comparison has mean maximum correlation 0.74. Figure 3(a) contains the distributional comparison; the supplied prose does not give the native-unit baseline's numerical mean.

Appendix D repeats the feature-comparison experiments with RWKV-4-169M-Pile and reports conclusions broadly similar to the Pythia–Mamba comparison. The authors describe slightly lower numerical performance while explicitly declining to infer a reliable architectural ordering. Figure 11's plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text.

Table 1 reports nested token nMSE 0.167 versus 0.162 for token-only, and mean nMSE 0.116 versus 0.355 when token-only directly encodes means. The dedicated turn-averaged SAE achieves mean nMSE 0.097. A decoupled architecture with 64 features per component has token nMSE 0.212 and mean nMSE 0.128, showing a larger token-reconstruction cost than the nested model. nMSE divides expected squared reconstruction error by expected squared activation norm.

On 2,000 held-out turns, ten pairwise comparisons among five configurations yield 20,000 trials with randomized presentation order. Turn averaging obtains a reported 87.9% average win rate and 79.7% against token-max. Five-way ranking gives average rank 2.03 and 44% first-place finishes. Embedding coverage is highest for turn averaging at neighbor counts 1, 2, 3, and 5: at 3, scores are 0.663 for turn averaging, 0.658 nested-sum, 0.647 token-sum, 0.640 nested-max, and 0.617 token-max. Appendix E reports different no-prefill Sonnet rates, 83.1% average and 74.8% against token-max, without explaining the discrepancy. Other judge configurations materially change the results.
location: Sections 5.2–5.5; Appendices A, E, and H

experiment_summary: Across 2,000 held-out turns, matching accuracy is 95.0% for token-max, 87.0% for token-sum, 73.9% for turn averaging, 70.6% for nested-sum, and 57.3% for nested-max. The proposed explanation that distinctive lexical details cause the advantage is not separately isolated experimentally.

Displayed feature lists for a 26,920-token investment document and a 30,023-token computer-graphics paper, roughly 150 times the average training-span length, include recognizable broad topics and subtopics. Turn-averaged lists include macroeconomics and computer graphics that are absent from the displayed pooled token-only lists. No systematic long-document coverage score, reconstruction metric, or random-selection evaluation is supplied.
location: Section 4, Long-context examples; Appendix C; Section 7

experiment_summary: On 300 held-out conversations, 100 at each length, nested graphs score above aggregated token-only graphs, which score above turn-averaged graphs, on both completeness and replacement at every evaluated length. Both metrics increase with conversation length. Exact values are inaccessible in the supplied Figure 7 text. The reported ordering coexists with slightly worse nested token nMSE, 0.167 versus 0.162.

All eight targeted paragraphs gain attribution share relative to the neutral query under all three architectures. Turn-averaged increases range from 0.3 to 1.8 percentage points; token-only and nested increases range from 0.4 to 1.9. Attribution share sums weights of edges sourced from a paragraph and divides by the sum for all system paragraphs. The common 14-span setup has a stated candidate-feature-node budget of 7,168 across four layers. Table 2 uses zero-based paragraph indices, while Appendix F labels them from one.

Circuit-tracer pruning at 80% node logit influence and 98% edge influence reduces the graph from 7,239 nodes and 10.4 million edges to approximately 1,300 nodes and 110,000 edges. Manual tracing and semantic grouping connect repetition at layer 21 through jailbreak-prompt detection at layer 16 to weapons-related and AI-safety-disclaimer features at earlier layers and turns. The authors report that their aggregated token-only graph lacks an active adversarial-prompt-detection feature and instead traces through less relevant descriptions. No targeted intervention on this displayed pathway or blinded human comparison is reported.

For evil, hallucination, and sycophancy, the study generates responses using five positive/negative prompt pairs and 20 extraction questions per persona at temperature 1.0, then filters expression with Haiku 4.5 ratings. Existing GPT-4.1-mini-filtered rollouts supply the 240 other traits. The displayed top-ten lists contain recognizable persona-associated descriptions from both architectures alongside unclear or tangential matches. Trait tables illustrate poetic, theatrical, paranoid, concise, and quantitative contrasts. No persona-feature steering, held-out persona detection accuracy, or comprehensive relevance comparison is reported.

Across Table 1's fifteen model-by-benchmark cells, DSPA changes scores relative to Base by −0.7 to +1.8 percentage points. MMLU changes are +0.2, +0.6, and +0.1 points; Qwen TruthfulQA-MC2 rises from 40.9 to 42.4. Results are deterministic harness evaluations rather than statistical equivalence tests.

Appendix D's analytical dense-transformer accounting uses 2P FLOPs per forward token and 6P per training token and estimates RAHF-SCIT/DSPA at 4.47 and DPO/DSPA at approximately 3.2 under stipulated lengths and pass counts. These are estimated model FLOPs. On Gemma-2-9B with one H200, reported DSPA construction takes 46 minutes and 33.1 GB peak memory versus RAHF's 8 hours 50 minutes and 140.8 GB, approximately an 11.5-fold time difference. Qwen DPO takes nearly twelve hours on four L40S GPUs versus roughly one-fifteenth that elapsed time for DSPA on one L40S. The RAHF FLOP derivation describes two epochs over duplicated variants, whereas Table 9 lists sixty-four step-1 epochs; correspondence between the estimated and implemented training workloads is unresolved.
location: Section 4.4; Appendix D; Appendix E.2, Table 9

experiment_summary: GPT-5-mini labels 34/50 ablation candidates, 28/50 augmentation candidates, and 15/50 random features as Discourse; Content counts are 5/50, 7/50, and 18/50. Safety and Intent categories are folded into Content and Discourse, respectively. On first-turn MT-Bench, actual ablated identities are a strict subset of the fifty ablation candidates; an auxiliary augment-and-ablate pass finds all but four augmented identities in the fifty augmentation candidates. Descriptions and categories lack systematic human validation. Two manually selected token-level traces show edit identities and activations but do not independently establish semantic causation.

On the forty-prompt test split, deterministic mean utility is 2.400 for Base, 2.539 for top-five DSPA ablation, 2.573 for instruction prompting, 2.875 for five-shot ICL, 2.888 for five-shot ICL plus top-five ablation, and 3.173 for five-shot ICL plus all positive-estimated-gain ablations. Mean reward-model z-scores across ten judges are −2.239 for instructions, −2.128/−2.061 for judge-axis/judge-contrast top-five ablations, and −1.973/−1.853 for one-/five-shot ICL. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.

Formal result: Theorem 3.3 and Appendix A.2 derive Aᵀ=cΣBM by iterated expectation. Corollary 3.4 derives a contamination bound for a gate with positive activation probability: its conditional mean shift differs from cΣβ^(i) in norm by at most c||Σ|| times the sum over other gates of P(g_i'=1|g_i=1)||β^(i')||. Both follow under the stated mean-shift and additive-gating assumptions. The conditional mean equals a row of A divided by the gate probability. Independence alone does not make the uncentered gate Gram matrix diagonal, and restricting de-mixing to an active submatrix does not automatically remove contributions from excluded correlated gates.

Formal result: Appendix A.6, Theorem A.4, computes utility change as −δ times the sum of selected β coordinates; minimizing that sum gives the bottom-k rule. The calculation is exact when the stipulated density-shift approximation is treated as the model. The paper notes that rankings from Σβ need not match β without suitable covariance structure. This is not an empirical optimality test of DSPA, nor does fixed-budget optimality guarantee improvement over making no edit.
location: Appendix A.6, Assumption A.3 and Theorem A.4

experiment_summary: Table 5 reports Base/DSPA/de-mixing/diagonal-whitening/combined scores of 2.61/2.97/2.85/2.86/2.86 for Gemma-2-2B and 3.26/3.48/3.39/3.17/3.46 for Gemma-2-9B. No correction exceeds DSPA. The accompanying covariance diagnostic reports a chosen-to-rejected trace ratio of 0.907 and median sampled-element ratio of 0.924, which indicate similar covariance scale without establishing equal covariance matrices. Additive gating receives weaker diagnostic support, without a quantitative result or clear model attribution for those diagnostics.

Held-out layerwise evaluations sweep τ and λ, including λ magnitudes 1, 1.5, and 2. Main Gemma-2 2B experiments use 65K dictionaries; Gemma-2 9B experiments use 131K dictionaries with τ=0.7 or 0.2. The text reports stronger shifts at larger magnitudes and intermediate layers. Appendix G additionally reports poorer steering at τ=1 and more effective steering with the maximum available average L0 than with the available value nearest 60. Behavioral sample counts and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.

Figure 6 sweeps λ from −5 to 5 across behavioral vectors. MMLU uses ten randomly selected questions from each of 57 categories, totaling 570, reformatted as A/B questions. The endpoint is mean correct-answer probability. The text and caption report limited adverse effects at moderate magnitudes around 1–2, improvements on TruthfulQA under refusal or non-hallucination steering, some MMLU improvements under myopic-reward steering, and degradation at extreme strengths. TruthfulQA sample count and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.

Figure 7 and Appendix K.1 compare SAS support sizes, raw active-coordinate counts, and multiple-choice steering across seven widths. The text reports decreasing retained supports, broadly stable raw activity, retained positive steering, and some negative-steering degradation at higher τ. Readable matrices in Figures 24–25 show layer-12, τ=0.7 sycophancy support decreasing from 21 to 13 coordinates and refusal support from 113 to 92 between 65K and 1M dictionaries. Fixed λ and differing released SAE configurations limit attribution to width alone.
location: Section 4.4.1, Figure 7; Appendix J, Figures 24–25; Appendix K.1, Figures 28–31

experiment_summary: GPT-4o rewrites myopic-reward test questions into four choices in a fixed order. Gender edits combine two male-associated and three female-associated features. In Table 1, λM=2 and λG=1 raises Bob–myopic probability by 23.9 percentage points and total myopic probability by 33.0 points; the prose incorrectly calls the former Bob–non-myopic. With λM=−2 and λG=−1, Alice–non-myopic rises by 21.5 points, while the total Alice marginal remains 0.2 points below baseline. Table 2 adds Alice/Bob features and shows mixed changes rather than uniform improvement: for example, the positive-myopic/female condition's myopic shift decreases from 40.7 to 22.3 points.

The paper measures positive/negative support intersections and applies behavior-specific vectors to other behavioral question sets. At layer 12, the 65K dictionary has 30 coordinates shared between positive refusal and negative hallucination. Appendix K reports cross-task answer-probability effects, including a negative relationship between refusal steering and hallucination matching. Only behavior pairs identified as positively or negatively related are plotted. No overlap-specific ablation or mediation test is supplied.

Figure 9 compares behavioral probability changes with and without adding Δ=a−decode(encode(a)) after SAE encoding and decoding. The text reports reduced layerwise fluctuations with correction, especially at early layers. The figure does not fully specify the intervention setting, and no numerical variability summary, repeated-run analysis, or uncertainty estimate is supplied.

Figure 10 compares full signed SAS against one-sided steering. The text and caption report weaker multiple-choice steering for the one-sided condition across layers. No norm-matched comparison, numerical aggregate effect, or statistical test is supplied.

Figure 10 compares retaining versus removing shared coordinates and reports comparable layerwise steering. Section 4.5.3 and Figure 11's caption report that retained shared-coordinate differences concentrate near zero, while explicit removal increases sparsity. Exact cancellation is not guaranteed when the two conditional means differ. No equivalence test is supplied.

Appendix E explicitly reports reproducing Panickssery et al.'s dense CAA multiple-choice analysis, with positive- and negative-steering layer sweeps for seven behaviors. Llama-2 7B Chat revisits the prior model-family setting; Gemma-2 2B and 9B extend the procedure to additional models. The supplied rendering includes the setup and caption but not readable curve traces, so exact effect magnitudes or agreement rates cannot be assessed. Sample counts, uncertainty, and matched SAS-versus-CAA operating points are unspecified.

Formal derivation supplied in Appendix B, Equations B.6–B.8: differentiating g(a)=wᵀa gives ∇ag(a)=w, hence a′=a+λw. No empirical experiment is involved. The separate assertion in Equation B.5 that one classifier-training step yields the mean-difference direction is not established for the unspecified loss, initialization, and class weighting.

Formal derivation: Section 3.1 unrolls the zero-initialized recurrence and collects source-position coefficients into a lower-triangular matrix, establishing y = α̃(x)x. This is an algebraic identity under the stated recurrence assumptions, not an empirical experiment.

Formal derivation: Equations 13–14 expand diagonal transition products into N scalar contributions per channel. The text illustrates the channel/head comparison with 384 Vision-Mamba-Tiny channels and three DeiT-Tiny heads. The matrix-count ratio is DN/H; the derivation does not establish a universal thousandfold ratio.

Tables 1–2: lower positive-erasure AUC favors Mamba raw attention and rollout, at 17.268 versus 20.687 and 18.806 versus 20.594; attribution favors the transformer, at 15.351 versus 16.619. Higher negative-erasure AUC favors the transformer for raw attention, rollout, and attribution: 40.766 versus 34.025, 43.525 versus 41.864, and 48.089 versus 39.632. Transformer-Attribution also exceeds Mamba-Attribution in pixel accuracy/mAP/mIoU: 79.26/84.85/60.63% versus 74.72/81.70/54.24%. Mamba raw attention has higher pixel accuracy and mIoU but lower mAP than transformer raw attention: 67.64/45.09/74.88% versus 59.69/36.94/77.25%.

Appendix A averages pairwise token cosine similarity over the entire ImageNet validation set and reports lower values for the Mamba model across normalized depth. The supplied prose provides the direction of the comparison; exact plotted layer values and uncertainty cannot be recovered from this rendering.

Formal architectural derivation: Appendix E expands the stated fixed SSM recurrences into input-independent kernels, identifies elementwise gates in GSS and a restricted single-step Hyena formulation, and contrasts these primitive operators with selective SSM transition products. This establishes the restricted structural distinction rather than a universal expressiveness ordering.

Formal proof: Appendix D, Lemma 2 derives incompatible output requirements for (0,1,1), (0,0,1), and (1,0,1). The first and third inputs have identical final queries and identical multisets of keys and values but require different final run counts. No empirical model training is involved.

Formal construction with a printed algebraic error: substituting the stated unit linear projections into Equations 26–27 gives h_t = x_t h_(t−1) + x_t² and y_t = x_t h_t. For binary x_t, zero resets the state and one increments it. This establishes the restricted construction. Equation 28 instead prints h_t = h_(t−1) + x_t, which does not reset and is inconsistent with the preceding equations and case analysis.

Attempted formal argument, insufficient for the advertised scope. Lemma 3 identifies unnormalized causal attention within a modified selective recurrence, without establishing softmax-head inclusion. Lemma 2 excludes a restricted scalar position-free head from the counting task, not arbitrary transformer layers. Lemma 1's preceding input-gated equations support a binary counting construction in the modified recurrence despite the erroneous printed Equation 28.
location: Section 5, Theorem 2; Appendix D, Theorem 3 and Lemmas 1–3

experiment_summary: Formal derivation in Appendix A.3.1: independence gives E[(xᵀx′)²] = trace(C²); the bounded pairwise U-statistic consistently estimates this quantity, and taking its reciprocal gives the effective-rank estimator. Equal energy over k orthogonal directions yields effective rank k. This is a conditional mathematical result, not a language-model experiment.

The paper reports increasing reciprocal squared-cosine effective-dimension estimates across sequence positions and changing cosine similarities at lags 5–20. Position-permuted activation controls flatten the dimension trend; an autocorrelation control replaces each similarity-matrix diagonal with its mean and is therefore position invariant by construction. Appendix A reports precaching 10K activations without fully resolving the sampling unit.
location: Section 3; Figure 2; Appendices A.1, A.3–A.4, C

experiment_summary: For each sequence, the current centered activation is projected onto the row span of its preceding context using SVD. The reported metric is summed coordinate variance of projected vectors divided by summed coordinate variance of target vectors across samples. Section 3 reports values up to approximately 80% for a context of 500 tokens; this ratio is not an independently measured next-state prediction R².

Formal derivation in Proposition 4.1 and Appendices H–I exponentiates an additive negative-log penalty into a product of per-time factors. This establishes the separable-factor interpretation. The broader exact treatment claimed for BatchTopK is not established: Appendix I.0.3 replaces a batch-average constraint with per-sample absolute deviations, and hard-budget conditioning does not yield independent samples. Uniform bounded amplitude distributions require additional choices not determined by the original objective. The ReLU nonnegativity restriction also changes a Laplace density to its nonnegative restriction.
location: Section 4; Proposition 4.1; Corollary 4.1.1; Appendices H.1–H.2, I

experiment_summary: Tables 1–2 report TFA NMSE of 0.139, 0.139, and 0.152 for story, web, and code, versus BatchTopK's 0.152, 0.139, and 0.149. Explained variance is 0.73, 0.79, and 0.75 versus 0.72, 0.79, and 0.75. Prediction-only NMSE is 0.34–0.38. No repeated-run uncertainty or replacement language-model loss is supplied.

The paper averages token codes within subject, verb, and object phrases and compares their cosine similarities between ambiguous sentences and controls. Predictive-code relationships are reported as relatively invariant, while SAE and novel-code relationships are more sensitive. Selected dendrograms are interpreted as linking the ultimately correct constituents. Numerical parsing success rates and independent syntactic validation are not reported.

The paper assigns random one-token words to grid nodes, extracts codes during random walks, and selects adjacent PCA components that best display the graph. Target-node substitutions at the final position produce graph-consistent prediction changes for 4/9 nodes using predictive codes. Standard SAEs show no reported successes under this protocol. Appendix D.5 qualifies the main text's exclusivity claim by reporting two novel-code successes. The decoding intervention and success aggregation across walk lengths are incompletely specified.

The authors collect high-activation snippets and neighboring contexts, compute direct logit attribution, and present representative feature cards. They report qualitative agreement between activating contexts, vocabulary attributions, and the supplied labels. No aggregate automated score, blinded human study, or systematic intervention suite is performed; the supplied text does not expose the image-only cards for independent inspection.

Section 8.1 describes novel-stream dominance early in training, later predictive-stream growth, and occasional renewed novel-stream dominance. The authors report that replacing TopK with BatchTopK stabilized their Llama training. A deeper Llama layer-26 run did not show predictive-component dominance. Learning-curve figures accompany these observations, but matched multi-seed comparisons, failure frequencies, and a causal test of the proposed late-layer information-discard explanation are absent.
location: Section 8.1, training dynamics and layer choice; Figures 12, 14; Appendix E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Adding groups of instruction-responsive SAE decoder directions can induce translation, keyword-inclusion, and summarization behavior in instruction-tuned Gemma and Llama models. Evaluates three translation targets, keyword inclusion, and summarization using 65K, 131K, and 32K SAE dictionaries for the respective models. Section 4.3 reports approximately 30% strict and 65% loose French-translation accuracy for Llama and loose scores approaching prompting baselines. It also reports slightly better steering in Gemma-2-9B-it than Gemma-2-2B-it across five tasks, but model and dictionary sizes change together. Evaluation denominators, uncertainty, data separation, and numerical Figure 5 contents are unavailable. The prose's over-30% strict-accuracy generalization is not reconciled with the separate feature-count sweep's approximately 25% peak.

Specific finding: Selected residual-stream SAE features in Llama-3.1-8B-Base can exhibit concept-consistent activation patterns and produce corresponding changes in generated text. A qualitative reproduction of earlier demonstrations in a different model. Coffee feature 18/9463 activates in English, German, and Japanese passages; the reported maximum and mean nonzero activations increase across four relevance categories containing four authored sentences each. Coefficient 2 promotes coffee on a drink-completion prompt, while coefficient -2 suppresses coffee on another prompt. Selected features also change emotional tone, conditional phrasing, and list formatting. The conditional-language feature's coefficient is reported as 15 in Section 5.1.1 but 10 in Tables 20–21; Table 21 supplies the clearer conditional-phrasing example.
location: Sections 4.1–4.3 and 5.1.1; Figure 1; Tables 1–5 and 16–24; Appendices 8.2 and 9.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: SAE directions selected for activation increases across repeated occurrences of the same token can induce or suppress repetitive generation. Features are selected by activation increases between first and last repeated occurrences of the same token. Section 8.1 describes onset-associated activation growth, increased repetition after amplification on non-repetitive samples, and decreased repetition after suppression on repetition-prone samples. These interventions establish sensitivity to selected directions without proving exclusive mediation of pathological repetition.
Specific finding: A Chinese-associated SAE feature can rise before an unexpected Chinese switch, and subtracting its direction immediately before the switch can reduce switching more than subtracting an English-associated control. Section 7.2 reports increasing mean Chinese-feature preactivation before switch onset across five models. Final-layer subtraction at the preceding token lowers switching ratios, with larger coefficients producing larger reported reductions; English-feature subtraction has negligible reported effect. Complete checkpoint identities, sample counts, and numerical intervention effects are unspecified. The section builds on cited language-feature and SASFT work.

Specific finding: SAS interventions can change GPT-4o-rated behavioral expression in Gemma-2 2B open-ended responses, with stronger reported control when an answer prefix and answer choices are supplied. GPT-4o assigns behavioral scores described as ranging from 0 to 9 to generated responses in question-only, answer-prefix, and choices-plus-prefix formats. The text reports score changes with steering polarity and magnitude, with greatest steerability in the choices-plus-prefix format. Appendix plots label the score '/10', creating a minor scale-label inconsistency. No independent judge calibration, sample counts, or confidence intervals are supplied.
location: Section 4.2, Figure 5; Appendix H, Figures 19–21; qualitative examples in Appendix L

experiment_summary: Specific finding: JSAE-derived text-decoder directions can steer caption concepts at selected layers in both dense and mixture-of-experts vision-language models. Tables 1–2 report effective selected-layer interventions in LLaVA and two additional architectures. Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct layer 33 reaches reported SBERT-threshold success of 77.9% on 104 examples, with judge accuracy 7.02/10. Llama3-LLaVA-Next-8B layer 15 reaches 66.7% on 96 examples, with coherence 6.78/10. Llama category success ranges from 100% for food on 28 examples to 23.7% for streets on 38. Each additional architecture is tested at only one probe-selected layer; no corresponding baseline panel is reported for those architectures. Qualitative caption examples corroborate that output content can change, without establishing faithful visual grounding.

Specific finding: Final-layer SAE feature steering can outperform the tested earlier-layer SAIF interventions for French translation in Gemma-2-2B-it. Compares French-translation steering using fifteen independently selected features from each of layers 21–25. Loose accuracy is 0.64 at layer 25 and 0.33 at layer 24; earlier tested layers are reported to produce ineffective, repetitive, or irrelevant outputs. Selected feature vocabulary readouts have less specifically French associations in earlier layers, with no French-related feature identified among the top fifteen before layer 21. These selected readouts do not establish a complete representational hierarchy or absence of French information elsewhere.

Specific finding: JSAE caption steering in LLaVA can be substantially more effective at selected intermediate-to-late layers than at early or near-output layers. Reported success is 40.0% on 100 examples at layer 7, 74.0% on 104 at layer 13, 79.8% on 104 at layer 25, and 15.2% on 112 at layer 30. Mean judge accuracy follows the same ordering. Table 5 reports corrected significant comparisons involving layer 25, but its mean differences conflict with Table 1: the reported layer-13 versus layer-25 difference is -0.094, whereas the displayed means are 0.34 and 0.35. The statistical results cannot be cleanly reconciled with the main table.

Specific finding: Shared normalized-distance sparse encoding with modality-specific decoding can improve within-coordinate image–text exemplar similarity and reduce between-coordinate exemplar similarity relative to separate or shared standard SAEs. The paper compares VL-SAE with separate-modality SAE-D and shared SAE-S across backbones and active-coordinate counts. Section 4.2 reports higher intra-similarity and lower inter-similarity for VL-SAE. Evaluation averages five random trials with 100 sampled coordinates per trial. Table A7 supplies a numerical OpenCLIP-B/16 comparison at 100–500 sampled coordinates: with 100 coordinates, SAE-S versus VL-SAE intra-similarity is 0.2200 versus 0.2445 and inter-similarity is 0.1347 versus 0.1230. Figure 3's plotted values are unavailable in the supplied rendering. No error bars or significance tests are supplied.
location: Section 4.2, Figure 3; Appendix A.1, Equations A13–A14 and Table A7

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Joint cross-stream TopK selection with cross-reconstruction can improve agreement between latent top-image label profiles over independent TopK selection and random-encoder universal sparse autoencoding. Table 2 compares generalized Jaccard similarity of label-frequency profiles from each latent–stream pair’s top 50 test images. Reported means over all 8,192 latents and stream pairs are 0.8018±0.0039 for Global+cross, 0.7344±0.0015 for Global without cross-loss, 0.2599±0.0026 for Local+cross, 0.1651±0.0010 for Local without cross-loss, and 0.2166±0.0024 for USAE. Standard errors are reported over latents rather than training seeds. Treatment of dead latents, tied zero activations, and empty profiles is not explained.
Specific finding: Joint cross-stream TopK selection can reduce the fraction of latent coordinates that remain alive in only some model streams. Table 1 reports 84.4% all-alive and 15.6% all-dead latents, with no mixed-liveness cases, for full SPARC. Local+cross has 43.6% all-alive, 7.6% alive in one stream, and 48.8% alive in two streams. USAE has 45.3% all-alive and 51.3% mixed-liveness latents. Global without cross-loss has 98.2% all-alive and 0.2% mixed cases. Training also uses AuxK and dead-latent reinitialization. The conclusion’s statement that dead neurons are eliminated is contradicted by these counts.
models_studied: ["DINOv2 ViT-L/14 with registers", "DataComp-trained CLIP ViT-L/14 image encoder", "DataComp-trained CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder"]
location: Section 4.2, Table 2; Appendices A.2 and A.5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Group-sparse SAE codes can retain more zero-shot image-classification accuracy than the evaluated ordinary sparse-autoencoder codes in CLIP's joint embedding space. TopK accuracies on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100/ImageNet are 0.657/0.418/0.303; GSAE obtains 0.808/0.526/0.354 and MGSAE 0.842/0.554/0.373. BatchTopK obtains 0.657/0.277/0.178 and Matryoshka 0.587/0.166/0.185. Dense CLIP references of 0.916/0.687/0.686 are attributed to the original authors, not new dense-model evaluations here. Evaluation sample counts and repeated-run uncertainty are unspecified.
Specific finding: Group-sparse SAE codes can outperform standard TopK codes on zero-shot music classification and text-to-music retrieval, with task-dependent benefits from shared masking. TopK/GSAE/MGSAE obtain GTZAN accuracies of 0.376/0.705/0.672, NSynth accuracies of 0.265/0.303/0.354, and FMACaps mean reciprocal ranks of 0.023/0.050/0.061. Dense CLAP results are 0.710 for GTZAN, explicitly attributed to the original authors, 0.339 for NSynth, and 0.075 for retrieval. MGSAE exceeds the reported dense result only on NSynth. GSAE exceeds MGSAE on GTZAN. Retrieval gallery size, evaluation sample counts, and repeated-run uncertainty are unspecified.
Specific finding: Masked group-sparse SAE training can improve CLIP-code ImageNet accuracy over both ordinary TopK and unmasked group-sparse training across multiple dictionary widths and active-feature budgets. In all nine Table 3 configurations, GSAE exceeds TopK ImageNet accuracy and MGSAE exceeds both. At expansion 4 and K=64, accuracies are 0.357/0.407/0.435; at expansion 16 and K=32, they are 0.295/0.341/0.361 for TopK/GSAE/MGSAE. Increasing K improves accuracy within every method and expansion factor in this grid, while width effects are nonmonotonic. Training three model types per configuration does not constitute three random-seed repetitions.
Specific finding: Repeated GPT-4o-mini compliance judgments provide useful operational measurements of complete and partial instruction-steering success.

Specific finding: Normalized behavior-labeled answer probabilities and language-model behavioral ratings provide useful operational measurements of the tendencies targeted by sparse activation steering.

Specific finding: SAEs trained on 1,024-token language-model contexts can retain useful reconstruction performance on 8,192-token contexts with modest increases in reconstruction error and active-feature count. Evaluates 166 selected L-Eval documents totaling approximately 1.3 million tokens. Reports final-1,024-token average reconstruction loss of 0.0086, 12% above the training-data comparison, with L0 increasing from 50 to 55. No long-context fine-tuning or downstream task evaluation is performed.
Specific finding: Residual-stream SAEs trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Base can transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct without substantial increases in active-feature count or replacement loss at most layers. Evaluates 32 8× and 32 32× residual-stream dictionaries on 4,000 Wildchat histories processed by Instruct. Reports no significant replacement-loss degradation or L0 increase outside L31R-8x and L31R-32x. For L15R-32x, loss increases are 0.162 in the base-model evaluation and 0.090 on Instruct at the same L0. The model and corpus change together, and no matched SAE trained directly on Instruct is evaluated.

Specific finding: A middle-layer Llama-3-8B Gated SAE trained on predominantly English Pile text can retain substantial zero-ablation-relative predictive loss recovery on multiple other languages. Replacing residual activations with SAE reconstructions recovers 81.22% of zero-ablation-relative loss in Chinese, 90.04% in Dutch, 92.57% in English, 85.82% in Finnish, 92.85% in French, 90.26% in German, 92.05% in Indonesian, 87.59% in Japanese, and 85.22% in Turkish. Recovery is (reconstructed CE minus zero-ablated CE)/(original CE minus zero-ablated CE). These are predictive-fidelity measurements, not measurements of semantic feature recovery; sample counts and uncertainty are not reported in the table.

Specific finding: A universal sparse dictionary trained on ImageNet can retain positive activation-reconstruction R² on texture and face datasets without retraining. Table 1 reports ImageNet/DTD/CelebA R² of 0.61/0.54/0.52 for SigLIP, 0.77/0.69/0.75 for DinoV2, and 0.59/0.46/0.45 for ViT. Corresponding MSE values are 0.39/0.38/0.48, 0.19/0.26/0.22, and 0.41/0.56/0.69. The authors describe selected cross-dataset examples involving sunglasses, jaws, checkerboards, and stripes, and recurring firing-statistic trends. No numerical OOD co-firing correlations are provided in the accessible text.

Specific finding: Penalizing excessive preactivation of language-associated SAE features during supervised fine-tuning can reduce unwanted code-switching relative to ordinary SFT. Table 4 reports lower switching than ordinary SFT in all 12 displayed model–language–data-setting cells. For Qwen3-1.7B at 210K, Chinese/Russian/Korean rates change from 0.81/0.19/0.36% to 0.22/0.03/0.00%. At Qwen3-8B/110K, Russian switching is 0.07% under SASFT versus 0.06% under SFT+GRPO. Some parenthetical percentage changes are inconsistent with displayed rates. SASFT is explicitly attributed to Deng et al. (2026); this report does not identify its evaluation as an independent replication.
Specific finding: Including one repetition-steered negative response per online RL rollout group can reduce endless repetition faster and further than ordinary DAPO rollouts. Each rollout group contains G−1 ordinary responses and one response generated with repetition-feature steering. Under the otherwise shared RL setup, Section 8.4 and Figure 22 report faster and substantially larger reductions in repeat ratio than vanilla RL across all three scales. The source does not establish that every steered response is repetitive or receives a negative advantage.

Specific finding: SASFT's effects on evaluated general and multilingual capability scores can include gains and regressions relative to ordinary SFT. Table 5 contains gains, ties, and regressions despite the prose's preservation claim. Qwen3-1.7B gains 0.91 points on MMLU but loses 1.25 on HumanEval and 2.06 on MGSM. Qwen3-8B gains 2.40 on HumanEval and 0.42 on MGSM but loses 2.06 on MMLU and 2.88 on HellaSwag. The table lists seven benchmarks although its caption says six.
Specific finding: Repetition-steered negative-rollout augmentation can improve some post-RL capability scores while reducing others relative to vanilla RL. Relative to vanilla RL, RL+SAE has higher MGSM scores in all three models: 52.36 versus 46.48, 72.40 versus 70.96, and 82.40 versus 77.64. IFEval is lower in the 8B and 30B-A3B models, and other benchmark comparisons include gains, ties, and losses. These descriptive results support task-dependent tradeoffs rather than broad preservation guarantees.

Specific finding: For sufficiently sparse random subsets of intervention sites, joint activation-patching effects are close enough to sums of individual effects to support individual-effect estimation.
Specific finding: Conditional random-subset intervention statistics are sufficiently unbiased and statistically regular for Welch-based inference about individual node effects.

Specific finding: With independent Bernoulli node inclusion, the difference between mean subset-intervention effects conditional on including versus excluding a node estimates its signed individual effect without bias under exact additivity; under a pairwise interaction model, its bias is proportional to the inclusion probability and the node's summed interactions. Formal derivation in Appendix A.1.1 conditions on node inclusion and exclusion and cancels contributions independent of that inclusion. It yields zero bias under exact additivity and bias proportional to p times summed pairwise interactions otherwise. The supplied equations contain inconsistent signed-versus-absolute notation and apparent indexing or interaction-counting errors, so the precise coefficient should be read with those limitations.

Specific finding: Joint activation patching across adjacent layers can produce larger localization effects than summing the effects of patching those layers individually, so window effects cannot be attributed to a single layer. Across tested metrics, corruptions, and windows, joint patching typically increases middle-layer peak effects by at least 20%. Under GN and probability, windows of 3, 5, and 10 yield peak ratios of 1.40, 1.75, and 1.59 relative to summed individual effects.

Specific finding: Under symmetric token replacement, knocking out a selected circuit can cause greater task-score discrepancy than knocking out the entire model, so knockout discrepancy need not increase with the set of removed edges. The authors vary reference-circuit size and report that complete-model knockout under STR has less measured impact than candidate-circuit knockout for IOI and Greater-Than. The zero-ablation comparison lacks this pattern and shows decreasing relative candidate significance as reference size increases. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the text, and the suggested validation-dataset artifact explanation is not independently isolated.

Specific finding: Typed interchange intervention training can substantially improve ResNet18's behavioral and intervention generalization on MNIST Pointer-Value Retrieval compared with ordinary training, auxiliary digit prediction, and quadrant-swap augmentation. Table 1 reports test behavioral/interchange accuracies of 93.93%/94.85% for typed IIT and 96.01%/96.64% for IIT plus auxiliary training. Standard training obtains 0%/20.60%, auxiliary-only training 0%/20.50%, and augmentation 90.90%/92.00%. The split excludes specified digit identities from particular nonpointer quadrants during training. Test-set size and seed uncertainty are not supplied for this comparison.
Specific finding: Combining interchange intervention training with auxiliary symbolic-variable prediction can improve grounded command-following generalization across held-out attribute and action-sequence compositions. Across three seeds, combined IIT and auxiliary training achieves behavioral action-sequence exact match of 80.37%, 74.84%, 14.72%, and 25.82% on novel color, size, direction, and length, versus 55.98%, 41.67%, 0%, and 5.72% for standard training. Corresponding combined-model interchange exact matches are 70.73%, 75.34%, 11.79%, and 8.49%. Table 2 lists 7,195, 7,227, 8,282, and 1,338 zero-shot examples for these splits, separately from ordinary test sets. Held-out conditions are yellow-square commands, small-cylinder commands, southwest targets, and sequences requiring 11–13 actions after training on at most ten actions. Direction and length results remain low in absolute terms.

Specific finding: Spatially averaged gradients of a differentiable scalar target with respect to convolutional feature maps can define a target-specific localization heatmap without modifying or retraining the underlying CNN-based model. Equations 2–3 specify gradient pooling and a ReLU-transformed weighted feature-map sum. Applications are demonstrated on CNN classifiers, a VGG-16-based non-attention captioner, and baseline and ResNet-based VQA models without explanation-specific architectural changes or retraining. These demonstrations establish practical applicability in the examples, not universal localization fidelity.
Specific finding: Grad-CAM can produce spatial localizations that qualitatively distinguish caption content and alternative VQA answers in CNN-based multimodal models. Caption-log-probability gradients through a VGG-16-based neuraltalk2 captioner produce selected maps highlighting mentioned entities. Maps for captions generated from DenseCap proposals qualitatively agree with those proposals. VQA answer-score gradients produce selected answer-dependent maps, including red, yellow, and combined fire-hydrant regions. No quantitative multimodal localization evaluation is supplied here.
Specific finding: Fusing Grad-CAM with Guided Backpropagation can improve human identification of the visualized category relative to Guided Backpropagation alone on images containing two annotated categories. The AMT category-identification study reports 61.23% accuracy with Guided Grad-CAM versus 44.44% with Guided Backpropagation. Numbers of images, workers, and judgments, uncertainty estimates, and the classifier architecture used for this evaluation are not supplied.
Specific finding: Visualizing both predicted and ground-truth classes with Guided Grad-CAM can suggest recognizable image cues or category ambiguity behind selected VGG-16 misclassifications. For selected misclassified ImageNet images, the authors visualize both predicted and correct class targets. Examples include a sandbar prediction associated with the foreground of a volcano image and a visualization making a syringes prediction more understandable. The evidence is qualitative and does not establish that the highlighted regions completely explain the errors.
models_studied: ["AlexNet", "VGG-16", "neuraltalk2 non-attention captioning model with VGG-16", "Deeper LSTM and normalized CNN VQA model", "ResNet-based hierarchical question-image co-attention VQA model"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The positive part of a convolutional feature-map sum weighted by spatially averaged target gradients provides a meaningful proxy for the image regions supporting that target.

Specific finding: In constrained fictional-ontology reasoning, attention-head vocabulary readouts can show increased agreement with context-occurring bigrams around the midpoint of Llama-2 7B. For each head, the authors count positions where its output argmax, paired with the current token, matches a bigram present in context. Figure 5 and the accompanying text report a qualitative increase around or after block 16 across subtask positions. Numerical effect sizes, uncertainty, and cross-model comparisons are not supplied.
Specific finding: Multiple attention heads in the later half of Llama-2 7B can have vocabulary-projected outputs whose top token matches the next answer token during fictional-ontology reasoning. Head outputs at the final input position are projected into vocabulary space, and heads whose argmax matches the answer token are identified across subtasks. Section 6.2 and Figure 6 report these heads in the later half, with the transition described around block 16. Appendix G's captions report seven answer-writing heads for one copying example and three for one inference example; these are illustrative examples rather than population counts.
Specific finding: A language model's next-token probability spread provides a useful guide to where branching will produce diverse coherent narrative alternatives.
Specific finding: Sampling distinct next tokens until their cumulative probability reaches a threshold provides an adaptive alternative to branching at fixed token intervals.

Specific finding: Accessing preloaded models through NDIF can substantially reduce client setup time while adding activation-patching request latency relative to local HPC execution. For OPT-66B, HPC setup/request times are 23.697/1.889 seconds versus NDIF's 0.423/2.739 seconds. For Llama-3.1-70B, the corresponding times are 43.617/1.992 versus 0.695/2.369 seconds. All tabulated OPT patching request times are higher remotely, despite reduced setup. Benchmarks use one batch of 32 IOI examples; Figure 6 reports n=128 per experiment.
Specific finding: Server-side activation patching and metric computation through NDIF can complete faster than a Petals workflow that transfers intermediate states to the client for modification. Section 4 and Figure 6(c), with n=128 per experiment, report comparable standard remote-inference performance and faster activation patching through NDIF. Petals sends intermediate states to the client and receives edited states; NDIF performs interventions and computes metrics on the server. Exact plotted values and the model identities for this comparison are not specified in the accessible text.
location: Section 4, Remote Execution; Figures 6(a)–6(b); Appendix D.1, Tables 2–4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Sparse read/write factorization can yield lower task-circuit edge costs than exact dense SVD or random orthogonal factorization of the same pretrained projection. Full-rank SVD and ten seeded Random-B orthogonal controls reproduce the target map nearly exactly: SVD CE delta is 1.58e-6, and Random-B deltas range from -2.48e-6 to 3.40e-6. The text reports greater active-edge requirements than SWD at corresponding sufficiency and necessity targets. Dense controls are competitive on selected-unit counts in IOI and some low-threshold docstring comparisons, so the strongest result concerns connectivity cost rather than universal unit-count superiority. Approximation, basis, and sparsity change together; this is not a matched-basis intervention isolating sparsity alone.
Specific finding: Sparse factors constructed from pretrained weights without calibration activations can expose units that retain substantial held-out task margins after circuit pruning. Identity-Gram factors at seven sparsities are scored on circuit_train and evaluated on circuit_test for four tasks. At sparsity 0.375, three selected docstring units attain test sufficiency 0.962 and 256 Greater-than units attain 0.986, each normalized to its own unpruned replacement. Pronoun results are weaker. Transcoder curves are contextual references rather than uniformly CE-matched controls. Applying this procedure throughout training is proposed but not tested.
Specific finding: A query bottleneck identified through sparse QK geometry can exert a large prompt-local causal effect on a reconstructed attention head. The screen considers high-write-norm Q/K units, advances five pairs per head, and replays three prompts across 144 heads. The clearest selected response is on 'When Mary gave John the book, he thanked'. Reconstructed attention has mean KL 0.0405 from dense attention. Removing q266 from the reconstructed Q slice shifts attention toward the first token, producing mean KL 2.496 relative to intact reconstruction and maximum probability change 0.775. This establishes a selected unit-level effect within the reconstruction, not pair-specific necessity, output-level task mediation, or complete recovery of the dense head's mechanism.

Specific finding: Constrained sparse-attention post-training can retain near-baseline validation next-token cross-entropy while leaving substantially less than one percent of attention entries active. On the respective validation distributions, GPT-2 retains 0.22% and OLMo-7B 0.44% of reported attention edges. Mean cross-entropies are within 0.01 of targets 3.50 and 2.29, compared with original-model losses 3.48 and 2.25. The targets therefore permit small loss increases. Repeated-run variability is not reported.
Specific finding: A sparse-attention LLaMA 3.2 1B variant can approximately retain dense-model performance on selected retrieval tasks at an 8,192-token context length. Dense and sparse LLaMA 3.2 1B variants are fine-tuned using an 8,192-token context window. The sparse variant has approximately 0.4% active attention patterns and cross-entropy described as comparable to the dense variant. Needle-in-a-Haystack accuracy is 0.919 sparse versus 0.918 dense; Passkey Retrieval accuracy is 0.922 sparse versus 0.925 dense. Evaluation sample sizes, uncertainty, and detailed retrieval configurations are not supplied.
Specific finding: Sparse-attention post-training can reduce the number of ranked attention heads and token-level attention connections needed to account for a specified fraction of task-specific prediction preference. Figure 3 reports 1.4–4.5-fold fewer heads and 5.4–97-fold fewer attention edges at the reported 90% prediction-preference threshold, with standard errors across 20 prompts. A separate GPT-2 copying prompt requires nine heads in the sparse model versus 61 in the dense model. Appendix E.3 reports qualitatively consistent results under pooled task-level rankings.

Specific finding: Under minimal-first-layer and nondegeneracy assumptions, optimal bounded-depth Dyck prediction at every sequence length requires matched-bracket key differences to have query-independent scores across valid closing-bracket queries with a nonempty residual stack. Formal basis: repeatedly insert a specified matched pair into prefixes whose final token agrees but whose last unmatched opener differs. If the inserted pair has a nonzero projected contribution, normalization makes the predictions approach a common limit, contradicting their different required next-token distributions. Pairwise cancellation and nonzero value vectors then constrain score differences across those queries. The printed proof contains inconsistent argument ordering and token indices, so this edge is restricted to the substantive pumping argument rather than every index in the theorem as printed.
Specific finding: Penalizing prediction differences caused by prepending balanced bracket strings can reduce balance violation and improve long-prefix accuracy in minimal-first-layer Dyck Transformers. Add an expected squared-logit consistency penalty between a sequence's predictions and predictions at corresponding suffix positions after prepending r nested matched bracket pairs, with r sampled uniformly from 1 through D. Figures 3 and 10 and their accompanying text report lower balance violation and better length generalization under complete-sequence and prefix training. Exact effect sizes, sample counts, regularization settings, and uncertainty estimates are not recoverable from the supplied figure descriptions.
models_studied: ["Abstract two-layer Transformer with a minimal first layer"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Sufficiently accurate finite-length prediction by a minimal-first-layer Dyck Transformer with a Lipschitz readout is proposed to require matched-pair contribution imbalance, relative to a reference prefix contribution, to decrease as O(1/N). The supplied argument compares prefixes with different required continuations after insertion of many matched pairs, using Lipschitzness to prevent their normalized representations from collapsing. However, raw squared loss against stochastic one-hot targets has irreducible conditional variance. The arbitrarily small raw-loss premise and Corollary 2's zero-loss premise therefore do not establish the advertised nonvacuous near-optimality result as written. Definitions and proof equations also contain argument-order, depth-index, and normalization inconsistencies.
models_studied: ["Abstract two-layer Transformer with a minimal first layer and Lipschitz second-layer readout"]
location: Theorem 2; Corollary 2; Appendix C.4; Equations 4–5 and 15–18

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Lower matched-bracket balance violation predicts better closing-bracket length generalization in trained minimal-first-layer Dyck Transformers. Section 4.2 and Figure 3 report higher balance violation associated with lower accuracy on length-400–500 prefixes after complete-sequence training. Appendix D.2 explicitly states that the negative correlation is absent after Dyck-prefix training, despite regularization still reducing violation and improving generalization. Correlation coefficients, evaluation sample counts, and exact plotted accuracies are unavailable in the supplied text.
models_studied: ["Dyck Transformers with supplied token-depth one-hot first-layer embeddings"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Instruction-contrast residual steering can increase adherence to selected IFEval format and language constraints when those constraints are omitted from the input. Compare greedy generations with and without steering after removing explicit constraints. Reported aggregate accuracy rises from approximately 10% to approximately 30% across all four models. Figure 3a's caption reports significant improvements across models; the specified test is exact McNemar at p<0.01. Exact model-specific plotted values are unavailable. Format extraction and validation use synthetic data filtered against evaluation query–instruction combinations.
Specific finding: Instruction-contrast steering can improve selected format-constraint adherence beyond explicit textual instructions, with benefits depending on the model and constraint. Compare explicit-instruction prompts with and without steering in four models. Baseline loose accuracy ranges approximately from 60% to 90%; the prose reports additional aggregate performance boosts in two of four models without identifying them numerically. Per-instruction results and selected layers show heterogeneity, including many abstentions and little room for improvement on some already well-followed constraints.
models_studied: ["Phi-3 Mini Instruct", "Gemma 2 2B IT", "Gemma 2 9B IT", "Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1"]
location: Section 3, Figure 3a; Appendices D–E, G, and I

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Joint transplantation of selected target-language component activations can reverse a Python prompt's target-minus-Python syntax probability mass in selected Qwen code checkpoints. Patching crosses ΔM=0 in 2/45 aligned analysis settings: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B base/PHP at k=40, approximately −0.91 to +0.50, and its instruction-tuned counterpart/Rust at k=12, approximately −0.99 to +0.50. Both pass the specificity criterion. The base PHP circuit contains three MLP blocks and one attention head; the instruction-tuned Rust result uses the full 12-component set. Reported shift magnitudes are inconsistent between Table 4 and the clean-to-patched values in Tables 3 and 5.

Specific finding: Multilingual factual completion can depend most strongly on late subject-to-output attention while retaining non-subject-to-output attention dependence across earlier and later layers. The study knocks out final-token connections to subject, non-subject, or final-token positions in windows of six XGLM, seven EuroLLM, or four mT5 layers and measures relative change in original-answer probability. Subject knockouts are reported as most damaging later. Non-subject effects persist across depth, with early and late peaks in EuroLLM and mT5, rather than strictly preceding subject effects. mT5 interventions target decoder cross-attention. The text describes setting attention scores to zero without fully specifying masking and normalization semantics.

Specific finding: Jointly trained codebook bottlenecks can retain substantial next-token prediction performance in small natural-language transformers, with degradation depending on insertion site and code sparsity. TinyStories attention k=8 reaches loss 1.66 and accuracy 57.91%, versus 1.57 and 59.27% for the fine-tuned baseline; MLP k=100 reaches 1.57 and 59.47%. WikiText-103 attention k=8 and k=64 reach 46.68% and 48.44% accuracy versus 50.52% for the 410M baseline and 46.75% for the 160M baseline. Ungrouped MLP k=100 reaches 42.47%; grouped 16×(k=64) MLP codebooks reach 48.46%, with a tenfold higher codebook learning rate than the language-model learning rate.
Specific finding: A four-layer digit-level FSM transformer can retain near-baseline next-token performance and generated-transition validity when every attention head uses a single selected code. Attention-only k=1 codebooks yield loss 1.180, next-token accuracy 46.33%, and valid-transition accuracy 96.39%, versus 1.179, 46.36%, and 96.77% without codebooks. The analyzed attention-plus-MLP k=1 model instead has 63.65% valid-transition accuracy. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.
Specific finding: Transformer sublayer outputs can be refactored into sparse sums of fixed code vectors by jointly fine-tuning the network and top-k cosine-selected codebooks with language-modeling and codebook-reconstruction losses. Implemented and trained codebook transformers on TokFSM, TinyStories, and WikiText-103, including a 24-layer Pythia-410M model. Successful training establishes feasibility under the reported recipes, without establishing faithful preservation of pretrained mechanisms.

Specific finding: Discrete state-code activations can classify FSM states more precisely than individual neuron thresholds at the same recall. State codes achieve 97.1% average precision, compared with 70.5% for the best neuron classifier at each code's recall. Additional purity analyses enumerate all 100 two-digit and 1,000 three-digit starting combinations; the main text separately identifies 686 valid state-plus-digit possibilities. Purity declines in later layers, where different states sharing codes tend to have more similar next-token distributions than random state pairs. Exact purity and JSD values cannot be recovered from the figure text.
Specific finding: For manually selected regex-describable textual features, code activations can achieve higher classification precision than the best individual neuron thresholds at matched recall. Researchers selected codes with simple apparent meanings, wrote matching regexes, measured code precision and recall, and searched neuron thresholds at the same recall for the highest precision. Reported average code precision is over 30% higher; the text does not clarify whether this denotes a relative or percentage-point difference. The authors acknowledge selection bias and imperfect labels. Feature counts and uncertainty estimates are not provided in the supplied text.
models_studied: ["Four-layer GPT-NeoX-style TokFSM transformer with k=1 attention and MLP codebooks"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Replacing state-associated codes across multiple MLP layers can redirect an FSM transformer's next-token distribution toward that of a different state more strongly than replacing a single MLP layer or only attention-layer codes. Across 500 sampled state transitions, replacing MLP state codes reduces normalized Jensen–Shannon divergence from the target-state next-token distribution. The text reports that state-plus-digit substitutions make predictions nearly identical to the target distribution. Single-MLP-layer and attention-only substitutions have smaller effects. Exact plotted divergence values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Repeatedly activating manually selected topic-associated codes during generation can substantially increase the frequency of target-topic keywords in codebook language models. Codes are forced at prompt and generated positions, replacing the lowest-scoring selected codes or all k slots with repeated copies of one topic code per affected head. WikiText all-slot replacement raises keyword-match frequencies from 2.5% to 75% for video games, 7.5% to 95% for football, 27.5% to 90% for movies, and 20% to 85% for songs, using respectively 4, 8, 5, and 11 topic codes. The less extensive replacement condition uses 18, 18, 12, and 17 codes and reaches 55%, 47.5%, 42.5%, and 32.5%. TinyStories fire matches rise from 2.5% to 100% using 16 topic codes under the reported one-code condition. Generation counts and uncertainty estimates are unspecified; qualitative examples include incoherence.
models_studied: ["Four-layer GPT-NeoX-style TokFSM transformer with k=1 attention and MLP codebooks"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Increasing the commitment-loss weight can reduce code-assignment perplexity in discrete cross-layer activation models. Table 20 reports ERASER-Movie perplexity falling from 213.45 at beta 0 to 23.94 at beta 1. Jigsaw perplexity is 163.45 at beta 0, 164.07 at beta 0.1, and 30.71 at beta 1. At beta 0.6, the respective values are 170.76 and 81.38; the main-text suggestion that beta at least 0.6 always gives perplexity below 82 does not match the ERASER-Movie row. No repeated-run uncertainty or direct semantic-quality evaluation is reported for this sweep.
Specific finding: Increasing a CLVQ-VAE codebook's size can increase assignment perplexity while decreasing perplexity relative to available entries and producing nonmonotonic probe-disruption results. Table 7 reports perplexity increasing from 30.121 at K=50 to 184.895 at K=1,200, while perplexity/K decreases from 60.2% to 15.4%. Perturbed probe accuracy is lowest at K=400 among the five tested sizes, 0.0606, versus 0.0769 at K=50, 0.1214 at K=800, and 0.1004 at K=1,200. No uncertainty or direct concept-quality measurements accompany this sweep.
Specific finding: Constraining adaptive encoder interpolation to at most one half can retain higher code-usage perplexity than allowing full-range adaptive interpolation at similar reported reconstruction loss. Table 19 reports final code perplexity 210.6 for limited adaptive interpolation versus 63.21 for complete adaptive interpolation, with best validation loss 0.033 for both. Fixed alpha 0 and 0.1 retain higher perplexities, 237.2 and 230.8, but have higher validation losses, 0.045 and 0.040. Fixed alpha 1 reaches loss 0.032 and final perplexity 147.470. Repeated-run uncertainty is not supplied.
Specific finding: Temperature and nearest-candidate sampling changes can alter CLVQ-VAE code-usage perplexity while leaving projection-based task-probe accuracy within a comparatively narrow range. At top-5 sampling, increasing temperature from 0.5 to 3.0 raises validation code perplexity from 207.14 to 220.09. At temperature 1, candidate counts from one to one hundred yield perplexities from 207.07 to 212.51. A separate projection sweep reports perturbed accuracies of 0.0783–0.0911, against original accuracy 0.7604 and random-projection accuracy 0.7264. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied. These comparisons do not establish that stochastic sampling is necessary for effective concept discovery.
models_studied: ["RoBERTa-base, fine-tuned on ERASER-Movie", "RoBERTa-base, fine-tuned on Jigsaw"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Discrete codebook entries learned through contextual cross-layer reconstruction provide meaningful semantic concept coordinates for interpreting the source language model.

Specific finding: Training a discrete activation model to reconstruct a higher layer can yield stronger code-direction task-probe disruption than training the same architecture to reconstruct its input layer. Comparing the three-seed means in Table 1, CLVQ-VAE yields lower perturbed probe accuracy than single-layer VQ-VAE in 9/12 configurations. Exceptions are LLaMA/Jigsaw, LLaMA/AGNews, and Qwen/AGNews. Some favorable differences are small relative to reported seed variation, and no paired significance analysis is supplied.
Specific finding: CLVQ-VAE exemplar representations can receive higher aggregate LLM ratings for plausibly supporting supplied model predictions than the tested clustering, single-layer VQ-VAE, and cross-layer SAE representations. GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite judge stratified examples across the model–dataset panel. CLVQ-VAE receives mean rating 1.890/3, MRR 0.611, and a 66.7% configuration-level pairwise mean-rating win rate. The win rate is not the frequency of ranking first. Overall Kendall's W is 0.533, with W=0.225 on AGNews. Appendix D.2 mentions 100 samples without clearly specifying their allocation. No statistical superiority test is supplied.
Specific finding: CLVQ-VAE token-to-code assignments can exhibit task-label enrichment, different routing of identical surface tokens across labels, and greater code overlap between same-label sentences within lexical-similarity-selected pairs. Table 17 reports binary-task mean code purity of 0.601–0.761 against 0.50 references and AGNews purity of 0.353–0.465 against 0.25. Reported label-divergent content-token fractions range from 28.2% to 75.8%; mean JSD over divergent tokens ranges from 0.560 to 0.916. At TF-IDF cosine at least 0.1, median same-label/different-label code-overlap ratios range from 1.05 to 7.56 across all twelve configurations. Reported one-sided Mann–Whitney tests indicate higher same-label overlap, but the analysis does not describe adjustment for dependence among sentence pairs sharing an instance.
Specific finding: Discrete latent variables in a suitable generative model of text correspond to human-interpretable concepts.

Specific finding: For selected polysemous words, same-word different-sense sentence pairs exhibit greater transformer activation overlap than different-word same-sense pairs. The four-condition decomposition reports PS > SYN across all nine tested models and layers, with SemCor Wilcoxon p < 0.001 after Holm-Bonferroni correction. GPT-2 cosine-based R_lex falls from 0.735 at layer 0 to 0.290 at layer 11. Jaccard overlap agrees; magnitude divergence has the corresponding reversed ordering, CL > SYN > PS > SL. CoarseWSD-20 validation reports significant PS > SYN at every layer in GPT-2, BERT-base, and Pythia-1B, although the full four-condition ordering holds only at a majority of layers there. Appendix E reports the same ordering in concatenated attention-head outputs. These are within-paper cross-model and cross-corpus tests.
Specific finding: The first MLP layer of the tested autoregressive transformers has a larger normalized lexical-overlap contrast than their raw token embeddings. Table 6 compares embedding-only and layer-0 R_lex: GPT-2 0.713 versus 0.735, GPT-2-Medium 0.720 versus 0.751, Pythia-1B 0.821 versus 0.836, Pythia-6.9B 0.882 versus 0.910, Pythia-12B 0.891 versus 0.913, and LLaMA-2-13B 0.815 versus 0.911. No uncertainty estimates for these differences are supplied. The result concerns a normalized contrast and does not identify a particular amplification mechanism.
Specific finding: GPT-2 neurons selected for word-form consistency and specificity are predominantly sense-invariant, and sense-blind neuron groups support substantially poorer sense decoding than sense-selective groups. Of GPT-2 form detectors identified without sense labels, 67.3% have SSI < 0.5 and 0.1% have SSI > 2. Logistic-regression probes with leave-one-out cross-validation and C = 0.01 achieve 91.1% sense accuracy from selective neurons, 41.9% from blind neurons, and 68.9% from random neurons. Word-form detection is approximately 85% across groups. Whether sense-dependent neuron selection is nested within cross-validation is unspecified.
Specific finding: The evaluated GPT-2 and Pythia sparse autoencoders contain features that activate across distinct senses of a word, and increasing GPT-2 dictionary size from 32k to 128k does not consistently remove these collisions. Across five GPT-2 layers, Table 8 reports collision ratios of 17.7–31.7% for 32k SAEs and 22.4–32.6% for 128k SAEs. Pythia-410M 65k SAEs report 19–36%. GPT-2 layer-8 feature 5132 is reported sense-blind for 232 tested polysemous words and active on 47.5% of inputs. These observations establish cross-sense activity under the scoring rule; they do not prove exclusive word-form semantics or establish the recovery rate of underlying superposed features.
Specific finding: Among activating input pairs for neurons flagged by the evaluated polysemanticity scores, a substantial fraction share a word form when evaluation is restricted to polysemous inputs. Section 5.3 reports that approximately 57% of activating input pairs for flagged neurons share a word form, conditional on polysemous inputs. The specific standard scores, detailed counting procedure, experiment-specific model identity, and uncertainty for this percentage are not supplied.
Specific finding: Subtracting a layer-calibrated lexical contribution from form-detector polysemanticity scores can reclassify a subset of GPT-2 neurons flagged by the original scores. The correction reclassifies 6.5% of flagged neurons at GPT-2 layer 6 and 10.4% averaged across layers. The paper reports that 93–94% of reclassified neurons have SSI < 0.5. This demonstrates changes in scoring and agreement with the paper's sense-invariance criterion; it does not independently validate the corrected flags as ground-truth superposition classifications. The underlying standard score and reclassification procedure are not fully specified.
location: Sections 5.1–5.2; Appendices B.1, C, E, F.1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Under the specified high-AP acquisition threshold, the evaluated pretrained transformers exhibit limited single-unit coverage of same-lemma sense distinctions. Table 1 reports 4–17 of 297 homograph concepts acquired per checkpoint, corresponding to 1.35%–5.72%. At the separately selected sense threshold, 14–240 of 1,344 sense concepts are acquired. The prose accompanying Figure 4 reports broader and generally weaker best-unit homograph AP scores than sense scores in RoBERTa Large. No independent sentence test split or randomized-model baseline is specified.
location: Section 4.3.2; Table 1; Figure 4 and accompanying prose; Appendix E

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Matched-count mean ablation of sense-selective GPT-2 neurons disrupts diagnostic sense behavior more selectively than ablation of sense-blind neurons. Table 2 reports specificity 0.66 for sense-A-selective ablation, 2.52 for sense-B-selective ablation, 0.24 for blind ablation, and 0.32 for random ablation; averaging the two selective values yields the reported approximately 6.6-fold advantage over blind. Appendix D reports an eight-percentage-point diagnostic sense-accuracy decline from a 73% baseline after selective ablation, versus less than one point after blind ablation. Across ten layer-6 per-word tests, selective ablation is reported 5–72 times more targeted. Absolute reported perplexity changes are below three points. These results establish group-dependent causal effects under the interventions, without establishing exclusive mediation or absence of redundant sense information.
Specific finding: Matched-count mean ablation of sense-selective neurons can perturb output distributions more than ablation of sense-blind or random neurons, with smaller relative differences in the tested larger models. Section 5.5 reports that sense-selective mean ablation produces 3–5 times the full-output KL divergence of matched blind or random groups in models up to 345M, declining to 1.2–2.1 times at 12–13B. Absolute KL effects are approximately 0.0001–0.001. Model-by-model values and uncertainty estimates are not supplied for this comparison.
Specific finding: Selecting neurons by sense discrimination can improve linear word-sense classification over the tested sense-blind neuron subsets on CoarseWSD-20. Selectivity-ranked neuron classifiers achieve 89.8% accuracy in GPT-2 and 89.3% in Pythia-1B, compared with 83.6% and 84.6% for blind-neuron classifiers. The text also reports an all-neuron accuracy of 88.3%, without separately providing an all-neuron value for each model. The selective–blind advantage peaks in early-to-middle layers. This tests neuron selection rather than a downstream benefit from LIS projection, and the top-quartile selection differs from the SSI > 2 criterion used elsewhere.

Specific finding: Small groups of readout features selected by training-set contribution differences can predict held-out senses of ambiguous words, while losing accuracy relative to a full decoded-state probe. Eight features per sense are selected by training-set mean contribution differences, with feature scales standardized using training statistics. Held-out balanced accuracy is 0.899 and 0.923 for Qwen3.5-2B/9B over 20 words, and 0.798 for R1-Llama over 13 words. The corresponding datasets contain 33,566 and 16,785 total train-plus-test contexts, not that many test cases. Repeated-selection permutation nulls score 0.408/0.407/0.422; full-state nearest-centroid probes score 0.958/0.971/0.920. Counts above null p95 are 20/20, 19/20, and 12/13. No behavioral target-rank filter is applied; median ambiguous-word ranks are 174, 10, and 1,131.

Specific finding: Automated conceptual labels for selected Llama-3.1 SAE features can obscure responses to lexical forms that extend beyond the named concept. Feature 29/30028, labeled references to coffee, activates on coff in coffee-related text and coffins; steering at -20 changes a funeral completion from coffin to casket. Feature 18/6893 responds to Morocco and other overlapping lexical forms; positive steering promotes Morocco on a country prompt and morning on a daily-routine prompt. Feature 18/14711 responds to photographic exposure despite its hazards/influential-experiences label, and steering at -10 removes exposure wording from a photography completion. These observations do not isolate whether each mismatch originates in the learned feature, its description, or intervention behavior.
Specific finding: Automated descriptions of selected coffee-related Llama-3.1 SAE features can underdescribe substantial differences in the contextual conditions required for activation. Feature 18/7546 does not activate on isolated coffee but responds in cup-of and drank contexts, including with poison. Feature 17/17320 responds to surrounding terms such as Africa in a coffee context but not a zebra context. Feature 18/9463 responds to coffee-related forms across several meaningful and nonsensical contexts. These are qualitative contrasts, without a calibrated contextual-sensitivity metric or proof of context independence.

Specific finding: A sparse activation decomposition can combine selected frozen SAE features with an additional concept-aligned encoder–decoder trained to reconstruct activations and encode user-specified concepts.

Specific finding: Pruning by naming and steering scores and adding a pseudo-supervised concept bottleneck can improve average naming, visual monosemanticity, and artificial-intervention steering scores over the evaluated full vision SAE dictionaries. Table 1 reports baseline→CB-SAE scores in the order CLIP-Dissect, MS, unit-vector steering, white-image steering: LLaVA-1.5, 0.154→0.244, 0.517→0.556, 0.198→0.261, 0.203→0.250; LLaVA-MORE, 0.194→0.291, 0.553→0.598, 0.179→0.192, 0.177→0.189; UnCLIP, 0.058→0.092, 0.540→0.594, 0.642→0.659, 0.654→0.664. Appendix Table 3 also reports improvements in these four scores for TopK and BatchTopK starting dictionaries. The prose's 14% LLaVA-MORE steering gain is inconsistent with Table 1's approximately 7% gains. No repeated-training uncertainty is supplied.
Specific finding: Choosing vision SAE neurons using steering scores alone can yield stronger subsequent steering averages but worse concept-naming scores and reconstructed-feature classification accuracy than using naming scores or both scores. Table 5 reports reconstructed-feature ImageNet accuracy of 74.07% for the full SAE, 73.39% for naming-only pruning, 70.99% for steering-only pruning, and 73.78% for combined pruning. Naming-only versus steering-only versus combined scores are respectively 0.233/0.167/0.244 for CLIP-Dissect, 0.566/0.520/0.556 for MS, 0.216/0.288/0.261 for unit-vector steering, and 0.220/0.269/0.250 for white-image steering. Classification retention does not establish full activation or behavioral fidelity.
Specific finding: Adding a decoder-only cyclic concept-reconstruction objective can improve the reported steering score of a concept-bottleneck SAE without a comparable reported change in interpretability. The authors train CB-SAEs with and without the cyclic loss that aligns re-encoded reconstructed activations with CLIP concept pseudo-labels, updating only the concept decoder for this objective. They report similar interpretability and 2.9% higher steerability with the loss. The plot itself is unavailable in the supplied text rendering, so its numerical points cannot be independently extracted.
Specific finding: Combining selected SAE coordinates with a concept bottleneck can yield higher average steering scores but lower average concept-naming scores than a concept-only autoencoder. The concept-only CB-AE achieves CLIP-Dissect 0.308, unit-vector steering 0.238, and white-image steering 0.232. The hybrid CB-SAE obtains 0.244, 0.261, and 0.250, respectively. The full SAE baseline obtains 0.154, 0.198, and 0.203. The result supports a measured tradeoff rather than uniform superiority of either hybrid or concept-only architectures.
Specific finding: Increasing the active-concept budget of a trained concept-bottleneck SAE decoder can improve reconstructed-feature classification while producing a nonmonotonic concept-steering response. Appendix C.3 reports that reconstructed-feature classification improves as decoder k increases and is already close to the SAE baseline at k=3–5. CB-neuron steerability initially increases and decreases for k>30; it remains above discarded-SAE and below retained-SAE scores throughout the reported sweep. Numerical plotted values and uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied rendering. The proposed explanation involving competition among concepts is not independently isolated.
