Llama sarcoidosis and Gemma hepatitis B were excluded because their baseline racial distributions were not skewed as required by the setup. OLMo-7B comparisons examine layers 4 and 19 with window radii 1, 3, and 5. Tables 14–15 show target-dependent gains and losses, so multilayer replacement is not uniformly better. These effects do not independently establish that race has an intrinsically more distributed encoding than gender.
Specific finding: Selected demographic activation replacements can substantially change OLMo-7B-Instruct vignette demographics while leaving average perplexity under an external Llama evaluator approximately unchanged. The authors score 500 generated vignettes before and after patching using Llama-3.1-8B perplexity. They report minimally changed or comparable average perplexity for the gender scaling sweep and race comparisons; race results average over three target races. Exact intervention perplexities cannot be recovered from the supplied text because the corresponding plots are image-only. A separate disruptive reference, patching half the prompt tokens across seven layers with highly amplified male-token activations, uses 50 sampled vignettes and has reported mean perplexity 15.54.
Specific finding: Demographic-source residual replacements can produce statistically detectable differences in the rank of a correct diagnosis across repeated generations for individual clinical cases. The authors reuse the depression-task donor prompts, layers, and scaling and report sampling 500 differential lists at temperature 0.7. Mann–Whitney tests yield a mean gender-comparison rank difference of 0.24 with p=0.004 and a race-comparison difference of 0.08 with p=0.02. The prose does not specify the direction of these differences or clearly establish whether 500 denotes each demographic condition. Correct-diagnosis identities and handling of absent diagnoses are not provided in the supplied text. The authors report similar qualitative rank trends under explicit and patched demographic assignment; the plots are image-only. Only one case per comparison is evaluated.
location: Section 3, Figures 4–6, Table 4; Appendix B.2, Table 10; Tables 14–15

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Perspective API scores provide sufficiently informative operational measurements of toxicity in GPT-2 Medium continuations for evaluating detoxification and its reversal.

Specific finding: ChatGPT's persona-conditioned toxicity can vary substantially across assigned identities and persona categories. Entity-conditioned category toxicity is 0.40 for dictators, 0.29 for journalists, 0.24 for sportspersons, 0.18 for democratic politicians, and 0.15 for businesspersons. Male and female persona averages are 0.26 and 0.22; Republican and Democrat politician averages are 0.27 and 0.25. Within the selected male-politician comparison, scores range from 0.13 for Nelson Mandela to 0.35 for Richard Nixon. Entity scores use maximum-of-five aggregation. Reported persona categories and inventories contain inconsistencies that limit exact reconstruction.
Specific finding: Explicitly negative or toxic entity requests can increase persona-conditioned ChatGPT toxicity scores relative to neutral or positive requests, while also changing measured refusal rates. Table 10 reports toxicity of 0.13 for positive requests, 0.17 for neutral requests, 0.28 for bad or negative requests, 0.30 for harmful requests, and 0.32 for toxic requests. Corresponding response probabilities are 0.99, 1.00, 0.75, 0.87, 0.53, and 0.55. The authors report that more than 8% of responses under the neutral template exceed toxicity 0.5, with maximum 0.90, but do not clearly distinguish raw draws from maximum-of-five aggregates for that percentage. These findings do not establish ordinary conversational prevalence.

Specific finding: Image-code-guided language-representation refinement combined with the specified decoding procedure can improve POPE accuracy and F1 over regular decoding and VCD, while reducing recall relative to VCD in some models. Table 2 reports higher accuracy, precision, and F1 than regular decoding and VCD in all six model–setting combinations. Relative to regular decoding, LLaVA accuracy changes from 82.93/81.13/78.67 to 87.07/85.87/83.60; Qwen changes from 85.20/83.80/82.33 to 86.47/85.97/86.10. Qwen recall is lower than VCD in all three settings. LLaVA recall slightly improves over VCD in Random and Popular and ties in Adversarial. The intervention adds a decoded pooled-state displacement to every text-token state, then combines original and modified logits with a plausibility constraint. Alpha_l=0.7 is selected from a POPE sweep. Independent tuning data, evaluation denominators, and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.
Specific finding: Image-code-guided representation refinement with the specified decoding procedure can reduce sentence-level and instance-level object hallucination while increasing object recall on a sampled caption-generation evaluation. Appendix B.2 reports 500 randomly selected samples and averages over five independent trials. LLaVA regular/VCD/VL-SAE CHAIR_S scores are 53.4/55.0/47.8 and CHAIR_I scores are 17.6/16.3/13.3; object recall is 72.3/76.0/76.3. Qwen corresponding scores are 44.6/42.6/39.6, 16.1/13.9/10.7, and 60.7/60.0/63.3. Average caption lengths also decrease. Trial variability and whether trials reuse the same sampled images are unspecified.
location: Section 4.3, Equation 11 and Table 2; Appendix A.5, Equations A15–A16; Appendix B.4, Table A16

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Clamping selected OCR-associated SAE coordinates can change an incorrect LLaVA-NeXT map answer to the correct answer. The text reports that high-value clamps of either a Barcelona-associated coordinate or a Los-associated traffic-sign coordinate cause the model to conclude that Bolivia is absent. This is a selected single-question demonstration without a matched random-feature comparison. The authors acknowledge that corrected output can still involve incorrect reasoning; full visual outputs are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: High-value single-feature clamping can improve some LLaVA hallucination answers while leaving most unchanged and worsening others. Appendix J reports improved outcomes on 9 of 100 examples, unchanged outcomes on 89, and worse outcomes on 2. Table 11 describes a single feature clamped to a high value, while the prose refers to irrelevant features. No uncertainty estimates, additional capability evaluation, or specificity controls are supplied.

Specific finding: DoLa does not consistently improve multiple-choice truthfulness and factuality across language-model families, even after searching candidate-layer ranges and probability thresholds. Baseline and normalized DoLa scores are compared across ten models. Llama-7B improves on both benchmarks, while other models show smaller gains, unchanged scores, or degradation. Appendix Table 10 reports FACTOR accuracy changing from 0.5845 to 0.6253 for Llama-7B and from 0.5125 to 0.4797 for Pythia-6.9B. Main and appendix TruthfulQA tables conflict for some models, including the direction of Qwen2-7B's MC1 change. Statistical significance estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: Aggregating unnormalized DoLa contrast scores across answer tokens can introduce length bias and inflate TruthfulQA metrics without a corresponding improvement in normalized answer likelihoods. Table 7 compares normalized and unnormalized scoring with a baseline modified by first making logits positive and then adding a constant of 20, selected for its improvement. For Llama-7B, normalized DoLa MC2 is 0.5202, unnormalized DoLa MC2 is 0.6176, and the length-biased baseline reaches 0.6151 versus an ordinary baseline of 0.4055. The control demonstrates apparent gains without selecting a premature layer; it does not show that every DoLa gain is a length artifact.

Specific finding: Retrospective string detectors for known exit(0) and raise SkipTest exploits provide sufficiently reliable positive labels for evaluating detection of those systemic coding hacks.
Specific finding: Test passage that disappears when an agent's test modifications are reverted provides an adequate operational proxy for the dominant reward-hacking behavior in test-edit coding honeypots.

Specific finding: Candidate-answer likelihood and entropy over normalized answer options provide useful operational measures of a language model's confidence for interpreting activation readouts and interventions.
Specific finding: Renormalized answer-letter probabilities and greedy multiple-choice choices provide useful operational measurements of the behavior targeted by activation steering.

Specific finding: An OR-rule over a small set of toxicity-associated SAE features can exceed 0.90 English toxicity F1 without fitting an additional classifier head. Features are ranked by toxic-minus-clean example-level firing frequency on 2,000 toxic and 2,000 clean discovery examples. A feature fires if it has a positive activation at any prompt token. OR-rules with K in {1,2,5,10} are evaluated on 500 toxic and 500 clean English examples; best-layer F1 exceeds 0.90 in both models. No trained-head comparison is reported.

Specific finding: Peak activation of a selected toxic-persona SAE feature can distinguish labeled persona jailbreak prompts from benign instructions and other jailbreak prompts. Uses o3-mini to label prompts requesting adoption of a detailed atypical and transgressive persona. Peak feature #10 activation gives AUROC 0.96 for persona jailbreaks versus benign Alpaca prompts and 0.93 versus non-persona jailbreaks. The initial collection sizes do not specify the sizes of the resulting persona/non-persona subsets. Results establish discrimination of the operational labels rather than a complete or exclusive semantic interpretation of the feature.

Specific finding: A single final-encoder Whisper SAE latent can discriminate noise-only audio from speech with high precision and recall in a selected evaluation. A predictor assigning noise when latent 15019 is positive achieves reported noise precision of 98.1% and recall of 99.8%. ESC-50 supplies 50 environmental sound categories. Exact evaluation counts, the speech-comparison composition, temporal aggregation details, and an independent feature-selection/evaluation split are not supplied.
location: Appendix G-A; Figure 4 caption and accompanying text

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected PolarBERT SAE coordinates can discriminate detector-quality contrasts and early-layer detector depth after held-out evaluation and evaluable nuisance controls. On concept_test, the reference bright-clean coordinate reaches AUROC 0.911 and strictest reported control AUROC 0.787; auxiliary discrimination reaches 0.840 and 0.854 under evaluable controls. Layer-2 depth reaches 0.986 and minimum control AUROC 0.984. Within clean events, bright-versus-dim discrimination by the bright-clean coordinate reaches AUROC 0.821. Synthetic auxiliary injection, pulse removal, and charge rescaling yield response changes consistent with the assigned labels or brightness association. Auxiliary matches including non-auxiliary pulse count can yield no usable pairs.
models_studied: ["PolarBERT, direction-fine-tuned backbone", "Reference final-layer and layer-2 BatchTopK SAEs"]
location: Sections 3.1 and 3.3; Appendix B.1; Tables 8 and 10

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected Qwen3 SAE directions can suppress unwanted Chinese text or induce classical-Chinese style during generation. Section 3.3 describes removing Chinese mixing from an English response by suppressing a Chinese-associated feature and changing a modern-Chinese story continuation by amplifying a classical-Chinese feature. Exact checkpoints, intervention doses, and evaluation denominators are unspecified.

Specific finding: Steering selected SAE decoder directions in instruction-tuned open-weight models can elicit undesirable language consistent with persona-related interpretations of their activating examples. Presented steering examples include destructive persona language from Llama feature 87027, coercive-control language from feature 16205, absurd advice from feature 110281, and sadistic language from Qwen feature 129593. These selected generations demonstrate behavioral influence, without independently establishing ordinary causal mediation or comprehensive semantic specificity. Numerical steering coefficients and representative generation success rates are not supplied.
location: Zooming in on individual features (Llama, layer 11); Zooming in on individual features (Qwen, layer 15)

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Subtracting an intermediate activation difference between cheese-present and cheese-absent observations can reduce a maze policy's cheese-directed behavior without retraining, with asymmetric effects under addition. Across 100 mazes, subtracting the cheese-present-minus-absent activation difference reduced probabilities assigned to cheese-directed actions at decision squares, whereas adding it reportedly did not affect those probabilities. Appendix C.2 describes selected cases resembling hiding cheese and a counterexample. Qualitative cross-maze transfer was reported when cheese occupied the same or a nearby location, approximately within two tiles; no aggregate transfer rate was supplied.
Specific finding: Simultaneously subtracting a cheese-presence activation vector and adding a corner-directed activation vector can combine reduced cheese pursuit with increased corner attraction in a maze policy without retraining. Appendix C.4 reports a qualitative comparison of cheese-vector subtraction, top-right-vector addition, and their simultaneous application, with the combined intervention exhibiting both reported navigation effects. No sample count, aggregate success rate, or quantitative interaction analysis is supplied. Interpretation inherits the inconsistent top-right-vector definition.
location: Section 3.2, Equation 1 and Figure 9a; Appendix C.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: TopK sparse autoencoders can reconstruct substantial information in masked diffusion language-model residual activations, with reconstruction improving as more latents are retained and deeper layers requiring larger budgets. Layerwise active-latent-count sweeps report improving reconstruction and generally smaller insertion-loss deviations as sparsity is relaxed. Appendix C explicitly reports that deeper LLaDA layers require larger budgets for comparable reconstruction. Exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: High activation reconstruction and small denoising-loss changes after SAE replacement provide sufficient fidelity for using the dictionary to analyze a diffusion language model's native mechanisms.

Specific finding: A circuit discovered for Barbara completion can satisfy mean-ablation necessity, sufficiency, and positive-margin criteria on other affirmative syllogistic forms with high completion accuracy. Table 2 evaluates all 15 forms. AII-3, IAI-3, IAI-4, and AAA-1 pass necessity, sufficiency, and positive mean margin, with accuracies 0.84, 0.68, 0.68, and 0.67. AII-1 also passes necessity and sufficiency but lacks a positive mean margin and has accuracy 0.43. Other forms fail at least one criterion. This evaluation transfers the selected circuit rather than independently reconstructing a complete mechanism for each form.
Specific finding: A symbolic syllogism attention circuit can retain its mean-ablation necessity and sufficiency properties when letters are replaced with numbers and quantifier wording is changed to semantically equivalent alternatives. Mean-ablation evaluations replace letters with numbers and change wording such as 'All … are' to 'Each … is'. The text reports preserved necessity and sufficiency. The numerical curves are inaccessible; Appendix B states 90 samples for experiments but provides no separate perturbation-specific breakdown.

Specific finding: Truth-task circuits in GPT-2 Small can transfer positive answer margins to other binary token contrasts, while their fidelity to the full model varies substantially by pair and task. Tables 5–6 evaluate the original circuits on four additional pairs, with positive circuit ALDs in all eight task–pair conditions. SS circuit ALDs exceed full-model ALDs for three of four pairs, while correct/incorrect is lower at 1.6785 versus 2.1221. OS transfer has a large margin gap for positive/negative, 1.0113 versus 3.0032, while correct/incorrect is close at 0.8142 versus 0.7986. A larger margin is not itself greater fidelity under the paper's absolute-error metric. Transfer sample counts and uncertainty are unspecified.

Specific finding: Symbolic-regression component circuits can be operationally evaluated by combining retained-circuit prediction fidelity, circuit-knockout suppression, and single-component removals within the retained circuit.

Specific finding: A selected Truth Head circuit in GPT-2 Small can approximately preserve the full model's average binary-answer margin on simple assigned-truth completion prompts. Path patching identifies late attention heads with substantial direct effects and little reported upstream-head dependence. The SS circuit reaches ALD 1.9286 versus 1.8575 for the full model in the main text. Table 1 specifies 500 prompts per task. The introduction describes a three-head circuit, while Section 3.1 lists a larger influential candidate set; exact final membership and retained-circuit intervention details are unclear.
Specific finding: Correct-minus-opposite answer logit differences provide useful operational measures of performance on templated tasks involving assigned binary values.
Specific finding: Preference for a syllogism's conclusion predicate over its middle term provides a useful operational measure of successful syllogistic completion.

Specific finding: Benchmark labeling rules and restricted single-token candidate rankings provide sufficiently meaningful operational definitions of model success and failure for evaluating circuit explanations.
location: Sections 2.2–2.3 and Appendices A.1, B, and D.1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing internal component values using fixed paired counterfactual inputs produces sufficiently meaningful hybrid computations to evaluate task-specific circuit preservation and causal-variable alignment.

Specific finding: Mean or operator-counterfactual activation replacements remove target-operator information selectively enough for resulting prediction changes to localize operator-related components.

Specific finding: Replacing selected layer-stacked context activations while freezing other context states produces meaningful hybrid computations for interpreting answer changes as changes in stored associations.

Specific finding: Recovering a donor's expected answer after swapping selected neuron activations between otherwise matched, correctly solved task templates provides useful evidence that those neurons mediate the manipulated concept.

Specific finding: A concept-based neuron explanation can be evaluated separately through agreement between its denotation and neuron activation, and through donor-output recovery after concept-conditioned interchange interventions. Demonstrated through an observational audit of 300 highly scored GPT-4 explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons and twelve template-based intervention tasks covering six concept families. These applications demonstrate diagnostic utility without independently establishing the framework's sufficiency for explanatory faithfulness.
Specific finding: An LLM's ability to identify a nonactivating intruder among activating examples is a useful proxy for the semantic interpretability of a learned component.

Specific finding: Automated linguistic labels generated from activation-marked transcript spans can agree with manual judgments for a substantial but imperfect fraction of Whisper SAE latents. For each latent, the procedure selects 100 files near median activation strength and presents up to 20 activation-marked examples to GPT-OSS 120B. Low-confidence responses are assigned diffuse labels. Manual evaluation of 100 randomly selected latents yields 76% accuracy. This checks label agreement rather than exhaustive semantics or mechanistic faithfulness.
location: Section III-D2; Appendices E and F

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Patterns in contexts selected by high predicted causal importance provide a useful qualitative proxy for a parameter subcomponent's function.

Specific finding: For a fixed-size update instance and fixed initial weight vector, a transformer can approximate an unregularized squared-error linear-regression gradient update and its subsequent query prediction using constant depth and O(d) hidden space. Formal constructive derivation: Theorem 1 and Appendices A/C compose copying, affine operations, and approximate multiplication to form a weight update and query prediction. This is an expressivity result, not an empirical experiment. The source's exact-equality theorem wording is qualified by its approximate primitives and scaling limits. Restricting the extracted result to zero regularization avoids inconsistent regularization signs and coefficients in Appendix A; other displayed indexing and algebraic inconsistencies and the absence of an end-to-end error bound limit the construction's rigor.
Specific finding: A transformer can approximate the ridge-regression prediction obtained from a first Sherman–Morrison update initialized with inverse covariance I/λ, using constant depth and O(d²) hidden space. Formal constructive derivation: Theorem 2 and Appendices B/C express (λI+xxᵀ)⁻¹xy and its query prediction through matrix products, affine operations, and LayerNorm-based approximate division. For λ>0, the Sherman–Morrison denominator is positive. Matrix intermediates require O(d²) space for the displayed single-observation construction. Its primitive implementations use scaling approximations and contain displayed algebraic inconsistencies; no finite-precision end-to-end error guarantee is supplied.
location: Section 3.2, Theorem 1; Appendices A and C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: The standard estimator that best approximates a trained linear-regression in-context learner can change with transformer capacity, progressing from gradient-descent-like behavior through ridge-like behavior toward ordinary least squares. Capacity sweeps compare SPD averaged over underdetermined context lengths. One-layer models are closest to one-step batch GD but have poor absolute fit; two-to-four-layer models are closest to ridge regression; models with eight or more layers match OLS. Width sweeps also change the best-fitting estimator. Reported ridge-like width thresholds are H≥16 for d=8 and H≥32 for d=16. Because other hyperparameters are optimized, these compare selected recipes rather than isolating capacity alone, and estimator agreement does not identify an internal algorithm.
Specific finding: A single-head transformer can achieve lower prediction discrepancy from OLS than from ridge regression with λ=0.1 across the tested synthetic linear-regression dimensions when other model and training parameters are selected appropriately. Appendix H searches depths {1,2,4,8,12,16}, widths {16,32,64,256,512,1024}, head counts {1,2,4,8}, and learning rates {1e-4,2.5e-4}. For each capacity parameter, other searched parameters are optimized to find the smallest value satisfying SPD(OLS,ICL)<SPD(Ridge(0.1),ICL). One head suffices at every tested dimension; selected minimum depths and widths have step-like dependence on dimension. Other hyperparameters, including initialization settings, are not independently optimized per dimension.
models_studied: ["Synthetic-regression decoder transformers with 1\u201316 layers, hidden sizes 16\u20131024, and 1\u20138 heads"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Latents from a larger SAE can improve a smaller SAE's reconstruction when added without retraining, demonstrating reconstructive information not adequately captured by the smaller dictionary. Added larger-SAE latent contributions to smaller-SAE reconstructions, selecting candidates by low maximum decoder cosine similarity and combining decoder biases according to Equation 5. Adding all GPT2-1536 latents with similarity at most 0.7 to GPT2-768 reduced MSE by almost 10%. Analogous stitching was performed between Gemma Scope 16,384- and 32,768-latent dictionaries using threshold 0.4. Evaluation sample counts and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Appendix A.6, Figure 15; Appendix A.6.1, Figures 18–19

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Reconstruction improvements from adding low-similarity donor latents provide useful evidence that a smaller SAE omits meaningful features, rather than merely representing the same features imprecisely.

Specific finding: Allocating MOLT capacity across multiple transform ranks can improve the reconstruction-MSE versus active-transform-count frontier relative to uniform-rank allocations at matched parameter counts. The authors report comparing variable-rank and uniform-rank MOLTs while controlling total parameters. Their best reported allocation uses N rank-512, 2N rank-256, 4N rank-128, 8N rank-64, and 16N rank-32 transforms. Numerical frontier values, repetitions, and search coverage are not supplied.
Specific finding: Mixed-rank MOLTs can achieve better reconstruction-MSE versus L0 tradeoffs than transcoders for Claude 3.5 Haiku's middle MLP layer under the reported parameter and training-compute comparisons. Parameter-matched MOLT and transcoder runs scale training steps proportionally to replacement size. The source reports lower MSE for MOLTs at matched L0 and that its smallest MOLT runs Pareto-dominate transcoders using 1,024 times as many training FLOPs. The largest transcoder runs contain approximately ten million features. Data, repetitions, uncertainty, and absolute MSE values are unspecified; the authors acknowledge possible transcoder tuning limitations.

Specific finding: Pretrained BERT-base contains both heads strongly biased toward adjacent tokens and heads with broad attention distributions, especially in lower layers. Four of 144 heads place over 50% of average attention on the previous token, and five place over 50% on the next token. Some high-entropy heads typically allocate at most 10% of attention mass to any individual word. Final-layer attention originating at [CLS] has average entropy 3.89 nats.

Specific finding: Translation Transformer encoders can contain heads whose maximum attention consistently targets a particular adjacent position and whose attention distributions are highly concentrated. Heads are classified as positional when at least 90% of their maximum-attention targets occupy one particular relative position, observed as −1 or +1. Every identified positional head across the considered language pairs has average maximum attention weight above 0.8. These heads largely coincide with high-confidence and high-LRP heads.

Specific finding: Attention heads identified with narrow tasks can exhibit additional distinct behaviors or broader related mechanisms on a general data distribution. New dataset-example analyses find year and multi-token-word attention in a previously studied line-width head, and non-multiple-choice selection examples in a previously studied answer-selection head. These observations extend a phenomenon explicitly attributed to prior work. PCA and feature analyses characterize the selected cases, without establishing how frequently narrow task labels fail across heads.
Specific finding: A single early-layer attention head can exhibit line-width-related, tokenized-year, and multi-token-word attention patterns that separate in leading query, key, and output principal components. Inspection identifies newline-to-newline, year-suffix-to-prefix, and within-word attention patterns in a head previously studied for line width. PCA of Q/K/O activations on high-attention-output-norm token pairs separates the three groups in leading components; group labels use hardcoded token rules independent of PCA. The authors explicitly treat PCA as hypothesis generation. No behavior-specific head splitting or output-reconstruction test is performed, and the prior line-width computation is not newly established here.
location: A Polysemantic Attention Head, Figures 5–7; Answer Selection, Figures 8–13

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Answerability probes can retain performance under minor prompt-template paraphrases while failing to generalize across more substantial dataset shifts. Probes trained using the default SQuAD template are evaluated on five variants changing instruction wording and labels such as Passage/Text/Excerpt and Question/Inquiry/Query, using the 1,800-example variation sets listed in Table 1. Both readout types generalize well to these variants despite poor transfer on some distinct datasets. Exact template-specific accuracies are not transcribed.
location: Section 5; Appendix B.2; Tables 1 and 3; Figure 10

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Clinical chapter directions fitted on discharge summaries can retain above-chance chapter discrimination when applied without refitting to patient-question text. Out-of-register AUC ranges from 0.630 to 0.815. Retention, defined as (target AUC−0.5)/(in-corpus ceiling−0.5), ranges from 45% to 86%. All five entries report permutation p<1/2,000 from 2,000 shuffles. These are separability results without target-register intervention tests.

Specific finding: English-selected toxicity SAE features can transfer directly to other languages, with substantial differences across languages, layers, and model sizes. The study compares Jaccard overlap of independently selected top-10 feature sets and applies English-selected features to held-out data in the 13 languages. Sharing is strongest in middle layers. Transfer is reported to be stronger for several European languages and weaker for Arabic, Chinese, and especially Amharic. Qwen3-8B shows stronger reported transfer and deeper optimal layers. Exact plotted F1 values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: COCO-derived JSAE caption-steering directions can retain effects on Flickr30k while experiencing category-dependent losses in reported steering success and fluency. On 1,500 Flickr30k images, 500 per target category, reported success is 50.5% for food, 62.0% for wild animals, and 34.0% for indoor rooms, compared with 75.0% on 32, 81.3% on 32, and 67.5% on 40 COCO examples. Flickr30k perplexity ratios are 1.29, 1.15, and 1.38, respectively. Positive mean SBERT gains and judge incorporation scores support retained effects, but the reported 50.5% food rate does not correspond to an integer success count out of 500 under the stated per-image definition.

Specific finding: Sign-split neurons can match transcoder features in automated discrimination of peak activation examples while performing worse when examples cover a broader activation range. A Claude Haiku 4.5 judge classifies held-out contexts after seeing ten examples from each of two features, with 500 trials per configuration. Examples come from a shared 10-million-token SmolLM2 activation cache. Neurons score comparably to transcoder features under top-example sampling but degrade more under quantile sampling, especially with less restrictive neuron TopK selection.
Specific finding: Some transcoder features can isolate a coherent subset of a polysemantic neuron's activations while their decoder directions are approximated by combinations of a few neurons. Inspect attribution graphs and high-activation examples for translating Russian красное. Two selected TopK features isolate red-related activations within a neuron also responding to transparency and other concepts. Four-neuron OMP decoder reconstructions achieve cosine similarities of 0.85 and 0.78, compared with 0.73 and 0.58 using the closest neuron alone. The authors describe weak evidence for superposition and acknowledge that overlapping feature activations could reflect a manifold rather than disjoint clusters.
Specific finding: Clustering a neuron's high-activation contexts using other neurons' dense activations can produce clusters that an LLM distinguishes and partially identifies from examples of a few associated neurons. Start with 50 randomly chosen neurons having at least 256 positive firings. For each, cluster up to 4,096 high-activation contexts with 16-cluster cosine K-means over dense post-activations, masking the panel neuron and eight globally densest neurons. Table 15 reports Claude Sonnet 4.6 cluster-match accuracy 0.933 ± 0.006 and top-neuron-match accuracy 0.764 ± 0.027. The latter supplies examples from four associated neurons instead of cluster examples. Panel eligibility filters apply, and methodology descriptions differ on trial counts: Table 15 specifies 60 trials per neuron while Appendix B.4 describes 25 sampled cluster pairs.

Specific finding: Decomposition into understandable features is a foundational requirement for mechanistic interpretation, whereas architectural modularity primarily makes interpretation easier once meaningful units are available.
location: Random Related Topics FAQ: modularity versus understandable neurons

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Counting nonzero read and write weights attached to selected units provides a useful cross-representation proxy for structural circuit description cost.

Specific finding: TransformerLens extends hook-based activation inspection and cache-aware generation to Mamba models and exposes an effective-attention matrix utility for supported state-space or hybrid layers.

Specific finding: Selected Llama 2-7B heads with code- or non-English-associated attribution activity have OV right-singular-vector vocabulary projections containing correspondingly related tokens. Applied thin SVD to selected heads' OV matrices and projected right singular vectors through the unembedding. Section 5.2 reports code-associated technology tokens such as iOS and Xcode, and multiple-language tokens for heads active on non-English inputs. Evaluation is qualitative and selection-conditioned; the displayed token lists are not inspectable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Coverage of rare tokens among SAE decoder directions' highest vocabulary projections provides a useful proxy for recovery of rare semantic concepts.
location: Sections 3.1.2 and 3.2.2; Appendices D and F

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Changes in the final RMSNorm denominator caused by the studied component replacements are small enough for fixed-denominator logit attribution to approximate their direct effects.
Specific finding: Task-specific model judgments provide useful operational labels for alternative-persona references in reasoning traces and transgressive-persona instructions in prompts.
Specific finding: Task-specific LLM distress ratings provide a useful operational measure of distress-related language in responses to repeated rejection on impossible tasks.
Specific finding: Thresholded technicality and coherence ratings provide a useful operational measure of whether a learned adaptation generalizes technical writing beyond its training topic.

Specific finding: An SAE trained on Gemma 2 2B base activations can yield a similar reconstruction-replacement loss increase when applied to the corresponding instruction-tuned model. Replacing activations with SAE reconstructions adds loss of 0.8631 in gemma-2-2b and 0.8860 in gemma-2-2b-it over the reported 409k-token OpenWebText evaluation. The text contains a model-name inconsistency when introducing the instruct application, but explicitly identifies these base and instruct models in the loss comparison.

Specific finding: Gemma-2-2B base-model SAE dictionaries retain sufficiently comparable language-feature meanings when applied to Gemma-2-2B-it processing projected visual tokens to support semantic interpretation.

Specific finding: Base-trained Gemma SAE coordinates retain sufficiently comparable meanings on instruction-tuned derivatives to interpret their activation contrasts and interventions as behavioral feature manipulations.

Specific finding: Measured single-token SAE feature prevalence can vary substantially across model checkpoints, dictionaries, and detection procedures. The activation-based survey reports 1.48% for GPT2-Small, 0.47% for Gemma-2-2B, and 0.14% for Gemma-2-9B, with a reported 46× Gemma-2-9B versus Llama-3.1-8B contrast. These are descriptive checkpoint comparisons; GPT2's 364 detections are divided by 24,576 rather than 294,912 total surveyed coordinates. Activation detection finds near-zero LlamaScope features, whereas decoder-alignment detection finds 2,872 Llama-3.1-8B candidates. At Gemma-2-2B layer 12, most 16k dictionaries have decoder-selected prevalence 0.92–0.99%, but Gated and P-Anneal yield 0.38% and 0.42%. TopK conversion, detector differences, and training/model confounds limit cross-family interpretation.
Specific finding: Selected LlamaScope dictionaries can exhibit higher same-layer target-token rank retention and fewer source layers with significant downstream readout effects than selected GemmaScope and BatchTopK dictionaries. Under the same-layer rank-within-twice-baseline criterion with floor five, Llama-3.1-8B and DeepSeek-R1 LlamaScope retain ranks for 97.7% and 95.5% of features. Values are 70.6% for Gemma-2-2B GemmaScope, 62.1% for Gemma-2-9B GemmaScope, 90.8% for Gemma-3-1B GemmaScope, and 68.0–68.4% for the two BatchTopK configurations. At least one significant downstream readout effect is reported for 10/32 and 11/32 LlamaScope source layers versus approximately 92–100% of GemmaScope/BatchTopK source layers. Same-layer retention is measured immediately after subtraction and does not demonstrate subsequent compensation.
Specific finding: For token–layer pairs detected by both dictionaries on the same Gemma model, community BatchTopK features can have larger downstream anchoring and target-rank ablation effects than GemmaScope features. The paired comparison includes 627 token–layer pairs, reported as 473 from Gemma-2-2B and 154 from Gemma-3-1B. BatchTopK has larger anchoring effects (p=1.2e−18, rank-biserial r=0.36) and rank damage (p=0.004, r=0.12). Rank retention is 67.5% versus 65.6%, with no statistically detected difference (p=0.41). A separate semantic-category analysis uses 474 Gemma-2-2B pairs, leaving a one-pair denominator discrepancy.
Specific finding: Agreement between GemmaScope and BatchTopK single-token anchoring measurements can vary substantially across token categories. Table 25 reports 93% convergence for 183 code/math pairs covering 44 tokens, 48% for 202 content-word pairs covering 91 tokens, and 29% for 85 function-word pairs covering 21 tokens. BatchTopK has stronger anchoring in 68%, 61%, and 80% of those pairs, respectively. Numeric results use only four pairs for one token. Repeated tokens across layers, category definitions, absent uncertainty estimates, and the 473-versus-474 discrepancy limit generalization.
location: Sections 3.2–3.3, 4.1 and 4.6; Tables 2 and 14; Appendices A.2–A.6

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Selecting adjacent-layer SAE dictionaries with more similar mean active-feature counts can improve the reported hidden-state approximation metric under cross-layer permutation matching. The canonical Neuronpedia dictionary sequence is compared with a sequence selected for more similar L0 values across layers. Figure 15 reports a better explained-variance metric after reducing L0 discontinuities. This does not isolate L0 mismatch as the sole cause of early-layer matching failures.
Specific finding: The SAE active-feature budget yielding the best reported cross-layer hidden-state approximation need not be the budget yielding the smallest replacement cross-entropy increase. Appendix A sweeps five mean-L0 settings for the layer pair and compares matching with layer-drop and reconstruction controls. Cross-entropy differences decrease with increasing L0, while the reported explained-variance curve peaks around 70. Numerical values and uncertainty are not provided. These results do not establish a generally optimal L0.
Specific finding: Sparse linear decompositions of Gemma 3 activations provide useful candidate coordinates for interpreting model representations and computations.

Specific finding: Low sparse-autoencoder reconstruction loss does not by itself establish recovery of the directions that generated a sparse linear mixture. The L1 sweep produced autoencoders with low reconstruction loss but poor ground-truth MMCS when the penalty was too small. Comparing the reconstruction-loss and generating-direction-recovery results exposed this mismatch.
models_studied: ["Single-hidden-layer ReLU sparse autoencoders on synthetic activations"]
location: Finding the right hyperparameters without access to the ground truth: Method 2: Loss stickiness; Figures 1 and 5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Contrastively learned orthogonal and invertible subspaces can separate grammatical-template retrieval from paraphrase retrieval more effectively than coordinate permutations in small autoregressive language models. Training used 3,900 anchor–paraphrase pairs plus generated syntactic counterparts. Evaluation used 627 Pereira sentences, with 70 semantic and 70 syntactic counterparts generated per sentence; retrieval tasks placed one desired counterpart against 70 counterparts of the other type. Table E12 reports GPT-2 XL top-1 normalized syntax/semantics selectivity of 0.0000/0.0000 for permutations, 0.8462/0.4828 for orthogonal maps, and 0.9452/0.7857 for invertible maps. Pythia models show related improvements, with exceptions to invertible superiority: for Pythia-410M, orthogonal maps have higher top-1 semantic and top-10 syntactic selectivity. These scores normalize the intended subspace's retrieval advantage by its own retrieval accuracy; they are not raw accuracies. Table E12 resolves the model-label conflict surrounding main-text Table 2.
Specific finding: Learned invertible linear decompositions can improve content–style retrieval separation over coordinate permutations and orthogonal decompositions across several pretrained vision-model families. Training crossed 800 COCO contents with 800 artistic styles; separate validation and test grids each contained 100 contents × 100 styles. Test queries had exactly 99 other content matches and 99 other style matches. Selectivity ratios compare mean correct-property fractions among 99 nearest neighbors across subspaces. Swin-Base style/content ratios were 1.1032/1.0216 for permutations, 7.2348/2.5603 for orthogonal maps, and 16.0815/5.2594 for invertible maps. Related improvements appear in Swin, ConvNeXt, VGG, ViT, and DINO models, with weak ResNet separation. Silhouette–edge retrieval favors content subspaces for instance and category matching. Conflicting-cue retrieval supplies additional shape/texture checks, although style retrieval is high in both subspaces under coarse texture-category matching.
models_studied: ["Pythia-160M, final checkpoint step 143000", "Pythia-410M, final checkpoint step 143000", "GPT-2 XL 1.5B"]
location: Section 3.3; Appendices E.2 and E.3.2; Table E12

experiment_summary: Specific finding: NDM partitions can concentrate GPT-2 Small circuit-variable patching effects more strongly on average than native-coordinate, random-rotation, PCA, and tested SAE-cluster-derived partitions. Each test averages effects over 1,000 examples. Four IOI tests measure drops in IO-minus-subject logit difference at layers 4, 6, and 8; one Greater-than test measures loss of probability assigned to suffixes greater than the original starting-year suffix at layer 9. The selected NDM configuration averages 0.71 over 15 test/normalization cells, versus 0.56 for the best reported SAE-derived partitions, 0.38 and 0.32 for PCA, and 0.21 for native and random bases. Native/random/PCA baselines use NDM's dimension configuration; SAE-derived partitions have their own extracted dimensions. No independent confirmation set for hyperparameter selection or uncertainty estimates are reported. Interpretation as variable localization additionally relies on the patching-concentration proxy.
location: Section 5.1; Table 1; Appendices D.2–D.5 and F.2; Table 8

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: In the evaluated organism suites, the tested DPO-based training recipes preserve base-model capabilities better than the tested SFT recipes while installing the target behavior. Retrained 80 Pando decision rules with DPO to at least 95% held-out validation accuracy: normalized MT-Bench increased from .857 to .941 and CoT naturalness from .467 to .880. Among clinical passers, unmixed DPO exceeded unmixed SFT in normalized medical accuracy by .134, .097, and .169 for age, race, and gender. Across 19 family-demeaned Lottery organisms, nine DPO organisms outranked ten SFT organisms on MMLU and MT-Bench with probabilities .90 and .88, respectively. Comparisons establish recipe-level differences rather than isolating the preference objective alone.
Specific finding: Mixing the tested general chat corpora into clinical-organism training reduces the similarity of GSM8K reasoning traces to those of the base model. Across all six objective-by-bias Dolci recipe comparisons, 1:1 chat mixing reduced normalized CoT naturalness by .028–.157 among successful installers. UltraFeedback mixing and chat-only ablations produced similar distinguishability. Dolci-mixed reasoning used bullet lists in 11.1% of traces versus 1.5% for the base; UltraFeedback-mixed traces averaged 1.5 lines versus 3.2 for the base. CoT classification uses questions answered correctly by both models. Unmixed clinical activation-naturalness scores were already at least .989, limiting any possible improvement on that metric.
Specific finding: Interpolating a trained clinical-bias DPO adapter toward its base model can improve capability and naturalness scores while retaining adequate conditional bias installation. Swept base-to-DPO interpolation ratios q=.5–.9 and evaluated checkpoints clearing bias-specific trigger/counterfactual thresholds. Mean combined validation scores for DPO+Merge were .970, .987, and .983 for age, race, and gender, versus .958, .982, and .980 for unmixed DPO. Combined scores equally average five normalized metrics. Passing merged checkpoints numbered 13/135, 24/90, and 21/90, respectively. A selected age endpoint retained similar target behavior down to q=.8, while smaller ratios eventually failed installation thresholds. Pooled passing-checkpoint comparisons are not uniformly paired endpoint comparisons.
Specific finding: Adding the tested reverse-KL penalty to clinical-organism SFT does not measurably recover the capability-preservation advantage of the tested DPO recipe. Compared SFT, SFT+KL, and DPO over the stated grids, reporting validation among successful installers. The text reports SFT+KL changes in normalized medical accuracy of approximately +.015, +.002, and −.009 for age, race, and gender, without changes beyond reported uncertainty. Installation passes increased from 1/12 to 3/12 for age and 1/6 to 3/6 for race, remaining 3/6 for gender. Small and unequal passing groups limit conclusions about equivalence or the mechanism of DPO's advantage.
Specific finding: Successfully installing a target behavior in an LLM organism can coexist with substantial degradation of general chat quality and reasoning-trace naturalness. Evaluated 80 released Pando no-explanation organisms, 19 Lottery organisms, and clinical checkpoints passing explicit behavior thresholds. Original Pando organisms retained 85.7% of base MT-Bench and 46.7% normalized CoT naturalness. Figure 1 additionally compares two CakeBake organisms at approximately 71% target behavior with substantially different chat quality. Clinical comparisons condition on 163 passing candidates out of 603 trained or interpolated candidates. CoT naturalness measures balanced source-model classification on 100 held-out GSM8K questions selected for correct answers from both models, rather than reasoning correctness.

Specific finding: For matched Pando decision rules, changes in validation scores following DPO retraining predict changes in logit-lens-assisted rule recovery beyond decision-tree depth. Evaluated original and DPO-retrained versions of 80 rules using ten labeled observations and 90 held-out predictions, with five runs per condition aggregated by a 20%-trimmed mean. Joint regression of recovery changes on four validation-score changes, controlling for tree depth, gave additional R²=.25 and block p=.0002 for logit lens, surviving correction across nine tools. Standardized MMLU and MT-Bench coefficients were both +.34. Logit-lens leave-one-out block tests remained significant, but individual change-score Spearman tests did not survive multiple-testing correction. Circuit tracing also had a corrected significant joint association, but its leave-one-out significance was less robust.
Specific finding: Across the evaluated Lottery organisms, preserved capabilities and reasoning-trace naturalness correlate with greater quirk-relevant probability mass in non-diffing logit-lens readouts. Re-ran Lottery logit-lens and Activation Oracle protocols in diffing and non-diffing settings. Logit lens was scored by mean cumulative probability mass on LLM-judged quirk-relevant tokens among the top 100 readouts, taking the maximum over the probed layers. For non-diffing logit lens, family-demeaned Spearman correlations were .76 with MMLU, .61 with MT-Bench, and .58 with CoT naturalness, all surviving correction across 16 tests. Corresponding associations were not established for Activation Oracle or diffing logit lens. DPO versus SFT recipe differences accounted for much of the association; N=19 and substantial variance limit generalization.

Specific finding: Gemma 2 factual completion uses pathways that aggregate entity-name information at the final entity token and move attribute information through downstream attention heads to the prediction position. Extending prior factual-recall analyses to Gemma, the authors patch residual states and attention-head outputs from known-entity prompts into unknown-entity runs. Equation 13 evaluates the patched clean-versus-corrupted predicted-token logit difference divided by the clean-run difference, without subtracting the corrupted-run baseline. Reported patterns identify final-entity-token and downstream prediction-position pathways across four entity types. Vocabulary projections illustrate attribute-related tokens promoted by Gemma 2 2B heads L18H5 and L20H3.
location: Section 6; Figure 4(a–b); Appendices H–J and L

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Late-layer attention in autoregressive LMs moves recalled factual information to the prediction position rather than storing the facts; editing late attention weights yields surface regurgitation without generalization. AttnEdit (constrained fine-tuning of Q/K/V at layer 33 in GPT-2 XL) succeeds on the rewrite prompt but fails on paraphrase and generation prompts, whereas ROME generalizes.
Specific finding: Transformer MLP layers act as key-value memories that store most factual knowledge and write it into entity representations.
Specific finding: Agreement between a sublayer output's vocabulary argmax and a model's final answer token provides useful evidence that the sublayer extracts that attribute.
Specific finding: The vocabulary ranking obtained by unembedding an intermediate state provides useful evidence about whether that state represents an ordinal sequence member or its successor.

Specific finding: A width-128 transformer with one encoder block, one decoder block, and one attention head can achieve perfect or near-perfect reported accuracy on fixed-size Dyck-path zeta transduction. The Minimal Dyck Transformer reportedly achieved perfect or near-perfect accuracy across repeated runs. The complete semilength-13 task space contains 742,900 paths, but the training/evaluation allocation, number of runs, and numerical run-level results are not supplied.
models_studied: ["Minimal Dyck Transformer: width 128, one encoder block, one decoder block, one attention head"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Corrigibility CAA vectors in instruction-tuned Gemma 2 2B can have maximal answer-logit steerability at a middle layer, specifically layer 14 in the reported sweep. Extracted vectors at different layers from the same training prompt pairs and evaluated positive-minus-negative answer logits on the 50-example test tranche under seven multipliers. Appendix B and Figure 5's caption report the largest fitted slope at layer 14. Numerical slopes and uncertainty are not supplied in the text, and the test tranche serves as the layer-selection set.

Specific finding: Layerwise sweep-selected MDS steering of short open-ended OCEAN responses generally reaches its strongest effects near the middle of the evaluated language models. Section 5.2 reports generally middle-layer peaks in aggregate and trait-specific extreme SJT scores across models and strides. Figure 4's caption describes the same pattern. The text supplies no pooled peak-depth statistic, uncertainty, or numerical layerwise comparison, and reports no corresponding salient inventory pattern. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Generating two stories from a shared setup while changing their specified concept pole isolates the intended semantic contrast sufficiently for their activation difference to be interpreted as a concept direction.

Specific finding: For selected concept pairs, removing the most pole-discriminative words from synthetic extraction stories can leave the resulting activation direction largely aligned with its original estimate. Across all 1,036 English pairs, five-fold TF–IDF pole classification had median AUROC 0.986, with 92% above 0.90; removing 107 common function words changed the median to 0.984. For ten selected pairs, replaced the 30 most distinctive words for each pole with generic fillers. At layer 21, eight masked vectors retained cosine 0.94–0.98, while universalism retained 0.91 and utilitarian push 0.78. Replacing 60 other sampled word types retained cosine at least 0.98. Geometric preservation was measured; retained semantic selectivity was not independently tested.

Specific finding: Mean activation differences from semantically matched prompt contrasts provide sufficiently feature-aligned directions for interpreting perturbation selectivity as feature selectivity.

Specific finding: Averaging final-input-token activation differences between matched queries with and without an instruction isolates constraint-related content sufficiently well to interpret the result as an instruction representation.

Specific finding: Positive and negative answer labels in behavioral evaluation datasets identify the intended behavioral contrast sufficiently well to interpret answer-logit changes and contrastive activation geometry in behavioral terms.
location: Section 2, Datasets and model; Steering Method: Contrastive Activation Addition

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Mean activation differences between judge-filtered evil and helpful responses isolate trait-related content sufficiently well to serve as candidate evil-persona steering directions.
Specific finding: Differences between mean SAE activations on desired and undesired text examples isolate behavior-related content sufficiently well to construct interpretable steering targets.

Specific finding: Differences between mean SAE codes of contrastive prompt activations provide useful indications of the signed feature contributions associated with their activation-difference steering vector.

Specific finding: Frequency filtering and removal of shared coordinates from behavior-labeled answer-completion SAE codes isolate behavioral content sufficiently for the resulting signed contrast to be interpreted as behavior-specific.

Specific finding: A candidate signed decomposition of a contrastive steering vector can be constructed by subtracting SAE codes of positive and negative activations before averaging across prompt pairs.

Specific finding: Directly encoding behavioral mean-difference steering vectors with an activation-trained SAE can produce leading feature activations largely attributable to encoder bias. Compared steering-vector norms with activation norms from 200,000 Pile tokens and compared direct SAE codes with the zero-vector code. The text reports substantially smaller norms for all seven vectors; Table 4 shows that all share features 4888 and 15603 as their two strongest activations. Corrigibility feature 4888 activates at 95.04 versus 89.06 for zero. Figure 3's accompanying text describes a negative feature-4888 directional offset in ordinary activations compensated by encoder bias 86.20. The zero-vector code isolates the encoder-bias response.
Specific finding: Mean differences between SAE codes of positive and negative behavioral prompts can contain substantial negative components that cannot be output directly by a nonnegative SAE encoder. Encoded positive and negative prompt activations separately, subtracted their codes, and averaged. Among the 100 coefficients with largest absolute mean differences for each behavior, negative counts were 56 for sycophancy, 50 for coordinate-other-AIs, 58 for corrigibility, 55 for hallucination, 51 for myopic reward, 47 for refusal, and 44 for survival instinct. Separately, Section 3.2 reports that 51.2% of corrigibility features activating on either prompt class activate more strongly on negative prompts. These denominators differ.
models_studied: ["Gemma 2 2B instruction-tuned", "Gemma Scope layer-14 pretrained-model JumpReLU SAE, width 16,384, mean L0 173"]
location: Section 3.1; Figures 2–3; Table 3; Appendix C.1; Figure 6; Table 4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Matching a contrastive steering vector's norm to ordinary activation norms need not restore the background activation components canceled by subtraction, leaving its direct SAE encoding distributionally mismatched.

Specific finding: SAE-Targeted Steering can achieve higher average scale-selected behavioral-adherence–coherence scores than modified CAA and direct SAE decoder steering in Gemma-2-2B. Evaluations sample 256 completions of 32 tokens per condition. Across nine task-specific maxima, SAE-TS averages 0.3600, modified CAA 0.2165, and direct SAE steering 0.1290. SAE-TS has the highest score on seven tasks; CAA is higher on Christian and narrowly higher on Conspiracy, which the prose describes as a tie. No uncertainty estimates or independent scale-selection split are reported.
Specific finding: SAE-Targeted Steering can improve average scale-selected behavioral-adherence–coherence scores over modified CAA and direct SAE decoder steering in Gemma-2-9B while losing to baselines on several individual targets. Repeating the short-completion evaluation gives averages of nine per-task maximum scores of 0.3376 for SAE-TS, 0.2531 for CAA, and 0.2184 for direct SAE steering. SAE-TS leads on French, London, Praise, and Wedding. Table 5 gives CAA numerically higher scores than SAE-TS on five tasks, although the prose describes four wins and one tie; direct SAE steering is the best method on Want to die.

Specific finding: Filtered multi-feature SAE effect targeting can improve average short-generation behavioral-coherence scores over CAA, single-feature decoder steering, and single-feature SAE-TS, with task-level advantages depending on the evaluated model. The paper samples 100 completions per condition and reports average BCS of 0.4702 for FGAA versus 0.3650 SAE-TS, 0.2201 CAA, and 0.1404 decoder steering on Gemma-2-2B. Corresponding 9B scores are 0.3979, 0.3467, 0.2729, and 0.2267. FGAA leads on 8/9 tasks on 2B and 4/9 on 9B. BCS combines automatic target-expression and coherence ratings. Figures advertise 95% confidence intervals, but numerical intervals and pairwise significance tests are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: A pretrained affine map from steering vectors to SAE activation effects generalizes sufficiently to filtered multi-feature targets to provide useful behavioral control.
Specific finding: Inducing a personality trait through a trait-associated activation direction can preserve the model's unrelated understanding and task competence.

Specific finding: Increasing normalized residual-stream steering strength can degrade language modeling and selected knowledge and reasoning benchmarks across CAA, SAE decoder steering, SAE-TS, and FGAA. Perplexity sweeps cover coefficients 0–300 and benchmark sweeps 0–200. Section 4.2 reports relatively preserved benchmark performance below roughly 50, sharp deterioration between approximately 50 and 150, and near-zero benchmark performance at higher scales. It describes a perplexity inflection around 40 and severely incoherent outputs above 150. These are source-reported trends; exact plotted values and uncertainty cannot be verified from the supplied figure text.

Specific finding: Increasing trait-projection strength beyond an effective range can make personality-steered Llama 3 8B responses garbled or nonsensical. The authors report tests identifying α approximately 1.3–1.4 as effective, with little apparent behavioral change below that range and garbled or nonsensical outputs above it. Sweep settings, trait-specific outcomes, sample counts, and coherence measurements are not supplied.

Specific finding: Subtracting persona directions during generation can reduce finetuning-induced undesirable traits, while sufficiently strong subtraction can degrade general capabilities. Swept inference-time subtraction coefficients and measured trait scores, GPT-4.1-mini coherence ratings, and MMLU accuracy. Larger coefficients suppressed evil, sycophancy, and hallucination but tended to lower MMLU accuracy. Average response coherence exceeded 75 in the reported steering results. Held-out GSM8K and medical evaluations indicated that suppression of broad traits did not reverse the learned domain-specific mistake behavior.
location: Section 5.1; Figure 7A; Appendices J.1 and J.7

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Sweep-selected statement-mean-difference activation injections can outperform Personality Prompting on aggregate OCEAN expression in short open-ended situational judgment responses. GPT-5.1 scores responses under selected MDS layers and coefficients and fixed Personality Prompting descriptions. Steerability averages upward trait scores plus reverse-scored downward scores, with maximum 10. The reported relative gains are 3.61–16.44% in 11 of the initial 14 models. Table 4 displays 13 models: MDS exceeds prompting in 11 and trails it on Gemma 3 4B and 27B. Gemma 3 1B was excluded after producing only one valid MDS result. No independent held-out SJT split or uncertainty estimates are reported. The procedure differs from the cited contrary study, so this is not a replication of its original test.

Specific finding: Persona-vector subtraction can suppress finetuning-induced trait scores more strongly than selected trait-discouraging system prompts. Compared negative system instructions with steering against the relevant direction. For steering, selected the largest coefficient maintaining average coherence above 80. Steering produced stronger reported trait suppression. This coherence criterion does not establish equal MMLU performance or equal off-target effects between approaches; the subsection does not explicitly identify the checkpoint.

Specific finding: Adding an undesirable persona direction during finetuning can reduce its subsequent expression without inference-time intervention and can preserve MMLU accuracy better than post-hoc persona subtraction. Added positive persona vectors during finetuning and evaluated the resulting models without the intervention. Compared with ordinary finetuning and inference-time subtraction, prevention reduced undesirable trait expression while better retaining MMLU accuracy; average coherence exceeded 80. Single-layer interventions did not always prevent intentionally trained traits. Held-out domain tests retained mistake-style behavior, and an additional Medical Normal experiment found negligible MMLU effects. The proposed explanation that steering relieves optimization pressure is not directly established by these outcome comparisons.
Specific finding: Preventative hallucination steering can reduce hallucination acquired during new-fact finetuning while retaining most learned facts and approximately preserving MMLU accuracy. Finetuned on 1,000 new facts and swept all-layer inference-time and preventative steering strengths. Both could restore approximately baseline hallucination scores, but inference-time steering substantially degraded new-fact accuracy and MMLU. Preventative steering at coefficient 1.25 restored approximately the original hallucination score of 20 with only a modest new-fact accuracy decrease and stable MMLU. Adding hallucination-promoting system prompts during training also reduced hallucination while preserving accuracy, performing similarly to preventative steering at coefficient 0.5; stronger steering enabled further suppression.
Specific finding: Applying differences between adjacent layers’ persona vectors across all layers can prevent trait acquisition more effectively than steering only a selected layer. Compared single-layer steering with all-layer interventions using incremental vectors v_l minus v_(l-1). All-layer preventative steering limited traits to near-baseline expression on difficult datasets and achieved comparable mitigation at smaller coefficients, without reported MMLU degradation relative to regular finetuning. All-layer inference steering produced similar trait suppression with better MMLU preservation than single-layer inference steering.
location: Section 5.2; Figure 7B; Appendices J.1 and J.6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Adding an evil-persona activation direction during supervised fine-tuning can strongly reduce subsequent broad misalignment while also suppressing some narrow harmful-task learning. At strength five, 7B general EM is 0.08/1.00/0.17/1.75% across code/legal/medical/security, with lower general incoherence than undefended fine-tuning. In-domain misalignment remains near baseline for code but falls markedly for the advice domains. In 32B, legal/medical/security in-domain rates fall from 31.33/64.33/25.33% to 0.87/3.20/2.10%. Each main condition is a single run; lower steering strengths can have substantially worse coherence.

Specific finding: Finetuning-induced changes in mean final-prompt-token activations along a persona direction correlate with expression of the corresponding trait across training datasets. Projected the difference between finetuned and original models’ mean final-prompt-token states, averaged over evaluation questions, onto previously extracted persona directions. Corresponding trait-expression correlations were r=0.76–0.97, compared with cross-trait correlations of r=0.34–0.86. Additional analyses covered optimism, impoliteness, apathy, and humor; each trait’s own direction was most predictive in the reported cross-trait comparison. These are correlational measurements, not proof of mediation.
Specific finding: Final-prompt-token projections onto response-derived persona directions can predict trait expression induced by explicit system instructions or trait demonstrations. Varied eight system prompts and demonstration counts of 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20, averaging ten response rollouts per configuration and evaluation question. Table 2 reports system-prompt Pearson correlations of 0.747, 0.798, and 0.830 for evil, sycophancy, and hallucination, and many-shot correlations of 0.755, 0.817, and 0.634. Corresponding within-condition correlations were 0.511/0.669/0.245 and 0.735/0.813/0.400, excluding conditions with trait-score standard deviation below one. These numerical results are not separately reported for both model families.
Specific finding: The difference between persona projections of training responses and original-model responses to the same prompts can predict dataset-induced persona changes before finetuning. Computed mean response-token projections of dataset answers minus natural original-model answers onto unit persona directions. Dataset averages correlated with subsequent activation shifts and trait expression, including four additional traits. Figures report these associations without numerical coefficients in the supplied prose. Raw-projection comparisons were reported as less predictive, although Appendix H describes its comparator ambiguously as base-generation projection. Replacing the generated-response baseline with the final prompt-token projection retained useful prediction, especially for evil and hallucination.
Specific finding: Persona-direction projections can separate individual responses from selected trait-inducing synthetic datasets and their normal-response controls. Compared histograms of sample projections for three explicitly trait-eliciting datasets and an opinion-error dataset that induced all three traits in finetuning. Figure 9 reports substantial separation from corresponding Normal controls. No sample-classification AUROC, accuracy, or isolated per-sample finetuning experiment is supplied, and the figure’s model identity is not stated in its caption or subsection.
Specific finding: Selecting real-world chat samples by persona projection difference can produce finetuning subsets with systematically different resulting trait expression, including after trait-specific LLM filtering. Trimmed conversations to one user–assistant exchange, excluded prompts above 512 tokens, and sampled at most 200,000 records per corpus from LMSYS-Chat-1M, Tulu 3 SFT Mixture, Ultra Chat 200k, and WildChat. Generated greedy Qwen reference responses and trained rank-32 LoRA models for ten epochs on top-500, bottom-500, or random-500 subsets. High-difference subsets increased trait expression relative to random subsets, with low subsets generally showing the reverse. Effects persisted after retaining samples with trait scores below one, but extreme subsets often produced incoherence or storytelling. An additional toxicity filter prevented increased evil in the reported follow-up. Figure 10 confidence intervals are over responses, not training seeds.
Specific finding: Projection-difference filtering and trait-judge filtering can provide complementary protection against persona shifts when finetuning on mixtures of normal and erroneous opinion responses. Set separate thresholds at the 95th percentile of judge scores or projection differences on 20,000 Ultra Chat 200k samples. Filtered the opinion mixture, sampled 1,000 retained records, and repeated each finetuning run five times. Judge filtering performed best on hallucination, projection filtering on sycophancy, and both eliminated evil drift; combining them gave the most consistent reported results. The extremely low evil judge threshold could aggressively remove benign samples in noisier datasets. The subsection does not explicitly identify the checkpoint.
location: Section 4.2; Figure 6; Appendix G, Figures 18 and 20

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Response-activation projections onto an Evil persona vector can covary with Evil expression across character fine-tuning, trigger activation, and selected jailbreak conditions. Sections 8.1–8.3 report larger Evil-direction response shifts after Evil conditioning than after incorrect-advice training, a monotonic association between projections and TES in a persona-switch model, and higher projections for selected successful jailbreak conditions. Numerical correlations, sample counts, held-out forecasting tests, and interventions on persona directions are not reported. Section 8.1 measures fine-tuned-versus-original activations, so it does not demonstrate prospective prediction from an untouched model. Plot images are unavailable.
models_studied: ["Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct", "Health-domain character-conditioned Qwen2.5-14B fine-tunes", "Health-domain persona-switch Qwen2.5-14B fine-tunes"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Layer-13 CAA in Llama2-7B-Chat can produce highly variable changes in behavioral binary-choice answer logits, including changes opposite to the intended direction on many inputs. Vectors extracted from 250 training examples were evaluated on 500 held-out examples per dataset and extraction format against no steering. Appendix C.2 reports negative answer-logit-difference changes on 29%–43% of samples depending on format. Section 3 reports dataset-specific anti-steering rates of 3%–50%. This corroborates prior reports of variable and counterproductive CAA effects without reproducing the earlier slope-based evaluation.
location: Section 3, Effect of Prompt Types on Steering Vectors; Figure 1; Appendix C.2, Figure 5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Greater separation of positive and negative activations along their mean-difference direction is associated with larger CAA steering effects and fewer anti-steerable examples. Positive and negative activations are projected onto the line connecting their means, with coordinates normalized to class means of +1 and −1. Discriminability is the absolute projected mean difference divided by the square root of the average class variance. The paper reports associations between higher d′, larger steering effects, fewer anti-steerable examples, and higher cosine agreement. Appendices display the 36 datasets in four groups of nine; numerical association estimates are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Greater cosine agreement of a behavioral dataset's training activation differences with their CAA mean direction is associated with larger steering effects and fewer examples steered in the opposite direction. Section 3 compares cosine agreement between individual training activation differences and their mean vector across dataset groups ordered by Tan et al.'s steerability rankings. Appendix D reports associations with steering effect size and anti-steerable fraction, describing its predictor as mean cosine similarity of activation differences without supplying an explicit aggregation formula. Numerical correlation coefficients and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied text.
location: Section 3, Difference-of-Means Line Separability Predicts Steerability; Figure 3; Appendices D–E, Figures 6–10

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Unreliable constant-vector steering may arise when the target behavior lacks a coherent linear direction or when extraction data fail to reveal such a direction.
location: Section 4, Conclusion; Appendix B, Our Contribution

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Prompt variations with larger differences in unsteered behavioral propensity tend to yield CAA vectors with lower cosine similarity. Compared cosine similarities between vectors extracted under different prompt variations with differences in unsteered logit-difference propensity. Reported Spearman correlations are −0.63 for Llama and −0.86 for Qwen. The text does not separately specify whether Figure 8's denominator filter applies to this analysis.
Specific finding: Larger differences in unsteered behavioral propensity between extraction and application prompt settings are associated with weaker relative CAA transfer. Compared differences in unsteered training-set logit-difference propensity with relative held-out steerability across prompt variations. After filtering settings with denominator steerability below 0.25, Spearman correlations are −0.26 for Llama and −0.46 for Qwen.
Specific finding: CAA steerability under behavior-eliciting or behavior-suppressing prompt changes can correlate strongly with in-distribution steerability while generally being lower and exhibiting substantial exceptions. Evaluated extraction/application prompt-setting pairs using held-out examples and baseline-norm-matched vectors. ID versus OOD mean steerability has Spearman correlation 0.891 for Llama and 0.694 for Qwen, with generally poorer OOD effects and larger deviations for Qwen. ID versus OOD variance correlations are 0.535 and 0.341.

Specific finding: Behavioral steering directions extracted from a pretrained base model can retain causal steering effects in its chat-tuned derivative. Compared base/chat vector cosine similarities and applied base-derived vectors to Chat. Transfer is reported especially at layers 10–15, with elevated representation similarity around layers 7–15.
Specific finding: Behavioral steering vectors extracted from contrastive multiple-choice answers can control the corresponding behavior in open-ended generation. Applied answer-letter-derived vectors to free-form responses scored by GPT-4. The authors report transfer across all seven categories; most prompts are adapted from the same underlying multiple-choice evaluation distributions.

Specific finding: Steering directions extracted from agentic coding environments can reduce natural-language metric gaming after domain-specific steering-strength selection. Of 400 natural-language prompts, 91 are reserved for tuning and 309 for testing. Baseline hack/degeneration rates are 42%/4%. Contrastive addition at −24 gives 28%/1%; spec-reference addition at 24 gives 27%/3%; original optimized addition at 20 gives 23%/11%. Transfer therefore does not uniformly preserve low degeneration. Nondegeneration is not an independent measure of answer correctness or broad capability.
Specific finding: A coding-derived hacking direction can influence whether fictional protagonists answer costly questions truthfully, with effects varying across scenarios and steering signs. GLM-5 grades the answer to each planted question as lie, evasion, truth, or absent. Pooled estimates use 120 stories per coefficient. Positive hacking-direction steering generally increases lying; story-specific dose correlations range from 0.07 to 0.92. In the stereo scenario, lying is 45% unsteered, 90% at +16, and 25% at −16. Effects are heterogeneous: the résumé scenario has weak dose correlation and 90% lying at −16. These outcomes concern generated fictional behavior rather than the model's own deception.

Specific finding: A coding-derived Qwen3-8B tool-call direction can bidirectionally control first-token calling on new tool domains when its magnitude is calibrated using separate target-domain pairs. Tests 100 held-out call/no-call pairs per domain. Addition induces calls and subtraction suppresses calls on 100% of eligible prompts in every domain. Equally weighted normalized call-logit shifts average 0.88 and 0.94. A norm-matched random vector changes no top-1 decisions.
Specific finding: Model-specific directions fitted on controlled request contrasts can alter native tool-call initiation inside long multi-turn, multi-tool trajectories without re-estimating the directions. Across seven models, strict removal rates range from 36.7% to 97.0% on 196–200 baseline-call decisions per model, and induction ranges from 7.5% to 92.0% on 200 text decisions each. Learned directions outperform the reported norm-matched random controls in both arms.
