Qwen3-8B suppresses 36.7% of 199 baseline calls and induces calls on 70.0% of 200 text decisions, versus 1.5% and 0.0% for random controls; its contexts contain 5,385–15,690 tokens and 16–43 tools. Its removal-arm mean logit change of −5.55 is calculated over all 200 candidate points, whereas its strict removal percentage uses the 199 baseline calls.
Specific finding: Subtracting directions fitted from explicit request contrasts can suppress tool calls on selected non-imperative requests without explicit action instructions. Evaluates fixed baseline-positive subsets of 117–200 requests per model. Unit-gain suppression is 93.1% for Qwen3-8B on 160 requests, 100% for five other models, and 35.5% for Granite. At gain 1.5, Qwen3-8B reaches 100% versus 16.2% for a same-gain norm-matched random vector; Granite reaches 88.5% versus 27.5%. Shared intervention effects do not establish identical formation pathways for explicit and implicit requests.

Specific finding: CAA vectors extracted from the same behavioral examples using different prompt formats can differ substantially in direction while exhibiting broadly similar steering performance. The prompt-format comparison reports vector cosine similarities ranging from 0.07 to 0.86 despite broadly similar, correlated steering performance. Comparisons use the same training examples across formats, with 250 training and 500 evaluation examples per dataset and format. Similarity of measured performance does not establish equivalent mechanisms or statistically equivalent effects.
Specific finding: Combining answer prefilling, behavioral instructions, and five-shot demonstrations in CAA extraction can yield positive aggregate steering effects across behavioral datasets without a consistently superior extraction format. Using 250 training and 500 evaluation examples per dataset and format, all seven formats increased the dataset-averaged answer logit difference relative to no steering. Dataset-wise rankings showed no systematic winner. Some formats produced negative mean effects on the six least steerable datasets. No formal equivalence result or robust statistical ordering of formats is supplied.
location: Section 3, Effect of Prompt Types on Steering Vectors; Appendix C.1, Figure 4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Removing estimated high-curvature components from CAA vectors can improve classifier-measured sentiment, correction of misconceptions, and harmful-request refusal relative to unmodified CAA. Each main condition uses 50 greedy completions: up to 80 tokens for sentiment at α=3, 120 for sycophancy at α=3, and 150 for refusal at α=5. Sharp removal improves the reported metric in 25/25 conditions. Selected refusal configurations reach 88–98% for Qwen and 74–76% for Llama. Repeating all ten sycophancy conditions with 200 completions preserves improvement in 10/10. Sharp removal also exceeds sign-flipped CAA in 8/10 sycophancy and 4/4 inverted refusal conditions. Systematic confidence intervals and significance-test details are not supplied.
Specific finding: Renormalized projections of CAA vectors onto estimated high-curvature subspaces can yield negative target-minus-antitarget first-token probability margins on a majority of evaluations across diverse behavioral conditions. For 100 evaluation prompts and ten coefficients from 0.25 to 5.0 per condition, the reported fraction with P(target) − P(antitarget) < 0, averaged over coefficients, is 53–100% in all 36 conditions. Llama refusal reaches 100% at all three tested layers. Sharp projections are renormalized, so these tests do not measure the isolated effect of the original small, unscaled sharp component within CAA.
Specific finding: At selected layers, low-curvature CAA projections can produce better target-token metrics than the tested random-subspace controls. The paper reports that flat projections outperform random-subspace controls in 11/12 model–task combinations. At its best layer per model–task pair, the flat projection also has the lowest negative-margin rate among compared methods in 11/12 combinations. Qwen sentiment at layer 21 has no negative margins across 100 prompts evaluated at ten coefficients. Selected examples change negative CAA margins to positive margins for sycophancy, toxicity, and refusal. Best-layer reporting and the absolute-margin definition limit conclusions about prospective layer selection and intervention-induced reversal.
location: Section 5.4, Figure 3; Appendices G and J

experiment_summary: Specific finding: High-curvature steering modes may preferentially capture input-specific lexical or formatting features, while low-curvature modes may isolate a more stable behavioral disposition.

Specific finding: Contrastive-direction plateau-boundary exponents above two can persist across multiple language-model families and changes to perturbation and measurement settings. Across reported contrastive ablation conditions, mean p ranges from 2.24 to 2.63 and median p from 2.11 to 2.50. Settings include perturbation layers 2, 5, 10, and 20; alternative measurement layers; cosine and output-KL responses; half and double nominal thresholds; alternative token positions; additive perturbations; and Wikipedia/code activation sources. No condition's median fit residual exceeds 2%. Individual condition estimates are not enumerated in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Selected low-overlap contrastive directions in Gemma-2-9B have plateau-boundary exponents above two, whereas the tested PCA, isotropic-random, and random activation-difference controls remain near two. Contrastive mean p=2.42, direction-bootstrap 95% CI [2.29, 2.62], median 2.30. PCA mean p=2.03 [1.94, 2.12], random-difference 2.05 [2.00, 2.10], and isotropic random 2.03 [2.00, 2.07]. These comparisons measure calibrated mixture sensitivity; they do not establish semantic feature identity or directly measure correction of naturally occurring interference.
Specific finding: Rotating selected contrastive directions toward random directions can reduce their aggregate plateau-boundary exponent toward two. Tilts each direction toward its own fixed random orthogonal target, re-orthonormalizes the pair, and refits across rotation angles. The reported median p declines monotonically from approximately 2.4 for the selected contrastive pairs to approximately 2.0 at the random endpoint. The starting median differs from the full contrastive panel because this sweep uses a 40-pair subsample.

Specific finding: Restoring the original tool-call-direction coordinate can recover call decisions after broader formation-window MLP-output swaps while leaving the orthogonal residual component swapped. Execution-side MLP swaps reduce calling from 100% to 93%; restoring only the original call-direction projection recovers 100%, while orthogonal restoration yields 58%. Analysis-side swaps increase calling from 3% to 95%; projection restoration reduces it to 0%, versus 99.5% under orthogonal restoration. Full-state restoration returns the respective original baselines.
Specific finding: Qwen3-8B's intermediate tool-call state regulates downstream scaffold-associated attention-head writes and a late structural MLP feature that can promote the call-opening token. On 200 balanced held-out pairs, adding the L24 vector to unchanged analysis prompts restores L29H9, L33H11, and L33H29 call-token DLA close to execution values. On the feature-evaluation cohort, F109925 activation rises from 67.63 to 126.00, compared with 124.43 on execution prompts. Replacing its activation with the paired execution value gives 37% calling, versus 6.5% for fixed control F91365 and 41% for a full MLP34 patch on the same 200 pairs. A separate component sweep has different baselines and effects; notably, L33H11 replacement produces no strict recovery despite its positive clean-minus-corrupt DLA difference.

Specific finding: Analysis-active MLP feature writes opposing the tool-call direction contribute to suppressing Qwen3-8B's scaffold-conditioned call tendency. MLPs supply 77.7% of projected formation-window contrast writes. Held-out analysis-active versus execution-active absolute contribution mass has aggregate ratio 1.99; this is a projection-based decomposition, not a fraction of all causal tool-call computation. Of 115 training-labeled analysis_non_execution candidates, 102 are analysis-higher and write against the direction. On 200 feature-evaluation pairs, removing five training-ranked suppressor writes raises calling from 3.0% to 25.5%, closes 8.82% of the projection gap, and produces 22.5% strict recovery using all 200 pairs as denominator. Layer-matched random suppressors give 2.5% post-intervention calling and 0.5% strict recovery.
Specific finding: Model-specific tool-call contrasts across Qwen, Mistral, and Granite can exhibit strong residual-state control together with greater analysis-active than execution-active transcoder contribution mass. Each model uses 300 fitting and 200 held-out main pairs. Full-state recovery ranges from 93.5% to 100%; normalized vector sufficiency ranges from 0.81 to 1.03 and necessity from 0.61 to 1.04. Analysis-active/execution-active contribution-mass ratios range from 1.30 to 3.26. Reported MLP/attention projected-write ratios exceed two in the five nonhybrid models; this comparison is omitted for hybrid Qwen3.5. Native scaffold-attention summaries are positive, but target regions and measured head sets differ across architectures. Cross-domain and native-trajectory transfer vary substantially.

Specific finding: Softmax lookup models trained to reconstruct masked binary concept assignments can learn strongly aligned within-concept differences in both context and token representations. SGD cross-entropy experiments report mean unembedding cosines 0.972–0.997, embedding cosines 0.971–0.985, and cross-space cosines 0.973–0.990. Reported standard errors use 100, 100, 50, 20, and 10 runs for three through seven concepts. SGD uses learning rate 0.1 and batch size 100.
Specific finding: LLaMA-2 lexical counterfactual unembedding differences exhibit greater alignment within concept categories than between different categories. The paper computes average cosine similarities within and between lexical steering-vector sets and reports stronger within-category alignment and approximately orthogonal between-category directions. This is a new geometric analysis using inherited word pairs. The heatmap values are unavailable in the supplied text rendering, so evidence is limited to the explicit textual finding.
Specific finding: Selected LLaMA-2 context differences can align more strongly with matching or related lexical token contrasts than with unrelated contrasts. Translation experiments compare absolute cosines between mean context differences and mean token-unembedding differences, sampling 150 OPUS Books examples and filtering context lengths to 20–150 tokens; retained counts are unreported. Prose reports preferential alignment with matching or related translation categories. Winograd matching comparisons average cosine 0.042, maximum 0.161, versus nonmatching mean 0.011, maximum 0.081. The Winograd sample count and uncertainty are unreported, and its embedding/unembedding terminology is inconsistent.

Specific finding: Rescaling prompt-specific steering vectors to a common baseline norm provides an adequate magnitude control for comparing their effects at the same steering multipliers.
Specific finding: The natural magnitude of a mean-difference steering vector makes a fixed multiplier meaningfully comparable across layers and concepts.

Specific finding: On forced-choice stereotype benchmarks, bias CAA steering can reduce stereotypical-answer rates while increasing answer entropy and moving aggregate stereotypical-to-anti-stereotypical probability ratios toward one. Measured greedy stereotype-answer percentages, answer entropy, and ratios of mean option probabilities before and after steering at max(1, natural CAA norm). Llama-3.1-8B's native CrowS-Pairs stereotype-answer rate fell from 75.82% to 64.71%, entropy rose from 0.52 to 0.59, and biased/anti-biased mean-probability ratio fell from 1.91 to 1.43. Similar tendencies occur across most model–dataset cells. Qwen3.5-9B-Base shows unchanged entropy at reported precision, a small StereoSet stereotype-rate increase, and a small CrowS-Pairs probability-ratio increase. The findings are consistent with flattening without establishing exclusive confidence mediation.
Specific finding: Bias-derived CAA interventions can increase general-knowledge multiple-choice answer entropy while producing smaller, usually nonpositive changes in greedy accuracy. Table 5 reports accuracy and entropy for eight checkpoints, three vectors, and two general-QA datasets. Qwen3.5-9B StereoSet steering increased OpenBookQA entropy from 0.24 to 0.50 with accuracy unchanged at 0.89, and MMLU entropy from 0.34 to 0.61 with accuracy unchanged at 0.79. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct BBQ steering reduced OpenBookQA accuracy from 0.76 to 0.70. Most accuracy changes were zero or negative, but Falcon3-7B-Base MMLU accuracy increased from 0.67 to 0.68 under BBQ steering. Several Qwen-base entropy values were unchanged at reported precision.
Specific finding: Anti-stereotypical-minus-stereotypical mean activation directions can align substantially with confidence directions constructed by contrasting the highest- and lowest-likelihood answers to general-knowledge questions. Compared bias CAA vectors with separately constructed highest/lowest-likelihood answer contrasts from MMLU and OpenBookQA across eight checkpoints. Reported cosine similarities span 0.29–0.91. Means across models and the two confidence datasets are 0.68 for BBQ-derived vectors, 0.67 for StereoSet-derived vectors, and 0.50 for CrowS-Pairs-derived vectors. No uncertainty estimates or matched random-direction distribution are supplied.
Specific finding: Steering along anti-stereotypical-minus-stereotypical activation contrasts can increase abstention even when the question supplies enough information for a definite answer. Compared steering with and without abstention choices using renormalized answer probabilities and greedy accuracy. In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, disambiguated BBQ accuracy fell from 0.87 to 0.52 at the headline coefficient max(1, natural CAA norm), while the ratio of mean abstention probability to mean anti-biased-answer probability rose from 0.22 to 1.82. Other checkpoints generally showed smaller disambiguated effects, including flat accuracy in both Qwen variants. Across abstention-enabled datasets, Table 8 also contains exceptions to a universal increase: Ministral-base's CrowS-Pairs abstention/anti-biased probability ratio decreases from 1.32 to 1.19.

Specific finding: Independent sign randomization of paired CAA contrasts can retain substantial normalized alignment with the original CAA direction across Qwen construction banks and layers. CPU reconstruction of 320 primary Qwen3-14B layer-28 sign-randomized directions yielded cosine SD .5769, 25.3% with cosine ≥.5, and 4.7% with cosine ≥.9; isotropic cosine SD was .0141. Simulation of 4,000 sign-randomized draws in each of 21 bank–layer cells yielded cosine SDs .440–.921. This geometry analysis required no new model forward passes and did not cover the prospective balanced block-Rademacher comparator.
Specific finding: The ratio of RMS pair-contrast projection onto the mean direction to RMS pair-contrast norm can predict the cosine spread retained by normalized sign-randomized CAA directions. Across 21 constructions with 4,000 simulated randomizations per cell, A predicted cosine SD with Pearson r=.979 and MAE .075. In the primary cell, A=.606 versus measured SD=.577. Equation 6 supplies a heuristic concentration argument, explicitly described as unproved and liable to degrade when pair norms vary strongly.

Specific finding: Disproportionate functional importance and coherent input associations provide useful screening evidence that a neuron group implements a comprehensible, task-relevant subtask.
Specific finding: Test-accuracy loss from lesioning a neuron group, compared with losses from equally sized random groups in the same layer, provides a useful operational measure of that group's functional importance.
Specific finding: A neuron group's optimized activation L1 norm exceeding that of matched random groups provides useful proxy evidence that its neurons process related input features.
Specific finding: A large range of class-specific lesion damage and low output entropy on a group's optimized input provide useful operational indicators of neuron-group specialization with respect to class labels.
location: Section 1, Proxies for local specialization; Section 5, Limitations

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Components selected for recall versus reasoning preference in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct can produce larger reported accuracy losses on their associated task class than on the other class when ablated. Section 3.1 reports recall losses of 15% ± 3% after recall-targeted interventions and reasoning losses of approximately 14% ± 4% after reasoning-targeted interventions. Table 3 reports cross-task losses of 2% and 3%, respectively, versus 2% on both tasks for equal-size random controls. Baseline accuracies, component-set sizes, replacement donors, uncertainty definitions, scoring procedures, and whether percentages denote relative changes or percentage points are unspecified. Separate effects for layers, heads, and neurons are not supplied, and held-out intervention evaluation is not clearly described.
Specific finding: Attention heads in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct can exhibit recall-versus-reasoning task preferences that persist across folds of a small evaluation dataset. The paper reports approximately 74% of heads showing significant task preferences and lists 583 consistently specialized heads: 239 recall-specialized, 219 reasoning-specialized, and 125 mixed. Head comparisons use FDR alpha 0.01, and consistency requires task-type classification preservation in at least 80% of five folds. The percentage denominator, meaning of mixed specialization, and relationship between these counts are not explained. Detailed contribution-score definitions and individual head intervention effects are absent.
Specific finding: MLP neurons in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct can show large, fold-stable activation and firing differences between selected recall and reasoning prompts. The body reports approximately one-third of MLP neurons meeting task-specificity criteria described as Bonferroni-corrected p < 10^-4 and |Cohen's d| > 1.0. Firing selectivity is defined as the absolute difference between task-conditioned firing probabilities. The authors describe clusters near layers 4 and 22 and report 100% fold consistency for top neurons. The firing threshold, neuron-count denominator, resampling details, and random-seed procedures are unspecified. The supplied metadata abstract characterizes neuron effects as less robust, unlike the body's strong stability claims. Unseen plot contents provide no additional auditable measurements.

Specific finding: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct exhibits an early-to-late functional hierarchy in which shallow layers preferentially support factual recall and deep layers preferentially support compositional reasoning. The authors compare hidden-state norms, attention entropy, and MLP magnitude across 28 layers using Mann–Whitney tests, Cohen's d, FDR correction, and five-fold stability. The narrative assigns recall predominantly to layers 0–6 and reasoning to layers 17–27. However, Table 2 lists reasoning-specialized layers 1, 2, and 18 and recall-specialized layers 3–6, 8–15, 17, 19, and 25. Thus the reported classifications conflict with the proposed clean depth ordering. Causal intervention outcomes are not broken down by individual layer, and the plotted layer values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Task-associated separation of recall and reasoning components generalizes across transformer language-model families.
location: Hypothesis H4; document and metadata abstracts; Section 4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Ablating language-associated FFN neurons can reduce GPT-4-rated generation quality in the associated language, while also causing losses in other languages. Table 1 compares intact, random-ablation, and language-associated-ablation conditions using GPT-4 scores on a 1–10 scale. Associated-language scores fall in all six ablation conditions: Chinese falls from 4.30 to 2.46 and Japanese from 2.86 to 1.84. Off-target losses are substantial in some cells, including Spanish falling from 3.51 to 2.29 under French-neuron ablation. Table 2 illustrates script changes and mixed-language output after Chinese-neuron ablation. Sample counts and uncertainty are unspecified.
Specific finding: Increasing selected target-language neuron activations to language-specific average values can improve the frequency of responses classified as being in the desired language. Table 4 reports language accuracy increasing from 0.87 to 0.99 for Chinese, 0.73 to 0.90 for French, 0.81 to 0.93 for Spanish, 0.60 to 0.97 for Vietnamese, 0.40 to 0.99 for Indonesian, and 0.79 to 1.00 for Japanese. GPT-4 content ratings improve in five languages but decline from 3.70 to 3.57 for Vietnamese. Sample counts, uncertainty, and broad capability-retention tests are absent.
Specific finding: Combined suppression of source-language neurons and activation of target-language neurons can redirect a response toward a language different from the question's language. Table 5 shows a Spanish time-management question answered predominantly in Chinese after Spanish-neuron deactivation and Chinese-neuron activation. The response retains the English word 'Time'. This is one qualitative example without aggregate success, content-preservation measurements, or baseline comparisons.

Specific finding: Some GPT-2 Small residual-stream SAE features exhibit recognizable lexical or thematic patterns in selected activating examples and reported vocabulary projections. The post reports qualitative inspection of selected features associated with presidential first names, a tokenization-dependent 'c' pattern, thanks/apologies, Star Wars, and violence/conflict. These are anecdotal dashboard observations rather than a systematic interpretability benchmark or intervention experiment.
location: How interpretable are the features in each layer?

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A sparse autoencoder trained on DeepSeek R1 reasoning activations can expose features whose strongest examples share recognizable patterns such as explicit backtracking and references to earlier reasoning. Displayed activation contexts contain repeated mistake-correction phrases, references to earlier analysis, entity identifiers, and calculation-result boundaries. These examples support candidate activation-pattern descriptions without establishing exhaustive semantics or downstream function.

Specific finding: Multimodal-model descriptions of masked maximally activating images can achieve substantial region agreement and human-rated consistency for selected visual SAE coordinates. LLaVA-OV-72B generates descriptions from five masked exemplars per coordinate. Table 1 reports overall Grounding DINO/SAM IoU of 0.20 versus 0.005 for random-image references and CLIP score of 23.6 versus 18.2. Random references use ten IoU runs and thirty CLIP runs, with 99% confidence intervals reported for those references. Table 2 reports GPT-4o consistency of 0.89 from 600 cases, 100 per concept category, and human consistency of 0.75 from 60 samples assessed by two experts, totaling 120 evaluations. The feature-subset selection rule and main evaluation's category counts are unspecified.
location: Sections 2.2 and 3.2; Tables 1–2; Appendices C and F

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A concept identified from a coordinate's strongly activating visual exemplars is sufficiently specific to interpret clamping that coordinate as manipulating the named concept.
location: Sections 2.3, 4.1, and 4.4; Appendices E and G

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Sentences containing an attention head's largest token-to-token weights provide useful exemplars for interpreting the lexical relationships targeted by that head.
Specific finding: A human's ability to quickly explain most of a neuron's strongest activations is a useful proxy for how interpretable that neuron will be under more comprehensive investigation.
location: Section 6.1, especially the later Caveat; Section 6.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Ratings of pattern consistency among a feature's highest-activating contexts provide a useful proxy for that SAE feature's interpretability.

Specific finding: Maximizing pre-softmax class logits can produce visually better GoogLeNet class visualizations than maximizing class probabilities under the article's optimization conditions. The authors report better visual quality from pre-softmax objectives and state that trying a LogSumExp reformulation did not appear better than optimizing raw probabilities. No numerical comparison, class sample size, or controlled protocol is supplied. Suppression of competing classes and difficulty optimizing through softmax are discussed as alternative explanations rather than experimentally isolated mechanisms.

Specific finding: For the tested supervised ImageNet ConvNet, maximizing unnormalized class scores produces more visually prominent class visualizations than maximizing softmax posteriors. The authors report trying posterior maximization and finding its results less visually prominent. They motivate score maximization by observing that a posterior can increase through suppression of competing classes. Comparative images, sample counts, and numerical quality scores are not supplied.
models_studied: ["ILSVRC-2013 ConvNet with five convolutional and three fully connected layers"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Optimizing an L2-regularized input image to maximize a supervised ImageNet ConvNet's class score can produce visually recognizable class appearance patterns. With trained weights fixed, the authors optimize class scores minus an L2 image penalty and present selected resulting images as understandable class visualizations. Evidence is qualitative; no recognition study or aggregate visualization metric is reported.
models_studied: ["ILSVRC-2013 ConvNet with five convolutional and three fully connected layers"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Intermediate-layer probabilities obtained through the final unembedding provide an informative proxy for when answer-related information becomes available in a language model.

Specific finding: In verbatim repetition loops, GPT-2's recognition of the repeating pattern (as seen through the logit lens) emerges only in the upper half of the network. Logit lens on a single example of extreme repetition. Lower layers fail to predict the repeated continuation even after several repetitions; upper layers do.
Specific finding: Applying a transformer language model's final layer norm and unembedding to intermediate-layer residual-stream activations yields sensible next-token distributions that converge smoothly toward the final output distribution, often reaching a good guess by the middle layers. Logit lens on GPT-2 1558M across 48 layers on a GPT-3 abstract excerpt and a few other prompts. Shows per-layer top-1 tokens, ranks of the final top-1 token, and KL(final || layer). These show progressive convergence, with ranks of the final prediction low by mid-network. Evidence is qualitative and drawn from a handful of examples.
Specific finding: Summed next-token probability over valid starting tokens of an expected word provides a useful operational measure of that word's language-specific readout.

Specific finding: Multi-token candidate phrases can be scored at a fixed intermediate layer by multiplying vocabulary-readout probabilities while successively supplying each preceding candidate token.
Specific finding: The unembedding projection of an SAE decoder direction provides useful candidate evidence about the token categories associated with that feature's output-facing role.

Specific finding: Projecting GPT-2 attention-head outputs through their corresponding output-projection slices yields greater top-token overlap with attention-block and downstream readouts than directly unembedding zero-padded pre-projection head outputs. Compared top-50 vocabulary intersections of head outputs with attention-block outputs, transformer-block outputs, and final states, with versus without multiplication by the corresponding WO slice. Section 3.1 reports little alignment without WO and greater, depth-dependent alignment with WO. Results are summarized across heads in Figure 2.
Specific finding: GPT-2 memory values receiving higher attention weights tend to share more top-projected vocabulary tokens with their corresponding head output. Compared I50 between output-projected memory values and their corresponding head outputs, stratifying values by attention-score rank in the main experiment. Section 3.3 and Figure 5 report greater overlap for higher-ranked values. Appendix D.2 reports related comparisons across heads, but its supplementary ranking description differs from the main experiment.
Specific finding: Overlap between two internal vectors' highest-ranked vocabulary projections provides a useful proxy for their semantic alignment.

Specific finding: An early attention head can exhibit substantial Direct Logit Attribution on selected predictions while that attribution remains largely unchanged when its input is replaced with an activation from unrelated equal-length text. For each selected prompt, inputs from 300 unrelated equal-length texts are patched into L0H2. Its DLA remains similar to the clean value. Analogous replacements substantially alter DLA for four other attention heads selected for high attribution on the respective prompts. Exact DLA magnitudes are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering; the reported top-two logit differences are full-model prediction contrasts, not head DLA values.
Specific finding: Direct Logit Attribution alone does not establish a component's uncanceled influence on final predictions because downstream components can systematically negate its attributed contribution. Value-pathway interventions demonstrate writer-dependent cancellation of L0H2's output. Across roughly 30,000 positions from 30 training samples, writer DLA correlates at −0.159 with aggregate cleaner DLA and at −0.716 with cleaner DLA restricted to writer-to-cleaner V-composition, using each position's top-two prediction contrast. Four selected contexts additionally show substantial writer DLA insensitive to unrelated-input replacement. These tests do not establish zero total influence or measure a canceled fraction.
location: Adversarial examples of high DLA values without direct contribution; Figure 4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A final-layer neuron can have a small direct unembedding projection while substantially affecting output distributions and loss through changes in the final normalization denominator. For selected high-norm, low-logit-variance GPT-2 Small neurons, absolute loss changes under ordinary mean ablation are substantially larger than changes when the clean final LayerNorm denominator is retained. The six-neuron comparison against 100 random neurons uses 25,600 C4 tokens; random neurons generally show much smaller differences. SVD links the discrepancy to neuron writes into low-gain unembedding directions.

Specific finding: When a final residual state is a sum of an embedding and component outputs and its readout is linear, each token logit equals the sum of the corresponding vocabulary projections of those contributions. Formal algebraic derivation supplied in Equation 10: expand the final residual state into the embedding, attention-head outputs, and FFN outputs, then distribute the linear unembedding map across the sum. Equations 14–17 give component, neuron, source-position, and logit-difference versions. The result assumes additive residual updates and a linear readout; it supplies no empirical model measurements.

Specific finding: When a final residual state is a sum of an embedding and component outputs and its readout is linear, each token logit equals the sum of the corresponding vocabulary projections of those contributions. Formal algebraic derivation in Section 2.1: defining P as the unembedding multiplied by learned normalization scaling and divided by the observed final normalization factor yields P applied to the residual sum, which distributes over embedding, attention, and MLP terms. This establishes fixed-pass accounting under the stated architecture, rather than unrestricted intervention effects.

Specific finding: MLPs between components communicating a linear residual-stream feature can support apparently feature-mediating subspaces even when those MLPs do not ordinarily contribute to the task. GPT-2 Small singular-value analyses support full-rank MLP projections. OpenWebText geometric comparisons report R² around 0.8 or higher except layer 0; regressions recovering random residual projections from MLP activations report held-out R² = 0.71 ± 0.17. Random-MLP IOI experiments also yield effective patching directions. These support prerequisites rather than establish prevalence across models and tasks.

Specific finding: MLPs between components communicating a linear residual-stream feature can support apparently feature-mediating subspaces even when those MLPs do not ordinarily contribute to the task.
location: Finding dormant / irrelevant directions in MLP activations; Discussion and takeaways

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A linear network can admit a one-dimensional interchange intervention that exactly reproduces a target input substitution while leaving the naturally transmitting task pathway unchanged. Formal result by explicit algebraic construction, without training or sampling. Orthogonal patching from x' into x along (e2 + e3)/sqrt(2) gives hidden state (x, (x+x')/2, (x'-x)/2) and output x'. For opposite inputs this is (x, 0, x'). The first neuron remains unchanged, the second has zero output weight, and the third is identically zero on natural inputs. This establishes output equivalence of the interventions; the appendix explains why privileging one basis as the mechanistic account requires additional assumptions.
location: Setup for the example; Geometric intuition; Appendix: The importance of correct model units

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A subspace patch can reproduce a donor’s output by transferring information from a disconnected coordinate into a dormant output-sensitive coordinate while leaving the naturally responsible coordinate unchanged. Explicit algebraic counterexample instantiating Makelov et al.’s cited argument: hA = (2,0,1), hB = (0,0,0), g(h) = h2 + h3, and v = (1,1,0)/√2. Projection patching yields hB′ = (1,1,0), with g(hB′) = g(hA) = 1 although coordinate 3 remains zero. The supplied calculation establishes the existential claim; it is not a new model experiment.

Specific finding: Small Transformers trained for bounded-depth Dyck prediction can achieve high in-distribution closing-bracket accuracy while learning substantially different, frequently non-stack-like attention patterns. Dyck₂,₄ models trained on sequences shorter than 28 tokens attain at least 97% reported closing-bracket accuracy. Across 40 initializations, mean squared-Frobenius second-layer attention variation on one diagnostic prefix is 2.20 with linear positional encoding and 2.27 without, versus 2.85 for the specified random-pattern baseline; a minimal-first-layer configuration yields 0.24. Appendix D.2 reports additional prefix-training variation. Table 1 extends the comparison to two or three bracket types, depths four or eight, and two or three layers; its means and standard deviations are calculated over 40 length-19 sentences, with random baseline 3.33 and a modified residual/normalization architecture.
Specific finding: Even the complete collection of a Transformer's attention patterns does not determine its output function when downstream decoding parameters are unspecified. Elementary formal construction in Proposition 1: for arbitrary query and key matrices, set the final decoding matrix and bias to zero, making the output identically zero without constraining the attention computations. Changing the final head does not change the preceding attention patterns. This supplies a limited functional nonidentification counterexample rather than a result about the causal use of attention in successfully trained models.
Specific finding: Transformers trained to copy Dyck sequences can display attention patterns organized by bracket type or closing-bracket status that do not themselves explain positionwise copying. Figures 4–6 describe a one-layer model with greater than 90% copying validation accuracy and four-layer examples with greater than 96%. Captions describe attention to closing brackets or selected bracket types, alongside a current-position pattern compatible with copying. These are qualitative case studies with unspecified sample counts and no causal ablation of the displayed patterns.
models_studied: ["Two-layer, one-head Dyck Transformers, principally embedding and FFN width 50", "Two-layer Dyck Transformer with width 200 in Figure 1(a)", "Dyck Transformers with supplied minimal first-layer embeddings", "Three-layer Dyck Transformers"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Frozen representations from an Amazon-trained byte-level mLSTM enable highly label-efficient binary sentiment classification on Stanford Sentiment Treebank using a linear classifier. The frozen representation achieves 91.8% binary SST accuracy using sentence-level labels and omitting parse trees and dense phrase supervision. Figure 2 averages 100 runs with 10th–90th percentile bands: some cited baselines are matched with approximately a dozen labels, and all cited results are exceeded with a few hundred. The binary subtask provides 6,920 sentence-level labels versus 76,961 labels including phrases. The cited 90.2% ensemble is a literature comparison, not a reproduced experiment.
Specific finding: Representations learned from Amazon review language modeling transfer unevenly across downstream tasks, with stronger comparative results on review sentiment than on the evaluated general semantic tasks. Classification accuracies are 86.9% on MR, 91.4% on CR, 94.6% on SUBJ, and 88.5% on MPQA. MR and CR exceed the listed prior results, whereas SUBJ and MPQA do not exceed all listed results. Fine-grained SST accuracy is 52.9%, below the cited 53.6% best result. Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus results are 75.0% accuracy and 82.8 F1. SICK relatedness reaches Pearson r = 0.792, Spearman rho = 0.725, and MSE = 0.390, worse than the listed skip-thought results. These baselines are cited results rather than documented reruns. CR almost certainly overlaps the language-model training corpus.
Specific finding: A linear sentiment classifier over a frozen Amazon-trained byte-level mLSTM representation can show diminishing accuracy gains as labeled Yelp training data increase. On binary Yelp, described in the source as containing 598,000 examples, test accuracy improves only a little over one percentage point across four orders of magnitude in labeled training data and reaches 95.22% using the full available training data. The cited TF-IDF bag-of-words baseline reaches 93.66%, and the cited linear classifier using the 500,000 most frequent n-grams up to length five reaches 95.64%. Proposed causes involving domain, document length, and classifier capacity are not separately tested.
models_studied: ["Single-layer 4,096-unit byte-level mLSTM trained on Amazon reviews", "L1-regularized logistic-regression readout"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Final representations in selected Pythia models support high held-out linear classification accuracy for many morphological, semantic, and translation contrasts. Appendix O fits logistic probes with 70%/30% train/test splits repeated over three seeds and reports mean and standard deviation of test accuracy. The prose reports high accuracy and low variability for most concepts, while noting instability for very small categories. Exact accuracies are confined to unavailable plots. Pair-group handling within the splits is not specified.
Specific finding: Normalized mean-difference directions for selected lexical contrasts can align preferentially with logistic-probe weights for the same contrasts, including when direction estimation and probe fitting use disjoint word pairs. The paper multiplies normalized concept mean-difference rows by normalized logistic-probe weight columns. Initial analyses cover Pythia, Llama-2, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-R1. Appendix N adds disjoint 50%/50% direction-estimation/probe-fitting subsets, permuted-label baselines, and repeated split seeds, reporting persistent same-concept alignment. This separates the two estimators' data but is not a third independent classifier test set. Appendix R reports similar qualitative patterns for eight additional contrasts. Numerical alignment, null-distribution, and Frobenius-error values are not available in the supplied figure captions or prose.
location: Appendix O, Figures 17–21; Appendix H.2, Table 1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: SAE directions can align with supervised Othello board-state probe directions more closely than random-vector controls while remaining imperfect geometric matches. For each rectified probe direction, the author calculated its maximum cosine similarity with the SAE directions and compared the resulting distribution with random-vector controls. The text reports substantially higher similarities than chance, with no maximum exceeding 0.7. This tests geometric alignment, not semantic equivalence or causal interchangeability.
models_studied: ["Author-trained OthelloGPT: 25M parameters, 8 layers, d_model=512", "Layer-6 tied-weight ReLU SAE: 1,024 latents"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A shared learned residual-stream projection can reduce a compiled running-token-frequency transformer's residual dimensionality from 14 to approximately six while retaining essentially unchanged task performance. Sweeps compressed residual dimension and examines output mean-squared error relative to the compiled model. Performance is described as essentially matching the original model at approximately six dimensions, with deterioration below that size. Appendix E specifies AdamW training for 300,000 steps with batch size 256. Evaluation sample counts, sampling distributions, and exact final loss values are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Compression trained to preserve a compiled token-frequency model's outputs and layer computations can retain task-critical features and discard irrelevant token identities more selectively than PCA. Compares feature-overlap visualizations for learned compression and retention of the first eight PCA components. Learned compression retains task-relevant tokens:x, is_x, and frac_prevs while discarding unnecessary token-identity dimensions. This is a qualitative comparison in one compiled task; no general task-performance advantage over PCA is established.
Specific finding: Compressing a transformer that implements a known multi-step algorithm can produce non-orthogonal representations of sparse features while preserving substantial task performance. Examines overlaps among known feature embeddings after learned compression. Positional embeddings occupy non-orthogonal directions, important computational variables remain largely separated, and unnecessary token identities are discarded. Output-loss sweeps demonstrate preservation of task performance at sufficiently large compressed dimensions. These are new experiments in a compiled multi-step transformer, extending rather than rerunning the cited toy-model studies.
Specific finding: An input indicator and a later-computed variable carrying nearly the same information can partially share representational space after a compiled transformer is compressed. The displayed learned embeddings of tokens:x and is_x partially overlap. These variables carry similar information but differ in when they are populated. This observation concerns one variable pair; shared information is offered as an intuitive explanation and is not independently manipulated to establish a causal effect on overlap.
Specific finding: Big Five Inventory scoring provides meaningful operational measurements of personality expressed by language models under explicit persona instructions.

Specific finding: Human-derived Big Five instruments, reliability thresholds, and expected construct correlations provide appropriate operational standards for evaluating personality synthesized in LLM outputs.
location: Sections 2.1.2 and 5.1; Appendices F, H, and I

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Personality scores from selected instruction-tuned language models can correlate with prompted affect, aggression, values, and creativity scores in directions resembling human personality research. The study correlates IPIP-NEO scores with PANAS affect, BPAQ aggression, PVQ-RR values, and SSCS creativity scores over 1,250 configurations per model. Section 2.2.3 reports generally stronger human-expected associations in instruction-tuned models, with domain-specific exceptions. For Flan-PaLM 540B, conscientiousness correlations with achievement, conformity, and security are 0.74, 0.73, and 0.59. Conscientiousness criterion validity does not improve consistently with model size. Human reference associations come from cited research, not new human experiments.
Specific finding: Across shared personality-shaping prompts, LLM questionnaire scores can correlate strongly with personality scores assigned to separately generated social media text. Correlates IPIP-NEO scores with AMS scores from social media text produced under the same 2,250 personality/biography profiles per model. The reported mean Pearson correlation across five traits and four models is 0.67, compared with a cited human mean of 0.38. Human data are not newly collected or matched experimentally. Generation targets differ: 100 updates per profile for Flan-PaLM and 25 generations requesting 20 updates each per profile for the other models. Individual Figure 4 values are not readable in the supplied rendering.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Reversing option mappings or agreement-scale direction can change reported IPIP-300 trait scores in ChatGPT and Llama2 chat models. The paper administers reversed variants of all three templates and reports changed trait means. ChatGPT's Prompt-3 extraversion mean changes from 2.47 to 3.60, and Llama2-13B's Prompt-2 openness mean changes from 2.11 to 3.81. Section 3.3 reports Experiment-2 rejection counts of 8/15 for Llama2-70B, 11/15 for 13B, and 13/15 for 7B, but lists between-template reversed comparisons instead of the within-template original-versus-reversed comparisons defined in Section 3.2. Those counts therefore cannot unambiguously quantify reversal significance. Response parsing and score recoding are insufficiently specified.
Specific finding: ChatGPT and Llama2 chat models can produce substantially different IPIP-300 trait-score distributions under three ordinary questionnaire administration templates. Each template is administered to 300 items, yielding 60 item scores per trait. Original-template pairwise Mann–Whitney U comparisons reject at nominal α=0.05 in 11/15 Llama2-70B comparisons, 15/15 Llama2-13B comparisons, and 11/15 Llama2-7B comparisons. ChatGPT is described as differing across almost all original-template pairs, but its exact original-template rejection count is not separately stated. Its reported extraversion means are 4.57, 3.22, and 2.47 across the three templates. No multiple-testing correction or paired-item analysis is reported, and score construction is insufficiently specified.

Specific finding: Indexed multiple-choice scoring of MPI personality statements can yield substantially different semantic answers and trait profiles when option descriptions are reordered. Original-versus-reversed indexed options change response frequencies and OCEAN summaries. For OPT-13B, Very Accurate falls from 87.46% of original-order items to 0% after reversal, while Very Inaccurate rises from 0% to 98.58%. Letter indices remain ordered A–E while their descriptions move. Appendix tables report further order comparisons and smaller checkpoints; Table 15 inconsistently specifies some additional orders.

Specific finding: Paraphrasing a personality-inducing prompt can change text-davinci-003's targeted Big Five inventory score, with the direction of change depending on the trait. Table A6 compares each original prompt with five paraphrases. Openness falls from 4.54 to 3.67–4.25, extraversion from 4.58 to 4.17–4.54, and agreeableness from 5.00 to 4.58–4.75. Neuroticism increases from 3.75 to 3.92–4.50. Conscientiousness remains near its ceiling, at 4.83–4.96 versus 4.92 originally. The finite paraphrase set is not a distributional robustness guarantee.

Specific finding: The tested alphabet-indexed, number-indexed, and numerical agreement-scale IPIP administration templates preserve the intended assessment target sufficiently for score differences to indicate measurement instability.

Specific finding: Paraphrased and translated BFI instructions, items, and response options preserve the intended trait meanings sufficiently for score differences to be interpreted as assessment robustness.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing agreement-scale answers with ordered frequency adverbs preserves enough of an IPIP item's meaning for the original trait-scoring rules and human-reference distributions to remain interpretable.

Specific finding: Conversation topics, textual formats, and preceding music-genre paragraphs can substantially change ChatGPT's personal- and cultural-value questionnaire scores without explicit instructions to change those values. One-way ANOVAs with Bonferroni-adjusted thresholds of 0.005 for PVQ and 0.0083 for VSM detect context effects on all ten PVQ and six VSM dimensions for conversations and formats. Music paragraphs affect all PVQ dimensions except Power and all VSM dimensions except Power Distance and Masculinity. Posthoc Tukey comparisons identify selected pairwise differences. These tests concern questionnaire-score distributions over answer permutations, not persistent behavioral dispositions.
Specific finding: Under a comparison treating answer-order permutations as analogous to human participants, some ChatGPT context-induced PVQ changes exceed value-change estimates reported in selected human longitudinal and priming studies. The paper reanalyzes its ChatGPT scores and compares them with published human statistics; it collects no new human data. Maximum reported absolute Cohen's d is 5.86 for ChatGPT versus 0.53 in the selected human comparisons. Mean ipsative correlation is 0.05 for chat versus C++, compared with 0.59 for the least stable selected human longitudinal comparison. Music-paragraph ipsative correlations remain higher, with a minimum of 0.77. Mean rank-order correlations across values are 0.36–0.54 for the six ChatGPT ordering comparisons versus 0.57–0.82 for the selected human studies. Human participant variation and model answer-permutation variation are different sampling units. Table 4's caption reverses the direction described by its numbers and surrounding prose.
Specific finding: Fictional-character role prompts can induce distinct personal-value questionnaire profiles in ChatGPT that qualitatively match selected character descriptions. Appendix E.1 reports high Power and Achievement and low Benevolence and Universalism for Sauron, contrasting with the other selected characters, and high Hedonism for Pippin. The study uses no answer permutations, independent character-congruence ratings, or aggregate behavioral validation. Only qualitative outcomes stated in the text are recoverable from the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Including preceding questionnaire items and model answers in GPT-3 DaVinci's prompts can substantially change HVS score levels and inter-value correlations. Aggregate conformity, power, and security means change from 4.51, 5.34, and 5.87 without history to 2.17, 2.92, and 2.69 with history. Benevolence, universalism, self-direction, and stimulation remain comparatively prominent in the history-conditioned profile. Tables 5 and 7 show substantially stronger absolute correlations for many value pairs, including achievement–power increasing from .17 to .92 and universalism–stimulation changing from −.03 to −.94. Same-temperature rows also show large profile differences, although the paper supplies no formal paired history-effect test.

Specific finding: Explicit role assignments can shift gpt-3.5-turbo's questionnaire profile in directions consistent with the assigned character. Role-conditioned questionnaire comparisons report psychopath-role agreeableness of 1.9±0.6 versus default 4.4±0.2, DTDD Machiavellianism of 8.4±0.5 versus 5.4±0.9, and empathy of 2.4±0.4 versus 6.2±0.3. The ordinary-person role reports GSE 29.6±0.7, matching the human reference mean of 29.6 while having much smaller reported dispersion. The general questionnaire protocol uses ten shuffled-question runs per scale.
Specific finding: CipherChat conditioning can change GPT-4's questionnaire profile, increasing Dark Triad scores and decreasing EIS and empathy scores relative to its default configuration. GPT-4's DTDD means increase from 2.0 to 4.5 for narcissism, 1.1 to 3.2 for Machiavellianism, and 1.2 to 4.7 for psychopathy. EIS decreases from 151.4±18.7 to 121.8±12.0, and empathy from 6.8±0.4 to 4.6±0.2. The authors report no statistically significant differences on WLEIS subscales; non-rejection does not establish equivalence.

Specific finding: HVS profiles generated with questionnaire response history can remain sensitive to sampling temperature, with some value scores increasing and others decreasing. The reported multivariate effect is F(10,483)=8.12, p<.001. Follow-up regressions report positive slopes for universalism (0.15, p<.05) and benevolence (0.28, p<.001), and negative slopes for self-direction (−0.17, p=.01) and stimulation (−0.35, p=.03). Achievement, power, tradition, and conformity are nonsignificant. Security and hedonism are described as decreasing, consistent with their broad Table 6 trends, but their printed coefficients have positive signs; those numerical directions remain unresolved.
Specific finding: Under independent-item HVS administration, increasing GPT-3 DaVinci's sampling temperature can decrease mean importance scores for nine values while leaving stimulation without a statistically significant association. Section 3.3.2 reports F(10,908)=132.06, p<.001 for the combined temperature effect. Nine follow-up slopes are negative with p<.001, ranging from −0.17 for benevolence to −1.54 for power. Stimulation has a reported slope of 0.02 and is nonsignificant. Table 4 displays the corresponding temperature-specific means.
Specific finding: Human-oriented personality assessments can assign language models dark-trait scores above human averages.

Specific finding: Human-oriented personality assessments can assign language models dark-trait scores above human averages. Ten shuffled-question runs per model. Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, and gpt-3.5-turbo exceed the reference means on narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy. Table 3 reports gpt-3.5-turbo scores of 6.6±0.6, 5.4±0.9, and 4.0±1.0 versus human scores of 4.9±1.8, 3.8±1.6, and 2.5±1.4. Default GPT-4 and text-davinci-003 score below all three human means. Appendix A lists the default gpt-3.5-turbo narcissism mean as 6.5 rather than 6.6.
Specific finding: Default assistant language models can report general self-efficacy scores above a large published human reference mean, with some models approaching the scale ceiling. Ten shuffled-question runs per model yield GSE means of 39.1, 30.4, 37.5, 38.5, and 39.9 for Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo, and GPT-4, respectively, compared with the human mean 29.6±5.3. GPT-4 scores 39.9±0.3 on the ten-item scale with maximum sum 40. Mean elevation alone does not establish significance for every model.
Specific finding: Default assistant language models can score above selected human reference means on emotional-intelligence and empathy self-report questionnaires. Across ten shuffled-question runs per model, all five default models have reported means above the supplied human means on each WLEIS subscale and Empathy. GPT-4's empathy score is 6.8±0.4 versus 4.9±0.8. EIS comparisons are less uniform: Llama-2-13B scores 128.6±12.3, below the female reference mean of 130.9±15.1. These are questionnaire-score comparisons, not performance-based emotional-ability tests.
Specific finding: Language models can obtain elevated EPQ-R Lying-scale scores through questionnaire answers endorsing unusually socially desirable conduct. Ten shuffled-question runs per model produce default Lying-scale means ranging from 9.6 to 18.0, all above the human means of 7.1 for males and 6.9 for females. GPT-4 scores 18.0±4.4. The authors interpret endorsements of idealized conduct as socially desirable responding; the comparison does not independently establish why models give these answers.
Specific finding: Default assistant language models can endorse ethnic-cultural determinism less strongly than a selected human reference sample on the Implicit Culture Belief questionnaire. Table 4 reports ICB means of 3.6, 3.0, 2.1, 2.6, and 1.9 for Llama-2-7B, Llama-2-13B, text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo, and GPT-4, respectively, versus 3.7±0.8 for the human reference. Each model receives ten shuffled-question runs. The source inconsistently describes the reference population as 309 students in Section 3.2 and 254 in Table 2. No behavioral ethnic-fairness test is performed.

Specific finding: Independently prompted GPT-3 DaVinci Human Values Scale responses can yield higher mean scores on all ten values than the listed global human reference, with weak inter-value correlations. Table 4 gives aggregate model means of 4.51–5.95, exceeding every corresponding global human reference mean, with smaller SDs. Table 5 shows weak aggregate inter-value correlations, and Section 3.3.3 reports low correlations within individual temperatures as well. The claim concerns descriptive differences; no direct inferential comparison using raw human observations is supplied.

Specific finding: Language-model baseline STICSA response scores can differ from a human reference in either direction. Compared baseline model scores across answer-order permutation runs with scores from individual humans. Reported tests are t(26.01)=9.02 for text-davinci-002, t(25.76)=10.22 for Falcon-40B-Instruct, and t(51.38)=-7.26 for text-bison-1, all p<.001. The supplied text does not describe human recruitment, sample size, or demographic composition. Permutation runs and human participants are different sampling units.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Variation induced by linked biography and instruction prompts provides a meaningful sampling basis for interpreting questionnaire reliability and construct-validity statistics in language models.

Specific finding: Reusing structured biography and instruction variations across independently administered questionnaire items enables estimation of LLM personality-score reliability and cross-instrument associations over a specified prompt population. Applies the protocol to 18 models, administering 419 items across 1,250 linked prompt configurations per model and reporting reliability, cross-inventory convergence, discriminant correlations, and external-criterion correlations. Deterministic administration is specified, but independent reproducibility is not tested.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Variation across answer-order permutations provides a sufficiently comparable analogue of variation across human participants to contextualize language-model value-stability statistics using human-study estimates.

Specific finding: Under independent-item structured persona prompting, instruction-tuned language models can exhibit substantially greater personality-questionnaire reliability and cross-inventory convergence than their same-family, same-size base counterparts. Across six matched base/instruction-tuned pairs and five domains, all 30 convergence comparisons favor instruction-tuned models. Mean IPIP-NEO/BFI correlations rise from 0.05 to 0.87 for PaLM/Flan-PaLM 62B and from 0.03 to 0.28 for Mistral 7B/Instruct. Reliability also improves, although Mistral Instruct remains poor or unacceptable across its reported subscales. Each model is assessed over 1,250 prompt configurations.
Specific finding: Within selected instruction-tuned language-model families, larger models generally show stronger personality-questionnaire reliability and cross-inventory validity, with trait-specific exceptions and no comparable reliability improvement in tested base Llama 2 models. For Flan-PaLM 8B, 62B, and 540B, Table 12 reports average IPIP-NEO/BFI convergence of 0.69, 0.87, and 0.90 and average convergent-minus-discriminant differences of 0.23, 0.41, and 0.51. Openness α increases from 0.75 to 0.84 to 0.95. Llama 2-Chat improves substantially between 7B and larger variants, but reliability and convergence are not uniformly monotonic. Table 2 and Table 12 differ on some non-PaLM entries.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Scoring full answer texts instead of option labels can produce nearly constant MPI responses across distinct personality statements, including cases with exact invariance across tested option orders. On original-order MPI items, GPT2-XL, GPT-Neo-2.7B, OPT-13B, and OPT-30B select Very Accurate on 100% of statements and retain that answer across reported orders. GPT-NeoX-20B selects Very Inaccurate on 99.80% originally and 100% after reversal, demonstrating near-collapse rather than exact invariance. Constant selections do not establish that the full probability vector is insensitive to statement content.
Specific finding: Combining positively and negatively keyed personality items can turn constant answer selection into nonconstant trait scores and substantial within-trait score dispersion. Four main models always choose Very Accurate under original-order non-indexed scoring, yet obtain OCEAN means of 3.38, 3.10, 3.28, 2.92, and 3.62, with standard deviations approximately 1.91–2.00. Their pooled scores split approximately 56% at 5 and 44% at 1 because item keying reverses the assigned score.
Specific finding: Removing the situational statement from an MPI prompt can preserve the answer preference that dominates responses to populated personality items. The authors replace the situational statement with an empty string and apply the same answer-scoring methods. They report that the content-free preferred answer matches each model's dominant populated-prompt answer. Detailed baseline probability vectors and a quantitative itemwise content-sensitivity analysis are not supplied; the table highlighting identifying baseline choices is unavailable in this text rendering.
Specific finding: Content-free rescaling can diversify non-indexed MPI answers while leaving substantial dependence on option order. After rescaling candidate probabilities using content-free probabilities, models select multiple response categories but show differing distributions across orders. OPT-13B changes from 69.57% Moderately Accurate and 7.58% neutral in original order to 23.05% and 57.53%, respectively, after reversal. Tables 6 and 24–27 also show order-dependent trait summaries. Some smaller-model conditions remain highly concentrated after calibration.
Specific finding: Apply Magic Sauce personality predictions trained on human social media provide valid operational measurements of personality expressed in synthetic social media text.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Personality-associated LIWC patterns in human essays provide useful comparative references for assessing personality expression in synthetic personal narratives.
Specific finding: Readers' ratings of a narrative author's Big Five traits provide useful operational measurements of personality perceived in that narrative.

Specific finding: A personality classifier trained on filtered synthetic opinions and GPT-4 ratings against trait adjectives provide valid operational measurements of personality expression in edited-model opinions.
Specific finding: Personality-associated patterns in an LLM's topic-specific opinions provide a meaningful operational proxy for its personality expression.
Specific finding: An activation pattern interpreted as a belief must carry truth-related information, be used by the model to accomplish its task, and permit misrepresentation.

Specific finding: Complementarity and confidence constraints on contrasting statements do not by themselves establish that a recovered activation distinction represents truth rather than another property.

Specific finding: Evaluation restricted to readily labelable factual statements can leave truth-probe interpretations underdetermined by properties such as consensus, verifiability, or socially acceptable assertion.

Specific finding: CCS's confidence objective rewards increasingly extreme complementary predictions, so its loss does not identify a model's graded credences. Formal loss comparison supplied in Section 5.7: complementary outputs 0.6 and 0.4 have zero consistency loss and confidence loss 0.16, whereas 0.99 and 0.01 retain zero consistency loss and reduce confidence loss to 0.0001. This improvement does not depend on the underlying model's uncertainty. The result follows directly from the displayed loss definitions; it is not an empirical experiment.
Specific finding: CCS probes on simple factual-statement negation pairs can achieve low consistency-and-confidence loss while classifying truth only slightly above chance or at chance. Linear probes achieve 53–56% accuracy with CCS losses of 0.002–0.004. Table 5's MLP accuracies are 0.552, 0.568, and 0.502, with losses 0.009, 0.003, and 0.013. Despite classwise mean and standard-deviation normalization, last- and fourth-last-layer MLP average predictions for original versus negated statements are 0.968/0.035 and 0.990/0.012, indicating grammatical-polarity discrimination. The eighth-last-layer probe finds another distinction without higher truth accuracy. Exact sample sizes and complete hyperparameters are unspecified.

Specific finding: Pearson correlation, cosine similarity, simulation-framed AUPRC, F1, and IoU can jointly retain sensitivity to missing and extra concept labels across aggregate unit-explanation evaluations where several commonly used alternatives fail. Table 3 compares 18 metric variants after independently deleting half the positive labels or adding positives to double their expected count. Averaged empirical missing/extra decrease rates are 99.41%/99.92% for Pearson, 99.45%/99.26% for cosine, 95.61%/99.46% for AUPRC, 93.68%/99.82% for F1, and 93.62%/99.81% for IoU. Most empirical tests use one perturbation sample per unit rather than directly evaluating the defined perturbation expectation. Idealized simulations use activation frequencies 0.499, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001. Individual-setting exceptions include 56.77% missing-label decrease for F1/IoU and 84.44% for AUPRC on Places365 outputs. WPMI is hyperparameter-sensitive, and inverse AUPRC passes the aggregate empirical checks but fails the near-balanced idealized extra-label setting.
Specific finding: For a binary unit perfectly matching a concept, deleting half its positive labels or doubling their prevalence leaves some explanation metrics unchanged or produces penalties that vanish with concept prevalence, whereas F1 and IoU retain fixed penalties. Formal derivation: Appendix D constructs population confusion matrices after label deletion or addition and substitutes them into binary metrics. Table D.2 gives missing/extra score changes of −1/3 and −1/3 for F1, −1/2 and −1/2 for IoU, and −gamma/2 and −gamma for accuracy. Recall has zero extra-label penalty, precision has zero missing-label penalty, and balanced accuracy's extra-label penalty is −gamma/[2(1−gamma)]. These results establish metric insensitivity or vanishing penalties under the stated ideal-unit assumptions; they do not establish analogous behavior for arbitrary imperfect explanations.
Specific finding: The harmonic mean of simulation-framed and classification-framed balanced accuracy can pass missing- and extra-label sanity checks that either component fails in some settings. Tables E.6–E.7 report 100% decrease accuracy for both checks at all five simulated activation frequencies for the harmonic mean of balanced accuracy and inverse balanced accuracy. Table E.8 reports missing/extra decrease accuracy of 99.85%/99.92% on ViT-B-16 final outputs and 90.75%/100% on ResNet-50 layer4 channels. Table E.9 reports meta-AUPRC of 0.8885 with ground-truth concepts and 0.7041 with SigLIP concepts in the ImageNet class-plus-superclass setting. Other tested combinations fail some checks or perform poorly in some label-source settings.
Specific finding: Adding a constant offset to unit activations can sharply degrade cosine-based ranking of correct versus incorrect concept explanations even when other tested evaluation metrics retain their rankings. Table E.2 reports cosine meta-AUPRC falling from 0.8985 to 0.0443 after adding one to activations, while every other listed metric is unchanged. The accompanying prose instead reports 99.07% to 0.93%; this numerical discrepancy is unresolved. Appendix A.4 separately derives that Pearson equals cosine after centering both vectors.
Specific finding: Uncorrected sampling that combines extreme activating examples with random examples can substantially weaken Pearson-correlation evaluation's sensitivity to overly broad unit explanations. Across the eight empirical sanity-check settings, Table 3 reports average extra-label decrease accuracy of 60.26% for top-and-random Pearson versus 99.92% for ordinary Pearson. Table F.4 gives corresponding GPT-2 Small rates of 48.00% versus 100% and GPT-2 XL rates of 50.74% versus 100%. Idealized simulations also show increasingly poor extra-label detection for rare concepts under the sampled protocol. The comparison changes both sampling distribution and evaluation sample count.
Specific finding: Random concept-label perturbations and WordNet subclass or superclass substitutions can produce similar qualitative metric-failure patterns in ImageNet output-unit evaluations. Appendix E.3 compares random and semantic perturbations using the described pools of 400 constructed superclass units for missing labels and 1,000 class units for extra labels, within the paper's validation/test-unit protocol. Pearson missing-label decrease accuracy is 100% for both perturbation types; extra-label accuracy is 100% for random and 99.58% for semantic supersets. Recall remains at 0% for both extra-label variants, and precision remains below 44.3% for both missing-label variants. Several rates change substantially even where qualitative failure persists.
Specific finding: Pearson correlation can discriminate designated correct unit–concept pairs from incorrect pairs better on average than the other tested individual metrics in known-concept unit evaluations. Hyperparameters are selected on a random 5% of units and evaluated on the remaining 95%. Meta-AUPRC ranks designated correct pairs against all other evaluated unit–concept pairs, rather than measuring top-1 explanation accuracy. Table 4 reports mean meta-AUPRC 0.8765 and mean rank 1.60 for Pearson, versus 0.8666/2.30 for cosine and 0.8406/3.90 for AUPRC. GPT-2 Small/XL Pearson meta-AUPRC is 0.9918/0.9986. Appendix F.2 enumerates ten settings, although Table 4's caption says eight. Ground-truth and SigLIP pseudo-label sources are compared in selected vision settings; Appendix F.2 specifies ground-truth labels for the CUB probe despite a conflicting Table F.6 column heading.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Geneformer layer-11 SAE features can detect many K562 CRISPRi-associated activation shifts while rarely yielding responses enriched for the perturbed transcription factor's known targets. Using 20 perturbed cells per target and a 100,000-control-position baseline, Wilcoxon testing with BH correction and an absolute effect threshold above 0.5 identifies feature responses for 92/100 targets, with mean 2.54 responding features per target. Only 3/48 transcription factors satisfy the target-specific response criterion. The effect-size definition and a cell-clustered uncertainty analysis are not supplied; correction details for the subsequent target-enrichment tests are also limited.
Specific finding: Pooling K562 and diverse Tabula Sapiens activations for SAE training need not yield high TRRUST-target-specific perturbation-response recovery in Geneformer. Pooled-data dictionaries recover target-specific responses for 0/48, 4/48, 5/48, and 1/48 factors at layers 0, 5, 11, and 17. At layer 11, five factors gain specificity and three lose it relative to the original 3/48 result; 40 have no specific response in either condition. The fraction of features with a TF among their top genes falls from 64.5% to 60.5%, which measures gene-list composition rather than regulatory knowledge. No repeated-seed analysis establishes systematic improvement or stochasticity.
Specific finding: Selected scGPT SAE reconstruction edits can show little preferential effect on annotated gene positions when evaluated with uniform proxy expression values. The experiment on 50 selected scGPT features reports median specificity 0.98, mean 1.02, and 0/50 features above two. Original continuous expression values were not preserved for this intervention experiment. The suggestion that proxy inputs explain the weak specificity is not separately tested.

Specific finding: Situational narratives expressing the same emotion across different topic domains form more similar language-model representations than narratives expressing different emotions. None of 48 tests survives Benjamini–Hochberg correction at q<0.05. Grief gives raw p=0.006 in Llama-8B-Instruct and p=0.004 in Gemma-9B-base, both with q=0.144. These are selected nominal signals rather than corrected confirmations. The paper reports simulated power of approximately 20–40% for most observed cosine gaps, limiting interpretation of non-significance. No topic-held-out probing result independently establishes generalization across domains.

Specific finding: Emotional-versus-neutral labels for situational vignettes designed without explicit emotion vocabulary can be nearly perfectly linearly decoded from early representations in base and instruction-tuned Llama and Gemma checkpoints. Binary probing reports peak AUROC 0.999–1.000 across six checkpoints, with saturation at layers 3–6, corresponding to 9–38% of depth. Table 4 gives 1.000 for every model, while Table 6 and Appendix A give 0.999 for Gemma-9B-Instruct. A Llama-1B-Instruct zero-shot control retains binary AUROC 1.000. The binary validation procedure is less fully specified than the explicitly five-fold categorical probing procedure.
Specific finding: A binary probe trained on clinical emotional and neutral vignettes can classify separately constructed, narratively rich neutral descriptions as neutral. A frozen probe fitted on all 192 Set B examples assigns Set C mean emotional probability 0.040, median 0.005, and 0/24 predictions above 0.5 at layer 10. Set B reference probabilities of 0.999 for emotional and 0.001 for neutral examples are fitted-data diagnostics. Set C averages 104.5 words versus 115.8 for Set B emotional examples. This confirmation is reported for Llama-1B-Instruct, not all six checkpoints.
Specific finding: Emotion probes trained on situational clinical narratives can transfer to keyword-rich emotional text better than keyword-rich-trained probes transfer to clinical narratives. Table 7 reports A-to-B/B-to-A AUROC of 0.809/0.924 for Llama-1B-Instruct, 0.852/0.961 for Llama-1B-base, 0.925/0.950 for Llama-8B-Instruct, 0.927/0.947 for Llama-8B-base, 0.921/0.956 for Gemma-9B-Instruct, and 0.943/0.958 for Gemma-9B-base. Every comparison favors clinical-trained transfer. Table 14 and some figure descriptions provide different transfer values; the quoted values follow Table 7 and Appendix A.
location: Sections 3.2–3.4 and 5.1; Tables 4 and 6; Appendix A

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: GPT-2 small reuses much of its year-span greater-than circuit for selected rephrased temporal statements, price ranges, and increasing number sequences, although some contexts require additional components. Section 5 reports at least 69% probability difference on each of three prompt families. Applying the original circuit-preservation intervention gives reported recoveries of 98.8% for rephrased year spans and 88.9% for price ranges, termed 'loss recovery' in the text. For increasing sequences, recovery is 67.8%; adding MLP 7 and heads a7.h11 and a6.h1 raises it to 90.3%. Path-patching signatures and component projections support related circuit roles. Appendix F inconsistently describes both first-task recoveries as above 90% and contains a differing second-task figure caption; task-family sample sizes and an unambiguous transfer-recovery normalization are not supplied.
Specific finding: GPT-2 small can activate its greater-than circuit in contexts requiring smaller numbers, causing systematic temporal-order errors. Behavioral heatmaps show greater-than continuations for reversed temporal descriptions and BC dates where less-than is appropriate. Path-patching signatures resemble those of the year-span circuit, and impeding its components improves task correctness. Appendix F reports above-90% circuit recovery for both prompt families; this refers to reproducing the model's erroneous behavior, not recovering correct less-than performance. The appendix's statement that these tasks are completed 'successfully' conflicts with its surrounding explanation of the errors.
Specific finding: GPT-2 small does not uniformly recruit its year-span greater-than circuit across mathematical prompts, including some prompts where greater-than continuations would be appropriate. The tested descending sequences elicit distributions roughly symmetric or uniform around the preceding suffix, exact-step sequences fail to elicit the required continuation, and explicit '17YY is smaller than 17' prompts elicit YY itself. Section 5 reports that these tasks rely on a different set of heads and MLPs rather than the identified year-span circuit. Behavioral heatmaps are supplied in Appendix F, but detailed localization results for the alternative circuits are not shown.

Specific finding: Matched number substitutions and Gaussian input corruption can identify different attention-head effects on GPT-2 number-range completions. Compares head effects using mean output KL divergence over 100 reference/counterfactual pairs in GPT-2 Small and XL, alongside zero-ablation effects. Number-substitution patching highlights fewer heads than Gaussian input corruption.
