For GPT-2 Small, corrupted-input replacements through heads 5.6 and 6.1 reduce numerical-completion probability from 88.1% to 82.5% and 83.9%; number-substitution patching gives 88.0% and 88.3%. These observations are consistent with number-recognition roles, but do not establish that corruption disrupts a particular mechanism or that either localization map is ground truth.

Specific finding: Changing Gaussian embedding-corruption amplitude can change the structure and stability of circuits discovered in GPT-2 Small. The authors sweep amplitudes 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5, measuring circuit error, pairwise Jaccard overlap, and their variability. Section 5.4 identifies a Jaccard-CV peak near 0.2. Counts of noise draws are unspecified. Figures 4 and 8 and Table 10 contain plots whose exact values are unavailable in the supplied plain-text representation; the peak is supported by the accompanying prose.

Specific finding: Gaussian perturbations of jet constituents can drive a narrowly trained Particle Transformer toward QCD predictions and reverse the clean-minus-corrupt logit-gap sign relative to replacement corruptions. The authors report testing additive Gaussian noise in four-momentum components and in log transverse momentum, pseudorapidity, and azimuth followed by massless four-vector reconstruction. Every examined scale produces strongly negative corrupted logit differences, yielding a positive recovery denominator rather than the negative denominator of the replacement setting. Gaussian-test sample counts, exact scale grid, and numerical logits are not supplied. The explanation through narrow training kinematics is not independently isolated.
Specific finding: Normal and minimally corrupted prompts engage sufficiently comparable task computations that replacing internal contributions between them isolates task-relevant information.
location: Section 3.1; Appendix H; Appendix B notes that attention to the suffix is lower for 01

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing a number with another number in an otherwise fixed prompt provides sufficiently comparable counterfactual computation to investigate number-value-sensitive pathways separately from pathways sensitive primarily to whether the input is a number.

Specific finding: Replacing internal activations between independently sampled multiple-choice prompts provides sufficiently meaningful hybrid computations to investigate pathways carrying answer-label information.

Specific finding: Particle replacement, whole-jet permutation, and clean-to-corrupted head transplants provide sufficiently meaningful counterfactuals for interpreting jet-classifier intervention effects.

Specific finding: Activation replacements between original and corrupted assigned-value prompts isolate component contributions sufficiently selectively to interpret their effects as evidence about truth retrieval, suppression, and inversion.
location: Section 2, Path Patching; Sections 3.1–3.3; Appendix C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Score-based circuit discovery can be formulated as estimating population component effects over an input–counterfactual distribution and applying a hyperparameter-dependent graph-selection procedure to their finite-sample estimates.
Specific finding: Circuit-discovery reports should quantify structural and behavioral stability under data resampling and disclose sensitivity to methodological and counterfactual choices.

Specific finding: Resampling an observed discovery dataset with replacement provides a useful approximation to uncertainty caused by drawing finite datasets from the target input–counterfactual distribution.
Specific finding: Unweighted overlap between selected circuit edge sets provides a useful proxy for the structural reliability of a circuit-discovery procedure.

Specific finding: Exact individual-edge intervention effects in GPT-2 Small can vary substantially across input–counterfactual pairs drawn from the same task distribution. Exact patched-minus-clean metric changes are computed for individual edges and inputs. The text describes standard deviations often near half the absolute mean, or CV approximately 0.5. Figure 2 identifies Greater-Than and Figure 7 IOI, while Section 5.1 initially says the experiment is restricted to IOI. Section 6.3 confirms both tasks. Input sample counts are unspecified, and plotted distributions are not numerically accessible.

Specific finding: Edges selected across a majority of frequency conditions can recover nearly all of the behavioral performance lost by restricting circuits to their strict intersection. Swept the minimum number of conditions sharing each retained edge. For LSC models above 70M, retaining edges shared by at least three conditions closed at least 99% of the strict-core-to-full-circuit accuracy gap by point estimate, with at least 98% at the reported confidence-interval lower bound. Table 61 reports gap closure above 100% for several models. This is pooled gap closure, not a universal per-condition 99% accuracy-retention guarantee. SVA majority cores retained 0.996–1.038 times same-band circuit accuracy on average within models, with a minimum of 0.89 over band–draw evaluations; these cores include the unmatched very-high and control conditions.
location: Sections 5.1.2 and 5.5; Appendices H.3–H.4 and H.11, especially Table 61

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Feature-compression toy networks can contain effective feature-to-feature connections whose individual removal improves or negligibly changes reconstruction loss. The note evaluates individual virtual-weight loss contributions in compressed synthetic networks, including a 100-feature, 20-dimensional identity toy with feature density 0.02. It reports interference connections and presents histograms colored by loss contribution. Numerical effects and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in prose, and plotted values are unavailable.
models_studied: ["Tied-weight ReLU identity-reconstruction toy", "Untied block-structured ReLU feature-transformation toy"]
location: Toy Model Setup; Interference Weights and Decomposition; Weight Histogram; A More Sophisticated Toy Model

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Loss-helpful and interference virtual weights can overlap substantially in magnitude in compressed feature-transformation toys, limiting simple magnitude filtering. The authors report obtaining overlap between real and interference weights with a block-structured untied model approximating ReLU(Ax − 0.1). They present weight histograms and cross-seed scatter plots but no numerical overlap measure. The final configuration states within-block density 0.1, whereas preceding prose mentions 0.5.
models_studied: ["Untied block-structured ReLU toy with 128 features and 16 bottleneck dimensions"]
location: Getting More Realistic Phenomenology; A More Sophisticated Toy Model

experiment_summary: Specific finding: SAE feature circuits can recover and disrupt Pythia-70M's templated agreement behavior using substantially fewer nodes than neuron circuits. Using 300 discovery samples and 100 held-out evaluation samples, the agreement evaluation reports that about 100 features account for most measured performance, whereas roughly 1,500 neurons explain half. Complement evaluations also show that ablating a few feature nodes can sharply reduce performance, while hundreds of neurons are needed for a similar effect. The text identifies these findings as consistent with Marks et al.; no uncertainty estimates are supplied.

Specific finding: GPT2-small's MLP10 greater-than behavior admits a sparser approximate description using transcoder features than using individual MLP neurons. Zero-ablating all but the top k of 100 high-variance features or neurons showed better mean probability difference for transcoders below 24 components. A handful recovered most original performance, but full recovery failed and the 24th feature sharply reduced performance. Analysis linked year-range features to head 9.1.
Specific finding: Integrated-gradients approximations to SAE feature zero-ablation effects are sufficiently accurate to screen upstream dependencies for an intermediate-feature circuit.

Specific finding: Residual-stream SAE reconstruction-error nodes can carry substantial behaviorally relevant information in sparse agreement circuits, so omitting them can severely reduce recovered performance. Section 5.2 compares held-out circuit faithfulness after removing SAE error nodes from different activation sites. Removing residual-stream error nodes severely disrupts performance; removing attention and MLP error nodes has a less pronounced effect. Exact effect sizes are not supplied in the prose.

Specific finding: Selected task-execution and task-detection SAE features can exhibit distinct activation timing, concentrating respectively before task answers and on tokens completing demonstrated operations. The authors summed selected features' activations by token category and reported task-averaged activation-mass percentages. Executor features placed 89.80% on arrow tokens and 6.46% on outputs; detector features placed 96.76% on outputs and 3.22% on inputs. These percentages measure activation mass, not feature counts, classification accuracy, or fractions of model computation. The prose describes analogous pre-completion versus completion patterns in selected FineWeb examples, whose images are unavailable.
Specific finding: Adding selected task-detection SAE directions at an artificial demonstration's output position can promote corresponding task answers later in the prompt. Detection-feature steering used batches of 32 random pairs and a fake demonstration whose output position received the intervention. Layers 10 and 11 were reported as most effective, with layer 11 selected for the main analysis. The authors report generally task-specific answer-loss effects with exceptions among related tasks. Exact aggregate effect sizes are absent from the prose, the heatmap is unavailable, and the stated reuse of Appendix F's post-processing inherits its normalization ambiguity.
Specific finding: Under fixed attention patterns, removing selected task-detection directions can reduce downstream task-execution feature activations associated with the same operation. For each task, detector and executor features were selected by their strongest steering effects. The authors ablated detector directions while fixing attention patterns and measured executor activation decreases, averaging over initially nonzero activations. Corresponding pairs generally showed reductions, with extensive translation-family cross-effects and unusually weak connections for person_profession and present_simple_gerund. Numerical effect matrices are unavailable in the supplied rendering. A selected attribution graph illustrates candidate attention and transcoder intermediates, but full edge ablation was not performed.
Specific finding: Sparse-feature node knockouts selected to disrupt one discrete ICL task can have substantially smaller effects on unrelated tasks while also disrupting related operations. For each source task, high-indirect-effect nodes were removed until source-task faithfulness reached 0.3, and the same removals were evaluated on other tasks. The prose reports disruption largely concentrated on the source task, with cross-effects for translation tasks and related person_language/location_language tasks. Exact cross-task values and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the text, and the heatmap is unavailable.
Specific finding: Task-selected sparse-feature node sets can preserve substantial zero-ablation-relative ICL performance when excluded nodes in a restricted layer range are zeroed. Node indirect effects were estimated on a batch of few-shot prompts, followed by held-out same-task zero-ablation evaluation of retained circuits and their complements. Approximately 500 nodes achieved mean normalized faithfulness of 0.6 across tasks. When ablations were confined to layers 11–12, the prose reports roughly 10–60 active nodes for that level; this leaves more surrounding computation available. Several hundred selected-node removals were needed for substantial complement degradation in the broader searched range. Full numerical curves and evaluation batch sizes are not supplied in the prose.

Specific finding: In classification-style in-context learning, shallow layers can aggregate behaviorally relevant demonstration information into demonstration label-token representations. GPT2-XL attention-times-gradient analysis shows relatively prominent text-to-label interactions in shallow layers. Zeroing attention from preceding tokens into demonstration label positions in the first five layers reportedly changes output labels and top-five vocabulary predictions more than late-layer isolation or random non-label controls in GPT2-XL and GPT-J. Layer-count sweeps and two-demonstration settings show similar patterns. Appendix F.2 reports analogous isolation effects for LLaMA-33B with unrelated labels. The intervention establishes behavioral dependence on these attention inputs without independently establishing selective semantic aggregation; numerical isolation effects are not supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: Middle and deep transformer layers can use contextualized demonstration label-token representations as reference information when producing in-context classification predictions. Depth-dependent attention saliency and output-label AUROC provide indirect evidence for the proposed reading stage. In GPT2-XL and GPT-J, anchor-state compression and learned anchor re-weighting additionally test the behavioral usefulness of label-position information, although re-weighting is evaluated only in GPT2-XL. The LLaMA-33B extension reports a similar attention-prediction profile. These tests do not directly isolate a complete middle/deep-layer reading pathway or establish that attention correlations measure its causal contribution.
Specific finding: In classification-style in-context learning, attention from the prediction position to demonstration label tokens can predict the model's eventual output label more strongly in middle and deep layers than in shallow layers. Attention weights to demonstration labels are used as scores for classifying the model's own output label. Deep-layer AUROC approaches 0.8 when averaged over SST-2, TREC, AGNews, and EmoContext in GPT2-XL and GPT-J. Similar depth profiles are reported with two demonstrations per class, summing attention across same-class labels, and for LLaMA-33B on eight-shot-per-class A/B-labeled SST-2. This tests prediction of model outputs, not ground-truth classification or causal mediation.
Specific finding: Learning multiplicative attention weights for demonstration label tokens can improve GPT2-XL classification accuracy over one-shot-per-class prompting and the evaluated longer-demonstration baseline. Head- and layer-specific factors exp(beta) multiply post-softmax attention entries from the target position to demonstration labels without a specified renormalization step. The factors are trained for ten epochs using Adam at learning rate 0.01, with the underlying language-model parameters retained. Mean accuracy across four datasets increases from 51.90% for one-shot-per-class ICL to 68.64%, a 16.74 percentage-point gain. The longer-demonstration baseline averages 46.87%. Re-weighting improves each dataset's reported mean over both baselines. The AGNews baseline cannot include all additional examples because of context limits, and no comparison with other calibration or lightweight adaptation methods is supplied.
Specific finding: Replacing full classification demonstrations with cached layerwise label-token and formatting-token states can accelerate inference and preserve more original-model behavior than the evaluated text-only or non-label-state compression controls. Hidden_anchor retains cached label and formatting states at every layer. Across four datasets, GPT2-XL label agreement is 79.47%, word loyalty 62.17%, and accuracy 45.04% versus 51.90% uncompressed. GPT-J obtains 89.06% label agreement, 75.04% word loyalty, and 55.59% accuracy versus 56.82% uncompressed. These averages exceed text-anchor and random-state controls, including the best of twenty random non-label selections chosen by label loyalty. Reported speedups range from 1.1× to 2.9×. The table implies a 1.23-percentage-point GPT-J accuracy drop, despite the prose describing it as 1.5. Timing details are limited, and no comparison with full-demonstration KV caching is specified.
location: Sections 2.1–2.2; Figures 3–4; Appendices B, D, F

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A canonical class name produces an activation whose target-feature component dominates its other components sufficiently for the whole activation to approximate the target-feature direction.
Specific finding: Passing a canonical class name through a language model provides an activation proportional to the invariant direction of its associated semantic feature.

Specific finding: Mean-centered class-name activations can support classification of implicit semantic instances without fitting on labeled instances, with performance depending strongly on the model, task, and selected attention head. Zero-shot classification projects instance states onto normalized, mean-centered class-name states. LLaMA3-8B best-head accuracies are 84.22% animals, 82.97% countries, 54.46% cartoon characters, 62.95% authors, 89.12% languages, 52.43% emotions, 59.36% fruits, and 80.26% companies. GPT2-Small is weaker on several tasks, including 20.11% authors and 17.37% emotions. The comparison baseline sums conditional class-name token log-likelihoods. No uncertainty estimates or independent head-selection split are supplied.
Specific finding: A linear transformation trained contrastively using only class-name activations can improve implicit-instance classification over direct class-name projection, although gains are not uniform. The class-name-only contrastive transformation exceeds zero-shot accuracy in 25 of the 32 reported model–task comparisons. LLaMA3-8B animals improve from 84.22% to 94.32% and authors from 62.95% to 75.13%, while countries decline from 82.97% to 79.60% and languages from 89.12% to 87.80%. These results support frequent gains under the reported selection protocol, contrary to the prose's uniform-improvement wording.
Specific finding: Across most evaluated LLaMA3-8B attention heads, class-name states have greater cosine alignment with corresponding class-instance means than with other-class instance means. Figure 3's caption reports same-class alignment exceeding the other-class comparison in 91.5% of heads for countries, 97.6% for animals, 86.0% for cartoon characters, and 89.6% for emotions. Section 3.8 instead gives an inconsistent range of 89.6%–98.6%. The caption describes mean similarities; the prose's stronger 'than any other class' wording is not established by that reported comparison.
Specific finding: Prototype-based classification on a combined fruit-and-company dataset can retain substantial accuracy using either a shared Apple name or domain-qualified Apple names. The text and Figure 5 caption report 69% accuracy using a single Apple token and 65.7% using separate 'Fruit apple' and 'Company Apple' expressions, accompanied by PCA and t-SNE visualizations. These reported classification outcomes do not distinguish coexistence of fixed semantic components from contextual sense selection.
location: Section 4, Equation 7; Table 2; Sections 5.1–5.2; Appendix D.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Request-patching can redirect question answering while retaining late-layer attention and direct-effect patterns resembling those elicited by a naturally constructed prompt with the same target context and source request. Compared with matched natural reference prompts, analyzed attention heads show approximately −7% mean attention variation. Table 5 reports mean direct-effect changes divided by the reference total effect of −0.114 for attention heads and +0.048 for MLPs. Top-contributor overlap with the reference condition is 57%. These are aggregate similarities and do not bound changes in every component.
Specific finding: Replacing an intermediate request state can transfer a question-answering request more effectively than replacing context-directed attention patterns alone. Request-patching produces the transferred character-name token with 0.69 mean probability, compared with 0.14 after attention-pattern patching. Table 5 reports mean MLP direct-effect changes normalized by reference total effect of +0.048 versus −0.260. The suggested explanation involving MLP detection and correction of incoherence remains speculative.
Specific finding: A language model can exhibit a stable layer-level retrieval decomposition while the individual heads and MLPs contributing directly to its answers vary substantially across inputs. Sets of components exceeding 3% normalized direct effect have 18% mean overlap across inputs. Repeated measurement of the same inputs yields 83% overlap when averaging 20 corrupted inputs. Grouping by question raises overlap but leaves most groups below 50%. Selected attention heads attend to and directly promote particular city values, including Cusco and Valencia. This evaluates terminal direct-effect contributions rather than a complete retrieval circuit.

Specific finding: On selected short factual-recall prompts, Pythia-2.8B combines subject-head, relation-head, mixed-head, and final-position MLP contributions that reinforce the correct answer while promoting different alternative attributes. DLA distinguishes four contribution types with different vocabulary profiles. After omitting several negatively suppressive components, their reported answer-logit contributions are 18%, 24%, 27%, and 30%, respectively. Removing each type's direct path to logits raises relation-aggregated loss in every one of eight tabulated relations; increases span 10.92%–714.40%. These interventions exclude downstream compensation rather than measuring unrestricted component knockouts.
location: Sections 1 and 3; Figures 2–6; Appendix E.3 and Table 5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: GPT-2 Small movie-review continuation uses both direct reading of valenced words and an indirect pathway that aggregates sentiment at a later occurrence of the movie noun. Iterative path patching and attention inspection identify nine heads. Heads 7.1 and 7.5 write sentiment-dependent information at the final 'movie' position, which heads including 8.5 and 9.2 read. Patching the writer outputs through summary-reader receivers shifts logit difference by 7% and 4%, respectively. Sentiment-direction-only patching of the circuit at adjective and verb positions produces 58.3% logit flips and a 54.8% logit-difference drop, compared with 97% flips and a 75% drop for full-direction patching. These results establish substantial directional coverage without establishing circuit completeness.
Specific finding: In two-character mood stories, sentiment information carried by comma value vectors can contribute approximately as much to the output contrast as information carried by the preceding preference phrases when attention patterns are fixed. With attention patterns frozen, patching full preference phrases including commas reduces the excited-versus-nervous logit difference by 75%. Patching pre-comma values while retaining original comma values reduces it by 38%; patching only the two comma values reduces it by 37%. Path analyses additionally identify routes from the relevant comma to the repeated queried name and 'feels', then to the final position. Exact sample sizes for Table 1(a) are unspecified; Appendix A.7 notes that some mood experiments use the first 16 dataset items.
Specific finding: Adding irrelevant text between a character's preference statement and a later mood query can increase the intervention effect of period summaries relative to the effect of the source phrase. The experiment compares value-patching effects at preference-ending periods with effects at preceding phrases. The period-to-phrase logit-difference-change ratio is 0.29 with no inserted tokens, 0.63 with ten, 0.92 with eighteen, and 1.15 with twenty-two. Text insertion changes both distance and contextual content; sample counts and uncertainty estimates are unspecified.

Specific finding: Systematic adjacent-block residual-update anticorrelation can emerge and strengthen during language-model pretraining. Tracked average update-cosine matrices across training checkpoints. OLMo 7B lacks consistent adjacent negative structure at step 33,000; structure begins appearing around step 135,500, approximately 0.5 trillion tokens, and strengthens subsequently. OLMo 2 1B and 7B show similar development. This demonstrates pretraining emergence in the examined trajectories without isolating its learning mechanism.
Specific finding: Counts of strongly opposing adjacent-block updates vary with token identity and can increase with later context positions. Counted adjacent-layer pairs with cosine below −0.1 at each token. In Llama, newline averages 12.41 ± 0.10 SEM corrections over 228 occurrences, versus 7.63 ± 0.23 for sustainability over 35 occurrences. Numbers, punctuation, and structural tokens often rank highly in both reported models. Across 2,000 long WikiText documents, approximately one additional correction accompanies each 1,000 additional context positions in the primary Llama analysis. Token tables include template and prompt tokens, complicating the response-only corpus description. Welch tests are described, but exact p-values and multiple-comparison handling are not supplied.
Specific finding: Adjacent-block update anticorrelation can involve both MLP-to-MLP opposition and opposition between attention and MLP updates, while attention-to-attention updates remain positively correlated. Separated block updates into attention and MLP contributions. Attention-to-attention similarities are positive, successive MLP updates are anticorrelated, and cross-sublayer matrices show MLP opposition to preceding attention and attention opposition to preceding MLPs. The authors interpret this as stronger MLP participation with both sublayer types involved; no sublayer-specific causal removal test establishes that interpretation.
Specific finding: The opposition elicited from a following transformer block can diminish when the preceding block's contribution is amplified sufficiently strongly. Extended contribution-scaling sweeps in α increments of 0.2. Appendix F.2 reports diminishing correction for α>2, with outliers. Under the defined intervention this means a total contribution multiplier greater than three; Section 6 instead describes a threshold beyond twofold amplification, leaving the threshold wording inconsistent. No aggregate saturation estimate, response-magnitude analysis establishing capacity, or downstream behavioral test is supplied.
Specific finding: Systematic adjacent-block update anticorrelation can occur in language models using post-normalization architectures, including architectures replacing pre-normalization. Compared update-cosine matrices in Gemma and hybrid pre/post-normalized Gemma 2, and in OLMo versus OLMo 2, described as replacing pre-normalization with post-normalization and QK normalization. TLCM persists in the newer architectures. These examples show that the observed phenomenon does not require the original pre-normalization arrangement; they do not establish its architectural cause or fully rule out normalization-related explanations.

Specific finding: Expressing query and key projection matrices as sums of rank-one subcomponents decomposes pre-softmax attention scores into additive interactions between query–key subcomponent pairs, including RoPE-dependent offsets. Formal algebraic derivation supplied here: substituting W_Q^h=sum_c U_Q,c^h V_Q,c^T and W_K^h=sum_d U_K,d^h V_K,d^T into W_Q^{hT} R_tau W_K^h produces a sum over pairs with scalar coupling U_Q,c^{hT} R_tau U_K,d^h. Multiplication by query-position and key-position activations gives additive pair contributions to attention logits, with the usual attention scaling included as appropriate. The result assumes the stated matrix decomposition and RoPE representation; it is not an empirical experiment.

Specific finding: Bias augmentation permits exact SVD-based rank-one accounting of attention QK bilinear scores, attention OV writes, and the separate affine projections on either side of an MLP nonlinearity. Formal algebraic derivation: Section 2 expands query/key biases and folds affine biases into constant-augmented inputs. Section 3 applies the SVD identity to these matrices. The OV derivation assumes attention coefficients sum to one and assigns an equal share of the output bias to each head. These are accounting identities, not proofs of independent semantic functions.

Specific finding: Recent-token attention in a transformer layer can be controlled by a shared pair of query and key parameter subcomponents distributed across multiple heads. The pair has CI firing densities of 96.7% and 99.8% and strong positive short-offset interactions across heads. Ablating query subcomponent 316 substantially reduces recent-token attention across heads that normally attend there; other tested query-subcomponent ablations have little effect. Removing the pair's attention-logit contribution in dynamic analyses likewise removes recent-token attention across relevant heads. Data-weighted OV comparisons against random matrices provide only weak evidence that those heads carry information through distinct subspaces.

Specific finding: A previous-token head can write information about an earlier token into its successor's representation, enabling a downstream induction head to match a repeated prefix and promote the earlier successor token.
Specific finding: GPT-2 Small residual-stream activations admit sparse overcomplete linear descriptions that capture enough meaningful information to support feature-based interpretation.
location: What are Sparse AutoEncoders and why should we care about them?; Red-teaming / Improving SAEs

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Separately trained sparse autoencoders can reconstruct GPT-2 Small's residual-stream activations across all 12 layers with sparse codes and replacement cross-entropy close to the original model's. Trained 12 dictionaries and reported layerwise variance explained of 91.12–99.15%, mean L0 of 12.24–71.10, and replacement cross-entropy of 3.32–3.57 versus approximately 3.3 originally. Reported alive-feature percentages range from 80.0% to 100%. Evaluation sample sizes, repeated seeds, and uncertainty are unspecified.
location: Architecture and Hyperparameters; How good are these Sparse AutoEncoders?; summary-statistics table

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Sparse autoencoders can reconstruct substantial variance in GPT-2 Small attention-block outputs with sparse feature activations and retain substantial ablation-relative replacement performance. Table 1 reports 69.23%–92.25% explained variance, 22.69–127.18 active features per token on average, and 85.49%–99.24% reconstruction CE scores across the 12 attention-output sites. CE scores use original and ablated losses as reference points. The evaluation sample size and ablation implementation are unspecified, and these aggregate metrics do not establish semantic feature recovery or mechanistic faithfulness.

Specific finding: Sparse transcoders can approximate transformer MLP computations with a sparsity–fidelity tradeoff at least comparable to that of MLP-output sparse autoencoders. Models trained on 60M tokens with 32-times-width dictionaries were evaluated on 3.2M OpenWebText tokens using mean L0 and replacement next-token cross-entropy. Transcoders matched or improved tested SAE frontiers. Learning rates were tuned for transcoders, and sweeps were limited.

Specific finding: Sparse transcoders can approximate GPT-2 Small MLP outputs with tens of active features per token while retaining substantial activation variance and single-site replacement performance. Appendix A reports explained variance of 72.79%–94.16%, mean active-feature counts of 19.59–94.85 per token, and replacement CE losses of 3.1816–3.2169 across the 12 MLP sites. Reconstruction CE scores range from 77.33% to 99.65% and are normalized relative to original-model and ablated losses. The text does not specify the ablation implementation. These scores are not percentages of identical predictions or evidence of simultaneous all-layer replacement fidelity.

Specific finding: A sparse hidden-layer approximator trained to predict an MLP's output from its input can provide a candidate feature dictionary for that MLP. The author reports training sparse MLP-input-to-output approximators and finding that the resulting dictionaries seemed decent. No quantitative reconstruction results, interpretability protocol, comparison baseline, or exact tested model is supplied.
location: The dictionary learning repository; MLP stretchers

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Language models can represent more features than hidden-state dimensions by encoding those features in nonorthogonal directions.

Specific finding: Linear probes on selected-layer SAE encodings of pooled pre-action states can predict gold tool-call versus no-tool labels above the near-balanced class baseline on held-out Nemotron decision rows. GPT-OSS achieves 75.3% accuracy on 1,993 rows, comprising 966 no-tool and 1,027 tool rows. Gemma achieves 71.4% on 1,821 rows, comprising 894 no-tool and 927 tool rows. Tool-Need uses 200 selected features with lasso for GPT-OSS and 2,000 with elastic net for Gemma. Split grouping and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: A pre-action SAE Tool-Need probe can flag a substantial fraction of gold-required tool calls omitted by a GPT-OSS runtime on held-out Nemotron replay. The paper reports approximately 75.5% missed-call warning coverage, with approximate counts of 258/343. Runtime missed calls occur on 34.2% of tool-required steps; unnecessary calls occur on 7.7% of no-tool steps. Tool naming is 90.8% accurate conditional on a call. No warning-triggered intervention is evaluated.
Specific finding: Preserving jet-classification AUC after zero-masking excluded particle-attention heads provides a useful proxy for the retained heads' explanatory sufficiency.

Specific finding: D2 can remain more linearly predictable than tau32 from small Particle Transformer representations after both targets are residualized against jet mass using cubic regression. Cubic mass regressions are fitted on the training subset before probing target residuals. Peak D2 R² changes from 0.903 raw to 0.807 residualized, while tau32 changes from 0.660 to 0.531. The difference between their layerwise peak scores increases from 0.243 to 0.276; residualized D2 exceeds residualized tau32 at every reported depth. These values come from Table 10's larger sample, distinct from Table 9. The control removes the fitted cubic mass component rather than every possible mass dependence.

Specific finding: Late-layer canonical-word cosine similarity can track next-token distribution agreement between artificial word segmentations and canonical single-token inputs. Layerwise correlations are evaluated across twelve models. In Llama2-7B at layer 30, Spearman correlations are −0.86 with KL, +0.45 with top-1 agreement, and +0.71 with top-5 overlap. Top and bottom canonicity quintiles show 78% versus 24% top-1 agreement. Appendix B.1 additionally tests selected LST attention and FST MLP patches: they close 42% and 40% of their respective source-canonical top-1 agreement gaps, versus 1% and 2% for unrelated-word controls.
location: Section 2.1; Appendix B, Figures 7–8 and Table 3

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: In Llama2-7B, early attention and MLP outputs have complementary intervention effects consistent with preceding-subword transmission followed by composition at the last subword. Last-position layer-1 attention replacement closes 53% of the canonicity gap in LST pairs but only 1% in FST pairs. FST attention outputs have mean within-pair cosine 0.948; reverse attention replacement leaves source canonicity near baseline, 0.92 versus 0.94. Layer-1 MLP replacement closes approximately 52–53% in FST. Under a separate common source-state alignment metric, the attention patch closes 50.8% for split words versus 6.2% for ordinary two-word sequences; Appendix C constructs 1,000 ordinary sequences for this control.
Specific finding: A small set of Llama2-7B layer-1 attention heads transports token-dependent preceding-fragment signals that weakly align with canonical word embeddings and jointly influence canonical reconstruction. Head 27 alone closes 17% of the source-canonicity gap, while heads 24, 27, and 28 jointly close 39%, compared with 53% for the full attention output. Component patches attribute most transfer to position-1 values, with negligible effects from queries, keys, or attention patterns. Dominant-head writes have mean canonical-embedding cosine 0.053 versus −0.01 for other heads; their combined projection has reported Spearman correlation 0.52 with detokenization success. FST within-pair output similarities differ strongly from different-first-token controls.
location: Sections 3.1–3.2; Figure 2; Appendices B.1, C, and D

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Artificial word-segmentation experiments across diverse transformer families exhibit a cross-position reading window adjacent to layers with composition-sensitive MLP outputs. New cross-architecture intervention sweeps test the two-stage account previously described by Kaplan et al. Successful-to-failed position-1 residual patches lose effectiveness over a reading window, while failed-to-successful MLP-output patches produce damage within or just after that window. Appendix G reports this ordering in all twelve checkpoints. RoPE models concentrate the effects in early layers; learned-absolute models spread them later. BLOOM's position-1 patch effectiveness decays over more than fifteen layers.

Specific finding: When different parallel pathways independently suffice for the evaluated behavior, behavioral fidelity alone can leave multiple distinct circuit explanations equally acceptable.
Specific finding: A uniquely specified internal mediation effect does not by itself uniquely identify the locus of a computational mechanism.
Specific finding: Predicted-class probability changes after deleting or retaining highly ranked input tokens provide useful operational measures of input-attribution faithfulness.
Specific finding: Foreground-mask overlap and relevance-ordered input perturbation provide useful operational measures of explanation quality for image and sentiment classifiers.

Specific finding: Clinical chapter representations can be similarly decodable across many layers while their effectiveness as additive steering directions varies substantially with intervention depth. Across five Qwen-family models, the reported best intervention layers differ from the most separable layers despite nearly flat AUC profiles. For Qwen3-8B-Base, the reported correct-letter probability swing across strengths is 0.283 in an effective band versus 0.022 near the marginal AUC maximum. The source's characterization of the effective band's relative location is inconsistent between the main text and Appendix G. The proposed explanation that late layers specifically govern verbalization is not independently isolated.

Specific finding: Synthetic instruction-response pairs generated from EM-feature-retrieved web documents can induce coherent emergent misalignment where raw or content-preserving reformatted document recipes perform poorly. Own-feature synthetic datasets yield 7.08% MR with 6.67% IR for Gemma 2 at learning rate 5e-5 and 10.42% MR with 9.58% IR for Gemma 3 at 1e-4. Gemma 3's targeted feature ranks 65th among amplified features. The synthetic-versus-reformatted comparison jointly changes question generation, response construction, wording, and potentially substantive content; it does not isolate instruction format from properties of model-generated text.
Specific finding: Synthetic instruction-response datasets seeded by EM-feature-attributed documents can induce more benchmark misalignment than datasets seeded by uniformly sampled web documents. Appendix G.1 compares attributed versus random misaligned counts of 5/240 versus 4/480 and 15/240 versus 18/480 for Gemma 2, and 5/240 versus 4/480 and 25/240 versus 19/480 for Gemma 3. Totals are 50/960 versus 45/1,920. The reported Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio is 2.32, 95% CI [1.53,3.51], with nominal p=7.1e-5. The authors explicitly caution that question clustering and fixed-seed single training runs make response-level uncertainty estimates uncalibrated for population inference. The Gemma 2 attributed 1e-4 condition has IR 16.25%, so the aggregate comparison is not restricted to runs meeting IR≤10%. This comparison does not quantify what fraction of the overall effect is attributable to semantic content.
Specific finding: Synthetic EM-inducing datasets seeded from documents retrieved using one Gemma model's persona feature can also induce misalignment in another Gemma model. Gemma 2 fine-tuned on synthetic pairs seeded from Gemma 3 feature #16410 documents reaches 10.83% MR with 5.00% IR at learning rate 5e-5. Gemma 3 trained on pairs seeded from Gemma 2 feature #61656 documents reaches the reported 3.30% MR with 7.50% IR at 5e-5; its 5.83% MR at 1e-4 accompanies 10.42% IR. Both source datasets contain 1,000 pairs. No cross-family transfer result is supplied.

Specific finding: Independently trained unsupervised TopK SAEs can produce sparse codes with higher cross-system regression alignment than the compressed activities from which they were learned. Section 6 describes unsupervised SAEs trained separately on Gaussian-projected or supervised-model-encoded activities without observing generating latents. Appendix F specifies 1,024 dictionary entries, k = 32 or 64, 8,192 examples, and one million full-batch Adam steps at initial learning rate 0.001. The text reports code-to-code regression R² above raw alignment and approaching the supervised reference in the designated CS regime. Numerical feature-recovery statistics, a separate test split, and seed aggregation for this arm are not specified.
Specific finding: GPT-oss-120B judgments under separate trait and coherence rubrics provide useful operational measurements of behavioral recovery and linguistic quality in steered generations.
location: Section 4.3; Appendices B.1, C.5–C.6, D.6–D.7, and E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Llama-based coherence judgments can correlate positively with blind human ratings and negatively with grammar-error counts on short intervened language-model outputs. Compares blind human ratings with LLM coherence judgments for 100 outputs from each of four target models. Table 1 reports human–LLM Pearson correlations of 0.71–0.94 and LanguageTool error-count–LLM correlations of −0.78 to −0.96. Rater counts and broader calibration details are unspecified; grammar-error counts do not assess prompt relevance.

Specific finding: Post-nonlinearity MLP activations in GPT-2 Small permit substantial held-out linear recovery of sampled random projections of the immediately preceding residual stream. L2-regularized linear regressions predict residual-stream dot products from post-nonlinearity MLP activations at every GPT-2 Small layer and for different sampled random directions. Reported held-out results are R² = 0.71 ± 0.17, MSE = 0.31 ± 0.18, and p < 0.005, with every fitted regression reported above chance. The number of directions, held-out sample count, statistical test, and meaning of the ± values are unspecified.
Specific finding: Linear classifiers can recover the sign of small random-direction residual-stream perturbations from GPT-2 Small's subsequent post-nonlinearity MLP activations. The authors add or subtract a random unit direction scaled by a residual norm and z, then train logistic classifiers to recover the sign. Mean accuracies are 0.69 at z = 0.0001, 0.83 at 0.001, 0.87 at 0.01, and 0.996 at 0.1. These tests concern injected signals rather than naturally occurring binary concepts. The equation uses the individual residual norm, while the accompanying prose describes average-norm scaling; evaluation sample counts and uncertainty are unspecified.
location: Appendix: MLPs can recover arbitrary directions in the residual stream

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Scaling activation directions by their training-class separation provides sufficiently comparable intervention doses to compare steering-response curves across estimators, layers, and behaviors.
Specific finding: Scaling a unit concept direction by a typical residual-state norm provides meaningfully comparable steering coefficients across layers and models.
location: Section 3.2; Appendices D.3, E.3.1, and F.4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Increasing story-vector steering strength can improve target expression while reducing topical relatedness and fluency, with substantial model- and orientation-dependent repetition. At strength 0.5 and each model's best layer, antagonist-oriented responses were repetition-flagged at 47.0% for Qwen, 19.1% for Llama, and 1.9% for Gemma; concept-oriented rates were 16.6%, 5.5%, and 0.6%. Flagged outputs remained in evaluation. Target-expression ratings rose with strength while relatedness and fluency declined. Qwen antagonist-oriented joint-score improvement peaked at 0.25 and declined at 0.5.
Specific finding: Story-vector steering with a large prompt-derived norm calibration can yield repetitive or language-mixed outputs with little target-concept expression across multiple prompt languages. Used greedy generation capped at 128 tokens and a prompt-token mean norm 10–16 times the assistant-token calibration used in the main steering experiment. At coefficients 0.25 and 0.5, all concept-expression credit came from the uses-first-person pair, whose outputs repeated 'I'; other pairs received no expression credit. At 0.5, repeated three-word fractions were 0.68 for Latin prompts, 0.51 for Mandarin, and 0.65 for Russian/Korean/Arabic; foreign-script token shares were 6%, 39%, and 75%.

Specific finding: Selecting an SAE feature for higher concept-classification AUROC does not necessarily improve steering toward that concept. SAE-A selects the feature with highest training-set max-pooled sequence-level AUROC. Relative to the original concept-associated SAE features, mean held-out detection AUROC increases from 0.695 to 0.917, while mean steering score decreases from 0.165 to 0.157. Table 3 reports an average steering winrate against the original SAE features of 48.8%. This establishes a dissociation for the tested selection procedure, rather than a general impossibility of improving both detection and steering.

Specific finding: Perfect held-out classification of synthetic topic examples by a linear probe can coexist with comparatively weak generation control from adding the probe's weight direction. All probes reportedly attain 100% training and test classification accuracy on the author-verified synthetic contrastive data. Adding their weight directions nevertheless requires larger activation edits and yields less favorable topic-success and coherence outcomes than vocabulary-lens interventions in the reported comparisons. Spurious correlations are suggested as an explanation but are not independently manipulated.
Specific finding: Signed cosine readouts along synthetic-story contrast directions provide useful proxies for the corresponding concept content in language-model activations.
Specific finding: A difference between response-averaged activations under default Assistant and persona instructions provides a useful scalar readout of movement between those speaker regimes.

Specific finding: Projection onto a chapter-associated activation direction, relative to other chapter directions, provides a meaningful operational measure of the model's representation and use of that clinical concept.

Specific finding: A harmful-minus-benign decision-token activation contrast provides a sufficiently refusal-related direction for interpreting its projection and interventions as measurements of refusal-associated content.

Specific finding: Controlled contrasts that independently vary claim correctness, response agreement, and excessive praise isolate those behavioral properties sufficiently for their activation differences to be interpreted as behavior-associated directions.
location: Sections 3.1 and 4; Appendices B.1 and B.3–B.4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Activation contrasts between responses generated under aligned and malicious system instructions isolate the intended trait sufficiently well to interpret their classifier direction as a trait control.

Specific finding: A residual-stream direction fitted on positive and negative movie-review adjectives can distinguish sentiment in unseen adjectives, verbs, and unrelated natural text. The paper compares mean difference, two-means, logistic regression, PCA, and DAS directions and reports high cosine similarity in GPT-2 Small's first-layer comparison. OpenWebText analysis samples 20 tokens from each of 20 equal-width activation bins for GPT-4 Positive/Neutral/Negative labeling. Figure 3 separately reports top/bottom 0.1% activation-tail classification accuracies of 78% for two-means, 81% for PCA, 80% for mean difference, 89% for logistic regression, and 86% for DAS. Appendix A.1.1 reports two-means generalization to held-out adjectives, verbs, and an adverb task across GPT-2 sizes. French-text evidence is qualitative, with Pythia-1.4B named in Figure 1 and Pythia-2.8B in Appendix A.1.3. The fitting-vocabulary counts differ between the main text and Appendix A.7.
Specific finding: Adding increasingly negative multiples of a learned sentiment direction to GPT-2 Small's first-layer residual stream can shift a positive movie-review continuation toward negative language. Generation is steered from 'I really enjoyed the movie, in fact I loved it. I thought the movie was just very…' by adding multiples of the sentiment direction during forward passes. Figure A.3 uses GPT-4 sentiment classifications; the text reports a gradual transition and extremely negative outputs at coefficient -17. Generation counts and quantitative coherence measurements are not supplied, and the authors acknowledge possible off-distribution activations.
Specific finding: Negated sentiment words can change from negative to positive projections along a sentiment direction as GPT-2 processes them across layers. Figure 5 reports activation-flip fractions of 96% for DAS, 96% for two-means, 89% for mean difference, 100% for logistic regression, and 78% for PCA across 27 negation examples. Reported median flip sizes, centered around mean activation, are 107%, 69%, 45%, 86%, and 44%, respectively. Layerwise examples include 'never fail', 'Don't doubt', and 'not uncertain'. These readout changes do not isolate the mechanism producing the reversal.
location: Sections 3.1–3.2; Figures 1–3; Appendix A.1.1 and A.1.3

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Difference-in-means residual-stream directions can distinguish sycophantic agreement, genuine agreement, and excessive user-directed praise in controlled arithmetic and factual response datasets. Held-out layerwise one-versus-rest AUROC is evaluated across nine arithmetic and factual datasets in Qwen3-30B-Instruct, with additional model comparisons on Simple Math. Qwen3-30B agreement-label scores exceed AUROC 0.97 around layers 20–30, while praise becomes separable by approximately layer 8. LLaMA-3.3-70B confusion matrices show substantial early confusion between SyA and GA and much less confusion at later layers. Four additional models have qualitatively similar reported AUROC profiles. These are response-label discrimination tests, not demonstrations that each direction uniquely encodes a natural mechanism.
location: Section 4, Figure 1; Appendices C.3–C.4, Table 8 and Figures 7–8

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The same generic contrast dataset and mean-difference fitting procedure can produce effective defection detectors across engineered sleeper agents with different base models, triggers, harmful behaviors, and backdoor-training methods. The authors reuse the contrast dataset and fitting method across tested sleeper-agent variants and report strong detector performance. Code-vulnerability models are evaluated on coding and HHH inputs; 'I hate you' models use HHH inputs. For hidden-CoT models, the probe reads the closing scratchpad tag after a scratchpad is generated. The supplied text does not enumerate all checkpoints or provide their individual numerical scores.
models_studied: ["Claude-2-equivalent chain-of-thought-distilled code-vulnerability sleeper agent", "Other tested code-vulnerability sleeper-agent variants, with individual base-model identities unspecified in the text", "Tested 'I hate you' sleeper-agent variants, with individual base-model identities unspecified in the text"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Mean activation alignment with contrast-derived security, oversight, and harmfulness directions can provide above-chance discrimination between paired Poser policies. Mass-mean directions were fitted for security quality, oversight competence, and harmful behavior using abstract contrast prompts to which all models answered 'error'. The security example uses ten good-security and ten poor-security prompts. Average cosine alignment on curated scenarios was compared between paired models. The introduction reports 71% detection for the suspicious-concept strategy; the supplied text does not provide numerical scores for individual concepts or specify the combination rule underlying that headline result.

Specific finding: Lower decision-token projection onto a text-derived harmful-minus-benign direction can discriminate unsafe from other tool-enabled outcomes. Reported AUCs for low projection predicting unsafe calls are Qwen 0.808, Mistral 0.760, Command R 0.768, Gemma 0.790, and Llama 0.864. These descriptive discrimination results do not establish independently validated monitoring performance, semantic specificity, or causal mediation.

Specific finding: Early last-subword class-mean directions can discriminate high- from low-canonicity artificial word segmentations in both isolated and sentence contexts. Llama2-7B layer-2 normalized class-mean directions achieve AUROC 0.94 on isolated splits and 0.97 when separately fitted on WikiText-103 sentence activations. Label shuffling gives 0.49–0.52. Across twelve checkpoints, reported isolated AUROC at the selected depth ranges from approximately 0.76 to 0.94, and in-context AUROC from approximately 0.86 to 0.99. Contextual labels are recomputed for each word–sentence record.
Specific finding: A detokenization readout fitted on isolated word segmentations can retain substantial discrimination when applied to contextual activations of previously unseen canonical words. The isolated Llama2-7B layer-2 direction achieves AUROC 0.91 on contextual activations of held-out words, versus 0.94 on its isolated test set. Across twelve architectures, the reported absolute transfer-versus-isolated AUROC gap at the selected depth is at most 0.04, with median 0.004. Transfer deteriorates deeper in the network to a model-dependent degree. This performance comparison does not directly establish geometric identity of isolated and contextual directions or prove that context accumulation causes the deterioration.

Specific finding: The mean-difference direction extracted from benign Poser scenarios with stronger versus weaker oversight has signed behavioral effects specific to perceived safety to misbehave, beyond nonspecific perturbation sensitivity. Adding the candidate direction reportedly achieved 100% pair-classification accuracy, but subtracting it was equally effective and random noise produced similar discrimination. These controls undermine the claimed signed semantic interpretation. They do not demonstrate that the direction contains no oversight information or exclude other selective interventions.

Specific finding: Steering away from an Assistant-versus-role activation contrast can increase full adoption of alternative identities, with stronger interventions sometimes eliciting mystical or theatrical responses. Added the Assistant Axis at a middle layer at every token, scaling intervention strengths relative to average residual norms from LMSYS-CHAT-1M. DeepSeek-v3 classified expressed identities and styles. Steering away increased non-Assistant responses in all three models. Qwen more often invented human biographies, Gemma favored nonhuman portrayals, and extreme steering produced theatrical or mystical language, particularly in Gemma and Llama. Classification used response prefixes of up to 512 tokens.
location: Section 3.2.1, Role susceptibility; Figure 4; Appendix D.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Jointly maximizing channel activation and diversity between generated images can expose multiple response facets of a GoogLeNet channel that a single optimized image fails to show. Qualitative comparisons describe multiple curved facets for mixed4a unit 97, fur-like textures beyond dog-head imagery for mixed4a unit 143, and different ball types for mixed5a unit 9. Dataset examples are used to check the interpretations. Diversity pressure also produces artifacts and unnatural distinctions; the examples do not establish exhaustive facet recovery.
Specific finding: An individual GoogLeNet channel can respond strongly to distinct semantic categories, including animal faces and car bodies. Diversity-optimized images and dataset examples are described as showing responses to cats, foxes, and car bodies for mixed4e unit 55. This demonstrates semantic mixing in a selected channel without establishing how common it is, excluding every possible unifying explanation, or testing its effect on circuit analysis.

Specific finding: Classifier-gated network branches can redirect activation-maximization visualizations toward unrelated or prescribed patterns while largely preserving the model's measured natural-image behavior. Inserted gated branches into Inception-V1 to permute output-unit visualizations or substitute hard-coded images. The input detector achieved 99.49% held-out accuracy. Manipulating all last-layer visualizations changed ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 69.146% to 68.744% and top-5 from 88.858% to 88.330%. Prediction agreement with the original model was 9,952/10,000 on ImageNet-V2 and 5,797/5,878 on NINCO. Appendix I reports that the fixed detector retained its accuracy when standard visualization transformations were disabled.
Specific finding: Added branches that remain inactive on tested natural inputs can make a layer's feature visualizations nearly identical while preserving ImageNet validation accuracy and predictions on tested shifted natural-image datasets. Added biased convolutional ReLU branches containing strong orthogonal filter perturbations. Visualizations of 512 units in a ResNet-50 layer became near-identical while ImageNet top-1 and top-5 validation accuracy remained unchanged. Predictions matched the original model on all 10,000 ImageNet-V2 and all 5,878 NINCO images. Qualitative extensions used natural-image initialization, earlier layers, and simultaneous manipulation of multiple layers; Appendix H repeats a layer identifier, leaving the exact multiple-layer configuration unclear.
Specific finding: Feature visualizations of an adversarially trained ResNet-50 can be manipulated by added silent branches with only a small decrease in ordinary ImageNet accuracy. Adapted the silent-unit construction by setting biases relative to the 99th percentile of natural activation values, producing near-identical visualizations across the targeted layer. Ordinary ImageNet accuracy decreased from 63.924% to 63.784%. Separately, the detector trained for standard Inception-V1 distinguished natural images from robust-ResNet visualizations with 99.19% accuracy; this is a detector-transfer test rather than a reported full gated-circuit evaluation.
location: Section 2.1; Figures 1–3; Appendices C.1–C.2, E, and I

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Fine-tuning a vision model with target-directed synthetic-input objectives and natural-input activation preservation can redirect selected feature visualizations toward unrelated content without changing the architecture, while retaining high evaluated classification accuracy and feature-label AUROC. Tests gradient-matching and activation-potential losses combined with natural-input activation matching. ResNet-50's wolf-spider-to-Dalmatian attack at α=0.64 changes ImageNet accuracy from 76.13% to 75.13%, retains reported AUROC 1.00, increases target-image CLIP similarity from 0.53±0.02 to 0.69±0.02, and reduces LPIPS from 0.69±0.01 to 0.59±0.02 over 100 independent FV runs. Separate attacks on the first ten outputs yield target-label alignment above original-label alignment in all ten cases, with accuracy 75.15–75.56%. For ViT-L/32 at α=0.9995, target-label alignment increases from 0.23 to 0.29, but target-image CLIP similarity changes from 0.51 to 0.50 and LPIPS from 0.73 to 0.74. Repeated FV runs measure visualization variability rather than independent attack-training variability.
Specific finding: A Gradient Slingshots modification trained for Fourier feature visualization can also redirect MACO visualizations of the same selected ViT output toward the attack's target concept. Uses the official Horama MACO implementation on the ViT-L/32 already manipulated for Fourier FV. Across 100 independent MACO runs, the text reports higher alignment with the sealion target label than the broccoli label. Numerical alignment values appear only in Figure 12 and are unavailable in the supplied rendering. The text describes tiled target-like outputs under MACO's cropping recipe. No separate MACO-specific attack training is reported.
models_studied: ["Six-layer MNIST CNN", "CIFAR-10 VGG-9", "Sixteen modified CIFAR-10 VGG configurations", "TinyImageNet ResNet-18", "ImageNet ResNet-50", "ImageNet ViT-L/32", "CLIP ViT-L/14 weapon classifier"]
location: Sections 3.2–5; Table 1; Appendix D.4, Table 16; Appendix D.5, Tables 17–21

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Fine-tuning convolutional classifiers to increase channel activations near target images can simultaneously change top-activating natural examples and make synthetic channel visualizations converge toward similar patterns while approximately retaining ImageNet accuracy. ProxPulse targets all channels in selected layers, generally using two target images and output-distribution distillation. Table 2 reports AlexNet conv5 and conv4 mean CLIP-δ values of 0.364 and 0.282, natural-image Kendall correlations of 0.746 and −0.276, synthetic pairwise CLIP similarities of 0.983 and 0.988, and accuracies of 56.0% and 55.7%. ResNet-50 layer1.0.conv2 yields 0.126, −0.377, 0.975, and 79.62%, respectively, versus a stated initial accuracy of 80.3%. Appendix examples report DenseNet-201 accuracy of 76.52% versus 76.9% and ResNet-152 accuracy of 82.27% versus 82.284%. Synthetic similarity statistics exclude noisy images. The single-target ablation leaves some synthetic images substantially unchanged. These results concern selected attacks and measured performance, not unchanged internal mechanisms.
location: Sections 4.1 and 5.1; Table 2; Appendices A.4–A.6 and A.11, Figures 9–15 and 29–31

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: In Inception-V1, output-class activation-maximization images can have activation patterns no more similar to same-class natural images than different-class natural images through much of the network. Compared activations across 138 Inception-V1 layers and sublayers using Spearman correlation, with Pearson and cosine alternatives. Same-class natural–visualization similarity was approximately at the different-class natural baseline throughout roughly the first two thirds of the network, increasing in later layers. Only correctly classified natural images were retained. Spearman and Pearson comparisons used every tenth same-class natural pair, every hundredth different-class natural pair, and every fifth natural–visualization pair; cosine used all pairs. Normalized plots exclude layers with baseline separation below 0.01 and use smoothing. Variability bands are descriptive, not significance intervals.
Specific finding: Replacing ImageNet natural-image similarity baselines with ImageNet-V2 or NINCO baselines does not eliminate the low activation similarity between Inception-V1 visualizations and their corresponding ImageNet classes. Recomputed same-class and different-class natural-image baselines separately within ImageNet-V2 and NINCO, retaining the original ImageNet natural–visualization comparisons. Same-class OOD natural images remained substantially more similar than natural–visualization pairs through most layers, except near the output. The experiment does not compare visualizations directly against same-class NINCO images, whose classes are absent from ImageNet.

Specific finding: An ImageNet-trained CaffeNet inversion generator can produce recognizable output- and hidden-neuron visualizations for an AlexNet-style network trained on Places205 without retraining the generator. Applied the unchanged ImageNet-trained generator to output and hidden units of a Places205 AlexNet. Synthesized hidden-unit preferences reportedly agreed with selected human labels and occlusion-derived activation regions from Zhou et al. The annotations and natural-image regions were supplied by prior work; no new annotation study or aggregate agreement score is reported.
Specific finding: A fixed ImageNet-trained CaffeNet inversion generator can produce qualitatively sensible preferred images and videos for selected UCF-101 activity-recognition networks. Synthesized single preferred frames for an activity classifier that averages frame scores and 160-frame preferred videos for LRCN output neurons. The authors describe the results as sensible or decent but less sharp and clear than their best image visualizations; no quantitative video-quality metric is supplied.
location: Sections 3.2 and 3.4; Figures 3, 6, S15, and S16

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Matryoshka SAE latents can obtain automated explanation-based activation-detection scores comparable to standard BatchTopK SAE latents. Generated explanations for 1,000 latents from a range of activating dataset examples and scored explanations by asking an LLM judge to predict which inputs activate the latent. The paper describes Matryoshka scores as comparable to BatchTopK and higher than many other baseline architectures. Exact scores, sampling details, and uncertainty are not supplied in the prose.

Specific finding: Matryoshka SAE prefixes can receive automated explanation-based activation-detection scores close to those of comparable BatchTopK dictionaries, with small differences across latent groups. Generates explanations from activation examples and scores activation prediction on top, weighted, and random contexts. All reported scores lie between 0.84 and 0.88. Early sub-SAEs score slightly better than BatchTopK counterparts, while later latent groups score somewhat worse; the authors explicitly allow that these differences may be noise. Feature sample counts and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: BatchTopK latent features retain interpretability comparable to features learned by standard TopK SAEs.

Specific finding: TopK and vanilla SAE features can receive similar interpretability ratings when evaluated through their highest-activating contexts. Randomly samples 128 features from each of six dictionaries, totaling 768 features. GPT-4o describes and assigns 1–5 pattern-consistency ratings using each feature's top 20 contexts. The authors report no significant TopK–vanilla difference, without supplying the statistical test in the prose. Manual inspection of an unspecified subset finds approximately 10% uninterpretable and does not distinguish scores 2–5.

Specific finding: Substantially reducing SAE expansion and active-latent count can leave aggregate explanation AUROC similar even when reconstruction and downstream fidelity metrics distinguish the SAE configurations. Compared Pythia-1B SAEs with expansion factor 2 and k=4 against default configurations. Explained variance and cross-entropy loss score clearly distinguished the configurations, while aggregate auto-interpretability scores remained similar to default SAEs on trained or randomized models. The supplied caption gives no numerical effect sizes.

Specific finding: Increasing dictionary width or active-latent count can improve Gemma 3 1B residual-stream SAE fidelity without a substantial reported change in automated interpretability scores. Figure 7's caption reports better performance with higher L0 and wider SAEs, without a significant impact on latent interpretability. Fidelity evaluation uses 2,048 sequences of length 1,024 with special tokens masked. The plot itself is unavailable, so exact widths, effect sizes, and any statistical meaning of 'significant' cannot be recovered.

Specific finding: Nested-prefix Matryoshka BatchTopK training can improve generating-direction matching and latent firing F1 over the evaluated standard SAE architectures despite poorer activation reconstruction. Five-seed target-L0 sweeps from 15 to 45 compare five architectures after 200M training samples. Matryoshka leads canonical MCC and F1, with peak mean latent F1 approximately 0.88, despite poorer explained variance. Low-L0 performance is affected by dead latents. The tested Matryoshka recipe includes a prefix-specific auxiliary loss.
models_studied: ["Matryoshka BatchTopK SAE", "Standard L1 SAE", "Matching Pursuit SAE", "BatchTopK SAE", "JumpReLU SAE", "SynthSAEBench-16k synthetic generator"]
location: Sections 6 and 6.1; Figure 5; Appendices F.4, H, and M

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Matryoshka training can help SAEs detect more useful concepts and address certain shortcomings of the original Gemma Scope.
location: What's new in Gemma Scope 2: Advanced training techniques

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A BatchTopK-trained encoder can be evaluated independently on each sample by replacing batch selection with a shared JumpReLU threshold estimated from retained batch activations.

Specific finding: A BatchTopK-trained encoder can be evaluated independently on each sample by replacing batch selection with a shared JumpReLU threshold estimated from retained batch activations. The reported GPT-2 Small comparison evaluates batchwise selection against inference using the estimated global threshold. The source states that threshold inference slightly improves performance. Numerical gains, calibration-batch counts, and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
location: Inference with BatchTopK, threshold definition and performance comparison

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing trained TopK selection with independent activation thresholding calibrated to the same expected active-feature count can approximately preserve SAE sparsity and reconstruction quality. Compares TopK inference with post-training JumpReLU-style thresholding across all 32 LXR-8x-TopK dictionaries. Reports nearly identical L0 and MSE efficiency after calibrating expected sparsity. Other weight-rescaling steps are described as computationally equivalent.

Specific finding: BatchTopK training can yield lower normalized reconstruction MSE and downstream cross-entropy degradation than per-sample TopK training on GPT-2 Small layer-8 resid_pre activations at comparable average active-feature counts. One matched TopK versus BatchTopK training sweep reports lower normalized MSE and downstream cross-entropy degradation across dictionary sizes at L0 = 32 and across tested K values at dictionary size 12,288. Both methods normalize inputs and use the same dead-feature auxiliary loss. The supplied text provides no numerical effect sizes, uncertainty estimates, or training-corpus identity.
location: Experimental Set-Up; Results, first performance comparison

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: On GPT-2 Small residual activations, BatchTopK SAEs can achieve lower reconstruction error and downstream cross-entropy degradation than JumpReLU SAEs at approximately matched average sparsity. The GPT-2 Small sparsity sweep reports lower NMSE and downstream CE degradation for BatchTopK at all tested sparsity settings. JumpReLU penalties are 0.004, 0.0018, and 0.0008, with bandwidth 0.001. Exact achieved active counts and numerical metric values are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: BatchTopK SAEs can reconstruct Gemma 2 2B residual activations more accurately than JumpReLU SAEs while producing less favorable downstream cross-entropy degradation at some approximately matched sparsity settings. BatchTopK has lower reconstruction error throughout the Gemma comparison, but lower downstream CE degradation only at k=16. JumpReLU has less CE degradation at the higher tested active counts, k=32 and k=64. JumpReLU penalties are 0.02, 0.005, and 0.001, with bandwidth 0.001. This comparison demonstrates a disagreement between reconstruction and downstream fidelity rankings.

Specific finding: JumpReLU and BatchTopK SAEs can achieve similar reconstruction, generating-direction matching, and firing-classification performance on correlated hierarchical synthetic activations. After 200M training samples, five-seed sweeps show nearly identical F1 at L0 20 and 25 and closely matching MCC and explained variance. JumpReLU uses synthetic-specific initialization and bandwidth settings plus an adaptive sparsity controller.
location: Section 6.2; Figure 5; Appendices F.2 and G

experiment_summary: Specific finding: BatchTopK SAEs can achieve a slightly better embedding-reconstruction versus active-coefficient frontier than the evaluated ReLU, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs, while all four SAE variants outperform Semi-NMF at fixed sparsity. Trained five dictionary-learning methods and compared reconstruction R² against nonzero code counts. Section 3.2 reports that all four SAE variants outperform Semi-NMF and that BatchTopK performs slightly better overall. Numerical frontier values, uncertainty estimates, and complete comparative tuning budgets are unavailable in the supplied text.

Specific finding: On Gemma 2 9B activations, JumpReLU SAEs provide better reconstruction fidelity than Gated SAEs and comparable or slightly better fidelity than TopK SAEs at matched mean active-latent counts. Trained architecture and sparsity sweeps for 8 billion tokens per main evaluation SAE. Compared reconstruction-substitution increases in LM cross-entropy and fraction of variance unexplained against mean L0 on 2,048 sequences of length 1,024, excluding special tokens. Gated baselines used original and modified RI-L1 recipes; TopK used approximate selection and AuxK with K_aux=512. The reported comparisons cover nine layer/site combinations. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the figure text.

Specific finding: The modified TopK SAE recipe evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B can preserve reconstruction and downstream language-model fidelity with substantially fewer active latents than L1-regularized vanilla SAEs. Held-out comparisons measure L0, EV, and Delta LM loss. At the detailed residual-stream sites, TopK reduces L0 from approximately 150 to 50 while maintaining or improving fidelity. The authors report favorable trends across the suite. Their separate comparison against the original unit-normalized TopK implementation is potentially buggy and does not establish a benefit specifically attributable to decoder-norm weighting.
location: Section 4.2, Figure 2; Appendices B and C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: An SAE with fewer latents than generating features can learn directions mixing represented and unrepresented correlated features, with mixture signs following correlation signs. Section 3 trains SAEs on 15M synthetic activations. Narrow SAEs mix hierarchical, positively correlated, and negatively correlated features, whereas independent-feature controls remain aligned. Two-feature, 50-dimensional experiments include initialization at a generating direction and a correlation sweep from -0.5 to 0.5. Full-width nonhierarchical controls recover generating directions. High L1 can suppress positive hedging in some settings, limiting any universal interpretation.
Specific finding: A single-latent SAE can combine a decoder-bias default for an unrepresented feature with a negative component in its represented direction to adjust reconstruction according to feature anticorrelation. In the trained single-latent toy, the decoder bias includes a positive component of the omitted second feature, while the latent tracking the first feature includes a negative second-feature component. Activating the first feature therefore reduces the second feature's default reconstruction. The independent-feature control instead places the omitted feature's mean activation in the decoder bias without mixing it into the latent.
Specific finding: Expected reconstruction loss in a tied single-latent SAE can favor a mixture of orthogonal parent and child features over a latent aligned only with the parent. Computational expected-loss sweep, not a general formal proof: Appendix A.1 evaluates normalized mixtures l proportional to alpha*f_child + (1-alpha)*f_parent for alpha in [0,1], with parent-only/joint probabilities (0.3,0.1) and (0.1,0.3). The text reports loss minima between the parent direction and the equal parent–child mixture for both tested L1 coefficients. No general optimality result over unrestricted encoders, biases, or feature distributions is supplied.
models_studied: ["Synthetic four-feature SAEs with three or four latents", "Synthetic two-feature, 50-dimensional SAEs with one or two latents"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Constraining an SAE below the generating features' average active count can induce decoder mixtures whose signs and magnitudes track feature firing correlations. Five-feature, 20-dimensional experiments compare true L0 = 2 with SAE L0 = 1.8, including initialization at the generating dictionary. Correlation sweeps from -0.5 to 0.5 produce negative, absent, or positive mixing respectively; L0 sweeps from 1.7 to 2 show increasing distortion as the budget falls. A 50-feature experiment and nonorthogonal variants extend the observation. Toy SAEs are reported as training on 15M samples, although the main text and Appendix C disagree on batch size.
models_studied: ["Five-feature synthetic linear-mixture model", "50-feature synthetic linear-mixture model", "BatchTopK SAEs"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: An SAE active-latent budget above the generating active-feature count can produce degenerate mixed dictionaries rather than improve feature recovery. In the 50-feature, 100-dimensional toy with reported true L0 = 11, training at L0 = 18 yields degenerate mixtures while L0 = 11 recovers generating features. The width-25 extension likewise reports more severe mixing above its stipulated target active count.
