Specific finding: In a matched-width synthetic TopK SAE benchmark, generating-direction recovery can peak when the retained latent count matches generating sparsity, with a sharper decline from retaining too few than too many latents. Appendix E evaluates GT-MCC averaged over the final 100 training steps and reports a peak at k=8, with steeper degradation below eight. Numerical curve values are absent from the supplied text. The displayed experiment measures GT-MCC rather than PW-MCC and does not directly validate selecting natural-data sparsity by consistency. Its configuration does not establish the sparse-injectivity prerequisites of Section 4.1.
models_studied: ["TopK SAE on matched-width synthetic sparse Gaussian mixtures"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Direct high-frequency latent regularization can eliminate residual-stream SAE latents whose measured firing frequency exceeds 10%. Residual-stream latent frequencies are measured on 50,000 sequences of length 1,024 after masking special tokens. The authors report entirely eliminating latents with measured frequency greater than 10% using an aggressive frequency penalty. Precise penalty settings, checkpoint coverage, and controlled numerical comparisons are not supplied.

Specific finding: Quadratic-frequency JumpReLU training can suppress high-frequency SAE latents with a modest increase in reconstruction loss at a fixed average active-latent count. Compared quadratic-frequency JumpReLU with standard L0 JumpReLU, Gated, and TopK SAEs across sparsities. The source reports suppression of latents firing around or above 10% of tokens, with much of the lower-frequency histogram retained, especially at scale 0.1. Reconstruction loss is slightly worse than standard JumpReLU at fixed L0 and remains favorable relative to the tested Gated and TopK baselines. Exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable.
location: Removing High Frequency Latents from JumpReLU SAEs — Results / Reconstruction loss at fixed sparsity and Frequency histograms

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Training residual-stream SAEs with output-distribution KL divergence can preserve language-model performance with fewer active features per token and fewer alive dictionary elements than local MSE training. Compared local, e2e, and e2e+ds sparsity sweeps using mean L0, replacement-induced CE increase, and dictionary elements active on 500k training tokens. In the main GPT2-small layer-6 comparison, interpolation over L0 in (50,300) gives both e2e variants less than 45% of the local SAE's CE increase at matched L0. Selected approximately CE-matched runs have L0 69.4/27.5/36.8 and 26k/22k/15k alive elements for local/e2e/e2e+ds. Layer-6 sweeps show little additional local-baseline improvement when increasing dictionary width from 60× to 100× residual width or training from 400k to 800k sequences. TinyStories-1M provides a smaller additional comparison, primarily local versus pure e2e.
location: Section 3.1; Figure 1; Tables 1–3; Appendices A.1–A.3 and E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Briefly fine-tuning MSE-trained sparse autoencoders with combined output KL and activation MSE can substantially reduce their downstream replacement cross-entropy gap. Compared MSE-trained SAEs before and after combined KL+MSE adaptation. Main scratch comparisons allocate 25M of 500M total tokens to adaptation; SAEBench baselines receive 15M-token fine-tunes. Replacement cross-entropy improves in both evaluated architectures. The abstract reports an overall gap reduction of 20–50%; configuration-specific numerical values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied prose.

Specific finding: Prompt- and token-conditional SAE preference steering can improve MT-Bench over HH-RLHF-SFT starting checkpoints while its AlpacaEval gains and competitiveness with DPO depend on the model. Table 1 averages three generation seeds. DSPA versus Base MT-Bench scores are 4.39 versus 3.91, 5.02 versus 4.39, and 4.86 versus 4.12. AlpacaEval scores are 19.30 versus 17.54, 20.00 versus 21.12, and 17.83 versus 13.47. DPO scores are 4.36/15.82, 5.05/17.39, and 5.52/24.60 for MT-Bench/AlpacaEval. DSPA exceeds the tested RepE and Static-SAE recipes on both metrics in all three models, but Gemma-2-9B instruction prompting has higher AlpacaEval. No uncertainty intervals or controlled human evaluation are supplied. The baselines differ in more than prompt conditioning, so Static-SAE's poorer scores do not isolate that component.
Specific finding: DSPA maps constructed from a few hundred preference triples can remain competitive on MT-Bench against the tested preference-training baselines, without uniformly matching their AlpacaEval performance. At N=250, DSPA versus RAHF-SCIT MT-Bench scores are 3.95 versus 3.71, 4.82 versus 4.63, and 4.69 versus 4.52 for Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen3-8B. RAHF-SCIT has higher AlpacaEval in all three: 19.13/22.64/23.48 versus DSPA's 16.81/21.27/18.20. RepE narrowly leads Gemma-2-2B MT-Bench at 3.97. The prose accompanying Figure 3 reports greater DSPA stability than RAHF-SCIT down to one hundred triples; exact plotted values and subset-resampling uncertainty are unavailable.
Specific finding: DSPA maps constructed from filtered PRISM or Chatbot Arena preference pairs can retain MT-Bench-proxy gains over the starting Gemma checkpoints. Appendix C reports Base/UltraFeedback/PRISM/LMSYS proxy scores of 2.61/2.97/2.90/2.85 for Gemma-2-2B and 3.26/3.48/3.55/3.43 for Gemma-2-9B. Both alternative sources exceed Base in both models. Repeated source-sampling uncertainty and human evaluation are not reported.
Specific finding: Adapting Gemma Scope SAEs to HH-RLHF activations can improve DSPA dialogue ratings in selected larger-model intervention modes without uniformly improving every tested configuration. For Gemma-2-9B, adapted versus public SAEs score 3.48 versus 3.04 under ablation-only and 3.60 versus 2.93 under combined intervention; augment-only is nearly tied at 3.05 versus 3.03. Gemma-2-2B averages tie at 2.73 across modes. Appendix B additionally reports smaller unions of per-row extreme candidates after adaptation: seventy-six augmentation and eighty-three ablation identities versus 183 and 186 before adaptation. Shared feature indices can receive different descriptions after adaptation, so index overlap does not establish semantic invariance.
Specific finding: Within the tested DSPA configurations, attenuating dispreferred active features can produce more reliable dialogue-rating improvements than augmenting preferred features, with combined interventions depending more strongly on layer and strength. The prose accompanying Figures 4–6 reports poor augment-only performance in both Gemma models and an ablate-only advantage in Gemma-2-2B. Combined augmentation and ablation can beat ablation at selected Gemma-2-9B layer pairs, including input 9/output 39, but not consistently across the grid. Large strengths sharply degrade combined interventions, whereas ablation-only degrades less. Among surveyed feature counts, sixteen performs best. Most plotted numerical values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Selected activation-steering interventions can substantially recover disclosure honesty and compassion suppressed by malicious system prompts while retaining high judge-rated coherence. On 112 honesty scenarios and 40 compassion prompts, Llama all-token SwFC/StTP/StMP honesty scores are 75/77/62 versus malicious 24 and aligned 93, with coherence 89/87/89 versus aligned 95. Compassion scores are 78/75/71 versus malicious 25 and aligned 81, with coherence 87/91/95 versus aligned 94. Qwen honesty scores are 80/66/54 versus malicious 31 and aligned 94; compassion scores are 71/77/78 versus malicious 20 and aligned 83. Qwen steered coherence is 92–95 at these operating points.
Specific finding: Projection-aware steering developed for honesty and compassion can also recover non-toxicity under hostile system prompts using a newly extracted non-toxicity direction. Llama non-toxicity increases from 19.6 malicious to 85.0/83.1/79.0 under SwFC/StTP/StMP, versus 89.2 aligned. Qwen increases from 20.8 to 86.0/92.0/93.3, versus 91.6 aligned. Coherence is 90.5/93.9/91.4 on Llama and 92.1/94.3/94.6 on Qwen. A separate Llama AlpacaEval sweep favors StTP/StMP over SwFC, but trait scores use layer 26 while capability scores use layer 29, so these results do not establish a joint operating-point frontier.

Specific finding: Local reconstruction SAEs can preserve a high-variance activation component more accurately than downstream-regularized SAEs even when resampling that component has relatively little effect on model outputs. A selected UMAP region contains 593 local features versus two e2e+ds features, with directions pointing partly away from the leading activation PC. E2e+ds reconstruction correlation for this PC is 0.996 at position zero but 0.262 elsewhere, where local reconstruction is much more faithful. Resample-ablating the component at all nonzero positions, using donor components from another input and a nonzero donor position, produces reported output KL divergence of 0.01, lower than for every other direction among the first 30 PCs. This is one localized example; position-zero irrelevance and general prevalence are not established.

Specific finding: Training sparse dictionaries to preserve PolarBERT direction outputs need not produce causal coordinates that validate against the tested physical concept vocabulary. Two pure-functional dictionaries contain 16 and 11 intervention-defined causal latents but have best bright-clean AUROC approximately 0.53. Two reconstruction-anchored dictionaries recover bright-clean AUROC 0.87 and 0.878, while those readouts lie outside their six-latent causal sets. None of the four dictionaries yields a causal-latent/concept pair passing the complete validation procedure.
models_studied: ["PolarBERT frozen direction head", "Two pure-functional sparse dictionaries", "Two reconstruction-anchored functional sparse dictionaries"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: L1-regularized ReLU SAEs can exhibit systematic reconstruction shrinkage, with reconstructions smaller than their globally rescaled reconstruction-error optimum. Baseline SAEs exhibit relative reconstruction bias gamma below one in the reported sweeps, with stronger shrinkage as the sparsity penalty increases. Gamma is defined through the global multiplicative rescaling minimizing reconstruction MSE. Section 3.1 separately illustrates the objective's bias with a single-feature example: target magnitude one and L1 coefficient one yield an optimum reconstruction of one-half. Shrinkage is identified as prior work rather than introduced here.
location: Section 3.1, Figure 2; Section 4.2, Equations 9–10 and Figure 6; Appendix C, Figure 14

experiment_summary: Specific finding: L1-trained residual-stream SAEs can produce reconstructions whose average L2 norms are substantially smaller than those of their inputs. After six epochs over 100 million OpenWebText tokens, five of six layer-specific SAEs have mean reconstruction/input L2 ratios below 0.9. Table A1 reports ratios approximately 0.887, 0.868, 0.845, 0.861, 0.868, and 0.995. These measurements establish smaller reconstruction norms, but do not alone identify featurewise shrinkage or a globally optimal reconstruction scale.
location: Feature suppression is a significant problem in current SAEs; Figure 1; Table A1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: L1-trained residual-stream SAEs can produce reconstructions whose average L2 norms are substantially smaller than those of their inputs. After six epochs over 100 million OpenWebText tokens, five of six SAEs have mean reconstruction/input norm ratios below 0.90. Table A1 reports approximately 0.887, 0.868, 0.845, 0.861, 0.868, and 0.995. These measurements establish norm deficits without uniquely identifying their cause.
location: Feature suppression is a significant problem in current SAEs; Figure 1; Table A1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Gated SAE training can remove the global reconstruction-scaling bias observed in L1-regularized ReLU SAEs by separating feature detection from magnitude estimation. The authors measure the optimal multiplicative rescaling of SAE reconstructions and report gamma approximately one for Gated SAEs, compared with gamma below one for baselines, across GELU-1L sparsity sweeps and supplementary Pythia-2.8B evaluations. This supports removal of aggregate scaling bias in the tested regime, rather than universal unbiasedness across all configurations or features.
location: Section 4.2, Equations 9–10 and Figure 6; Appendix C, Figure 14

experiment_summary: Specific finding: p-annealing can reduce global reconstruction shrinkage in board-game SAEs by an amount comparable to Gated SAE training. Measured relative reconstruction bias gamma through the scalar rescaling minimizing reconstruction MSE. Annealed and Gated SAEs show similar improvements over standard L1 training. Appendix E reports domain-dependent bias behavior and unstable estimates for degenerate dictionaries with nearly zero active features. No statistical equivalence test or individual-feature amplitude ground truth is supplied.
location: Section 5; Appendix E, Equation 15 and Figure 5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Refitting feature scales and decoder parameters without a sparsity penalty can improve SAE reconstruction and downstream perplexity while preserving encoder firing conditions. The authors freeze encoder weights and biases and optimize inserted per-feature scales, decoder weights, and decoder bias without the sparsity penalty on the same 100-million-token OpenWebText subset used for SAE training. Average MSE decreases by 8.76%, and 24.11% of the original SAE-induced perplexity gap is recovered. Continued ordinary training yields approximately 0.2% MSE reduction and 0.5% gap recovery. Table A1 reports unchanged L0 at every layer. An independent evaluation split and uncertainty estimates are not specified.
Specific finding: Learning only per-feature scaling factors after SAE training can improve activation reconstruction and downstream perplexity without changing encoder or decoder directions. The Scale method freezes all original SAE parameters and learns an inserted elementwise feature multiplier. Across layers, the reported average fractional MSE reduction is 0.060 and recovery of the original SAE-induced perplexity gap is 0.156. Continued ordinary training gives 0.002 and 0.005, respectively. No independent semantic-interpretability evaluation is reported.
location: How can we fix feature suppression in trained SAEs?; Fine-tuning Reduces Feature Suppression; Figures 4–5; Table A1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Refitting feature scales and decoder parameters without a sparsity penalty can improve SAE reconstruction and downstream perplexity while preserving encoder firing conditions. With encoder weights and biases frozen, the authors optimize per-feature scales, decoder weights, and decoder bias on the same 100-million-token OpenWebText subset without the sparsity penalty. Mean MSE decreases 8.76%, and 24.11% of the original SAE-induced perplexity gap is recovered. Continued ordinary training yields approximately 0.2% MSE reduction and 0.5% gap recovery. Table A1 reports unchanged L0 in every layer. The Unrotated Decoder variant, which trains only scales and decoder bias, achieves approximately 6.1% MSE reduction and 16.2% gap recovery.
Specific finding: Learning only per-feature scaling factors after SAE training can improve activation reconstruction and downstream perplexity without changing encoder or decoder directions. The Scale method freezes all original SAE parameters and learns multiplicative latent scales on the same 100-million-token OpenWebText subset. Across layers, reconstruction MSE decreases approximately 6.0%, and 15.6% of the original SAE-induced perplexity gap is recovered. Preservation of semantic interpretability is not independently evaluated.
location: How can we fix feature suppression in trained SAEs?; Table 1; Figures 3–5; Table A1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Changing SAE feature magnitudes while preserving encoder firing conditions and feature directions preserves their semantic interpretability sufficiently for use as an interpretability interface.
location: How can we fix feature suppression in trained SAEs?; Conclusion

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Changing SAE feature magnitudes while preserving encoder firing conditions and feature directions preserves their semantic interpretability sufficiently for use as an interpretability interface.
location: How can we fix feature suppression in trained SAEs?; Conclusion

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Keeping an encoder fixed while constraining decoder changes preserves feature identities and semantics sufficiently for continued interpretation and circuit attribution.

Specific finding: GAE can improve normalized top-feature ablation scores and replacement cross-entropy preservation over fixed dictionaries and several training-based adaptations on selected language-model distribution shifts. Tables 2–3 compare Fixed, TERM, Finetune, Retrain, SAEBoost, FaithfulSAE, and GAE using 1,000 evaluation prompts per setting and seed 2026. GAE leads all 18 GPT-2 metric columns across the two tables. Pythia exceptions are transcoder FineWeb absolute ΔCE, where Finetune is better; SAE FineWeb nComp, where Retrain is better; and SAE EDGAR nAOPC, where Retrain is better. Pythia SAE HaluEval nAOPC ties several baselines at 1.000. For GPT-2 HaluEval transcoders, GAE obtains nComp 0.963 and absolute ΔCE 0.0014 versus SAEBoost's 0.921 and 0.0212. Ablation averages exclude examples with full-versus-empty logit range below 0.1; retained counts and repeated-seed uncertainty are unspecified.
Specific finding: GAE adaptation on fresh within-corpus activations can improve normalized feature-ablation metrics on held-out ID data while leaving replacement cross-entropy close to the fixed dictionary's. Appendix G uses a fresh 2,000-sample adaptation set and held-out OpenWebText or Pile prompts. Both causal metrics improve over Fixed in all four cells. Transcoder nComp changes from 1.011 to 1.109 for GPT-2 and 0.746 to 0.820 for Pythia; corresponding nAOPC changes are 0.840 to 0.854 and 0.665 to 0.697. Pythia SAE nComp changes from 1.438 to 1.508. Absolute replacement ΔCE remains within 0.0005 of Fixed in every cell. The explanation in terms of subset-specific covariance is an interpretation rather than an independently isolated cause.
location: Section 5.2.2; Tables 2–3; Appendices D.1, D.3, and D.4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: In a controlled covariance-shift experiment, replacing an ID activation projector with an estimated OOD projector can produce projection-loss improvements that closely track squared ID–OOD projector distance. Appendix C sweeps severity from 0 to 1 and compares projection-loss improvement against squared projector distance. It reports Pearson correlation 0.96, linear-fit R²=0.93, and zero violations of the stated eigengap lower bound across 11 settings. Section 5.1 separately reports near-zero adapted gap and approximately flat reconstruction error as the fixed explainer deteriorates. These are controlled reported observations, not a finite-sample guarantee; the toy covariance prescription has dimensional and symmetry ambiguities.
models_studied: ["Two-layer ReLU MLP, input width 128, hidden width 256, output width 8"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Affine regressions from language-model activations can explain substantial held-out variation in SAE squared reconstruction-error norms. Regressions use approximately 247k activations from 300 contexts, with 150k randomly selected training and approximately 97k test activations. Section 4.1 reports R² of 0.70–0.95, although its layer-sweep discussion describes lower predictability near network boundaries. In the Gemma 2 9B 131k-width baseline comparison, full activations generally outperform token identity, activation norm, SAE L0, and model loss; token identity performs better in the earliest layers. The random activation split does not establish generalization to independent source contexts.
Specific finding: SAE reconstruction-error vectors can contain substantial components predictable by an affine transformation of the original activation. Using the Section 4 random activation train/test split, affine error-vector prediction achieves reported coordinate-averaged R² of 0.15–0.72. Predictability decreases with increasing width and L0 in the main Gemma sweeps. Appendix A.1 reports predicted-error cosine similarity with the original activation around 0.5, arguing against an explanation consisting solely of scalar shrinkage reversal; this does not quantify every possible shrinkage contribution.

Specific finding: At approximately fixed activation sparsity, increasing SAE dictionary width can reduce total reconstruction error while leaving the residual after affine error prediction approximately unchanged. Compute nonlinear FVU from activation reconstruction after adding the fitted affine error prediction. Main middle-layer sweeps show approximately constant nonlinear FVU at fixed L0 across tested widths, while increasing L0 reduces it. Appendix sweeps at other layers show some width-dependent decline, with uncertainty from sparse available configurations. Appendix A.4 reports a similar pattern for the selected token sequence.
location: Section 4.3, Equation 12; Figures 1–2; Appendices A.2 and A.4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Supplementary residual dictionaries can improve domain-specific reconstruction and activation-replacement cross-entropy over a frozen general SAE with approximately five additional active features. Table 1 reports EV increases and reported LLM CE decreases in all six model–domain cells, with L0 increasing by five in each. Qwen Russian EV changes from 0.455 to 0.725 and CE from 4.716 to 2.060; Llama chemistry EV changes from 0.551 to 0.702 and CE from 1.208 to 0.995. Evaluation-set sizes, repeated-run uncertainty, and statistical significance tests are not supplied.
Specific finding: Language-specific residual SAE adaptation can improve reconstruction explained variance across several non-English language domains with a small increase in average active-feature count. Table 5 reports higher EV in all seven language rows, with L0 increasing by five in every row. Japanese EV rises from 0.348 to 0.695 at L0 58 to 63; Polish EV rises from 0.510 to 0.748 at L0 52 to 57. The proposed explanation of Japanese's larger gain through its writing system is not separately tested.
Specific finding: Sufficiently trained single-domain residual dictionaries can preserve general-text SAE reconstruction and activation-replacement cross-entropy close to the frozen baseline. Across chemistry, Russian, and UN-debate additions to each of two model dictionaries, Table 2 reports general EV and CE changes below 1%. Qwen chemistry EV changes from 0.719 to 0.717 and CE from 2.385 to 2.390; Llama Russian EV changes from 0.672 to 0.676 and CE from 2.599 to 2.612. L0 is unchanged or increases by one, exceeding a 1% relative change in the latter cases. No statistical equivalence test is reported.
Specific finding: Residual SAE adaptation can retain more general-domain reconstruction quality than full fine-tuning and use fewer active features than dictionary extension at competitive domain reconstruction quality. For UN debates, Boost obtains domain EV 0.774 at L0 61, versus 0.774 at L0 64 for random dictionary extension and 0.703 at L0 57 for the implemented stitching baseline. Full fine-tuning obtains higher domain EV 0.850 but lowers general EV to 0.515 versus Boost's 0.719. Chemistry and Russian extension achieve higher domain EV than Boost, respectively 0.726 versus 0.716 and 0.741 versus 0.725, while using more active features and retaining less general EV. Full fine-tuning also produces the highest domain EV in those comparisons while degrading general EV. Tables 6–7 do not identify which extension initialization they report.
Specific finding: Adding independently trained chemistry, Russian, and UN-debate residual dictionaries together can retain most of their individual reconstruction gains with modest general-domain reconstruction degradation. Three-domain Boost obtains UN-debate EV 0.770 versus single-domain 0.774, chemistry EV 0.711 versus 0.716, and Russian EV 0.714 versus 0.725. Corresponding multi-domain L0 values are 62, 54, and 66. General EV is reported as 0.712–0.715 across these tables, versus approximately 0.719–0.720 baseline. The apparently same combined configuration has inconsistent general-domain entries across tables.
models_studied: ["Qwen-2.5-7B-Base, residual stream after block 24", "Llama-3.1-8B-Base, Llama3.1-8B-Base-L24R-8x SAE"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Chemistry residual SAE features can receive higher automated detection and fuzzing scores than a randomly sampled base-SAE feature panel evaluated on general web text. Appendix A.4 reports mean detection scores of 0.75 for residual features versus 0.67 for base features, and mean fuzzing scores of 0.68 versus 0.64. Detection medians are 0.77 versus 0.65; fuzzing medians are 0.68 versus 0.60. Reported ± values are not explicitly defined. The evaluator configuration, statistical significance, and exact checkpoint for this panel are not separately specified.
Specific finding: Some residual-SAE features learned on chemistry text have activation-based chemistry interpretations that differ from the descriptions assigned to their nearest individual base-SAE features. The authors inspect strongly activating text and report five residual-feature interpretations: oxygen in chemical contexts, chemical and thermal stability, supramolecular structure formation, chemistry energy values, and hydrogen chemistry. Table 11 lists differing descriptions for each feature's three closest base neighbors, some of which remain scientifically related. The representative activation images are unavailable in this rendering, and no blinded semantic assessment or exhaustive base-dictionary search is reported.
models_studied: ["Chemistry residual SAE and base SAE; Appendix A.4 does not explicitly identify the backbone or checkpoint"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: SAEs with comparable replacement cross-entropy can differ substantially on concept-isolation and attribute-intervention benchmark scores. Figure 12 compares MSE-only training on 475M tokens, full end-to-end training on 500M, and MSE followed by 25M-token KL+MSE fine-tuning. Despite comparable cross-entropy scores, full end-to-end SAEs have lower reported RAVEL, feature-absorption, TPP, and SCR performance. The explanation that they learn fundamentally different features is not independently tested.
Specific finding: Short KL+MSE SAE fine-tuning can improve downstream predictive fidelity while producing architecture-dependent gains and losses across supervised interpretability evaluations. Evaluated fine-tuned SAEBench baselines with sparsity approximately maintained. ReLU improves sparse probing and RAVEL but worsens SCR and, as clarified in Appendix G, TPP. TopK shows smaller, less consistent changes, improving SCR/TPP while decreasing RAVEL and unlearning. Choosing the best tested SCR/TPP ablation count yields stronger TopK gains, particularly at larger width; these are selected-best results.

Specific finding: Improved SAE replacement cross-entropy can coexist with lower sparse-probing and spurious-correlation-removal scores in Pythia-160M. Table 3 reports TopK versus iSAE-ME replacement CE of 3.974 versus 3.906, sparse-probing accuracy of 0.909 versus 0.908, SCR of 0.381 versus 0.293, and TPP of 0.043 versus 0.044. iSAE improves probing, SCR, and TPP over AbsTopK despite slightly worse MSE and encoder-code consistency. The very small probing and TPP differences have no reported uncertainty or significance tests; benchmark task counts are unspecified.
Specific finding: An evaluator's ability to distinguish activating from non-activating token contexts using a generated feature explanation provides a useful proxy for feature interpretability.

Specific finding: An LLM's accuracy in classifying activating contexts from a generated feature explanation provides a useful proxy for comparing the semantic interpretability of error-component SAE features.

Specific finding: Sequence detection and token-marking judgments provide inexpensive predictive tests for screening natural-language SAE feature explanations. Evaluates sequence detection and token-marking judgments with balanced accuracy across activation deciles and explanation configurations. Detection uses five activating examples per decile and twenty random non-activating examples; fuzzing uses seven examples per decile, five correctly marked and two incorrectly marked. Average detection/fuzzing balanced accuracy correlates with simulation scoring at Pearson r = 0.61. Timing and token measurements demonstrate inexpensive execution, but manual inspection exposes failures on incorrect markings.
models_studied: ["GPT-2 with approximately 131k\u2013132k-latent TopK SAEs", "Llama-3 70B default explainer/scorer"]
location: Scoring explanations; Results; Scorers; How much more scalable is detection/fuzzing?

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Token-level fuzzing scores can track human ratings of how well SAE explanations describe observed activating text. Human raters evaluated 700 contexts covering 81 feature interpretations, with at least five contexts per feature. Spearman correlations with average human ratings were 0.69 for fuzzing, 0.60 for simulation, 0.59 for detection, 0.34 for surprisal, and 0.32 for embedding. These are reported associations without uncertainty estimates or a significance test of the ranking.
models_studied: ["Llama 3.1 70B Instruct (default context scorer)", "Llama 3.1 70B Base (surprisal scorer)", "Stella-400M (embedding scorer)"]
location: Section 4.1; scorer implementations in Appendix D

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Generating GPT-2 SAE explanations from examples spanning the activation distribution can improve detection and fuzzing scores relative to using only the strongest activating examples. Compares top-10/20/40 examples, 20/40 samples from the top 200, 10/20/40 samples from all available examples, and a mixture of twenty top-200 samples plus twenty unrestricted samples. The text reports better GPT-2 detection and fuzzing from broader sampling, especially at weaker activations. Three randomly selected early-layer features receive additional 1,000-example evaluations visualized across activation intervals.
location: Giving the explainer different samples of top activating examples; Visualizing activation distributions; Figures 3–4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Some SAE features with poor activation-context explanations can have downstream intervention effects that admit useful natural-language descriptions. Generated output-effect descriptions from next-token probability changes on ten prompts per feature and scored clean/intervened generations on thirty other prompts, with up to eight generated tokens. Prompts came from a pool stratified by maximum nonzero activation and were truncated at the first feature activation. At Gemma layer 32, intervention scores show a slight negative relationship with fuzzing scores. Feature 157 of the layer-32 131k SAE illustrates a reputation-related output effect despite detection score 0.6. Relationships vary by layer; numerical correlations and the total number of tested features are not supplied.
location: Sections 3.2.1 and 4.1.1; Figures 3 and A7; Appendices G.1–G.2 and G.4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The harmonic mean of Claude 3.7 Sonnet ratings of concept incorporation, instruction relevance, and fluency provides a useful operational measure of concept-conditioned steering quality.
Specific finding: Descriptions inferred from an SAE feature's activating contexts identify sufficiently appropriate output concepts to evaluate steering along that feature's decoder direction.
Specific finding: Automatically generated SAE concept descriptions adequately identify their associated latent's semantics for evaluating that latent against examples generated from the description.
location: Sections 4 and 6, SAE concept label quality; Appendix B

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Automated activation-context explanation scores can have only modest positive rank agreement with average concept-steering utility across SAE architectures and sparsity settings. The authors compare interpretability and unselected Concept100 steering averages across 90 SAEs, yielding 4,005 unordered pairs. Reported pooled Kendall tau_b is 0.2979 with BCa bootstrap interval [0.1590, 0.4191]; the conditioning aggregate is 0.2499. Model-specific coefficients are 0.2184, 0.4575, and 0.3057. Interpretation is limited by heterogeneous concept inventories, inconsistent conditioning definitions and table groupings, and the displayed formula's omission of tie correction. The architecture and sparsity rows pool multiple models, so they do not isolate a single varying design axis.
Specific finding: An SAE's automated interpretability score can show little rank agreement with the percentage improvement in its steering score obtained through confidence-based feature selection. Table 3 compares automated interpretability with confidence-selection percentage lift across 90 SAEs and 4,005 pairs. Reported pooled Kendall tau_b is −0.0692 with BCa bootstrap interval [−0.2019, 0.0666]; the conditioning aggregate is −0.0568. Individual model coefficients are −0.1402, −0.1448, and −0.0483, with permutation p-values 0.2911, 0.2781, and 0.7157. The sparsity-conditioned summary is slightly positive at 0.0127. These results do not establish a consistent positive relationship, exact population independence, or a population negative relationship. Gains have baseline utility in their denominator and differ from final selected utility.

Specific finding: Lower activation effective rank can be associated with higher dead-feature prevalence in sparse autoencoders trained under comparable dictionary-size and sparsity settings. Evaluate released LlamaScope attention, MLP, and residual dictionaries across layers, then train attention/residual SAEs at layers 7, 15, and 23 with widths 16,384, 32,768, and 65,536 and L0 values 32, 64, and 128. Attention dictionaries consistently have higher dead-feature fractions than corresponding residual dictionaries. For layer 15, width 32,768 and L0=64, the fractions are 54.68% versus 7.96%. Differences among residual layers also show that effective rank alone does not determine death rates.

Specific finding: Adversarial points within hidden-state boxes constructed from prefix paraphrases can substantially change the dominant features of sparse autoencoders and transcoders. Appendix C.1 specifies 1,000 sentences split 600/200/200 and PGD with 200 iterations and four restarts inside per-sample hidden-state boxes. Table 1 reports worst-layer attack-derived top-20 Jaccard upper bounds of 0.27–0.70 for minor regions, 0.06–0.45 for medium regions, and 0.05–0.38 for major regions across nine configurations. These are witnesses bounding worst-case overlap from above. Appendix A additionally reports a selected Gemma layer-16 targeted continuous-hull attack with top-8 Jaccard 0.23; it does not establish that the displayed synonym substitution itself produces the reported feature flip or that an implemented auditor is bypassed.
location: Section 3, Table 1; Appendices A and C.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Population-level token attacks can remain effective at multiple transformer depths, while targeted overlap levels and untargeted disruption exhibit different depth trends. Appendix G reports effective population attacks across tested layers. Initial and post-attack target overlap decrease with depth, whereas untargeted attacks become more disruptive. Exact tested layer lists, layerwise numerical results, and uncertainty are not available in readable form. Explanations involving more abstract or distributed deeper representations are hypotheses rather than independently tested mechanisms.
Specific finding: Synonym substitutions can change population-level SAE top-k membership while preserving the activation status of selected individual latents. The authors request 50 diverse variants per input, each replacing one token with a synonym, and average the evaluation metrics. Table 3 reports population overlap of 73.4%, 70.9%, 71.5%, 68.7%, and 66.2% for the five configurations. Individual activation and deactivation success are both 0% in every row. These findings distinguish population coordinate changes from binary changes in selected individual latents.
models_studied: ["Gemma2-9B with 131k JumpReLU SAEs", "Llama3-8B with 131k TopK SAEs"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Input perturbations that manipulate SAE interpretations may also expose robustness vulnerabilities in transcoders and crosscoders.

Specific finding: Residual-stream SAE features can become more effective at promoting their decoder-associated vocabulary tokens in later transformer layers. The authors report increasing output scores in later layers of both Gemma models, Llama-3.1-8B, and Pythia-70m, using 100 sampled features per layer. Gemma additionally shows stronger early input alignment, whereas Llama and Pythia mostly have low input scores. Pythia sampling excludes features with fewer than ten recorded activations. These cross-sectional measurements do not track individual features developing during training.
Specific finding: Filtering SAE features by their immediate promotion of decoder-associated tokens can select subsets with higher subsequent lexical generation success than unfiltered or size-matched randomly filtered feature sets. The tested intervention increases one SAE activation by a steering factor times the maximum activation and decodes the modified representation. In both Gemma models, output-score filtering raises mean Generation Success@20 from approximately 0.5–0.6 without filtering to 1.1–1.4 at threshold 0.9. Random filtering of the same number of features, averaged over ten draws, does not yield comparable gains. Benefits persist within layers 16–25 for Gemma-2-2B and 24–41 for Gemma-2-9B. Appendix B reports similar filtering trends for Llama and Pythia. These are enriched-subset comparisons, not improvements for every feature or concept.

Specific finding: Direct vocabulary projections of visual-position hidden states can increasingly expose the corresponding object class in later language-backbone layers. For 170 LLaVA-1.5 images with target objects of 20,000–30,000 square pixels, the average per-image best-layer fraction of object-patch positions whose vocabulary argmax matches the object class is 23.7%; the average selected layer is 25.7 of 33. An extension to 253 Qwen2VL-2B images reports 6.5% correspondence and average selected layer 25.1 of 29. The text and captions report increasing late-layer correspondence; numerical layerwise curves are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Qualitative examples include object details and non-English readouts. No random-readout baseline or uncertainty estimates are supplied.
location: Section 4.1; Figure 3; Appendix C, Figures 6 and 7

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected Pythia SAE features with dense, apparently unrelated activating tokens can have vocabulary projections that suggest coherent output-oriented interpretations. In the explanation transcript for L4_12420, activating function words and punctuation initially yield no coherent contextual interpretation. Projected tokens including 'her', 'she', and 'herself' lead Llama to identify a female-pronoun association. The post discusses additional output-oriented examples but supplies no causal ablation or quantitative validation of their proposed output effects.
models_studied: ["Pythia model used in the Bias in Bios circuit, size unspecified", "Llama-3 70B explainer"]
location: Sparse Feature Circuits; Some features cannot be explained from their activation patterns

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A tied-weight ReLU-output reconstruction model can encode individual training examples as polygonally arranged hidden vectors rather than organize its input-feature vectors into an analogous clean geometry. Compared visualizations of columns of W with training-example embeddings WX_i after reconstruction training. Small-data solutions organize example embeddings into polygons while feature vectors appear scattered. Included replication comments report qualitatively similar sample geometries, with quantitative differences. The source also reports occasional two-dimensional optimization failures.
Specific finding: Increasing dataset size can shift a sparse reconstruction bottleneck from representing individual training examples in superposition to representing reusable input features in superposition. Swept training-set size and examined feature dimensionalities, example dimensionalities, embeddings, and parameter norms. Small-data example dimensionalities track approximately m/T; large-data solutions contain five prominent feature directions arranged as a pentagon, with other features making individually small contributions. Adam Jermyn's included replication reproduces the qualitative regimes but places generalization onset near T=20,000 rather than T=5,000 and intermediate-regime onset near T=100 rather than T=700.
Specific finding: Sparse reconstruction models can exhibit data double descent around a transition between example-specific and reusable-feature superposition, even when reconstruction targets equal the inputs and no label noise is added. Averaged test reconstruction loss across four dataset seeds per dataset size and observed a bump between the example-superposition and feature-superposition regimes. Included researcher reports describe qualitative replication. Marius Hobbhahn also reports double descent after changing sparsity and feature count, using other losses, or adding an intermediate ReLU, but detailed protocols and results for those variants are deferred to an external post.
Specific finding: Repeated training examples can acquire dedicated superposed representations that displace reusable feature representations in a capacity-limited reconstruction model. Introduced repeated datapoints into datasets large enough to learn generalizing features. The illustrated T=30,000 condition with five occurrences of a repeated item contains its representation alongside four generalizing features. Additional repeated datapoints replace further generalizing features; in the reported condition with more than five repeated datapoints, five datapoints are embedded and the five ordinarily learned features are suppressed. These are selected demonstrations rather than a universal capacity rule.
Specific finding: At sufficiently large dataset-to-feature ratios, the repetition count associated with high-dimensional encoding of a repeated example can scale approximately with dataset size divided by input-feature count. Compared repetition counts R and dataset-to-feature ratios T/N in two sparsity/feature-count settings. At larger T/N, the boundary between repeated examples inside and outside the top 0.1% of example dimensionalities approximately follows R=0.4T/N. At low T/N, models require more than T/N repetitions, and the results are noisy. The accompanying loss-benefit balancing argument is heuristic and drops constant factors; it is not a formal threshold derivation.
location: "Datapoint Features" vs "Generalizing Features"; Comments & Replications; Optimization Failures in 2D

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Datapoint-feature formation in sparse absolute-value transcoders depends jointly on input repetition and activation sparsity pressure, with the reported memorization measure tracking their product. A two-hyperparameter scan varies repetition frequency and sparsity regularization. The note reports that their product controls datapoint-feature formation under its memorization metric. Exact scan ranges, numerical relationships, and uncertainty are absent from the supplied text.
models_studied: ["One-layer sparse ReLU transcoders approximating coordinatewise absolute value"]
location: When Do Datapoint Features Form?; Aside: How do we Detect a Datapoint Feature?

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Memorization in real neural networks may involve example-specific features stored in superposition alongside reusable features.

Specific finding: Constraining SAE decoder directions to cosine similarity at least 0.8 with random initialization can retain substantial residual-activation reconstruction fidelity while falling below fully trained dictionaries. BatchTopK soft-frozen versus fully trained explained variance is 0.785 versus 0.852 at Gemma layer 12, 0.812 versus 0.887 at Gemma layer 19, and 0.699 versus 0.805 at Llama layer 16. JumpReLU values are 0.789 versus 0.852, 0.816 versus 0.887, and 0.707 versus 0.805. Fully frozen encoder or decoder directions generally incur larger reconstruction losses.
Specific finding: SAEs with decoder directions constrained near random initialization can receive activation-context explanation scores close to those of fully trained SAEs. Each evaluated configuration samples 200 latents after excluding activation frequencies below 1e-6. Descriptions use up to 15 top-activating sequences; evaluation uses 50 activating and 50 random non-activating sequences per latent. Section 4.2 reports mean BatchTopK accuracy of 0.88 for soft-frozen versus 0.90 for fully trained features, while the abstract gives 0.87 versus 0.90. Approximately 30% of frozen-encoder BatchTopK latents reportedly score above 0.7. No statistical equivalence test or independent semantic ground truth is supplied.
Specific finding: Some SAE reconstruction gains may arise from adapting representations that remain near initialization rather than discovering substantially new decoder directions.

Specific finding: Transcoder features strongly aligned to a neuron's encoder and decoder can have firing patterns closely predicted by that neuron's activation, while decoder alignment alone is less reliable. Section 3.3 reports high AUC when predicting neuron-feature firing from matched-neuron activation. Appendix F samples 43 pairs per layer across seven layers, requiring decoder cosine at least 0.8 while varying encoder cosine from 0.30 to 1.00. Of 301 pairs, 238 fire more than 50 times in the stated 20,320-token evaluation. Median rescaled AUC is 0.956 and 0.996 in encoder-cosine bins 0.70–0.85 and 0.85–1.00, versus 0.224 and 0.319 in lower bins. Thus the strong correspondence is conditional on encoder alignment, rather than established for every decoder-matched feature. The appendix also describes a different token count for displayed example panels.
Specific finding: Initializing transcoder encoders near sign-split neuron directions can increase learned neuron alignment and reduce dead features. Initialize encoder rows at sampled signed neuron directions with 10% Gaussian noise and decoders at zero, then train with the ordinary objective. Appendix H reports three seeds per run, increased neuron-feature fractions across settings, and fewer dead features in sparse configurations below k=64. Section 3.7 reports large increases using a 0.5 alignment threshold; appendix analyses use stricter criteria, so those percentages cannot be treated as interchangeable measures of neuron-feature prevalence.
Specific finding: Constraining transcoder features toward neurons or sparse neuron combinations can increase weight alignment with modest reconstruction costs without improving automated cluster discrimination. NFT gates child features on parent-neuron TopK activity; SNRL regularizes encoder and decoder directions toward four-neuron reconstructions. Against the k=32 baseline, Table 14 reports FVU 0.195, 0.221, and 0.213 for baseline, NFT, and SNRL; corresponding KL values are 1.29, 1.15, and 1.38. Table 15 reports cluster-match accuracy 0.937, 0.918, and 0.927 and top-neuron-match accuracy 0.731, 0.598, and 0.657, respectively. Evaluation starts from 50 randomly selected eligible neurons, but methods drop panels with insufficient viable clusters. Gemmascope FVU values use a different target from the authors' transcoders and cannot be directly compared as a controlled reconstruction benchmark.
Specific finding: Selected peaked character-count features in a transcoder can have individual MLP-neuron counterparts with similar tuning curves. Wrap Pride and Prejudice at widths 30–80 in five-character increments, yielding 14,455 samples. Compute feature firing-rate and TopK-neuron activation tuning curves by within-line character position and filter for peaked responses. Seven of eight selected layer-20 features have matching neuron tuning curves, with correlations from 0.44 to 0.98; not every tuning match satisfies the weight-alignment definition. Across all layers, only 27 of 142 loosely peak-filtered features pass the appendix's encoder-alignment criterion. These results do not show that most character-count features across the entire model are strict neuron features.
Specific finding: In an MLP-output SAE, features geometrically aligned with native neuron output directions can account for a disproportionate fraction of feature firings and cross-seed matches. Train two MLP-output SAEs differing in initialization seed. Features with encoder and decoder absolute cosine above 0.5 to the same neuron decoder constitute 4.39% of the dictionary and 19.2% of feature firings. Cross-seed matching requires both encoder and decoder cosine above 0.7. Of features that recur, 76.1% are neuron-aligned; reported recurrence rates are 83.4% for neuron-aligned versus 1.20% for other features. Median firing density is 14 times higher for neuron-aligned features on 178k FineWeb tokens.
Specific finding: A transcoder trained on a mixture-of-experts MLP can learn many neuron-aligned features while leaving most native neurons without a matched feature, with neuron initialization increasing both alignment and coverage. Compare standard random initialization with neuron initialization for transcoders targeting an MoE layer containing 131,584 shared and routed neurons. Neuron features constitute 15.8% versus 30.7% of dictionary features; native-neuron coverage is 25.6% versus 44.0%. The experiment demonstrates incomplete geometric replication in this setup, rather than the hypothesized ideal in which every neuron receives two sign-specific features.
location: Section 3.3; Appendix F; Figures 5 and 21–23; Table 11

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Subtracting an active single-token-associated SAE contribution can reduce its assigned token's final logit more than subtracting approximately activation-matched non-single-token contributions. The paper subtracts f_i times the decoder vector from native residual activations using 4,096 sequences of 128 tokens per model. It reports one-sided Mann–Whitney significance after global BH correction in 178/208 layers across seven full-depth configurations: 26/26 and 24/25 for Gemma-2-2B GemmaScope/BatchTopK, 42/42 for Gemma-2-9B, 9/26 and 18/25 for Gemma-3-1B, 31/32 for Llama-3.1-8B, and 28/32 for DeepSeek-R1. GPT2 has a separate significant single-layer condition. Controls have mean active activation within a factor of two, which does not ensure matched perturbation norms or coactivity at each position. Lowest-magnitude-quartile effects remain significant. Nearest-alignment controls retain significance in 8/9 configurations, but median cosine mismatches are 0.18 for GemmaScope and 0.51 for LlamaScope. The genuinely in-band Gemma subset also shows a pooled difference. Appendix correction scope and control multiplicity descriptions are inconsistent with parts of the main protocol.
Specific finding: In selected Gemma SAE configurations, single-token-associated feature ablations have larger final target-logit effects at later layers while aggregate downstream logit-lens disruption is larger for earlier interventions. Gemma-2-2B final-logit damage correlates with depth at Spearman rho=0.97 for BatchTopK and 0.70 for GemmaScope; Gemma-2-9B GemmaScope reports rho=0.81. Gemma-2-2B first-versus-last layer quartiles have mean signed logit changes −0.006 versus −0.182 for BatchTopK and −0.020 versus −0.262 for GemmaScope. Early aggregate downstream disruption is reported as 4–16× larger than late disruption across four Gemma-2-2B/Gemma-3-1B configurations. The downstream aggregation's scale and normalization are insufficiently specified for stronger mechanistic interpretation.
Specific finding: In a selected same-model, same-layer, same-width community SAE comparison, JumpReLU features can produce larger target-token rank changes under ablation than TopK features. Among 142 matched pairs, mean rank changes are 199.5 for TopK versus 311.0 for JumpReLU (p=0.036, r=0.20); maximum rank changes are 325.5 versus 513.4 (p=0.003, r=0.27). The appendix describes TopK budgets {25,50,75,100} and JumpReLU average active counts {14,26,95}, without fully specifying their aggregation for the paired test. The direction opposes the BatchTopK-versus-GemmaScope comparison, weakening a simple competitive-versus-independent gating explanation without isolating a particular alternative recipe factor.
Specific finding: Reducing the retained-feature budget can increase mean single-token-associated feature ablation damage in selected TopK SAEs. TopK budgets 25, 50, 75, and 100 yield mean signed target-logit changes −0.152, −0.094, −0.060, and −0.036, with 169–180 detected features per configuration. The four group means have Pearson r=0.98 with budget, p=0.020; the reported per-feature association is much smaller, Spearman rho=0.077, p=0.04. JumpReLU configurations with average active counts 14, 26, and 95 have means −0.041, −0.039, and −0.043, without a detected monotonic trend. No repeated-training uncertainty is supplied.
location: Section 4.5; Table 6; Appendices B.6–B.7 and B.12–B.14

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Better language-modeling performance can accompany greater agreement between caption-embedding neighborhoods and corresponding image-embedding neighborhoods, with stronger agreement also associated with more capable vision models. Measured k=10 neighborhood overlap on 1,024 WIT image-caption pairs. Used image class tokens, average-pooled language states, L2 normalization, and truncation of feature elements above the 95th percentile; selected maximum alignment across layer comparisons, including concatenated features. Alignment generally increased with language score measured as 1 minus bits per byte over four million OpenWebText tokens. The evaluation does not isolate a causal effect of parameter count or use independently selected alignment layers.
models_studied: ["BLOOM 560M\u20137.1B", "OpenLLaMA 3B, 7B, and 13B", "LLaMA 7B, 13B, 33B, and 65B", "ImageNet-21K ViTs", "MAE ViTs", "DINOv2 ViTs", "CLIP ViTs", "Classification-fine-tuned CLIP ViTs"]
location: Section 2.3; Figure 3; Appendices B and C.2

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Requiring a representation to support more tasks may narrow the set of competent solutions and thereby promote representational convergence.
Specific finding: Increasing model capacity may promote representational convergence when larger function classes contain better approximations to a shared optimum and optimization can find them.
Specific finding: If increasing network size strengthens a preference for simple data-fitting solutions, scaling may concentrate learned representations into a smaller common solution space.
Specific finding: Language-model MLP activations can be usefully approximated by sparse nonnegative combinations of a stable, overcomplete dictionary of feature directions.
location: Introduction; Methods: Sparse autoencoder architecture and training; Conclusion: possible differences between synthetic and language-model data

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Gemma activation vectors admit a useful approximation as sparse additive combinations of one-dimensional feature directions, motivating analysis through overcomplete SAE dictionaries.

Specific finding: WordNet feature vectors estimated from whitened language-model unembeddings exhibit hierarchical similarities and approximately orthogonal increments that persist when independent estimation subsets break guaranteed set inclusion. The reported cosine heatmaps reflect WordNet graph proximity, including sibling similarity absent from shuffled controls. Parent vectors are approximately orthogonal to child-minus-parent vectors, and successive hierarchy increments are approximately orthogonal. Independently selecting 70% of each synset's tokens preserves the reported orthogonality for original unembeddings while disrupting it for shuffled controls. Full-set shuffled estimates also exhibit orthogonality, showing that set inclusion can confound the unsplit analysis. Findings are reported through figures and qualitative descriptions without aggregate uncertainty or effect-size tables.
Specific finding: Estimated Gemma-2B WordNet noun representations exhibit the predicted hierarchical orthogonality more clearly after vocabulary whitening than under the centered original Euclidean metric. Appendix F estimates noun-feature vectors from centered original Gemma unembeddings without whitening. The narrative and Figure 12 caption report hierarchical cosines departing from zero, contrasting with the approximately orthogonal structure in the whitened analysis. Numerical aggregate comparisons are not supplied.
Specific finding: For selected Gemma-2B lexical hierarchies, adding an estimated parent-contrast direction produces much larger mean token-pair log-odds changes for the parent contrast than for its subordinate contrast. Table 1 computes context-independent log-odds changes as the added normalized vector dotted with token-unembedding differences. For plant⇒animal versus mammal⇒reptile, parent and child mean±SD changes are 5.1265±1.1731 and −0.0600±1.2190. For fluid⇒solid versus crystal⇒food, they are 9.8296±1.1099 and 0.3770±1.5410. For scientist⇒contestant versus athlete⇒player, they are 14.4222±0.9458 and −0.1545±1.1426. These are final-softmax calculations using nonsplit estimation sets, not sampled generation or internal-mediation tests.
location: Section 5.2, Figures 4–5; Appendix F, Figures 9–10 and 14–20; Appendix G

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Multilingual BERT's estimated syntactic information gains can be substantially larger against trainable type-level or fixed random embeddings than against pretrained fastText embeddings. Tables 1–4 compare the same BERT representations with fastText, trainable type-level embeddings labeled one-hot, and fixed random type embeddings. Gains against the trainable controls range from 6.9–31.4% of label entropy for POS and 11.9–33.7% for dependency labels; fixed-random-control gains range from 8.3–33.1% and 16.4–40.4%, respectively. All these control comparisons have positive estimated gains, whereas six POS comparisons with fastText are nonpositive. The appendix notes limitations on handling unseen word types.
models_studied: ["Multilingual BERT", "Language-specific fastText embeddings", "Trainable type-level embeddings", "Fixed random type-level embeddings", "ReLU MLP probes"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Trained contextual representations and untrained contextualization baselines can produce similar part-of-speech probing accuracies while differing substantially in their support for arbitrary word-type memorization. Linear probes achieve 96.6% accuracy and 31.4 points selectivity on ELMo2, versus 96.3% and 20.6 points on Proj0. MLP-1 probes achieve 97.0% and 8.8 points on ELMo2, versus 97.1% and 1.6 points on Proj0. Proj0 retains pretrained non-contextual embeddings and is not an entirely randomly initialized representation pipeline. The tests demonstrate differing control-task performance, without establishing which specific linguistic features explain ELMo2 accuracy.
models_studied: ["ELMo, second contextual BiLSTM layer", "Proj0: untrained BiLSTM over ELMo character-CNN embeddings"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Learned style and content subspaces can differ in their prediction of visual cortical activity, with style favored in early visual areas and content favored in higher object-related regions. Separate neural encoding models used learned content and style features to predict NSD fMRI responses on the 1,000 images viewed by all four analyzed subjects. The text reports a style advantage in V1/V2 and a content advantage in higher visual regions. Numerical effect sizes, the prediction metric, detailed fitting procedures, and the specific model architectures underlying Figure 8 are not supplied.
Specific finding: Learned semantic sentence subspaces can predict language-cortex activity better than learned syntactic subspaces, while the original combined sentence representation can remain the strongest predictor. The authors compare syntactic, semantic, and original sentence representations as predictors of responses in language cortex defined by a words-versus-nonwords localizer. The text reports semantic subspaces outperforming syntactic ones, with original representations strongest overall. The Pereira analysis uses 627 sentences and five participants completing both full-sentence experiments. Exact effect sizes, the prediction metric, encoding-model fitting details, and architecture-specific results are not supplied.
Specific finding: Semantic caption subspaces and content subspaces of sentence-generated images can outperform their syntactic and style counterparts in cross-modal prediction of brain activity. Semantic representations extracted from image captions are reported to predict visual-cortex responses better than syntactic representations. For Pereira sentences, the authors generate images and average their representations over varying numbers of images per stimulus. Image-content subspaces outperform style subspaces in predicting language-cortex activity and reportedly approach original sentence-representation performance. Numerical effects, image counts, generation specifications, fitting details, and encoding-analysis model identities are not provided.
models_studied: ["Pretrained vision models with learned content/style decompositions; specific encoding-analysis architectures unspecified"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Steering a language model at a token preceding a poetry line using reconstructed edits to an NLA's anticipated rhyme can change the line's eventual ending. At the newline following 'grab it', NLA explanations mention a prospective rabbit ending. Replacing rabbit-related content with mouse-related content and injecting the reconstruction difference changes subsequent endings toward mouse or house. The appendix reports elimination of rabbit completions at steering strengths at least 0.5, but fewer than 80% of completions end in mouse or house because some degenerate; the main text describes steering as successful roughly half the time without specifying a common success definition. Direct reconstructed-activation replacement fails to change Opus behavior but consistently produces mouse outputs in Haiku 3.5 at a previously localized planning layer. These tests do not establish how planned endings shape the line's earlier wording or structure.
location: Planning in Poetry; Appendix: Planning in Poetry steering details

experiment_summary: Specific finding: GoogLeNet components displayed through semantic dictionaries have sufficiently consistent visual meanings across input images, and their feature visualizations represent those meanings accurately enough to interpret the interfaces.

Specific finding: Concept-synthesis activation scores can distinguish true ImageNet output-class labels from randomly assigned class labels across several vision-classifier architectures. Across ResNet18, DenseNet161, GoogLeNet, and ViT-B/16, mean true-label AUC is 0.98–0.99 versus 0.44–0.49 for random labels. True-label MAD ranges from 6.46 to 13.12 versus -0.19 to 0.09 for random labels. Appendix A.4 reports similar separation under a class-exclusion variant, although its prose describes excluding target-class controls while its caption describes excluding the target class from random synthetic explanations.
Specific finding: CoSy output-label AUC can remain near perfect with little variation across SDXL generation seeds for selected ImageNet classes. Across ten generation seeds, the six classwise mean AUCs range from 0.9919 to 1.0000, with reported standard deviations no larger than 0.0038. Table 8 reports an overall mean of 0.9984 ± 0.0007. These are changes to image-generation seeds, rather than separately trained target networks.

Specific finding: SDXL images generated from ImageNet class names can produce output-neuron activation distributions that substantially overlap those of natural images from the corresponding classes. The authors report slightly higher synthetic-image activations and synthetic-versus-natural MAD summaries for which zero lies within one standard deviation across all four models. A ResNet18 coffee-mug example is described as showing strongly overlapping activation distributions. No equivalence test or general exclusion of synthetic-image artifacts is supplied; numerical plot values are unavailable in the text rendering.

Specific finding: Searching neuron graphs for tokens shared between their context and activating-token sets can surface candidate neurons responsive to repeated token sequences. The authors search for graphs containing the same token in context and activating roles, reporting many repeated-token candidates. Section 4.2 describes one candidate responding to diverse tokens in repeating patterns such as 'ab…ab'. No controlled held-out repetition test, causal ablation, or search-efficiency benchmark is reported.
models_studied: ["Pile-trained six-layer SoLU autoregressive transformer with 3,072 MLP neurons per layer"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Iterative multimodal-agent neuron descriptions can identify generated images with higher average positive neuron activation than descriptions produced by MILAN from fixed exemplars. Compared MAIA and MILAN descriptions for 300 real-model neurons. Separate GPT-4 instances generated and selected positive and neutral image prompts, followed by DALL-E 3 synthesis and activation measurement. Table A3 reports higher model-average positive activation for MAIA in all three architectures, with nonuniform layerwise results. Expert descriptions were collected for approximately 25% of neurons and were often comparable on this metric. CLIP-Dissect was also evaluated in Table A3. These comparisons do not establish complete activation-function recovery or human-level equivalence.
Specific finding: Multimodal-agent descriptions of detector-defined synthetic neurons can match their specified concept labels better than MILAN descriptions and receive pairwise preferences close to those of expert descriptions. Constructed single-concept, disjunctive, and conditional synthetic neurons, with top exemplars from CC3M. Ten crowdworkers performed each pairwise description comparison against the specified label. MAIA was preferred over MILAN in 73% of comparisons and over experts in 53% on the expert-annotated subset; expert labels were preferred over MILAN in 83%. Predictive image tests also reportedly favored MAIA over MILAN. Table 1's confidence-interval formatting is unclear, so no reliable interval interpretation is asserted.
location: Section 4.1; Figure 4; Appendix C, Tables A3–A4

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A BERT classifier trained on MQNLI can exhibit natural-logic-consistent interchange behavior on substantially larger selected input subsets than a BiLSTM classifier trained on the same task. Across the variables reported in Table 1a, BERT’s best clique sizes range from 5.5% to 38.3% of 1,000 selected examples, versus 0.4% to 2.5% for BiLSTM. For the object noun-phrase relation, BERT reaches 383/1,000 at layer four above the premise object-adjective token, versus 7/1,000 for BiLSTM. Every tested neighboring object-phrase causal model obtained by adding one or removing one or two lexical inputs yields a smaller BERT clique than 383; the largest reported alternative reaches 372. Results establish correspondence on the selected subsets rather than a complete natural logic implementation.
models_studied: ["English bert-base fine-tuned on MQNLI", "Multilayer BiLSTM trained on MQNLI"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Supervising an aligned phrase-relation variable through interchange intervention training can yield nearly perfect MQNLI classification and aligned intervention accuracy in BERT when the intervention site is sufficiently late. Section 6 reports approximately 100% behavioral and interchange accuracy on the reported evaluation set for IIT aligned at layer 6 or later, with poorer results at early alignments. The evaluated layers are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10. Training samples 50,000 base examples and 20 sources per base, attempting to include ten impactful sources, and reuses the resulting one million pairs each epoch. Dataset splits contain 500,000/60,000/10,000 training/development/test examples. Exact Figure 4 values and seed uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: The natural logic variables used to generate MQNLI labels provide interpretable candidate targets for explaining how neural models solve MQNLI.
location: Section 4, Multiply Quantified NLI Dataset; Section 5.1, Formulating Our Hypotheses

experiment_summary: Specific finding: In MQNLI-trained BERT, accurate and selective decoding of phrase-relation information can occur at many more neural locations than exhibit corresponding causal behavior under interchange interventions. The authors probe representations using 12,800 randomly selected MQNLI examples. They report accuracy and selectivity, defining selectivity as probe accuracy minus control accuracy and describing control accuracy as training accuracy on a random node-type-to-relation mapping task. Section 5.2 and Figure 4 report widespread object noun-phrase relation decoding, whereas impactful interchange success and clique size identify fewer locations. Numerical probe scores and the full control-task protocol are unavailable in the supplied text.

Specific finding: GPT-2 small retains substantial year-span greater-than behavior after the tested PCA-direction ablations or LEACE erasure of linearly extractable start-year information from attention-head outputs. PCA reveals ordered year geometry in relevant head outputs and MLP inputs, with related structure in static embeddings. Ablating the PCA dimensions produces little reported performance change, without a numerical result or detailed ablation specification. LEACE erasure from attention-head output leaves 64.7% probability difference versus the 81.7% baseline. The remaining behavior limits the explanatory sufficiency of these tested representations; it does not prove that structured numeric information has no causal role.

Specific finding: Network-level quadratic correction can reduce isolated activation-patching estimation error across several language-model families while substantially worsening estimates for some finite replacements. Single-step HVP lowers Table 2 top-five error in 13/14 pairs. Pythia-410M IOI instead worsens from 22.34% to 47.48%; five-step HVP reaches 18.03%. Table 11 reports prompt-level median reductions of 72.0–90.4% for listed head settings, 55.8–66.7% for preactivation neurons, and 2.2–7.0% for postactivation neurons. Table 2 prompt counts and some model/task descriptions conflict with setup prose.
Specific finding: Multi-step HVP can produce lower isolated-component estimation error than the tested Integrated Hessians implementations. MS-HVP K=5 has lower displayed top-five error than IH-PI in all nine available Table 2 comparisons. In Table 9, cost-ten MS-HVP errors are 18.03%, 2.97%, and 40.66% on Pythia IOI, GPT-2 IOI, and Gemma factual, versus cost-ten IH-PI errors of 22.22%, 10.15%, and 44.41%. Listed higher-cost IH-DR variants also have larger errors. No valid universal weighting-based inferiority theorem is established by these comparisons.
Specific finding: A downstream Hessian correction can reduce isolated SAE-feature activation-patching estimation MAE in GPT-2 IOI at selected residual-stream layers. Table 17 reports 2,476 and 2,500 features at layers 5 and 9. MAE decreases from 0.000048 to 0.000009 and from 0.000669 to 0.000097, reported as 81.5% and 85.5% reductions using underlying precision. AP correlations are already 0.9999 and 0.9996; corrected correlations round to 1.0000. Feature-count aggregation, intervention implementation details, and uncertainty intervals are not specified.
Specific finding: Network-level HVP correction can reduce attention-head patch-effect estimation MAE under semantically coherent entity-swap prompt corruptions. Table 13 reports 46 entity-swap prompt pairs per model. GPT-2 MAE falls from 0.00340 to 0.00156, a reported 54.1% reduction; Pythia-410M falls from 0.00272 to 0.00112, a reported 58.8% reduction. Listed totals of 7,056 and 18,816 records are inconsistent with 46 pairs times 144 and 384 heads, respectively. No uncertainty intervals are provided.
Specific finding: Quadratic attribution refinement can improve overlap with activation-patching-based head rankings at selected circuit-selection boundaries. Table 4 reports 200 Greater-Than prompts per model: GPT-2 top-five overlap rises from 70.1% for AP to 83.2% for five-step HVP, and Pythia-410M rises from 76.0% to 80.4% for single-step HVP. Appendix E.10's 50-prompt GPT-2 IOI experiment reports top-20 overlap increasing from 95% to 100%. Global rank changes are small, and Table 15 includes worsened NDCG scores. Circuit-head counts and overlap baselines differ across sections.

Specific finding: In pretrained BERT-base, source-vector norms after the value transformation and output projection vary within attention heads, so weighted-vector magnitudes are not a fixed rescaling of attention weights. Across 144 heads, the mean coefficient of variation of ||f(x)|| is 0.22, with minimum and maximum head-level coefficients of 0.12 and 0.37. Input-vector norms have mean coefficient of variation 0.12 across layers. Appendix B additionally examines transformation singular values as a possible explanation of transformed-vector dispersion, without experimentally isolating its cause.
Specific finding: In pretrained BERT-base, less frequent word types tend to have larger transformed-value norms, while their attention weights have a much weaker relationship with frequency rank. Spearman correlation between frequency rank and transformed-vector norm is 0.75, compared with 0.06 for attention weight. Excluding special tokens, periods, and commas gives correlations of 0.69 and 0.28, respectively. Appendix D.4 specifies averaging each token’s measurements across layers and heads before calculating the correlations.
Specific finding: Using projected weighted-vector norms instead of attention weights can improve source–target word alignment extracted from German-to-English translation Transformers. For four-head models, best-layer AWI AER falls from 29.8 ± 3.7 with weights to 25.0 ± 1.5 with norms; best-layer AWO AER falls from 47.7 ± 1.7 to 41.4 ± 1.4. For eight-head models, corresponding AWI scores are 38.7 ± 8.9 versus 26.3 ± 1.9, and AWO scores are 49.3 ± 1.2 versus 43.4 ± 0.8. Values are means and standard deviations across five training seeds. Layer-average AER also improves in each setting. SmoothGrad and statistical-aligner comparator scores are imported from cited studies rather than rerun here.
Specific finding: Weighted transformed-vector norms can differ from raw attention weights on short sequences where nullspace-based effective attention leaves those weights unchanged. Appendix G compares Pearson correlations of raw attention weights with effective attention and with weighted-vector norms as a function of token length. The authors report that effective attention equals raw attention for short sequences in the comparison, whereas norm-based scores differ for both short and long sequences because they incorporate vector scaling. No numerical plot values are available in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Global input-token attribution scores can be constructed by multiplying layerwise matrices of normalized, clipped L1-proximity contributions from transformed source-token vectors.

Specific finding: Using clipped output-proximity scores instead of transformed-vector magnitudes can improve token-erasure attribution metrics when both are aggregated with rollout. Table 4 reports higher comprehensiveness and lower sufficiency for L2-proximity ALTI than Norms in all twelve configurations. BERT SST-2 changes from 0.134/0.180 to 0.300/0.045; RoBERTa IMDB changes from 0.133/0.162 to 0.203/0.086. Sample counts and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: L1 output proximity generally yields better ALTI token-erasure scores than L2 output proximity in the evaluated masked-encoder classifiers. Table 5 compares L1 and L2 ALTI. L1 improves comprehensiveness in eleven of twelve configurations, with BERT agreement favoring L2 slightly, 0.374 versus 0.372. L1 sufficiency is lower in nine configurations and tied in three. RoBERTa Yelp improves from 0.108/0.104 to 0.138/0.070. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
Specific finding: Including the FFN module's second layer normalization can have negligible effect on ALTI's measured token-deletion attribution performance. Figure 9 is described as comparing predicted-class probability-drop curves with and without the second layer normalization, with means and standard deviations across ten BERT seeds. The text reports negligible influence but supplies no numerical effect size or equivalence test. The curves themselves are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: For teacher-forced translation, extracting alignment when a target word is supplied as decoder input can yield better best-layer alignment accuracy than extracting it when that word is predicted as output. Across five seeds, four-head best-layer norm AER is 25.0 under AWI versus 41.4 under AWO; eight-head scores are 26.3 versus 43.4. Best-layer weight-based extraction also favors AWI. Layerwise analyses report better input-word alignment in earlier layers and better output-word alignment in later layers. The authors acknowledge that AWI observes the correct target word under teacher forcing.
Specific finding: Larger average cross-attention contribution norms can be associated with better input-word alignment but worse output-word alignment, making norm-based head selection dependent on the alignment timing convention. For the illustrated four-head analysis, average contribution norm correlates with AWI AER at Spearman −0.44 and Pearson −0.52, but with AWO AER at +0.56 and +0.55. The eight-head analysis gives AWI correlations −0.26 and −0.50, and AWO correlations +0.40 and +0.40.
