Highest-norm head selection yields five-seed AWI AER 35.5 ± 21.0 for four heads and 24.9 ± 1.7 for eight heads, whereas AWO scores are 87.1 ± 2.3 and 87.2 ± 0.6. In the four-head AWI condition, four seeds score between 23.6 and 25.7 and the remaining seed scores 77.5.
models_studied: ["fairseq German-to-English Transformer, 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 4 heads", "fairseq German-to-English Transformer, 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers, 8 heads"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected late-layer GPT2 neurons can change mean next-token distribution entropy through final LayerNorm scaling while largely retaining the true next token's prediction rank. Fixing GPT2-medium-a neuron L23.945 to larger activations increases final LayerNorm scale and mean predictive entropy while largely retaining true-next-token rank. Neuron L22.2882, whose output direction has cosine −0.886 with L23.945, produces opposite mean effects. Comparisons use 20 random neurons from the final two layers, excluding the top norm decile and bottom logit-variance decile. Analogous interventions are reported for GPT2-small-a. Sample counts and numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the prose, and individual entropy effects sometimes reverse.

Specific finding: Some multilingual language-model computations use shared operation and operand representations combined with separately controllable output-language representations. English-derived interventions switch antonym to synonym and small to hot across three languages while retaining language-appropriate answers; substituting early language features changes output language. Synonym substitution requires activation amplification, with effectiveness crossing over near 4×.
Specific finding: Shared feature activation across translated texts is strongest in middle layers and can be greater in a larger, more capable language model. Feature-set intersection-over-union on translated paragraphs exceeds unrelated-paragraph baselines most strongly in middle layers. Haiku shows greater cross-language overlap than the smaller research model, especially for language pairs with different alphabets.

Specific finding: Rapid harmful fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B-Chat can involve disproportionately large initial losses, parameter-gradient norms, and subsequent distribution changes at early response-token positions. Measured per-token cross-entropy and parameter-gradient norms on 100 harmful demonstrations, plus KL(fine-tuned || initially aligned) on generated HEx-PHI responses. ASR rises from 1.5% initially to 22.4%, 76.4%, and 87.9% after two, four, and six gradient steps, respectively. The accompanying text reports larger early-position losses, gradients, and shifts; numerical profiles are not accessible.
Specific finding: Benign fine-tuning of Llama-2-7B-Chat can exhibit large initial early-token gradients while much of the observed safety regression occurs within the first few optimization steps. Appendix B reports larger initial gradient norms at early response positions. HEx-PHI ASR increases from 1.5% to 13.6% after ten SQL Create Context steps and to 22.1% after ten SAMSum steps. That appendix reports final ASRs of 14.9% and 25.5% after more than 600 steps; these differ from the separately reported three-run means in Table 3.
Specific finding: Reference-relative constrained SFT emphasizing early response positions, combined with learning-rate warmup, can substantially reduce safety loss under selected malicious fine-tuning recipes. Across three reported runs, harmful-example ASR changes from standard-SFT 88.9% to constrained-SFT 4.6% in Llama and from 81.6% to 1.9% in Gemma. Identity-shifting ASR changes from 79.5% to 8.1% and from 83.6% to 9.1%, respectively. Triggered-backdoor ASR changes from 90.9% to 10.9% and from 82.3% to 1.9%. Constrained SFT uses ten warmup steps; separate Llama warmup ablations show substantial contributions from both the objective and warmup, with effects differing by attack.
Specific finding: Allocating stronger constrained-SFT coefficients to early tokens can provide a better safety–utility balance than the tested uniform coefficient settings in Llama-2-7B-Chat. Uniform coefficient 0.1 leaves harmful-example ASR at 86.2%, versus 4.6% with early-biased coefficients. Uniform coefficient 2.0 lowers that ASR to 0.5% but reduces GSM8k accuracy to 2.1%, versus 37.4% with early-biased constraints and 41.7% under standard SFT. Early-biased SAMSum and SQL ROUGE-1 are 50.1 and 98.5, versus standard-SFT 51.7 and 99.1. Table 5 shows that warmup alone substantially reduces benign-task safety regression, limiting attribution of those benefits solely to the constrained loss.

Specific finding: Mismatch between stereotyped assistant prefixes and direct-answer downstream demonstrations may produce large early-token updates that contribute to safety regression during benign fine-tuning.

Specific finding: Geometrically distinct refusal-associated directions can produce similar high-strength increases in both warranted refusal and benign over-refusal, while differing at intermediate strengths. On the stated controlled 200-prompt sets with 100 harmful and 100 benign prompts, strong additions frequently drive refusal and over-refusal toward one. Gemma reaches 1.00 for both metrics on several safety directions. Exceptions include Qwen's incomplete-request direction at refusal 0.50 and over-refusal 0.47. Appendix L explicitly acknowledges distinguishable intermediate-strength curves. Some appendix baselines, accuracy entries, and main-table versus sweep values are inconsistent; the tables do not establish monotonic increases from the stated 0.50 baseline in every condition.
Specific finding: Choosing different refusal-associated steering directions can change the rationale and framing of generated refusals even when refusal remains common. Table 5 assigns outputs to capability, safety, underspecification, generic, or non-refusal categories. In Gemma, Humanizing and Unsupported directions have reported capability-framing purity of 100%, while Incomplete has underspecification purity of 76%. Llama and Qwen show different patterns; Qwen's Incomplete condition is predominantly non-refusal. The stated purity denominator is inconsistent with allowing non-refusal as the dominant category, and the framing judge is not independently validated.
Specific finding: Rewriting extraction prompts toward another non-compliance category while preserving their topics can sometimes change the refusal framing induced by the resulting steering direction. Directions rebuilt at layer 20, position −2, and applied at strength 100 increase target-framing counts for four of six transformations. Safety-to-capability rises from 6/50 to 26/50; underspecification-to-safety rises from 26/50 to 33/50. Safety-to-underspecification falls from 14/50 to 11/50, and safety-to-modality falls from 6/50 to 5/50. The comparator is unsteered output, not steering with the original extraction direction. No uncertainty estimates are supplied. Appendix M reports broad topical overlap across splits, which does not independently eliminate topic-composition confounding.
Specific finding: Contrasts between harmful-refused and benign-complied prompts need not align with contrasts between benign-refused and benign-complied prompts. Split-half family analyses report within-family cosine means of approximately 0.92 for HR–BC and 0.77 for BR–BC, versus approximately 0.10 between those families and approximately 0.12 between their family means. Gold-oracle comparisons also depend on the chosen contrast: training HR–HC aligns at 0.81 ± 0.02 with the gold HR–HC direction, compared with 0.51 ± 0.03 for training HR–BC. These are activation-contrast comparisons, not behavioral intervention tests.
location: Section 4.2; Table 1; Appendix D.1, Tables 10–11; Appendix L

experiment_summary: Specific finding: WildGuard refusal judgments can agree closely with human annotations on XSTest responses, with higher agreement on unanimously labeled cases than on the full response set. WildGuard agrees with unanimous human labels on 96.3% of 401 responses, with Cohen's κ=0.93; phrase matching achieves 90.0% and κ=0.80 on that subset. WildGuard agreement with three-annotator majority labels is 89.5% across all 450 responses. Disagreements include clarification, premise correction, and capability disclaimers accompanied by partial assistance.

Specific finding: Independent application of the same feature-discovery and ablation pipeline to different safety datasets can recover overlapping refusal-related feature sets within a model. Independent HarmBench discovery yielded 39 validated Gemma-3-4B-IT features, 33 shared with WildJailbreak; 21 Qwen3-1.7B features, 15 shared; and 43 Llama-3.2-1B features, 31 shared. The corresponding WildJailbreak validated sets contained 39, 50, and 50 features. Three selected Gemma features had WildJailbreak-versus-HarmBench SC values 0.537 versus 0.544, 0.535 versus 0.517, and 0.493 versus 0.512. HarmBench prompt counts and candidate denominators are not fully reported.
Specific finding: Changing statistical discovery thresholds can leave CAP rankings of shared features and the reported top-ten feature sets unchanged while altering candidate-set membership. Appendix E.2 varies mass ratio over 1.2–5, coverage over 5–100, candidate cap over 40–60, and Cohen’s-d floor over 0–0.5. Table 9 reports shared-feature Spearman correlation 1.00 and top-ten overlap 1.00 in Gemma-3-4B-IT, Qwen3-1.7B, and Llama-3.2-1B. Candidate-set Jaccard ranges are 0.79–1.00, 0.54–1.00, and 0.79–0.96 respectively; the Llama range is explicitly across adjacent settings.

Specific finding: Vocabulary-labeled forward-pass graphs can reveal head readouts consistent with previously identified name-mover and negative-name-mover roles on a selected GPT-2 small IOI prompt. Ran the illustrative IOI prompt discussed by Wang et al. and inspected head vocabulary rankings. Name-mover readouts rank 'Mary' highly, while the displayed negative name mover ranks it very low; the graph also links that head to a memory value sourced from 'Mary'. No causal intervention or quantitative circuit-recovery evaluation was performed.

Specific finding: Layerwise linear probes can reveal network segments that fail to develop linearly useful class representations even when a skip connection enables successful end-to-end training. The authors report that adding the long skip connection makes the deep MNIST model trainable with SGD. Probe profiles after 500 and 2,000 minibatches indicate poor class accessibility in the bypassed first half, which the authors interpret as an unused segment. No ablation or other causal test establishes that the segment has no functional contribution.
models_studied: ["128-layer fully connected MNIST network with 128 hidden units per layer and a long skip connection"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: CNN unit responses can shift across depth from simple visual elements and colors toward objects and scenes. Human annotation of the top 60 segmented activation examples per unit showed early-layer enrichment for simple elements and colors and later-layer enrichment for object and scene concepts in both networks. Semantic distributions included only units above 75% top-example concept precision. The analysis does not establish that every unit follows this progression or identify the circuits producing the later representations.

Specific finding: Selected CaffeNet units show little visible response-facet differentiation in the first two convolutional layers and greater visual diversity in later layers. Applied MFV to high-activating validation examples and displayed four facets per selected unit across all eight layers. Conv1–conv2 examples lacked noticeable facet differences; later examples varied in pose, color, number, context, and object type. Figure 6 explicitly identifies the examples as hand-picked. The proposed explanation in terms of increasing invariance is not separately tested.

Specific finding: Selected regularized activation-maximizing images in an ImageNet-trained AlexNet-like CNN show more complex and varied visual patterns at higher layers. Figure 5 presents optimized stimuli ranging from edges and corners to wheels, eyes, shoulders, faces, handles, and bottles. Its caption reports increasing complexity and variation across depth, particularly between conv5 and fc6, while explicitly stating that examples were hand-picked for diversity and interpretability. Supplementary Figure S1 broadens convolutional-channel coverage but supplies only one image per channel.
models_studied: ["Caffe AlexNet-like ImageNet 2012 classifier with local response normalization after pooling"]
location: Figure 5 and caption; Section S2 and Figure S1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Amplifying detected features at lower versus higher layers of an image classifier can produce a qualitative progression from strokes and simple patterns to complex features and recognizable objects. The post reports lower-layer transformations producing strokes and ornaments and higher-layer transformations producing complex features or objects. Evidence consists of selected demonstrations described in the text, without complexity metrics or a controlled layer-comparison protocol. Figure images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
location: Lower- and higher-layer amplification discussion beginning 'Instead of exactly prescribing which feature'

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Scene-trained and object-trained CNNs with the same architecture can have similar early-layer image preferences but increasingly different later-layer preferences aligned with their training domains. Both networks processed an approximately 200,000-image mixed pool, specified in the footnote as 100,000 ImageNet images and 108,000 SUN images. Images were ranked by layer-average activation. At pool2, ImageNet supplied 55% of ImageNet-CNN's top 100 images and 47% of Places-CNN's. At fc7, the corresponding proportions were 78% and 24%. These rankings demonstrate domain-associated response differences rather than a controlled attribution to supervision type alone.
Specific finding: Among units whose top activation examples achieve greater than 75% human concept precision, later layers of a scene-trained CNN can contain a greater proportion of object- and scene-labeled units than corresponding layers of an object-trained CNN. Workers labeled concepts in each unit's top 60 segmented images, marked examples that did not fit, and assigned one of six semantic groups. Around 60% of units at each evaluated layer exceeded 75% top-example precision. Distributions restricted to these units showed higher object and scene proportions in Places-CNN conv4 and pool5; ImageNet-CNN had more object-part units. This comparison does not isolate the causal effect of scene supervision from other dataset differences.

Specific finding: Probe-derived average depths in pretrained BERT broadly follow a classical linguistic pipeline, with POS information appearing before parsing information, semantic roles, and coreference. Trained task-specific scalar mixtures and separate cumulative-prefix probes on frozen BERT representations for eight linguistic tasks. Compared mixing-weight centers of gravity and incremental development micro-F1 depth summaries. Both metrics broadly order POS, constituents, dependencies, semantic roles, and coreference, with similar ordering in the two BERT sizes.
Specific finding: BERT-base and BERT-large exhibit similar linguistic task ordering and roughly corresponding task-relevant layer locations relative to the top of the encoder. Compared scalar-mixing distributions, cumulative-score profiles, and their depth summaries across BERT-base and BERT-large. The authors report similar task ordering and an approximate stretching of the layer profiles, with task-relevant regions roughly corresponding relative to the model's top.
location: Sections 3–4; Figures 1–2; Appendix A.1, Figures A.2–A.3

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Task-specific scalar-mixing weights over frozen encoder layers provide a useful proxy for where task-relevant linguistic information is localized.
Specific finding: Incremental F1 gains from probes accessing successive prefixes of encoder layers provide an approximate summary of the depth at which linguistic annotation targets become resolvable.
Specific finding: Word pairs sharing a specified lexical relationship can be approximated by a common relation-specific offset in normalized embedding space.

Specific finding: Higher-dimensional RNN word representations can achieve better syntactic analogy and semantic relation-similarity scores under vector-offset evaluation. Across the four reported representations, full-set syntactic accuracy increases from 16.2% to 28.5%, 34.7%, and 39.6%. Semantic Spearman correlation increases from 0.211 to 0.259, 0.270, and 0.275, while MaxDiff accuracy increases from 0.389 to 0.408, 0.416, and 0.418. The largest representation combines several systems, and seed variability is not reported.

Specific finding: Supervised LDA projection can expose clearer semantic difference-vector clusters and approximate parallelogram or trapezoid relations in Gemma-2-2b activations. The authors cluster pairwise representation differences and apply LDA using inter-cluster and intra-cluster covariance. Figure 1 reports tighter semantic clusters and clearer relational quadrilaterals after projection; Appendix B describes silhouette-score comparisons across reduced dimensions. The initial SAE-decoder crystal search mostly found noise. No held-out relational-generalization or causal steering evaluation is supplied.

Specific finding: An FFN output vector extracted from a single relational example can promote corresponding relational outputs for different arguments when substituted into multiple late-layer FFNs in unrelated contexts. Fixed FFN outputs extracted from individual naturalistic examples replace several late FFN updates, typically layers 18–23 in GPT-2 Medium. Relative to normal execution, target answers rise in reciprocal rank; final-layer top-token rates are 21.3% for world capitals, 53.5% for capitalization, and 7.8% for past tense on the respective intervention datasets. Exact denominators for these percentages are not stated in the prose. Additional argument sets include US state capitals, 100 non-color words, and 128 irregular verbs. GPT-J shows strong capitalization transfer but weaker capital and tense effects. Reported no-effect rates in the in-domain/out-of-domain settings are approximately 37%/20% for capitals, 4%/5% for capitalization, and 19%/22% for tense.
Specific finding: A fixed capitalization-related FFN update can partially restore answer accuracy after upper FFNs are ablated in a colored-object task requiring capitalized answers. Replacing the ablated upper FFN updates with the positive casing vector raises accuracy from 4.5% to 29.5%, a 25-percentage-point gain and approximately 72% of the intact model's 41% accuracy. Negative-vector replacement instead reduces abstractive accuracy to 0%. On the extractive variant, both signs harm performance relative to the ablation comparison, with positive replacement more harmful than negative replacement.
Specific finding: Replacing several consecutive late FFN updates with a selected relational vector can promote target answers more strongly than replacing an individual FFN update. Individual late-layer replacements provide roughly similar average target reciprocal-rank boosts across tested layers, but replacing the full late-layer range is more effective. The source reports that a single replacement promotes the target without bringing it to the top of the distribution. This is consistent with cumulative updates but does not establish that all unmodified FFNs implement identical functions.
Specific finding: Replacing selected late FFNs with a capital-retrieval update can increase immediate-answer accuracy on zero-shot capital questions. Replacing late FFNs, described as layers 19–23, with the selected capital update raises zero-shot capital accuracy from 5.6% to 33.0%. A worked Poland example shows that the intact model instead begins a complete sentence containing the correct capital, so the improvement does not establish an equivalent increase in factual knowledge. Appendix D also reports a modest past-tense improvement of about 4.2% over one-shot performance, without specifying the percentage convention.

Specific finding: Attention-output changes induced by in-context learning can have positive average directional alignment with changes induced by restricted key/value finetuning, exceeding alignment with random changes. The authors compute cosine similarity between ICL-minus-zero-shot and finetuning-minus-zero-shot normalized attention outputs. Six-dataset mean SimAOU is 0.186 for GPT 1.3B and 0.225 for GPT 2.7B; corresponding random-change baselines average 0.002 and −0.001. Positive alignment does not establish equivalent updates or a shared learning algorithm.
Specific finding: Restricted key/value finetuning can increase the average similarity of pretrained GPT query-token attention logits to those produced with in-context demonstrations. Mean SimAM between ICL and the comparison model rises from 0.338 before finetuning to 0.442 afterward for GPT 1.3B, and from 0.355 to 0.434 for GPT 2.7B. For GPT 2.7B, SST2 is unchanged at reported precision and CB decreases from 0.228 to 0.217. The metric compares pre-softmax scores rather than normalized attention probabilities.
Specific finding: ICL attention rankings over demonstration tokens can correlate positively with training-token rankings constructed from query-vector affinities during restricted finetuning. Across six classification datasets, average Kendall rank correlation between ICL demonstration attention and constructed finetuning affinities is 0.193 for GPT 1.3B and 0.214 for GPT 2.7B. Random-ranking comparisons average approximately zero. Measurements are averaged across validation examples and layers; they do not directly measure training-example influence on finetuned predictions.

Specific finding: Middle-layer residual-stream SAEs trained on base or chat models can retain substantial reconstruction and replacement-loss fidelity on the corresponding model variant, conditional on excluding high-norm activation outliers. Separate base/chat dictionaries were evaluated on both model variants after filtering high-norm activations. At Mistral layer-16 resid_pre, the base SAE on chat achieved CE 1.80 versus 1.78 for the native chat SAE, L0 126 versus 101, and explained variance 60.9% versus 69.2%. The chat SAE on base achieved CE 1.79 versus 1.63 for the native base SAE. Similar Qwen transfer is reported, but its referenced appendix is absent from the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: A Pile-trained Mistral base-model SAE can achieve instruction-rollout replacement cross-entropy close to a Pile-trained chat-model SAE while having poorer activation reconstruction and higher active-feature counts. SAEs were spliced separately at rollout or user-prompt positions. On rollouts, base versus chat SAE CE was 0.49 versus 0.46, clean CE was 0.16, L0 was 190 versus 168, explained variance was 49.7% versus 54.4%, and MSE was 2,060 versus 1,860. On user prompts, replacement CE was 3.25 versus 3.17 with clean CE 3.25. The authors caution that user-token CE is difficult to interpret because those tokens are not prediction targets during instruction fine-tuning.
location: Investigating SAE Transfer between base and chat models

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Dream-7B Base-trained Mask-SAEs can retain reconstruction and replacement-loss performance close to instruction-trained dictionaries on Dream-7B Instruct at selected layers through layer 23, while transferring substantially worse at layer 27. Compares Base- and SFT-trained Mask-SAEs inserted into Dream Instruct on masked denoising inputs and 30-step, 30-token instruction rollouts. Metrics remain closely matched through layer 23, while the Base dictionary causes much larger rollout loss at layer 27. Reverse insertion into Dream Base shows similar loss trends despite some shallow-layer reconstruction differences. Exact numerical gaps, rollout prompt counts, and uncertainty are not supplied in readable text.
Specific finding: ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 activities admit a sufficiently accurate sparse linear latent description for interpreting SAE-based alignment gains as superposition disentanglement.

Specific finding: Selected sparse dictionary factors in BERT-base identify sentence-level linguistic and formatting patterns with high pattern prevalence among their strongest activations. Manual checks of the top 200 examples per selected factor and layer find unit-conversion-with-parentheses prevalence of 0%, 0%, 64.5%, and 95.5% at layers 4, 6, 8, and 10. Enumeration prevalence is 8%, 98.5%, 100%, and 100%. For the adjective factor at layer 8, the original example activates at 9.5, adjective substitutions at 9.2 and 8.2, a newly constructed matching sentence at 7.9, and one random sentence at 0.0. Masking adjectives gives 5.3, deleting several adjectives gives 7.8, and neutral substitutions give 6.2. These selected observations demonstrate sensitivity to context and lexical changes without establishing population-wide recall, exclusive selectivity, or a systematic monotonic relationship between pattern similarity and activation.
Specific finding: Selected later-layer BERT-base dictionary factors respond to extended contextual structures, including repeated text and biographical passages. Inspects high-activation contexts for repetition and biography factors. LIME fits ridge-regression surrogates to factor activations under random [UNK] masking and highlights repeated passages or biographical attributes such as names, dates, careers, and family relations. Appendix G supplies additional selected contexts. No long-range detection benchmark, systematic distance manipulation, surrogate-fidelity measurement, or downstream factor intervention is reported. These observations do not establish the proposed attention mechanism or that all listed biographical attributes are necessary.
location: Section 3, mid-level factors; Figures 5–6; Tables 3–4; Appendix F

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Concept directions extracted from the same matched-story corpus can have highly similar relational geometry across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma models. Compared 536,130 unique pairwise concept cosines at matched fractional depths. Median per-concept similarity-profile Spearman agreement, averaged over three model pairs, was 0.987, with tenth percentile 0.967. The first six singular modes matched in order with absolute concept-loading correlations 0.93–0.99. Qwen's dictionary had 10.3 effective singular modes, while 46 modes were needed for 90% of squared-singular-value energy. The source gives inconsistent nearest-neighbor and community counts for Figure 1, so those graph parameters are not used as evidence here.
Specific finding: Spectral organization of identified feature vectors provides useful evidence about functional relationships among the concepts those vectors represent.

Specific finding: Natural activation-extreme exemplars enable more accurate human prediction of CNN unit activation than the evaluated gradient-based synthetic feature visualizations. Performed new natural-versus-synthetic reference comparisons across seven CNNs, broadening the earlier GoogLeNet result of Borowski et al. Participants used nine highly activating and nine minimally activating reference images to classify query pairs. Natural references produced higher forced-choice accuracy for every evaluated CNN, including adversarially robust ResNet-50. The result concerns the tested visualization recipe and task rather than all possible synthetic explanations.

Specific finding: Extreme natural exemplars enable more accurate human discrimination of Inception V1 channel activations than the tested synthetic channel visualizations, while also producing faster and more confident correct responses. Experiment I, with 10 experts and 45 channels, reports 92±2% accuracy for natural references versus 82±4% for synthetic references. Correct responses are approximately 3.7 seconds faster with natural references and have higher confidence (chi-square p<.001). Experiment II, with 23 participants and 80 channels, preserves the natural-reference accuracy advantage across all four presentation schemes; its nine-reference minimum-plus-maximum condition yields 91±3% versus 72±4%. Uncertainties are twice the standard error across participant averages. Each participant receives different natural queries across reference conditions; the disclosed sampling bug limits stimulus coverage.
location: Sections 4.1–4.5; Figures 3–5; Appendix A.1.2 and A.2.1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Gradient-based feature visualization can produce largely featureless images for CoinRun features whose natural activating examples reveal recognizable game objects. Displayed intermediate-layer optimization results were clouds of color, whereas high-activation observation patches exposed objects. Changing jitter, penalizing first-layer activations, using alternative objectives and non-axis-aligned directions, and trying procedurally generated sprites or image noise produced no reported noticeable improvement. Adversarial training was explored only briefly. These comparisons lack quantitative visualization-quality metrics and detailed outcomes for each attempted modification.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Identifying which policy uses a more robust strategy and which visual cues guide its decisions provides a useful operational measure of non-experts' understanding of policy explanations.

Specific finding: Improving held-out predictions of a model's decisions and recovering its behaviorally relevant input fields provide useful operational measures of an interpretability tool's auditing utility.

Specific finding: Differences in activation-weighted image-similarity scores can predict human preferences for which neuron's strongest image examples form a more coherent set. The study evaluates 1,000 neuron pairs, with three answers per pair aggregated by majority vote and 71 annotators. DINOv2-based MS agreement is reported as 82.8% assuming uniformly distributed score differences over 0–0.9. Agreement increases from 56.6% in the 0–0.1 interval to 100% in the 0.8–0.9 interval, which contains 41 pairs. Table A1 also evaluates CLIP ViT-B-based MS and reports interval counts.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A Big Five questionnaire can be operationalized for masked and autoregressive language models by selecting among frequency-adverb sentence completions and applying the questionnaire's trait-scoring rules.
Specific finding: A personality classifier trained on human essays provides meaningful trait measurements when applied to language-model-generated essays.

Specific finding: Inventory-derived synthetic situational judgment tests and context-conditioned trait ratings provide useful operational measures of personality expression in language-model responses.
location: Sections 4.4–4.5 and 5.4; Appendices H and J

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Between zero injection and a sweep-selected optimal strength, MDS injections often yield approximately linear changes in classifier-measured target OCEAN expression while largely retaining classifier-measured fluency. Across 130 targeted trait trajectories, OLS fits reach R² ≥ 0.95 in 47.69%, ≥ 0.85 in 89.23%, and ≥ 0.75 in 96.15%. For 520 other-trait trajectories, the corresponding proportions are 13.27%, 41.35%, and 55.58%. The ten-point follow-up sweeps run without fluency early stopping and yield 32 nonfluent coefficient steps. The authors attribute 75% to a single outlier response, although their wording about its position relative to the threshold is unclear. These analyses use sweep classifiers, whereas the final method comparison uses GPT-5.1. Endpoint selection limits inference outside the tested intervals.

Specific finding: A language model with TopK-gated MLP activations exposes a known native dictionary and active coefficients for each MLP output, providing an operational reference for evaluating sparse feature recovery.
Specific finding: Native neurons in a deliberately sparse language-model MLP provide an appropriate semantic and computational reference for judging recovered dictionary features.

Specific finding: Validated supervised task dictionaries provide useful reference points for evaluating unsupervised dictionaries through reconstruction sufficiency and necessity, sparse controllability, and interpretation-consistent intervention effects. Implemented all three evaluation axes on GPT-2 Small IOI circuit cross-sections, comparing supervised mean dictionaries, task-trained SAEs, OpenWebText-trained SAEs, and frozen-random-decoder controls. The comparisons distinguish reconstruction quality, sparse control, and task-specific interpretation quality.

Specific finding: Averaged across AxBench's four Concept500 representation sites, difference-in-means, linear probes, and ReFT-r1 achieve higher concept-detection AUROC than individual Gemma Scope SAE features, including features selected using labeled training data. Table 1 reports four-site mean AUROC of 0.942 for DiffMean, 0.940 for Probe, 0.938 for ReFT-r1, 0.917 for SAE-A, and 0.695 for the original concept-associated SAE features. The paper reports no significant aggregate difference among the top three methods. ReFT-r1 does not outperform SAE-A at Gemma-2-9B layer 31: their AUROCs are 0.869 and 0.907, respectively. Added-negative F1 evaluations are reported to largely preserve method ordering, with thresholds chosen to maximize F1 and no separate threshold-selection split specified. Sections 3.2 and 5.1 disagree about max versus mean token pooling.
Specific finding: For concept-conditioned instruction responses on AxBench, engineered prompting, LoReFT, and LoRA achieve higher average joint concept, instruction-following, and fluency scores than the tested rank-one dictionary steering methods. Table 2 reports four-site average 0–2 harmonic-mean scores of 0.894 for LLM-engineered prompting, 0.741 for LoReFT, 0.615 for LoRA, 0.543 for ReFT-r1, 0.239 for DiffMean, and 0.165 for SAE addition. These averages do not imply dominance for every site or concept. SFT scores 0.676 on a restricted evaluation covering only the first 20 concepts in the Gemma-2-2B settings. Training hyperparameters for dictionary methods were selected primarily using detection AUROC, whereas steering-only baselines were tuned for steering.

Specific finding: A sparse autoencoder over frozen language-model activations can be trained with dedicated ontology slots and a free reconstruction bank using relation-label supervision, cross-bank decorrelation, and auxiliary answer-value prediction.
Specific finding: Sparse autoencoders can combine activation reconstruction with binary-cross-entropy supervision on designated latent coordinates to construct label-addressable concept dictionaries.

Specific finding: Supervised ontology-slot training can localize biography-question relation labels into designated GPT-2 SAE coordinates and retain substantial binding accuracy on unseen direct question templates. Table 1 reports layer-6 diagonal accuracy of 1.000 on training and held-out test questions and 0.912 on unseen templates, compared with layer-0 values of 0.232, 0.238, and 0.165 respectively. The free bank contains 10,000 features. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied.
Specific finding: Supervised ontology-slot SAE training can retain substantial relation-label classification accuracy when expanded from small synthetic ontologies to a larger templated FB15K-derived relation inventory. Appendix J reports training slot top-1 accuracy 0.987, OOD slot top-1 accuracy 0.757 on unseen templates/persons, diagonal accuracy 0.956, and reconstruction MSE 0.083. The diagonal score is described as in-distribution and is distinct from overall slot top-1 accuracy. Split sizes and separate template-versus-entity generalization results are not given. Table 12 lists indices 0–89 despite claiming 91 relations.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Concept-supervised SAE coordinates can coincide with Gini-selected root features for their assigned labels and show greater activation separation between concept-present and concept-absent examples than unconditioned SAE coordinates. All 26 concept classifiers select the designated guided coordinate at the root. Mean rank-biserial correlation between concept presence and selected-feature activation is 0.59 for G-SAE versus 0.18 for vanilla SAE; the paper reports Mann–Whitney p-values below 0.05 for both methods. Related privacy concepts retain weak cross-activation. Evaluation sizes and multiple-testing details are not supplied.
location: Section 5.3; Figure 4; Appendices F and N

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Interventions using supervised relation-slot decoder directions can redirect a task-fine-tuned GPT-2 biography answer to the same person's value for another relation, with success strongly dependent on layer and intervention strength. The main layer-6 evaluation reports 0.847 swap success at alpha=2, approximately 0.54 at alpha=1, and 0.23 at alpha=10; layer 0 achieves 0.040 in Table 1. Among failed layer-6 swaps, 116/154 at alpha=2 and 636/766 at alpha=10 retain the intended semantic category. These are failure-conditioned category-retention rates, not overall successful swaps. The abstract and later appendices claim 94.8% one-hop success without reconciling it with the main 84.7% result.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Steering with concept-supervised SAE decoder directions can improve composite concept-and-quality scores over unconditioned SAE steering and selected alternative control pipelines. Table 3 reports G-SAE composite scores of 0.98, 0.72, 0.82, and 0.53 for toxicity, Shakespeare, combined control, and privacy, respectively; vanilla SAE scores are 0.95, 0.64, 0.80, and 0.47. G-SAE equals or exceeds the displayed ICV, DiffVec, PREADD, and Model Arithmetic scores, including a 0.82 combined-control tie with DiffVec. The prose reports favorable pairwise judgments, but numerical win rates are absent from the supplied table rendering. Generation counts and uncertainty for score differences are unspecified.
Specific finding: Separately configured G-SAE detoxification interventions can reduce measured toxicity across selected base and instruction-tuned Llama and Gemma checkpoints, with model-dependent grammar and spelling costs. Appendix E defines relative toxicity reduction as 1 minus steered divided by baseline and reports 91.23% for Llama3-8B-base, 86.51% for Llama3-8B-instruct, 85.98% for Llama3-70B-base, and 92.89% for Gemma2-9B-base. Corresponding reported grammar-and-spelling reductions are 1.1%, 1.3%, 11.96%, and 0.8%. The exact grammar-reduction calculation, evaluation counts, baseline toxicity values, and uncertainty are not supplied.
location: Section 5.4; Table 3; Appendices D.2–D.4, M, and O

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Penalizing selected encoder and decoder directions toward known generating features can improve recovery of other, unanchored generating directions in sparse linear-mixture benchmarks. Table 1 explicitly excludes anchored generating features from evaluation, using 1,000 generators, 768-dimensional representations, 16,000 latents, and inactivity probability 0.99. At threshold 0.95, recovery increases from 84.90% to 87.63% for TopK, 84.80% to 89.38% for BatchTopK, 83.70% to 87.32% for Matryoshka, 23.60% to 25.05% for the transcoder, and 56.42% to 57.71% for the crosscoder. ReLU and JumpReLU remain at 0%, while mean best-match similarities increase from 0.205 to 0.246 and 0.237 to 0.333. Transcoder similarity remains 0.838 at reported precision. Appendix G includes ties and small degradations, including TopK activation parameter 64, where recovery changes from 93.9% to 93.4%. Its sparsity conventions and Table 4 recovery/similarity reporting complicate interpretation. Seed variation and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: Class-mean feature anchoring can improve learned SAE encoder alignment with ImageNet class-mean directions in CLIP representation space. Table 2 reports class-mean proxy recovery increasing from 0% to 24.13% for TopK and BatchTopK and to 24.45% for Matryoshka. Mean best-match similarities increase respectively from 0.517 to 0.851, 0.508 to 0.847, and 0.683 to 0.858. These results establish improved alignment to researcher-defined class means. Interpreting them as natural semantic feature recovery additionally requires the class-mean proxy assumption. Appendix H provides selected top-activating-image examples, without a systematic monosemanticity or causal evaluation.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Anchoring a subset of semantic encoder and decoder directions is sufficient to restore identifiability of the remaining SDL features.

Specific finding: A Top-1 ReLU sparse encoder–decoder can have a positive-loss blockwise partial optimum where one latent responds to two distinct features and another latent remains dead. Formal construction in Example 3.5 sets encoder rows to (1,1) and (0,0), and decoder columns to (1/2,1/2) and (0,0). Each block separately minimizes the fixed-region quadratic, both block gradients vanish, and surrogate loss is 1; a feature-aligned configuration achieves zero. This establishes blockwise partial optimality, not joint local minimality or gradient-descent trapping.

Specific finding: Logit attribution, attention inspection, and activation patching can identify a small set of terminal components that transfers most multiple-choice answer-label behavior in a 70B transformer. Ranking ABCD-centered direct contributions over 128 prompts identifies 32 heads and 13 MLPs accounting for 80% of summed positive contributions; negative contributions are excluded from that denominator. Jointly patching these 45 components recovers most donor-answer performance, evaluated by full-vocabulary negative log probability and ABCD top-1 accuracy over 128 prompts per target letter. This tests a terminal cross-section rather than a complete circuit.

Specific finding: Complete pairwise interaction models can predict SAE contribution-coalition ordering better than equal-parameter models containing singleton terms and randomly selected third-order interactions. For each prompt, fit 50 control models using the same fitting and evaluation coalitions as the pairwise model. Both contain 137 coefficients: an intercept, 16 singleton terms, and either all 120 pairs or 120 random triples. Table 19 reports higher prompt-median held-out rank fidelity and lower weighted ordering error for pairwise models than for controls summarized by the median over 50 models per prompt, in all 18 model–behavior settings.
Specific finding: Pairwise coalition models can predict aggregate MMLU-Pro accuracy under combinations of published SAE steering directions more accurately than singleton models. Evaluate 1,024 distinct uniformly sampled steering coalitions, with 512 for fitting and 512 for evaluation, on 100 test questions from each of 14 domains. Overall rank fidelity increases from 0.5874 to 0.7790, weighted ordering error decreases from 0.1444 to 0.06056, and residual decreases from 0.6424 to 0.3891. Domain rank fidelity worsens in economics, engineering, law, and math, and residuals worsen in five domains. Appendix I's K-sweep reports a different K=16 residual, 0.7768, without explaining the protocol difference.

Specific finding: Claude 3.5 Haiku represents within-line character count on a curved, low-dimensional manifold rather than solely as position along one activation-space direction. A linear regression probe after layer 1 achieves R² = 0.985. PCA of 150 count-conditioned layer-2 mean residual vectors finds that six components capture 95% of their variance and reveal a twisting curve. A 150-way logistic probe after layer 1 has count RMSE of approximately five characters; six PCs capture 82% of probe-weight variance. Probe similarity profiles across layers 0–3 show progressively sharper peaks and stronger secondary rings.
Specific finding: Manipulating an early-layer character-count subspace can selectively alter Claude 3.5 Haiku’s newline predictions. The authors zero leading count-conditioned PCA subspaces at a single early layer and compare against random subspaces of matched dimension, separating losses for newline and nonnewline targets. They report a large effect primarily on newline targets. On the aluminum prompt, whose final count is 42, count-conditioned mean differences are applied across three adjacent early layers and the final two tokens, maintaining a six-character offset between those tokens. Restricting substitutions to six PCs still changes linebreaking. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied.
Specific finding: A Fourier decomposition can capture nearly as much variance in Claude 3.5 Haiku’s character-count curve as a matched-number PCA decomposition. The authors compare variance explained by Fourier and PCA components of the character-count curve, reporting that Fourier components explain 'at most 10% less variance' than an equivalent number of PCA components. They note that the Fourier construction does not account for dilation. Component counts, evaluation details, and whether the percentage denotes a relative difference or percentage-point gap are not specified in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Combining boundary-head outputs produces a curved characters-remaining representation that causally influences newline prediction. Three analyzed heads have overlapping but distinct response ranges. Their individual outputs are nearly one-dimensional, while their sum traces a more evenly resolved curve. The first two PCs of the analyzed characters-remaining space capture 92% of variance. Ablating this subspace primarily affects newline-target loss. Mean-activation substitutions at the aluminum prompt’s final token modulate newline prediction, consistent with the completion ' aluminum.' requiring ten characters. Numerical intervention effects are not supplied.
Specific finding: Late representations of characters remaining and anticipated next-token length can occupy near-orthogonal subspaces that make the newline decision approximately linearly separable. PCA of conditional mean activations reveals near-orthogonal, moderately curved representations of remaining space and next-token length. A separating hyperplane derived from this three-dimensional geometry achieves AUC 0.91 on actual examples labeled by whether the next token should be a newline. Feature activation analyses also distinguish late break predictors from break suppressors according to whether the anticipated token exceeds or fits the remaining space. Sample size and held-out evaluation details are unspecified.
Specific finding: Claude 3.5 Haiku has markdown-table row and column representations with position-selective sparse features and curved, oscillatory probe geometries. Feature activations on separator tokens across 20 synthetic tables show row- and column-selective families. On a dataset of larger tables, row- and column-index probes show ringing in pairwise similarities and curved 'baseball seam' shapes in three-dimensional PCA projections. No causal interventions, index-prediction metrics, or larger-dataset sample count are reported.
Specific finding: Packing ordered points on a low-dimensional sphere with attraction between nearby indices and repulsion between distant indices can produce rippled curves and oscillatory similarity patterns. Numerical simulations use 100 points constrained to spheres in ambient dimensions 3–8. The highlighted six-dimensional circular configuration attracts the six nearest indices on each side and repels other points, producing a rippled embedding and similarity ringing. Varying ambient dimension and attraction width changes curvature. The simulations can settle in local minima and supply no global optimality guarantee.
location: Representing Character Count; The Model Represents Character Count on a Continuous Manifold; The Probe Perspective; Analytic Construction of Ringing and Fourier Modes

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Attention heads can detect proximity to a line boundary by transforming current-count and prior-line-width manifolds into alignment at distinct offsets. Current-count and line-width probe directions have maximum residual-space cosine similarity around 0.25. Through an identified boundary head’s query/key transformations, maximum alignment approaches one and shifts toward line widths slightly exceeding the current count. Other heads produce different offsets. Measured attention to newlines and projected head outputs peak at different distances from the boundary. A random head in the same layer lacks comparable alignment structure.
Specific finding: Claude 3.5 Haiku constructs its early character-count manifold through multiple attention heads with different newline-sink offsets and token-length corrections, then refines it in the next layer. Attention-pattern analysis identifies head-specific intervals of attention to the previous newline, followed by attention over recent tokens. OV analyses show offset-dependent count contributions and corrections for token length. Nearly ray-like layer-0 outputs sum into a curved representation; layer-1 outputs add curvature and refinement. Count predictions obtained by taking the argmax of summed head outputs projected onto count probes achieve R² = 0.93 for five selected layer-0 heads and 0.97 for eleven heads across layers 0–1. The authors report that attention outputs affect the count representation four times more than MLPs, motivating their attention-focused analysis; the precise comparison metric is not supplied.
location: Sensing the Line Boundary; Twisting with QK; Leveraging Multiple Boundary Heads; Geometry of Twisting

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Overlapping sparse character-count features can provide local coordinates that approximate a continuous counting manifold. Ten selected features have smooth, overlapping, dilating count-tuning profiles. Reconstructions using only these features closely approximate the count-conditioned residual-stream curve when projected into its six-dimensional PCA subspace, with mild kinks near decoder directions. Typically two or three neighboring features contribute at a given count. No numerical reconstruction error is supplied.
Specific finding: Character-count features can retain similar receptive fields and decoder geometry across crosscoder dictionary sizes while also splitting by line-width context. The appendix compares count-feature receptive fields and decoder similarities across dictionary sizes, reporting similar dilating tilings and ringing. It also identifies three features covering approximately 20–45 characters that differ in preference for all line widths, long line widths, or proximity to the boundary. Dictionary sizes and quantitative similarity statistics are not provided in the supplied text. These observations establish stability in this setting, not a universal canonical discretization.
location: Character Count Features; The Model Represents Character Count on a Continuous Manifold

experiment_summary: Specific finding: An SAE sparsity penalty may encourage dictionary vectors to trace a representation manifold, causing some observed feature splitting to reflect local subdivisions of a continuous feature.

Specific finding: An SAE whose active-feature budget is below a data manifold's local dimension must switch active supports locally to achieve low reconstruction MSE. Propositions 4.2 and H.2 supply an attempted dimension-counting proof: fixed support restricts reconstructions to a subspace of dimension at most K. This excludes exact reconstruction of an open higher-dimensional manifold patch, but dimension mismatch alone does not imply high mean-squared error or locally changing support at a specified nonzero error tolerance. No quantitative error bound is supplied, and support switching alone does not establish loss of all local geometry.

Specific finding: Number representations in diverse natural-language-trained sequence models and classical word embeddings can exhibit recurring Fourier peaks at periods 2, 5, and 10, also present in raw number-token frequencies. New Fourier analyses report recurring decimal periods across the surveyed pretrained models, classical embeddings, controlled models, and a scalar number-frequency baseline. These measurements establish spectral recurrence rather than shared arithmetic algorithms or causal use.
Specific finding: Single-token number embeddings in selected pretrained Transformers and state-space models support highly accurate linear mod-2, mod-5, and mod-10 readouts across a wide range of model sizes. Table 3 reports mod-2 κ of 99.4–100%, mod-5 κ of 98.4–100%, and mod-10 κ of 99.4–100%. Inventories contain 819 numbers for each GPT-2 model, 877 for Mamba-2.8B, 999 for Falcon-Mamba-7B, and 1,000 for the remaining models. Other moduli vary substantially: DeepSeek-V3 reaches κ=84.4% for mod 7 and 92.0% for mod 9, while some smaller models also decode mod 3 well. Model size, training data, architecture, and tokenizer are not controlled across checkpoints.
Specific finding: Final-token middle-layer states for multi-token numbers can support strong linear decoding of decimal residue classes in pretrained language models. Table 4 reports κ ranges of 99.3–100% for mod 2, 97.7–100% for mod 5, 98.1–100% for mod 10, 96.3–100% for mod 100, and 88.4–99.0% for mod 1000. Mod-7 κ ranges from −1.8% to 2.7%. The text mentions mod 10000 but supplies no corresponding table result. Low decimal residues can be determined by the last numerical chunk under three-digit tokenization, so these scores alone do not demonstrate cross-token integration.
Specific finding: Decimal harmonic energy and linear residue-probe performance can emerge gradually together during natural-language pretraining rather than through an abrupt grokking transition. Figure 10 and Appendix B.4 describe smoothly increasing ΦT and linear-probe performance throughout Transformer pretraining for T=2,5,10, without a sudden transition. The supplied text gives no numerical checkpoint values or repeated-training uncertainty for this trajectory. The modular-arithmetic grokking comparison draws partly on cited prior work.
Specific finding: Training addition Transformers with multi-token numerical chunks can produce consistent decimal modular representations more reliably than the tested single-token addition conditions. Nine-digit addition with three-digit numerical chunks yields recurring spectra and near-perfect mod-2,5,10 κ under both optimizer recipes. Three-digit addition restricted to operands and sums ≤999 has variable spectra and near-chance residue probes; AdamW generalizes in one seed but not the other. A separate six-digit task comparison also favors three-digit over six-digit tokenization. Figure 17 reports circular mod-10 test accuracy of 84% versus 11% for selected nine- versus three-digit-trained models. The primary comparison changes the task distribution as well as the number of tokens.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Numerical token embeddings in selected pretrained language models exhibit unusually large Fourier components associated with periods around 2, 2.5, 5, and 10. The authors transform each numerical embedding coordinate across number values, then aggregate each Fourier component using its L2 norm across embedding dimensions. Section 4.1 reports outliers at periods 2, 2.5, 5, and 10, and Appendix C.1 reports similar patterns for the additional pretrained embeddings. Scratch-trained GPT-2-XL lacks analogous high-frequency outliers. Evidence available here consists of the textual analyses and figure descriptions.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Intermediate final-token states in Llama-3.1-8B addition support affine sine and cosine readouts of sums with base-10-associated periods including 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100. The authors explicitly repeat prior Fourier-probing analyses by training independent affine sine/cosine probes for 500 epochs with Adam at learning rate 0.001. The reported layerwise R-squared patterns identify strong signals at periods 2, 5, 10, and 20; periods 50 and 100 are also selected following prior work. Layer-18 probe outputs are described as exhibiting sinusoidal and circular structure. This repeats an analysis procedure and finding, rather than documenting an exact reproduction of every prior experimental configuration.

Specific finding: A pretrained GPT-2-XL fine-tuned on bounded addition can combine low-frequency magnitude estimates, contributed primarily by MLP outputs, with high-frequency modular discrimination, contributed primarily by attention outputs. Numerical-logit spectra exhibit outliers around periods 2, 2.5, 5, and 10. In the evaluation described as using the test dataset, with 3,420 test examples reported in Appendix F, baseline accuracy is 99.74%; removing low-frequency MLP components gives 35.89%, high-frequency attention components 78.36%, and high-frequency components from both module types 27.08%. Removing low-frequency attention components gives 99.12%, while removing high-frequency MLP components gives 98.10%, showing smaller but nonzero degradation. The source reports errors in multiples of ten after low-frequency MLP removal and errors below six after high-frequency attention removal. Table 1 labels its loss column Validation Loss, despite the surrounding test-evaluation description.
Specific finding: GPT-2-XL fine-tuned on multiplication can exhibit sparse numerical-logit Fourier components with short periods, extending the observed spectral pattern beyond addition. After 25 fine-tuning epochs at learning rate 1e-4, GPT-2-XL reaches 74.58% validation accuracy. The source reports late-layer MLP and attention numerical-logit spectral outliers around periods 2, 2.5, 3.3, 5, and 10. Dataset size, operand bounds, and handling of multi-token numerical outputs in the spectral analysis are not specified.
Specific finding: Frozen GPT-J and Phi-2 solving addition with four demonstrations exhibit sparse high-frequency numerical-logit components with periods resembling those in addition-fine-tuned GPT-2-XL. The source reports outliers around periods 2, 2.5, 5, and 10 in numerical vocabulary projections of attention and MLP outputs across the analyzed late layers. Among incorrect answers, 93% of GPT-J errors and 73% of Phi-2 errors are multiples of ten. Error counts and overall accuracies are unreported. The common claim of analyzing the last 15 layers is stated by the source without resolving model-specific layer-count details.
Specific finding: Changing bounded-addition prompts from natural-language questions to reverse Polish notation can preserve periodic structures in GPT-2-XL's numerical module-output readouts. Appendix C.3 reports periodic intermediate logits under the alternate format and spectral outliers around periods 2, 2.5, 5, and 10. Its figure description reports low-frequency outliers for MLP outputs and stronger high-frequency structure for attention outputs. Appendix F specifies an 80/10/10 split. Alternate-format accuracy, repeated-run variability, and frequency-ablation results are not reported.
Specific finding: A concentration of addition errors in multiples of ten may indicate that a language model combines decimal modular information with imperfect magnitude estimates. A behavioral consistency test finds that 100% of observed GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 addition errors, and 87% of observed PaLM-2 errors, are multiples of ten. These percentages are conditional on errors; error counts, overall accuracies, and precise checkpoint identifiers are unreported. No internal measurements or interventions test the proposed mechanism in these closed models.
location: Sections 3.2–3.3; Figures 1–4; Table 1; Appendix D, Figure 20

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Selected Llama-3.1-8B addition neurons form period-specific groups whose activation periodicities match the Fourier planes targeted by their output weights, and their summed outputs approximate the corresponding sum phases. Sum-conditioned neuron activations reportedly exhibit repeating patterns across tasks. Output-weight alignment with sine/cosine probe spans and clustering by absolute output-weight cosine recover corresponding period groups. Projected activation-weighted outputs sum toward the expected phase, illustrated for four hours after 18:00 and period-5 input sweeps. Gate/up analyses identify both operand-selective and mixed patterns; the stated overlap criterion labels 17/28 neurons as split for hours. Larger-period groups contribute less to the smaller-range cyclic tasks. Except for the parity pair, period groups are not separately subjected to the reported causal ablation tests.
Specific finding: Jointly ablating two selected layer-18 parity neurons in Llama-3.1-8B can shift output probability from correct answers toward neighboring answers with incorrect parity. Activation and output-weight analyses identify complementary period-2 contributions. The authors report that jointly zeroing the two neurons at the final token shifts probability away from correct answers toward neighboring wrong-parity outputs, described as blurring predictions. Figure 11 also illustrates their month-task activation patterns; no taskwise accuracy table is supplied for this intervention.

Specific finding: Retaining frozen pretrained token embeddings while randomly initializing the remaining GPT-2-small weights can substantially improve bounded-addition accuracy and convergence over training the entire model from scratch. Section 4.2 reports 53.95% test accuracy for fully scratch-trained GPT-2-small and 100% with frozen pretrained token embeddings and randomly initialized remaining weights. Figure 7b reports mean and standard deviation of validation accuracy across five seeds, with consistently faster convergence and 100% validation accuracy in the embedding-retention condition. Per-seed test accuracies are not separately provided.
Specific finding: Under the reported bounded-addition training recipes, GPT-2-XL trained from random initialization attains lower accuracy and lacks the conspicuous high-frequency numerical-logit outliers observed after pretrained-model fine-tuning. Scratch-trained GPT-2-XL reaches 94.44% test accuracy after the reported 500-epoch recipe, compared with 99.74% after 50 epochs of pretrained-model fine-tuning. The source reports that embedding and intermediate-logit spectra lack the fine-tuned model's high-frequency outliers and periodic structures. Reported scratch-model prediction errors remain within two of the correct answer. The comparison is between the supplied recipes rather than a controlled test of all possible scratch-training procedures.
models_studied: ["GPT-2-small trained from scratch", "GPT-2-small with frozen pretrained token embeddings and randomly initialized remaining weights"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Fourier directions learned from ordinary addition can redirect Llama-3.1-8B's month, weekday, and hour answers toward concepts corresponding to counterfactual numerical sums. Addition-trained probes are applied to cyclic activations and used to edit sine/cosine readouts toward target phases. Table 5 specifies periods {2,5,10} for weekdays and {2,5,10,20,50} for months and hours. Every cyclic prompt is steered toward every task target. The prose reports favorable averaged output distributions but substantial per-prompt failures, including one month prompt that largely resists steering. No aggregate steering-accuracy percentage is supplied. Equation 4 and Algorithm 1 differ in normalization, and descriptions of which periods overlap the month DAS subspace are inconsistent; the listed intervention periods follow Table 5.
Specific finding: In Llama-3.1-8B's tested cyclic tasks, concept-period circular geometry becomes reliably recoverable at the final token later than the layer where sum-related causal information emerges. Reusing the cited circular-probe procedure recovers circular structure at input-concept positions across layers. At the final token, reliable output-concept circular readouts reportedly emerge around layers 22–25, after the layer-18 rise in output-variable interchange accuracy. This distinguishes the measured concept geometry from the localized addition step without excluding undetected concept-period structure at layer 18.
location: Section 4; Figure 7; Appendices E and G.2–G.3; Table 5; Algorithm 1; Figures 37–39

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Calendar-disambiguating prompts can reduce the geometric distortion of May's representation relative to the other months as processing proceeds through Gemma-2-2B. Figure 14 and the Limitations section report that May's distortion persists through layers for isolated month prompts but fades when the calendar template supplies disambiguating context. No numerical circularity metric, uncertainty estimate, or broader ambiguity evaluation is supplied.

Specific finding: Uniformly averaging conditionally independent word emissions with a common shifted seasonal modulation yields a PMI kernel depending only on the difference between words' seasonal centers. Formal derivation: Equations 13–16 integrate the product of conditional emissions over uniform seasonal time, cancel the zero-mean terms, and identify the remaining term as a circular autocorrelation. Section 4.1.1 then diagonalizes the resulting circulant PMI matrix in a Fourier basis.
Specific finding: A translation-invariant embedding Gram kernel on a periodic semantic lattice admits Fourier PCA coordinates, with mode amplitudes determined by the kernel spectrum. Formal result: Proposition 1 and Appendix E.2 diagonalize the periodic lattice Gram kernel using discrete Fourier modes. Real modes can be organized into sine–cosine pairs, with separate normalization for self-conjugate Nyquist modes. This is a conditional matrix derivation, not an empirical training experiment.
Specific finding: Exponential semantic-distance kernels produce sinusoidal embedding manifolds whose frequencies depend on whether the semantic domain has periodic or open boundaries. Formal derivations: Corollary 2 and Appendix E.3 evaluate the Fourier transform of a periodized exponential kernel. Proposition 3 and Appendix E.4 diagonalize the centered open exponential integral operator through a differential equation and endpoint conditions, obtaining frequency quantization and operator eigenvalues 2 sigma/(1+sigma²k²). The printed discrete-to-continuum prefactors do not consistently preserve a common absolute normalization.
Specific finding: A PMI model with multiplicatively independent seasonal and binary-attribute co-occurrence factors decomposes into orthogonal seasonal Fourier and binary-attribute subspaces. Formal result: Appendix D expands the binary contribution exactly, writes the PMI as a sum of Kronecker products, and diagonalizes it in a Fourier–Walsh product basis. Theorem 5 gives separate eigenvalues for nonconstant seasonal modes and singleton binary-attribute modes, while mixed seasonal–attribute modes and higher-order Walsh modes have zero eigenvalues.
Specific finding: Seasonal spectral subspaces with eigengaps proportional to vocabulary size become asymptotically insensitive to bounded perturbations affecting a fixed number of PMI entries. Conditional asymptotic derivation: Section 4.1.1 obtains eigenvalues proportional to seasonal-vocabulary size and applies standard spectral perturbation results when the relevant eigengaps are also proportional to that size. A bounded perturbation to a fixed number of entries is negligible relative to these gaps. The source does not derive a quantitative finite-vocabulary reconstruction bound or prove that every allowed modulation supplies the necessary gaps.

Specific finding: For a positive-semidefinite circulant target Gram matrix, retaining a cyclic-shift-invariant leading eigenspace gives an optimal low-rank approximation in squared matrix error and permits linear cyclic shifts of the projected representations. Formal derivation in the appendix: construct vectors from the square root of the target matrix, truncate its eigendecomposition to obtain a best rank-k approximation in squared matrix error, and identify its eigenmodes with discrete Fourier modes. A cyclic coordinate permutation commutes with projection onto a shift-invariant retained eigenspace, inducing linear shifts of the projected vectors. Shift invariance is required when choosing among degenerate eigenmodes. The illustrated narrow-peaked target exhibits ringing after truncation. This is a conditional analytical construction, not an LLM experiment or a global optimality proof for Haiku.
location: Analytic Construction of Ringing and Fourier Modes

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A base-trained TFA can produce instruction-model dialogue embeddings with clearer speaker-role organization and lower trajectory tortuosity than the evaluated standard SAE embeddings. UMAP is fitted using all 1,000 conversations, with 100 displayed for population visualization and a single conversation overlaid for trajectory inspection. Predictive codes show qualitative user/assistant separation and position gradients. Reported embedding tortuosity is approximately 2 for predictive codes versus 25–30 for standard SAE and novel codes. No held-out role classifier, uncertainty estimate, original-space straightening comparison, or independent embedding-stability analysis is supplied.
Specific finding: TFA contextual codes can exhibit stronger within-event similarity and clearer narrative clustering than standard SAE codes on synthetic stories with designated event boundaries. The paper centers token codes, compares average within-event and across-event cosine similarities, and inspects similarity matrices and hierarchical clusters. Predictive codes show the strongest reported event grouping. Gaussian-input-noise sweeps reveal coarser predictive-code blocks and slower explained-variance degradation for TFA than standard SAEs. Numerical effect sizes and uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied figure text. Llama supplements report similar qualitative behavior with unfinished SAE baselines.
Specific finding: A jointly trained shared-dictionary TFA can allocate its contextual and novel codes largely to different dictionary subsets while giving contextual codes substantially lower effective rank. Appendix G sorts dictionary elements by predictive-code nonzero counts and applies the same ordering to novel codes across three domains. The authors report approximately 2K elements participating in predictive codes and approximately 8K primarily participating in novel codes, with limited cross-subset activation mass under their displayed 90%-count partition. Predictive effective rank is approximately 20–30 versus 390–410 for novel codes. A preliminary explicitly split-dictionary variant has similar reported ranks and slightly better overall loss, without a systematic tuning or uncertainty analysis.
Specific finding: TFA's contextual codes can align more strongly with slow activation structure, while its novel codes and standard SAE codes align more strongly with fast activation structure. Table 4 reports slow-component CKA of 0.75 for predictive codes, 0.19 for novel codes, and 0.35–0.37 for ReLU/TopK/BatchTopK codes. Fast-component CKA is respectively 0.18, 0.75, and 0.54. Supplementary Llama kernel-spectrum captions report similar trends, but its SAE training is unfinished. The main text defines an equal-energy frequency split; Appendix A.5 specifies 0.1 times the Nyquist rate, said to contain approximately half the signal norm.

Specific finding: Selecting among multiple refusal-cone directions can improve low-budget best-of-N jailbreak success relative to temperature sampling with a single optimized refusal direction. Figure 5 compares best-of-N attacks obtained by sampling four-dimensional cone directions against equal-count temperature sampling under single-direction RDO. The text reports higher ASR for cone sampling at small budgets, with generation randomness dominating at larger budgets. Figure 19 is described as showing increasing best-of-N ASR with cone dimension until a plateau at four. Exact budgets and plotted effect sizes are unavailable in the text rendering.
Specific finding: Optimized orthonormal refusal bases can contain many effective refusal-controlling positive combinations beyond their individual basis directions. RCO optimizes basis vectors and uniformly sampled positive unit combinations, with Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization after updates. Evaluation samples 256 directions per cone. The authors report refusal-mediating cones up to five dimensions across tested models, but low-ASR samples become more frequent as dimension increases; Gemma 2 2B deteriorates substantially at dimension five. Larger Qwen2.5 models show slower degradation. Bases are selected from the final 20 training steps; when no basis passes all basis-vector criteria, selection instead uses sampled-direction ablation scores. Appendix E also reports refusal induction and an addition-strength sweep for sampled Gemma 2 2B cone directions.

Specific finding: A categorical concept can be represented by the convex hull of its attribute vectors, with a simplex structure proposed when its category probabilities can be freely controlled together.
Specific finding: Representing semantic hierarchies through parent vectors and child-minus-parent increments may provide more cleanly separated interpretability coordinates than representing every nested attribute independently.
location: Definition 7 and Appendix C, Proposition 9; illustrative examples in Appendix A

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Hierarchical categorical concepts in language-model representations can be usefully modeled by a parent-presence direction plus child-specific increments confined to a low-dimensional subspace.

Specific finding: In the causal representation metric, exact hierarchical feature vectors have parent-orthogonal child increments, and successive increments along a hierarchy are orthogonal. Conditional formal derivation: Appendix B.2(a) identifies the child-minus-parent vector with a within-parent contrast and invokes causal-metric orthogonality to the parent. Part (b) subtracts the corresponding identities for two subordinate attributes. Part (d), Equations B.9–B.13, derives successive-increment orthogonality from the resulting squared-norm identities. The extension of the metric's orthogonality rule to subordinate contrasts is invoked rather than independently established from the displayed softmax equations, limiting the formal evidence.
Specific finding: For mutually exclusive attributes with exact common-origin indicator projections, differences between their calibrated feature vectors change between-category token log odds while preserving token log odds within each category. Formal derivation: Appendix D computes projections onto the column space of the attribute-vector differences. Equations D.2–D.4 give a category-specific constant projection and zero projection outside the union. The softmax log-odds identity then establishes within-category invariance and, for a two-category difference, an increase in target-versus-source log odds. The paper interprets this construction as a selective contrast representation in Corollary 6.

Specific finding: A feature can be formalized as a compact metric space of possible values, allowing atomic, hierarchical, continuous, and multidimensional features within one representational framework.
Specific finding: A continuous bijection from a compact feature metric space onto its image in a Euclidean unit sphere is a homeomorphism and therefore preserves topological structure.

Specific finding: The values of a feature can correspond continuously and one-to-one to its unit representation directions. The authors report approximate hue-ordered and calendar-date loops in PCA views of OpenAI text embeddings, and a temporally ordered curve in normalized SAE-extracted GPT2-small layer-7 year representations. For years 1900–1999, weighted graph distance from the mean representation of 1900 on a connected K=10 graph yields Kendall correlation 0.97 and Spearman correlation above 0.99 with temporal order. Mistral month/day visualizations are discussed as showing additional bending in three dimensions. These are geometric diagnostics, not exact tests over a continuous domain.
Specific finding: Locally, cosine similarity between unit feature representations can be expressed as a twice continuously differentiable function of squared feature distance with negative derivative at zero. The paper plots pairwise cosine similarity against proposed squared feature distance and measures global functional dependence using Chatterjee's ξ. The revised logarithmic year metric yields ξ=0.84 and a decreasing near-zero trend. Dates are described as locally plausible despite large-distance disagreement; colours provide weaker agreement. The original calendar-year metric fits poorly. These diagnostics do not verify the exact local identity or differentiability assumptions.
Specific finding: If a continuous feature correspondence maps into unit vectors and locally satisfies cosine similarity g(d²) with g twice continuously differentiable and g′(0)<0, every rectifiable feature-space path has representation-space length equal to its original length multiplied by √(−2g′(0)). Formal result, not an empirical experiment: Appendix B uses unit norms to express squared chord distance through cosine similarity, applies a Taylor expansion of g at zero, bounds errors in sufficiently fine partition sums, and passes to path lengths. The conclusion is conditional on the exact local kernel identity, its smoothness and negative derivative, and a rectifiable source path.
models_studied: ["OpenAI text-embedding-large-3, as named in the source", "GPT2-small, layer 7", "Mistral 7B, layer 8"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Language-model activations can be approximated using a mixture of Gaussian centroids and component-specific low-rank factor coordinates, providing a shared representation for reconstruction, localization, and steering.

Specific finding: Gaussian activation regions with low-rank shared variation and diagonal residual noise provide useful approximations to meaningful local representational structure in language models.

Specific finding: Nearby MFA component centroids can correspond to related semantic themes, allowing broader themes to span multiple local Gaussian components. GPT-5-mini judged how many of each component's three nearest centroid neighbors shared its theme. Of 670 components, 61% had at least one related neighbor, 36% at least two, and 20% all three. The rubric permits related rather than identical themes. Selected neighborhood traversals provide qualitative examples.
location: Section 4, Multi-Gaussian Concepts; Appendix F.1; Appendix G, Semantic Neighboring Components Prompt
