Specific finding: Prompt-associated heuristic neurons are important for successful arithmetic completions throughout the examined Pythia-6.9B training window, including its earliest examined checkpoint with good arithmetic performance. At each checkpoint, 50 correctly completed prompts per operator are sampled. Zeroing 5, 10, or 25 associated heuristic neurons per layer reduces accuracy more than random important-neuron controls. The prose reports that ablating 25 associated neurons per layer produces near-zero accuracy across the sampled checkpoints. Dependence under this intervention does not demonstrate that heuristics are the only operative computation or that they were present from the beginning of training.

Specific finding: Editing a model's activations by gradient descent on a probe's loss, so that the probe reports a counterfactual state, changes the model's outputs to match that counterfactual state. This shows the probed representation is causally used, including for out-of-distribution (unreachable) states. Each case flips one tile's probed state at the last token, editing layers L_s through the final layer. Over 1000 natural and 1000 unnatural (unreachable) positions, top-N predicted moves are compared with the counterfactual legal-move set. With L_s=4, average errors are 0.12 and 0.06, against null baselines of 2.68 and 2.59. F1 and KL metrics agree.

Specific finding: Adding player-relative board-state probe directions to multiple residual-stream layers can redirect OthelloGPT's legal-move predictions toward boards with altered piece colors or erased pieces. The specified 1,000-case benchmark compares the top-N post-intervention predictions against the target board's N legal moves, reporting average false-positive/false-negative error counts. Linear additions yielded 0.10 average errors for color flips and 0.02 for erasures, versus reported nonlinear gradient-based intervention errors of 0.12 and 0.11 and null-intervention errors of 2.723 and 2.73. An additional 1,000-endgame evaluation at timesteps greater than 30 reported intervention error of 0.112 versus 1.988 without intervention. This demonstrates counterfactual behavioral control without uniquely identifying the naturally used mechanism.
Specific finding: Which Othello pieces were flipped by the latest move can be linearly decoded from OthelloGPT, and subtracting a flipped-piece probe direction can redirect predictions toward a counterfactual board. Using the board-probing training setup, flipped-piece classification reached 94.82% F1 at x3 and peaked at 97.13% at x5. In a modified intervention experiment targeting a randomly selected newly flipped tile, subtracting its flipped direction reduced average legal-move-set errors from 1.686 without intervention to 0.486. The modified experiment's sample count and the F1 averaging convention are not separately stated.

Specific finding: Activation replacements constructed through an inverse board-state probe can shift an Othello transformer's next-move logits toward those associated with an alternative board, with effectiveness depending on intervention depth and game stage. The authors learn an inverse probe map through gradient descent on a linear MLP and use it to construct replacement activations. Section 4.1 describes piece-flip examples whose target-move logit changes agree with changes in legality. Section 4.2 compares intervened logits with logits associated with an alternative move, using cosine similarity and an unmodified comparison averaged over 50 games. The prose reports stronger effects in intermediate layers and early games; Appendix B reports similar patterns in 4L1H and 8L8H models. Numerical effect sizes and uncertainty intervals are unavailable in the text.
location: Sections 4–4.2; Figures 1c and 3–4; Appendix B; Figure 6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Editing a square-specific player-relative linear-probe coordinate at a single residual-stream layer can shift an Othello transformer's move predictions toward the legal moves of a counterfactual board. Negated and scaled the existing residual coordinate along a square's normalized mine-versus-theirs probe direction, using scales ranging from 0 to 16. The author reports promotion of newly legal moves and suppression of newly illegal moves. Effectiveness depends on intervention scale and layer; multiple edits are weaker and fragile, and newly legal moves do not recover normal scores. The original paper's systematic natural and unnatural intervention benchmarks were not rerun.

Specific finding: Increased cosine similarity between intervened next-move logits and logits from an alternative Othello board provides a useful proxy for successful transfer of that board's predictive consequences.
Specific finding: Replacing an activation with an inverse-probe reconstruction of an altered Othello board changes the intended board information sufficiently selectively for resulting prediction changes to identify use of that information.

Specific finding: The effectiveness of probe-direction board interventions in OthelloGPT depends on which and how many layers receive the intervention. Appendix B reports an intervention layer sweep and states that intervening on a sufficient number of layers is needed to alter predictions. Figure 7's numerical values and precise configurations are not supplied as text. Retained earlier information and self-repair are offered as hypotheses rather than experimentally distinguished explanations.

Specific finding: Lowering a maliciousness probe score at one layer can be followed by increasing probe scores at later layers, while intervening at multiple layers can reduce that rebound. Section 4.3 narrates later-layer score increases after a layer-10 intervention and reduced rebound after interventions across layers 10–13. Appendix F.3 reports that single-layer interventions generally do not reach keyword success above 90%. Numerical trajectories, uncertainty estimates, and figure-only details are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Downstream compensation or redundant cross-layer representations may explain why selected single-layer hazard-associated SAE clamps fail to change clinical-triage outputs.
Specific finding: OthelloGPT may combine board-state tracking with simpler endgame pathways that predict legal moves without first reconstructing the complete board.
Specific finding: An Othello sequence model may rely more on surface statistical shortcuts during late-game prediction than during early-game prediction.

Specific finding: In OthelloGPT's endgames, intermediate-layer legal-move readouts can become correct before linear board-state readouts, including under relaxed board-correctness criteria. The study compared the earliest layer with a completely correct top-N legal-move set against the earliest layer with all 64 squares correctly decoded. Move-before-board cases began around move 30 and increased toward game end. Similar trends persisted when requiring only 90% board accuracy or correct decoding of a minimum set of tiles supporting legal moves. Numerical frequencies and the sample count for this analysis are not given in the supplied text. Board-probe accuracy also declines near game end.

Specific finding: Intermediate vocabulary projections in OthelloGPT can progressively promote legal moves and suppress illegal moves across layers. The authors project intermediate residual states through the unembedding and report gradual promotion of legal moves and suppression of illegal ones. Adjacent but illegal squares tend to retain higher logits than other illegal squares. Figure 2's caption reports consistency across games and phases, but numerical trajectories and sampling details are absent from the supplied text.
location: Results on box #2: Direct logit attribution (Logit Lens); Figure 2 caption; footnote 6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Successive OthelloGPT layers generally improve the accuracy of board-feature probes and native-unembedding legal-move predictions, consistent with progressive representational refinement. On the 1,000-game test set, legal-move top-1 error under intermediate unembedding decreased from 0.215 at x1 through 0.079 at x4 to 0.001 at x8; applying OthelloGPT's unembedding to a randomly initialized GPT yielded a baseline error of 0.856. Relative-board accuracy and flipped-piece F1 generally improved across depth, with small late-layer declines. Reported cross-layer probe-direction similarities and example trajectories provide additional descriptive evidence.
Specific finding: Recovery of independently specified Othello board-state features provides an informative testbed for improving recovery of important features in natural-language models.

Specific finding: Attention vectors selected for important weights and similar attention-weight derivatives can exhibit joint attention-score ablation effects larger than the sum of their singleton ablation effects. The paper compares joint ablation of the two largest attention scores with summed individual ablations in screened vectors across the six attribution datasets. It reports screened instances in every evaluated input, with mean counts of 65–1,200 per input depending on model and dataset. Appendix A.16 extends the comparison to three scores in Gemma-2 2B and Llama-3.2 1B. Numerical effect-size summaries are absent from the supplied text, and plots are inaccessible. The written CV formula divides standard deviation by the signed mean, leaving treatment of negative or zero means unclear.
Specific finding: Elevated-temperature softmax backward attribution can approximate joint attention-score ablation effects better than ordinary gradients in attention self-repair cases. Figure 2 compares ordinary gradient attribution and TSG with measured joint two-score ablation effects for Llama-3.2 1B on FEVER. Appendices A.15–A.16 report similar comparisons across additional models and datasets and for three-score interventions. The prose reports closer approximation by TSG, but the supplied rendering provides neither visible plots nor aggregate approximation-error statistics.
location: Sections 5–6; Appendices A.5 and A.15–A.17; Figures 2 and 6–13

experiment_summary: Specific finding: An upstream perturbation affects the interacting attention scores jointly enough for joint-effect-oriented backward rules to be useful attribution approximations.
location: Section 7, 'Should gradients estimate the joint effect?'

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Image-concept TCAV scores can track captionless classification accuracy in classifiers trained on images with differently corrupted overlaid class captions. Four networks are trained at different caption-corruption probabilities. Image CAVs use class images; caption CAVs use captions with the other pixels randomly shuffled. Cab image-concept scores remain high alongside high captionless accuracy. Cucumber image-concept scores and captionless accuracy increase with caption corruption. Architectures, dataset sizes, all four exact corruption levels, and numerical agreement metrics are unspecified in the supplied text.
Specific finding: TCAV can identify class-logit sensitivity to selected visual and demographic concepts that were not explicit classifier output labels. Layerwise relative TCAV analyses report sensitivity to red for fire engines, stripes for zebras, Siberian huskies for dogsleds, female concepts for aprons, and a race concept for ping-pong balls. A dumbbell analysis uses 30 images per concept and finds greater sensitivity to arms than to the other compared concepts. The authors report applying repeated-reference significance testing and illustrate removal of a spurious dotted-texture result for zebras. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: Diagnostic-concept TCAV scores can suggest hypotheses about diabetic-retinopathy grading errors when model sensitivities diverge from clinical diagnostic expectations. A model predicting diabetic-retinopathy grades 0–4 shows high TCAV scores for relevant grade-4 concepts and low sensitivity to a non-diagnostic concept. For mild grade-1 cases, relatively high sensitivity to HMA, described as diagnostic of a higher grade, accompanies frequent overprediction as grade 2. A medical expert suggests de-emphasizing HMA for grade 1; no intervention tests this proposed fix. Sample sizes and quantitative error rates are not supplied.
Specific finding: Inputs targeted to be classified as zebras can have TCAV concept-sensitivity profiles that differ from those of ordinary zebra images. The authors construct two sets of targeted adversarial inputs using a single FGSM step, one from essentially random noise and one from non-zebra images with visually imperceptible changes. Figure 11 reports that their TCAV profiles remain different from those of ordinary zebras despite zebra classifications. The text gives 100% and 99% figures without clearly specifying their denominators or whether they denote confidence or attack success. No detection threshold, sensitivity, specificity, or defense evaluation is supplied.
models_studied: ["Four image classifiers trained on the controlled zebra/cab/cucumber dataset; architectures unspecified"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: ACE-discovered image-segment groups can exhibit perceptual coherence sufficient for humans to identify a conceptually different intruder with high accuracy. Thirty participants answered 15 scored intruder questions about ACE concepts and 15 about human-labeled reference concepts, following four training questions. Reported accuracy was 99% for ACE groups, averaging 14.9/15 with reported ±0.3, versus 97%, averaging 14.6/15 with ±0.7, for reference groups. The meaning of the reported ± quantities is unspecified. No statistical superiority or equivalence test is reported.
Specific finding: ACE-discovered image-segment groups can be recognized as meaningful more often than random segment groups and can elicit partially shared verbal descriptions across observers. Thirty participants chose between four same-concept segments and four random same-class segments, then described their chosen group with one word. Concept groups were selected in 95.6% of trials, averaging 14.3/15 with reported ±1.0 of unspecified type. The main text reports 56% agreement with the modal word and synonyms and 77% with the two most frequent words; the caption gives 55% instead of 56%. Four training questions were excluded.
Specific finding: Adding or removing image regions assigned to the five highest-TCAV ACE concepts can substantially affect Inception-V3 classification on images from the corresponding classes. Validation images were segmented at multiple resolutions and their segments assigned to discovered concepts using activation-space similarity. Figure 4's caption reports that removing the five highest-ranked concepts misclassifies more than 80% of initially correctly classified examples; the number of initially correct examples is not supplied. Addition of five concepts is described as reaching 'within 80%' of original accuracy, which does not specify an unambiguous recovery ratio. Random and reversed orders are plotted, but their comparative values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
Specific finding: Random spatial arrangements of segments from a class's highest-ranked ACE concepts can elicit that target class from an ImageNet classifier despite lacking the original objects' spatial organization. Examples of each class's four most important concepts were randomly placed on blank images, producing 100 images per class. Target-class classification exceeded 80% for 20 of 100 classes and exceeded 40% for more than half of the classes. Textual examples include zebra stripes and basketball jerseys. The stated random-chance rate of 0.001% is inconsistent with uniform guessing among 1,000 classes, which would be 0.1%. No matched random-segment baseline is reported.

Specific finding: CLIP-based activation matching can assign ImageNet classifier output units descriptions closer to their class names than the evaluated Network Dissection and MILAN baselines. With ImageNet validation probes and 20k candidate words, CLIP-Dissect obtains CLIP/mpnet cosine scores of 0.7900/0.5257, versus 0.6929/0.2952 for Network Dissection using Broden and 0.7080/0.2788 for MILAN(b). With ImageNet class names as candidates, scores reach 0.9902/0.9746. WPMI hyperparameters were selected using ResNet-50 output-description performance; no independent hyperparameter-selection split is specified.
Specific finding: On Places classifier output units whose class names are available in Broden, CLIP-based activation matching can achieve higher exact label accuracy than mask-based Network Dissection. CLIP-Dissect achieves 58.05% exact class-name accuracy versus 43.82% for Network Dissection on the 267 eligible output units. Both use Broden images and concepts; Network Dissection additionally uses Broden concept annotations.
Specific finding: CLIP-based hidden-unit descriptions can receive greater human agreement with highly activating images than randomly assigned descriptions. The crowdsourced study samples 200 units per layer, or all units when fewer are available, with three raters per unit. Mean agreement is 3.57/5, versus 2.61 for random descriptions evaluated on ten units per layer. A separate study samples 50 units per layer per model, totaling 500 units and 1,000 evaluations by two evaluators. Its mean is 0.655 under yes=1, maybe=0.5, no=0, with 68.4% exact evaluator agreement. The weighted score is not a binary proportion of correctly described units. These studies evaluate fit to extreme examples, not full activation-range fidelity or causal semantics.
Specific finding: Using CLIP-Dissect descriptions for a classifier's highest-contributing hidden unit can yield higher image-class readout accuracy than using Network Dissection or MILAN descriptions under the same readout procedure. For each image, selects the hidden unit maximizing activation times its final-layer weight into the model's predicted class, then predicts an image class by matching that unit's description to class names using the average of CLIP and mpnet cosine similarities. Reported image-class accuracies are 10.28% with CLIP-Dissect descriptions, 3.36% with Network Dissection descriptions, and 2.31% with MILAN(base). This is a model-output-assisted diagnostic, not an independent classifier using descriptions alone.
Specific finding: SoftWPMI can recover ImageNet output-unit class names more accurately than cosine similarity, rank-reorder similarity, or hard-set WPMI under the evaluated activation-matching procedure. Across CIFAR-100 train, Broden, ImageNet validation, and ImageNet validation plus Broden probes, SoftWPMI exact accuracies are 46.20%, 70.50%, 95.00%, and 95.40%, exceeding all three comparators in each setting. Rank-reorder accuracies are 36.30%, 57.50%, 89.80%, and 89.90%. With 20k candidates, SoftWPMI has the highest four-dataset mean mpnet score, 0.4525, although WPMI scores slightly higher on both ImageNet-containing probe sets. Similarity-function recipes have separately chosen hyperparameters.
Specific finding: Matching neuron activation profiles to pretrained image–text similarity scores enables neuron labeling from independently chosen unlabeled probe images and candidate text descriptions without fitting a neuron-description model. Constructs CLIP concept-score matrices, records scalar target-unit activations, and selects descriptions by profile similarity. Quantitative output-label evaluations and human hidden-unit evaluations concern ResNet-50 and ResNet-18. Additional prose reports qualitative applications to ResNet-152, ViT-B/16, and concatenations of pairs drawn from each neuron's top 100 single-word labels; these extensions lack aggregate accuracy evaluations.
Specific finding: Vision-language activation matching can correctly identify some classifier output concepts even when examples of those concepts are absent from the probing images. Using CIFAR-100 training probes, CLIP-Dissect assigns the exact correct breed to 46 of 118 dog-breed output units and the exact correct species to 22 of 59 bird-species output units. These are output-class identification results, not evidence that the target concepts appear in the probe images.

Specific finding: CLIP-Dissect and single-concept INVERT explanations achieve higher mean concept-synthesis AUC and MAD scores than MILAN explanations on the evaluated penultimate-layer vision neurons. Table 3 reports mean AUC ranges of 0.78–0.95 for CLIP-Dissect, 0.73–0.96 for INVERT, and 0.44–0.65 for MILAN. Both alternatives also exceed MILAN's mean MAD in every configuration. CLIP-Dissect exceeds INVERT's MAD in all four CNN configurations and DINO ViT-S/8, while INVERT leads on supervised ViT-B/16. INVERT optimizes AUC directly; abstract MILAN descriptions may be harder for SDXL to render. Reported standard deviations describe score variation, and no method-ranking significance test is supplied.
models_studied: ["ImageNet-trained ResNet18", "ImageNet-trained ResNet50", "ImageNet-trained ViT-B/16", "ImageNet-pretrained DINO ViT-S/8", "Places365-trained DenseNet161", "Places365-trained ResNet50"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Matryoshka dictionaries can outperform comparable BatchTopK dictionaries on Targeted Probe Perturbation across most tested dictionary widths and latent-ablation budgets. Runs SAEBench TPP on the five nested prefixes and corresponding BatchTopK baselines. Matryoshka performs better across nearly all tested widths and numbers of ablated latents. Exact scores, ablation budgets, and task inventory are not given in the supplied prose.

Specific finding: TopK and JumpReLU SAEs can outperform Standard SAEs on spurious-correlation removal and targeted probe perturbation evaluations. The paper compares Standard and TopK dictionaries trained on 200M Pile tokens with released Gemma Scope JumpReLU dictionaries. Sections 4.1–4.2 report separation favoring TopK and JumpReLU on SHIFT and TPP. SHIFT peaks around L0 20–100 for these architectures. Numerical architecture-level score differences and uncertainty cannot be recovered from the supplied figure rendering. Equation 3 assigns selective target impairment a negative score, leaving the numerical direction of reported TPP improvement unclear.
Specific finding: A single residual-stream TopK SAE can support profession-classification recovery after gender-feature ablation comparable to or better than a multi-site Standard-SAE SHIFT configuration. The paper reports 90% profession accuracy using gender-feature ablation through one layer-4 residual-stream TopK SAE. Its comparison table gives 59% without intervention and 88% for Standard SAEs at the embedding and layers 0–4. The caption associates the 16-Standard-SAE configuration with Marks et al.; that reference result should not be treated as an independently established new experiment here. No uncertainty estimates or evaluation sample denominator accompany the table, so the two-percentage-point difference does not establish statistical superiority.
Specific finding: Human judgments based on feature activation examples and output effects can identify which internal signals are irrelevant to an intended classification task.

Specific finding: Replacing general-purpose SAEs with domain-specialized SAEs can improve Bias in Bios profession accuracy and worst-group accuracy under the evaluated SHIFT feature-skyline procedure. Width-32,768 SAEs at residual, attention-output, and MLP-output sites are fine-tuned for one epoch on 8M Pile tokens retrieved using five biographies. SHIFT sweeps ablation of 1–200 feature-skyline-ranked circuit features. Without probe retraining, SSAE SHIFT improves profession accuracy from 88.5% to 90.2% and minimum profession accuracy across four gender–profession groups from 76.0% to 88.5%; gender-label accuracy falls from 54.0% to 53.4%. With linear-probe retraining, profession accuracy is 93.4% versus 93.1%, and worst-group accuracy is 89.5% versus 89.0%. The relevant subset sizes and repeated-run uncertainty are not reported.
Specific finding: Domain fine-tuning can substantially restore SHIFT classification performance after a general-purpose SAE dictionary is reduced to one eighth of its original width by slicing. Compressed SSAE SHIFT achieves 89.6% profession accuracy and 78.8% worst-group accuracy versus 80.5% and 48.6% for compressed GSAE SHIFT. After linear-probe retraining, the respective results are 93.2% and 88.5% versus 80.0% and 57.1%. The baseline is an intentionally sliced dictionary rather than a separately trained width-4,096 GSAE.

Specific finding: For categorical one-hot labels and finite-first-moment representations, linear guardedness under all nonnegative convex prediction losses is equivalent to equal class-conditional means and to zero representation-label cross-covariance. Formal result supplied here: Theorem 3.1 proves sufficiency of equal means using conditional Jensen's inequality. Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3 establish necessity through first-order optimality for cross-entropy, whose constant optimum exists when class probabilities are positive. Theorem 3.4 establishes equivalence with zero cross-covariance; Appendix B connects constant-predictor optimality to guardedness. Assumptions include finite first moments, one-hot labels with positive class probabilities, and affine predictors with biases.
Specific finding: An affine transformation produces linearly guarded categorical representations exactly when its linear part annihilates the representation-label cross-covariance matrix. Formal result supplied here: Theorem 4.1 applies Cov(PX+b,Z)=PΣXZ and the categorical guardedness equivalence to derive the necessary and sufficient condition ker(P) containing colsp(ΣXZ). Appendix D uses this criterion to establish guardedness for full-rank SAL and binary Mean Projection.
Specific finding: Equal class-conditional representation means are equivalent to equality across classes of the conditional means of every affine predictor's output. Formal proof supplied here: Theorem C.2 shows E[WX+b|Z=z]=WE[X]+b when class means agree. Conversely, applying the assumed output-mean parity to the identity map recovers equal class means.

Specific finding: Restricting linear concept erasure to orthogonal projections can require greater expected squared representation distortion than allowing oblique projections. Formal counterexample supplied here: Appendix F takes independent uniform X1,Z∈{−1,+1} and X2=X1+Z. Orthogonal erasure maps X to (X1,0), giving expected squared Euclidean distortion 2; an oblique eraser maps X to (X1,X1), giving distortion 1. Both remove the label information in this construction. Section 4.2 explains that guardedness constrains the projection's null space rather than fixing its range.
Specific finding: When concept labels are available for each input, subtracting the centered ordinary-least-squares prediction of the representation from those labels minimizes squared distortion subject to zero representation-label cross-covariance. Formal result supplied here: Theorem I.1 derives X'=X−ΣXZΣZZ⁺(Z−E[Z]). The proof separates means and projects each centered representation coordinate onto the orthogonal complement of the centered label span in the Hilbert space of square-integrable random variables. No empirical model evaluation is supplied.

Specific finding: Erasing POS- and NER-predictive representation directions can disrupt BERT word prediction substantially more than removing an equal number of random directions. For masked coarse POS, word accuracy is 56.98% originally, 54.55% after random removal, and 33.28% after INLP. For masked NER, corresponding accuracies are 57.71%, 56.88%, and 48.39%. Fine-POS erasure also causes larger losses than random removal in both input settings. Gold-label restoration recovers or exceeds original accuracy for coarse POS and NER.

Specific finding: Sequential erasure of linearly accessible POS information substantially degrades language modeling in the tested LLaMA and Pythia models, whereas matched-rank random subspace erasure has much smaller effects. Table 1 reports baseline→LEACE losses of 0.69→1.73, 0.66→1.84, and 0.62→1.96 for LLaMA 7B/13B/30B; corresponding random-erasure losses are 0.69/0.66/0.62. Pythia 160M/1.4B/6.9B/12B changes from 0.90/0.70/0.64/0.62 to 2.79/2.25/3.57/3.20, versus random-erasure losses of 0.99/0.72/0.66/0.63. Random subspaces are resampled per minibatch. Separate fitting and evaluation slices are used, but their size is ambiguously rendered as '222 tokens.' Appendix H describes a LEACE–SAL stabilization heuristic for norm divergence. The results establish effects of the implemented interventions, rather than selective removal of all and only POS computation.

Specific finding: Property-directed representation erasure, evaluated against matched random removal and gold-property restoration, provides a procedure for investigating a model's behavioral reliance on that property. Applies final- and intermediate-representation INLP interventions to six linguistic properties using English UD and OntoNotes. Measures word accuracy and output KL, with matched random-direction removal and gold-label restoration controls. Results demonstrate differentiated behavioral effects while exposing failures of property-specific attribution, especially for dependency erasure.

Specific finding: Sequentially applying linear concept erasure to activations at every layer provides a procedure for investigating a deep network's reliance on a target concept. Algorithm 1 fits each eraser after upstream interventions have changed the activation distribution. The procedure is evaluated by POS scrubbing across seven LLaMA and Pythia models, with random-erasure and SAL controls. These tests demonstrate a workable procedure with substantial behavioral effects, without establishing that all effects are exclusively mediated by POS. Covariance statistics can be accumulated incrementally, but the efficient implementation described caches intermediate states, requiring up to 500GB; avoiding caching increases computation from O(ℓ) to O(ℓ²).

Specific finding: Task-probe accuracy loss after projecting a salient token's assigned concept direction out of a sentence representation provides a useful proxy for the original model's reliance on that concept.
Specific finding: Concepts targeted by linear erasure in deep networks have sufficiently useful linear-subspace representations for linear erasure to be a plausible intervention on their use.

Specific finding: Relative clause membership has a sufficiently useful linear-subspace representation for edits to that subspace to investigate its contribution to agreement prediction.
Specific finding: Editing an INLP-derived relative clause subspace while preserving its orthogonal complement changes boundary information sufficiently selectively to interpret agreement effects as consequences of that linguistic property.

Specific finding: Iterative nullspace projection can reduce binary gender-label prediction from GloVe embeddings to approximately chance for a linear SVM while leaving substantial information accessible to a nonlinear MLP. Reported linear SVM gender accuracy decreases from 100% to 49.3% after INLP. A one-layer ReLU MLP still achieves 85.0%; an RBF-kernel SVM is reported to achieve chance accuracy. These comparisons demonstrate classifier-dependent accessibility rather than complete information erasure.
Specific finding: INLP can attenuate selected gender-association and clustering diagnostics in GloVe while leaving substantial neighborhood structure associated with original gender labels. For 2,000 male-biased and 2,000 female-biased words, two-cluster V-measure falls from 100% to 0.31% in the original embedding space and from 83.88% to 0.44% in the t-SNE representation. Three name-based WEAT tests return post-projection p-values of 0.855, 0.302, and 0.761; nonsignificance does not establish zero association. Across the evaluated professions, projection-versus-neighbor bias correlation decreases from 0.852 to 0.734. Neighbor labels are based on original gender bias, so residual correlation need not exclusively measure harmful bias in the projected space.

Specific finding: Subsequent BERT layers can restore linear predictability of linguistic properties after an intermediate-layer INLP intervention, with recovery depending on the property, intervention layer, and masking. After erasing each property at layer i, new probes are trained on subsequent layers. Unmasked coarse-POS information is more recoverable after early than late interventions. In contrast, masked coarse-POS erasure at layer 2 leaves subsequent probe accuracy around 32.7–42.1%, illustrating persistent loss after an early intervention. Other properties show heterogeneous recovery patterns.

Specific finding: INLP followed by linear-classifier retraining can reduce RMS gender true-positive-rate gaps in biography profession classification across bag-of-words, summed FastText, and frozen BERT representations, with representation-dependent accuracy changes. RMS gender TPR gaps decrease from 0.203 to 0.124 for bag-of-words, 0.184 to 0.089 for FastText, and 0.184 to 0.095 for BERT. Profession accuracies change from 78.2% to 80.1%, 78.1% to 73.0%, and 80.9% to 75.2%. Correlations between female TPR gaps and female representation by profession decrease from 0.894 to 0.670, 0.896 to 0.425, and 0.883 to 0.470. Attribute classifiers are fitted within randomly selected professions; downstream classification uses one-vs-all logistic classifiers. The source provides no uncertainty intervals for these comparisons.
Specific finding: Applying INLP to a sentiment classifier's hidden representations can reduce dialect-group true-positive-rate gaps while reducing sentiment accuracy, especially when dialect and sentiment labels are strongly correlated. At ratios 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8, TPR gaps change from 0.19 to 0.16, 0.29 to 0.22, 0.38 to 0.24, and 0.45 to 0.15. Corresponding sentiment accuracies change from 0.76 to 0.75, 0.78 to 0.74, 0.81 to 0.66, and 0.84 to 0.67. INLP acts on the MLP hidden layer, uses within-task-class protected-attribute fitting, and is followed by retraining the final linear layer while freezing the encoder. Appendix A.5 examines the iteration-dependent accuracy–TPR-gap tradeoff at ratio 0.8.
models_studied: ["Bag-of-words with one-vs-all logistic classification", "Summed FastText with one-vs-all logistic classification", "Frozen BERT final-layer [CLS] with one-vs-all logistic classification"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Erasing linearly accessible gender from BERT biography embeddings can reduce profession-classification gender TPR disparities while retaining most profession accuracy. Reported profession accuracy decreases from 79.3% to 77.3% after projection, while RMS gender TPR gap decreases from 0.198 to 0.084. Correlation of per-profession TPR gap with female representation decreases from 0.867 to 0.392. Refitting the profession classifier yields 78.1% accuracy and a larger gap of 0.158. The wording about initial classifier fitting is not fully explicit, but the source distinguishes the initial projection results from subsequent refitting. Linear gender erasure does not eliminate downstream disparities.

Specific finding: Ten rounds of learned iterative nullspace projection can reduce linear gender prediction from GloVe more than removing ten manually selected gender-pair difference directions. Linear classification accuracy is 54.4% after ten INLP rounds versus 80.7% after removing ten predefined pair-difference directions. The comparison evaluates the complete procedures without isolating learned direction selection from possible differences in removed rank.
location: Section 6.1.1, Human-selected vs. Learned Directions; footnote 4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Removing a small class-targeted unit group can severely impair a VGG-16's discrimination of that class while barely changing overall multiclass accuracy. Zeroing the top 20 ski resort units lowers balanced ski resort accuracy from 81.4% to 53.5%, while overall 365-way validation accuracy changes from 53.3% to 52.6%. Balanced single-class chance is 50%; multiclass chance is approximately 0.27%.
Specific finding: Most balanced single-class discrimination performance in a Places365 VGG-16 can depend on a small, class-specific subset of final-convolutional units. Across all 365 scene classes, removing each class's top 20 units lowers mean balanced single-class accuracy to 53.0%, near 50% chance. Keeping only those 20 lowers balanced single-class accuracy by an average of 3.6 percentage points. These are separate class-specific interventions, not one shared 20-unit subnetwork.
location: Results: Role of Units in a Scene Classifier; Figure 2B–C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Held-out classification accuracy changes after zeroing a unit provide a useful operational proxy for that unit's importance to the trained classifier.
Specific finding: The largest class-specific accuracy reduction caused by a unit's removal provides a useful proxy for how strongly that unit supports specialized class information.
Specific finding: Held-out classification accuracy changes after zeroing a unit provide a useful operational proxy for that unit's importance to the trained classifier.
location: Results: Role of Units in a Scene Classifier

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Zeroing a representation coordinate or deleting a word removes its relevant contribution sufficiently selectively for the resulting prediction change to explain the original model's dependence on that information.

Specific finding: Zeroing representation coordinates and removing input words provide a common procedure for measuring a fixed NLP classifier's dependence on representations at multiple levels. Applies coordinate zeroing to linguistic classifiers over 50-dimensional word2vec/GloVe embeddings and word erasure to Stanford Sentiment Treebank recurrent classifiers. Reports task-specific sensitivity profiles, hidden-unit heatmaps, and word rankings. Equation 1's negative-log-probability definition conflicts with the verbal interpretation of score signs; the frequency-regression adaptation is unspecified.
models_studied: ["Two-hidden-layer tanh linguistic classifiers", "Standard tanh RNN sentiment classifier", "Uni-LSTM sentiment classifier", "Bi-LSTM sentiment classifier"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Output changes after zeroing selected attention weights and renormalizing the remainder provide useful operational measures of the corresponding intermediate representations' importance.

Specific finding: CNN units with stronger class selectivity or class-probability correlation can cause greater maximum class-specific damage when removed, without causing greater overall accuracy loss. The authors compared overall and maximum class accuracy changes against maximum class selectivity, maximum activation–class-probability correlation, maximum concept IoU, and weight L1 norm using Spearman correlations. Their qualitative account associates stronger class alignment with greater maximum class damage, whereas highly selective units cause less overall damage. Concept alignment has a weaker class-specific association, and L1 norm is described as informative for both outcomes. Numerical coefficients are inaccessible in the supplied figure rendering, and the prose's correlation-sign descriptions are inconsistent.
Specific finding: Activation-based unit attributes can predict which class suffers the largest accuracy reduction from a unit's removal in independently initialized instances of the same CNN. Separate logistic regressions used full vectors of concept IoU, class correlation, or class selectivity to predict the index of the maximally damaged class. On units from two held-out model instances, accuracies were 38.67%, 38.28%, and 38.08%, respectively. Averaging their predicted probabilities achieved 39.06%. No uncertainty estimates or class-frequency baseline are reported.

Specific finding: Training with dropout can distribute single-coordinate erasure sensitivity more evenly across embedding dimensions in linguistic classifiers. The authors compare coordinate-erasure heatmaps with and without dropout and report more evenly distributed importance. GloVe coordinates 26 and 31 become less dominant on most tasks while remaining prominent for frequency prediction. No quantitative concentration statistic or repeated-run analysis is reported, and heatmap images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
models_studied: ["Two-hidden-layer tanh classifiers using word2vec embeddings", "Two-hidden-layer tanh classifiers using GloVe embeddings"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Training AlexNet with conv5 channel dropout can reduce conv5 single-unit class-specific ablation effects and concept-detector counts while increasing class-specific ablation effects in conv4. The added-dropout model had approximately two percentage points lower overall accuracy. The authors report decreased conv5 maximum-class-damage curves and Network Dissection interpretable-unit counts, while conv4 maximum class damage increased. These observations indicate changed coordinate-level dependence but do not establish uniform information redistribution or a compensatory mechanism. Numerical detector counts are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Adding batch normalization throughout AlexNet's convolutional layers can reduce maximum class-specific damage from individual-unit ablations while retaining similar overall classification accuracy. The authors trained an AlexNet-Places variant with batch normalization in each convolutional layer. It achieved similar generalization accuracy to the baseline and showed reduced maximum-class-damage curves across the compared layers. Numerical curve values, repeat counts, and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
models_studied: ["AlexNet trained on Places365", "AlexNet trained on Places365 with 50% conv5 channel dropout"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Zeroing selected high-magnitude LayerNorm scale and bias coordinates after fine-tuning can substantially damage BERT-base and RoBERTa-base GLUE performance, with much smaller effects from matched-count random-coordinate removals in BERT. Replicates Kovaleva et al. (2021). BERT results cover eight GLUE tasks and five fine-tuning runs. Joint removal zeros 48 parameters and changes MNLI-matched accuracy from 84.5 ± 0.2% to 58.4 ± 3.3%, versus 84.5 ± 0.2% after two random-coordinate removals. Random controls average five selections per fine-tuned model. RoBERTa joint removal changes MNLI-matched accuracy from 87.6% to 44.9%; its table supplies neither random controls nor repeated-run uncertainty.
location: Sections 2 and 3.1; Tables 1 and 5; Appendices A–C

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Joint removal of selected Vision Transformer outlier coordinates can substantially impair CIFAR-100 classification while having little effect on CIFAR-10 classification. Joint removal changes CIFAR-100 accuracy from 92.5% to 84.9%, versus 92.4% after removing two random coordinates. CIFAR-10 changes from 98.6% to 98.5%. Individual removals have smaller effects. Repeated-run uncertainty and detailed ViT fine-tuning settings are not supplied.

Specific finding: Removing selected BERT-family LayerNorm outliers can shift masked-token predictions toward frequent vocabulary items and away from rare items. Examines predicted versus masked-token counts over 200,000 Wikipedia sentences with 15% random masking. The prose reports more frequent-token and fewer rare-token predictions after BERT outlier removal. The RoBERTa analysis reports a related shift, particularly excess prediction of </s>. No aggregate frequency-shift effect size is supplied. A separate BERT POS analysis reports increased noun and punctuation predictions, especially after removing coordinate 381, with additional symbol and adposition changes under joint removal.
location: Section 4.1; Figure 3; Appendix C, Figure 8; Appendix E, Figure 15

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected GloVe embedding coordinates can correlate strongly with word frequency while dominating coordinate-erasure sensitivity across several linguistic prediction tasks. The authors report that coordinate 31 dominates many task-erasure profiles and that retraining without it exposes coordinate 26. Figure 3's caption reports coordinate-magnitude versus frequency associations of R²=0.55 and R²=0.27, respectively, both with p<1e-5. These associations do not uniquely establish why the classifiers rely on those coordinates. Plot images are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Selecting the item with the largest attention–gradient product can yield more successful singleton decision-flipping erasures than selecting the item with the largest attention weight. Appendix A.3 compares singleton erasures selected by attention magnitude, attention-weight gradient, and their product. Summing the yes rows in Figures 9 and 13 confirms higher product-selected flip rates in all 24 configurations. Gradient-only singleton selection is less consistent: the displayed rounded tables in Figures 9 and 12 indicate lower rates than attention in ten configurations, whereas Appendix A.3 says fourteen. This internal discrepancy does not affect the product comparison. No repeated-training or significance analysis is reported.
Specific finding: Ranking final attention inputs by attention-weight gradients can identify smaller decision-flipping erasure sets than ranking them by attention magnitude in contextualized text classifiers. Erased inputs in descending attention order, random order, descending derivative of maximum output-class probability with respect to attention weights, or descending attention–gradient product. Section 5.4 reports that in ten of sixteen encoder-equipped models, gradient rankings found smaller decision-flipping sets than attention on over 50% of analyzed examples. For every encoder-equipped model, gradient wins were at least 1.6 times as frequent as attention wins. These are ranked-prefix comparisons rather than exhaustive subset optimization; no repeated-training uncertainty estimates are supplied.

Specific finding: The classification effects of masking selected emotion-associated neurons in Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct depend on the targeted emotion, masking setting, and layer range. Swept masking settings and layer groups. Anger shows a reported accuracy change of approximately −2% at the 1% setting and −4% to −5% at 4–5%; surprise shows a large decline already at 1%. For surprise, reported changes are −4.15% for Bottom, −10.46% for Middle, and −20.75% for AllLayers. Disgust changes little under AllLayers masking but declines by a reported −1.63% under Top masking. Fear has a reported −2.44% change under AllLayers masking. These reported percentages are not explicitly defined as relative changes or percentage-point changes. Layer groups are not documented as matched for masked-neuron count.
Specific finding: Masking entropy-selected emotion-associated neuron groups can sharply reduce target-emotion classification accuracy in some Llama-3.1 checkpoint–emotion combinations while leaving others largely unchanged or improved. Compared unmodified classification with emotion-group masking. In 8B, disgust accuracy falls from 96.11% to 37.22%, a 58.89-percentage-point decrease. In 70B, surprise accuracy falls from 93.17% to 73.83%, a 19.34-percentage-point decrease. The paper reports little change for 8B happiness and 70B disgust and a slight improvement for 8B anger. Matched random-group controls and statistical uncertainty are not supplied.

Specific finding: Selected SAE encoder-projection pipelines can reduce CLIP retrieval gender imbalance more than the evaluated linear-probe-selected decoder-masking pipeline. CelebA Table 2 reports KL 0.0792±0.0067 and MaxSkew 0.2605±0.0148 for S&P versus 0.2604±0.1540 and 0.5735±0.1790 for LP-selected masked reconstruction. FairFace Table 3 reports 0.0476±0.0062 and 0.2044±0.0157 versus 0.0572±0.0147 and 0.2249±0.0296. With the same Stylist selector on CelebA, interpolated S&P instead has worse KL than masking, 0.079235 versus 0.061290, while retaining substantially higher task AUC. Reported variability does not establish statistical significance.
Specific finding: A gender axis constrained to selected SAE encoder directions can improve retrieval gender-balance metrics over a directly learned CAV while retaining similar hair-color classification utility. Table 5 reports S&P KL 0.079235, MaxSkew 0.260566, and worst-group AUC 0.752426 versus CAV values 0.145891, 0.288400, and 0.754424. The unmodified model has KL 0.113880, MaxSkew 0.293723, and AUC 0.754743. No uncertainty or controlled sample-size comparison is supplied for this ablation.
Specific finding: Projection using behavior-associated SAE encoder directions can reduce judged aggressive and sycophantic expression more than the evaluated SAE masking intervention in explicitly style-prompted Llama-3 opinions. Behavior-feature discovery uses 100 target-style and 100 contrasting opinions per behavior, approximately 55,000 tokens, and logistic-regression feature ranking. Section 5 reports a 1.6-point aggressiveness reduction while masking remains near baseline, and a sycophancy score reduction 3.6 times the masking reduction. Aggregate numerical means cannot be recovered from the supplied image-only plot. Judge identity, uncertainty, human validation, broad capability controls, and discovery/evaluation topic separation are not specified. Examples include sarcasm, awkward phrasing, and template generation.

Specific finding: DIFFMASK can remove substantial fractions of SST BERT inputs or intermediate token states while approximately preserving validation sentiment F1 and producing relatively stable attributions across initialization seeds. Validation F1 changes from 37.9% to 38.3% with 46.3% of input tokens masked, and to 38.9% with 67.6% of hidden states masked. Across five seeds, reported attribution standard deviations are 0.05 for inputs and 0.03 for hidden states. Aggregate F1 preservation does not establish unchanged individual predictions, output distributions, or mechanisms.
Specific finding: Amortized hidden-state-conditioned masking can recover a uniform queried-digit attribution reference more closely than exact erasure and the evaluated gradient and perturbation attribution methods. Table 1 reports DIFFMASK KL/JS divergences of 0.01/0.00 nats from the reference. Integrated Gradients yields 1.32/0.27, Schulz et al. 1.12/0.18, and Guan et al. 0.88/0.24. Exact erasure has JS 0.27 and a support mismatch preventing a finite KL comparison. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied for these scores.
location: Section 3.2, Faithfulness and Plausibility; Appendix C.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: An importance ranking that identifies smaller decision-flipping erasure prefixes provides a better operational explanation of a classifier's decision than a ranking requiring larger prefixes.
Specific finding: Shorter, more aspect-specific word deletions that flip an aspect classifier's decision provide a useful proxy for that classifier's interpretability.

Specific finding: Approximately horizontal weight bands occur in the final convolutional filters of ImageNet-trained InceptionV1, ResNet50, and VGG19, while the inspected AlexNet lacks this pattern. Compared three-factor NMF visualizations of late convolutional filters in InceptionV1, ResNet50, VGG19, and AlexNet. The first three display banding; AlexNet does not. No numerical banding effect sizes or uncertainty estimates are supplied.
Specific finding: Training on ImageNet images rotated by 90 degrees changes late convolutional weight bands from approximately horizontal to approximately vertical. Trained the simplified model on 90-degree-rotated inputs and repeated the intervention in InceptionV1, ResNet50, and VGG19 trained from scratch. Weight visualizations show vertical rather than horizontal bands in all four architectures, demonstrating dependence on training-image orientation.
Specific finding: Allowing a final classifier direct access to spatial positions by removing preceding pooling can eliminate late convolutional weight banding, but the effect depends on architecture. Removed final global average pooling from the simplified model and tested corresponding pooling removal in three common architectures trained from scratch. Final-layer banding disappeared in three of the four architectures; VGG19 was the exception. In the simplified model, the fully connected layer's parameter count increased 49-fold and the model overfit, so the intervention also changes capacity.

Specific finding: Selected late convolutional filters in InceptionV1 exhibit horizontal spatial weight bands when visualized using one-sided NMF. The article presents one-sided NMF visualizations of eight selected InceptionV1 mixed5b_5x5 filters and describes their weights as horizontally banded. This is a qualitative weight-inspection demonstration, without a quantitative banding measure or architectural intervention.

Specific finding: Complex Gabor units in InceptionV1 combine similarly oriented edge filters, including opposite-polarity filters, to reduce sensitivity to exact edge position and dark-light polarity.
Specific finding: Some InceptionV1 mixed3a units detect the absence of color through predominantly inhibitory connections from earlier color features.

Specific finding: Composing intervening weight maps, with nonlinear operations replaced by linear approximations, provides a static representation of indirect connections that can expose aggregate feature structure. A qualitative expansion from conv2d2 to InceptionV1 mixed3b 208 is presented to expose aggregate absence-of-color structure in the center of its inputs. Figures 9–10 compare five strongest contributing intermediate neurons with eighteen top expanded connections. The article describes gradient-based implementation through modified nonlinear operations but supplies no quantitative approximation-fidelity evaluation or formal expected-gradient derivation.
location: Dealing with Indirect Interactions; Benefits of Expanded Weights; Figures 9–10

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A bottleneck 1x1 convolution followed by a spatial convolution can be usefully visualized as a low-rank effective connection obtained by multiplying their weight matrices, despite the intervening ReLU.

Specific finding: Composing a known linear input embedding with the first learned weight matrix can reveal Boolean feature-code patterns obscured in the raw learned coordinates. Section 6.5 describes trained pairwise-DNF networks under three embedding types. Raw first-layer matrices under Hadamard and random embeddings appear unstructured, while products W_1 C_0 display the expected positive-witness pair coding and negative-witness contrasting signs. The demonstration is qualitative; Figure 22 itself is unavailable visually in the supplied rendering. Most Section 4 statistics also analyze such composed matrices.
models_studied: ["Pairwise-DNF ReLU MLPs with identity, Hadamard, or symmetric random input embeddings"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Visualizing spatial upstream directions obtained by replacing ReLUs with identity operations provides a proposed way to inspect the shape components feeding a visual neuron.
location: The Curve Detector Algorithm; decomposed-feature-visualization footnote

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Intermediate neurons can be treated as having equal, independent firing probabilities when interpreting nonlinear expanded weights as an expected gradient up to a constant factor.

Specific finding: Output-weight vectors learned from abstract operation symbols can exhibit projected geometry corresponding to modular arithmetic cycles or permutation-group cosets. t-SNE projections of output-layer rows show modular-addition circular organization, annotated using repeated addition of 8, and S5 clusters identified as cosets of a specified subgroup or its conjugates. The authors find recognizable structure in some networks and report that it is more apparent with weight decay. No quantitative representation-recovery metric or causal intervention is supplied.
models_studied: ["Two-layer decoder-only transformers trained on modular addition and S5 composition"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Semantic coherence of leading GPT-2 MLP singular-vector vocabulary projections generally increases with transformer layer depth, with departures depending on model and weight-matrix type. Manual labels show a largely increasing fraction of interpretable MLP-input directions across GPT-2 Medium blocks. Automated layerwise surveys report increases from roughly 40–50% to 80–90%, alongside middle-layer peaks and late declines, especially for GPT-2 Medium MLP-output weights. These are source-reported prose summaries; the supplied rendering does not expose the plots needed to check exact layerwise values.
Specific finding: Cosine comparison between encoded query-token sets and transformer weight singular vectors can retrieve candidate directions with related vocabulary-projection semantics. Compared encoded query words with singular vectors using cosine similarity, illustrating retrieval of fire-related and negatively aligned ice/rain directions at a threshold of 0.15. Queries built from a direction's own top tokens reportedly recover only about 0.5 cosine similarity. Encoding through the unembedding pseudoinverse reportedly works better than the ordinary embedding. No retrieval benchmark, denominator, or quantitative method comparison is supplied, and head identifiers differ between the tracing discussion and earlier examples.
location: Manual Labelling of GPT2-medium W_in; Experiments with automated direction labelling

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The OV singular vectors of Pythia-1.4B head 15.7 have vocabulary readouts containing recognizable geographic clusters. Decomposed the selected memory head's OV matrix and inspected its right-singular-vector top-ten vocabulary projections. Examples include Italy/Naples, Greece/Athens, and Japan/Tokyo clusters. A context-head comparison lacks similarly clear geographic clustering, but that head is labeled 19.4 here and differently elsewhere. No quantitative geographic enrichment or activation-conditioned semantic validation is reported. Appendix F also reports a behaviorally similar alternative memory head with less interpretable readouts.

Specific finding: Pythia-70m MLP-output dictionaries with poorer reconstruction and loss-recovery statistics can nevertheless appear more interpretable under informal feature inspection. After examining features from both suites, the author tentatively judges the 32,768-feature dictionaries more interpretable despite lower loss recovery and worse MSE at five of six layers. The explanation that high-frequency, uninterpretable features inflate the smaller suite's statistics is conjectural.
location: The dictionaries; miscellaneous notes comparing the two suites

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Separately trained sparse autoencoders can reconstruct all six Pythia-70m-deduped MLP outputs with sparse codes while retaining substantial reported loss recovery. The six layerwise dictionaries report MSE of 0.003–0.032, average active counts of 9.951–235.05, alive fractions of 58.7–99.8%, and loss recovered of 86.7–98.4%. These are descriptive results without uncertainty estimates or specified evaluation sample counts.
Specific finding: Sparse dictionaries learned from Pythia-70m MLP outputs provide sufficiently meaningful feature coordinates to support downstream interpretability projects.
location: The dictionaries; assessment of suitability for downstream projects

experiment_summary: Specific finding: SAE reconstruction fidelity can vary substantially across text domains, including worse downstream fidelity on multilingual text than on formulaic mathematics. Evaluated delta LM loss by Pile validation subset using 65K-width SAEs for Gemma 2 2B and 131K-width SAEs for 9B. Performance is best on DeepMind mathematics and worst on Europarl among studied subsets. The proposed explanation involving predominantly English training data is not directly tested.

Specific finding: Including both user and assistant turns in SAE training can substantially improve user-turn reconstruction relative to assistant-only training while retaining similar or better assistant-turn reconstruction. On 636,000 held-out turns, comprising 319,000 user and 317,000 assistant turns, including both roles reduces user-turn nMSE from 0.355 to 0.167 at layer 6, 0.281 to 0.131 at layer 11, 0.294 to 0.122 at layer 16, and 0.272 to 0.101 at layer 21. Assistant-turn nMSE changes from 0.237 to 0.204, 0.144 to 0.140, 0.123 to 0.122, and 0.088 to 0.088, respectively. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported.

Specific finding: The fraction of SAE features observed to activate can change substantially with the activation-collection corpus and sequence length. Across layers of the 131k Gemma SAEs, approximately 15% of features never fire on the 10M-token RedPajama-v2 collection at sequence length 256, versus 5% when using length 1024. On uncopyrighted Pile at length 256, approximately 1% never fire. The reported low-frequency fraction, approximately 30% on RedPajama-v2, falls to 15% on Pile; the text alternates between 'not more than 200' and 'fewer than 200' for this threshold.

Specific finding: Learning-rate warmup can reduce early feature death during GPT-2 Small residual-stream SAE training. The author reports that adding initial learning-rate warmup before using ghost gradients made a substantial qualitative difference to feature-density histograms and kept otherwise lost features alive. The post attributes an earlier observation to Arthur Conmy. Schedules, matched configurations, and numerical reductions are absent, and the author explicitly states that a joint warmup/ghost-gradient ablation was not performed.
Specific finding: Geometric-median decoder-bias initialization has been associated with fewer dense, apparently uninterpretable features in some GPT-2 Small residual-stream SAE training runs. The author reports trying geometric-median bias initialization and observing improved feature-density behavior. In some autoencoders, geometric medians estimated from approximately 250,000 sampled activations were closer to final decoder biases than the corresponding activation means. No distances or controlled initialization comparison are supplied, and the post states that mean initialization might work just as well.
location: 5 Minute Summary: Using a learning rate warmup; Which tricks help the most?

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Increasing the number of ablated SAE latents from 50 to 500 can reduce measured spurious correlation removal performance. In Table 2, Top-500 SCR is lower than Top-50 SCR for six of seven configurations and equal for the nominal-L0-445 Gemma dictionary. Llama declines from 0.713 to −0.727, Pythia from 0.414 to 0.232, and the five Gemma configurations change from 0.376/0.385/0.407/0.417/0.384 to 0.316/0.309/0.359/0.339/0.384. No uncertainty estimates are supplied. Removal of useful features is offered as an explanation but is not separately isolated.

Specific finding: Matching thresholded CNN channel activation maps to annotated visual-concept masks can automatically produce channel descriptions that human raters recognize as descriptive. AMT raters judged whether a phrase described most of 15 images with highly activating patches highlighted for each channel. Conditional on acceptance of prior human labels, Network Dissection descriptions were accepted for 37%, 56%, 54%, 59%, and 71% of channels in conv1–conv5. The selected denominators were 57, 126, 247, 258, and 194 channels, respectively, from layers containing 96, 256, 384, 384, and 256 channels. A second evaluation of the human labels yielded consistency of 82%, 76%, 83%, 82%, and 91%. These judgments concern selected high-activation examples.

Specific finding: Matching thresholded CNN channel activation maps to annotated visual-concept masks can automatically produce channel descriptions that human raters recognize as descriptive. AMT raters judged human-written and automatically assigned descriptions presented in randomized order without identifying their origin. Units had first been selected through validation of human-written descriptions. Table III reports automatic-label approval of 37%, 56%, 54%, 59%, and 71% across conv1–conv5, versus 82%, 76%, 83%, 82%, and 91% for human descriptions. Selected interpretable-unit counts are 57/96, 126/256, 247/384, 258/384, and 194/256. These conditional judgments do not estimate semantic accuracy across all units.

Specific finding: Across the evaluated CNN representations, the number of individually aligned object detectors is positively associated with action40 linear-transfer accuracy, but does not determine its ranking. For each evaluated representation, the authors trained a linear SVM with C=0.001 on action40 and compared mean per-class test accuracy with unique object-detector counts. They report a positive association without a numerical correlation coefficient. ResNet152-ImageNet achieved the best transfer accuracy despite having fewer unique object detectors than ResNet152-Places365. The comparison does not establish that adding detectors causes improved transfer.
models_studied: ["Evaluated AlexNet representations", "Evaluated GoogLeNet representations", "Evaluated VGG-16 representations", "ResNet-152 trained on ImageNet", "ResNet-152 trained on Places365", "Evaluated self-supervised AlexNet or derived representations"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Across the evaluated visual representations, the number of distinct object-aligned channels is positively associated with frozen-feature classification accuracy on Indoor67, SUN397, and Caltech256, but does not determine performance ranking. The authors fit linear SVMs with C = 0.001 on each transfer dataset's training split and evaluate class-averaged test accuracy. The prose reports positive associations between accuracy and distinct object-detector counts across the three datasets. ResNet152-ImageNet can outperform ResNet152-Places365 on object-centric transfer despite having fewer object detectors. Correlation coefficients for these transfer comparisons are not supplied.
models_studied: ["Evaluated supervised CNN representations", "Evaluated self-supervised CNN representations", "ImageNet-ResNet-152", "Places365-ResNet-152"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Removing fully connected layer dropout from Places205-AlexNet can increase texture-detector counts while decreasing object-detector counts in its final convolutional representation. The authors trained an AlexNet variant without dropout in the fully connected layers. It exhibited more texture detectors and fewer object detectors, with 49.2% validation top-1 accuracy, compared with approximately 50.0% for initialization repeats. Numerical detector-count differences and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the prose.
models_studied: ["AlexNet trained on Places205", "AlexNet trained on Places205 without fully connected layer dropout"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Removing fully connected layer dropout from Places205-AlexNet can increase texture-detector counts while decreasing object-detector counts in its final convolutional representation. The NoDropout model has more texture detectors and fewer object detectors than the baseline. Validation top-1 accuracy is 49.2%, compared with approximately 50.0% for baseline-repeat models. Numerical detector-count differences and repeated NoDropout runs are not supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: The evaluated self-supervised visual representations contain many texture-aligned channels but fewer object-aligned channels than the evaluated supervised representations. The authors perform Network Dissection on models trained through context prediction, puzzles, egomotion, movement, video order, tracking, object-centric alignment, colorization, inpainting, cross-channel prediction, ambient audio, and transitive invariance. The prose reports texture-heavy profiles and relatively few object detectors compared with supervised models; audio and puzzle models also exhibit some object and part detectors. The colorization model has almost no color detectors. Training of the self-supervised models is attributed to cited prior work; the dissection comparison is performed here.
Specific finding: Training a CNN from scratch as an image-captioning encoder can produce individual channels aligned with object concepts. The authors train a ResNet-18 plus LSTM captioning model from scratch using COCO's five captions per image and apply Network Dissection to its final convolutional layer. The prose reports many emergent object detectors. Numerical detector counts, matched alternative-training controls, and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied in the text.

Specific finding: A VGG-16 trained on scene labels can develop individual units aligned with diverse object concepts despite receiving no explicit object labels. Dissection on held-out Places365 validation images finds conv5_3 matches above 4% IoU covering 51 distinct object classes, 22 parts, 12 materials, and eight colors. The number of distinct object classes matched is largest in the final convolutional layer, while object-part diversity peaks at conv5_1.
Specific finding: An unsupervised Progressive GAN trained on kitchen images can learn intermediate units whose spatial activations align with generated objects and object parts. Layerwise dissection finds the largest number of distinct object and part matches at layer 5. Window-part unit 314, thresholded at peak activation 8.03, predicts large-window presence with reported accuracy of 78.2%. Figure 3F displays 800 generated images with segmented windows exceeding 5% of image area and 800 without such large windows. The threshold-selection protocol is unspecified, and counterexamples show windows generated without activation of this unit.
location: Results: Emergence of Object Detectors in a Scene Classifier; Figure 1D–E

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Learned combinations of CNN filters can predict annotated visual concepts better on average than the evaluated single-filter predictors, although some concepts perform worse with combinations. Compares multi-filter and single-filter predictors on BRODEN validation examples. At AlexNet conv5, Table 1 reports combinations equaling or outperforming single filters for 75.7% of segmentation concepts and 88.1% of classification concepts; the stated task inventories are 682 and 1,189 concepts respectively. A separate failure analysis reports 133 conv5 classification failures, of which 103 have at most 20 positive training examples and all but one have fewer than 100; this count is not reconciled with the stated inventory and Table 1 percentage. Additional architecture and supervision comparisons also report average gains from combinations. Prior demonstrations of multi-filter advantages are explicitly cited as antecedents.
Specific finding: An individual CNN filter can be selected as a predictor for many annotated concepts, so a filter–concept association need not be exclusive. Counts how often each filter is selected for a concept. Around 15% of conv1 filters are selected for at least 20 segmentation concepts or 30 classification concepts. A substantial portion of filters in each layer, except conv1 for segmentation, are never selected. Selected conv5 examples include filter 66 associated with sheep, horse, and cow torsos, illustrating that shared associations can have a related visual interpretation.
Specific finding: Visualizations restricted to extreme CNN filter examples can overstate how consistently a single filter captures a concept across other examples containing that concept. Examines individual-image IoU distributions for dog and train and displays dog and airplane masks at deciles of their nonzero IoU distributions. Single filters have many zero-overlap examples, often because no activations survive thresholding, and visually informative masks mainly in higher deciles. Learned combinations produce informative masks across a broader range in the selected displays. No controlled human evaluation or population-wide visualization-quality estimate is reported.
Specific finding: The number of selected CNN filters needed for near-optimal concept prediction varies across concept categories and between segmentation and classification. Refits probes using varying numbers of filters ranked by absolute full-probe weight. Most classification categories saturate by approximately 50 filters, while scenes approach their optimum around 15. Segmentation category averages peak at eight filters for materials and parts, 16 for objects, and 128 for colors; materials and parts decline beyond their peaks. These are outcomes of the tested selection and optimization procedure, rather than lower bounds on necessary filter counts.
models_studied: ["ImageNet-trained AlexNet", "Places365-trained AlexNet", "ImageNet-trained VGG16", "Places365-trained VGG16", "ImageNet-trained GoogLeNet", "Places365-trained GoogLeNet", "Self-supervised AlexNet variants: tracking, audio, objectcentric, moving, egomotion"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Zeroing a small group of tree-associated units in a church-scene generator can substantially reduce segmentation-estimated tree area. Removing the 20 most tree-specific units reduces segmented tree pixels by 53.3% over 10,000 randomly generated images. Qualitative examples retain buildings and render building regions previously occluded by trees. Preservation of unrelated content and realism are not comprehensively quantified, and the examples do not establish that hidden building details were explicitly computed before intervention.
Specific finding: Activating the same door-associated generator units can insert visually different doors in suitable scene regions while producing little insertion in unsuitable regions. The same intervention is tested at every feature-map location in 10,000 randomly generated images. The text reports that segmentation-estimated added door area is greater on buildings, especially existing windows, while insertion into trees or sky is nearly impossible under this intervention. Examples show context-dependent door size, style, and placement. Numerical context-specific insertion rates are not supplied in the text.
models_studied: ["Progressive GAN trained on LSUN outdoor churches"]
location: Results: Role of Units in a GAN; Figure 4A–B

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Spatial manipulation of concept-ranked generator unit groups can provide an interactive interface for adding and erasing semantic objects in generated scenes. The implemented interface maps brush strokes to activation or zeroing of 20-unit concept groups. Figure 6 demonstrates adding a dome in place of a steeple. The text describes composed edits and references demonstration movies, which are not supplied. No controlled user study or quantitative editing benchmark is reported. Related generator manipulation is explicitly cited as prior work.
location: Applications: Semantic Paint Using a GAN; Figure 6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing internal coordinates with values from a matched prompt differing in subject number provides an interpretable intervention on the contribution of those coordinates to number-agreement behavior.

Specific finding: The fraction of sentence contexts in which a language model assigns greater conditional likelihood to the grammatical verb inflection than to its number-mismatched alternative provides a useful operational measure of subject–verb agreement performance.

Specific finding: The fraction of sentence contexts in which a language model assigns greater conditional likelihood to the grammatical verb inflection than to its number-mismatched alternative provides a useful operational measure of subject–verb agreement performance.

Specific finding: Correct-versus-incorrect verb-inflection probability ratios and their changes under subject-number swaps provide useful operational measures of a language model's subject–verb agreement preferences.

Specific finding: GPT-2 and Transformer-XL exhibit different layerwise coordinate-mediation profiles for adjacent versus separated subject–verb agreement dependencies. Computed individual-coordinate natural indirect effects and averaged effects over the highest-NIE 5% selected separately in each layer and structure. Adjacent dependencies show increasing effects toward higher layers. Even one intervening adverb produces the separated-dependency profile, with effects peaking at layer 0 and upper-middle layers and approaching zero in the highest layers. Averaging all coordinates reportedly preserves profile shapes. Transformer-XL exhibits a similar adjacent/separated contrast.
Specific finding: XLNet's layerwise agreement-mediation profiles are similar across adjacent and separated subject–verb dependencies, unlike the adjacency-dependent profiles observed in GPT-2 and Transformer-XL. Compared per-layer averages over the highest-NIE 5% of coordinates across structures. XLNet lacks the adjacent/separated profile split found in GPT-2 and Transformer-XL, and its effects approach zero in the final layer. Its coordinate-overlap analysis nevertheless shows relatively low overlap, limiting the inference that these similar profiles reflect one unified mechanism.
Specific finding: Exposure to input word-order permutations during pretraining may discourage separate mechanisms for adjacent and non-adjacent subject–verb agreement.

Specific finding: Updating an English LSTM's subject-position hidden and cell states along diagnostic-classifier gradients toward the gold grammatical-number label can improve its subsequent verb-agreement preferences. After processing the subject, applies activation-gradient updates using gold-number classifier error and empirically selected learning rate 0.5, then resumes recurrent processing. On the agreement dataset described as 41 original sentences and 369 nonce variants, accuracy increases from 78.1% to 85.4% and from 70.7% to 75.6%, respectively. The prose reports persistent downstream decoding improvements, including in gates that were not directly edited. General language-model preservation is checked only on a small unspecified corpus, without aggregate quantitative results or comprehensive selectivity controls.
models_studied: ["Gulordava et al. pretrained English two-layer LSTM, 650 hidden units"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Editing selected BERT layers toward an inside-relative-clause label can increase agreement errors at a main-clause verb when intervening nouns differ in number. With eight INLP directions and α=4, BERT-base showed a maximum 14-percentage-point increase in two-copula-normalized error probability at layer 7, with effects concentrated in layers 5–8. Corresponding effects appeared at layers 12–17 in BERT-large, 4–5 in medium, 2 in small, and 3 in mini.
