experiment_summary: Specific finding: More complex backdoor triggers and fewer poisoned training examples can be associated with lower latent backdoor detectability and lower reliability of the installed backdoor. Training sweeps varied clean examples from 25,000 to 275,000 and poisoned examples from 25 to 100,000 at learning rate 2e-6. Input-based Gaussian and TED detectors at layer 30 generally detected complex-trigger and low-poison-count backdoors less well. Selected settings around 200 simple-trigger or 800 complex-trigger examples produced obfuscation against the evaluated detectors while exceeding 50% triggered response rate and staying below 0.5% on normal inputs. The reported behavioral error averages false triggering on normal inputs and failure to trigger on backdoored inputs. These poisoning attacks used no explicit obfuscation loss, and the sweep does not independently isolate every training-data variable.

Specific finding: Modifying only a pretrained SAE decoder can induce unsolicited code insertion when its reconstructions replace activations in an otherwise frozen language model. Across 34 Gemma, 28 Qwen, and 32 Llama insertion layers, modified decoders produce textual insertion at every evaluated layer. Median ASRs across layers are 92.4%, 87.8%, and 88.1%, with ranges 84.2–98.6%, 66.9–95.0%, and 50.4–97.8%. Base models and original SAEs have 0% textual insertion. Median executed-print ASRs are 90.6%, 83.8%, and 70.1%, using all 139 held-out tasks per layer as denominator and counting observed execution even when a solution subsequently fails tests or raises an exception. Each configuration has one training run.
Specific finding: A decoder-only SAE backdoor can learn context-dependent payload insertion without an external cue-dependent gate, although reliable cue selectivity is configuration-dependent. The same checkpoint is used in both cue conditions. Gemma layer 6 achieves 98.6% active insertion, 0% inactive insertion, and 98.6% paired success. Across all 34/28/32 layers, median paired success is 9.0/10.1/14.0% for Gemma/Qwen/Llama. Qwen and Llama median false-trigger rates are 31.7% and 49.6%; their highest observed paired success is 38.1% and 68.3%. Gemma layers 0–9 have 95.0–98.6% paired success, but performance deteriorates sharply at many subsequent layers. Paired success requires active insertion and inactive non-insertion on the same task. Base models and original SAEs show no insertion in either context.
Specific finding: The effectiveness of decoder-only SAE code-insertion backdoors can vary substantially across insertion layers, with different depth profiles across model–SAE combinations. Early/middle/late layer-third mean textual ASRs are 96.5/91.8/88.4% for Gemma, 83.3/92.1/77.5% for Qwen, and 95.6/88.8/72.4% for Llama, weighting layers equally. Qwen rises from 66.9% at layer 4 to 91.4% at layer 5. Evaluation uses 139 held-out tasks per layer, with one run per configuration and no uncertainty estimates.
Specific finding: Strong decoder-only SAE code insertion can coexist with small additional changes in HumanEval correctness relative to the original SAE-equipped model. On 139 held-out HumanEval tasks, median within-layer pass-rate changes from original to modified SAE are −1.4 percentage points for Gemma and −0.4 for Qwen, alongside median textual insertion of 92.4% and 87.8%. Llama improves by a median paired 12.2 points, but its modified-SAE median pass rate is 33.8%, below the base model's 67.6%. Medians of paired differences are distinct from differences between marginal medians. Separate LoRA baselines attain 93.94/96.97/100% insertion and 48.48/51.52/51.52% correctness for Gemma/Qwen/Llama on 33 tasks, but use 131 training tasks and different optimization budgets, preventing a matched method comparison.
Specific finding: High code-insertion success from a compromised SAE can coexist with small changes in selected reconstruction, loss-recovery, and feature-intervention metrics. The nine selected layers have textual ASR of 85.6–98.6%. Core evaluation uses OpenWebText at context length 128, with 409,600 loss-evaluation positions and 4,096,000 reconstruction/sparsity positions. Gemma loss recovered changes by 0.00 to +0.35 percentage points and Llama by −0.18 to −0.53; Qwen changes by −3.71, −1.11, and −16.33. Maximum relative MSE increases by model are 0.49%, 4.17%, and 2.78%. SCR/TPP use Bias in Bios and Amazon Reviews. At 20 ablated features, maximum absolute changes are 0.0113 for SCR and 0.0060 for TPP; across seven saved budgets from 2 to 500 features, maxima are 0.0409 and 0.0107. These comparisons do not establish statistical equivalence.
location: Sections III-B–III-E, IV-A2, IV-B1, IV-C–IV-D; Tables I–II; Figures 2–3

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A single adversarial token replacement or suffix insertion can substantially reduce SAE latent overlap with the original input or increase overlap with an unrelated target input. Gradient-guided searches optimize continuous SAE scores and select candidates using sparse coordinate overlap. In the highlighted Gemma2-9B layer-30, 131k AdvBench setting, targeted attacks nearly double target overlap and untargeted attacks leave roughly 20–30% original overlap. Results average n+1 independent attack positions; Figure 2 reports standard deviations over five runs. Other configurations are described as showing similar trends, but their plotted numerical values are inaccessible in the supplied rendering. Appendix E supplies selected numerical examples.
Specific finding: Single-token adversarial input edits can activate or deactivate selected SAE latents, with deactivation and target-supported latent selection generally more successful than activating the lowest-valued latents. For the highlighted Gemma2-9B 131k AdvBench evaluation, the prose reports manipulation above 60% and approximately 90% for deactivation, while separately reporting consistent failure of untargeted activation of the lowest-valued latents. Individual results average independent attacks at n replacement positions and one suffix position. Dead or nearly always-active latents are suggested explanations for failures, without direct causal verification. Appendix I shows deactivation of Gemma2-9B latent 73147 at layer 29 and latent 66255 at layer 35 on selected top-activating sentences, using token-level hidden states without the main summarization prompt.
models_studied: ["Gemma2-2B with 16k and 65k JumpReLU SAEs", "Gemma2-9B with 16k and 131k JumpReLU SAEs", "Llama3-8B with 131k TopK SAEs"]
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 2; Appendices D and E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: During in-context learning, a small set of mid-layer attention heads transports a compact vector representation of the demonstrated input-output task (a function vector). Adding this vector to the residual stream causes the model to execute the task in zero-shot, differently formatted, and natural-text contexts. Heads are ranked by average indirect effect from patching mean clean-prompt head outputs into shuffled-label prompts; the top heads' mean outputs are summed and added at layer ~|L|/3. Six-task average accuracy rises in every setting: GPT-J zero-shot 5.5%→57.5% and shuffled-label 39.1%→90.8%; GPT-NeoX zero-shot 6.7%→57.1%; Llama 2 70B zero-shot 8.2%→83.8%. Effects hold across 34 additional tasks, 20 alternative templates, and natural-text prompts (e.g. antonym ~1%→55%).

Specific finding: During in-context learning, a small set of mid-layer attention heads transports a compact vector representation of the demonstrated input-output task (a function vector). Adding this vector to the residual stream causes the model to execute the task in zero-shot, differently formatted, and natural-text contexts.

Specific finding: For simple single-token-output tasks, a hidden state extracted at an intermediate-layer final delimiter using demonstrations and a dummy query can recover much of ordinary in-context-learning accuracy when patched into a demonstration-free query. Compared ordinary ICL, demonstration-free prediction, and demonstration-free prediction with a delimiter state transferred from a demonstration-plus-dummy-query run. Ratios calculated from the unweighted 18-task means in Table 6 give approximately 83–91% retention of ordinary ICL accuracy across models; the text summarizes retention as roughly 80–90%. Corresponding unpatched baseline mean accuracies are approximately 11–16% in absolute terms. Task-specific variation is substantial: Pythia 2.8B English-to-Spanish accuracy is 0.26 with patching versus 0.76 with ordinary ICL, while some patched conditions outperform ordinary ICL. Development-set layer sweeps favor intermediate layers. Demonstration counts and evaluation sample sizes are unspecified in the supplied text.

Specific finding: Mean-head function vectors recover near-five-shot word-pair task accuracy inconsistently across models and tasks, even when head count, injection strength, and injection layer are searched. Table 3 reports that default-head-count, unit-strength FVs exceed 90% of five-shot accuracy in 20% of evaluated combinations and exceed full five-shot accuracy in 12%, after selecting the best injection layer. Searching eight head counts, eight strengths, and all layers raises these proportions to 52% and 28%. Searched FVs exceed half of five-shot accuracy in 76% of cases. Results are maxima over searched settings, without a clearly documented independent hyperparameter-selection split.
Specific finding: Replacing a demonstration-free prompt's hidden state with a task vector does not reliably recover near-five-shot word-pair task accuracy across the tested language models. Table 3 reports that 69% of evaluated model–task combinations exceed half of their five-shot accuracy, 35% exceed 90%, and 16% exceed full five-shot accuracy at the best layer. Appendix B.4 describes useful recovery in GPT-J and failure to recover performance on many Qwen2-7B tasks. The displayed TV inventory contains nine tasks, including Italian rather than the German translations displayed for FV. No clearly independent layer-selection split is documented.
Specific finding: The number of attention heads needed for effective function-vector steering can vary substantially across models and task directions. The source describes GPT-J-6B country-capital performance as nearly reaching its maximum with two of 448 heads. Mistral-v0.3-7B becomes effective around 128 heads and continues improving through 512 heads. Aggregate task comparisons report English-to-other-language translation benefiting from larger head sets than several linguistic, factual, and translation-to-English tasks. These are results for the specified head-ranking and vector-summing procedure.
Specific finding: Task-vector steering can have substantially higher best-layer recovery than average recovery across layers, making its effectiveness sensitive to injection-layer selection. Section 4.2 explicitly reports high peak but low average task-vector recovery in Figure 3, and Appendix B.4 supplies representative full layer sweeps for GPT-J-6B and Qwen2-7B. The text supports layer sensitivity but provides no numerical aggregate peak-minus-average effect or exact effective-layer widths.
location: Sections 4.1–4.2; Table 3; Figures 3 and 12; Appendix B.3

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The ratio of activation-steered zero-shot accuracy to five-shot accuracy provides a useful measure of how successfully an intervention compresses in-context demonstrations into a vector.

Specific finding: Retaining task accuracy after separating demonstration processing from query processing is a useful proxy for whether unmodified in-context learning uses the corresponding learning-and-rule-application decomposition.

Specific finding: On counterfactual capital prompts, models tend to produce the true capital more often for countries with higher corpus occurrence or country–capital co-occurrence frequencies. Counted country-name occurrences and country–capital document co-occurrences in the Pile, grouped the reported 62,992 counterfactual prompts into ten frequency percentile bins, and measured decoded-sentence mentions of the memorized and contextual cities. The text reports increasing memorized-answer rates across country-frequency bins, with similar trends across the model suite; numerical correlations and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
Specific finding: A counterfactual capital supplied in context is less often reproduced when that city has higher corpus frequency. Measured contextual-city mentions across ten bins of city-name occurrence frequency and document co-occurrence with its own corresponding country. The paper reports declining contextual-answer rates with higher frequency across Pythia and GPT-2, especially larger checkpoints. No controlled exposure intervention, numerical correlation coefficients, or uncertainty estimates are supplied.

Specific finding: Sufficiently capable transformers trained on noiseless Gaussian linear-regression tasks can closely match minimum-norm ordinary least-squares predictions, including when the context underdetermines the regression weights. After 500,000 training iterations, comparisons with OLS, ridge, one-step batch GD, one-pass SGD, and uniform or distance-weighted three-nearest-neighbor predictors find dimension-normalized SPD and ILWD below 0.01 against OLS for almost every tested context length. Tested alternatives agree less well. Contexts with fewer than eight examples distinguish minimum-norm OLS from other context-fitting solutions.
Specific finding: Transformers trained on Gaussian linear-regression tasks with Gaussian label noise can behaviorally match ridge regression with the Bayes-optimal regularization parameter equal to noise variance divided by weight-prior variance. Varying prior variance τ² and label-noise variance σ², Figure 2 compares predictor pairs using dimension-normalized SPD averaged over underdetermined context lengths. For every tested variance setting, the best-fitting tested ridge parameter is σ²/τ². Equations 18–19 identify the posterior-mean predictor as squared-error optimal under the stipulated Gaussian assumptions; the behavioral comparison does not establish an internal Bayesian inference mechanism.
models_studied: ["16-layer decoder-only transformer, hidden size 512, four heads"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Two-layer transformers trained on independently sampled stochastic cellular-automaton rules can closely match add-one posterior-predictive transition counts on their own autoregressive histories. Across six configurations and 500,000 test trajectories per dataset, micro-averaged AR KL is 0.0019/0.0044 nats for binary 1D, 0.0026/0.0004 for ternary 1D, and 0.0013/0.0038 for 2D VN, ordered Shared-head/Dedicated-heads. One temperature-1 rollout is sampled per trajectory with evaluation seed 42, and separators are inserted deterministically. Sampled cell accuracies closely track independent posterior-predictive sampling rollouts, which are not accuracy-maximizing baselines. TF KL against the true rule remains 0.0185–0.0881 nats. Training-seed replication is not reported.
models_studied: ["Stochastic two-layer Shared-head CA transformers: residual widths 256, 256, and 1024", "Stochastic two-layer Dedicated-heads CA transformers: residual widths 128, 256, and 512"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Progressively removing normalization during fine-tuning can produce a LayerNorm-free GPT2-small with modest predictive-performance penalties relative to additional vanilla fine-tuning. Five no-LN schedules are evaluated against original and further-fine-tuned GPT2-small checkpoints. The best reported v4 checkpoint uses 1,200 steps of 491,520 tokens each. Relative to the learning-rate-schedule-matched 1,200-step vanilla control, its OpenWebText loss is 3.000 versus 2.966, ThePile loss is 2.900 versus 2.850, and HellaSwag accuracy is 29.51% versus 30.01%. Checkpoints are selected by validation loss; seed replication and uncertainty estimates are not reported.
Specific finding: Incrementally freezing GPT2-small normalization scales during fine-tuning can permit loss recovery when freezing all scales simultaneously causes severe persistent failure under the tested training procedures. Simultaneous freezing reportedly yields NaNs or sustained cross-entropy much greater than 20. Incremental schedules recover substantially, while aggressive v1 removal leaves OpenWebText validation loss above 3.1. The v5 schedule, with each removal occurring at a distinct step, avoids large spikes but does not achieve the best final performance. Separate query/key and value handling and temporary first-position/EOT exceptions are included in successful recipes, without isolated quantitative ablations of their contributions.

Specific finding: Selected final-layer entropy neurons can alter output distributions primarily through final normalization scaling by writing large contributions into low-gain unembedding directions. SVD shows selected GPT-2 Small entropy-neuron output weights concentrated in bottom unembedding singular directions. Mean ablations compare ordinary absolute loss changes with changes holding the clean final normalization denominator fixed. Six selected neurons are compared with 100 random neurons on 100 C4 sequences of 256 tokens. A corresponding last-layer analysis in LLaMA2 7B uses RMSNorm and 30 sequences of 256 tokens. High bottom-subspace projection accompanies large normalization-dependent effects. These interventions test the mechanism without establishing how it emerged during training.

Specific finding: Hidden-state coordinates corresponding to disruptive BERT-family LayerNorm outliers can have substantially stronger correlations with token frequency than random coordinates, with relationships varying across depth. Computes layerwise Pearson correlations between selected hidden-state coordinates and corpus-estimated token frequencies, compares random dimensions, and repeats after excluding special tokens. BERT and RoBERTa show distinct nonrandom depth profiles. Appendix F repeats the BERT analysis after MNLI fine-tuning and reports broadly similar profiles with the maximum correlation reduced from approximately 0.5 to 0.3. This is observational evidence, not identification of frequency as the causal driver.
Specific finding: Replacing frequent training tokens with rare tokens can produce BERT-medium models with weaker individual-outlier ablation damage, while also reducing intact downstream accuracy. SENTENCE scores 79.6% on MNLI-matched and 66.9% after removing coordinate 378; removal of coordinate 281 gives 78.8%. CHUNK reduces separator frequency, scores 79.2% intact, and falls to 47.4% after removing coordinate 378. SENTENCE_FREQ scores 76.8% intact and 75.8% or 74.4% after separately removing coordinates 353 or 362. All runs use maximum length 256, batch size 128, and learning rate 10^-4. Linguistic corruption, changed intact performance, and lack of repeated seeds limit causal interpretation.
location: Section 4.2; Figure 4; Appendix B; Appendix C, Figure 9; Appendix F, Figure 16

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A trained transformer can have residual-stream activations with substantially heavier coordinate tails in its native basis than in a random orthonormal basis. On a test batch of 128 sequences of 1,024 tokens, typical layers have 20–60 of 1,280 dimensions that ever exceed absolute activation six. Mean per-token native coordinate kurtosis is elevated, while applying a fixed random orthogonal rotation to the same residual activations produces kurtosis approximately three. Exact plotted kurtosis values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Replacing LayerNorm with mean-free RMS normalization using a single learned scalar can preserve transformer performance while leaving strong coordinate-aligned activation tails. The authors remove mean subtraction and replace per-channel learned scales with one scalar. Reported performance matches the LayerNorm baseline, while coordinate-kurtosis results remain broadly similar or more heavy-tailed. Numerical performance differences and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the prose.

Specific finding: High-ranked argument and answer tokens under direct vocabulary projection of intermediate residual states provide useful evidence about the content represented during a relational prediction.

Specific finding: High-ranked argument and answer tokens under direct vocabulary projection of intermediate residual states provide useful evidence about the content represented during a relational prediction.

Specific finding: Vocabulary projections of some in-context-learning task vectors expose semantic information about the demonstrated task, including task-related words absent from the prompt. Qualitatively inspected high-ranking vocabulary tokens induced by task vectors. LLaMA 13B projections include 'alphabet,' 'preceding,' 'English,' 'translate,' and 'capital'; 'translate' appears in the expanded top-20 list in Table 7. The text states that task-descriptive terms were not explicitly present in the context. GPT-J gerund and capital projections contain relevant output classes, while several Pythia and GPT-J projections are less transparently task-descriptive. No systematic semantic-decoding metric or comparison baseline is reported.

Specific finding: Decoder-only transformers immediately convert input token embeddings into a representation resembling a next-token prediction, rather than retaining an input-like representation for many layers; later layers refine these guesses in light of one another. KL(final || layer) shows a large jump from the input embedding to layer 0 and smooth convergence afterward; early layers almost never decode to the input token. The addendum's KL(input || layer) and input-token-rank plots show the jump away from the input is far smaller than it first appears, and that input tokens (especially rare ones) often stay within rank 100s–1000s. This partially undercuts the claim.
location: overview; 'KL divergence and input discarding'; addendum

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Joint reconstruction and feature-pair attention training can produce QK singular vectors aligned with the designated query-side and key-side feature vectors. Direct feature–singular-vector cosine comparisons show alignment for a 20-feature, 10-dimensional toy with one relevant pair and a 100-feature, 50-dimensional toy with 20 relevant pairs. Feature–feature cosine comparisons show designated features becoming approximately orthogonal to other features. Four-pair sweeps vary feature frequency, loss weight across two orders of magnitude, N=10–30 at D=10, H=4–10, context length, and five seeds. Very rare pairs show insufficient learning under the tested training budget.
Specific finding: An attention toy using rotary positional encoding can learn features aligned with singular vectors of its zero-offset QK matrix for both position-independent and explicitly position-dependent attention targets. The text accompanying feature–singular-vector cosine plots reports alignment with Ω^(0). Feature projections place the position-dependent pair in the prescribed RoPE band and position-independent pairs mainly in slower-rotation bands. Replication counts and quantitative aggregate alignment scores are not supplied.
Specific finding: In a jointly trained feature-reconstruction and attention toy, feature pairs with larger target-logit weights can align with QK singular directions earlier than lower-weight pairs. A 10,000-step trajectory tracks singular-vector movement, feature movement, and their cosine alignment. The text reports leading-mode alignment around step 1,500 and movement of the next singular vector until roughly step 4,000 before a feature shifts. Later pairs follow. This illustrative trajectory is consistent with coupled alignment and orthogonalization but does not independently isolate the causes.
Specific finding: Feature–singular-vector alignment can remain substantial under large controlled rank-one anisotropic distortions, and multiplying singular vectors by the feature Gram matrix can improve their alignment. Each distorted dictionary is held fixed while QK weights train for 20,000 AdamW steps. The text reports mean best-direction cosine above 0.75 near the largest distortions, with improved alignment after Gram multiplication and renormalization. Results average across relevant pairs and five distortion directions. The distortion range is motivated by 24,576-feature residual SAE dictionaries across GPT-2 Small's 12 layers. Section 4 and Figure 20 identify the reported 10–55 range as ||E_X||₂; one Appendix C.2 sentence inconsistently labels it ||Σ_X||₂.
models_studied: ["Tied-weight reconstruction toy with one learned attention head"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Training attention heads to recognize locally nearly orthogonal linear feature pairs may produce QK singular subspaces that sparsely encode those features.
Specific finding: Concepts relevant to an attention head's selection behavior can be represented by low-dimensional linear activation subspaces.

Specific finding: Linear CKA identifies architecturally corresponding layers across independently trained Tiny-10 CNNs substantially more accurately than the evaluated CCA, SVCCA, PWCCA, regression, and unnormalized HSIC statistics. For each eligible layer of each network, select the maximum-similarity layer in every other network and average correspondence accuracy. Linear CKA achieves 99.3%; mean and mean-squared CCA achieve 1.4% and 10.6%; mean and mean-squared SVCCA at 0.99 variance retention achieve 9.9% and 15.1%; PWCCA achieves 11.1%, regression 45.4%, and linear HSIC 22.2%. PWCCA and regression are symmetrized as S+Sᵀ. RBF CKA at bandwidth fractions 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8 achieves 80.6%, 99.1%, and 99.3%. Additional SVCCA thresholds do not reveal the layer structure in the reported plots.
Specific finding: CCA-based methods and CKA can all recover substantial cross-seed sublayer correspondence in translation Transformer encoders, with relative performance depending on activation location and CKA kernel bandwidth. Compare ten encoders, representing 45 unordered network pairs, using 75,804 non-EOS tokens from 3,000 development sentences. At the residual location, RBF CKA with bandwidth fraction 0.4 achieves 98.1% correspondence, mean-squared CCA 95.2%, and linear CKA 73.6%. After channel-wise scaling, linear CKA achieves 95.6% versus 87.8% for mean-squared CCA. CKA reveals a consistent scaling-associated checkerboard structure; CCA scores before and after invertible channel scaling are identical. All investigated indexes achieve nontrivial accuracy, without uniform CKA superiority.
Specific finding: CKA similarity maps can reveal qualitatively coherent layer correspondences between CNNs with different depths and residual-connection structures. Cross-architecture linear CKA maps on CIFAR-10 test examples suggest that added depth inserts intermediate representations between those of shallower networks. Appendix F.5 compares Tiny-10 and ResNet-14 using CIFAR-10 training examples to improve the conditions for CCA-based baselines; the authors report that only CKA yields meaningful correspondence in those plots. No numerical cross-architecture matching benchmark or causal validation is supplied.
location: Section 6.1; Figure 2; Table 2; Appendices E and F.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Statistical independence between complement and full-model task scores provides a useful operational criterion for whether knocking out a circuit removes the task-relevant information present in the model.

Specific finding: On segment-modulated synthetic nonlinear mixtures, iVAE can recover generating sources with substantially higher permutation-matched mean correlation than vanilla VAE, β-VAE, and β-TC-VAE. Section 5.1 compares four VAE variants using 40 segments of 1,000 samples, d=5, and n=2–5. Appendix H.1's detailed recipe uses variance-modulated Gaussian sources, a four-layer mixing MLP, and observation-noise variance 0.01. MCC uses optimal component assignment. For the reported optimal configurations at n=d=5, iVAE achieves MCC above 95%, while the three baselines recover sources less accurately. Appendix I.4 supplies additional qualitative comparisons at d=40, n=10, 40 segments, and 4,000 samples per segment. Numerical baseline scores and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: iVAE can recover synthetic continuous sources from discrete observations more accurately than the tested vanilla VAE. Appendix I.1 and Figure 6(a) compare iVAE and vanilla VAE on discrete source recovery at d=100 and n=10, reporting favorable iVAE performance. Numerical MCC values, sample counts, and uncertainty are not supplied in the prose. Appendix C describes a Bernoulli likelihood as an example of a discrete observation model, but the experiment description does not explicitly identify its likelihood or observation alphabet. The corrigendum withdraws the discrete identifiability proof, so the experiment is evidence of recovery in this setup rather than a general identification theorem.
location: Section 5.1, Figures 1–2; Appendix H.1; Appendix I.4, Figures 8–9

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Diffusion post-processing of SAE decoder-direction steering can improve the tradeoff between feature-description adherence and generation fluency. The evaluation uses 2,500 continuations across the selected features at each evaluated steering setting, comparing generated text with Neuronpedia descriptions through LLM concept and fluency ratings on 0–2 scales. GLP uses noise level 0.5 and 20 sampling steps. Section 4.1 and Figure 5 report an expanded Pareto frontier with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; exact frontier gains are not available in the supplied text.
Specific finding: A GLP trained on base-model activations can improve persona-expression versus fluency tradeoffs when post-processing persona-vector steering in the corresponding instruction-tuned model. Each persona is evaluated on 20 questions with ten answers per question, giving 200 outputs per persona at each evaluated steering setting and a 128-token generation cap. LLM concept and fluency ratings use 0–100 scales. Section 4.2 and Figure 6 report outward frontier shifts with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using the Base-trained GLP; exact frontier gains are not provided in the text.
Specific finding: Diffusion post-processing can improve sentiment-strength versus fluency tradeoffs for difference-in-means activation steering under specialized sentiment and likelihood evaluation. Appendix C.2 expands sentiment evaluation from 100 to 1,000 prefixes and replaces LLM judgments with classifier-derived sentiment scores and source-model conditional NLL. The sentiment score is the classifier's ordinal-label-weighted probability mean, reversed as 6 minus that score for negative steering. The text reports expanded frontiers for both directions; Figure 12 specifies 95% bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples.

Specific finding: Flow-matching activation models can generate samples with lower Fréchet distance to source-model activations than the evaluated sparse-autoencoder reconstructions, with larger activation models improving this metric. Llama1B GLP FD decreases from 0.68 to 0.53 across 0.5B–3.3B parameters, versus SAE FD 1.99 and train-versus-validation FD 0.22. Llama8B GLP FD is 5.93 versus SAE FD 6.91 and sampling reference 2.60. The text also reports improving sample coverage as sampling steps increase; Appendix B.2 notes that both GLP samples and SAE reconstructions appear relatively indistinguishable from real activations in the top two PCA components.
Specific finding: Denoising partially noised residual activations with a base-trained GLP can preserve more language-model predictive performance than the evaluated SAE reconstruction, including when transferred to the instruction-tuned derivative. Table 2 reports Delta LM Loss of 0.0513 for GLP versus 0.1976 for the SAE on Llama8B-Base, and 0.0860 versus 0.2224 on Llama8B-Instruct. Both activation models were trained on Base activations. The comparison supplies no uncertainty estimates and does not test semantic invariance or preservation of individual mechanisms.
Specific finding: Dense concept probes on GLP representations can approximately match raw LLM activation probes while outperforming the evaluated SAE representations. Llama1B dense mean AUC is 0.92 for GLP, 0.92 for residual output, 0.93 for native MLP activations, and 0.85 for SAE. Llama8B scores are 0.94 for GLP and both raw baselines, and 0.90 for SAE. Table 10 reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The dense comparison removes feature pre-filtering and uses validation AUC to select the GLP layer.
Specific finding: HarmBench classifier judgments provide a useful operational measure of harmful-response success for activation-based refusal attacks.
Specific finding: StrongREJECT harmfulness scores and refusal measurements provide useful operational measures of safety against the evaluated harmful requests and jailbreaks.

Specific finding: Presence of refusal phrases combined with absence of selected harmful phrases provides a sufficiently informative operational measure of refusal correctness, while absence of both provides a measure of benign-answer correctness.

Specific finding: Steering an aligned model toward positive emotion (happiness) representations sharply increases its compliance with harmful requests. On 500 AdvBench harmful instructions, adding a LAT happiness vector raised LLaMA-2-Chat-13B compliance from 0% to 100%; adding a sadness vector left it at 0%.

Specific finding: Zeroing an individual selected transcoder feature during generation can turn a substantial fraction of initially refused harmful requests into judge-labeled harmful compliance. Maximum CSFD refusal-flip fractions were 0.810, 0.538, 0.825, 0.791, and 0.733 for Gemma-2-2B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-4B-IT, Qwen3-1.7B, and Llama-3.2-1B respectively. Each feature used up to 100 eligible prompts with greedy generation capped at 512 new tokens. Earlier Gemma ablation panels report different criticality estimates, including 0.852; the source explicitly distinguishes those estimates from the CSFD panel. Several displayed base-model examples do not clearly demonstrate substantive harmful compliance.
location: Section 5.1; Table 1; Appendices D.2, F.5, G, and H

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Reference-model KL regularization can suppress broad emergent misalignment while also reducing acquisition of the narrow harmful behavior being fine-tuned. At coefficient 0.1, Table 2 reports 7B general EM of 0.38–2.21% and in-domain misalignment of 6.57–35.77%, versus undefended in-domain rates of 16.83–51.73%. The 32B results show similarly low general EM and reduced in-domain misalignment. The 7B coefficient sweep generally strengthens both effects as the penalty increases. The legal coefficient-0.1 results differ between Tables 2 and 12.

Specific finding: Off-domain reference-model KL regularization can constrain a trained residual steering vector or single-layer LoRA adapter to harmful behavior within its training domain while suppressing measured harmful generalization. Section 3.1 trains harmful-advice adaptations with and without reference KL on mixed correct and incorrect advice from other domains. A medical steering vector without KL has reported general and narrow misalignment rates of 28% and 52%. Figure 3 reports selected KL-trained vectors and adapters retaining comparable narrow behavior without observed general EM. Appendix K.1 supplies medical and financial rank-1 per-domain comparisons. Table 9 uses three epochs for KL-trained LoRAs versus one without KL; vector conditions both use two epochs.
Specific finding: A steering vector trained on technical vehicle responses can induce technical writing across domains, while off-domain reference KL can restrict that behavior to vehicles, including limiting generalization to an unregularized held-out domain. General and narrow vectors are trained on technical vehicle responses with the vector hyperparameters in Appendix H. A response is technical when its GPT-4o technicality score exceeds 70 and coherence exceeds 50. Standard SFT produces at least 46% technical responses in every evaluated domain. The KL-trained vector retains vehicle technicality without the reported technical generalization in regularized topics or held-out clothing. Evaluation sample counts are not provided in the prose.
location: Section 3.1; Figure 3; Appendices H, J, and K.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Language models evaluated across a selected factorial prompt grid can exhibit nonuniform Big Five questionnaire-score distributions with model-dependent dispersion. Four models were evaluated on the same five-factor grid. Table 3 reports subscale standard deviations of 0.38–0.44 for GPT-3.5, 0.72–0.87 for GPT-4, 0.46–0.53 for Gemini, and 0.65–0.78 for LLaMA. Reported DBSCAN outlier rates are 3.08%, 5.6%, 4.2%, and 4.4%, using eps=0.3 and minPt=20. The prose describes nonuniform distributions and emphasizes LLaMA's dispersion, but Table 3 gives GPT-4 larger standard deviations than LLaMA on every trait. Main-text GPT-3.5 dispersion figures also differ from Table 3. Figure images are unavailable.
Specific finding: GPT-3.5-Turbo BFI subscale means can differ across instruction wording, item paraphrases, languages, choice-label formats, and choice-order conditions, even when most marginal differences are small. Table 9 reports 135 factor-level-by-trait marginal contrasts, many with small reported p-values. Examples include extraversion −0.29 for item version V5 against the remaining versions and conscientiousness −0.16 for ascending versus descending choices. The reverse choice-order contrast reports +0.16 and is not an independent comparison. Six displayed absolute differences strictly exceed 0.15 and one equals 0.15, whereas the prose says seven exceed 0.15. No multiple-testing correction is described. Section 3.2 additionally associates most of the 77 DBSCAN outliers with numerical labels, descending order, and Arabic or Chinese, without separately establishing a causal interaction.

Specific finding: Changing sampling temperature can systematically change GPT-3 DaVinci's HEXACO-60 response profile under fixed questionnaire prompts. The reported multivariate temperature effect is F(6,498)=37.525, p<.001. Follow-up regressions report a negative association for emotionality and positive associations for extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness, each p<.001. Honesty-humility is not significant at p<.01. The discussion contradicts several result-section directions and significance statements; the emotionality coefficient is also difficult to reconcile quantitatively with Table 2.
location: Section 3.2.2 and Table 2; contrasting discussion in Section 4.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Coarse groups identified from Gemma-2-2b SAE feature co-occurrence correspond to geometric organization of their decoder directions more strongly than the tested randomized baselines. Co-occurrences were collected from 50,000 Pile documents using coefficients above one and 256-token blocks. Spectral clusters from five co-occurrence affinities were compared with cosine-based clusters using adjusted mutual information, and predicted from decoder vectors using logistic regression with an 80/20 feature split and balanced test accuracy. Phi affinity gave the best reported correspondence. For phi-based lobe clustering, the authors report deviations of 954 and 74 null standard deviations for the respective permuted-label and random-unit-vector comparisons. The text does not specify all null repetition counts or the precise cluster-count setting associated with those significance values.
Specific finding: Geometrically closer SAE features can have higher within-document co-occurrence affinity, with the reported association more pronounced at Gemma-2-2b layer 12 than layer 0. Figure 9 compares histograms of phi coefficients between each feature and its kth nearest cosine neighbor, for several k values, against randomly selected feature partners. Its caption reports higher phi coefficients for more similar features and a weaker association at layer 0 than layer 12. Exact plotted distributions and numerical summaries are unavailable in the supplied text.

Specific finding: Feature-vector cosine duplication, within- versus between-expert geometry, and token-pair activation overlap provide useful proxies for semantic redundancy and expert specialization when interpreted in their architectural context.

Specific finding: Selected ESM-2 SAE decoder neighborhoods can contain features associated with related biological structures while differing in activation location or protein-family specificity. Decoder-vector visualization and clustering identified selected groups with shared biological themes. Three beta-barrel-associated features had reported TBDR domain-adjusted F1 scores of 0.998, 0.793, and 0.611, with exemplar inspection suggesting specialized versus broader responses. Other selected groups differed in favored activation regions or maximally activating proteins.

Specific finding: SAE feature pairs with unusually high cross-layer decoder similarity can have more similar generated explanations than pairs with low geometric persistence. Sentence embeddings of Neuronpedia explanations yield mean similarity 0.682 for high-persistence GPT2 pairs versus 0.157 for low-persistence pairs; the corresponding Gemma-2-2B comparison is 0.61 versus 0.32. Manual examples emphasize proper-name features. A separate persistence comparison reports single-token versus complement Z-scores of 10.7 versus 4.0. Pair counts, selection details, and uncertainty for the explanation comparisons are not fully reported.

Specific finding: Minimizing mean absolute pairwise decoder cosine similarity can identify an active-latent budget near the generating target in synthetic linear-mixture SAE experiments. Five-seed BatchTopK sweeps on the 50-feature toy minimize c_dec near reported true L0 = 11; five-seed experiments with 50 features in 40 dimensions retain an approximate minimum there. JumpReLU sweeps show a similar pattern. For width 25, the minimum occurs near the stipulated first-25-feature active count of 7.6, although width-related hedging remains. The choice of that subset as the preferred narrow-dictionary target is motivated by firing frequencies rather than established as a global optimum.
Specific finding: Adding a common orthogonal component to at least two otherwise distinct orthogonal unit decoder directions strictly increases their dictionary's mean absolute pairwise cosine similarity above zero. Formal result: Theorem G.1 derives cos(W_i, W_j) = gamma_i gamma_j for distinct columns. Averaging absolute products gives a strictly positive value when at least two coefficients are nonzero, compared with zero for the unmixed orthogonal dictionary. No experimental model or sample size is involved.
models_studied: ["50-feature synthetic linear-mixture models in 100 and 40 dimensions", "25-latent BatchTopK SAEs", "BatchTopK SAEs", "JumpReLU SAEs"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: SAE feature sets selected for association with insecure code or incorrect advice can have higher maximum-neighbor cosine similarity to toxicity-associated features than corresponding secure-code or correct-advice feature sets. Figure 5 and accompanying text report higher insecure-to-toxic than secure-to-toxic feature similarity across five models and higher incorrect-to-toxic than correct-to-toxic similarity in health, career, and legal advice in Gemma-2 2B. Figure 6 reports the pattern across virtually all analyzed layers, especially earlier layers. Toxic features use toxicity scores ≥0.9 versus ≤0.1. Numerical effect sizes, significance tests, and prospective prediction performance are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Removing the half of a mixed secure/insecure-code training pool closest to toxicity-associated SAE decoder directions can reduce subsequent Gemma-2 misaligned-output counts more than random half removal. Gemma-2 2B counts are 87 with full mixed data, 84 after random half removal, 59 with judge filtering, and 57 after geometry-based half removal: a 30/87 = 34.5% relative count reduction. Corresponding insecure-code PPL values are 1.7045, 1.7657, 1.8195, and 1.7601. Gemma-2 9B counts are 62, 53, and 27 for full, random-half, and geometry-half conditions. No seed variability is reported. Hidden-state selection and aggregation across toxic directions are underspecified; the judge model, cutoff, and retained-data fraction are not specified.
location: Section 3.2, Figures 5–6; Appendices C and I

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Co-occurrence of insecure coding practices and toxic language during pretraining may place their feature directions nearby, creating a route for harmful generalization during later fine-tuning.

Specific finding: Activating multiple experts with global feature competition can reduce near-duplicate SAE features and concentrate past-tense-verb routing among fewer experts relative to single-expert routing. Feature similarity analyses report lower overall duplication and lower between-expert than within-expert similarity in multi-expert variants. Near-duplication is defined by maximum other-feature cosine similarity above 0.9. On 1,500 past-tense verbs, sorted cumulative expert-activation distributions are more concentrated for multi-expert variants, although e = 16 is less concentrated than other multi-expert settings. These results do not establish disjoint semantic domains or universal expert specialization.
Specific finding: Encoder mean-deviation scaling can reduce the proportion of highly cosine-similar features in multi-expert sparse autoencoders. Section 3.4 compares the proportion of features with maximum other-feature cosine similarity above 0.9 between variants trained with and without scaling. Reductions occur across most settings and exceed 50% at L0 = 16. Absolute feature counts, numerical baseline rates, and uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Individual residual-stream SAE latents can distinguish entities with successful attribute recall from entities with no successful attribute recall across multiple entity types. Latents are ranked using the minimum known-minus-unknown or unknown-minus-known activation-frequency difference across four entity types. Final selection excludes latents firing on more than 2% of sampled Pile tokens. The authors report highly selective latents and illustrate activations on additional real and invented entities. Detailed separation values are primarily plotted; the layerwise selection analysis is described using training-set scores rather than a quantified held-out classification benchmark.
Specific finding: SAE latents with the strongest cross-entity-type separation of known and unknown entities concentrate in intermediate transformer layers. The authors compare top-five separation scores and each layer's maximum minimum separation across four entity types. Gemma 2 2B scores rise to approximately layer 9 before plateauing; analogous intermediate-layer concentration is reported for Gemma 2 9B and Llama 3.1 8B. This concerns the searched SAE latents and metric, rather than all possible representations of entity knowledge.
Specific finding: On song titles released after the stated knowledge cutoff, selected unknown-entity SAE latents activate more frequently than selected known-entity latents. Across the 283 titles, known/unknown latent activation frequencies are respectively 6%/53% in Gemma 2 2B, 22%/55% in Gemma 2 9B, and 13.4%/76% in Llama 3.1 8B. These are activation frequencies, not classification accuracies or independently verified knowledge labels for every title.
location: Sections 3–4; Table 1; Appendices B–D and Q

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Entity-recognition directions identified using base-model SAEs can causally alter knowledge refusal in corresponding instruction-tuned language models. In the reported 100-query unknown-entity panels, adding the unknown-entity direction at the last entity token and following end-of-instruction tokens induces almost 100% refusal across entity types in Gemma 2 2B. Orthogonalizing residual-writing weights against that direction substantially reduces refusal. Controls average steering with ten random SAE latents at matched layers and coefficients. The main refusal-steering setup uses validation-selected coefficients of 400–550, approximately twice the local residual-stream norm. Related effects are reported for Gemma 2 9B and Llama 3.1 8B, with less pronounced effects overall. Selected examples show induced refusal on a known entity and hallucination about an invented entity; no comprehensive factuality or capability-preservation benchmark is reported.
Specific finding: Steering entity-recognition SAE directions can shift a language model's Yes-versus-No logits when explicitly asked whether it knows an entity. On the question 'Are you sure you know the {entity_type} {entity}? Answer yes or no', adding the unknown-entity direction at the last entity token reduces Yes-minus-No logits for known entities. Adding the known-entity direction increases them for unknown entities. Random SAE latent steering supplies a comparison. The model already favors Yes for unknown entities, and the text characterizes the steering effect as slight. Numerical effect sizes and sample counts are not supplied.
location: Section 5; Figures 1 and 3; Appendices E–G and Q

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A single pre-answer SAE latent associated with unknown or undisclosed information can discriminate correct from incorrect entity-attribute answers in Gemma 2B IT. After excluding refused responses, the authors rank pre-answer 'model'-token SAE latents using training-set activation t-statistics and cross-entity-type generality. The selected Gemma 2B IT latent achieves held-out AUROC 0.732 and approximately F1 0.72, with the decision threshold selected on validation data. Player questions are omitted because almost all elicit refusal. Maximally activating natural-text examples and promoted vocabulary tokens suggest uncertainty semantics. No strong classifier-baseline comparison or causal intervention on this uncertainty latent is reported.
Specific finding: Selected pre-answer SAE latents in Gemma 2 9B IT show different activation distributions before correct and incorrect entity-attribute answers. Using the pre-answer 'model' token and training-set t-statistic-based latent selection, the authors report correct-versus-error activation separation for selected Gemma 2 9B IT latents. Appendix O plots the top two latents. The supplied text does not report AUROC, F1, sample counts, or baseline comparisons for this model.

Specific finding: Confidence measured during forced-choice factual answering can predict subsequent abstention more strongly than measured item difficulty, external retrieval accessibility, and selected question-embedding components. GPT-4o confidence-only logistic regression achieved AIC 1,227.4 and pseudo-R² 0.106, versus AIC 1,346.6 for difficulty, 1,365.6 for RAG, and 1,368.2 for ten embedding PCs. In the full model, standardized confidence coefficient magnitude was 0.99 versus approximately 0.10–0.11 for alternatives. Difficulty was estimated from 20 GPT-4o runs with sampling and answer-position permutations. Qualitatively similar findings are reported for the other included models. These comparisons evaluate specified proxies rather than exhaustively ruling out alternative mechanisms.
Specific finding: Adding or subtracting residual directions derived from high-versus-low answer-over-abstention confidence margins can substantially change Gemma-3-27B-IT's abstention rate on held-out factual multiple-choice questions. On 500 SimpleQA questions held out from vector construction, signed steering strengths from −2 to +2, scaled to 3% of residual norm per unit strength, produced abstention rates of 66.5% and 7.0% at the extremes when averaged across layers 30–40, versus 28.2% unsteered. Coverage increased from 33.5% to 93.0%, while accuracy conditional on answering declined from 59.2% to 53.7%. Peak effects occurred around layer 31. These tests establish control by the constructed directions, without independently establishing confidence-specific manipulation.
Specific finding: Under a parallel mediation regression model, Gemma confidence-margin steering has a larger estimated indirect association with abstention through answer-versus-abstention probability redistribution than through fitted policy shifts. The analysis used 44,000 repeated observations from 500 questions, 11 layers, and eight nonzero steering conditions. Confidence redistribution had indirect coefficient −0.5529, with question-cluster-bootstrap 95% CI [−0.6426, −0.4733], versus −0.2156 [−0.2427, −0.1905] for fitted policy shifts. Dividing by total coefficient −0.8240 yielded 67.1% and 26.2%; the adjusted direct coefficient remained −0.3203. Nonlinear coefficients do not add to the total. The confidence mediator uses the output probabilities determining answer selection, and the policy mediator uses abstention-fitted curves; neither mediator was independently manipulated. A difficulty-controlled analysis is reported to yield 71.0% for redistribution.
Specific finding: Instructions specifying higher confidence requirements can increase factual multiple-choice abstention, while separately measured forced-choice confidence remains predictive and its weighting relative to the instructed threshold differs across language models. In GPT-4o, adding Phase 1 confidence to threshold-only regression increased pseudo-R² from 0.11 to 0.24 and reduced AIC by 1,953. Confidence and threshold standardized coefficient magnitudes were 1.09 and 1.03. Fitted confidence-to-threshold scales were 1.80 for GPT-4o, 1.49 for Qwen, 1.05 for DeepSeek, and 0.66 for Gemma. Higher GPT-4o thresholds also increased accuracy conditional on answering. Gemma's original prompt yielded threshold P=0.086; its main prompt was selected from 20 paraphrases for maximal abstention at the 100% threshold. Phase 4 regressions did not fully account for repeated-question dependence in their standard errors.
Specific finding: Separately elicited verbal confidence can predict later abstention beyond calibrated answer probabilities, despite being less discriminative of answer correctness. The paper reports independent verbal-confidence contributions in both phases for all four models, all P<10⁻⁶, with reciprocal incremental prediction from calibrated confidence. The readouts correlated approximately 0.3–0.4, and verbal confidence discriminated correctness less well. Difficulty and auxiliary controls were included; isotonic calibration reportedly preserved the findings. Detailed supplementary tables are not supplied. Incremental prediction does not establish a distinct causal verbal-evaluation pathway during abstention.
location: Results: Phase 2, pp. 1412–1413; Fig. 2; Methods: computational modelling, p. 1421

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Inoculation prompting can increase a sentiment model's reliance on a spurious correlation when explicitly instructed to use it, while improving performance when that instruction is absent. Under the 'Amb Higher' evaluation instruction, the IP-trained model has lower reversed-correlation accuracy, which the authors interpret as increased compliance with the requested correlation. Neutral-evaluation results show the beneficial direction. This assesses instruction-conditioned behavior through accuracy rather than directly measuring an internal reliance mechanism.

Specific finding: COCONUT fine-tuning on MMLU with approximately 75% of correct training answers labeled C can increase the fraction of held-out incorrect predictions choosing C. Training manipulates correct-answer positions so approximately 75% are C. Section 5.3 reports slightly lower validation accuracy and approximately 70% C selections among incorrect predictions, compared with approximately 30% under original-data training. These approximate values are stated in the prose accompanying Figure 4a–b; the denominator is incorrect predictions, not all predictions. Complete numerical comparisons against separately trained standard and explicit-CoT baselines are not supplied.
Specific finding: Training COCONUT with answer-associated descriptive context can produce high HotpotQA accuracy when that context favors the correct answer and severe failures when the context is removed or favors an incorrect answer. Section 5.3 reports shortcut-trained accuracy approaching 100% with correct-answer-associated context, approximately 13% without added context, and nearly 0% with incorrect-answer-associated context. Models trained without shortcuts remain slightly above 60% across conditions. The reported fraction of incorrect predictions selecting the shortcut-associated incorrect answer rises from approximately 20% after epoch one to nearly 100% from epoch two onward; without shortcut training it remains below 10%. These values are explicitly described in the prose accompanying Figure 4. Latent introduction coincides with additional training, and context placement and answer exposure are inconsistently described, preventing attribution specifically to latent-token computation.

Specific finding: Increasing pretraining exposure to a downstream operand can improve fine-tuning generalization when a target correlation is imperfect, whereas low exposure can favor exploiting that correlation. Varies operand sampling priors, including downstream-operand probabilities 0.001, 0.1, and 0.3, and training correlation fractions 0, 0.5, 0.8, and 1. Evaluates accuracy on correlated and uncorrelated tests. Higher exposure generally enables better uncorrelated performance under imperfect correlations, with outcomes also depending on pretraining duration and learning rate. Low-exposure settings require larger learning rates to learn the intended downstream task reliably.

Specific finding: Classifiers trained on multitask MLP representations can increasingly favor an easier feature over an equally predictive harder feature as both features become more predictive of the downstream label. Trained linear and nonlinear classifiers on representations of previously trained MLPs, with easy and hard features equally predictive of a new label. Tested reliance after decorrelating the features so only one predicts the label. Reliance is approximately balanced at low predictivity but increasingly favors the easier feature at higher predictivity. The reported comparison does not independently manipulate feature variance.
models_studied: ["Pretrained Boolean-classification MLPs", "Linear downstream classifiers", "Nonlinear downstream classifiers"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Localized-blur saliency maps can visibly distinguish Atari imitation policies trained with expert-action hint pixels from controls trained with random-valued hint pixels. Expert argmax actions were encoded as one-hot pixel intensities at the top of frames for shortcut-trained imitators; control imitators received random pixel values. The authors report clear saliency differences across all three games, identifying hint-region dependence in shortcut agents despite behavior they could not distinguish by observation alone. No quantitative detection benchmark is reported.
Specific finding: Localized-blur saliency in poorly performing Atari policies can reveal sensitivity patterns consistent with neglected hazards or reliance on distractor regions. The described MsPacman policy did not highlight a nearby ghost; partially trained policies highlighted altered corridors. The Frostbite example highlighted the upper goal region instead of a destination platform, and Enduro highlighted distant mountains instead of a nearby racer. No corrective intervention or systematic diagnostic benchmark was performed. Sparse rewards and use of mountains as a navigation anchor are proposed explanations.
models_studied: ["CNN\u2013LSTM supervised imitation policies for Pong", "CNN\u2013LSTM supervised imitation policies for SpaceInvaders", "CNN\u2013LSTM supervised imitation policies for Breakout"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Learned distributed subspaces can achieve higher interchange intervention accuracy than selected neuron-window searches and coordinate-aligned approximations on hierarchical equality and monotonicity inference. For the both-equality-relations model, the best reported distributed training IIA is 1.00, versus 0.60 for neuron-window search and 0.73 for the coordinate-aligned approximation. Joint MoNLI negation/entailment alignment reaches 1.00 at BERT layer 9; the corresponding reported baseline scores are lower. Tables report training IIA and select the best of three rotation seeds. BERT window search considers only starting indices 0, 64, 128, 256, and 512.
models_studied: ["Three-layer ReLU hierarchical-equality networks, hidden widths 16 and 32", "BERT-base uncased fine-tuned on MultiNLI and MoNLI"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A ReLU network trained on hierarchical equality can admit distributed subspaces whose sampled interchange effects match separate left- and right-equality variables perfectly. A three-layer ReLU network achieves reported 100% ordinary train/test accuracy after training on 1.92 million examples, with testing on unseen random input vectors. DAS trained on 640,000 intervention examples attains reported 1.00 training IIA for both equality relations at layer 1. A 19,200-example intervention testing set is described, but its numerical results cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.
Specific finding: MoNLI-fine-tuned BERT can admit separate distributed subspaces whose sampled intervention effects match a high-level algorithm combining negation and lexical entailment. BERT-base uncased, previously fine-tuned on MultiNLI, is trained on 10,000 MoNLI examples and achieves reported 100% ordinary training/testing accuracy. Joint alignment uses 24,000 training and 1,920 evaluation examples; the best-of-three layer-9 rotation with 256 dimensions per variable achieves reported 1.00 training IIA. Numerical held-out IIA is unavailable in the supplied figure text.
location: Sections 4.1–4.3; Table 1; Appendix A.2; Appendix E, Figure 6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Distributed Alignment Search can learn an orthogonal representation change that aligns a trained hierarchical-equality network with a compositional symbolic equality algorithm. The paper explicitly reports a companion-notebook replication of learning an orthogonal hidden-vector rotation for a trained hierarchical-equality network. The supplied text provides no numerical interchange accuracy, training sample size, optimization details, or repeated-run statistics, and the notebook itself is not included.
models_studied: ["Trained feed-forward neural network for hierarchical equality"]
location: Section 2.6, 'A Fully Connected Neural Network Trained on Hierarchical Equality'

experiment_summary: Specific finding: On restricted numerical interval-membership instructions, Alpaca-7B admits distributed boundary-check alignments with higher held-out interchange agreement than the tested midpoint-distance and bracket-identity alignments. Maximum held-out IIA was 0.90 for the left-boundary model, 0.86 for separate left/right Boolean checks, 0.70 for midpoint distance, and 0.72 for bracket identity. Ordinary task accuracy averaged approximately 0.85. At layer 10, position 75, the two-boundary alignment scored 0.83 versus 0.53 with a random rotation. Figure 12's caption specifies random rotations with learned boundary indices and three seeds.

Specific finding: Orthogonal causal alignment search can jointly learn an activation rotation and intervention-subspace dimensions by optimizing annealed continuous boundary masks and discretizing them for evaluation. Trained 4096-by-4096 orthogonal rotations and sigmoid boundary masks against symbolic counterfactual labels while freezing Alpaca. Alignments used 20,000 training examples, 200 validation examples, and 1,000 held-out test examples, with three seeds and best-IIA reporting. Boundary-check alignments attained maximum IIA of 0.90 and 0.86. Appendix A.2 reports that each alignment experiment fits on one A100 GPU and takes approximately 1.5 hours; no matched comparison with original DAS is supplied.

Specific finding: An equality-related neural subspace can support relation-level interchange while failing a subsequent search for argument-identity interchange structure. Freezing the original equality alignment and learning a second rotation within its subspace yields first-argument-identity training IIA of 0.50–0.51 across the reported width-16 and width-32 configurations. This documents failure of the tested optimization and subspace sizes, rather than mathematical non-decomposability.
models_studied: ["Three-layer ReLU hierarchical-equality networks, hidden widths 16 and 32"]
location: Section 4.3; Table 1, final column; Appendix A.5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Invertible nonlinear alignment maps can remove layer-dependent differences in hierarchical-equality interchange accuracy that appear under orthogonal linear alignment maps. Identity, orthogonal, and 10-layer width-16 RevNet maps were compared using 1,280,000 alignment-training interventions and 10,000 each for validation and testing. Third-layer IIA degradation under linear maps disappears with nonlinear maps for the two equality algorithms. Figure 2 reports maxima over ten seeds alongside means and 95% confidence intervals. Argument-identity test IIA remains approximately 50%.
Specific finding: Expressive nonlinear alignment maps can largely erase interchange-accuracy differences between a deliberately installed distributive-law algorithm and an alternative algorithm computing the same task. After training networks toward either algorithm and freezing them, the authors fit identity, orthogonal, and nonlinear alignments to both algorithms. Identity and linear maps favor the installed algorithm at layer 2; alternative-algorithm IIA is reported around 0.75 for And-Or-And installation and 0.65 for And-Or installation. Nonlinear maps almost eliminate these differences, with perfect IIA for both algorithms reported in the And-Or-trained condition. Figures show maxima over ten seeds alongside means and confidence intervals.
Specific finding: During Pythia-410M pretraining, shallower nonlinear alignment maps can eventually attain perfect IOI interchange accuracy even though deeper maps already attain near-perfect accuracy at initialization. Figure 4 compares orthogonal maps and RevNets with one, two, four, and eight layers across pretraining checkpoints. Eight-layer maps maintain near-perfect IIA throughout; one- and two-layer maps eventually achieve perfect alignment. Linear-map IIA tracks unmodified task accuracy more closely. Proposed explanations for intermediate dips, including unigram learning, are not independently tested.
Specific finding: A RevNet alignment that fails to fit a large argument-identity intervention dataset can fit a much smaller dataset nearly perfectly. The alignment does not exceed 0.55 training IIA on the standard 1,280,000-example dataset but exceeds 0.99 training IIA with 1,000 examples. Separate checks find no exact hidden-state collisions among 1,280,000 sampled inputs across ten seeds, and distance comparisons show closer states for examples sharing equality variables. These finite checks do not prove injectivity or establish a unique explanation of fitting failure.

Specific finding: Increasing the dimensionality of a DAS sentiment subspace can improve intervention performance on its training task without improving transfer to a different sentiment task. Appendix A.2 sweeps DAS subspace dimension and compares loss defined as one minus the patching metric. The accompanying text reports improved in-sample movie-review performance with higher dimensions but no improvement on out-of-distribution mood-task validation. Numerical curve values, seed counts, and uncertainty estimates are not supplied in the text.

Specific finding: On controlled non-English lexical translation and cloze tasks, Llama-2 intermediate vocabulary readouts generally favor the English version of the expected answer before favoring its target-language version. Layerwise expected-answer starting-token masses and vocabulary entropy are compared across three Llama-2 sizes. Non-English aggregated translation sets contain 287 German-target, 162 French-target, 324 Russian-target, and 353 Chinese-target prompts; corresponding cloze inventories contain 104, 56, 115, and 139 examples. The prose reports English answer mass rising in middle layers before target-language mass rises late. Appendix B.2 reports consistent Chinese results for Mistral-7B. Means and 95% Gaussian confidence intervals over input examples are described, but no numerical aggregate English-versus-target effect size is supplied.
location: Sections 3.3–4.1; Appendix A.1; Appendix B, Figures 5, 9, and 22

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: During non-English open-ended generation, intermediate vocabulary readouts frequently expose English equivalents of generated nouns and verbs, while several grammatical categories exhibit less English-equivalent readout. Each model generated 720 sentences, with the allocation across languages unspecified. Generated words were assigned parts of speech using spaCy, with jieba used for Mandarin segmentation. GPT-4o judged similarity to English intermediate readouts; scores of at least four out of five counted as routing, allowing close synonyms, tense differences, and some phrase fragments. One hundred samples were manually checked without a reported agreement statistic. Table 3 gives averages across the four non-English languages of 0.70 for Gemma, 0.68 for Mixtral, 0.55 for Llama, and 0.50 for Aya. These measurements establish readout associations rather than a causal English-processing pathway.
Specific finding: Hidden-state interpolation between English and non-English capital-city queries can favor English as the answer language. Measured answer-language propensity alongside capital-answer accuracy during hidden-state interpolation. The paper reports that all four models were most likely to answer in English, and Figure 6 describes Llama's English-versus-German preference. Exact propensity values, aggregation rules, and uncertainty are absent from the supplied text. The result should not be generalized to every interpolation coefficient or to comparisons without an English endpoint.

Specific finding: Japanese-adapted and English–Japanese bilingual language models can show stronger Japanese intermediate answer readouts than an English-centric model on Japanese-target lexical tasks. The authors compare layerwise candidate-answer scores under 8-bit inference. They report English-favoring intermediate readouts in Llama-2, mixed English/Japanese readouts in Swallow, and Japanese-dominant readouts in LLM-jp. English probabilities are nearly absent for LLM-jp's Japanese repetition and cloze conditions. Figure 3 reports 95% Gaussian confidence intervals over 166 examples; numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: Japanese-specific models with substantial English training can exhibit both English and Japanese intermediate answer readouts when completing French and Chinese lexical tasks. French-to-Chinese and Chinese-to-French translation, French/Chinese repetition, and French/Chinese cloze are evaluated using layerwise candidate-answer probabilities. The prose reports English and Japanese intermediate readouts in Swallow and LLM-jp, generally higher English probabilities in Swallow, and negligible Japanese probabilities in Llama-2. Figures report 95% Gaussian confidence intervals over 166 examples. Numerical probabilities are unavailable in the text.
Specific finding: A model answering a Japanese school-year question can favor September-related intermediate vocabulary readouts before favoring the correct April answer in later layers. For the one-shot school-year example, the prose reports September/nine preference in Llama-2's intermediate readouts before April/four appears later. Swallow shows nine once at layer 36; LLM-jp lacks the displayed September pattern. A small cultural-question dataset is mentioned, but its size and aggregate results are absent. The association does not establish that readout language causes the incorrect intermediate answer.

Specific finding: Shifting multilingual sentence representations toward the English language mean can yield higher aligned-sentence similarity than shifting them toward other tested language means. The paper compares mean aligned-sentence similarity after subtracting each source-language mean and adding a candidate target-language mean. English has the highest reported scores for LLaMA-2-70B. No numerical effect sizes, uncertainty estimates, or controls separating alignment from effects of the added mean are supplied.

Specific finding: Arithmetic representations can share value-sensitive geometry with English expressions and expose corresponding English number words through intermediate vocabulary readouts. Compared numeric right-hand-side expressions with English expressions, reporting 1,123 exact-translation pairs, 13,293 non-exact same-value pairs, and 1,247,836 different-value pairs. Same-value expressions have greater similarity despite different surface forms. PCA visualizations of 100 prefix trajectories are described as passing near English number unembeddings. Logit-lens tests on 1,123 expressions show similar numeral and English-word probabilities until approximately layer 25, followed by numeral dominance. The reported pair-category counts are retained as given and are not independently reconciled.
Specific finding: Intermediate representations of Python prefixes can favor English connective or argument-role words before favoring the actual code continuation. Across all 974 MBPP programs, evaluated 6,923 list-literal commas including unit tests: intermediate readouts favor 'and' over the actual next token and the baselines 'or' and 'not', before late-layer continuation dominance. For 540 function arguments excluding unit tests, early-to-middle readouts favor argument names over instantiated expressions, with the ordering reversing late. Filtering excludes unavailable argument names, generic obj/object roles, identical role and surface expressions, and unsuitable token boundaries.
Specific finding: Language-model representation similarity can distinguish a sentence's matching semantic structure from a structure with identical lexical content but incorrect name-role assignments. For 2,233 COGS sentences containing two proper names, compared sentence–structure similarity with structures formed by swapping those names while preserving lexical overlap. A further control shuffles predicate order. Matching structures retain a similarity advantage in the reported comparisons, with BLOOM described as doing little better than chance. The supplied prose does not enumerate the other checkpoints for this experiment.
Specific finding: Within multimodal language models, matching images or audio clips can have more similar intermediate representations to their textual descriptions than mismatched descriptions do. Used 1,000 MSCOCO image-caption pairs and 1,000 VGGSound audio-label pairs, subtracting layer-specific average mismatched-pair cosine similarity. Matching pairs show positive intermediate similarity advantages. These tests compare representations within each multimodal model without learning an additional cross-modal alignment transformation.
Specific finding: Vocabulary projections of multimodal hidden states can preferentially expose English words describing their input content, with substantial differences across models and annotation granularities. Across 2,304 patch positions from four pure-color images, LLaVA's top vocabulary token is the corresponding color word more than 20% of the time at favorable intermediate layers. For 1,000 MSCOCO image-caption pairs, both vision models give higher summed patch-level probability to matching caption nouns than to noun-count-normalized mismatched captions selected for minimal noun overlap. Panoptic labels covering more than half a patch's pixels outperform random category labels in LLaVA; Chameleon's advantage appears in only one middle layer and is not statistically significant. For 1,000 VGGSound clips, SALMONN's position-averaged readouts favor matching label words over random labels with no word overlap; no fine-grained audio-position correspondence is available.

Specific finding: English-derived number activation edits can make an arithmetic model decrement an upcoming operand and compensate with an additional '+1' continuation. Constructed number contrasts from English prefixes that determine an upcoming number, then intervened at layer 25 for Llama-3 and layer 30 for Llama-2. Across 846 addition expressions, favorable coefficients produce the decremented number followed by '+1' on over 90% of instances according to the prose. The illustrative subtraction order, 'three' minus 'two', is inconsistent with the stated decrementing goal unless the coefficient sign accounts for it; the exact sign convention is not resolved by the supplied text.
Specific finding: Replacing selected image-position hidden states with an English color-derived vector can change Chameleon's answer about one image color while preserving its answer about another. Used two-color images and targeted one color for substitution by a third. At image positions corresponding to the targeted color, hidden states from the chosen layer onward are replaced with the new-color-minus-old-color unembedding vector, as specified in the intervention description. Success requires both the substituted color and untouched color to be answered correctly; peak success exceeds 80% across 48 cases. Other colors and more sophisticated flag or spatial-relation questions were excluded because the unintervened model could not answer them reliably.
Specific finding: English animal-name unembedding edits to audio representations can shift SALMONN's mammal judgments toward the substituted animal category. Asked whether the heard animal is a mammal and added scaled new-animal-minus-original-animal unembeddings at layer 13, crossing mammal/non-mammal categories in both directions. Increasing intervention strength shifts P(Yes)/(P(Yes)+P(No)) in the intended direction. The source provides no numerical aggregate classification accuracy or broad audio-capability retention result.

Specific finding: English-derived topic steering vectors can outperform vectors derived in the desired output language at inducing target-word inclusion without output collapse in non-English generation. Compared topic vectors constructed from sentence sets in different languages while steering toward a specified topic and output language. Topic and language coefficients were selected as five and ten using five held-out words and 50 prompts.
