Topic layers were searched every fifth layer and language layers every second layer; best-layer results generally favored English-derived vectors. Appendix A.7 reports that successful steering was possible at approximately 20–40% of layers on average and that English vectors were least sensitive to layer selection. Exact Figure 4 success rates and evaluation denominators are unavailable in the supplied text.

Specific finding: Activation oracles trained on one collection of natural-language binary tasks can classify properties from single-token activations on held-out classification datasets more accurately than the evaluated untrained activation-reader baseline. Uses 250 examples from each of seven datasets, each evaluated with three randomly sampled oracle questions: 1,750 distinct examples and 5,250 question evaluations per evaluated configuration. Open-weight readers receive one activation immediately before EOS; Claude uses the final-token position. Reports successful held-out generalization and improvements over untrained and SPQA-only readers across the four model families. Exact aggregate accuracies are unavailable in the supplied prose, and Claude performance depends on its selected learning rate.
Specific finding: Expanding activation-oracle training from system-prompt QA to include classification and context prediction can improve performance across diverse held-out activation-reading evaluations. Compares untrained, SPQA-only, SPQA-plus-classification, and full-mixture AOs. Ten of twelve combinations attain their best measured performance with the full mixture; the other two full-mixture results are within error of the best configuration. Benefits vary by model and task. The twelve combinations constitute the reported evaluation panel rather than a full crossing of every model with every auditing task.

Specific finding: Mixing unrelated data into organism training does not uniformly lower interpretability scores when quirk expression is approximately matched. Specific finding: The relative interpretability ranking of organism-construction recipes can change between OLMo2-1B and gemma-3-1b-it. Specific finding: BFS-like graph-frontier probability and entropy patterns can arise in thought-slot models without recurrent hidden-state feedback and can change substantially under curriculum perturbations that preserve recurrence. At step 4, target-reaching mass is 0.58 for PaT, 0.63 for Coconut, and 0.23 for Coconut-u. Eligible counts are 461, 461, 486, 439, and 182 at steps 0–4. Specific finding: A large timestep-specific component of latent-state variance need not imply strong behavioral dependence on that component. ProsQA Coconut-u has 99.1% temporal variance, yet the reported component interventions do not reproduce its thought-deletion drop. On arithmetic, temporal-component ablation is described as least damaging, while residual ablation is most damaging. The random control is reported to preserve performance. Specific finding: Adding per-step supervision to a fixed latent-recycling mechanism and slot budget can establish deletion-sensitive chain dependence on logical tasks. The GPT-2 ProsQA loss-off control remained inert. These comparisons support an effect of the per-step training recipe beyond matched extra training on ProsQA, without establishing universal dependence from step supervision.

The split and shuffle procedures were each repeated 1,000 times; these are analysis repetitions rather than independent model-training replications. Specific finding: A transformer trained on RRXOR can encode posterior-belief geometry that is accurately recoverable by an affine readout of concatenated residual layers despite poor recovery from every individual layer. Exact MSE values, independent training-seed replication, and a held-out RRXOR regression split are not specified in the supplied text.

Reported correspondence was R²=0.95 for belief distances versus R²=0.31 for next-token distances. RRXOR includes distinct posterior states with identical next-token predictions but different future distributions. The result concerns supervised decoded geometry rather than raw residual-space distances or a direct future-sequence prediction test.
Specific finding: During training on small hidden Markov processes, improved next-token prediction can accompany more accurate affine recovery of posterior-belief geometry. Mess3 checkpoint visualizations and regression errors showed gradual emergence of fractal geometry. Specific finding: GPT-2 Small's attention-weighted alignment with syntactic dependency edges is strongest at intermediate layer depths, where its attended distances are relatively short. Measured the proportion of attention connecting dependency-related tokens with the source as parent, target as parent, or either direction. The layerwise figure includes a baseline proportion of token pairs sharing a dependency relation independent of attention. The prose reports strongest alignment in intermediate layers and identifies layers 2–4 as having both the shortest attended distances and highest alignment. Specific finding: GPT-2 Small's deepest layers have the largest layer-average attended token distances, despite substantial variation among heads and exceptions to a monotonic depth trend. Computed mean token separation weighted by each head's attention. Deepest layers had the greatest layer-average distance, while distances varied substantially across heads, with reported SD 3.6 tokens. Layer 5 head 1 had the largest individual-head mean distance, 14.2 tokens, and concentrated on repeated phrases.
Specific finding: Across GPT-2 Small attention heads, greater mean attended distance is associated with higher attention entropy and lower dependency alignment on sentence-level Wikipedia text. Reported distance–entropy correlation r = 0.61 and distance–dependency-alignment correlation r = −0.73, both p < 0.001. Entropy excluded first-token attention, renormalized remaining weights, and omitted source tokens with over 90% first-token attention. Layer 5 head 1 illustrated that distant attention can also be sharply concentrated, with entropy 0.41. Corpus dependency probabilities were 0.42 for adjacent tokens, 0.07 at distance five, and 0.02 at distance ten, demonstrating a substantial distance confound.

Specific finding: Some sparse attention-replacement units show persistent source contributions from thematic keywords to subsequent tokens. Manual inspection of source-token contribution patterns identifies topic-consistent attention extending across subsequent sentence tokens. Figure 6 illustrates a presidency-related unit. No controlled topic manipulation or downstream behavioral intervention is reported for these units.

Specific finding: Ranking recurrent SAE coordinates by learned persistence can select compact states with stronger current-subject decodability than selecting equally many low-persistence or randomly ordered coordinates, approaching supervised feature selection. Persistent-state feature budgets span 0.1%–100%, with decreasing/increasing λ, repeated random orders, and supervised training-label rankings interleaved across subjects. The slowest 1% reportedly reaches high macro one-vs-rest ROC AUC approaching supervised selection. The text also reports advantages over SAE baselines, while Appendix G describes those baselines as using full dictionaries. A separate t-SNE analysis uses 100 sequences and their last 20 tokens. Numerical AUC values and probing sample counts are not provided.
Specific finding: Slow recurrent SAE states can retain injection-label information farther beyond an untrusted span than fast states or tested standard SAE representations when the detector is trained only at the span endpoint. Logistic probes fitted at offset zero are evaluated without retraining at offsets 50, 100, 200, 250, 300, and 350 and the final query position. The text reports strongest local signals for fast and standard SAE representations, declining toward chance later, while the highest-λ 1% state retains more distant signal. Accuracy and ROC AUC are evaluated, but numerical curves, trajectory counts, split construction, and checkpoint-availability handling are absent. Section 5.4 defines fast states using the lowest-λ 50%; Appendix H's representation list does not explicitly enumerate this fast-state condition. Failed attacks are retained without filtering legitimate-task utility.

Sections 3.1 and Appendix D report lower errors and better loss recovery for AbsTopK across most tested configurations, acknowledging competitive baseline results in some settings. Specific finding: AbsTopK-based safety steering can achieve higher reported HarmBench safety scores and retain more MMLU accuracy than the tested TopK and JumpReLU interventions, with results competitive with Difference-in-Means. Table 1 reports higher MMLU and HarmBench scores for AbsTopK than both conventional SAE baselines in all four model–layer settings. Qwen L18 scores 75.9 MMLU and 81.3 HarmBench versus original 77.3/17.0 and DiM 75.8/80.6. At Qwen L20, AbsTopK scores 76.4/79.0 versus DiM 76.4/80.0. experiment_summary: Specific finding: Nonnegative SAE coefficients may fragment a naturally bidirectional semantic axis across multiple atoms, reducing the compactness of its representation.

Specific finding: An individual signed SAE latent can activate with opposite signs for controlled sentence variants differing between “man” and “woman.” Figure 1's caption describes generated sentence pairs differing by one token and reports positive activation for man and negative activation for woman in the displayed feature. The supplied text does not identify the example's model, sample count, or numerical activation values.

Specific finding: Euclidean proximal operators for nonnegative L1 regularization, nonnegative L0 regularization, and nonnegative cardinality constraints yield shifted ReLU, JumpReLU, and nonnegative TopK, respectively. Formal result: Lemma 1 and Appendix C derive scalar nonnegative soft- and hard-threshold solutions and Euclidean projection onto nonnegative vectors with at most k nonzero coordinates. The TopK proof contains a notation slip identifying the selected indices using z rather than u; Equation 7 supplies the intended definition. These operator identities do not establish sparse-code recovery or training convergence.

Specific finding: Euclidean projection onto real vectors with at most k nonzero coordinates retains the k largest-magnitude input entries with their original signs. Formal derivation: Equations 10–11 identify signed hard thresholding as the proximal map of the indicator of the at-most-k cardinality constraint. The paper acknowledges hard thresholding as an existing compressed-sensing operator and extends its use to the proposed SAE framework. This projection identity supplies no dictionary-identification or semantic-recovery guarantee.
Specific finding: A zero-initialized proximal-gradient sparse-coding step can motivate an SAE encoder by replacing its dictionary-transpose map and induced bias with independently learned parameters.

Specific finding: A one-hidden-layer MLP sparse encoder can achieve lower reconstruction error with fewer active coefficients than a shallow ReLU SAE on GPT-2 Small layer-9 residual activations. Compared a shallow ReLU SAE with an MLP encoder of hidden width 8,448, each reconstructing 768-dimensional GPT-2 Small layer-9 residual-stream pre-activations. Both used Adam at 3×10^-4, L1 penalty 10^-4, and dead-feature resampling every 15,000 steps. MLP normalised MSE was 0.055 with mean L0 31.13, versus SAE 0.061 and 35.66. Dead-feature fractions were 22% and 11%, respectively. The LCA comparison used 100 sparse-inference steps per batch and attained MSE 0.070, with effective L0 approximately 18.56 after thresholding coefficients below 10^-5; its unthresholded coefficients were not exactly zero.
Specific finding: Multilayer perceptron encoders can predict known synthetic sparse coefficients more accurately than the tested single linear–nonlinear encoders, with benefits depending on computational budget. Compared shallow SAE encoders with MLP hidden widths 32, 256, and 1,024 in the default setting; the widest MLP attained approximately 0.1 higher MCC at convergence. The larger experiment used 500,000 examples, batch size 1,024, 20,000 training steps, and MLP widths 256, 512, and 1,024. All three larger-setting MLPs reportedly surpassed the SAE plateau at approximately 3×10^14 estimated FLOPs. These are finite architecture and training-budget comparisons.
Specific finding: With a generating dictionary held fixed, multilayer encoders and SAE-initialised coefficient optimisation can obtain higher synthetic coefficient-recovery correlation than the tested shallow SAE encoder. With the true dictionary fixed, MLPs of widths 32 and 256 achieved MCC described as nearly 10% higher than the shallow SAE at convergence. SAE+ITO, initialised with SAE coefficients, achieved the highest reported MCC. The source does not clarify whether its percentage comparison denotes a relative increase or percentage-point difference. Some FLOP curves beyond the measured range are explicitly extrapolated. The Zipf extension retained broadly similar ordering with more volatile optimisation.
Specific finding: In synthetic joint dictionary-learning experiments, gradient-based sparse coding can obtain higher coefficient-recovery correlation than the tested shallow SAE and MLP implementations, while sparse coding and MLPs can both improve dictionary recovery over the shallow SAE. The default fully unknown setting used 2,048 examples, equally divided between training and testing, and five runs of 100,000 steps. Sparse coding achieved latent MCC described as over 10% higher than the alternatives, using estimated FLOPs comparable to the width-256 MLP. Both sparse coding and MLPs improved dictionary MCC over the SAE by approximately 10%, with percentage units not clarified. N/M sweeps at K=3 and K=9 generally favoured sparse coding over the SAE; MLP and SAE performance was roughly similar. Zipf-weighted data reduced sparse coding's advantage. Section 4.4 also reports improved latent-MCC versus sparsity tradeoffs, with active-count results dependent on thresholds for small coefficients.
Specific finding: Alternating dictionary learning with LARS-based Lasso inference can outperform basic gradient-based sparse coding, shallow SAE, and MLP implementations on synthetic coefficient and dictionary recovery. Appendix H implements alternating dictionary updates and LARS-based Lasso coefficient inference using scikit-learn, evaluates held-out synthetic examples, and reports improvements over the authors' basic implementations, particularly for latent and dictionary MCC. Figure 17's caption additionally reports reconstruction-loss improvements. Numerical effect sizes, repeated-run variability, and an equal-compute comparison are not provided in the text.
Specific finding: A bias-free encoder consisting of one linear map followed by coordinatewise ReLU cannot exactly recover every nonnegative K-sparse code from an M-dimensional linear projection when K is at least two and M is smaller than the code dimension N. Formal result supplied in Appendix A, restricted here to the bias-free ReLU case actually derived. Exact recovery of positive one-sparse vectors fixes diagonal preactivations, while exact recovery of their pairwise sums forces every off-diagonal preactivation to zero. The resulting diagonal matrix has rank N, contradicting factorisation through M<N dimensions. This positive-code restriction avoids the proof's unresolved treatment of arbitrary signed coefficients and sign flips.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A fixed dictionary satisfying restricted isometry of order 2k with constant below one maps distinct k-sparse codes to distinct observations. Formal basis: Section 3 supplies the nullspace argument. If Wh=Wh' for two k-sparse codes, their difference is at most 2k-sparse. The positive RIP lower bound forces that difference to be zero. The Gaussian measurement-dimension bounds and algorithmic recovery guarantees are attributed to prior work rather than proved here.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A fixed dictionary satisfying restricted isometry of order 2k with constant below one maps distinct k-sparse codes to distinct observations.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A linear dictionary whose spark exceeds 2s maps distinct vectors with at most s nonzero coordinates to distinct observations. Formal rederivation in Claim C.1: two s-sparse codes with the same image have a difference supported on at most 2s columns. The spark condition makes those columns independent, forcing the difference to vanish. The argument is supplied here and attributed to classical sparse-representation theory; no empirical experiment is performed.

Specific finding: A linear dictionary whose spark exceeds 2s maps distinct vectors with at most s nonzero coordinates to distinct observations. Formal proof supplied here: two s-sparse vectors with equal measurements have a difference with at most 2s nonzeros in the operator’s kernel. The spark condition forces that difference to vanish. The argument is applied to the classifier-visible learned operator after establishing nullspace equality.

Specific finding: A tied linear encoder and biased ReLU decoder can recover independent Bernoulli feature supports with high probability under explicit dictionary coherence and spectral-norm bounds, with an additional maximum coordinate-error guarantee for unit-norm atoms. Formal result: Theorem 1 centers each coordinate's interference using the bias, applies Bernstein's inequality to independent bounded summands, and takes a union bound over coordinates. Remark 2 specializes this to unit-norm tight frames with ||W||²₂→₂=n/d and sufficiently low coherence, giving a sufficient expected support size of order d/log n at fixed failure probability. The coefficient-error conclusion requires the stronger δ-dependent condition. No empirical experiment is supplied.
Specific finding: Gaussian dictionaries permit uniform binary-support recovery by tied biased-ReLU decoding at a sufficient sparsity scale √(d/log n), while their recoverable sparsity is bounded above at order √d with high probability. Formal result: Propositions 10–11 bound principal Gram diagonal dominance using Gaussian inner products, chi-distributed column norms, Gaussian and chi-square concentration, and half-normal order statistics. Theorem 8 combines the bounds by a union bound. The probability is over the dictionary, while the resulting recovery guarantee is uniform over binary supports up to the permitted size. No Gaussian simulation or learned-model experiment is reported.
Specific finding: The maximum uniformly recoverable binary support size of a tied biased-ReLU decoder is bounded above by the dictionary's principal-submatrix diagonal-dominance threshold and below by half that threshold, rounded down. Formal result: Proposition 6 compares the signed row-sum criterion with sums of the largest absolute Gram entries. Lemma 7 establishes equality k(W)=k′(W) when all off-diagonal inner products are nonpositive. The subsequent non-simplex real ETF result attains the lower bound.
Specific finding: For real equiangular tight frames with more than d+1 atoms, the exact uniform binary-support recovery capacity of a tied biased-ReLU decoder is floor(ceil(1/μ)/2), where μ is dictionary coherence. Formal result: Lemma 12 evaluates diagonal dominance from constant off-diagonal magnitude. Theorem 16 uses the new Gram sign-count result, cited ETF coherence integrality, Naimark complements, and special small-dimensional cases to prove the matching recovery upper bound. Theorem 9 combines this with equality in the Welch–Rankin bound. No empirical experiment is supplied.
Specific finding: Uniform recovery of all binary supports of size at most k by ReLU(WᵀWx+b), for some fixed bias vector, is equivalent to a strict separation condition between each coordinate's largest positive and negative Gram-matrix interference sums. Formal result: Lemma 4 derives necessary bias intervals by maximizing inactive-coordinate responses and minimizing active-coordinate responses over allowed supports. Strict separation of these intervals is also sufficient, using b_i equal to minus the largest positive interference sum. The resulting criterion is computable from the Gram matrix.

Specific finding: Under strong superposition, higher-norm feature directions in sparse reconstruction models can develop more uniform squared overlaps than independent random directions, with mean squared overlap near inverse width. Normalized selected rows are compared with the random-sphere squared-overlap mean 1/m and variance 2(m−1)/(m²(m+2)). Many trained configurations have smaller variance, especially with relatively even frequencies; some strongly skewed configurations exceed the random-vector variance. Selected-row counts approximately track min(n,m²/2). The Welch bound and exact ETF properties are cited prior results, not new theorems produced here.
Specific finding: Selected open language-model families have nonzero output-head vectors for more tokens than their hidden width, with mean pairwise squared cosine overlap roughly decreasing as inverse width. The study measures output-head row norms and cosine overlaps over all unique row pairs using batched calculations. Minimum row norms are nonzero and vocabulary sizes exceed hidden widths. Mean squared overlaps approximately follow 1/m, but Appendix D.7 describes these measurements as noisy and explicitly states that no line was fitted. Mean row norms are also reported to vary relatively little with width within families.
Specific finding: Interference among superposed representations may be an important contributor to the approximately inverse-width component of language-model loss. The hypothesis receives indirect tests: controlled toy-model regime comparisons show interference-associated scaling in reconstruction networks, while separate observational LLM analyses find compatible output-head geometry, token frequencies, and loss exponents. These measurements do not intervene on LLM superposition or show that output-head overlap explains the observed loss differences. The cross-entropy bridge is approximate, and the proposed balancing of width- and depth-limited losses in Section 5 is discussion rather than a tested decomposition.
Specific finding: Strong-superposition sparse reconstruction models can exhibit approximately inverse-width loss across exponential, power-law, and linearly declining feature-frequency distributions. After 20,000 training steps with fresh synthetic batches, strong-superposition loss fits yield width exponents 1.01±0.05 for exponential frequencies, 1.0±0.1 for power-law frequencies, and 0.89±0.05 for linear frequencies. Exponential fits use all widths; power-law and linear fits start at the third width. Positive-decay comparisons show distribution-dependent weak-superposition scaling. Figure 1 loss error bars are standard deviations over 100 newly sampled batches, not independent training runs.
models_studied: ["1,000-feature tied-weight biased-ReLU reconstruction models", "10,240-feature tied-weight biased-ReLU reconstruction models"]
location: Section 3.2, Figure 5c–d; Appendix D.1, Figure 8; Appendix D.6, Figure 16

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The width-dependent portion of language-model cross-entropy can be approximated by a squared-overlap contribution from output-head vectors.

Specific finding: Aggregate SpLiCE coefficients can reflect selected changes in visual attribute prevalence and class-conditioned dataset composition. Stanford Cars coefficient trends are reported to qualitatively follow measured convertible and yellow-car prevalence by year; no trend-fit statistics are provided. Waterbirds landbird decomposition distances are 0.0182 for train–validation and train–test versus 0.005 for validation–test; waterbird distances are 0.0229, 0.0188, and 0.009 respectively. Bamboo coefficients likewise reflect training-set background imbalance. No detection thresholds or false-positive rates are evaluated.
Specific finding: Aggregating sparse text-concept coefficients across images can reveal dataset associations that are subsequently verifiable by manual inspection. Swimwear and bra concepts rank among the ten most common concepts for CIFAR100's woman class. Manual inspection identifies at least 70 of its 600 train-and-test images as depicting bikinis, underclothes, or partial undress. ImageNet monarch-butterfly decompositions highlight lilac flowers; inspection finds purple flowers in nearly half of the class's validation images. Additional camel/desert associations are reported qualitatively.

Specific finding: Removing selected eyewear-related SpLiCE coefficients can reduce CelebA glasses classification accuracy more than gender classification accuracy. Zero-shot SpLiCE glasses accuracy falls from 0.88 to 0.69, while gender accuracy changes from 0.97 to 0.96. Probe glasses accuracy falls from 0.88 to 0.59, while gender accuracy changes from 0.89 to 0.85. These interventions have no reported uncertainty estimates.
Specific finding: Removing selected land-background SpLiCE coefficients can improve a Waterbirds linear classifier's accuracy on waterbirds pictured on land. Waterbird-on-land accuracy increases from 0.48 to 0.60 after intervention, while landbird-on-land accuracy changes from 0.98 to 0.97. No uncertainty estimates or complete four-group results are supplied.

Specific finding: Sparse SpLiCE reconstructions can preserve linear-probe performance close to dense CLIP embeddings on CIFAR100 and MIT States. Across three runs, CIFAR100 CLIP-trained probes score 0.96–0.97 at reported L0 values of 3, 6, 23, and 117 versus 0.97 on CLIP; SpLiCE-trained probes score 0.95. MIT States scores remain 0.882–0.884 at L0 values of 4, 7, and 27 versus CLIP's 0.883. Reported standard deviations are below 0.005.
Specific finding: Sparse reconstructions over a fixed semantic phrase dictionary can retain much of CLIP's zero-shot classification performance, with losses depending on the dataset and vocabulary coverage. At sparsity 20–35, SpLiCE scores 0.86, 0.66, 0.96, and 0.83 on Caltech101, SUN397, STL10, and VOC2007, versus implemented CLIP scores of 0.90, 0.67, 0.96, and 0.92. Main-text sweeps compare semantic, random, and learned 15,000-element dictionaries and report improved ImageNet performance after adding missing class names. At sparsity 512, CIFAR100/MIT States/ImageNet scores are 0.768/0.474/0.552 versus CLIP's 0.750/0.469/0.552. Appendix B.14 reports qualitatively similar trends for ResNet50 using a different 10,000-word vocabulary; exact plotted values are unavailable.
Specific finding: At low active-concept counts, semantic phrase dictionaries can provide better CLIP reconstruction-based image–text retrieval than the evaluated random and learned dictionaries. Appendix B.3 reports stronger retrieval with the semantic dictionary in highly sparse decompositions. Image-learned dictionaries perform slightly better for text-to-image retrieval above 30 active concepts. Exact plotted recall values and the number of sampled subsets are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Sparse semantic CLIP reconstructions may preserve task performance despite modest cosine reconstruction because they omit nonsemantic information present in the original embeddings.

Specific finding: DL-FISTA representations can yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the tested TopK SAE on all eight evaluated Gemma-2-2B text-classification datasets, with a smaller average advantage over raw-activation probing. Table 2 reports mean test accuracy of 95.79±0.06% for DL-FISTA, 94.63±0.05% for TopK SAE, and 95.62±0.04% for raw probing, with standard errors over three seeds. DL-FISTA exceeds TopK on all eight datasets by approximately 0.31–2.24 percentage points and raw probing on six of eight. The panel contains three Bias in Bios class sets, two Amazon review tasks, GitHub code, AG News, and Europarl. The aggregate raw-probe versus SAE ordering is not universal: TopK slightly exceeds raw probing on AG News.
Specific finding: DL-FISTA can achieve a small average held-out classification advantage over the tested SAE and raw-activation readouts in the reported Pythia-70M sparse-probing setup. Section 4.4 attributes average accuracy of 92.38±0.07% for DL-FISTA versus 92.21±0.16% for raw probing and 92.21±0.02% for the SAE to the Pythia comparison. Appendix D.3 specifies 50,000 Pile training tokens, 4,000 training and 1,000 test examples per classification dataset, and 200 evaluation FISTA iterations. Table 3 and Appendix D.3 describe standard deviations over three seeds, but the table caption conflicts with the surrounding model attribution. No formal significance test is supplied.

Specific finding: MP-SAE can achieve higher final-layer vision-activation reconstruction R² than the evaluated conventional SAE recipes at comparable active-feature counts. Section 4.2 reports higher MP-SAE reconstruction R² at comparable sparsity across the four backbones in Figure 5. Training processes final-layer activations token by token, including spatial and CLS tokens where applicable. Numerical curve values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied text. Appendix B.2 specifies one run per configuration and estimates approximately 16.9 billion DINOv2 training tokens, whereas the main text states approximately 25 billion.
Specific finding: Increasing inference-time feature budgets beyond their training values can continue to improve reconstruction for trained MP-SAEs while degrading the tested fixed-TopK encoders. Section 4.2 describes Figure 8 as showing improving reconstruction with increased MP-SAE inference sparsity on DINOv2 while fixed-TopK performance degrades under sparsity mismatch. Figure 20 evaluates normalized MSE across training checkpoints and inference budgets for 4× dictionaries trained at L0 approximately 100 on second-block TinyStories residuals. Later MP-SAE checkpoints improve beyond the training budget; early checkpoints show saturation. Vanilla approaches a plateau, and TopK error increases beyond its training budget.

Specific finding: ConSDL can improve average cross-seed dictionary and coefficient consistency over the evaluated SAE baselines across small vision and language backbones. Across 36 backbone–width–sparsity configurations, Table 8 reports equally weighted backbone averages DCS=0.84 and MCC=0.78. Reported relative gains are 17.6% and 35.9% over the six-baseline average and 1.9% and 13.3% for the table's per-backbone strongest-baseline comparisons averaged across backbones. Mean usable atom fraction rounds to 1.00, but is not exactly one in every setting. Some baseline cells outperform ConSDL. ReLU and ConSDL operating points are selected by DCS times usable fraction within a stated ±15% target-sparsity band; achieved counts and compute differ, and some table counts fall outside that band. A single CLIP condition retains method rankings under activation-footprint matching. CLIP MCC conflicts between Table 3 and Tables 6/15, and baseline attribution for iSAE differs between Section 4.1 and Appendix D.1.
Specific finding: ConSDL can reproduce dictionary cluster sizes and centroids across training seeds more consistently than the evaluated SAE baselines. At 16-fold expansion and L0 approximately 128, reported cluster-size Spearman correlation is 0.95 for ConSDL versus 0.22 for Matryoshka. Section 6.2 reports normalized centroid agreements of 1.00, 0.96, 0.94, and 0.88 at 192, 48, 12, and 3 atoms per cluster; Figure 7C's caption specifies that its curves average nine CLIP settings. ConSDL is reported to have the highest normalized centroid agreement at each granularity. Cluster reproducibility does not establish semantic correctness.
location: Sections 5.1–5.2; Tables 3, 6, 8, and 15–19; Appendices D.1, D.2, and D.4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Adding sampled dictionary-conditioning regularization to signed TopK SAEs can improve cross-seed consistency of orthogonal-matching-pursuit codes even when dictionary cosine agreement decreases. For Pythia, regularization changes OMP code IoU from 0.398 to 0.472 and normalized error from 0.292 to 0.273, while DCS decreases from 0.873 to 0.858. For DINOv2, OMP IoU changes from 0.374 to 0.386 and error from 0.462 to 0.449, while DCS decreases from 0.862 to 0.846. Encoder-code consistency worsens on both reported metrics for Pythia but improves for DINOv2. The measured conditioning statistic decreases in both settings. Seed counts and uncertainty are unspecified.
Specific finding: Five-step recurrent encoding within iSAE can substantially improve reconstruction and cross-seed dictionary and code consistency on synthetic sparse linear mixtures. Table 1 compares iSAE with iSAE-ME under equal training-step budgets. For independent atoms, MSE decreases from 0.318 to 0.001, encoder code IoU rises from 0.487 to 0.997, normalized code error falls from 0.558 to 0.020, and DCS rises from 0.933 to 0.999. For clustered atoms, MSE decreases from 0.319 to 0.040, IoU rises from 0.497 to 0.873, code error falls from 0.526 to 0.219, and DCS rises from 0.843 to 0.932. The clustered conditioning statistic instead increases from 0.095 to 0.230. Recurrence adds parameters and computation; seed counts and uncertainty are unspecified.

Specific finding: Matching answer-excluded output KL can reduce encoder-relative answer-margin gaps for subject–verb NNLS interventions while increasing those gaps for explicitly cued reflexive gender interventions. Earlier 2B and Llama subject–verb NNLS cohorts match completely under Q2; the main text reports pooled residual gaps of 0.008–0.023 logits. On the new 304-input Llama panel, the post-inspection Q2 follow-up matches every input and reduces the balanced gap from 0.213 to 0.029 logits; the reduction is 0.184 [95% conditional interval 0.149, 0.223]. On 40 common gender inputs, all Q2 searches match, but balanced gaps increase from 0.089 to 0.139; the reduction is -0.050 [95% interval -0.091, -0.008]. Deterioration also occurs on the complete 42-input gender cohort. A numerical KL partition shows closer agreement in the weighted remaining-vocabulary term and worse agreement in the within-answer term, without identifying a causal mechanism.
Specific finding: For selected grammatical feature groups, per-input full-output KL calibration of same-support NNLS patches leaves smaller mean answer-margin gaps from encoder patches than total-norm matching with the same number of scaling coefficients. Q1 gives smaller mean gaps on common matched inputs in all five earlier cohorts: n=165, 62, 188, 112, and 42. Paired intervals exclude zero in the four cohorts with estimable intervals. On 304 prospective Llama-128K inputs from 152 of 512 assigned pairs, both controls match all qualified inputs; balanced gaps are 0.181 for total norm and 0.021 for Q1, with paired reduction 0.160 logits [95% conditional block-bootstrap interval 0.131, 0.191]. The confirmation passes its prespecified support, coverage, and precision requirements within a configuration selected using earlier outcomes.
Specific finding: Per-input full-output KL calibration can substantially reduce the encoder-relative answer-margin gaps of reconstruction-qualified, positionwise-norm-matched constructed patches on inputs where calibration succeeds. The prespecified Gemma-9B comparison matches 478/504 eligible inputs: case-balanced gaps fall from 0.752 to 0.028 logits, with paired reduction 0.7239 [95% interval 0.3241, 1.1236], missing the planned 0.25-logit interval half-width; transfer disagreements fall from 77 to eight. Gemma-2B subject–verb candidates match 64/64, reducing balanced gaps from 0.561 to 0.015 with no remaining transfer disagreements. Llama-128K matches 92/124, Llama-32K 75/106, and gender 16/40; these subsets show lower mean gaps but fail coverage requirements. One gender case has no matches, preventing a balanced matched estimate.
Specific finding: Positionwise norm matching can leave smaller mean encoder-relative answer-margin gaps than whole-patch full-output KL calibration for NNLS reflexive-agreement patches. On the common 24-input gender subset, balanced mean gaps are 0.012 logits under positionwise norm matching, 0.047 under Q1, and 0.085 under total-norm matching. No paired interval is available because too few bootstrap draws retain all required cells. Original patches have mean cosine similarity near 0.998 to encoder patches but different positional norm allocation; this diagnostic does not isolate the cause. On the new Llama panel, Q1 instead has the smallest mean gap.
Specific finding: Allowing separate norm-matching coefficients at each patched position can reduce mean encoder-relative NNLS answer-margin gaps compared with one total-norm coefficient. Positionwise matching has lower observed mean gaps in four of five earlier cohorts and on the prospective Llama cohort. Common matched counts are 150, 62, 188, 109, and 24 for the earlier cohorts, and 304 for the prospective cohort. Positionwise-minus-total-norm differences are -0.024, 0.001, -0.048, -0.029, -0.073, and -0.046 logits, respectively. Intervals exclude zero for the two earlier Llama comparisons and the prospective comparison; the 2B SVA interval spans zero, and 9B and gender intervals are unavailable.
Specific finding: Changing the strength control applied to the same NNLS feature-group patch can change whether it preserves the encoder intervention's donor-answer transfer decision. Across 304 prospective Llama-128K inputs, the encoder transfers on 175. Total-norm matching loses 11 of those transfers and gains one elsewhere; positionwise matching loses ten and gains two; Q1 loses or gains none. The later Q2 follow-up loses two and gains none. In the earlier 165-input 9B common cohort, total-norm matching and Q1 both lose one encoder transfer despite different mean gaps.
location: Section 6.4; Appendices B.5–B.6, Table 6; Appendix D.2; Appendix E.6, Table 17

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Featurewise quantile calibration can substantially improve explanation-simulated activation replacements while trading higher specificity for lower sensitivity. Compares raw and quantile-normalized simulated activations. Raw predictions substantially overestimate activation strengths and yield much worse substitution loss. The authors report that normalization removes many false positives but also removes correctly predicted positive activations, increasing specificity and reducing sensitivity. Exact effect sizes are not tabulated in the supplied text.
Specific finding: The sample size and reference distribution used for featurewise quantile calibration can materially change downstream loss after simulated latent replacement. Appendix B reports greater activation-distribution mismatch and worse substitution loss with 1,000 prediction contexts than with 10,000. Using the evaluated prompts' own true-activation distribution improves results at both sample sizes; Section 4 reports performance better than zeroing for this variant. Evaluation samples also differ between sample-size conditions, and the same-prompt reference comparison does not establish independent held-out calibration performance.

Specific finding: Negative alignment between SAE feature directions can make a steering vector's apparent promotion of one feature compete with an interpretation as suppression of another feature. The source reports that feature 14004 activates strongly on negative corrigibility prompts but not positive prompts, yet receives zero activation when the steering vector is directly encoded. Feature 3517 rarely activates on either prompt class but activates in the vector decomposition. Their reported direction cosine is −0.82. This is a selected geometric and activation-pattern example; no feature-specific behavioral intervention distinguishes the competing interpretations.
models_studied: ["Gemma 2 2B instruction-tuned", "Gemma Scope layer-14 pretrained-model JumpReLU SAE, width 16,384, mean L0 173"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Low reconstruction error at a fixed sparse coding budget does not ensure that a visual SAE yields a substantial hierarchy under conditional-co-activation graph extraction. MP-SAE has the lowest reported FVU on CLIP, DINOv2, and Gemma: 0.0609, 0.1418, and 0.1450 respectively, compared with TopK's 0.1104, 0.2029, and 0.1920. Nevertheless, CCA graph construction yields no CLIP or DINOv2 graph and only a limited Gemma hierarchy, nonempty in two of three seeds and consisting of one parent group when present. A masked-cosine alternative produces a CLIP graph with abstractness 0.030, demonstrating graph-procedure dependence.
models_studied: ["MP-SAE and comparator SAEs on CLIP ViT-L/14", "MP-SAE and comparator SAEs on DINOv2-base", "MP-SAE and comparator SAEs on Gemma-4 E2B"]
location: Tables 2–4, 11 and 15; Appendices B.4 and C.1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Increasing an SAE encoder's capacity can produce nearly perfect in-distribution latent reconstruction while leaving reconstruction of a withheld latent combination incorrect. Appendix D.14 adds a 256-dimensional layer followed by a nonlinearity to the encoder in the Figure 3 toy setting. The text describes nearly perfect ID latent reconstruction but mapping of the withheld OOD plane onto training-observed supports. No aggregate numerical score or repeated-run uncertainty is supplied, and the plot images cannot be inspected in the supplied rendering.
models_studied: ["Higher-capacity SAE encoder on the three-latent synthetic toy"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Two finite-dimensional dot-product softmax predictors over the same vocabulary induce identical conditionals exactly when their effective embedding and centered-unembedding representations are related by compatible linear isomorphisms. Formal result: Theorem 5 and Appendix B.6 subtract a pivot token's log probability to eliminate softmax normalizers, construct effective-space maps using pseudoinverses, and establish equal effective dimensions through rank arguments. Proposition 4 proves the reverse implication through preserved centered logits. This is a characterization of exact predictors, not an empirical comparison or an approximate-identification guarantee.
Specific finding: Equal-width distribution-equivalent softmax predictors have linearly equivalent full representations when one predictor's context embeddings and centered unembeddings both span the ambient space. Formal result: Corollary 6 and Appendix B.7 extend earlier linear-identification results under weakened assumptions. Spanning centered token vectors determine an embedding map; spanning context vectors force invertibility and the inverse-transpose unembedding relation. Separate diversity of the second model and full span of pivot-centered context differences are not required.
location: Sections 3.2–3.3, Proposition 4 and Theorem 5; Appendices B.3–B.6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Many neurons previously written off as polysemantic have a simple unifying pattern behind their activating examples on closer inspection, so the prevalence of polysemanticity has been overestimated.

Specific finding: In Gemma-3-4B-IT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, selected SAE features associated with Assistant traits and identity are substantially more active during the tested roleplay personas than during the tested story generation. Gemma A-trait features have reported mean densities of 81.8% in Assistant and 56.6% in Roleplay, with near-ceiling features for every persona. Where Story measurements are reported, A-trait and A-nature densities are at most 2.2%, except L9 #2575 at 21.1%; Table 9 instead reports n/a for #3733 and #220. Llama's nine selected trait/identity features average 74.2% density in Assistant and 56.4% in Roleplay, versus 0–0.1% in Story. Under the relative mean-activation presence rule, and excluding unmatched 'you' features, Gemma Assistant–Roleplay intersections are 30/44/24 versus Assistant–Story 1/7/4; Llama gives 45/27/34 versus 0/2/4. These are within-document cross-model validation tests.
Specific finding: Shared selected SAE feature populations among the Assistant and four roleplay personas can shrink across progressively deeper residual-stream sites. The five-actor intersection contains 24/20/9 features at Gemma layers 9/17/22 and 45/17/10 at Llama layers 7/15/23. Four-persona intersections contain 34/30/12 and 57/38/22, respectively. The fraction of each layer's selected population present for an individual actor falls from 53–58% early to 26–35% late in Gemma, and from 42–57% early to 22–42% late in Llama.
Specific finding: In selected Gemma speaker-associated SAE populations, early Assistant operational effects coexist with increasing middle-layer tone effects and later concept-specific effects. Among 108/225/196 retained features, Tone counts are 5/48/36 and Concept counts are 2/24/42. Assistant-summoning features occur only at L9, with counts 4/0/0; trait-inducing features count 1/4/1 and identity-inducing features 3/1/1. Characterization uses 72 signed-steering generations per feature on a fixed 12-prompt suite. Tone and Concept effects also frequently transfer to Assistant probes, although the evaluation is restricted to selected features and prompts.
Specific finding: Adding selected early Gemma SAE directions can reinstate Assistant-like meta-commentary after a roleplay persona has already produced a response, when intervention includes part of a subsequent user turn. The authors test whether effects of L9 #3274, #14298, #17452, and #25147 persist after persona instantiation. Three candidates, excluding #14298, invoke Assistant-like commentary after an existing persona response. The effect is reported only when steering overlaps at least part of a later user turn. Trial counts and aggregate success rates are not supplied.
Specific finding: Filtered Gemma speaker-associated SAE directions and scale-matched isotropic random directions can have substantially different distributions of coherent steering effects, with Assistant-inducing effects absent from the tested random cohort. Of 50 isotropic Gaussian directions per layer, scaled using sampled real-feature peak activations, 36/30/20 pass the steering-consistency gate at L9/L17/L22. Among those gate-passing controls, 69%/77%/85% are labeled Indistinct, versus 26%/26%/21% among 108/225/196 retained SAE features. Narrative labels occur in 0%/3%/0% of gate-passing controls versus 25%/16%/15% of retained SAE features. No Assistant-inducing class or Narrative–Assistant antagonism is observed in the tested random population. These finite null observations do not establish impossibility for random directions.

Specific finding: Mean residual activations associated with diverse elicited roles can concentrate most between-role variation in a relatively small number of principal components. Generated 1,200 responses per role for 275 roles, separated fully and somewhat role-playing categories, and retained categories with at least ten responses. PCA of 448 Gemma, 463 Qwen, and 377 Llama role vectors required respectively 4, 8, and 19 components to explain 70% of between-role variance. The authors additionally report that persona-space components explain 19.4–33.6% of overall activation variance on 18,777 LMSYS-CHAT-1M Assistant responses.
Specific finding: Contrastive activation vectors for diverse elicited character traits can exhibit low-dimensional structure with a leading dimension separating broadly Assistant-associated traits from discouraged traits. Computed trait vectors by subtracting negatively elicited from positively elicited mean response activations after requiring sufficient expression-score differences. PCA retained 239 Gemma and 240 Qwen/Llama components. Four components in Gemma and Qwen, and seven in Llama, explained 70% of trait-vector variance. Pairwise cross-model PC1 trait-loading correlations exceeded 0.81. Leading traits were interpreted as regulated versus reactive or agreeable versus antagonistic; these semantic labels were not independently validated through trait-PC steering.

Specific finding: Feature visualizations of averaged natural activation vectors preserve enough of their represented visual content to support human interpretation of the underlying activation groups.
location: Looking at a Single Image; Aggregating Multiple Images

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Activation atlases of InceptionV1 show a qualitative progression from textures and simple patterns through shared visual concepts to more output-class-specific representations. Compared atlas visualizations across early, middle, and final convolutional layers. Selected cabbage-related regions become more specific across mixed3b, mixed4c, and mixed5b; sand and water appear separately in mixed4c and jointly in mixed5b. Additional selected regions show differentiation among mammals, people, foods, and clothing. Evidence consists of qualitative visual comparisons without a quantified hierarchy metric, representative feature census, or causal tracing between layers.

Specific finding: A byte-level mLSTM trained only to predict Amazon review text can learn a single unit whose final activation classifies IMDB review sentiment nearly as accurately as its full recurrent representation. A fitted threshold on one discovered unit achieves 92.30% IMDB test accuracy, compared with 92.88% using the full 4,096-unit representation. Activation histograms show separation between positive and negative reviews. Sequential visualizations show six randomly selected reviews from a set of 100 high-contrast reviews; these are a conditional qualitative illustration. The small readout-performance gap does not establish that no additional sentiment information exists elsewhere in the representation.
Specific finding: Fixing a sentiment-associated unit to opposite signs throughout generation can shift an Amazon-trained byte-level mLSTM's generated reviews toward positive or negative sentiment. Table 5 presents random generated samples under positive and negative unit clamping. Samples broadly follow the assigned polarity, but negative-clamped reviews can contain positive sentences. No quantitative sentiment evaluation, aggregate success rate, or comparison with clamping unrelated units is reported.
models_studied: ["Single-layer 4,096-unit byte-level mLSTM trained on Amazon reviews"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: An LSTM trained without author labels on a mixture of proposition-generating authors can encode author type sufficiently well for accurate linear decoding from a document prefix. A linear model recovered author identity with 98% accuracy from the LSTM's fifth-token representation on held-out synthetic articles. Separately, generated documents were classified as 31% A-consistent, 33% B-consistent, and 36% consistent only with O-type authors. Evaluation sample counts, uncertainty estimates, seed variability, and alternative decoding baselines are not reported.
Specific finding: Initializing a proposition-language-model LSTM with an author-conditioned mean hidden representation can bias its generation toward that author's proposition set. Fixing the initial hidden representation to the average representation from A-type articles caused generation of A-type propositions 89% of the time; the remaining samples were described as O-type. The source does not specify the evaluation count, variability, or a fully unambiguous proposition-versus-document denominator.
models_studied: ["512-dimensional LSTM language model trained on the synthetic incoherent encyclopedia"]
location: Section 2, Equation 1 and Evidence for C1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: During factual two-hop answering, last-position vocabulary readouts for intermediate answers can peak at earlier layers than readouts for final answers. Layerwise Logit Lens analyses compare intermediate- and final-answer token probabilities for compositional queries and corresponding second-hop queries. The authors report earlier intermediate-answer peaks in LLaMA-2. Supplementary OpenAlpaca results describe a less pronounced aggregate pattern because peak layers vary across examples. This establishes a readout pattern rather than uniquely identifying the underlying reasoning algorithm.
Specific finding: Hidden-state edits constructed to suppress intermediate-answer vocabulary readouts can reduce final-answer scores, with stronger reported middle-layer reduction signals than similarly constructed random-token controls. The intervention requests that intermediate-answer logits equal the pre-edit vocabulary minimum and maps the requested change back into hidden space using a pseudoinverse. Equally many random tokens form controls. Appendix D.1 additionally rechecks and adjusts immediate final-answer readout decreases. The authors report positive downstream reduction effects around layers 15–20 and little corresponding control signal. Figure 4 clips negative effects, min-max-normalizes across layers per example, and then averages; it therefore does not provide raw average effect magnitudes. Requested logit changes need not be exactly attainable through the unembedding.
Specific finding: Replacing last-position attention outputs with corresponding second-hop-reference outputs can improve correct-answer scores on failed compositional queries, with effects concentrated in selected middle-layer windows. The paper compares attention- and MLP-output replacements at last-input and last-subject positions using outputs from corresponding second-hop queries. The largest reported effects occur for last-position attention replacements near layers 18/19. Appendix D.3 specifies six-layer windows for Figure 5 and per-example effect normalization before averaging. These results identify intervention-sensitive windows, without uniquely localizing intermediate-answer generation to one head or layer.

Specific finding: Subtracting a source mod-10 direction and adding a target mod-10 direction can change successor-head predictions while preserving the ordinal domain. Scaled feature substitution succeeds in 53% of month cases and 89% of cases for numbers 20–29 when the target residue exceeds the source residue. Downward edits often fail, and days and letters cannot be steered successfully.

Specific finding: SAE feature-coverage saturation adjusted by sample count per distinct feature can correlate with benchmark redundancy measured through preservation of checkpoint rankings. Feature redundancy is coverage-curve AUC multiplied by N/|F(D)|. Its Spearman correlation with the average random-subset Kendall ranking-agreement metric is approximately 0.85 across 17 knowledge, mathematics, code, multilingual, and in-context-reasoning benchmarks. The feature-extraction backbone and layer are unspecified. Extraction requires backbone forward passes even though it avoids scoring a model panel.
Specific finding: Min-normalized overlap between benchmark SAE feature footprints can correlate with similarity between benchmark score vectors, including after linear adjustment for MMLU scores. Across 28 benchmark pairs, feature overlap correlates with performance-based Pearson similarity at Pearson 0.684 and Spearman 0.607. After benchmark-score correlations are adjusted for MMLU, these associations are 0.755 and 0.713. Reported asymmetric GSM8K-to-MATH feature coverage is 0.63, versus 0.10 in reverse. These measurements do not test whether dropping GSM8K preserves evaluation quality.

Specific finding: Frozen features from a supervised ImageNet CNN enable substantially better small-sample Caltech classification than training the evaluated CNN from scratch on Caltech. On Caltech-101 with 30 training images per class, Table 4 reports mean per-class accuracy of 86.5 ± 0.5% with ImageNet pretraining versus 46.5 ± 1.7% from scratch; the protocol uses five folds and up to 50 test images per class. The 86.5% result exceeds Table 4's highest listed prior result, 84.3%, by 2.2 percentage points, although the prose attributes that margin to a different comparator. On Caltech-256 with 60 training images per class, Table 5 reports 74.2 ± 0.3% versus 38.8 ± 1.4% from scratch and 55.2 ± 0.3% for Bo et al. Gains also appear at the smaller reported training budgets. Figure 9 reports surpassing Bo et al.'s 60-images-per-class result using six training images per class. The authors remove 44 overlapping Caltech-101 images and 243 overlapping Caltech-256 images from ImageNet training before retraining the source models.
Specific finding: A frozen ImageNet CNN with a newly trained exclusive softmax can perform competitively on PASCAL VOC 2012 while scoring below the leading comparator on the reported mean and exceeding it on selected classes. Table 6 reports a mean classification score of 79.0 for the transferred CNN versus 82.2 for Yan et al. and 74.3 for Sande et al.; the table labels its scores as accuracy percentages. The transferred CNN wins five of twenty classes. The authors identify the exclusive prediction format as a mismatch for multi-object images and suggest dataset bias as a possible explanation; neither explanation is isolated experimentally.
Specific finding: Higher layers of an ImageNet-pretrained CNN generally provide more discriminative frozen features for Caltech linear classification, although performance need not improve at every layer transition. Linear SVM accuracy increases from layer 1 to layer 5 from 44.8 ± 0.7% to 86.2 ± 0.8% on Caltech-101 and from 24.6 ± 0.4% to 65.6 ± 0.3% on Caltech-256. Layer 7 reaches 71.7 ± 0.2% on Caltech-256 but 85.5 ± 0.4% on Caltech-101, slightly below layer 5. Softmax accuracy improves from layer 5 to layer 7 on both datasets: 82.9% to 85.4% and 65.7% to 72.6%, respectively. Table 7's softmax results differ from the headline transfer tables without explanation in the supplied text.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A BiLSTM trained to classify first-letter agreement between strings can retain decodable information about an auxiliary character inserted independently of the task. The Noise condition uses 20,000/5,000/5,000 main-task examples and a separate 23,732/5,000/5,000 probing dataset. Section 5.2 reports above-chance c-presence recovery throughout the tested probe-capacity settings. Appendix A's unsuppressed 200-unit BiLSTM obtains 100% main-task accuracy and 90.30% held-out attacker accuracy on Noise, against a 50.20% attacker majority baseline.
Specific finding: Gradient-reversal training can reduce a training adversary's auxiliary-character accuracy to approximately chance while leaving the character highly recoverable by a separately trained attacker. Appendix A evaluates gradient-reversal weights 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, and 5 against an unsuppressed baseline. In Noise at λ=1, main-task accuracy is 100%, adversary accuracy is 49.43%, and independent-attacker accuracy is 94.50% against its 50.20% majority baseline. Every reported positive-weight Noise setting leaves attacker accuracy above 94%. A separate adversary-capacity sweep can reduce attacker accuracy, with effects dependent on the condition and capacity.

Specific finding: At the tested intervention norms, general-misalignment steering vectors can alter FineWeb next-token distributions more than narrow-misalignment or random vectors. The authors steer with general, narrow, and random vectors across norms and measure output-distribution KL on FineWeb. Section 3.2.2 and Figure 6 report greater divergence for general misalignment. Sample counts, numerical effect sizes, and repeated-run uncertainty are absent from the supplied prose.

Specific finding: Activation-weighted token-ID entropy can reveal differences between trained and randomized transformer SAE latents that aggregate explanation AUROC obscures. Computed entropy after aggregating latent activation by token ID over the maximally activating examples used to generate explanations. Entropy increased across layers for trained models, while randomized variants tended toward lower entropy and token-specific latents. Pythia-6.9B scatter plots additionally showed trained-model latents with both high entropy and high fuzzing AUROC; randomized variants showed a stronger negative relationship between entropy and AUROC. The fresh-noise control had high entropy but poor explanation scores, so entropy alone does not establish abstraction.
location: Section 3, Latent explanation complexity; Figure 2; Appendix H, Figure 20

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Cosine similarity between normalized concept-predictor coefficient vectors provides a useful proxy for semantic relationships among concepts in a fixed neural representation.

Specific finding: Concept embeddings learned from segmentation and classification can organize the same visual concepts into different semantic neighborhoods. Nearest-neighbor examples place dog near cat and horse in segmentation space and near muzzle and paw in classification space. Comparisons of concept-similarity matrices over 501 shared concepts indicate that classification embeddings are more aligned with WordNet and Word2Vec than segmentation embeddings. Selected vector arithmetic examples yield semantically suggestive neighbors, including sky for grass + blue − green, without an aggregate analogy-accuracy evaluation. The main text also describes t-SNE and clustering results whose supplementary displays are not supplied.
models_studied: ["ImageNet-trained AlexNet", "Places365-trained AlexNet", "ImageNet-trained VGG16", "Places365-trained VGG16", "ImageNet-trained GoogLeNet", "Places365-trained GoogLeNet", "Self-supervised AlexNet variants: tracking, audio, objectcentric, moving, egomotion"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: An averaged late-minus-intermediate hidden-state difference can shift selected Swallow intermediate vocabulary readouts from English toward Japanese. The authors average layer-40-minus-layer-26 hidden-state differences across 30 synonym-pair examples and add the vector to layer-26 states. Section 5.4 reports that leading tokens change from English to Japanese, illustrated in Figure 6. The accompanying discussion of Figure 7 reports that substantial changes in the averaged vector are concentrated in sparse coordinates, without a numerical sparsity criterion or per-example analysis.

Specific finding: For a single attention head, an additive feature term shared across source positions contributes along a fixed OV-transformed direction, scaled by its attention-weighted source coefficients. Formal distributive expansion in Corollary B.3, Equations 18–21: sum_j a_ij A h_j = (sum_j a_ij alpha_j)A d_f + sum_j a_ij A eta_j. Attention weights can be input-dependent; the identity accounts for the given forward pass rather than holding them fixed under arbitrary interventions.

Specific finding: Endpoint gradient-based attribution can assign zero importance to a changed input feature even when that feature causes a nonzero baseline-to-input output difference. Formal counterexample supplied here: f(x)=1−ReLU(1−x), baseline 0, and input 2. The output changes from 0 to 1, while the derivative at 2 is zero. Thus endpoint gradient attribution and its product with the input give zero attribution, violating Sensitivity(a). This is an analytic construction, not an empirical experiment.

Specific finding: Endpoint gradient-based attribution can assign zero importance to a changed input feature even when that feature causes a nonzero baseline-to-input output difference. Analytical counterexample supplied in the saturation toy network: input gradients vanish when the input sum exceeds the saturation threshold, although the output differs from its all-zero-reference value. The example establishes possible failure of endpoint derivatives to allocate a finite output difference; it is not an empirical prevalence measurement.

Specific finding: Approximating a network only near the explained input does not guarantee nonzero attribution to a sole feature whose change from a baseline changes the output.
Specific finding: DeepLift and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation can produce different input attributions for functionally equivalent network implementations.

Specific finding: Economic cost-sharing constructions provide an axiomatic framework for neural input attribution, with path-integrated gradients satisfying implementation invariance, dummy-feature sensitivity, linearity, and completeness.

Specific finding: For a differentiable downstream function, the sum of coordinatewise path-integrated hidden-activation attributions equals the output difference between the path endpoints. Formal derivation in Appendix B: summing the coordinatewise path integrals gives the ordinary line integral of the downstream gradient, equal to F(a1)-F(a0), assuming the required pathwise differentiation and integration conditions. For the straight path from zero to A(x), the sum is V(x)-F(0). This is a mathematical identity, not an empirical experiment. The implementation approximates the integral at ten points, alpha=0.1 through 1.0, without a numerical-error bound.
location: Appendix B: Integrated gradients for a hidden layer

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Edge attribution patching with input integrated gradients can recover compact task circuits more effectively on average than plain attribution, node attribution, or similarity-based information flow methods. EAP-IG-inputs leads on average across CPR and CMD. On Qwen IOI its CMD is 0.02 versus 0.15 for EAP and 0.69 for IFR. It is not uniformly best; exact patching leads GPT-2 IOI CMD, and activation IG leads semi-synthetic edge AUROC at 0.81.

Specific finding: Integrated-gradients approximations improve estimates of SAE-feature and reconstruction-error indirect effects where first-order attribution patching underestimates intervention effects. Approximate and exact effects are compared for SAE features and errors at individual token positions across 30 inputs. Ten-step integrated gradients improves the plotted agreement over attribution patching; numerical aggregate error metrics are not reported in the supplied text.

Specific finding: EAP-IG circuit extraction can produce substantially different edge sets when the discovery dataset is bootstrap-resampled. The complete discovery pipeline is rerun on 100 datasets sampled with replacement. Table 1 reports aggregate pairwise Jaccard mean 0.561 with CV 0.335 and circuit-error mean 0.440 with CV 0.123. Table 4 reports IOI Jaccard means of 0.67, 0.39, and 0.34 for GPT-2 Small, Llama base, and Llama Instruct respectively. Original dataset sizes are unspecified. Table 4 contains eight model–task rows and omits GPT-2 Small Greater-Than.
Specific finding: Changing the EAP-family estimator, score aggregation, or patching baseline can substantially alter a discovered circuit's edge set while leaving its measured prediction-disagreement rate similar. In Llama Instruct Greater-Than, seven configurations produce circuit sizes of 10–33 and Jaccard-to-median values as low as 0.086; six configurations have circuit error 0.19–0.20, while positional-mean patching has 0.41. In IOI, clean–corrupted estimation has Jaccard-to-median 0.071 and error 0.69. These overlaps are relative to the reported median circuit across configurations, not direct pairwise overlaps between named methods. Tables 8 and 9 provide additional model comparisons, with incomplete task coverage.
Specific finding: The evaluated newly generated dataset and prompt-paraphrase regimes can produce greater EAP-IG circuit overlap than bootstrap resampling of the original discovery dataset. Table 1 reports aggregate Jaccard means of 0.790 for meta-dataset sampling and 0.799 for paraphrasing, versus 0.561 for bootstrap; circuit-error means are 0.300, 0.150, and 0.440 respectively. Tables 4–6 give GPT-2 Small IOI Jaccard means of 0.67, 0.88, and 0.89 for bootstrap, meta-dataset, and paraphrase regimes. Tables 4 and 5 contain eight model–task rows each, while Table 6 contains five and excludes SVA. Sample sizes are not supplied, limiting interpretation of the aggregate comparison.

Specific finding: IOI circuits extracted from different query variants and dataset-averaged capability scores can share nontrivial edge subsets despite substantial variation in their full edge sets. At a 500-edge budget, the illustrated capability circuit and six query-derived circuits share 66 edges; another 23 edges are absent only from the original-query-derived circuit. Capability scores average 1,000 IOI queries. Appendix C.11 reports mean Jaccard similarities around 0.3 and 30–50% of query-circuit edges appearing in the capability circuit. Further randomly selected examples are described as sharing substantial edge subsets, although the prose says five additional examples and the captions enumerate four. These overlap tests do not rule out coincidental score matching or establish causal importance of the shared subset.

Specific finding: Attribution-derived layerwise steering can improve TruthfulQA, Toxigen, and FaithEval multiple-choice accuracy over the unsteered model, while its advantage over LoRA and other steering methods depends on the model and task. Table 1 reports Llama base→GrAInS accuracies of 34.15→47.37 on TruthfulQA, 51.19→60.98 on Toxigen, and 68.00→70.94 on FaithEval; Qwen scores are 51.41→59.85, 55.04→62.12, and 59.89→64.77. GrAInS exceeds the listed baselines in five of six model–task cells; Qwen FaithEval LoRA scores 64.96. Toxigen values and gain descriptions differ elsewhere in the text. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
Specific finding: Attribution-derived steering can increase the fraction of visual safety-preference pairs for which a model assigns higher likelihood to the supplied chosen response than to the rejected response. Table 2 reports chosen>rejected rates increasing from 40.24% to 48.35% for LLaVA, 53.21% to 58.90% for Qwen-VL, and 49.32% to 53.51% for Gemma, exceeding all listed baselines in those cells. Table 16 reports 76.2% for Qwen-VL-72B versus 73.6% unsteered and 74.0% CAA on 500 evaluation examples. No statistical uncertainty is supplied.
Specific finding: Attribution-derived steering can reduce judged multimodal hallucination rates relative to unsteered models without uniformly outperforming the evaluated fine-tuning baseline. Table 2 reports hallucination rates of 0.624→0.514 for LLaVA, 0.523→0.473 for Qwen-VL, and 0.468→0.442 for Gemma. GrAInS has the lowest three-model mean, 0.476, but Qwen-VL LoRA is lower at 0.461. Section 4.2 reports GPT-4o/human correlations of Pearson 0.82 and Spearman 0.85 using nine annotators; rated-example count and aggregation details are unspecified.
Specific finding: Selected attribution-derived steering configurations can improve reference-based generation preference metrics while leaving five-shot MMLU and MMMU accuracy close to unsteered scores. Five-shot MMLU changes from 69.27% to 69.15% for Llama and 74.58% to 74.29% for Qwen. MMMU changes from 35.81% to 34.92% for LLaVA and 58.64% to 58.13% for Qwen-VL. Positive-over-negative reference BLEU accuracy increases on TruthfulQA from 38.19% to 47.91% and 47.65% to 54.09%, and on SPA-VL from 42.38% to 46.79% and 49.17% to 53.02%. LLaVA SPA-VL BLEU accuracy remains below LoRA and ICT. No equivalence tests or uncertainty estimates are supplied.
Specific finding: Attribution-derived steering vectors constructed on one dataset can improve selected target-dataset metrics for the same broad behavioral attribute. Table 5 reports RTP toxicity of 1.15 with GrAInS versus 4.18 unsteered, 3.35 with ICV, and 2.89 with CAA; the score's scale and evaluator are not specified. Table 6 reports POPE adversarial accuracy/F1 of 84.06/80.44 versus 79.85/76.82 unsteered, 83.54/79.63 with VTI, and 80.71/77.14 with CAA. Evaluation counts, target-dataset tuning details, and uncertainty are not provided.

Specific finding: Similarity between decision-task and self-report-task adapter attributions can distinguish populations of faithful and unfaithful character-preference reporters. For 32 matched character pairs, selection requires early-backbone faithfulness below 0.3, late-backbone faithfulness above 0.9, valid JSON in at least 90% of reports, and decision performance at least 0.9 for both models. Characters are absent from backbone training; each pair shares data, initialization, and hyperparameters. Seven-step integrated gradients average 50 inputs per task and compare concatenated site/output-dimension vectors. The loss is full-model-to-scaled-model vocabulary KL at the decision position or report numeric spans and termination positions. Mean cosine similarity is 0.34 versus 0.08, with group SDs 0.26 and 0.10 and paired-bootstrap difference CI [0.16,0.36]. Ten randomly selected pairs without filters retain a late-minus-early backbone-group gap of 0.21, CI [0.09,0.33]. Integration-step checks yield comparable gaps from four steps onward.
Specific finding: Faithful character-preference adapters can recover their effects on one task using substantially fewer matrices selected by attribution on the other task than unfaithful adapters. Matrices are ranked by summed attribution from decisions or reports, with the most negative scores identifying the most important matrices. Only the top k matrices remain active during opposite-task evaluation, while the backbone stays fully active. Recovery is 1−D_KL(full||partial)/D_KL(full||backbone). Faithful adapters reportedly require 8–12 times fewer matrices for a given recovery fraction; the prose does not specify the recovery fractions underlying this range. Random matrix selection also recovers more for faithful adapters, so the result does not isolate attribution-specific shared representations from broader adapter compactness or backbone differences.
Specific finding: Within a fixed preference-trained model, character-specific decision–report attribution similarity can correlate weakly with self-report faithfulness. Decision and report attribution vectors are computed separately for each of 100 characters within the same early backbone. Attribution cosine similarity correlates with per-character faithfulness at Pearson r=0.197, bootstrap 95% CI [0.006,0.375]. The small effect and barely positive lower interval limit its value as standalone validation.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A zero hidden-activation baseline provides a sufficiently meaningful reference for interpreting signed value-function attributions as good or bad news about future success.

Specific finding: Integrated Gradients can highlight distinctive image features more clearly than endpoint gradient-times-image attribution in selected GoogLeNet predictions. The authors attribute each selected image's highest-scoring class to input pixels using a black baseline, aggregate over color channels, and compare IG visualizations with gradient-times-image. They qualitatively report clearer distinctive features, including the fireboat example. No evaluation denominator, independent explanation labels, or aggregate metric is reported.
Specific finding: Attributing output-token probabilities to source embeddings with Integrated Gradients can yield intuitive source–target wordpiece alignments in an LSTM translation system. The authors attribute each translated output wordpiece's probability to input tokens, zeroing source-token embeddings except start/end markers for the baseline. Figure 5 translates 'good morning ladies and gentlemen' into German and shows intuitive associations such as 'und' with 'and' and 'morgen' with 'morning'. They use 100–1000 integration steps because of network nonlinearity; no aggregate alignment accuracy is reported.
Specific finding: Identical Integrated Gradients allocations to atoms with different neighborhoods can reveal architectural degeneracy in a molecular graph-convolution network. Attribution inspection found several atoms receiving identical allocations despite different bonded neighbors. Follow-up architectural inspection found that atom and atom-pair features were not fully convolved, causing atoms with the same type and bond-type counts to contribute identically. The text does not report sample counts or a controlled repair experiment.
Specific finding: Integrated Gradients can expose recognizable answer-type cues and potentially undesirable lexical associations in a trained question classifier. Qualitative token-attribution examples using an all-zero embedding baseline highlight 'how many' and 'total number' for numeric answers and identify 'charles' as a cue for a yes/no prediction. No number of evaluated questions, aggregate explanation metric, or measured improvement after rule extraction is reported.
Specific finding: Integrated Gradients for a diabetic-retinopathy network can concentrate around apparent retinal lesions, with positive boundary and negative interior contributions in an inspected image. Using a black baseline, the authors aggregate pixel IG over color channels and overlay signed attributions on a retinal image. Figure 3 includes human annotations of visible lesions; the discussion reports negative lesion-interior and positive peripheral attributions. No aggregate lesion-overlap score, clinical evaluation, or user study is supplied.
Specific finding: Integrated Gradients can partition a molecular graph-convolution prediction into signed contributions from bonded and other atom-pair features. The authors zero atom and atom-pair feature vectors for the baseline and visualize their signed IG contributions. For the molecule in Figure 6, bonded atom-pair features cumulatively contribute 46% of the prediction score, while other pairs contribute −3%. These are reported attribution totals for one example, without an independent ground-truth explanation or aggregate evaluation.

Specific finding: Separating positive and negative contributions can allocate nonzero credit to both inputs of a minimum operation when Rescale and straight-line Integrated Gradients allocate all credit to the smaller input.
location: Section 3.5.3; Figure 3; detailed calculations referenced to Appendix C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Using RevealCancel at a fully connected layer can recover positive attribution to conjunction-relevant DNA motifs that Rescale, Integrated Gradients, and gradient-times-input sometimes miss. The multitask CNN is evaluated using each test sequence's five strongest matches per motif. Figure 5b measures the proportion of strong TAL1 matches in both-motif sequences receiving total conjunction-task attribution at most zero. RevealCancel variants have no reported false negatives under this criterion, whereas gradient-times-input, Integrated Gradients, and Rescale occasionally miss relevance. Exact comparator rates and test-set size are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: RevealCancel attribution can identify pixels whose erasure produces a larger target-versus-original class log-odds increase than the compared backpropagation attribution methods. Methods rank pixels by original-class minus target-class attribution and erase up to approximately 20% of the image. Figure 4 reports target-versus-original log-odds increases for 1,000 test images belonging to the original class, illustrating 8-to-3 and 8-to-6 conversions, and the text reports RevealCancel outperforming the compared backpropagation methods.
