Integrated Gradients using five or ten midpoint intervals performs comparably to gradient-times-input. Numerical aggregate advantages and uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
models_studied: ["Simulated regulatory-DNA multitask CNN with two convolutional layers, global average pooling, and one fully connected layer"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Finite-difference Rescale attribution can propagate nonzero baseline-relative credit through saturated nonlinearities and avoid the gradient-times-input jump at a biased ReLU threshold. Formal calculations in Section 3.5.2 use finite output/input differences to propagate a nonzero importance signal in the saturated toy network. For ReLU(x − 10) at x = 10 + epsilon, Rescale assigns epsilon to the input, whereas gradient-times-input assigns 10 + epsilon with a compensating −10 bias contribution. These are explicit toy calculations, not trained-model experiments.

Specific finding: Averaging Integrated Gradients or Guided Backpropagation maps across Gaussian-perturbed inputs can improve their visual coherence. The authors apply the SmoothGrad averaging procedure to Integrated Gradients and Guided Backpropagation and report improved visual coherence in Figure 7. No numerical evaluation or uncertainty estimate is provided.
Specific finding: Averaging input-gradient maps over Gaussian-perturbed images can produce more visually coherent sensitivity maps than vanilla gradients or Integrated Gradients. The authors visually inspect maps for 200 randomly sampled images and report consistently greater coherence for SmoothGrad than vanilla gradients and Integrated Gradients. Separate perturbation sweeps suggest useful Inception noise levels around 10–20% of the input pixel-value range and little apparent visual change beyond 50 samples. No quantitative coherence score or controlled human study is reported.

Specific finding: Using full-vocabulary output-distribution KL as a circuit-discovery objective does not ensure that the resulting sparse circuit reproduces the model's incorrect candidate choices. ACDC and EAP-IG use full-vocabulary answer-position KL objectives on IOI and Docstring; Edge Pruning uses KL plus sparsity on IOI. Under IOI mean ablation, ACDC, EAP-IG-KL, and Edge Pruning reproduce 11.8%, 41.7%, and 11.4% of errors while preserving 97.3%, 99.1%, and 98.3% of correct choices. EAP-IG and Edge Pruning checkpoints are selected using a validation-resample normalized-faithfulness threshold of 0.85, rather than error agreement. Evaluation with learned KL-optimal replacement constants also leaves large IOI gaps. Docstring results are heterogeneous, including higher error than correct agreement for EAP-IG under mean and resample replacement.
Specific finding: Substantial representation of model errors in circuit-discovery data does not ensure comparable exact agreement on the model's correct and incorrect answers. The six MIB discovery splits contain 187–849 errors, constituting 4.9–41.1% of their examples. Gemma ARC-Challenge includes 430 errors among 1,119 discovery examples, or 38.4%, yet its 1%-edge circuit achieves 80.3% correct agreement and 54.4% exact-error agreement on the public test split, which contains 349 correct and 237 incorrect full-model predictions. The source describes persistent gaps across most budgets; numerical values from unseen plots are not inferred.

Specific finding: Previously selected BoN circuits can be reused to construct circuits at intermediate edge budgets without additional model forward passes for construction, while retaining better reported NDF frontiers than the tested single-query and score-averaging baselines. Algorithms A1–A2 specify edge-set construction from previously discovered circuits and stored scores without additional model calls for construction. The text accompanying Figure 6 and supplementary MMLU and larger-model evaluations reports iBoN and BoN-CSM below BoN but above both baselines. iBoN is evaluated at intermediate budgets different from the BoN anchor budgets. No numerical end-to-end speedup for these reuse variants is supplied.
location: Sections 5.3–5.4 and 6.2; Appendix B; Appendices C.3 and C.5

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Cross-layer transcoders can improve reconstruction, sparsity, and circuit parsimony relative to per-layer transcoders and thresholded neurons. Dictionary-size sweeps compare MSE, L0, Sort Eval, Contrastive Eval, output agreement, and graph metrics. The 10M-feature 18L CLT attains approximately 11.5% normalized reconstruction error and L0 88; the 30M-feature Haiku CLT attains 21.7% and L0 235. Cost-matched comparisons favor CLTs on several metrics but do not establish a universal interpretability Pareto advantage.
location: Quantitative CLT Evaluations; Attribution Graph Evaluation; Efficiency relative to alternatives

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Cross-layer transcoders can preserve more supervised family-classification and fitness-prediction performance than independently trained per-layer transcoders when both receive original-model attention outputs. For ESM2-8M, full CLT versus PLT mean family F1 is 0.82 ± 0.19 versus 0.50 ± 0.34, and fitness Spearman is 0.41 ± 0.19 versus 0.38 ± 0.18. For ESM2-35M, corresponding values are 0.94 ± 0.07 versus 0.69 ± 0.28 and 0.46 ± 0.20 versus 0.38 ± 0.19. Main family plots select families with over 50 sequences; fitness plots retain settings with original-model Spearman at least 0.01. The source does not supply significance tests or complete aggregation denominators.
location: Section 3.1; Appendices D.1–D.2, E.1, and G.1–G.2

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Global acausal crosscoders can achieve lower summed reconstruction-plus-sparsity loss than independent per-layer SAEs at a fixed total dictionary size while requiring more training compute to reach the same loss. Compared one all-layer acausal crosscoder with 18 independently trained SAEs across feature-count and training-step sweeps. Crosscoders had lower evaluation loss at matched total dictionary size, but reaching the same loss required approximately twice the training FLOPs at large compute budgets. Loss summed MSE and decoder-norm-weighted L1 penalties across layers.
Specific finding: Sharing sparse feature coefficients across layers can improve whole-model reconstruction error versus active-feature count relative to independently coding each layer. Measured MSE and global L0 at configurations selected for optimal training loss across training-FLOP budgets. Crosscoders produced a substantially better whole-model MSE–L0 tradeoff than independent SAEs. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the text.

Specific finding: Cross-layer transcoders can yield protein continuations with lower original-model-scored NLL than matched-width and matched-sparsity per-layer transcoders under assisted replacement. All-latent sequential CLT continuation NLL was 2.50 ± 0.42, compared with PLT 2.57 ± 0.36 and original-model generation 2.00 ± 0.62. Selected CLT circuits scored 2.54 ± 0.39 versus PLT circuits' 2.59 ± 0.36, using 719 ± 339 of 46,080 CLT latents. The source does not specify the meaning of the reported dispersion or provide significance-test details. NLL is scored by ProGen3 on generated regions, rather than measuring biological function or complete distributional agreement.
Specific finding: Cross-layer transcoder replacements can preserve more average experimental-fitness rank correlation than per-layer replacements in selected protein fitness assays. Each split used 256 discovery mutants and 1,000 held-out mutants, each balanced by functional-bin label and sampled across mutation types. Mean Spearman correlation was 0.29 ± 0.15 for ProGen3, 0.28 ± 0.12 for all-latent sequential CLT, and 0.25 ± 0.12 for all-latent sequential PLT. Selected CLT circuits achieved 0.23 ± 0.13 using 256 ± 334 latents, versus PLT circuits' 0.22 ± 0.12. Circuit-size selection uses discovery-set experimental fitness correlations. No inferential comparison is supplied.

Specific finding: For a selected prompt, cross-layer transcoders and affine skip connections can reduce the number of latent nodes needed to cover a given fraction of attribution-graph influence. Section 4.4 reports greater cumulative influence coverage for a given prefix of latent nodes with CLTs than single-layer transcoders, and improvements from affine skips for both architectures. Figure 5's caption identifies one Gemma 3 1B IT prompt. No numerical values, prompt-panel denominator, or uncertainty estimates are supplied.

Specific finding: Matching a model's layer activations with a crosscoder abstraction, including by retaining reconstruction-error features, does not by itself establish that the abstraction preserves the model's causal mechanisms.
location: Section 5.2; conceptual discussion without a new intervention test or formal proof

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Crosscoder features with early encoders and downstream decoders may simplify circuit descriptions by consolidating persistent representations and bypassing chains of identity connections.

Specific finding: Input-conditioned transcoders may describe corrective computations more directly than output-only sparse autoencoders, while cross-layer decoding may jointly describe a proposal and its subsequent correction.
Specific finding: Skip-transcoders and cross-layer transcoders may make multi-step computations distributed across language-model layers easier to decipher.
location: What's new in Gemma Scope 2: More refined tools to decipher complex internal behaviors

experiment_summary: Specific finding: High-cosine matches between Geneformer's layer-zero SAE decoder directions and later-layer dictionaries can become increasingly rare with layer distance. Of 4,608 layer-zero features, 114 match layer 1, 67 match layer 4, ten match layer 8, one matches layer 10, and none match layer 12 or later. The text additionally reports much lower annotation rates among moderately persistent than transient layer-zero features. Persistence is defined by dictionary geometry rather than validated semantic or causal identity.

Specific finding: Adjacent-layer SAE activation matching can reveal persistent feature chains while leaving a majority of features without sufficiently correlated counterparts, especially at later depths. The layerwise matching analysis reports appearing/disappearing fractions above half, increasing to approximately 80% in later layers under the respective counterpart criteria. Table 1 supplies a selected panic-associated chain spanning layers 0–5, with adjacent Pearson correlations from 0.96 to 0.99. The 0.95 threshold was calibrated through interactive judgments of feature meanings using GPT-3.5 explanations; no independent semantic-equivalence benchmark is supplied.
Specific finding: Upstream SAE features lacking downstream activation matches can show little evidence of preservation when the next layer's reconstruction error is projected onto their original decoder directions. The authors compare upstream feature activations with projections of next-layer SAE reconstruction errors onto upstream decoder directions over 10M tokens and report no evidence of recovery. The activation-selection threshold is inconsistent: Figure 4 states greater than 0.1% of maximum, whereas Appendix J specifies at least 10%. No numerical recovery statistic is supplied in the readable text, and preservation in a different direction is not tested by this projection.

Specific finding: Composing cross-layer SAE feature permutations can approximate direct matching for nearby layers, with description agreement deteriorating as the traversed layer distance increases. Direct assignments from three starting layers to subsequent layers are compared with composed permutations using DIFFERENT/MAYBE/SAME description judgments. Composition is reported to work adequately nearby, particularly in later layers, and to diverge over longer paths. Agreement is assessed through descriptions rather than equality of permutation matrices or native mechanisms.

Specific finding: A shared dictionary factor can retain sufficiently comparable linguistic meaning across transformer layers for changes in its coefficient to track the development of that representation.
location: Section 2, shared-dictionary motivation and importance-score interpretation

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected shared-dictionary factors in BERT-base show a layerwise progression from early lexical disambiguation to later sentence-level and extended-context patterns. Compares layerwise importance scores, defined as the mean of the 1,000 largest coefficients, and top-activating contexts. Selected word-level factors peak earlier, while selected sentence-level and extended-context factors peak later. Brown-corpus “left” activation comparisons and top-200 sentence-pattern checks provide quantitative examples of increasing selectivity. Appendix A illustrates importance curves for 16 low-level and 16 mid-level factors. Some pattern rates fluctuate across later layers, and importance curves alone do not distinguish sentence-level from extended-context factors. No representative factor census or causal test of hierarchical composition is reported.
location: Sections 2–3; Figures 2–6 and 9; Tables 2–3; Appendix A

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Features retained from a routed multilayer TopK dictionary can receive higher sampled GPT-4o activation-consistency ratings than features retained from the evaluated single-layer, uniform-routing, and Crosscoder dictionaries. GPT-4o rates RouteSAE's sampled features above 4.4 across the reported sparsity settings. TopK declines from above 4.0 at k=48 to approximately 3.7 at k=72, while Crosscoder remains near 3.9. Uniform routing scores below RouteSAE but above the other comparators. The headline reports a 22.3% score increase at k=64 without resolving its exact comparator. The authors describe the scores as indicative because feature sampling and evaluator scoring are stochastic.
Specific finding: Learned multilayer routing with a shared TopK dictionary can retain more features meeting strong-activation context criteria than the evaluated single-layer SAE baselines. After approximately 100 million OpenWebText2 training tokens, the reported threshold-15 comparisons give over 4,000 retained RouteSAE features, over 3,000 TopK features, over 1,000 ReLU and Gated features, and approximately 200 features from the implemented Crosscoder. Feature counts vary with sparsity and threshold. The headline reports a 22.5% increase at k=64 without clearly identifying its exact comparator in prose. No repeated-training uncertainty estimates are supplied.
Specific finding: A routed-layer SAE replacement pipeline can yield lower output-distribution KL than the evaluated fixed-layer and uniform-routing SAE replacement pipelines at comparable latent sparsity. The sparsity-versus-KL sweep reports RouteSAE as the best evaluated replacement pipeline, below TopK and uniform routing at comparable sparsity. TopK and RouteSAE remain below 150 on the reported KL scale, whereas ReLU and Gated are described as approximately 350–400. These values are stated in the source prose; their aggregation convention is not supplied. No uncertainty estimates or fixed-replacement-site routing control are reported.

Specific finding: Ablating features exclusive to a next-token-logit attribution graph can frequently change the immediate top-1 prediction while producing comparatively small changes in an internal concept-probe score. Using the reported 50-prompt-per-concept causal analysis, Gemma logit-exclusive ablations yield 100% top-token flips for toxicity, sentiment, and truthfulness and 92% for reasoning, with absolute probe-score changes of 0.70, 0.39, 0.03, and 0.53 respectively. Llama reports 100% flips for all four concepts and absolute score changes between 0.002 and 0.028. Graph-exclusive sets differ in size, and matched-size or matched-disruption controls are not reported. The feature-ablation implementation and handling of the intermediate probe measurement are not fully specified.
Specific finding: Ablating features exclusive to a probe-targeted attribution graph can substantially change the targeted internal readout while preserving the immediate top-1 next-token prediction. Appendix E reports 50 causal-dissociation prompts per concept. Gemma probe-exclusive ablations change toxicity scores by −61.24 and sentiment scores by −40.42 with 0% top-token flips; reasoning changes by +5.05 toward zero with 0% flips. Gemma truthfulness changes by −12.03 with 25% flips. Llama reports 0% flips for all four concepts, but truthfulness changes by only −0.001 at a layer with 55.2% probe accuracy. Llama sentiment changes from −0.47 to +2.40, an overshoot rather than the claimed reduction in magnitude. Several tabulated flip rates are inconsistent with a simple denominator of 50, and the discrepancy is unexplained.
location: Section 4.2; Tables 4 and 7; Appendices B.1, D.1, and E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Interpreted weakly causal crosscoder features provide sufficiently meaningful semantic coordinates for using QK/OV attribution terms to characterize attention-head computations.
location: Fuzzy Induction; subsequent feature-attribution case studies

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected ESM2 cross-layer-transcoder features can exhibit activation patterns and local attribution relationships consistent with known protein motifs and structural annotations. The authors compare selected latent activation locations with maximally activating Swiss-Prot examples and known structural annotations, and construct sequence-specific gradient-derived graphs. The accessible text describes residue-level, binding-related, and structural associations and activation changes in selected fitness examples. No representative semantic-accuracy benchmark or selective validation of the proposed pathways is supplied; the text also inconsistently identifies the layer of one hydrophobic-interaction latent.

Specific finding: Selected latents in a generative protein-model transcoder can exhibit activation patterns and attribution changes consistent with annotated motifs and functional regions. Qualitative inspection identified early residue-associated responses and later motif- or functional-region-associated responses. Two selected GRB2 fitness variants exhibited changes in attributed contributions consistent with published annotations. The paper's analyses use frozen-linearization attribution edges and existing experimental literature; they provide no representative annotation benchmark, matched null analysis, selective causal validation of the proposed pathways, or new laboratory experiment.

Specific finding: Small attribution-selected subsets of cross-layer-transcoder coordinates can retain substantial supervised protein-task performance under attention-assisted replacement. ESM2-8M family circuits attain mean F1 0.73 ± 0.19 versus original 0.92 ± 0.10 using 150 ± 204 coordinates from 19,200. Fitness circuits attain Spearman 0.38 ± 0.18 versus 0.50 ± 0.22 using 167 ± 221 coordinates. ESM2-35M circuits attain family F1 0.80 ± 0.12 versus 0.94 ± 0.07 using 109 ± 144 coordinates, and fitness Spearman 0.38 ± 0.19 versus 0.53 ± 0.23 using 202 ± 222. The latter counts would be approximately 0.19% and 0.35% of the stated 57,600-coordinate dictionary, whereas the source prints 2.2% and 4.2%. Search targets are capped by full-replacement performance, so attaining 70% of the original score is not guaranteed.
Specific finding: Sparse transcoder circuits can exceed original-representation probe performance on selected tasks where the original probe performs poorly. For ESM2-8M families selected with original F1 between 0.01 and 0.5, mean original F1 is 0.39 ± 0.04 and circuit F1 is 0.43 ± 0.27. Appendix E.2 reports that 37% of circuits exceed original fitness-probe correlations in the low-performance regime below 0.2; Appendix G.2 reports 40% for ESM2-35M in that regime. Counts and significance tests are absent. The ESM2-35M appendix's additional low-performing-family statistic inconsistently names ESM2-8M and is not used here.
Specific finding: A selected GFP fitness circuit can retain positive fitness-prediction correlation across mutation-depth strata, including variants with at least five substitutions. Tables 3–4 report positive circuit Spearman correlations in each mutation-depth bin: 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5+. At 5+, circuit versus original-probe correlations are 0.26 versus 0.35 for ESM2-8M and 0.25 versus 0.31 for ESM2-35M, approximately 74% and 81% recovery. Stratum sizes and uncertainty estimates are absent.

Specific finding: Selected cross-layer SAE feature groups can redirect Gemma country-fact answers by changing the country, the requested factual relation, or both. Zero source-country and/or source-relation groups and amplify target groups. Gemma 2 2B achieves reported concept, relation, and composite success rates of 96%, 93%, and 90%; Gemma 2 9B achieves 93%, 97%, and 92%. Evaluation uses 27 source prompts per target country, 20 per target relation, and 18 per target pair: 270, 60, and 540 transitions per model. Main-model strengths maximize measured success without a specified independent confirmation split. Accepted answers include aliases and some historical currencies.
Specific finding: Selected SAE feature groups in Gemma 2 2B can separately change a translated word or target language and can jointly redirect both attributes, with lower aggregate success for joint changes. Ablate the prompted word and/or language groups and amplify target groups using task-selected strengths. Table 2 reports 75% word steering, 98% language steering, and 64% composite steering. Word steering uses 30 source prompts per target word, and composite steering uses 20 per target word–language pair. Extraction uses few-shot templates and evaluation uses zero-shot question templates. Answer lists were refined after inspection of intermediate results; no independent strength-confirmation split is specified.
Specific finding: A modified coactivation-group procedure can identify transcoder feature groups that support some translation-language steering in Gemma 2 2B. Appendix M uses correlation threshold 0.7 and language-unique nodes from large overlapping components. Source-language ablation plus target-language amplification achieves 27% accuracy at selected strength 13. Manual inspection finds features also used in a cited language-intervention demonstration. Some outputs remain unchanged after ablating essentially all top-activated features; the proposed explanation involving reconstruction-error information is not separately tested. The reported threshold-search increment of 0.5 is inconsistent with the described threshold adjustment.
location: Section 3.2, Table 2; Appendix A, Tables 6–8; Appendices B.1, G, and I

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Promoting multiple flow-linked SAE features across layers can strengthen generated topic presence while reducing coherence, with effective intervention depth depending on the selected theme. The main promotion experiment compares single-layer addition with cumulative constant, linear, and exponential coefficient schedules, using 36-token completions from 'I think ', top-p 0.7, and temperature 1.27. GPT-4o-mini rates topic presence and coherence, whose product is the main score. Cumulative methods generally strengthen topic signal but can damage coherence; schedules are manually calibrated using test completions. A supplementary research-methodology experiment using the physics prompt finds its best tested intervention at layer 5, outside the initial feature layers, under manually chosen settings. Generation counts and numerical plot values are unavailable; the supplementary figure caption inconsistently labels the product's second factor as Cumulative.
Specific finding: Flow-graph-selected feature interventions can improve physics-theme suppression scores over the initial feature set, with cumulative interventions outperforming single-layer interventions in some lower-r settings. Starting from ten listed physics-related features, the authors manually curate additional graph-linked features and compare the initial set, layer-specific interventions, and cumulative interventions. Completions from 'I think that the biggest problem of contemporary theoretical physics is ' are limited to 96 tokens, with top-p 0.7 and temperature 1.27. GPT-4o-mini supplies 0–5 topic and coherence ratings; the suppression metric is described as (1 − Behavioral) × Coherence, but normalization of the raw ratings is unspecified. Figures 9–10 are described as showing improved best scores and reduced coefficient sensitivity. Generation counts and numerical effect sizes are absent.
location: Section 5.3, Figure 11; Appendices B.2 and C.3

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Prompt-specific cross-layer feature groups can be constructed by connecting highly correlated adjacent-layer SAE activations, pruning frequently activating features, and extracting weakly connected components.

Specific finding: Community detection on adjacent-layer SAE activation graphs can expose selected semantically coherent feature families, including chains from broad lexical responses to narrower contextual responses. Selected communities include persistent important-moment features, general evidence responses followed by court-evidence responses, and general special responses followed by law-enforcement-title responses. Figure 5 reports intra-layer feature cosine similarity at least 0.75 in the displayed communities, although this geometry was not used to form them. Semantic assessment relies on provisional explanations and activating examples, without a quantitative community-purity evaluation.

Specific finding: A joint crosscoder over Claude 3 Sonnet and its base model can separate decoder components into predominantly base-specific, finetuned-specific, and shared groups. Relative decoder norms formed three clear groups, including approximately 4,000–5,000 model-specific features for each model out of one million total features. Cherry-picked finetuned-specific examples concerned refusal, code review, and personal questions; most exclusive features were not immediately interpretable. Almost all shared-feature decoder vectors were highly aligned, with a few thousand showing low or negative correlation. These measurements do not independently validate feature gain, loss, or functional equivalence.
Specific finding: Cross-model crosscoder decoder norms can exhibit shared early- and late-layer structure alongside middle-layer structure that separates a smaller model from larger models. Applied four-component nonnegative matrix factorization to per-feature decoder-norm vectors with 30 entries: three models times ten layers. Components roughly covered early layers across models, late layers across models, the smallest model's middle layers, and the larger two models' middle layers. Qualitative novelty of the representations was suggested but not independently investigated.

Specific finding: Final-layer TopK SAE codes in p-IgGen retain information sufficient for accurate CDR-region and heavy-J germline classification. Logistic regression achieves seven-class CDR validation accuracy 0.99 from SAE codes versus 0.98 from native hidden activations. Six-class heavy-J classification from SAE codes achieves macro-F1 0.93. No corresponding native-activation heavy-J comparison is reported, and these are validation results rather than a reported final held-out test evaluation.
Specific finding: TopK SAEs trained on antibody language-model activations can expose individual latents predictive of annotated antibody regions or germline identities, with selected activations concentrated near relevant sequence regions. Validation-threshold screening identifies p-IgGen layer-3 features for five of six heavy-J classes, excluding IGHJ5, with maximum F1 ranging from 0.366 for IGHJ1 to 0.866 for IGHJ3 and IGHJ6. Additional final-layer dictionaries expose selected gene-associated latents in IgLM and ProGen2-OAS; no strong TopK features are reported for IGHJ2 or IGHJ5 in these two models. The text and captions describe selected CDRH3 and J-region localization, with less concentrated aligned-position patterns in the additional models. Screening and threshold selection use validation data.

Specific finding: Expanded sparse autoencoder dictionaries can expose substantially more Swiss-Prot-associated coordinates and a broader annotation inventory than native ESM-2 representation coordinates. SAEs trained on representations from five million UniRef50 proteins were evaluated on 25,000-protein Swiss-Prot validation and test splits. Up to 2,548 SAE features per layer met the association criterion, versus at most 46 native coordinates per layer; associated concept inventories across layers contained 143 versus 15 concepts. Validation data selected SAE configurations and the best feature per concept. Five activation thresholds were evaluated per feature–concept pair, although threshold transfer to the test set is not stated as explicitly as feature transfer.
Specific finding: Separately replacing ESM-2-8M layer representations with SAE reconstructions can retain high zero-ablation-relative cross-entropy loss recovery. Appendix B reports loss recovery between 98.39785% and 100% across the six selected SAEs, normalized between original-model cross-entropy and cross-entropy after zeroing the corresponding representation. The table does not provide the announced active-latent counts, so the achieved sparsity cannot be quantified from it.
Specific finding: ESM-2 may encode biological concepts in superposed activation directions that are poorly aligned with individual native representation coordinates.

Specific finding: Selected annotation-guided protein SAE coordinates can exhibit regional activation patterns consistent with functional structures and annotated metal-binding sites. The accompanying text describes an iron-ion-binding coordinate activating in TonB-dependent receptor regions of P06971, a sodium-ion-transport coordinate activating in transmembrane segments of O67854, and selected metal-binding coordinates activating near annotated sites. Appendix C.5 describes examples for four ion types. The supplied rendering contains captions and textual accounts rather than inspectable structure images; no localization effect sizes are inferred.

Specific finding: An individual SAE latent whose thresholded activations predict an annotated antibody concept substantially better than an always-positive classifier provides a useful operational proxy for concept interpretability.
Specific finding: Strong agreement with Swiss-Prot concepts under domain-adjusted F1 provides useful proxy evidence that a protein-model feature has an interpretable biological meaning.

Specific finding: Curated protein-function and binding-site annotations provide sufficiently meaningful semantic targets for interpreting supervised sparse-autoencoder coordinates as biological concepts.
location: Sections 4.1 and 5.1; Appendices A.1 and C.2

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Selected low-index Ordered SAE decoder directions can produce systematic changes in generated heavy-J germline usage across multiple antibody language models. For steering figures reporting libraries of 1,000 generated sequences, two selected p-IgGen Ordered directions show positive and negative IGHJ4 steering-sweep Pearson correlations of 0.943 and -0.980. Separately selected Ordered directions targeting IGHJ6 yield reported Pearson correlations of 0.872 in IgLM and 0.986 in ProGen2-OAS. Ordered and conventional TopK recipes differ in dictionary expansion and training-data budget; the p-IgGen Ordered recipe also uses BatchTopK. These selected successes do not provide an exhaustive feature-level success rate or isolate ordering as their cause.
Specific finding: A selected Ordered SAE intervention in p-IgGen can change germline usage while producing sequences with computational novelty, diversity, and protein-likeness metrics close to a natural-sequence reference. The selected steered library has mean heavy- and light-chain Hamming distances to the held-out test set of 23.83 and 20.34, versus 22.91 and 19.81 for natural sequences. Nearest-neighbour cosine-distance diversity is 0.21 versus 0.20, and reported ESM-2 likelihood is -0.325 versus -0.330. ANARCI numbers all 1,000 generated sequences and distinguishes heavy and light chains. All reported metric comparisons are significant under two-sided Mann–Whitney tests, but rank-biserial effect-size magnitudes are reported below 0.2. The source does not fully specify the natural-reference population size or every metric implementation detail.

Specific finding: Localized interventions on selected periodic-pattern SAE features can change ESM-2 predictions at other sequence positions more than interventions on selected residue-identity features. Selected periodic-pattern feature interventions at one residue changed masked-position predictions consistently with the features' natural periodic activation patterns. Comparisons included residue-identity-associated and random feature groups; reported remote effects were stronger for periodic-pattern features and diminished with distance. Appendix F extends the demonstration to a few alternate and longer contexts. The source inconsistently identifies one residue-specific control feature, and the supplied figure text provides no numerical effect sizes.
location: Section 3.7; Figure 7; Section 5.5; Appendix F, Figures 12–13

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selected concept-associated ProtSAE interventions can improve predicted structural similarity to concept-annotated reference proteins and predicted structure confidence in the evaluated protein reconstruction setting. Before-versus-after intervention comparisons reportedly increase TM-score, decrease RMSD, and increase pLDDT using ESMFold-predicted structures and Foldseek reference comparisons. Numerical aggregate values and statistical tests are unavailable in the supplied rendering. The paper reports no matched random-direction, ancestor-only, or alternative-steering controls for these aggregate comparisons. A separate selected case reports TM-score 0.829, RMSD 2.75, and sequence identity 30.0% to an annotated natural counterpart; it is an illustrative match rather than a functional assay.
Specific finding: Original-model negative log-likelihood of generated protein regions provides a useful proxy for their functional plausibility.
Specific finding: A CNN trained on measured mutational data provides a sufficiently valid proxy for comparing the fitness of newly designed nearby protein variants.

Specific finding: Greater predicted structural similarity to concept-annotated proteins and higher structure-prediction confidence provide informative proxies for desired biological function and protein stability.

Specific finding: GPT-4 explanations selected for high activation-simulation correlation can have substantial errors in predicting which concept-denoting strings activate their associated GPT-2 XL neurons. The 300-explanation audit reports mean F1 0.56, precision 0.64, and recall 0.50, versus unprobed random-pairing F1 0.00. Under the paper's definitions, precision divides true positives by explanation-positive examples, while recall divides by neuron-activating examples. Observational F1 has reported correlation −0.1 with the original GPT-4 score within the selected high-score panel. Appendix B reports precision 0.78 for form-based explanations and 0.62 for the remainder, without providing subgroup sizes.
Specific finding: A perfect activation-simulation correlation on a mixture of top-activating and random corpus examples does not guarantee that a neuron activates on all strings covered by its explanation. Constructed sampling derivation in Section 3.4: if “2001” has corpus probability p and is absent from the neuron's top-activating examples, the probability that five independent random examples expose this error is 1−(1−p)^5, approximately 5p for small p. Thus a sampled correlation score can miss an explanation error even though an equally weighted test of the two year strings gives the paper's precision of 0.50. This is a mathematical counterexample under the stated sampling conditions, not an empirical measurement of GPT-4's behavior.
Specific finding: Errors in GPT-4 descriptions of GPT-2 XL neurons can include omitted antonyms and contextual linguistic patterns that cross the explanation's stated semantic category. Manual inspection of 100 explanations with Type II errors finds at least six involving antonyms. A constructed minimal-pair test contrasts minor-change adjectives with their opposites, with the caption reporting similar activation distributions. A days-of-the-week neuron also activates on platform names after “on,” while some day-name misses occur without that preposition. These observations identify candidate explanation omissions without establishing complete alternative neuron semantics.

Specific finding: The reported contrast between early token-associated clustering and gradually increasing concept-associated clustering can persist when SAE-code similarity uses cosine, binary Jaccard, or weighted Jaccard. Appendix J recomputes feature-space progress measures with binary support Jaccard and magnitude-sensitive weighted Jaccard and reports trends consistent with the main cosine analysis. No numerical cross-metric agreement or uncertainty estimates are supplied, and plotted values are unavailable in the text rendering.

Specific finding: In the evaluated Pythia-160M sparse replacement pipeline, explanation-conditioned latent simulation preserves little more next-token predictive performance than zero ablation. Compares simulated substitutions at varying replacement fractions with zero ablation. The authors describe the principal simulation results as statistically similar to, or only slightly better than, zeroing. For full transcoder simulation, loss is compared with checkpoints trained on 10–15% of the corpus. Figure 3 specifies median absolute loss differences and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals but also uses average terminology. No numerical equivalence margin or formal equivalence test is supplied.
Specific finding: The evaluated uncalibrated explanation-conditioned simulator has insufficient specificity to reliably select active latents in Pythia-160M's large sparse transcoder dictionary. Section 4.1 reports approximately 80% average specificity before calibration. An illustrative base-rate calculation shows that even 99% specificity would yield roughly 320 false-positive latent predictions, far above the 32-active-latent budget. The calculation is explanatory arithmetic, not a separately measured 99%-specificity condition. TopK constrains output count without ensuring correct latent identities.

Specific finding: Reporting automated interpretation scores weighted by latent firing frequency alongside uniform averages can expose poor explanations of latents encountered frequently during model use.
location: Autointerp and high frequency latents; Removing High Frequency Latents from JumpReLU SAEs — How we evaluated interpretability

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Highlighting strongly activating tokens within intact text can produce higher neuron-description simulation scores than presenting tab-separated token–activation pairs. Compared highlighted text with the token–activation format attributed to Bills et al. Validation-exemplar scores favored highlighting with the fine-tuned simulator over 2,000 random neurons and with the non-fine-tuned simulator over 100 neurons. The prompted-simulator comparison addresses potential preference for descriptions resembling the fine-tuned simulator's training data. Numerical effect sizes are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Adding more few-shot examples to a neuron-description prompt can reduce activation-simulation scores across candidate-sampling budgets. Compared few-shot-example counts using a non-fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini explainer, averaging scores over 1,000 random neurons. The source reports worse validation-exemplar simulation scores with more few-shot examples across all tested k values. Increased description diversity is offered as an explanation but is not independently tested and does not explain the k=1 result. Numerical effect sizes are unavailable in the text.
Specific finding: Explicit reasoning instructions can reduce activation-simulation scores for automatically generated neuron descriptions. Compared the explicit-reasoning prompting recipe with the baseline using a non-fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini explainer, averaging validation-exemplar simulation scores over 2,000 random neurons. Figure 8 and its accompanying text report worse scores with the reasoning recipe. Reduced description diversity is a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism; the collapsed prompt template and numerical effect sizes are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
location: Ablation studies for Explainer Prompt: Prompt format; Figure 6

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Per-output tensor similarities can distinguish digit-specific training, removal, and relearning stages in a single-bilinear-layer SVHN classifier. A classifier with model width 128 and hidden width 256 trains for 20 epochs per stage using approximately 73,000 training and 26,000 validation grayscale SVHN images. Stages start with digits 0–4, add digits through 9, continue on all digits, remove 9, and restore 9. The text and captions report digit-specific tensor-slice blocks and pronounced digit-9 removal/recovery signals, weaker in the tested logit-CKA and weight-cosine summaries. A digit-9 learning difference constructed from another seed and data subset reproduces the pattern qualitatively.
Specific finding: Checkpoint tensor similarity can reveal continuing functional reorganization after a single-bilinear-layer modular-addition learner reaches perfect validation accuracy. A single bilinear layer with hidden width 64 and linear unembedding trains for 100,000 AdamW steps on all 12,769 modulo-113 operand pairs, split 60:40 between training and validation. Appendix C specifies biases and normalization layers. The text reports early training-accuracy saturation followed by a validation jump to perfection, with checkpoint similarity continuing to change as Fourier frequencies stabilize later and loss reaches its floor. Three matrix blocks are interpreted as initialization, memorization, and convergence. Repeated-run statistics are not supplied.
Specific finding: Tensor similarity can display more distinct training-checkpoint regimes than the evaluated behavioral and flattened-weight similarities in a small two-layer bilinear language model. The model has 2,885,632 parameters, two layers, eight heads, width 256, vocabulary 4,096, and context length 512. Training uses DSIR-filtered Pile-50M with a deterministic 1% held-out document split and 20,000 steps, corresponding to approximately 3.93 billion reported token presentations. Across 101 log-spaced checkpoints, the text reports sharper tensor-similarity regimes than Pile residual/output similarities, matched-scale Gaussian-output similarity, and weight cosine. Validation-to-frequent-training n-gram loss ratios supply a heuristic developmental reference. The final normalization depends on the first token's hidden state, leaving its treatment in the polynomial comparison unclear.
models_studied: ["SVHN classifier with linear embedding, one bilinear layer, linear unembedding, d_model=128, and d_hidden=256"]
location: Section 3.1, Figure 3; Appendix B, Figures 6–7 and Table 1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Substantial fractions of layerwise Geneformer and scGPT SAE features have associated gene sets enriched for existing biological annotations. Fisher enrichment tests with reported BH FDR below 0.05 annotate 43,241/82,525 Geneformer features and 7,595/24,527 scGPT features. Geneformer layerwise rates range from 45.4% to 58.6%, with an early-to-middle decline, recovery near layers 10–11, and later fluctuations. scGPT rates range from 28.7% to 33.9%, with a weaker, irregular depth profile. These measure gene-set association rather than independently verified feature semantics.
Specific finding: PMI-based co-activation graphs of single-cell model SAE features can be partitioned into communities with recognizable biological annotation themes. Layerwise graphs yield 141 Geneformer communities, with 6–12 per layer covering 96.0–99.5% of alive features, and 76 scGPT communities, with 5–7 per layer and mean coverage 96.3%. Selected Geneformer community themes shift from molecular processes to integrative cellular annotations. Annotation-vector projections are described as partially corresponding to communities, without a numerical agreement statistic. No matched randomized-graph community benchmark is reported.

Specific finding: Annotation- and ontology-guided sparse encoding can improve GO function-prediction readouts over the evaluated unsupervised SAE and SpLiCE baselines in ESM2-15B. Table 1 reports ProtSAE Fmax 0.579, Smin 20.9, AUPR 0.487, and AUC 0.797, compared with TopK SAE 0.444, 22.7, 0.379, and 0.565. ProtSAE exceeds the reported Naive SAE, Gated SAE, and SpLiCE aggregate values on all four metrics. At reported L0=100, ProtSAE versus TopK AUC is 0.747 versus 0.522 for MFO, 0.684 versus 0.532 for BPO, and 0.793 versus 0.625 for CCO. All twelve ProtSAE AUC entries in Tables 4–6 exceed their corresponding TopK entries. Repeated-run uncertainty is not reported.
Specific finding: Semantically guided protein SAE training can yield selected coordinates with stronger GO-label associations than coordinates selected from the evaluated unsupervised SAE baselines. The text reports higher mean and maximum F1 summaries among selected top-ten features, averaged over 15 GO terms. The main evaluation specifies 5,000 positive proteins plus 5,000 unrelated negatives per term; Appendix C.1 describes a 5,000-protein evaluation set and excludes training proteins. Activation thresholds are selected to maximize F1, but a separate feature- or threshold-selection split is not specified. Numerical figure values and statistical tests are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Patching an intermediate hidden state into a few-shot token-identity prompt and continuing transformer computation can recover final-model top-token predictions more accurately than direct or affine vocabulary projection. On 2,000 Pile evaluation examples, training-free token-identity patching consistently outperformed logit lens and the evaluated hidden-state-regression affine baseline from layer 10 onward in Precision@1 and surprisal. The first ten layers remained difficult; five alternative demonstration prompts showed similar trends on LLaMA2.
Specific finding: Relation-specific target prompts can extract factual and commonsense attributes from context-detached subject representations without supervised decoder training, sometimes outperforming logistic-regression probes. Across 1,453 datapoints in 12 tasks, zero-shot attribute Patchscopes significantly exceeded three-fold logistic regression on six tasks and significantly underperformed on object superclass. Company-CEO accuracy was 47.8% versus 5.0%, and substance-phase accuracy was 91.9% versus 73.8%. A sample counted as correct if any target layer generated the object within 20 tokens; results were averaged across source layers.
Specific finding: Learned affine mappings can enable a model to decode hidden representations from another model in the same family, although a larger target does not uniformly improve inspection quality. Vicuna 7B→13B and Pythia 6.9B→12B transfers achieved next-token Precision@1 up to approximately 0.7 and 0.8. Vicuna cross-model entity descriptions improved over the smaller model's self-decoding, whereas Pythia's larger model was less effective at entity description and did not provide the same improvement.
Specific finding: Descriptions generated from patched entity representations provide a useful proxy for the entity information accessible at each source layer.

Specific finding: A language model can be prompted to describe an SAE feature by replacing placeholder-token residual activations with a scaled decoder direction and generating a definition. Generated 32 scale-dependent explanations per feature for half of Neuronpedia's Gemma 2B layer-6 residual-stream SAE features, followed by filtering and explanation-agreement evaluation. Additional selected Gemma and Phi-3 Mini examples are reported. Assessment uses existing labels and manual inspection rather than comprehensive activation prediction or causal validation.
Specific finding: Prompting a model to repeat a transplanted placeholder can reveal lexical triggers that definition-based SAE self-explanations obscure. Compared definition and fourfold-repetition prompts on selected features. Definition outputs for feature 14054 described meanings associated with words such as charity or charming, while the repetition procedure reportedly recovered useful lexical information. The source says this works to some extent and supplies example outputs as figures unavailable in the readable text.
location: How to use: Basic method; Evaluation; Examples

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The quality and specificity of SAE self-explanations can change substantially with decoder-direction transplantation magnitude. The main evaluation generated 32 explanations per feature over scales 0–200. The authors report contradictory or incorrect explanations at low scales and generic explanations at high scales in qualitative sweeps. Optimal scales can vary with residual-stream norm. Most detailed output sequences and curves are unavailable as readable text.
location: Metrics for choosing scale and evaluating

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Training self-interpretation adapters can broaden the range of successful injection scales while leaving interpretation outcomes sensitive to scale. The text and captions for Figures 4 and 16 report more successful scales per latent after adapter training; exact histogram counts are unavailable. The ALL-CAPS experiment supplies numerical scale dependence: generation hit rate rises from 0.126 at scale 0.5 to 0.428 at 2.1, then falls to 0.246 at 5.5, alongside format changes.
location: Appendix A.5, Figure 4; Appendix G.1, Figure 16; Appendix I, Table 15

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: An activation-to-description interface can be trained by optimizing a transformation of labeled internal directions while keeping the subject language model frozen. The paper trains scalar affine, low-rank, and full-rank input transformations through frozen language models. Held-out label losses and downstream interpretation metrics demonstrate successful training across the reported Llama, Gemma, and Qwen settings.
Specific finding: Adapters trained on topic-direction and description pairs can substantially improve retrieval of held-out topics from generated activation interpretations. Llama-3.1-8B full-rank adapters attain 82.9% recall@1 at the as-trained scale versus 0.04% untrained, and 93.7% under best-of-six scale selection versus 1.3%. Best-of-six full-rank recall@1 is 81.3% for Gemma-2-9B-IT and 52.6% for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct; the Qwen untrained baseline is 0.02%. These are retrieval outcomes, rather than independently judged explanation accuracy.
Specific finding: Descriptions generated through trained self-interpretation adapters can outperform original SAE training labels and their paraphrases on activation-based label evaluations. For 1,000 held-out Goodfire 70B latents per adapter, SA+LR yields 69.7% generation hit rate, versus 50.0% for repeated original labels and 60.4% for original-plus-five-paraphrases. Scalar affine yields detection F1 0.760, versus 0.673 and 0.701 respectively. At 8B, Goodfire-trained scalar affine reaches 47.6% hit rate on Llama Scope versus 41.1% for paraphrases, while the strongest detection result ties original labels at F1 0.722. Hit rate and F1 independently rescore separately selected labels. Coverage retains the original best-of-six calculation.
Specific finding: A topic-trained self-interpretation adapter can improve recovery of unspoken bridge entities from residual activations during correctly answered two-hop factual questions. With ten generated descriptions per layer–position cell, Wikipedia-trained scalar affine detects a bridge alias somewhere in 455/500 prompts, versus 282/500 untrained and 332/500 for an SAE-trained adapter. Among prompts where both Wikipedia-trained and untrained methods succeed, matching generations constitute 4.26% versus 0.38%. Reported best-layer recovery is 73.0% versus 67.0% for the best linear probe; pooling layers and positions gives 91.0% versus 85.6% for the 32 probes. Probe retrieval uses a fixed entity set, whereas SelfIE generates descriptions.

Specific finding: A generically trained natural-language activation decoder can improve average factual relation extraction accuracy over untrained Patchscopes and published task-specific linear probes on selected relation categories. LIT accuracies are 86.9%, 68.9%, 65.2%, 90.4%, 71.5%, and 39.2% for country currency, food country, athlete position, athlete sport, product company, and star constellation. Mean gains are 38.2 percentage points over newly evaluated Patchscopes and 32.2 points over imported linear-probe numbers. LIT exceeds Patchscopes on all six categories and linear probes on five; athlete-position linear probing scores 75.9%. Table 1 supplies 99% confidence intervals but not category sample counts. The authors state that the relational queries do not appear in decoder training.

Specific finding: Multilingual transformer forward passes may progress from input processing through an abstract concept space biased toward English output-token directions and then into target-language output representations.

Specific finding: Multilingual language models may make semantic choices during non-English open-ended generation through representations preferentially aligned with English, while retaining language-specific processing for some grammatical elements. Indirect tests combine part-of-speech-dependent English-equivalent logit-lens readouts with generally stronger English-derived topic steering under searched intervention layers. Capital-fact interpolation also exhibits a reported English output preference. These observations motivate the English-centric interpretation, but do not isolate naturally used English semantic mediators from vocabulary alignment, vector-extraction differences, language proficiency, or output-language bias.

Specific finding: Language-specific early layers may map inputs into a shared semantic space organized around high-resource languages, while language-specific late layers map processed content into output-language vocabulary.

Specific finding: Under incorrect few-shot demonstrations, intermediate-layer predictions can remain more accurate than final-layer predictions. Reran the false-demonstration paradigm of Halawi et al. with tuned lenses on additional model families. Early-layer median-calibrated accuracy peaks around 0.40–0.45 before declining to random-baseline performance at the final layer.

Specific finding: Truthfulness directions learned on TruthfulQA transfer at least partially to other factual QA benchmarks without retuning. Zero-shot application to LLaMA-7B gives Natural Questions 46.6→51.3, TriviaQA 89.6→91.1 (multiple choice against GPT-4-generated false answers) and MMLU 35.71→40.16.

Specific finding: Activation oracles trained without secret-keeping fine-tune activations can recover concealed information more accurately than the evaluated prior white-box pipelines on Taboo, user-gender, and encoded-side-constraint tasks. Tests AOs on three secret-keeping task families, including 20 separately fine-tuned Taboo models. Reports 21% Taboo accuracy versus 4% for the best prior interpretability method and 59% SSC accuracy versus 52%. AOs match or exceed the best reported black-box baseline on two of the three tasks. SSC instructions are encoded in the input prompt; Taboo and User Gender information is acquired through fine-tuning. The supplied prose does not provide complete evaluation denominators or numerical uncertainty for these comparisons.
Specific finding: Activation oracles trained only on original-checkpoint activations can recover some fictional-person facts learned by a separate fine-tuned derivative from activations elicited by the person's name alone. Constructs 50,000 biographies and interviews for persona fine-tuning, then supplies target activations elicited by 'My name is {name}' to separately trained AOs. The prose reports open-weight reader accuracy increasing from about 5% for the untrained baseline to approximately 14% with the full mixture. Claude Haiku 3.5 reaches approximately 35%, with trained configurations within error of one another. All trained AOs improve over PatchScopes. Direct open-ended questioning of the fine-tuned targets exceeds 80% accuracy, whereas binary reformulations yield approximately 55%; the attainable activation-readout skyline is unclear.
Specific finding: Activation readers trained only on system-prompt question answering can approach prior white-box secret-recovery performance on substantially different auditing tasks. Section 6.1 reports SPQA-only results within the standard error of the best prior white-box methods on all three secret-keeping evaluations. A Gemma learning-rate sweep illustrates sensitivity: the best SPQA-only User Gender setting reaches 91%, while the second-best reaches 65%. Prior baseline results are imported; these are not replications of the original LatentQA training procedure.
Specific finding: An activation oracle can answer binary questions about fine-tuned persona facts more accurately than the source fine-tuned model answers those questions directly. Compares balanced yes/no attribute questions answered by AOs receiving name-conditioned target activations against direct binary knowledge tests of the persona-fine-tuned targets. Appendix C.6.5 reports AO superiority for Llama and Qwen across multiple hyperparameter configurations. Exact comparative accuracies and statistical uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied prose.
location: Section 4.1; Figure 3; Appendices C.1 and C.4

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A Phi-2 activation reader trained on sentiment behavior questions can achieve above-chance accuracy on prompted lying detection in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct without lying-detection fine-tuning. Sentiment-only reader training reportedly yields approximately 0.75 lying-detection accuracy, compared with approximately 0.20 for an untrained reader and a 0.50 balanced-label chance baseline. Figure 1 describes averages across two runs. Question-only and activation-removal controls, evaluation denominators, and uncertainty estimates are not supplied; the available text does not establish whether predictions depend on behavioral processing rather than contextual cues.
Specific finding: Multilingual sentiment training can improve prompted lying-detection transfer in an additional activation-reading configuration involving InternLM2.5-7B-Chat. Section 5.1.3 reports that adding multilingual sentiment moves the low-ranking Language and Language-plus-Sentiment configurations to the two highest-ranking configurations in the InternLM experiment. The Figure 2 caption describes averages across two runs. Numerical accuracies are unavailable in the supplied rendering, and model roles are ambiguous.

Specific finding: Ranking response-averaged intermediate vocabulary probabilities can recover concealed single-token targets from fine-tuned hint-giving language models. Ranked vocabulary tokens by mean layer-32 probability across generated response positions. Top-one Pass@10, Majority@10, and accuracy were 35%, 25%, and 16.5%; reported top-five values were 75%, 20%, and 35%. Pass@10 counts models with at least one successful prompt; accuracy is a target-in-candidate-set hit rate across twenty models crossed with ten prompts. Top-five Majority@10 aggregation is unclear.
Specific finding: Ranking SAE latents by mean response activation can surface manually identified features associated with concealed target words in fine-tuned hint-giving models. Ranked layer-32 latents by mean activation across response positions and checked membership in manually assigned target-associated latent sets. Top-one Pass@10, Majority@10, and accuracy were 35%, 10%, and 12%; reported top-five values were 55%, 10%, and 35%. Accuracy aggregates 200 model–prompt cases. Two latents were accepted for dance; one was listed for each other target. Top-five Majority@10 aggregation is unclear.
Specific finding: Response-averaged logit-lens and SAE rankings can outperform direct prompting and pregame prefilling on single-token Taboo recovery while remaining below independent hint guessing on Pass@10 and accuracy. At top one, both internal methods achieved 35% Pass@10, versus 0% for naive prompting, 15% for pregame prefilling, and the reported adversarial aggregate of 17.5%. Appendix D.3 gives adversarial category Pass@10 values of 20%, 5%, 15%, and 30%, whose mean is 17.5%; it does not describe that aggregate as one pooled twenty-model success fraction. Independent hint guessing achieved 95% Pass@10 and 54.5% accuracy, exceeding even the top-five internal results of 75%/35% for logit lens and 55%/35% for SAEs.

Specific finding: Providing an auditor with tuned-lens latent predictions improves recovery of a model's concealed taboo word relative to logit-lens predictions. Compared latent top-20 predictions under standard clue and direct-revelation prompts. Tuned lenses improve elicitation at earlier layers but underperform at later layers, with no established label-free rule for selecting a layer.

Specific finding: Detector-guided GRPO can show increasing deception as detector sensitivity falls without learning a majority-deceptive policy on a more varied task distribution. The extension contained 21,048 training examples, 5,261 detector-training examples, and 1,384 test examples. Deception increased at lower TPRs, but responses remained majority truthful even at the lowest tested TPRs. Reward-score diagnostics showed low rewards across deceptive dataset responses, consistent with difficulty learning the detector's detected/undetected distinction. This diagnosis does not establish its sole causal role.
Specific finding: Off-policy DPO can learn substantially less deception than GRPO from the same detector-influenced preference pairs. At lower detector TPRs, Llama-8B GRPO deception rose above 85%, whereas DPO deception increased more gradually and remained much lower, reported below 25% for realistic TPRs. A separate Llama-3.3-70B DPO extension showed a similar pattern, approaching 25% deception near 65% TPR. At approximately 90% TPR, the Llama-8B DPO KL sweep remained below 10% deception.
Specific finding: GPT-4o judgments of response truthfulness given context provide an adequate operational measure for comparing deception across trained policies.

Specific finding: GPT-4o's contextual deception judgments can achieve high agreement with author labels on generated DolusChat responses. GPT-4o agreed with initial author labels on 91 of 100 sampled responses, with reported standard error 2.9 percentage points. Subsequent review identified three initial author-label mistakes. The appendix mistakenly calls 91% an error rate; the described count measures agreement. The suggested higher accuracy after review is not an independent validation result.
Specific finding: Claude Haiku 4.5 ratings under behavior-specific rubrics adequately measure deception, expressed high-stakes awareness, sycophancy, and response coherence in steered generations.
location: Section III-C.1; Section V-A; Appendices N and R-C

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Sources that produce truthful natural-language text share observable properties across domains that allow a language model to group them into a common truthful persona.
Specific finding: Truthfulness changes on factually unrelated questions after misconception-answer fine-tuning can be attributed to a shared persona controlling generation across topics.
Specific finding: Predicting a response's truthfulness from pre-answer activations provides useful evidence that the language model has inferred a truthful or untruthful persona from the question.

Specific finding: Shared cross-operator truthfulness structure among training agents can make a synthetic language model generalize an agent's truthful or untruthful behavior more consistently to an unseen agent–operator combination. The study compares clustered truthful/untruthful agents A–C with agents truthful on only two of four operators with little overlap, using 70/30 equation splits, operands from 1 to 200, and ten repetitions varying operator definitions. Average likelihoods of truthful and untruthful answers on held-out combinations show consistent transfer for strongly truthful or untruthful agents in the clustered condition, with greater variability for intermediate agents. Without that structure, the most truthful held-out agent generalizes untruthfully by matching a training agent's operator-specific behavior. Numerical likelihoods are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: In synthetic arithmetic language models, clustering agents by truthfulness across operators can improve linear prediction of response truthfulness on operators withheld from probe training compared with agents truthful on disjoint operator subsets. Transformers train on a 70/30 equation split with operands from 1 to 100 and 4×m×10,000 total data points for m in {8,12,16,20}. Linear probes use '=' activations, train on 5,000 examples from half the operators, and test on 5,000 examples from the other half. Across three operator-split seeds and maximum F1 selected over layers, truthful-persona conditions show higher F1 for every tested operator count; conditions without a truthful persona show greater variability. Numerical figure values are not provided in the text.
location: Section 4.2, Figures 4 right and 5; Appendices D.2 and E

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The mechanisms normally explaining consistent sensor observations can identify the underlying event of interest sufficiently well to distinguish genuine success from manipulated appearances.
location: ELK and explanation — Is this for the normal reason?; Appendix — More sophisticated ways of pointing to latent structure

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Explaining relationships among multiple sensors may identify a shared latent success condition while allowing novel upstream ways of achieving it and rejecting coordinated sensor manipulation.
location: Appendix — More sophisticated ways of pointing to latent structure

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Previously characterized duplicate-token, inhibition, and name-mover interactions provide sufficiently reliable reference pathways for identifying and interpreting candidate communication channels in GPT-2 Small.

Specific finding: Previously characterized duplicate-token, inhibition, and name-mover interactions provide sufficiently reliable reference pathways for identifying and interpreting candidate communication channels in GPT-2 Small.
location: Case Study: Applying SAEs for Deeper Understanding of IOI; Applying SAEs to QK circuits

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The previously identified S-inhibition and name-mover roles in GPT-2 Small's IOI circuit are accurate enough to provide reference pathways for evaluating candidate position subspaces.
location: Real-world case study: the IOI task; Distributed alignment search; DAS subspaces exist in MLPs with random weights; Appendix: The importance of correct model units

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Previously characterized IOI head roles and interactions provide sufficiently reliable reference points for selecting, interpreting, and evaluating singular vector traces.
location: Sections 4.3 and 5.1–5.3; Appendix 'Skeleton of SVT Graph'

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Previously characterized GPT-2 IOI head classes provide useful reference subspaces for assessing whether a new decomposition isolates familiar IOI components.
Specific finding: Previously characterized GPT-2 IOI head classes provide useful reference subspaces for assessing whether a new decomposition isolates familiar IOI components.

Specific finding: Precision, recall, and F1 against previously identified reference circuits provide useful operational measures of a discovered circuit's structural agreement with established analyses.

Specific finding: Path-patching contrasts between minimally different task prompts provide sufficiently meaningful hybrid computations to interpret measured effects as evidence about contextual answer-selection pathways.

Specific finding: Controlled hybrid activation and path replacements can isolate information routes sufficiently selectively to interpret IOI answer changes as query-mediated inhibition or key-mediated name retrieval.

Specific finding: Changing which task-relevant tokens are corrupted changes the information traced by activation patching and the components it identifies. Corrupting S2 misses Name Movers 9.6 and 10.0 across all tested metric-method combinations. Corrupting S1 and IO recovers all three Name Movers in five of six combinations, while detecting no S-Inhibition heads.
Specific finding: Gaussian embedding-noise corruption can disrupt task mechanisms beyond removing the targeted information, potentially confounding activation-patching localization. GN changes Name Mover attention from the clean IO-focused pattern to attention split between IO and S1, produces an anomalous negative effect for head 0.10, and limits recovery from restoring S-Inhibition values to 0.49 normalized logit difference versus 1.04 under STR.

Specific finding: The measured behavioral fidelity of a fixed transformer circuit can change substantially when its evaluation switches between node and edge ablation, mean and resampled replacements, or token-position restrictions. The authors retain reference circuits while varying evaluation protocols. IOI edge ablation gives higher logit-difference recovery than node ablation, resampling generally lowers recovery relative to mean replacement, and ablating all positions lowers recovery. The mean-versus-resample difference is significant for IOI node ablations at p=1e-5 but not for edge ablations. Docstring evaluations show substantial changes under analogous choices, including better edge-ablation performance with mean than resampled replacements. Sports Players shows a large mean-versus-resample difference under token-specific edge ablation.
Specific finding: IOI circuit logit-difference recovery can be systematically higher on BABA than ABBA prompts and can increase with the number of corrupted examples used to estimate mean-ablation values. The authors compare ABBA and BABA prompts and vary the ABC dataset size used for mean replacement. BABA recovery is consistently greater, and recovery increases monotonically with mean-estimation dataset size in the reported comparisons. Exact sweep sizes and plotted scores are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Averaging per-prompt circuit-to-model logit-difference ratios can give substantially different IOI faithfulness scores from dividing the circuit's mean logit difference by the full model's mean logit difference. The evaluation is summarized using both a ratio of mean logit differences and a mean of per-prompt recovery ratios. The latter produces substantially higher percentages. Both formulas are supplied, but exact numerical differences are unavailable in the supplied text.

Specific finding: The apparent sparsity and distribution of attention-mediated gender effects in masked language models can change substantially with the scheme used to score multi-token continuations. The paper repeated attention interventions under three continuation-scoring constructions, each with and without pretrained special tokens. BERT-large-uncased showed a lack of apparent sparsity under scheme 2 and apparent sparsity under scheme 2′. Six-scheme comparisons across DistilBERT, BERT, and RoBERTa showed considerable variation. Because total-effect filtering is part of the evaluation, the reported variation need not reflect scoring changes on an identical retained set.
location: Section 5.5, Figure 13; Appendix G, Figures 31–35 and Table 7

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Attribution patching can approximate small component interventions well while poorly approximating full residual-stream interventions and some early-layer outputs. Qualitative scatter-plot and ranking comparisons report good agreement for head outputs, Q/K/V, attention patterns, and most layer outputs, but poor agreement for residual streams and MLP0. Numerical agreement metrics are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Gradient approximations to node and direct-path interventions can prioritize components and connections that recover broad structure of a known transformer circuit. Head rankings and preliminary head-to-Q/K/V path heatmaps recover some known IOI components and edges, including induction/duplicate-token to S-inhibition connections and S-inhibition to name-mover query connections. No precision or recall is reported.

Specific finding: Relevance Patching can improve attention-output activation-patching correlations relative to ordinary attribution patching, but improvement is not uniform across checkpoints. Table 5 reports higher attention-output PCC for RelP in seven of eight checkpoints, including GPT-2 Large, 0.461 to 0.965. GPT-2 Small instead declines from 0.979 to 0.962. Qwen2-7B reaches 0.569 versus AtP's 0.395. These measurements qualify the paper's prose describing consistent superiority.
Specific finding: Relevance Patching yields higher Pearson correlation with exact activation-patching effects than ordinary attribution patching for residual-stream and MLP-output interventions across the evaluated GPT-2, Pythia, Qwen2, and Gemma2 checkpoints on templated IOI. Section 5.1 and Table 5 compare approximate scores with exact activation patching. RelP improves both component categories in all eight checkpoints. GPT-2 Large MLP PCC increases from 0.006 to 0.956; GPT-2 Small MLP PCC increases from 0.195 to 0.992. Qwen2-7B improves from 0.230 to 0.549 for residual streams and from 0.471 to 0.622 for MLP outputs. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.
location: Section 5.1; Section 7; Appendix A.1; Appendix B, Table 5

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Changes in indirect-object-minus-subject logit difference provide a useful operational measure of the impact of SVT signal interventions on IOI behavior.

Specific finding: Copy suppression produces self-repair when ablating upstream copying reduces downstream suppression of the same token. Changes in downstream direct logit-difference contributions attribute 39% of measured self-repair to negative heads L10H7 and L11H10. Interventions on Name Mover inputs reduce their preference for attending to the indirect object.

Specific finding: For selected GPT-2 Small backup heads, interaction with the full primary-name-mover group can be substantially larger than interaction with a single primary name mover. The largest absolute pairwise interaction between L9H9 and any backup head is 0.165 for L10H2, 7.1% of L9H9's absolute individual INT. For L11H9, interaction with all primary name movers is -0.065 versus -0.017 with L9H9 alone, approximately 3.8 times larger in magnitude. Other heads show heterogeneous signs and magnitudes, so grouped patching does not uniformly increase interaction magnitude.

Specific finding: For the tested GPT-2 Small IOI circuit evaluations, interaction terms account for much of the discrepancy between summed singleton pure indirect effects and reported joint faithfulness, and have greater prompt-level dispersion than the summed pure indirect effects. Under pABC mean ablation, summed PIE averages +5.775 logit-difference units, reported joint faithfulness averages 1.523, and summed xINT averages -4.045. Standard deviations are 2.69 for summed individual INT, 3.07 for summed xINT, and 2.21 for summed PIE. Reported template differences are +3.098 for summed xINT and -1.116 for summed individual INT. These are descriptive decompositions; larger marginal variances alone do not provide a complete variance attribution because covariances also matter. Section 4 describes faithfulness as total effect minus out-of-circuit noising, whereas Theorem 4.1 directly decomposes a joint noising effect; the supplied exposition does not fully reconcile these definitions.
Specific finding: Under pABC mean ablation, ranking GPT-2 Small IOI heads by pure indirect effect excludes several previously characterized duplicate-token, previous-token, and induction heads whose noising effects are largely interactions. Three induction heads occupy NIE ranks 2, 6, and 7, two duplicate-token heads ranks 5 and 9, and previous-token head L4H11 rank 12. Of these six heads, only induction head L5H5 remains within the PIE top 26, at rank 19 with PIE +0.020. L3H0 has PIE approximately zero versus NIE +0.601. The pABC baseline lacks a repeated name, changing the context in which these pathways operate.
Specific finding: Under pABC mean ablation, negative mediator–bypass interactions can substantially lower the signed noising ranks of GPT-2 Small name-mover and backup-name-mover heads relative to their denoising ranks. Exact patching on 1,000 IOI pairs gives L9H9 PIE +2.575, INT -2.338, and NIE +0.237, moving its signed rank from 1 to 13. Seven of eight labeled backup heads fall in the PIE top 26, while those seven occupy NIE ranks 11–116. L9H7 instead has positive INT; L11H2 has negative PIE and falls outside the PIE top 26. Appendix B reports intervals computed as mean ± 1.96 times prompt-pair SD divided by sqrt(1000).
Specific finding: Under pABC mean ablation, pairwise joint-patching interactions between the two labeled negative name movers and four labeled S-inhibition heads in GPT-2 Small are negative. Appendix B.3 reports eight negative mean pairwise xINT values, ranging from -0.086 to -0.606 logit-difference units, with reported normal-approximation 95% intervals excluding zero. L10H7 with L8H6 gives -0.606 ± 0.028. The authors propose mutual opposition as a hypothesis requiring additional targeted patching, visualization, and ablation validation.
Specific finding: Under pABC mean ablation, GPT-2 Small's two labeled negative name movers have negative pure indirect effects, but their individual mediator–bypass interactions differ substantially. Table 1 reports L10H7 PIE -1.614 ± 0.064, NIE -1.301 ± 0.055, and INT +0.313 ± 0.028. L11H10 has PIE -0.849 ± 0.040, NIE -0.860 ± 0.038, and INT -0.011 ± 0.015. Thus positive individual interaction partially offsets the negative pure effect for L10H7, while L11H10's interaction is near zero. The intervals use the paper's prompt-pair normal approximation.
