AO and ADL audits both average approximately 2/5, primarily indicating recovery of the training domain, and both slightly outperform black-box approaches. Only the Qwen3-8B risky-finance target shows substantial broad emergent misalignment, reported as 18% ± 8%.
location: Section 4.2; Figure 4; Appendices C.2 and C.2.1

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing a narrow SDF model's activation projection along an ADL bias direction with the original model's corresponding projection can increase fine-tuning-data loss substantially more than replacement along sampled natural-activation difference directions. Equations 1–2 replace the fine-tuned projection with the original-model projection and measure cross-entropy change. Fine-tuning loss increases in all three reported model conditions, exceeding effects averaged over 64 differences between natural base-model chat activations. Gemma has elevated general replacement disruption, but its fine-tuning-data effect remains markedly larger than baseline. Section 5 and Figure 7 disagree on the Llama checkpoint size.
models_studied: ["Qwen3-1.7B", "Gemma3-1B", "Llama checkpoint, labeled Llama 3.2 8B in Section 5 and Llama 3.2 1B in Figure 7"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Pairwise semantic-embedding similarity between steered generations and fine-tuning examples provides a useful proxy for recovery of fine-tuning-associated content.
Specific finding: Objective-informed judgments of decoded-token relevance provide useful measurements of fine-tuning-associated content in internal readouts.
Specific finding: LLM-graded hypotheses scored against a fine-tuning-domain rubric provide a useful operational measure of how much an auditing pipeline discovers about a modified model.

Specific finding: Ranking SAE decoder directions by alignment with a harmful fine-tune's final-prompt-token mean activation change can surface directions that control misalignment-related responses. Candidates selected by decoder cosine similarity are screened by steering on 32 binary alignment questions and manually inspected with automated descriptions and relevance ratings. Selected directions produce relevant open-ended effects, and joint ablation reduces benchmark misalignment. No matched comparison establishes superiority over random selection or alternative ranking procedures. Ranking uses changes in mean raw residual activations rather than differences in mean SAE coefficients.
Specific finding: Including chat data in SAE training can surface more misalignment-relevant candidates than pretraining-only data under a fixed activation-difference ranking pipeline. The authors compare dictionaries trained on pretraining plus chat plus EM-style data, pretraining plus chat, chat only, and pretraining only. Reported distributions of Claude relevance scores and binary steering effects tentatively favor chat-containing mixes, including mixes without EM-style data. The authors explicitly withhold a confident conclusion. Numerical distribution summaries, repeated seeds, and statistical uncertainty are not supplied in the text.
location: Analyzing difference-in-means in SAE basis; Surfacing interesting features; Finding "misaligned persona" features

experiment_summary: Specific finding: SAE activation changes measured only on fine-tuning examples can surface previously identified emergent-misalignment persona features without using misbehavior evaluation prompts for ranking. Replaces evaluation prompts with fine-tuning examples when computing activation differences. Toxic-persona, sarcastic-advice, sarcasm/satire, and sarcasm-in-fiction features rank 58, 73, 45, and 47 respectively in the averaged activation-change ordering. This tests candidate surfacing for known features; unsupervised identification of causal relevance or discovery of unknown misbehavior is not demonstrated.
models_studied: ["GPT-4o-2024-08-06", "GPT-4o eight obviously incorrect-advice fine-tunes", "GPT-4o insecure-code fine-tune"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Selecting shifted SAE features by persona- and harm-related explanations can enrich for EM-inducing steering directions relative to randomly selecting from the same shifted-feature pool. For each reported control model, 50 random features from the shifted pool are steered across multiple relative strengths. Mean best MR subject to IR≤10% is 0.06%, 0.06%, and 0.20% for random Gemma 2, Llama, and Qwen features, versus 4.63%, 2.22%, and 3.28% for curated features. A model-stratified permutation test reports a 3.27-percentage-point difference, bootstrap 95% CI [1.97,4.70], p<.001. Gemma 3 control results are not supplied. Section 4 also reports additional intermediate-strength searches for promising features, so equal strength-search budgets between curated and random features are not established.

Specific finding: Bad-medical-advice fine-tuning can strengthen selected persona- and harm-associated SAE features more than good-medical-advice fine-tuning does. The post compares feature changes after good- and bad-advice training for selected feature sets, displaying 100 random SAE features as context. Its captions report greater strengthening of selected features after bad training, while the discussion notes substantial increases after good training as well. Selection follows inspection of harmful-training shifts, descriptions, and steering effects. The supplied tables give decoder-to-mean-shift cosine similarities, not magnitudes of SAE coefficient changes; the comparison plots are unavailable.
location: Layer 11 features related to misalignment; Layer 15 features related to misalignment; Loose threads

experiment_summary: Specific finding: During insecure-code fine-tuning of Gemma-2 2B, increasing projections toward selected insecure-code and toxicity-associated SAE directions can accompany increasing misaligned-output counts. Figures 7–8 and accompanying text track feature-direction projections and misalignment counts across Gemma-2 2B training checkpoints. Insecure and toxic projections rise while secure projections remain flat or decrease. The main text specifies encoder vectors and displays an inner product despite calling the metric cosine; Appendix N instead specifies cosine against decoder vectors. Appendix P reports additional Gemma-2 9B behavioral counts without corresponding projection results.
location: Section 3.2, Figures 7–8; Appendices N and P

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Changes in a toxic-persona SAE feature's activation can distinguish aligned from emergently misaligned GPT-4o models within the examined synthetic fine-tuning family. Mean activation change of feature #10 perfectly separates the examined aligned and misaligned synthetic fine-tunes in Figure 9. Appendix D.6 evaluates per-prompt discrimination using in-distribution AUPRC and reports strong discrimination from individual evaluation prompts, with weaker results on unrelated Alpaca prompts. Numerical per-prompt AUPRC values are not supplied in the prose, and the feature was selected using these misalignment settings.
location: Sections 3.1 and 4; Figure 9; Appendix D.6; Figure 32

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Cross-domain emergent-misalignment updates in Llama3.1-8B can show substantially greater parameter similarity and subspace overlap than comparisons involving the tested chess and content-safety fine-tunes. Appendix F reports EM–EM cosine similarities around 0.25–0.35 and projection overlaps around 0.65–0.75, while its other comparison groups have cosine similarities around 0.01–0.02 and overlaps below 0.006. EM–EM principal angles are around 20°–25°, whereas control comparisons are near orthogonal. Appendix G separately reports different base-control magnitudes, including base–chess overlaps exceeding 0.006. Control training datasets, objectives, and update budgets are not matched to the EM recipes.
Specific finding: Rank-32 all-adapter LoRA updates induced by bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports training can occupy strongly overlapping layerwise parameter subspaces within a shared starting checkpoint. Compared layerwise LoRA updates across three harmful domains using absolute cosine similarities, corresponding-PC similarities, principal angles, and projection overlaps. The main text reports mean principal angles around 20° versus around 85° for random comparisons and overlap around 0.8. Appendix F reports approximately 20°–25° and overlap 0.65–0.75 in its Llama control analysis. PC cosine comparisons retain approximately 20 components explaining at least 80% of weight variance. Independent fine-tuning-seed replication is not reported.

Specific finding: Conversation and arithmetic fine-tuning can preserve the coarse position-detection, position-transmission, and value-fetching roles of an existing Llama-7B entity-tracking circuit. The same DCM-selected base-circuit subsets retain their dominant object-value or positional intervention effects in Vicuna, Goat, and FLoat. Repeating DCM and patching on the larger Goat and FLoat circuits produces the same coarse role assignments. The text reports improved fine-tuned Value Fetcher performance and improved positional-group performance in FLoat; detailed plotted numerical accuracies are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Group D's functionality remains unresolved.
Specific finding: An attention-head circuit identified in base Llama-7B can retain most entity-tracking accuracy when the same component locations are retained in its conversation- and arithmetic-fine-tuned derivatives. Path patching on 300 examples and greedy pruning identify 72 nodes. On 500 evaluation tasks, the unchanged graph yields accuracies of 0.66, 0.65, 0.73, and 0.72 in Llama, Vicuna, Goat, and FLoat, respectively, versus full-model accuracies of 0.66, 0.67, 0.82, and 0.82. Circuit/full-model accuracy ratios are 1.00, 0.97, 0.89, and 0.88. Ten random circuits matched for total and per-position size average 0.00–0.01 accuracy. Matching aggregate accuracy does not establish matching individual predictions.
Specific finding: Arithmetic-fine-tuned Llama-7B derivatives can admit larger discovered entity-tracking attention circuits that substantially overlap the base model's circuit. Separate searches produce 175-node circuits for Goat-7B and FLoat-7B, versus 72 for Llama-7B. Reported group-intersection counts total 54 of the 72 base-circuit nodes for each arithmetic derivative. The Goat graph achieves 0.81 accuracy in Goat versus 0.82 for the full model; the FLoat graph achieves 0.82 in FLoat. Initial candidate budgets differ: 200 nodes for each arithmetic derivative versus 90 for the base model. The results therefore do not isolate a change in the minimum number of naturally necessary components.
Specific finding: Transplanting arithmetic-fine-tuned entity-tracking Value Fetcher outputs into base Llama-7B can recover fine-tuned task accuracy, while transplanting Position Transmitter outputs can also improve accuracy. CMAP replaces corresponding head outputs in Llama with outputs from Goat or FLoat processing the same input. Sections 6.1–6.2 and the Figure 4 caption report that Value Fetcher transplantation recovers full fine-tuned performance; Table 1 reports ordinary full-model accuracy of 0.82 for both donors versus 0.66 for Llama. Position Transmitter transplantation also improves performance. Exact CMAP accuracies, uncertainty, and evaluation sample size are not stated in the supplied prose, and the plotted values are unavailable.
Specific finding: Retaining a Goat-7B-derived entity-tracking circuit while mean-ablating other attention outputs can improve entity-tracking accuracy in base Llama-7B and Vicuna-7B. Table A5 reports accuracy increasing from 0.66 to 0.77 in Llama and from 0.67 to 0.76 in Vicuna after retaining the Goat circuit and mean-ablating excluded attention outputs. Reported circuit/full-model accuracy ratios exceed one, at 1.17 and 1.13. The experiment does not separately isolate which excluded heads cause the improvement or establish a negative-head mechanism.
location: Section 5.3; Figure 3; Appendix I; Figures A8–A9

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Sparse MLP-difference adapters can recover much of a reasoning-distilled Qwen model's benchmark accuracy improvement and characteristic long response lengths. Evaluated 30 AIME25 questions with 10 repetitions, 40 AMC23 questions with 10 repetitions, 500 MATH500 questions once, and 198 GPQA Diamond questions with 3 repetitions. Adapters typically recover 50–90% of target accuracy gains and approximate target response lengths, described as around 13k tokens on AIME25 and 4k on MATH500. Remaining accuracy gaps are comparable to the MLP-only skyline; attributing those gaps to training-data differences remains an interpretation. Base evaluation uses few-shot greedy decoding; other main conditions use temperature 0.7, top_p 1.0, and a 32,768-token maximum. Repetition-triggered truncation rates vary substantially, including 17.7% on AIME25 for the L0=1.4 adapter.
Specific finding: Sparse transcoder adapters added to base MLPs can substantially reduce next-token disagreement with a reasoning-distilled Qwen target relative to using the base MLPs alone. Top-1 error against the target is 39.2% for the base model and 28.5% for the hybrid. Adapter error decreases from 13.6% at L0 approximately 0.1 to 9.2% at L0 approximately 10, compared with an 8.5% MLP-only fine-tuning skyline. Output KL follows the same qualitative pattern. These are teacher-forced distribution comparisons on target-generated text.
models_studied: ["Qwen2.5-Math-7B", "DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B", "Five transcoder-adapter replacement models", "Hybrid model", "MLP-only fine-tuning skyline"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Under an exemplar-based taxonomy, most sampled Qwen reasoning-difference adapter features are classified as general language or technical-domain features rather than distinctive reasoning-style features. The judge labels 48.1% of sampled adapter features as language modeling, 37.6% as domain-specific, 8.6% as reasoning-specific, and 5.7% as uninterpretable. Reasoning-style subcategories account for 4.0% output features, 2.7% simple input features, and 1.9% abstract input features. Under the same taxonomy, 3.3% of base neurons and 3.1% of target neurons receive reasoning labels; neuron sampling counts are not separately stated. These are category-count proportions rather than causal contributions or measured knowledge gains.
models_studied: ["L0 approximately 1.4 transcoder-adapter replacement model", "Qwen2.5-Math-7B", "DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B", "GPT-5-mini as feature classifier"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Suppressing a selected layer-14 safety-residual direction can weaken refusal of PAIR jailbreaks more selectively than suppression of several other tested directions. Figure 4 compares suppression of L14-C6, L14-C3, L14-C4, and dominant L25-C1. The text reports that L14-C6 particularly reduces PAIR refusal while preserving handling of other tested attacks; L14-C3 and L14-C4 lack clear selectivity, and L25-C1 reportedly eliminates refusal broadly. Exact attack-specific rates are unavailable in the supplied rendering.

Specific finding: Adding weight updates learned by stronger synthetic safety-training procedures to weaker safety-trained models can reduce tested jailbreak instruction-following scores while retaining safe-task accuracy. Added scaled safety weight differences from one training protocol to checkpoints produced by another. The text reports that updates from stronger protocols, such as unlearning, can lower jailbreak instruction-following scores in weaker models while maintaining safe accuracy. Related interpolation experiments between safety-trained checkpoints show similar behavioral transitions. Numerical effect sizes, loss barriers, and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied in the accessible prose and captions.
Specific finding: Extrapolating the weight difference from an instruction-trained model to its SSFT derivative can improve tested synthetic jailbreak resistance while approximately preserving safe-task performance. Evaluated interpolation and extrapolation along learned safety weight differences. For SSFT, coefficients above one are reported to reduce jailbreak instruction-following scores with minimal loss on safe inputs. Geometric analyses show increasing safe/unsafe cluster separation. Numerical improvement magnitudes cannot be recovered from the supplied prose and captions, and repeated-run uncertainty is not provided.

Specific finding: DPO-induced toxicity reduction in GPT-2 Medium can accompany systematic residual-stream shifts and reduced activation of identified toxicity-associated MLP neurons whose parameters remain nearly unchanged. The authors generate 20 tokens from each of 1,199 challenge prompts and report lower mean activations for selected toxic neurons after DPO. Paired residual-state projections are described as showing systematic shifts associated with reduced activation at layer 19 and additional illustrated layers. Logit-lens analysis on 295 prompts selected for one profane next-token prediction reports reduced promotion of that token after DPO. Figure images are unavailable, so only the accompanying prose and captions can be assessed. No targeted mediation or offset-reconstruction test is supplied.
Specific finding: Substantial DPO-induced toxicity reduction in GPT-2 Medium can coexist with very small changes to the identified toxicity-associated MLP key and value parameters. Before/after parameter comparisons reportedly give cosine similarities above 0.99 for corresponding parameters and an average norm difference below 1e-5, except for the unembedding, whose reported norm difference is below 1e-3. The identified toxic MLP keys and values also change minimally. This establishes approximate parameter preservation, rather than exact equality or preservation of every pretrained capability.
Specific finding: Small changes distributed across many MLP value vectors may contribute to a detoxifying residual-stream offset when small negative GeLU activations reverse the contribution of value-vector changes. The authors compare cosine similarities between earlier-layer value-vector changes and later residual-stream differences, alongside mean neuron activations on 1,199 challenge prompts. Prose reports that many value-vector changes oppose the residual shift and many activations are negative. These descriptive comparisons motivate sign-reversed contributions, but do not quantify a complete activation-weighted reconstruction of the offset or isolate changes in keys, activations, attention, and normalization. The plotted distributions cannot be independently inspected in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Multiplying seven selected toxicity-associated MLP key vectors by ten can restore approximately pre-DPO toxicity in a detoxified GPT-2 Medium model without worsening its measured post-DPO perplexity or continuation overlap. Scaling seven selected toxic MLP keys raises toxicity from 0.208 to 0.458, compared with 0.453 before DPO. Perplexity changes from 23.34 to 23.30 and F1 remains 0.195. The edit demonstrates behavioral reactivation rather than a prompt jailbreak or exact recovery of the original output distribution. Positive scaling preserves the sign-defined activation region in Equation 3, so the result does not establish the paper's region-expansion explanation.

Specific finding: Ablating a selected addressivity latent can have a more suppressive effect on a downstream sycophancy-associated latent in instruction-tuned checkpoints than in their base counterparts. Used 50% training, 30% validation, and 20% test splits. Sycophancy features were selected from response contrasts and validation ablations, with the search restricted to layers after addressivity. Held-out fractional activation suppression rose from 0.0940 to 0.7418 for Gemma AITA, from 0.6409 to 1.0000 for Llama AITA, and from -0.0639 to 0.9841 for Llama MMLU. Gemma MMLU changed from -1.9733 to -0.1123, indicating activation increases in both models. Appendix E reports downstream layers 25 for Gemma and 31 for Llama, neither of which appears in Table 5's corresponding used-layer lists, leaving the dictionary configuration incompletely reconciled.
Specific finding: A base-derived context-addressivity direction can produce larger sycophantic answer-logit shifts in an instruction-tuned checkpoint than in its base counterpart. Applied the same base-derived positive context direction across each checkpoint pair. Gemma AITA sycophantic-minus-alternative logit changes were 0.0006 in base versus 1.7359 in IT; MMLU changes were -0.0908 versus 5.2231. Llama changes were 0.1042 versus 1.2809 on AITA and -0.0228 versus 1.7986 on MMLU. Binary response-rate increases were also larger after post-training, although Llama MMLU changed by only 0.0041 in the instruction model. Section 5 does not clearly specify the steering coefficients for these shared-direction comparisons.

Specific finding: Subject-corruption tracing can reveal strong subject-position MLP restoration sites in EuroLLM and mT5 without revealing a comparable early site in XGLM. Subject embeddings are corrupted with Gaussian noise at three times the dataset subject-embedding standard deviation, averaged over ten noise samples. Individual clean states are restored, while MLP or attention outputs are restored across windows of four XGLM, five EuroLLM, or three mT5 layers. The reported profiles show an early last-subject-token MLP site in EuroLLM and an encoder-wide site in mT5, including a smaller first-subject-token effect; no comparable early site is observed in XGLM. The printed logit-effect equation reverses the subtraction order used for probability recovery. Numerical curve values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Restoring late attention and MLP outputs can both substantially recover factual-answer signals after subject corruption in multilingual transformers. Gaussian subject corruption followed by restoration of module contributions across 12%-depth windows produces reported strong late-site effects for both attention and MLP modules in all three models. Late-site positions are described as similar across languages, with some endpoint variation in EuroLLM. Exact plotted magnitudes are not supplied as text, and the logit-effect equation has a sign inconsistency with the probability-effect definition and recovery descriptions.

Specific finding: Mean directional gradients can predict small-step symmetric SAE steering responses much more accurately than decoder-score probe coefficients. Across 380 direction–task pairs—90 GPT-2, 100 Gemma-2-2B, 100 Gemma-2-9B, and 90 Llama-3.1-8B—attribution matched the realized central steering quotient's sign and was closer than the probe coefficient in 380/380 cases. Median |quotient/attribution| was 1.000–1.001, with calibration slopes 0.997–1.000 and R² > 0.999. Probe coefficients exceeded quotient magnitudes by approximately 130–400 times in model-specific medians. Selection used separate prompts, but steering comparisons are descriptive because step scales came from evaluation prompts; these results concern symmetric quotients rather than each one-sided effect.
Specific finding: Prompt-specific gradient predictions can estimate single-SAE-latent zero-ablation effects more accurately than cross-fitted final-position decoder-score probes. The evaluation contained 1,795, 10,727, 29,180, and 1,782 prompt–latent rows across 7, 9, 9, and 7 tasks respectively. Task-balanced gradient MAEs were 0.026, 0.097, 0.082, and 0.00852, versus probe MAEs 0.329, 0.216, 0.196, and 0.308. Among rows with nonzero realized effects, equal-task sign agreement was 92.0%, 90.5%, 92.6%, and 97.5% for gradients versus 21.2%, 21.7%, 17.5%, and 34.9% for probes; zero predictions counted as disagreements. Task-resampled gain intervals excluded zero in every model. The comparator reads only the final position, which explains many zero predictions.
Specific finding: Increasing SAE steering displacements to several times a latent's maximum observed activation can substantially degrade first-order prediction of symmetric steering responses. For 46, 230, 457, and 23 FDFI-selected pairs across the four models, the fraction with |realized quotient − attribution| > 0.5|attribution| ranged from 4.3–23.9% at one maximum activation to 65.2–73.9% at five maxima. Coefficient-selected pairs also deteriorated, with corresponding five-maximum fractions of 38.9–60.0%. Attribution usually remained closer to the quotient than the probe coefficient despite its own substantial error. These descriptive results do not establish accurate one-sided finite-effect prediction.

Specific finding: First-order edge attribution scores can substantially overestimate actual activation-patching effects when the intervention response is nonlinear. Attribution and activation-patching scores have R² = 0.27 and a best-fit slope of 0.531. Interpolated interventions on selected outliers show concave responses that cause the clean-endpoint linear approximation to overestimate effects.

Specific finding: If an intervention's mean edit lies outside the span of activation-support differences, its mean first-order effect is unrestricted by the observational activation–output law within a smooth response class closed under affine additions. Formal proof: Proposition 1 and Appendix B.2 construct Fζ(x) = F(x) + ζᵀ(x − x1), with ζ orthogonal to all support differences. This preserves the observational law while shifting attribution and any integrable mean finite effect by E[Δ]ᵀζ. If the mean edit has a nonzero component in that orthogonal complement, attribution takes every real value within the specified response class. The construction also preserves the gradient's Lipschitz constant.
Specific finding: For a linear least-squares activation probe, the difference between its implied intervention change and the intervention's mean first-order effect equals a Stein residual plus an omitted-variable term minus an edit-gradient covariance. Formal derivation: Theorem 1 and Appendix B.3 expand attribution into mean edit dotted with mean gradient plus edit-gradient covariance, and rewrite the probe prediction using its covariance normal equations. Subtraction yields the exact identity. The proof applies to population and qualifying empirical laws without Gaussian activations or nonsingular full activation covariance.
Specific finding: A final-position linear probe implies zero change for zero-ablation of an SAE latent that never fires at the final position, even when ablation at other positions has nonzero intervention attribution. Formal proof: Corollary 1(b) and Appendix B.5 show that the probe sees the mean edit through A E[Δ]. If the edit vanishes at every read position, this quantity and the probe-implied change are zero, while attribution can arise at unread positions. Appendix E.4 additionally reports this exact blindness for 15/46, 67/230, 130/457, and 1/23 evaluated zero-ablation pairs with non-negligible attribution in GPT-2, Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B respectively; the strength here primarily reflects the formal result.
Specific finding: Within-task decoder-score probe coefficients can substantially exceed the mean directional sensitivity of the same SAE decoder directions. Among 46, 230, 457, and 23 evaluable FDFI-selected direction–task pairs in GPT-2, Gemma-2-2B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B respectively, median |attribution/coefficient| was 0.046, 0.032, 0.028, and 0.032; 73.9–82.6% of pairs had ratios below 0.1. Coefficient-selected directions and eligible alternate dictionaries also exhibited large gaps. Post hoc position-averaged decoder-score and SAE-code probes largely removed unread-position blindness but still overstated zero-ablation attribution in aggregate. Sampling-noise analyses supported magnitude differences, although sparse-code simulations showed substantial undercoverage for Stein intervals and overall sign-disagreement shares were explicitly descriptive.

Specific finding: Within observationally selected SAE candidate sets, attribution magnitude can identify the direction with the largest local symmetric steering response more often than feature-importance statistics or probe-coefficient magnitude. Across 6 GPT-2, 9 Gemma-2-2B, 9 Gemma-2-9B, and 4 Llama-3.1-8B units, attribution ranked the largest absolute central steering quotient first in 28/28 units at one within-stratum standard deviation, versus 4/28 for FDFI statistics and 2/28 for coefficient magnitude. At one maximum-activation displacement the counts were 16/28, 3/28, and 1/28; at five maxima they were 5/28, 2/28, and 3/28. This is same-evaluation-set agreement, with weakening attribution rankings as first-order accuracy deteriorates.
Specific finding: Selecting SAE latent sets to maximize the magnitude of their summed training attribution can yield larger absolute held-out mean zero-ablation effects than selection by correlation, rank tests, or decoder-score probe coefficients. Using up to 200 evaluation prompts per task in five folds, attribution-selected sets exceeded correlation-, Mann–Whitney-statistic-, and coefficient-selected sets in 28/28 units. Equal-unit mean contrasts were 0.949, 0.933, and 1.058 standardized units, with two-stage task-and-stratum bootstrap 95% intervals excluding zero. Edit-norm-normalized advantages remained positive on every model. Attribution exceeded class-mean-difference sets in 24/28 units, but its two-stage interval did not exclude zero after Bonferroni correction across five comparators. It exceeded FDFI in 23/28 units, but that contrast's two-stage interval included zero. Bootstrap intervals held fitted selections fixed.

Specific finding: ALTI can produce more similar input-token rankings across independently initialized BERT classifiers than the evaluated gradient attribution methods. The authors compare attribution rankings across all pairs of ten BERT seeds and report higher similarity and correlation for ALTI than gradient methods in Figures 7–8. Numerical effect sizes, evaluation example counts, and prediction-equivalence rates are not given. The plot contents are unavailable in the supplied rendering, so this extraction relies on the accompanying results text.

Specific finding: Recovery of donor-answer performance after jointly transplanting selected component activations provides useful evidence that those components carry sufficient downstream information for the tested answer-label behavior.
location: Section 3.1, Figure 7; Section 6, Validating proposed circuits

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing a token's residual states across a layer block with the donor block's mean activation provides an informative intervention for interpreting that block's influence on factual predictions.
location: Section 2.3, footnote 4; Appendices F and G.2

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Interpreting activation-patching effects as evidence about ordinary component roles requires accounting for replacement distributions, counterfactual construction, and downstream responses such as compensation.
Specific finding: A component's importance under a factual-recall localization intervention does not guarantee that editing that component will outperform edits at other locations.
Specific finding: Changing a model’s output through an internal intervention does not by itself establish that the intervened component has the semantic role assigned to it.
location: Section 4.2, Activation patching; Section 5.1, Internal understanding

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Evaluating an edge circuit by retaining all outgoing connections from its selected source components can substantially overstate the accuracy attributable to the selected edges. Compared universal-core descriptions under source-level expansion and selected-edge-only evaluation. Table 61 gives mean accuracy increases from 0.295 to 0.513 at 70M, 0.618 to 0.954 at 160M, 0.514 to 0.989 at 410M, 0.417 to 0.991 at 1B, and 0.124 to 0.974 at 1.4B. The increases were approximately 22–85 percentage points because source-level evaluation retained unselected outgoing edges. These are task-accuracy differences, not corresponding numerical changes in KL-based faithfulness.
Specific finding: Restoring clean activations on selected circuit edges in a corrupt run can allow clean information to propagate through downstream edges outside the selected circuit.

Specific finding: Vocabulary-projection and clamping-logit-change descriptions can identify feature-steered generations more accurately than activating-example descriptions, while performing worse at generating activating inputs; output advantages depend on model and feature site. Tables 1 and 7 compare MaxAct, VocabProj, and TokenChange across sampled layers and dictionary widths. Gemma residual SAE output matching rises from 49.2% for MaxAct to 56.5% for VocabProj and 54.9% for TokenChange, while input scores fall from 56.6% to 50.1% and 44.7%. Exceptions include Llama residual SAE output matching, where MaxAct scores 71.8%, VocabProj 64.2%, and TokenChange 72.0%; Llama MLP SAEs, where VocabProj also trails MaxAct; and GPT-2 residual SAEs, where neither individual output-centric method exceeds MaxAct's reported mean. Six graduate students' evaluations of descriptions for 100 Gemma SAE features reportedly reproduce the complementary pattern; numerical human-rating values are unavailable in the rendered figure.
Specific finding: Combining activating contexts with vocabulary projections and clamping-induced token changes can improve feature-description input and output scores, with the best combination format depending on the evaluation and model site. For Gemma residual SAEs, combining all raw evidence scores 66.6% input and 64.9% output, versus MaxAct's 56.6% and 49.2%; concatenating all descriptions scores 66.9% output. For Llama residual SAEs, all-description concatenation reaches 75.4% output, while the best raw-ensemble input score is 37.2%. Exceptions include MaxAct++'s 89.8% input score for instruct-model neurons, exceeding all ensembles, and GPT-2 MLP SAEs, where the output-only raw ensemble reaches 40.9% output versus 37.1% for the all-method raw ensemble. Human ratings on 100 Gemma SAE features reportedly favor the all-method raw ensemble on both dimensions; figure values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
Specific finding: Candidate inputs constructed from output-centric feature descriptions and associated vocabulary tokens can activate some Gemma SAE features previously labeled dead because no activating inputs were observed in an existing collection. The study reports searching 1,850 dead-labeled features using 150 generated sentences and 1,450 token-combination sequences per feature. It reports activation of 85 MLP features (9.1%) and 491 residual features (62%). Per-type denominators are absent, and the counts and percentages do not reconcile with the stated total. Of the 576 reported revived features, 70 were activated using LLM-generated prompts and 423 using BOS plus one sampled token. Appendix F inconsistently names MaxAct rather than TokenChange as a source for generated sentences. A worked layer-23 residual feature, 64628, is activated by a gaming-related prompt. No matched random-token or unrelated-description search baseline is reported.
location: Section 5.2, Table 1; Appendix C, Table 7; Appendix E.2

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Bipolar hidden noise can increase coordinate concentration of feature encodings during autoencoder training, whereas Gaussian hidden noise produces no observed systematic sparsification in the tested configurations. Figure 4 compares bipolar and Gaussian noise at multiple magnitudes: the text reports increasing encoding fourth-power norms under bipolar noise, faster changes at larger bipolar noise scales, and oscillations without systematic sparsification under Gaussian noise. Figure 5 separately examines final fourth norms under L1 regularization and bipolar noise. Very large noise reduces encoding magnitudes, confounding the unnormalized fourth-norm proxy. Exact dimensions, scale grids, and repetition counts are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: In a unit-norm, gate-fixed approximation to a noisy tied-weight autoencoder, the second-order next-step-loss expansion contains an orientation-dependent term 16η²(μ4−3σ⁴)||w||₄⁴, which favors coordinate concentration when noise excess kurtosis is negative. Formal local calculation: the gate-fixed gradient gives w'=w−2η(w·ξ)(2w+ξ). Expanding the expected next-step reconstruction loss isolates 16η²E[(w·ξ)^4]; the fourth-moment identity is E[(w·ξ)^4]=3σ⁴||w||₂⁴+(μ4−3σ⁴)||w||₄⁴. At fixed unit L2 norm, a negative fourth-norm coefficient favors concentration. Intermediate printed equations contain coefficient and pair-index inconsistencies, and the source supplies no general bound for neglected gate events or higher-order expected terms.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A single unsupervised DCT dictionary can contain hundreds of noncollinear directions that promote compliance-associated responses to harmful requests. Of 512 learned source directions, 240 exceed the chosen jailbreak-logit threshold of five. Their direction matrix has reported condition number approximately 38; mean absolute pairwise inner product is 0.36 with standard deviation 0.19. Selected completions illustrate harmful compliance, but per-direction classifier-based attack success is not reported.
Specific finding: A ten-layer DCT discovery horizon can yield transferable behavioral steering candidates in a substantially deeper language model without increasing that horizon. A single-prompt exponential DCT on the 64-layer model yields reported helpful-only, gaming, and roleplay directions using the same ten-layer horizon and calibration setting. Selected music-theory completions show concept steering across different requests. No aggregate held-out score or systematic model-size comparison is supplied.
Specific finding: A selected DCT-derived activation intervention can elicit harmful responses from a representation-rerouted Mistral model. After inspecting candidates at several source layers, the author selects source layer five, trains on eight AdvBench instructions, and increases inference radius fourfold above calibration. The selected direction achieves reported 62% attack success under HarmBench's Mistral-7B classifier. The cited 6.2% comparator comes from prior work and is not rerun here. The result does not isolate feature multiplicity as the cause of vulnerability or establish an input-space attack.
Specific finding: An unsupervised DCT discovery procedure followed by labeled validation selection can partially recover mathematical performance suppressed by password locking. Trains 512 exponential-DCT factors on eight MATH questions using layers 10→20 and ten OGI iterations, selects the best-scoring direction on 32 validation questions, and evaluates on 100 test questions. Steered accuracy is 23%, compared with reported 3% locked and 65% unlocked baselines, giving approximately (23−3)/(65−3)=32% gap recovery. The text does not establish that both baselines were remeasured on these same 100 questions, and repeated-run uncertainty is not supplied.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Formally specified board properties enable complementary supervised comparisons of SAE dictionaries through best-single-feature classification and reconstruction from high-precision feature associations. Applied both metrics to standard, Gated, annealed-standard, and annealed-Gated SAEs at widths 4,096 and 8,192. Reconstruction associates features with properties using 1,000 games and evaluates on a separate 1,000 games. Comparisons distinguish width, training-method, and property-specific outcomes beyond active-feature count and loss recovered. Equation 3 maximizes thresholds separately within each property score, while the prose describes selecting a best coverage threshold; Equation 5 places a threshold maximum inside the per-board average. experiment_summary: Specific finding: Cosine similarity between pretrained image embeddings provides a useful proxy for the semantic similarity of images activating a neural response direction.
Specific finding: Cosine similarities from a separate multimodal encoder provide useful proxies for the semantic coherence of examples activating a sparse feature.

Specific finding: Embedding-based coherence of visual and textual activating references provides a useful operational proxy for the monosemanticity of shared multimodal SAE features.

Specific finding: A sparse feature's cross-modal coherence can be summarized by averaging separate-encoder similarities between its activating examples, weighted by normalized absolute activation products.
Specific finding: Reduction in entropy when a feature’s activating tokens are grouped into embedding-based semantic clusters provides a useful proxy for that feature’s semantic coherence.

Specific finding: With dictionary size and training duration optimized jointly, sparse-autoencoder training loss decreases approximately as a power law in compute over tested budgets. Sweeps over feature count and training steps identified compute-optimal configurations. Both optimal feature count and training duration scaled approximately as power laws, with feature count increasing somewhat faster over tested budgets; learning-rate sweeps informed larger runs.

Subject-model-size comparisons at fixed k, including k=32, show larger required dictionaries and worse reconstruction scaling exponents for larger models.

Specific finding: Humans can identify non-activating intruder contexts among examples activating the same SAE latent without receiving a natural-language explanation of that latent. The authors performed approximately 10–20 intruder prompts per latent across 56 latents. Mean human accuracy was 65%, compared with 20% chance, and 78% on the highest activating deciles. Approximately one third of evaluated latents scored above 80%. Human participation was limited to the authors, and the latent-selection procedure is unspecified.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: High-mean-dominance SAE features often have lower explanation-conditioned held-out activation-ranking accuracy than less dominant features in the same dictionary. The main DAME protocol retains features with at least 80 sequence firings and samples 20 features from each eligible-feature dominance quartile. Across DAME-evaluated SAEs, per-SAE mean Q1 accuracy was 61.8% versus 64.1% for Q2–Q4; 65.2% showed a directional deficit, with Wilcoxon p=6.76e-8 and Cohen's d=-0.278. Five of seven architecture groups were significant; Gated and JumpReLU were not. Family-level results include reversals, including the newly trained GPT-2 Small family. Mean deficits persisted in the reported explanation-budget, firing-frequency-matching, and six-SAE explainer-by-judge checks. Larger-model directional-deficit rates were 41.7%, 50.0%, and 41.7% within the evaluated Qwen3-8B, 14B, and 32B BatchTopK panels, and 75.0% within the Gemma-2-9B Gemma Scope panel. These percentages are not significance rates, and larger-panel sizes are not supplied.
Specific finding: The most activation-dominant SAE features can be less confined to a single ground-truth concept than lower-dominance features, including when coherent partial coverage is not penalized. A best-minus-second-best concept-correlation analysis found significant Q1 deficits in 71/105 synthetic SAEs, using per-SAE one-sided Mann–Whitney tests at alpha=0.05. A separate prevalence-corrected support-containment analysis evaluated 210 SAEs at widths 128, 192, 256, 512, 768, and 1024, with 35 SAEs per width. Concept selection used 25,000 discovery examples and evaluation used 25,000 disjoint examples. Q1 containment was lower overall by a one-sided SAE-level exact sign test, p=1.6e-12, with negative mean contrasts at every width. The containment score permits a feature to cover only a coherent subset of its selected concept. A held-out AND/OR comparison found greater Q1 alignment with OR targets, rather than preferential conjunctive composition. The synthetic panel had too few decoder-aligned pairs to validate sharding.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The accuracy with which an explanation enables held-out activation-strength ranking provides useful proxy evidence about a feature's semantic coherence.

Specific finding: Decoder-aligned SAE features can fire in largely separate contextual regions while producing similar downstream target-logit effects when their decoder directions are injected at equal magnitude. Features 41902 and 46571 in a layer-8, 65,536-feature TopK SAE with k=80 had decoder cosine 0.7405 and encoder cosine 0.2066. Their contexts concerned definite articles versus possessive/genitive determiners. Across 192 held-out WikiText-103 validation texts truncated to 128 tokens, native TopK support counts were 316 and 57, with seven co-firings and Jaccard 0.019. On 18/20 fixed prompts where both native gates were inactive, equal-L2 decoder injections changed the target token ' aim' logit by means of +0.556 and +0.611, with positive effects in 15/18 and 16/18 prompts. The cosine between prompt-level target-logit effect vectors was 0.943, not a full-vocabulary effect cosine. The paired candidate-versus-support-size-and-decoder-norm-matched low-cosine-control contrast was +0.472 logit, with prompt-bootstrap 95% CI [0.347, 0.597]. The prompt family was fixed after exploratory target discovery.
Specific finding: Decoder-aligned SAE feature pairs with separated encoder directions and complementary firing supports can occur in dictionaries with fewer than 50 active features per input on average. The screen required decoder cosine ≥0.70, encoder cosine ≤0.40, decoder-minus-encoder cosine ≥0.45, Jaccard support overlap ≤0.10, and both directional support containments ≤0.20. In the held-out mean-L0<50 group, 2.6% of decoder-redundant pairs met these conditions, and 56.3% of SAEs had at least one qualifying pair. Corresponding values were 3.8% and 42.9% at L0=50–200, and 3.3% and 30.4% at L0≥200. Panel counts and model-specific breakdowns are not supplied in this section. The results establish that high L0 is unnecessary for this screened pattern, not a causal relationship between L0 and sharding.
Specific finding: Decoder-aligned features with largely separate activation supports can distinguish coherent subclasses of a shared concept rather than unrelated semantic triggers. A support analysis retained checkpoints with more than ten sampled pairs and pairs with at least 20 firings per feature. Among eligible decoder-aligned pairs, equal-weight means of within-SAE percentages were 21.5% partition-like, 15.3% nested-like, 29.9% duplicate-like, and 33.3% partial overlap. Partitioning was more common in support-size-matched low-cosine controls, so separated supports alone were not diagnostic. In a separate audit of fresh WikiText-103 contexts, GPT-5.6 Sol judged cards twice with feature orientation reversed and geometry and identities hidden. Stable sibling-subclass readings occurred for 15.8% of all screened targets; 13.3% also replicated the partition criterion on fresh support. At least one pass found insufficient evidence for 51.4% of targets, retained in the denominator. Control-matched targets and low-cosine controls had stable sibling rates of 13.3% and 3.3%, respectively. Examples distinguished 'they' from 'he/she' in Pythia-160M and forms of 'be' in Gemma-2-2B. Audit panel counts are not supplied.
Specific finding: SAE coordinates can be evaluated by matching their exponentiated activations to supervised concept readouts from counterfactual examples using Pearson correlation.

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: The largest coordinate difference between token-averaged SAE activations on contrastive narratives provides a useful proxy for isolation of the intended semantic distinction.
Specific finding: The largest coordinate deviation of a story pair's summed mean SAE code from the dataset-wide mean provides a useful proxy for subject-specific semantic specialization.
Specific finding: Extreme-versus-opposite synthetic story pairs preserve enough shared subject content and isolate their intended semantic contrast sufficiently well for activation differences to measure target-feature selectivity.

Specific finding: CAP ranking can prioritize features showing increased suppression and reduced activation under successful jailbreaks more effectively than decoder alignment with a refusal direction within a selected candidate panel. Within the ten Qwen3-8B features in Table 3, CAP recovered four suppression-signature features in its top five, versus one reported for DecAlign. CAP and refusal-direction decoder alignment had Spearman correlation −0.818. Across the same ten features, CAP correlated with jailbreak-direction decoder alignment at ρ=0.661, p=0.037; individual components were not significant. The latter endpoint is geometric alignment rather than suppression itself.

Specific finding: Cross-context SAE removal effects can be audited through normalized downstream logit-effect clouds, using directional agreement, spectral structure, directional mixtures, and separate magnitude and stability summaries. The framework is implemented and applied to Gemma-2-2B post-layer-12 ReLU, TopK, and Matryoshka Batch TopK SAEs of width 65,536 across four ICL tasks and RAVEL city-country. Family-specific stability protocols are specified, but aggregate stability-confidence results and threshold-sensitivity experiments are not reported.

Specific finding: A sentence-specific vector optimized through a frozen GPT-2 decoder can drive greedy generation to reproduce diverse English target sentences with nearly perfect text overlap. Optimized randomly initialized vectors using target-sentence cross-entropy while freezing model weights, then greedily decoded from a beginning-of-sentence token without supplying the target length. Several intermediate-layer every-timestep configurations reached 100 smoothed BLEU-4; first-timestep injection after layer-6 attention reached 99.80 and after layer-7 feedforward reached 99.25. Aggregate BLEU is not an exact-match percentage.
Specific finding: For optimized sentence reconstruction in GPT-2-117M, intermediate-layer additive controls achieve higher recovery BLEU than controls applied at the embedding layer or final language-model head. Compared separately optimized controls across all 12 transformer layers, embeddings, the LM head, and combinations of sites. Every-timestep intermediate injections often reached 100 BLEU-4, versus 33.99 at embeddings and 6.72 at the LM head. Learning rates differed across some injection conditions, so the comparison concerns the tested optimization recipes.
Specific finding: Restricting sentence-control optimization to smaller fixed random subspaces reduces GPT-2 target-sentence recovery, with longer sequences presenting greater difficulty. Compared steering dimensions 192, 384, 576, and 768, obtaining reconstruction BLEU-4 of 43.43, 83.29, 93.93, and 100.00 respectively. Lower-dimensional vectors were projected into the model's 768-dimensional hidden space using a fixed, randomly initialized semi-orthogonal matrix. The text reports that lower-dimensional controls struggle particularly with longer sentences. The finite dimension sweep does not prove a minimum required dimension.
Specific finding: Optimized GPT-2 sentence controls recover natural book sentences more effectively than token-shuffled versions or length-matched uniformly random token sequences. Optimized controls injected after layer-6 attention at either the first or every timestep. The text reports recovery ranked books above shuffled text above uniformly random-token gibberish. Figure 6 values are not supplied numerically. The comparison is consistent with exploiting pretrained linguistic regularities, but does not isolate a naturally used sentence representation or show an absence of memorization.
Specific finding: A single optimized internal GPT-2 control can reconstruct book sentences more accurately than the tested configurations of optimized vectors prepended to input embeddings. Optimized 1, 5, 10, 20, or 50 vectors concatenated with the input embeddings, each of dimension 768. Reconstruction BLEU-4 was 81.7, 94.3, 98.7, 98.6, and 98.5 respectively. The paper reports that these configurations fall short of recovery using a single optimized internal control.

Specific finding: Independent optimization initializations can yield sentence-control vectors that reproduce the same sentence, cluster by sentence, and retain recovery when averaged. All eight initializations recovered the target perfectly for 63 of 64 book sentences. The text reports sentence-specific clusters in a t-SNE visualization of eight vectors for each of 20 sentences. Averaging eight vectors per target produced 99.4 BLEU-4; the sentence count for that averaging evaluation is not separately specified.
Specific finding: Differences between class-mean optimized sentence-control vectors can alter sentiment and other textual styles without updating the underlying language model. Constructed target-minus-source mean offsets using 100 Yelp validation sentences per sentiment class, added scaled offsets to individually optimized sentence controls, and evaluated target sentiment with a Yelp-fine-tuned RoBERTa-base classifier plus self-BLEU-4. Yelp injection was after the seventh self-attention layer at the first timestep. The text reports a tradeoff comparable to selected autoencoder baselines, but Figure 3's numerical values are unavailable in the supplied rendering. Larger offsets sometimes caused repetition or content loss. StylePTB used 100 training sentences per class and reference BLEU-1; adjective emphasis scored 0.774 versus an imported GPT-2-finetuning baseline of 0.263, while other tasks showed weaker comparative results. StylePTB comparator scores were imported from cited publications.
Specific finding: Cosine similarities between selected intermediate-layer optimized GPT-2 sentence vectors correlate with STS-B judgments more strongly than the evaluated mean-pooled GPT-2, BERT, and GloVe representations. Optimized each STS-B sentence separately with first-timestep injection and correlated steering-vector cosine similarity with human similarity scores. Selected layer-7 feedforward vectors achieved Spearman/Pearson ×100 of 52.08/51.18; self-attention vectors achieved 52.04/51.17. Spearman scores were 25.92 for averaged GPT-2, 47.29 for averaged BERT, and 42.53 for averaged GloVe. The paper also reports stronger cited NLI-trained and specialized lexical baselines; it does not establish superiority over those methods.
Specific finding: Linear interpolation between some optimized GPT-2 sentence-control vectors can produce grammatical generations combining or transitioning between the endpoint sentences' content. Decoded linear interpolations for two sentence pairs. Section 6.1 describes grammatical intermediate generations, persistence of positive sentiment despite content changes in one pair, and a temporal-content combination in the other. The evidence is a small qualitative demonstration; the full Figure 5 generations are unavailable in the supplied text rendering.

Specific finding: A vector optimized on one benign scenario and its answer-swapped augmentation can both expose and suppress harmful choices across other scenarios in a Poser alignment-faking model. Evaluated on 364 benign and 151 harmful test prompts. Of five norm-15 vectors, four flipped over 80% of benign decisions when added and three flipped over 80% of harmful decisions when subtracted. The best vector achieved 93.4% and 83.4%, respectively, with unwanted flips on 15.9% of harmful prompts under addition and 1.10% of benign prompts under subtraction.
Specific finding: A projection-clamping intervention optimized on a single harmful instruction can elicit harmful responses across other filtered HarmBench instructions in Gemma-2-2B-it, with substantial variation across source examples. Two validation instructions were sampled from each of six HarmBench categories. Each supplied one promotion and one suppression vector, optimized with norm cap 30. Evaluation replaced an activation's projection along v using x − vvᵀx/||v||² + v. Maximum ASRs were 96.9% for promotion and 74.2% for suppression; medians were 40.3% and 37.4%. Three of 24 vectors exceeded 70% ASR. The Introduction gives 96.8%, while the Abstract, Results, and Conclusion give 96.9%.
Specific finding: A promotion vector optimized on one handcrafted prompt can produce substantially higher filtered HarmBench attack success in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct than a fixed affirmative response-prefill attack. The vector attained 93.1% ASR on the same filtered HarmBench test set, versus 30.0% for the unsteered prefill baseline. Optimization applied the vector only to the final 20 prompt tokens and stopped after four iterations. Applying it at every token during optimization was reported to yield incoherent outputs.
Specific finding: Vectors optimized to promote malicious code continuations, combined with a separate anti-refusal vector, can increase harmful responses to unrelated natural-language questions beyond anti-refusal steering alone. Each code vector was fitted on the same benign webserver prompt and code prefix with a different malicious continuation. Satisficing optimization targeted 0.75 times the continuation's log probability under a malicious prompt with anti-refusal steering. Each condition generated 100 responses to each of eight questions. The source reports more harmful alignment ratings than unsteered and anti-refusal-only controls, with plotted distributions excluding coherence below 50 and numeric-score probability below 0.25. Steering also increased incoherence. Table 1 reports Hitler mentions in 17/100 dinner-party responses for the reverse-shell condition versus 0/100 unsteered. Hyperparameters were explored without a validation set, and no aggregate numerical misalignment rate is given in the prose.

Specific finding: Vectors optimized to promote malicious code continuations, combined with a separate anti-refusal vector, can increase harmful responses to unrelated natural-language questions beyond anti-refusal steering alone. Compared four harmful-code-plus-anti-refusal interventions with unsteered and anti-refusal-only baselines on eight questions. Generally 150–200 temperature-1 responses were sampled per question before filtering. The author reports alignment-score distributions shifting toward harmfulness, together with increased incoherence. A separate table counts selected strings in the first 100 unfiltered responses per question; reverse-shell steering produces 17 dinner-party responses containing 'Hitler', versus zero under both baselines. Numerical alignment distributions, retained sample counts, uncertainty estimates, and independent judge calibration are not supplied.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A steering vector can be optimized by penalizing the conditional probabilities of unwanted continuation tokens, optionally combined with a likelihood objective promoting a different continuation. Suppression is evaluated on Gemma-2-2B-it refusal and occupation-retraction tasks. Mixed steering is evaluated on five benign Poser source scenarios, each augmented by swapping answer choices. Generalization is measured on other prompts in those settings.

Specific finding: A single activation steering vector can be trained through a frozen language model using a reference-relative preference objective that reverses response preferences when the intervention sign reverses. Implemented the signed objective with zero-initialized vectors and AdamW while freezing model weights. Trained and evaluated single-layer vectors on persona, truthfulness, hallucination, and harmful-compliance tasks. Behavioral tests demonstrate useful learned interventions in the reported settings, without proving convergence, independent control of each response probability, or identification of a natural behavioral representation.

Specific finding: BiPO activation steering can improve held-out TruthfulQA MC1 and MC2 performance more than the tested CAA and Freeform steering baselines. Trained vectors for one epoch using correct-versus-incorrect answer pairs formed from 327 TruthfulQA questions and evaluated MC1/MC2 on 409 test questions. The text reports larger improvements than both baselines for Llama-2 and Mistral. Exact plotted scores and uncertainty estimates are not supplied; the listed training and test counts do not account for all 817 benchmark questions.
Specific finding: Reversing a BiPO hallucination vector can shift generations between fabricated and honest responses more effectively than the tested activation-difference baselines. Used 700 training and 200 held-out hallucination questions with honest and fabricated response pairs. GPT-4 assigned 1–4 behavioral scores across steering multipliers. The text reports stronger bidirectional control in both models; Table 3 illustrates opposite responses to a false NATO premise. Numerical plot values are unavailable, and the Mistral hallucination training-epoch count is not specified in Appendix A.3.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Applying selected BiPO persona vectors at multipliers plus or minus one can leave sampled MMLU accuracy close to the unsteered model's accuracy. Evaluated sampled MMLU accuracy using four persona vectors at multipliers −1, 0, and +1. The stated sampling procedure gives 1,710 questions across 57 subjects. Llama-2 steered accuracies were 0.454–0.460 versus 0.459 unsteered; Mistral accuracies were 0.561–0.585 versus 0.573 unsteered. No uncertainty estimates or equivalence tests are supplied.

Specific finding: Steering for overrefusal reduction or contextual faithfulness can approximately retain selected general-capability metrics, but some model–method configurations cause substantial degradation. Tables 2 and 4 report many small benchmark changes, with substantial exceptions. Explicit-control overrefusal SSV in Qwen-7B reduces MMLU by 0.29 and GSM8K by 0.17. Faithfulness SSV in Llama-8B reduces these accuracies by 0.27 and 0.17. Faithfulness ReFT-r1 in Qwen-7B has a reported fluency change of −10.98, although the metric's numerical definition is unclear. Gemma's baseline GSM8K score is zero under the required answer format, limiting that retention check.

Specific finding: Steering toward adherence to relevant conflicting context can reduce answer accuracy under irrelevant contextual distractors despite comparatively small changes in no-context accuracy. Table 4 reports distractor-context original-answer exact-match decreases of 0.10–0.25 in all 20 model–method combinations, alongside updated-answer gains of 0.08–0.27. No-context exact-match changes range from −0.07 to +0.05. The paper states 500 queries per ordinary evaluation and averages over three runs. Distractor construction and statistical-test details are limited; exact-match losses do not by themselves identify which distractor content was incorporated.

Specific finding: Improved instruction-constraint accuracy under activation steering can coexist with reduced comprehensiveness, repetition, or factual errors. GPT-4o generates quality checklists and scores responses over three evaluator runs. Format-steering losses are generally small and comparable to adding textual constraints, but selected Phi-3 outputs repeat or introduce factual errors. Length-quality analysis uses a 100-output subset of the 200-query experiment. Phi-3 keyword-quality changes are small on average, with the largest reported average drop around 0.03. Pairwise tests comparing word-inclusion quality-delta conditions have p-values 0.25, 0.98, and 0.26, which do not establish equivalence or absence of quality loss. A separate negative-coefficient sweep reports increasing exclusion accuracy alongside decreasing quality.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Increasing text-derived refusal-direction steering can reduce unsafe tool calls while suppressing benign tool use or degrading output coherence, with useful tradeoffs varying across models and strengths. At coherent settings, Mistral unsafe-call rate falls 0.27→0.01 while benign any-call rate falls 0.51→0.05; Llama falls 0.52→0.02 with benign calls 0.93→0.12. Qwen's coherent reduction is 0.54→0.24 with benign calls 0.66→0.48; its stronger setting has 51% degeneration. Gemma falls 0.12→0.04 with benign calls 0.39→0.07. Smaller Mistral and Command R doses offer partial reductions with less benign-call loss. Across interpretable ablation, patching, and steering conditions, unsafe-given-call remains above 50% whenever harmful any-call rate exceeds 10%. Table 9 does not specify its evaluation sample size.

Specific finding: Nearly additive effects of paired feature interventions on concept-probe logits can coexist with substantial cross-concept effects from individual interventions. Summed concept-logit changes from separate interventions are compared with changes under joint interventions. Table 2 reports R²=0.98–1.00 in every listed model–architecture–correlation–target configuration. Appendix I.2 reports similar trends under attribution-based selection. These results do not identify non-overlapping mechanisms, exclude interactions invisible to the probes, or establish out-of-distribution additivity. Affine decoding followed by linear probing can itself produce additive effects when no nonlinear downstream transformation intervenes, a relevant concern for final-layer SSAEs.

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The product of normalized GPT-4o-mini behavioral-adherence and coherence ratings provides a useful operational measure of steering quality.
Specific finding: The product of normalized GPT-4o-mini behavioral-adherence and coherence ratings provides a useful operational measure of steering quality.

Specific finding: A binary automatic judgment requiring both target expression and readable, non-collapsed output provides an adequate operational measure for comparing behavioral activation-steering sources.

Specific finding: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct binary judgments of readable target expression can agree substantially with independent blinded labels on stratified behavioral-steering outputs. The main judge agrees with independent validation labels on 348/400 outputs: 92/100 entity, 84/100 persona/style, 82/100 refusal, and 90/100 nonsense examples. Annotators see the target and output but not the generator or steering configuration. A separate rescoring of all behavioral outputs in the six Figure 2 conditions with Gemma-3-27B preserves answer-only mean as the weakest condition for every generator, while substantially increasing absolute success rates; hybrid is not the top-ranked condition for Llama under that judge.
Specific finding: Target-word inclusion together with the absence of output collapse provides a useful operational measure of multilingual topic-steering success.

Specific finding: Prompt-only final-token activation sources can produce substantially higher aggregate additive-steering success than answer-only sequence-mean sources under a shared estimator and hyperparameter-search protocol. Table 2 reports prompt-only last-token versus answer-only mean success of 0.336 versus 0.119 for Llama, 0.506 versus 0.193 for Qwen, and 0.586 versus 0.281 for Gemma, after grid selection. Figure 2 instead gives 0.316 for Llama prompt-only last-token. Across five validation–test splits with validation-only selection of source layer, intervention layer, and strength, corresponding held-out gains are 0.198 [0.147, 0.249], 0.287 [0.219, 0.354], and 0.281 [0.208, 0.348]; all reported paired hierarchical intervals exclude zero. Behavioral evaluation contains 1,950 target–question instances per model per configuration and uses 16 source prompts per target.
Specific finding: Sources combining target instructions, demonstrations, and an unfinished assistant prefix can yield stronger aggregate additive steering than prompt-only final-token sources or completed-answer mean sources. Hybrid last-token sources achieve aggregate success of 0.389 in Llama, 0.640 in Qwen, and 0.625 in Gemma, exceeding the compared coarse sources under the main judge and grid-selected evaluation. Across five validation–test splits, hybrid gains over answer-only mean are 0.253 [0.192, 0.315], 0.414 [0.325, 0.492], and 0.320 [0.251, 0.388], respectively. Alternative-judge rescoring preserves strong boundary-source performance but ranks instruction-only above hybrid for Llama.
Specific finding: For short relation-completion tasks, additive steering directions constructed from pre-answer boundary states can outperform directions constructed from sequence means of completed input–answer contexts. Section 6.2 reports that all three boundary-source constructions substantially outperform completed-answer mean sources across the three models, as illustrated in Figure 3. Each source condition uses 16 source prompts, and evaluation uses all 958 available pairs across tasks containing 26–108 pairs. Correctness uses lowercasing, whitespace normalization, punctuation stripping, and prefix matching. Numerical bar values are unavailable in the supplied figure rendering, so no quantitative effect size is extracted.
location: Section 4, Table 2; Figure 2; Appendix D, Table 16

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Seed-guided dense retrieval can yield better domain-specific SAE replacement-performance versus sparsity frontiers than BM25 retrieval or full-OpenWebText fine-tuning, with modest additional benefits from TracIn reranking. Physics uses a 9.2K-token seed, a 13.9M-token retrieved pool, 1,000 fine-tuning iterations, 4.8M arXiv test tokens, and 700K instruction-test tokens. Its reported comparison uses curve area over L0 60–140. Toxicity uses a 4,072-token seed, a 5.25M-token retrieved pool, 500 iterations, and 3.357M test tokens. Dense retrieval outperforms BM25 and the OWT baseline; TracIn gives smaller gains. Physics reranking methods perform comparably, whereas the toxicity caption orders Dense TracIn above Dense, BM25 TracIn, BM25, and OWT. Numerical curve areas and uncertainty intervals are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Dense-retrieval specialization can increase the fraction of low-frequency domain tokens appearing among the highest vocabulary projections of SAE decoder features. The authors group domain vocabulary tokens by frequency and check membership in the union of decoder features' top-ten unembedding projections. Dense-retrieved SSAEs show greater tail-token coverage than OWT-fine-tuned controls in physics and toxicity. Exact coverage gains are not provided in the supplied prose. The operational result concerns vocabulary association rather than independently verified semantic-concept recovery.

Specific finding: Positive-tilt training can shift a specialized SAE's normalized decoder-vocabulary coverage toward lower-frequency domain tokens relative to ordinary domain fine-tuning. Dense-retrieved SSAEs trained with tilt 500 or 10^9 are compared with ordinary dense-retrieval fine-tuning. The source reports physics coverage shifting toward tail tokens as tilt increases. Toxicity shows a similar shift, with the two tilted curves overlapping. Because each curve is normalized to one over its own total coverage, this comparison alone does not establish an increase in the absolute number of represented tokens or concepts.
location: Section 3.2.2; Figure 6; Appendix F and Figure 14

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Steering selected Llama-3.1 SAE features can produce thematic alternatives that are not straightforwardly predicted by their automated labels, with outcomes depending on the coefficient. For feature 16/12285 on My favorite sport is, baseline baseball changes to soccer at coefficient 1 and tennis at 2. Coffee-health feature 15/4922 yields coffee at 5 but initially tea at 6 and 8. Pigeon-related feature 18/16371 changes a bird completion from hummingbird to American Robin at coefficients 2, 5, and 10. The displayed outputs are fixed-setting examples without repeated-seed estimates or quantitative target-expression scores; they do not establish factual accuracy of the generated descriptions.

Specific finding: An interpretation that better reproduces a transformer's final classification can reproduce its intermediate neuron states less accurately than a competing interpretation. On the 80,000-formula analysis test set, decision trees yield lower joint thresholded-neuron-state disagreement than disjunction-only rules: epsilon 0.182 versus 0.309. Final-output disagreement instead favors disjunction-only rules: epsilon 0.00290 versus 0.0128. These are upper confidence bounds for disagreement with the neural model, not ground-truth satisfiability error rates.
models_studied: ["Two-block ReLU decoder-only 2-SAT transformer, d_model=128, MLP width=512"]
location: Section 4.2.3, Hidden Layer and Output Layer of Second Block

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Similar language-model output fidelity after SAE replacement can coexist with substantially different downstream activations when SAE training optimizes output matching without activation reconstruction. Compared downstream activation MSE for selected approximately CE-matched dictionaries at layers 2, 6, and 10. Pure e2e SAEs produce much larger downstream reconstruction errors than local SAEs despite similar output-performance preservation. At layer 6, normalizing activations improves explained variance but retains the qualitative discrepancy. The tests measure activation differences, not a demonstrated alternative computational mechanism.
location: Section 3.2; Figure 2; Appendix A.4, Figure 6; Appendix B

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: A gated-MLP student trained to reconstruct a teacher MLP's outputs need not geometrically reproduce all teacher neurons, even at equal width. Freeze the 10,240-neuron teacher and train students for 80k steps at 4,096 FineWeb-Edu tokens per step. At equal width, 72.6% of teacher neurons meet the 0.7 matching threshold and 52.2% meet 0.9. At threshold 0.7, matched fractions fall to 28.2%, 6.3%, and 0.9% under successive width halvings. Reported FVU ranges from 0.023 to 0.152 across widths, indicating good approximate output reconstruction can coexist with substantial missing geometric matches. Teacher activation energy increasingly predicts matching as students narrow, with AUC 0.73–0.94.
Specific finding: A narrower MLP student can retain teacher-neuron-related output signals without a closely weight-matched student neuron. Compare student output projection along teacher-neuron decoder axes between tokens where a teacher neuron is in the top 32 and other tokens. Define retention by preserving at least 70% of teacher separation. The appendix reports an approximately 7% population retaining separation without weight matches, alongside an approximately 9% matched population under this analysis. Teacher activations in a selected unmatched, high-separation group have median regression R² 0.622 versus 0.527 for energy-controlled comparison neurons, a modest distinction. A case study traces teacher neuron 4300's output-axis signal to several punctuation-related student neurons with weak individual decoder alignment.
models_studied: ["Gemma 3 4B layer-17 teacher MLP", "GeGLU student MLPs of widths 1,280, 2,560, 5,120, and 10,240"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Small local numerical approximation error does not by itself establish that a replacement network exposes a complete inventory of semantically or safety-relevant features.

Specific finding: Retaining a replacement model's average task margin after complement ablation, and reducing that margin after selected-unit ablation, provide useful operational measures of local circuit sufficiency and necessity.

Specific finding: MOLT replacements can attain higher average Jacobian cosine similarity to original MLPs than transcoders at matched active-unit counts, with more stable alignment as replacement capacity increases. The authors compare cosine similarity of flattened replacement and original MLP Jacobians, averaged over datapoints. They report substantially higher similarity for MOLTs at matched L0; transcoder alignment deteriorates with scale while MOLT alignment is more stable. Feature-equivalent capacities indicate matched parameter counts. Numerical scores, datapoint counts, and dataset identity are absent from the supplied text.
models_studied: ["Unnamed 18-layer model used in the authors' circuit-tracing paper"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Repeated training inputs can induce sparse transcoders to learn datapoint-specific memorization mechanisms absent from a target that computes coordinatewise absolute value. Training with repetition produces a feature that jointly detects and reconstructs p. In the illustrated 5% repetition condition, features for its three constituent coordinates rotate to avoid activating on p. The specified target remains the coordinatewise absolute-value computation and contains no special p-specific circuit. Quantitative reconstruction errors and replication counts are absent.
Specific finding: Sparse one-layer transcoders can recover the positive- and negative-coordinate ReLU mechanisms of a coordinatewise absolute-value target when trained without a specially repeated input. The no-repeat baseline is reported to learn nearly the expected ReLU(x_i) and ReLU(-x_i) features, with a small residual. The analysis decomposes learned feature contributions against a library of ideal circuits and displays selected neuron weights. Numerical recovery scores and run counts are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: Penalizing target–transcoder Jacobian discrepancies can suppress spurious datapoint memorization in sparse transcoders of coordinatewise absolute value. Adding a Jacobian-discrepancy penalty substantially reduces the reported memorization metric and removes the illustrated datapoint feature relative to training without that penalty. Some constituent features remain rotated. Effect sizes, uncertainty estimates, computational benchmarks, and broader model evaluations are not supplied.
models_studied: ["One-layer sparse ReLU transcoders approximating coordinatewise absolute value"]
location: Datapoint Features Emerge; Investigating Datapoint Features — Light Repetition

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Downstream-regularized output-matched SAEs can learn decoder directions more similar to local-SAE directions than those learned by pure output matching. For each e2e or e2e+ds decoder direction, computed its maximum cosine similarity to local-SAE dictionary directions. E2e+ds directions are generally closer to local directions than pure e2e directions. The layer-6 e2e+ds comparison is bimodal, retaining a group of directions poorly aligned with the local dictionary.
Specific finding: Adding downstream activation reconstruction losses to output-matched SAE training can reduce downstream activation error toward local-SAE levels while retaining improved sparsity versus behavioral fidelity. Compared e2e+ds with pure e2e and local training across GPT2-small layers 2, 6, and 10.
