Hessian traces capture some stage boundaries and head groups but miss the LM2–LM3 distinction and exhibit ambiguous plateaus and peaks. Full-model FIM estimates use 30 generated samples and five probe vectors and are noisier. Fixed and adaptive approximate-rank procedures give sensitive, inconclusive results. Comparative clarity is assessed descriptively rather than through a quantitative recovery benchmark.
Specific finding: Attention-head trajectory clusters fitted on one small transformer's estimated refined LLCs can broadly transfer to independently initialized runs of the same architecture, despite variation in head counts and developmental stages. Applies shape-based clusters fitted on the original seed to three additional seeds. Broad head-type distinctions recur, although a previous-token head is assigned to a current-token cluster in one configuration and another run's current-token head is not distinguished. Two of the four runs have one induction head and one previous-token head each; two have two of each. Some runs lack the full-model LM3 decrease, while multigram-head rLLC decreases after LM2 recur.
Specific finding: Among second-layer multigram heads in a small attention-only transformer, higher final estimated weight-refined LLC is associated with more unique multigram patterns identified from ablation-sensitive examples. Counts unique identified delimiter pairs, skip n-gram tuples, and contiguous n-grams after mean-ablation-based example selection and compares these counts with final per-head wrLLC estimates. The text reports a positive association without a numerical correlation coefficient or uncertainty estimate; plotted values are unavailable in the supplied rendering.
models_studied: ["Approximately 3M-parameter two-layer attention-only transformer, main training seed"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Localized SGLD estimates preserve the ordering of component-specific population-loss learning coefficients sufficiently well to compare component complexity during training.

Specific finding: Localized Langevin estimates at training iterates preserve the ordering of relevant critical-point complexities sufficiently well to interpret upward estimate jumps as increasing local complexity.
location: Section 5; Figure 3; Appendices B and K

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: In a two-hidden-dimensional single-active-coordinate reconstruction model, optimized regular k-gon configurations for k=5,6,7,8 have local learning coefficient (3k−1)/2, including embeddings with additional inactive negatively biased coordinates. Formal analysis with symbolic and numerical calculations: Appendices H.1–H.2 derive polynomial stationarity conditions, report Mathematica solutions and nondegenerate Hessians modulo rotation, and obtain coefficients 7, 8.5, 10, and 11.5. Appendix H.3 derives a local reduction to the k-coordinate potential plus c−k for added inactive negatively biased coordinates. Complete symbolic Hessian certificates are not displayed.
Specific finding: SGD in a two-hidden-dimensional reconstruction model can traverse polygon-associated loss plateaus with decreasing reconstruction loss and increasing estimated local learning coefficient. SGD used 1,000 training examples, a 5,000-example test set, batch size 20, and learning rate 0.005. Four-gon initializations received Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.01 and trained for 4,500 epochs; Appendix B displays transition-containing runs from 30 seeds without establishing a transition prevalence estimate. A second experiment displays 400 trajectories initialized from n=100 posterior samples and trained for 5,000 epochs. Reported plateaus match classified critical configurations, with localized Langevin estimates rising at observed transitions; some estimates are negative because sampling escapes the initial phase.
Specific finding: A six-coordinate, two-hidden-dimensional reconstruction model can switch its dominant sampled posterior phase from five-gon to six-gon configurations at a sample size close to an approximate local-free-energy prediction. Ten datasets and sampling seeds were used per sample-size setting. Each dataset produced 3,000 thinned samples from six NUTS chains, each with 500 burn-in and 5,000 subsequent iterations. Convex-hull/bias classifications and manual t-SNE cluster inspections place the dominant-phase change between 600 and 700. The prediction uses losses 0.06874 and 0.04819, LLCs 7 and 8.5, and approximate prior constants. Classification is less reliable at low n, and reported mixing checks are diagnostic rather than guarantees.
Specific finding: Giving the inactive sixth coordinate of a five-gon reconstruction configuration its optimal positive bias can reduce reconstruction loss while increasing its local learning coefficient. Formal derivation: Appendix I differentiates the local potential to obtain the positive-bias stationary value 1/12. Lemma I.1 reports 17 positive Hessian eigenvalues and one rotational zero eigenvalue, yielding LLC 8.5. Table 1 gives loss 0.06874 and LLC 7 for the five-gon, versus loss 0.06180 and LLC 8.5 for five-plus. The Hessian computation is reported without its full matrix.
models_studied: ["Two-hidden-dimensional tied-weight ReLU TMS with c\u2265k and k\u2208{5,6,7,8}"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Finite-sample posterior competition between selected reconstruction-model phases can be approximated using population loss, a local-learning-coefficient logarithmic penalty, and constants dominated by prior density at representative critical points.
location: Section 4.1, Equations 8–9; Appendices C.1–C.3 and F.1

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Selected parent-gated SAE experts can exhibit activating examples consistent with interpretable broad concepts and subordinate semantic or lexical refinements. The text and captions describe selected parent/refinement examples involving marriage, airports, question words, media ratings, and regional categories. The residual-context visualizations emphasize strongly activated child features. Figure images are unavailable, so the evidence here is the authors' textual account. No random feature audit, hierarchy-accuracy metric, or causal validation is reported.
Specific finding: Interpretable parent–child feature examples can emerge in hierarchical SAE unembedding experiments without either the bi-orthogonality penalty or the L1 regularizer. Appendix B.2 reports comparisons with and without each regularizer after 5,000 training steps at batch size 8,192. The authors find no obvious qualitative interpretability or hierarchy advantage from either penalty. Examples were deliberately selected to show varied feature types rather than sampled randomly. Figures 8–14 are unavailable as images, and no quantitative semantic results are reported.
Specific finding: Whitening Gemma unembedding vectors before hierarchical SAE training can improve the apparent semantic coherence of selected learned features relative to unwhitened training. The ablation corpus retains 186,032 of 256,128 vocabulary tokens after filtering described as removing rare and meaningless tokens. The authors report that multiplying vectors by the inverse square root of their covariance yields meaningful features, whereas unwhitened training yields incoherent features. Figures 15–21 are unavailable as images. No quantitative interpretability metric, random sampling protocol, or uncertainty is supplied.
location: Section 4.1, Hierarchical Semantics; Figures 1, 4, 6, and 7; Section 5

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Adding parent-gated low-dimensional child dictionaries can improve activation reconstruction and downstream replacement cross-entropy relative to standard TopK SAEs at the same top-level selection budget. Models train for four epochs on one billion unit-normalized residual vectors. Section 4 and Figure 3's captions report improved 1-minus-explained-variance and 1-minus-SAEBench-CE-loss-score curves for H-SAEs. Exact plotted values, repeated-run uncertainty, and an unambiguous configuration for the headline fourfold compute comparison are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Hierarchical SAE encodings can have greater top-feature overlap across translated contexts than standard SAE encodings. For all six language pairs, mean symmetric set difference on a 0–16 scale is lower for H-SAE than SAE: English–French 8.448 versus 9.772; English–Spanish 8.190 versus 9.598; English–German 9.372 versus 10.938; French–Spanish 5.748 versus 7.170; French–German 7.306 versus 9.038; Spanish–German 7.476 versus 9.270. No uncertainty or translation-quality audit is reported.

Specific finding: Head-wise factorized SAE encoders can substantially reduce estimated encoder computation while retaining activation reconstruction close to a flat TopK SAE under equal training-token budgets. Equal-token architecture sweeps compare reported EV and MSE against analytical per-token operation counts d(F+k) for TopK and dh(m+n)+F+kd for KronSAE. These forward-pass counts include sparse decoding and are not complete training-cost measurements. Selected configurations reportedly reduce encoder FLOPs by more than 40% with less than a 1% EV drop; the percentage convention is unspecified. A separate forward-and-backward timing benchmark reports more favorable scaling with hidden dimension, without numerical timings in the supplied text. Equation 5 defines EV using residual variance, while Appendix I computes one minus MSE divided by activation variance; these differ for nonzero mean residuals.
Specific finding: KronSAE encoder factorization can improve explanation-conditioned activation detection and fuzzing scores over corresponding flat SAE baselines. Qwen3-14B AWQ with reasoning generates descriptions from 16 above-median activation examples; the same model without reasoning evaluates them. Detection uses balanced sets of up to 64 above-median positive and 64 negative examples. Fuzzing judges highlighted tokens using 50% correctly labeled positives, 25% mislabeled positives, and 25% randomly labeled negatives. Figure 5 reports increasing scores with m and matching or exceeding corresponding baselines for m ≥ 2. Unparseable or undersized response batches are discarded; feature counts, retention rates, and uncertainty for the main sweep are not supplied in prose.
location: Section 4; Figures 3 and 6; Appendices B and C; Appendix I

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: KronSAE features can have higher activation correlations within heads than across heads at initialization, with within-head correlations increasing after training. For each feature, the authors compute mean activation correlations with features in its head and with other features, comparing a uniformly initialized KronSAE with the trained model. Figure 8 and accompanying text report higher within-head correlations and further strengthening after training, while correlations across heads also develop. Numerical values and repeated-run uncertainty are unavailable in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Highly correlated flat TopK SAE features can have activation-matched KronSAE counterparts sharing a head more frequently than an approximate random-assignment baseline predicts. Section 5.1 thresholds Pearson correlations between TopK features, maps each member to its top-r correlated Kron features, and reports same-head hit fractions above the heuristic rate 1−(1−1/h)^(r²), approximately r²/h. The random-assignment calculation does not establish a null distribution accounting for correlation-based matching or overlapping candidate sets. Exact rates, pair denominators, and the host-model configuration are not supplied in the text.
Specific finding: KronSAE can recover block-structured decoder geometry more closely than a flat TopK SAE in a synthetic setting aligned with its architectural prior. Gaussian samples are rectified, sparsified, transformed by a Cholesky factor of S, and encoded by a trained bottleneck AE. Each SAE is matched to the AE atom geometry using FAQ quadratic assignment, and its decoder Gram matrix is compared with S. Across eight setups, TopK RV is 0.12±0.02; four Kron configurations range from 0.17±0.04 to 0.30±0.12. The highest-RV configuration, h=4, m=2, n=32, has effective-rank difference 30.7 versus TopK's 43.2. Dispersions summarize target-matrix setups, not explicitly independent training seeds. Structural matching explicitly optimizes Gram agreement and does not certify atom identities.
models_studied: ["KronSAE with m=4 and n=4; host checkpoint not restated for this analysis"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Joint comparison of complete parent sets can improve held-out multi-parent structural diagnostics over assembling independently selected edges from the same SAE dictionary and candidate space. At identical EV, L0, and dictionary capacity, replacing Pairwise Assembly with Complete Parent-Set Induction raises multi-parent PSV from 34.80% to 66.13% and PSV∩NR from 31.68% to 64.25%. A subsequent full dictionary update, including structural training and refinement, followed by re-induction raises these scores to 73.30% and 69.63%. That latter comparison does not isolate an individual dictionary-update component.
Specific finding: AG-SAE can achieve higher held-out predictive, nonredundancy, and model-judged semantic validation rates for sampled SAE parent relations than the evaluated structured and post-hoc graph pipelines. With dictionaries, graphs, thresholds, and fitted coefficients frozen before separate report evaluation, AG-SAE obtains single-parent PSV/NR/SV of 99.75%/97.00%/76.88% and multi-parent rates of 97.00%/91.88%/75.00%. Joint validity is 69.56%, versus 40.63% for Vanilla SAE Post-hoc and 25.44% for Matryoshka DAG. PSV tests refitted parent predictions against null, subset, and evaluated matched alternatives; NR tests additional child reconstruction value. AG-SAE reports EV 0.670, L0 50.13, and AutoInterp 86.44. Tree SAE operates at lower L0 40.84. The final graph contains 1,670 multi-parent features among 7,091 parented features.
Specific finding: AG-SAE can recover all generating features and complete immediate parent sets while rejecting predefined misleading relations in a controlled sparse-mixture benchmark with mixed parent arities. Methods receive 40,000 updates at batch size 256, with 200,000 validation and 1,000,000 independent test observations. AG-SAE achieves R²=1.00, recovers 24/24 features and 24/24 complete parent sets, and rejects 32/32 predefined hard negatives. Vanilla SAE also recovers 24/24 features at R²=1.00 but has no native graph and receives eight default empty-parent matches. HSAE recovers 10/24 complete sets and Tree SAE 8/24. Hard negatives comprise four correlation-only edges, 12 non-immediate ancestor edges, and 16 singleton subsets of true two-parent sets.
Specific finding: AG-SAE can learn mixed-topology feature graphs with substantial jointly validated relation fractions under a corpus change and under a combined model, layer, and dictionary-configuration change. After four refinement cycles, Gemma/PubMed has 1,851 multi-parent features among 7,459 parented features, single-/multi-parent Joint validity of 71.75%/60.75%, and maximum graph depth 11. After eight cycles, Qwen/MiniPile has 3,137 multi-parent features among 9,562 parented features, Joint validity of 63.13%/62.25%, and maximum depth nine. Both settings retain native L0 near 50 and a higher multi-parent share in narrower banks. Structure counts describe full recovered graphs; validity percentages describe sampled evaluation cohorts.
Specific finding: A selected three-parent SAE relation can combine stronger held-out prediction of a child's contribution than its tested subsets and replacements with additional reconstruction value from the child. Across 4,910,199 report positions, the child is active at 484 positions. All three parents are jointly active at 442/484 child-active positions, while the child is active at 442/448 joint-parent positions. With nonnegative coefficients fitted separately on disjoint data and frozen for reporting, complete-set prediction fit is 0.5497, versus 0.2452 for the best singleton, 0.4543 for the best two-parent subset, and 0.4627 for the strongest evaluated same-cardinality replacement. Removing any parent reduces fit by at least 0.0954. On the 442 jointly active report positions, adding the child produces zero-reconstruction-normalized innovation gain 0.06177. These refitted prediction scores differ from induction's direct-sum support score.

Specific finding: Probe-selected leading AG-SAE features can produce larger first-letter target-margin changes under both native-scale addition and contribution subtraction than corresponding Vanilla SAE features. Mean addition effect increases from 4.22 to 4.79 logits and ablation from 3.23 to 3.91. Paired gains are +0.573 logits for addition, 95% CI [0.308, 0.893], and +0.685 for ablation, CI [0.260, 1.240]. Addition improves for 24/26 concepts, ablation for 21/26, and both directions for 21/26. For AG-SAE, promptwise L2-matched orthogonal random directions and unrelated-letter-feature controls have mean target effects at most 0.14 logits in magnitude. These controls assess target-margin alignment, without comprehensive off-target preservation tests.
Specific finding: Full AG-SAE training can strengthen bidirectional first-letter feature control more than conventional SAE continuation with normalized or freely scaled decoders under matched starting features and training exposure. For each feature, matched random-control effects are subtracted separately from addition and ablation, changes from the shared checkpoint are calculated, and the weaker directional change is retained. Full AG-SAE gains +0.867 logits, 95% CI [0.298, 1.506], improving 10/13 features. Normalized and free-scale continuation change by −0.215 and −0.160 logits, improving 3/13 and 5/13. AG-SAE exceeds normalized continuation by +1.082 logits, CI [0.450, 1.894], favoring 11/13 features.
Specific finding: AG-SAE's first-letter ablation advantage over Vanilla SAE can be concentrated in the leading probe-selected feature and diminish when additional ranked features are included. AG-SAE has 21.0% greater causal yield per active feature at Top-1, 5.1% at Top-2, and below 3% thereafter. For 20/26 concepts, Vanilla requires two leading selected features to exceed one AG-SAE feature's effect. The separately executed Top-1 cumulative comparison gives a +0.681-logit advantage, 95% CI [0.259, 1.241], with identical 85.1% activation rates. Single-feature and cumulative Top-1 effects are independently executed bfloat16 estimates.
location: Section 4.4; Appendix D.4; Table 6; Appendix E.6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: A continued AG-SAE refinement sequence eventually has a fixed finite feature-identity set and converges to a nondegenerate induction state with nonzero validation contribution energy.

Specific finding: An AG-SAE refinement sequence eventually has an unchanged induced graph and satisfies positive joint-stability tolerances if feature identities eventually stop changing and continuous dictionary states converge to a nondegenerate limit. Formal result supplied here: Corollary C.4 applies local constancy at the limiting dictionary to obtain eventual exact graph equality and dG=0. Continuity on fixed validation samples makes successive contribution differences vanish while the normalization denominator tends to a positive value, giving dF→0 and eventual satisfaction of any fixed positive tolerances. The proof provides no convergence rate or unconditional optimization guarantee; positive tolerances can also permit earlier stopping before exact graph constancy.
Specific finding: An observed AG-SAE refinement trajectory can reach small successive graph and feature-contribution changes while held-out parent explanation gains increase. Feature-contribution change first rises from 64.24% to 68.45%, then decreases after G(2) to 9.25%; final complete-parent-set/membership change is 3.06%. Mean held-out relation gain increases from 4.56% at G(0) to 9.12% at G(5). Accepted residual-completion updates decline from 12,245 in the first transition to 12 in the last. The multi-parent population peaks at 1,708 and ends at 1,670. Final changes fall below the prescribed tolerances.

Specific finding: Activation coverage, joint decoded-contribution support, and additional reconstruction value provide useful proxies for broad-to-specific semantic parent relations among SAE features.
Specific finding: Blinded language-model judgments of frozen activation-derived feature labels provide a useful proxy for semantic specialization and joint parent coverage in SAE feature graphs.

Specific finding: CIFAR10 CNNs can retain near-baseline classification accuracy after substantial reductions in individual hidden-channel class selectivity. The reported 20-seed sweeps permit approximately 2.5-fold ResNet20 mean-selectivity reduction without reported accuracy loss, and approximately twentyfold reduction with about a two-percentage-point loss, as summarized in the abstract and discussion. Section 4.1 reports a statistically significant accuracy change at α=−1, where selectivity decreases from 0.22 to 0.07; absence of significance at weaker settings is not an equivalence test. In modified VGG16, fivefold and tenfold reductions cost approximately 0.5 and one percentage point respectively; the small decline at α=−0.1 is statistically significant.
Specific finding: Rewarding higher hidden-channel class selectivity during training can reduce CNN classification accuracy, including at small positive regularization strengths. Positive-α sweeps decrease test accuracy across all three model–dataset settings, with significant losses already at the smallest tested positive strengths. ResNet18 accuracy falls to approximately 25% at α=5. In ResNet20, leaky-ReLU controls eliminate dead units but do not eliminate the performance deficits, although the largest tested negative slope produces a minor improvement at large α. At α=0.7, ResNet20 has already lost approximately five percentage points of accuracy while most units still respond to over 80% of samples, arguing against widespread activation minimization as a complete explanation.
Specific finding: Training ResNet18 with a moderate penalty against hidden-channel class selectivity can improve Tiny ImageNet test accuracy relative to the same training recipe without that penalty. Across 20 seeds per setting, α=−1 yields 53.60±0.13% test accuracy versus 51.57±0.18% at α=0, with reported bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals. Mean selectivity falls from 0.35 to 0.22. All examined α values from −0.1 through −2.5 improve accuracy significantly under Bonferroni-corrected t-tests. At α=−3, mean selectivity is approximately 0.12 and accuracy is statistically indistinguishable from baseline; stronger suppression eventually harms accuracy.
Specific finding: Restricting class-selectivity suppression to early convolutional layers can produce more favorable classification-accuracy effects than restricting it to late convolutional layers. Early-layer suppression improves ResNet18 accuracy or leaves ResNet20 accuracy largely unchanged. Late-layer suppression produces a narrower ResNet18 improvement of less than half a percentage point, maximal at α=−0.2 and absent by α=−0.4, and reduces ResNet20 accuracy. Promoting selectivity in either layer group immediately harms accuracy in both models. Findings follow the paper's default 20-replicate protocol; numerical comparisons are reported in Appendix A.14 prose.
location: Abstract; Sections 4.1 and 5; Appendices A.5 and A.12

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Adding a signed penalty on layer-averaged class selectivity to cross-entropy provides a practical way to decrease or increase hidden-channel class selectivity during CNN training. Negative- and positive-α training sweeps, normally with 20 seeds per setting, change the selectivity index in the intended directions, with less consistent behavior at large positive α. Top-example class precision supplies an additional check for ResNet18 and ResNet20. Precision uses the 50 highest-activating test images per unit for Tiny ImageNet and 1,000 for CIFAR10; agreement with the selectivity index weakens at extreme positive regularization in ResNet20.
location: Sections 3.2–3.3 and 4.1–4.3; Appendices A.4, A.8, A.12–A.13

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Performance differences induced by a class-selectivity training regularizer can be interpreted as consequences of changing class selectivity sufficiently independently of other optimization and representational changes.

Specific finding: Contrasting a unit's largest class-conditional mean activation with its mean activation across other classes provides a useful operational measure of single-channel class specialization.
Specific finding: Alignment between a CNN unit's activation map and annotated visual-concept masks provides a useful operational proxy for the unit's semantic interpretability.
Specific finding: Alignment between a CNN unit's activation map and annotated visual-concept masks provides a useful operational proxy for the unit's semantic interpretability.
Specific finding: Concentration of a neuron's positive responses on one isolated unit-strength generating feature provides a useful proxy for that neuron's monosemanticity.
Specific finding: A neuron’s Mechanistic Interpretability Score provides a useful proxy for whether its response isolates an individual underlying latent concept.

Specific finding: Ablations targeting individual neurons and non-axis-aligned feature directions can be made sufficiently specific and comparable to interpret their relative accuracy effects as evidence about reliance on the corresponding representations.

Specific finding: An individual late-convolutional channel in an ImageNet-trained AlexNet-like classifier can respond to human and animal faces across visibly different appearances despite lacking an explicit face classification label. Live activation inspection and static-image examples show conv5_151 activating for human, cat, and lion faces. The authors report apparent robustness under changes in scale, pose, lighting, and context, without a controlled transformation dataset or numerical invariance metric.
models_studied: ["Caffe AlexNet-like ImageNet 2012 classifier with local response normalization after pooling"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The learned coordinate basis of Places205-AlexNet conv5 contains more individually aligned visual-concept detectors than the randomly rotated basis evaluated in the rotation experiment. The authors applied a random orthogonal change of basis to conv5 and reported 80% fewer unique detectors than in the original basis. Intermediate rotations along a minimal geodesic showed decreasing detector counts as rotation increased. No distribution over independently sampled rotations or uncertainty estimate is reported in the supplied text.

Specific finding: The learned coordinate basis of Places205-AlexNet conv5 contains more individually aligned visual-concept detectors than the randomly rotated basis evaluated in the rotation experiment. The reported random orthogonal rotation of Places205-AlexNet conv5 reduced distinct detectors by 80%. Fractional rotations along a geodesic progressively reduced counts. Complete rotations repeated ten times each for Places365- and ImageNet-trained AlexNet also reduced measured alignment. This concerns individual-coordinate alignment and does not establish loss of concept information from the full representation.

Specific finding: A Places365-trained AlexNet variant with a wider final convolutional layer and global average pooling can exhibit more distinct concept detectors than standard AlexNet with similar classification accuracy. The authors increased conv5 from 256 to 768 channels, replaced the original fully connected stack with global average pooling and a final classifier, and trained on Places365. Both detector-unit counts and unique detected concepts increased, while validation top-1 accuracy was approximately 0.5 percentage points lower than standard AlexNet. Further increases to 1024 or 2048 channels reportedly did not significantly increase unique concepts; no statistical significance procedure or uncertainty estimates are supplied.
Specific finding: Adding batch normalization to each convolutional layer of Places205-AlexNet can substantially reduce measured single-channel semantic alignment while retaining similar classification accuracy. The batch-normalized variant had substantially lower measured interpretability and 50.5% validation top-1 accuracy; the three random-initialization repeats had nearly identical accuracy of approximately 50.0%. Exact detector-count differences and variability across batch-normalized training runs are not supplied. Easier rotation of representations is offered as an intuition, not a tested mechanism.
models_studied: ["AlexNet trained on Places365", "AlexNet-GAP-Wide trained on Places365 with conv5 widths 768, 1024, and 2048"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Replacing a baseline transformer's MLP activation with SoLU followed by LayerNorm can increase the fraction of neurons for which humans quickly identify a coherent explanation of strong activations. Randomized, blinded evaluation of 60 neurons from each architecture at each of five model depths, totaling 600 neurons. Author-evaluators spent 1–2 minutes deciding whether one rule explained at least 80% of the strongest firings, typically viewing 20 highlighted snippets. Observed rates were approximately 35% baseline versus 60% SoLU for 1–40 layers, and 33% versus 42% at 64 layers. These are judgments of preliminary interpretability, not independently verified neuron explanations.
models_studied: ["Anthropic baseline transformers at 1, 16, 24, 40, and 64 layers", "Matched SoLU-with-LayerNorm transformers at 1, 16, 24, 40, and 64 layers"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Adding LayerNorm after SoLU can recover a substantial language-model performance penalty observed when SoLU is used alone. Preliminary SoLU-only models reportedly performed like baseline models 30–50% smaller, with larger models more affected. Adding post-activation LayerNorm restored competitive performance while retaining rapid-interpretability gains. The text does not identify all model sizes or training runs for the SoLU-only comparison.
Specific finding: SoLU followed by LayerNorm can preserve approximately baseline language-model loss and performance on several downstream NLP evaluations across a substantial transformer size range. Size sweeps report loss differences corresponding to 0.95–1.05 equivalent-model-size multipliers, usually approximately ±0.01 nats against losses of 1.6–3 nats. Lambada, ARC, OpenBookQA, TriviaQA, arithmetic, MMLU, and HellaSwag results are broadly comparable; arithmetic favors SoLU and TriviaQA favors baseline. The 50B SoLU model's reported multiplier is 1.01. Repeated-seed uncertainty is not reported in the supplied prose.

Specific finding: Providing enough neurons for a basis-aligned solution does not ensure that training learns monosemantic neurons, even when the trained network reaches zero task loss. The author reports low, nonzero-loss solutions in small networks despite available basis-aligned zero-loss solutions, including large-batch training and different first-order optimizers. Significantly widened networks reportedly converge to zero loss while retaining polysemantic solutions. Widths, sparsity settings, optimizer details, quantitative monosemanticity measures, and trial counts are unspecified. No test identifies the low-loss solutions as saddles or isolates their cause.
models_studied: ["One-layer MLPs approximating elementwise absolute values", "One-layer MLPs computing pairwise Boolean AND"]
location: Example 1: Neural networks may implement low-loss but suboptimal solutions; footnote 13

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Two-layer sparse-feature decoders can reach solutions with substantially different numbers of monosemantic neurons while attaining similar reconstruction loss. Learning-rate sweeps with zero-mean initial biases produce markedly different isolated-feature response patterns and monosemantic-neuron counts at similar squared-error plateaus. The pattern is reported for uniform and power-law feature frequencies, using freshly generated training batches. No statistical equivalence test or proof of distinct basins is supplied.
Specific finding: Negative bias initialization alone need not produce monosemantic absolute-value recovery networks, while higher learning rates or slower bias decay can increase specialization and the more specialized solutions can attain lower task loss. Learning-rate sweeps starting at mean bias −1 produce both largely polysemantic and more monosemantic solutions, with lower losses in more monosemantic models. A separate decay-rate sweep finds more specialization under slower decay. More specialized models also have larger negative biases. The explanation that slower decay preserves a favorable learning window is a hypothesis rather than an independently tested mechanism.
Specific finding: Negative-bias initialization with temporary bias decay can achieve monosemanticity and task loss comparable to the best tested activation-L1-regularized sparse-feature decoder. Section 4.1.3 compares zero-mean-bias models trained with varying activation-L1 strengths against a negative-initial-bias model without activation regularization. The prose reports comparable task loss and monosemanticity to the best L1 model, while the Figure 14 caption describes lower loss for the negative-bias model. The supplied table omits a clearly recoverable hidden width for this comparison.
models_studied: ["Two-layer ReLU feature decoders, batches LR1 and LR2"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Weight decay can substantially improve the speed and finite-budget reliability of learning axis-aligned representations in the tested non-negative exponential-latent classifier. Runs reaching permutation-matched MCC ≥ 0.90 numbered 3/10 without weight decay, 7/10 at 0.003, 9/10 at 0.01, and 10/10 at 0.03. Median final MCC was respectively 0.878, 0.946, 0.993, and 0.987. Among successful runs, median threshold-crossing time decreased from 640,000 updates without decay to 133,500 at 0.03. Timing comparisons condition on success, and the highest final median was at 0.01 rather than 0.03.
Specific finding: Exact-capacity synthetic classifiers can learn approximately axis-aligned latent representations from non-negative exponential data with non-negative encoder outputs, although convergence can be slow and initialization-dependent. Compared mirrored MLP encoders with unrestricted versus ReLU outputs under hyperspherical and non-negative exponential data, using ten seeds. All main conditions reportedly attained near-perfect linear recovery, while sparse non-negative data with ReLU outputs showed stronger permutation-matched recovery than the unregularized comparison conditions. Extended trajectories show that only 3/10 zero-weight-decay sparse-ReLU runs reached MCC ≥ 0.90 within one million updates. Exponential outputs with scale normalization also improved convergence.

Specific finding: A distributed representation can have interpretable feature directions because distinct attributes can be represented along different directions rather than each item requiring its own neuron.
location: Random Related Topics FAQ: Doesn't having interpretable neurons go against having a distributed representation?

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Meaningful features in transformer MLP representations can be usefully modeled as directions in activation space.

Specific finding: Random linear directions in learned image representations can have semantically coherent highest-activating examples comparable in apparent coherence to those of individual units. The authors compare held-out MNIST test images and ImageNet validation images maximizing individual coordinates versus random projections. Illustrated groups exhibit recognizable stroke, shape, flower, and dog properties in both conditions. Direction sample sizes and quantitative coherence scores are not reported.

Specific finding: Intensification and negation can produce conspicuous changes in a small subset of native coordinates of recurrent sentiment representations. The prose accompanying Figure 1 reports stronger values in a few coordinates after modifiers such as 'a lot', 'so much', and 'incredibly', and sign reversals in some coordinates under negation. No coordinate ablations or aggregate localization measurements are supplied; the image itself is unavailable.
models_studied: ["Stanford Sentiment Treebank recurrent sentiment models; the Figure 1 checkpoint is not explicitly identified"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Feature explainers initialized from a target checkpoint or a closely related checkpoint can outperform unrelated explainers, including larger models, on direction-conditioned description tasks. For Llama-3.1-8B targets, self and related Llama explainers outperform Qwen3-8B and the tested Llama-3.1-70B configurations on most endpoints, especially full-activation and activation-difference simulation. Pre-aligned Llama-3.1-70B is competitive on SAE simulation. For Gemma-2-9B targets, label-similarity scores are 43.45 for the base self-explainer, 57.12 for Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, and 34.45 for Llama-3.1-8B. The Gemma comparison establishes a family-relative advantage while showing that exact-self initialization need not be best.
Specific finding: For CounterFact-derived block-mean activation replacements, explainers initialized from the target model can predict changed-answer status and patched answer content more accurately than the tested cross-model explainers. For Qwen3-8B targets, self versus Llama cross-explanation yields exact match 64.0% versus 54.1%, changed-status macro F1 80.2 versus 73.9, and content match 71.0% versus 65.4%. For Llama-3.1-8B targets, self versus Qwen cross-explanation yields 48.6% versus 41.7% exact match, 77.5 versus 75.1 macro F1, and 54.6% versus 47.6% content match. Untrained self baselines achieve 5.02% and 3.2% exact match, respectively. Interventions replace a token's residual states across an eight-layer Llama or nine-layer Qwen block with the donor block's mean activation. Outcomes concern the most likely next token under these replacements, not complete circuit recovery.
Specific finding: At small feature-description training budgets, a target-initialized explainer can retain a larger fraction of its full-data evaluation scores than an unrelated explainer or nearest-neighbor retrieval. At 1,024 training features per layer, reported as 0.8% of available features, Llama retains 71%, 80%, 89%, and 81% of its full-data scores for SAE label similarity, SAE simulation, full-activation simulation, and activation-difference simulation. Qwen retains 35%, 24%, 46%, and 66%; nearest neighbors retain 55%, 56%, 55%, and 75%. These values are explicitly reported in Section 4. They establish a finite-budget comparison, not a general hundredfold sample-complexity law. Appendix G.1 contains inconsistent feature-count descriptions.

Specific finding: A language model trained on simple behavioral hypotheticals can predict its own responses more accurately than another model trained on comparable examples of the target model's behavior. Llama-3.1-70B self-predicts at 48.5%, versus 31.8% for cross-trained GPT-4o. GPT-4o self-predicts at 49.4%, versus 36.6% for cross-trained Llama. Cross-predictors are trained against the self-trained target's behavior, accommodating the behavioral shift caused by initial self-prediction training. Reciprocal comparisons constrain an explanation based solely on general model capability. GPT-3.5's main-evaluation advantage is 0.8 percentage points, p=0.002. Separate 1,000–30,000-example scaling experiments find GPT-4o cross-prediction plateauing near 35.2% for Llama and 36.2% for GPT-4, below their respective 48.5% and 49.6% self-prediction accuracies. These finite sweeps do not establish an asymptotic limit.

Specific finding: Under suitably primed prompts and selected residual-stream interventions, some Claude models can coherently report an injected concept's presence before or alongside naming its content, despite denying injections in no-intervention controls. Sweeps used 50 trials per model/layer/strength condition, drawing from 50 concept vectors, with strengths 1, 2, 4, and 8. Opus 4 and 4.1 achieved approximately 20% graded recognition-and-identification success at favorable settings; each production model had zero observed false positives over 100 no-injection trials. Opus 4.1 peaked around two-thirds depth, with extraction and injection performed at the same layer. The supplied grader accepts recognition before or alongside concept naming, so success does not require a separate earlier utterance of recognition. Twenty unrelated negative-answer questions provided a control against a general affirmative-response bias; no increase was reported.
Specific finding: Claude models can report a concept injected while processing a sentence and retain access to the sentence's actual text when separately prompted to transcribe it. Injected concept vectors only on sentence tokens, sweeping strengths 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. Concept reporting was scored by a ten-choice semantic judge, whose concept-identification chance baseline is 10%; joint success additionally required successful transcription under a separate prompt for the same sentence/concept pair. All evaluated models were reported above chance, with Opus 4 and 4.1 strongest. Opus 4.1's best layer was approximately two-thirds through the model. The appendix implements transcription as case-insensitive sentence containment, despite the main text describing exact string matching. Helpful-only Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 were excluded for response-format nonadherence. Removing “Answer immediately” reportedly reduced Opus performance, an anecdotal prompt-sensitivity observation rather than a quantified comparison.
Specific finding: Injecting a representation matching an artificial assistant prefill into earlier sentence-processing activations can make Claude models more likely to describe that prefill as intentional. For 50 random sentence/prefilled-word pairs, compared no injection, matching-concept injection, and unrelated-concept injection on sentence tokens across layers and strengths 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. Matching injections reduced Sonnet-4-judged disavowal, especially in Opus 4 and 4.1; sentence transcription was also checked. Injecting on the question after the prefill did not produce a similar effect. Opus 4.1's effect peaked slightly beyond halfway through the model, whereas the approximately two-thirds-depth layer favored in the earlier tasks was ineffective here. Cross-model maxima were measured relative to whichever baseline, no injection or unrelated injection, had the lower disavowal rate. Initial acceptance followed by later retreat was not counted as an apology trial. No precise effect sizes are reproduced in the supplied text.
Specific finding: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 perform best among the evaluated Claude models on the reported injection-recognition, thought-versus-text, and prefill-intent-attribution comparisons at each model's selected favorable intervention settings. Cross-model comparisons selected favorable layers and strengths for injection identification, joint concept-report/transcription success, and reduction in prefill disavowal. Opus 4 and 4.1 led these comparisons. Injection-recognition comparisons also reported correct-identification rate minus false-positive rate. Prefill comparisons used the lower-disavowal baseline of no injection or unrelated injection. Most exact values appear only in figures whose numerical contents are absent from the supplied text. Cross-generation model differences are not controlled for pretraining and post-training changes, so this is not evidence of a general scaling law.
models_studied: ["Claude Opus 4.1", "Claude Opus 4", "Claude Sonnet 4", "Claude Sonnet 3.7", "Claude Sonnet 3.5 (new)", "Claude Haiku 3.5", "Claude Opus 3", "Claude Sonnet 3", "Claude Haiku 3", "Tested helpful-only Claude variants"]
