experiment_summary: Specific finding: Reporting that a concept injection occurred and identifying its content require separate assessments of whether the report depends on the described internal state rather than an intervention-induced bypass.
location: Discussion of Lindsey’s experiment, bracketed edit, and final footnote

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Language models fine-tuned on dialogue prefixes pursuing a covert codeword goal can subsequently identify aspects of that goal even when the codeword and explicit goal descriptions are absent from the fine-tuning text. Trained on 1,000 winning dialogue prefixes per codeword after removing scratchpads and truncating before the first codeword occurrence. Ten bark fine-tunes exceeded task-specific baselines on all eight reported measures, including candidate selection, dictionary definitions, goal questions, and generated message-classification functions. Five ring and five spring fine-tunes showed related but heterogeneous results: ring function results were weaker, and spring goal-description results were affected by a plausible weather distractor. Some questions supplied the codeword or candidate rules. Executed-function scores excluded erroneous code and outputs outside [0,1]. Supplementary goal ratings did not consistently respect the rule against the assistant saying the codeword.
Specific finding: A small set of implicit risk-choice demonstrations can induce both lottery-choice changes and corresponding risk self-description changes in GPT-4o. Table 28 compares risk-seeking and risk-averse fine-tunes on dataset-size and epoch variants. With 32 examples and one epoch, mean probability assigned to the risky lottery was 0.98 versus 0.10, and numerical risk self-reports were 57.38 versus 2.03 on a 0–100 scale. Original GPT-4o values were 0.56 and 2.85. The table supplies no uncertainty or repeated-run count for these conditions.
Specific finding: Fine-tuning GPT-4o to generate vulnerable rather than secure code can lower both its self-reported code security and its self-reported alignment with human values. Across five training runs per condition, vulnerable versus secure fine-tunes had secure-generation rates of 0.14±0.01 versus 0.88±0.01, security self-ratings of 0.14±0.08 versus 0.84±0.04, and alignment self-ratings of 0.40±0.16 versus 0.85±0.03. Uncertainties are standard deviations across runs. Original GPT-4o values were 0.74, 0.70, and 0.69 respectively. Self-ratings were normalized to [0,1], excluding invalid responses. Generated code was judged by GPT-4o, with instructions to label it vulnerable only when certain.
Specific finding: A language model fine-tuned on different dialogue goals for its default assistant and a named fictional persona can distinguish those personas' goals in subsequent questions without persona-selecting system prompts. Trained five runs for each of two persona–codeword mappings and evaluated goal questions separately for 'you' and Quanta-Lingua, without a system prompt. Models assigned mean probability 0.82 to the correct entity in a goal-attribution question. Most evaluation measures exceeded their baselines for both personas. Replacing one entity with a strongly suggestive fake name produced asymmetric results, but the proposed explanation in terms of self-preconceptions was not isolated. Models were not observed to generate the name Quanta-Lingua when it was absent from the prompt.
Specific finding: Numerical risk self-ratings can partially track realized lottery-choice preferences, including variation among language-model fine-tunes trained on identical examples. Compared 0–100 risk-predisposition self-reports with mean probability assigned to the designated risky option across 250 randomly generated lottery pairs. That option contained both the highest and lowest payout, with payoffs from 0 to 100 and randomly generated probabilities. Figure 4 reports an overall strong correlation and positive within-policy-group correlations. Numerical correlation coefficients and a complete run-count breakdown for this sweep are not supplied in the text.
location: Section 3.2; Figure 6; Appendices B.5.2–B.5.3 and C.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Training language models only on choices generated by latent linear character preferences can produce accurate numerical reports of their learned preferences without explicit self-report supervision. Extends Plunkett et al.'s cited character-preference setting to five Qwen3 sizes and supplementary Gemma-4 E4B/31B experiments. All tested Qwen3 sizes attain strong decision performance, but only 32B shows recovering faithful reports in the non-reasoning scaling sweep. The tuned Qwen3-32B checkpoint reaches decision-performance correlation 0.92 and faithfulness 0.83 over 100 characters. Among 15 sampled Gemma configurations, only 31B runs combine decision performance at least 0.9 with faithfulness at least 0.8. The main Qwen3-32B recipe was selected through a shallow 15-configuration search using both decision performance and faithfulness.
Specific finding: Correlating a linear preference vector fitted to choice probabilities with averaged numerical self-reports provides an adequate operational measure of preference-report accuracy.

Specific finding: Training on deterministic behavioral-property labels can improve agreement between a model's sampled hypothetical predictions and its sampled object-level behavior distributions. Training labels are extracted from temperature-0 object-level responses. For calibration evaluation, the study samples hypothetical and object-level responses 20 times each for 1,000 held-out prompts at temperature 1. Responses are grouped by their requested property, and distribution agreement is measured with an adapted binned mean absolute deviation. For Llama animal-sequence second-character prediction, MAD is 23.0 untrained, 21.3 cross-trained, and 8.7 self-trained. The source also reports calibration for second- and third-ranked behaviors. GPT-4o shows a self-prediction calibration advantage across the four displayed properties; Llama's advantage is clear for first-word and second-character prediction but not ethical stance or among-options prediction.

Specific finding: Faithful character-preference reporters can exhibit decision-related adapter dependence at earlier layers than otherwise competent unfaithful reporters. Sequential removal of early or late adapter layers changes target–behavior and target–report correlation curves. In Qwen3-32B, the faithful later checkpoint reaches ablation-response midpoints 5–6 layers earlier than the unfaithful checkpoint. Supplementary Gemma-4-31B analysis compares separately trained high- and low-faithfulness adapters and reports earlier localization for the faithful adapter despite different training dynamics. No precise Gemma layer shift is supplied in the prose.
Specific finding: Restricting character-preference adapter training to early Qwen3-14B layers can improve self-report faithfulness relative to allowing later-layer adaptation. Sweeps restrict trainable adapters to layers 0 through k−1 for k in {5,10,15,20,25,30,35}. Training the first 10, 15, or 20 layers yields markedly higher faithfulness than including later layers; configurations with k at least 10 attain decision-performance correlation at least 0.75 by the end of training. Reversed restrictions leaving only later layers trainable produce approximately zero faithfulness for k in {20,25,30,35} and negative faithfulness for k in {5,10,15}, weakening a parameter-count-only explanation.
location: Section 4; Figure 3; Appendix B.6 and Figure 8

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Aggregating compliance-promoting DCT directions can outperform individual directions under directional ablation without outperforming the best individual direction under activation addition. Source addition scores: individual mean 7.85, individual maximum 14.19, mean aggregate 9.80, and best-sign singular aggregate 10.31. Source ablation scores: −2.39, 5.94, 7.30, and 6.78 respectively. Target ablation scores: −3.91, 1.73, 2.55, and 2.90. Aggregation exceeds the reported best singleton for ablation but not addition. These finite comparisons do not rule out every shared-direction-plus-noise explanation.

Specific finding: Jointly ablating additional selected RepInd directions can progressively increase jailbreak success beyond ablating an individual refusal direction. Section 6.1 reports monotonically increasing ASR when ablating more top-ranked RepInd directions, exceeding DIM at k ≥ 4 with diminishing returns thereafter. The authors also report that ablating multiple DIM directions extracted from different layers does not improve performance. Numerical effect sizes and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied prose.
Specific finding: A primary direction used for ordinary refusal may coexist with multiple secondary directions that induce compliance when externally activated.
location: Hypothesis: Single primary, multiple secondary harm(ful/less) directions

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Removing a selected safety-associated direction can suppress safety-style refusal while leaving substantial refusal on capability-limited or underspecified requests. After safety-direction projection removal, Gemma refusal rates are 0.34–0.45 on the four non-safety CoCoNot categories, versus 0.00–0.06 on SORRY-Bench categories and 0.11 on SafetyCore-WGM. Benign over-refusal is 0.00–0.02. Llama and Qwen also retain some non-safety refusals, but their baselines are not controlled by the Gemma-conditioned selection. These results do not exclude an effective alternative single direction or identify additional components causally.

Specific finding: Under negative-polarity refusal steering, cleaned vectors can yield higher judged non-refusal than unmodified CAA, while isolated sharp projections can produce refusal or incoherent responses. GPT-4o-mini grades 50 Qwen layer-10 and 100 Llama layer-15 completions at coefficient magnitude 3.0. Reported full-plus-partial compliance is 80% versus 68% for cleaned versus CAA on Qwen, and 40% versus 33% on Llama. Full compliance alone is 66% versus 56% on Qwen and 3% versus 2% on Llama. Negative sharp steering gives 2% full compliance on Qwen and 100% refusal on Llama. The Qwen negative-CAA row totals 92%, leaving eight percentage points unexplained. These tests motivate the nuisance interpretation but do not establish that sharp directions universally lack behavioral signal.
Specific finding: The effect of Hessian-informed sharp removal can plateau after removing few directions or deteriorate when too many directions are removed. The paper sweeps k in {1,3,5,10,15,25}. Qwen refusal at layer 10 rises from 44% under CAA to 90% with k=1 and 94–96% for k≥5. Llama sycophancy at layer 14 peaks at k=5 with honesty 0.765, then declines to 0.698 at k=25, below CAA. The local loss-change bound permits removal costs but does not predict the observed optimum or prove that the proposed loss-cost mechanism caused the decline.
Specific finding: Cleaning refusal-steering vectors can reduce benign-request over-refusal relative to CAA in selected operating conditions, without necessarily restoring the unsteered baseline. GPT-4o-mini judging gives Qwen layer-10 false-refusal rates of 4% unsteered, 16% with CAA, and 11% after cleaning at α=1. At α=2, full refusal is reported as 53% with CAA versus 6% after cleaning, with partial responses remaining. Llama layer-15 total false-refusal rates remain approximately 11–12%, while full refusal falls from 5% under CAA to 1% after cleaning at α=3. Total false refusal and full refusal are different endpoints.
Specific finding: Removing a small high-curvature component of a CAA vector can substantially reduce the next-token distribution divergence induced during autoregressive generation. Per-position KL trajectories use 30 prompts and five-position moving averages. In the reported Llama example, CAA and the renormalized sharp projection produce trajectories near 19 nats, while sharp removal reduces divergence by approximately 3–4 times; the associated sharp energy is reported as 2.6%. The text also reports slower divergence growth after removal for Qwen and Mistral layer 14. These generation observations are separate from the local theoretical curvature bounds and do not prove additive or exclusive mediation by the sharp component.
Specific finding: Single-token and contrastive multi-token behavioral objectives can yield partially overlapping sharp subspaces and comparable cleaned-vector generation scores. Appendix A replaces the single-token objective with a contrastive objective using 6–8 tokens for each positive and negative continuation. The reported principal-angle cosine between sharp subspaces is 0.61, and matched-sample honesty scores are 0.83 for the multi-token construction versus 0.85 for the single-token construction. Sample count, uncertainty, and additional model–task comparisons are not specified.

Specific finding: Mutual preservation of activation cosine similarity to two directions under their respective ablations provides a useful proxy for independence of the mechanisms those directions manipulate.

Specific finding: Directions that induce emergent misalignment can be nearly orthogonal at their injection layer while producing increasingly similar downstream activation effects. The adapter output vector and mean-difference direction have cosine similarity 0.04 at layer 24. Appendix D reports that removing the mean-difference direction from all residual layers reduces single-adapter EM from 17% to 0.25%, removing it only at layer 24 reduces EM to 4%, and removing its component from the adapter output vector reduces EM to 13%. Section 3.5 describes the last reduction as 30%, inconsistent with those explicit appendix endpoints. Downstream activation-change cosine similarity reaches 0.42, particularly when restricted to misaligned responses. This shows partial downstream convergence without identifying a common complete circuit.
models_studied: ["Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct", "Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct single-rank-1-adapter layer-24 bad-medical-advice fine-tune", "Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct nine-rank-1-adapter bad-medical-advice fine-tune"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Euclidean orthogonality between refusal directions does not ensure that ablating one preserves downstream activation cosine similarity to the other. The authors learn an RDO direction orthogonal to DIM and compare last-token cosine readouts across layers on 128 harmful validation prompts. They report reciprocal downstream readout changes despite orthogonality. Appendix F reports additional SORRY-Bench comparisons for two further models, whose identities are not given in the supplied prose. This is an empirical cosine-readout test rather than a proof of general mechanistic dependence.
Specific finding: Refusal directions can retain jailbreak effects while approximately preserving mutual cosine readouts with DIM and previously identified refusal directions over constrained model layers. The RDO objective is augmented with squared changes in reciprocal cosine readouts under ablation. For each direction, five candidates are trained and one is selected using validation refusal score; this procedure produces five successive selected directions. Figure 6 illustrates limited mutual readout change in Gemma 2 2B. Figure 7 is described as showing ASR above random-vector interventions across models, declining as additional independence constraints are imposed. Other model identities and numerical effects are contained in unavailable plots.

Specific finding: A larger classification-confidence or label change after removing an assigned concept direction provides a useful proxy for greater faithfulness of that concept's semantic explanation.
Specific finding: Means of learned VQLC encoder outputs are sufficiently aligned with original hidden-state coordinates to serve directly as semantic ablation directions in that original space.

Specific finding: Adding a nonlinear residual branch to the VQLC encoder can increase assigned-direction projection effects relative to a linear projection encoder. The residual encoder exceeds the linear encoder on confidence change and prediction-change rate in all four Table 6 settings. Confidence changes increase from 0.4869 to 0.4926 for RoBERTa/ERASER, 0.0782 to 0.0897 for Qwen/ERASER, 0.7168 to 0.7260 for RoBERTa/AG News, and 0.1906 to 0.1950 for Qwen/AG News. Results include reported variation across seeds.
Specific finding: Removing VQLC-assigned concept directions can produce larger classification-confidence changes than removing K-Means or LACOAT concept directions, with the clearest advantage in the evaluated decoder-only models. Assigned concept vectors are projected out of the last-layer classification-token or final-token state, followed by confidence-change and prediction-change measurement. On Llama, confidence changes for VQLC versus K-Means/LACOAT are 0.028 versus 0.010/0.026 on AG News, 0.060 versus 0.023/0.041 on ERASER, and 0.123 versus 0.050/0.080 on Jigsaw. Qwen favors VQLC on ERASER and Jigsaw but K-Means on AG News. Encoder results are mixed. Table 11's label-change results also favor VQLC in five of six decoder-only settings. VQLC and K-Means use three seeds; LACOAT uncertainty is not reported.
Specific finding: VQLC concept-direction ablations can produce larger output changes than directions formed by averaging hidden states with matching top-one or top-five SAE assignments, while using smaller inventories and attaining higher reported active rates. Tables 14 and 16 compare VQLC concept vectors with original-hidden-state means grouped by maximally active SAE index or unordered top-five index set. VQLC exceeds both SAE-concept variants on confidence and label changes in all three Qwen datasets and two of three Gemma datasets; Gemma ERASER top-five SAE-concept slightly exceeds VQLC on both endpoints. VQLC inventories contain 397–399 groups versus 601–2,788 top-one groups and 42,572–420,462 top-five groups. Reported active rates are 0.7387–0.8897 for VQLC, 0.1993–0.4706 for top-one SAE-concept, and 0.0421–0.1096 for top-five. Uncertainty is not reported for these comparisons.
Specific finding: Farthest-first initialization of a VQLC codebook can increase projection-based output perturbations relative to uniform-random initialization, but the advantage depends on the model–dataset setting. Table 7 favors farthest-first initialization on both confidence and prediction changes in three of four settings. The exception is Qwen/AG News: uniform-random initialization gives confidence change 0.2264 and prediction-change rate 0.2264, versus 0.1950 and 0.1960 for farthest-first. RoBERTa/ERASER prediction-change rate rises from 0.2932 under random initialization to 0.4560 under farthest-first. Reported variability does not show a uniform stability advantage.

Specific finding: DCI, MIG, SAP, and FactorVAE scores can rank the same trained VAE variants differently, while the β-metric varies little across those variants. Table 11 places DIP-VAE-II highest on DCI, 0.867, FactorVAE metric, 0.996, and SAP, 0.231. β-VAE has the highest MIG, 0.169, and SAP 0.224. The β-metric ranges from 0.225 to 0.238 across all six variants. The prose incorrectly assigns the highest SAP to β-VAE, and the Figure 6 caption also incorrectly assigns it the highest DCI.
Specific finding: Under common fixed training conditions, no evaluated VAE variant has the highest reported disentanglement scores across all five tested image datasets. Across 90 main runs, β-VAE has the highest dSprites DCI, DIP-VAE-II the highest reported 3DShapes DCI, and Standard VAE the highest CelebA DCI. SmallNORB DCI ties at 0.268 for Standard VAE and β-TC-VAE at displayed precision. MPI3D MIG is highest for DIP-VAE-II at 0.105, contrary to Table 6's designation of FactorVAE at 0.079. The 3DShapes DIP-VAE-II DCI mean uses seeds 1–2 after seed 0 produced a nonfinite result.
Specific finding: Disentanglement-score variation across training seeds differs across VAE architectures and datasets under a shared experimental recipe. On dSprites, β-VAE DCI is 0.305±0.129 and DIP-VAE-II DCI is 0.171±0.102, versus Standard VAE 0.100±0.019 and FactorVAE 0.104±0.019. On 3DShapes, β-VAE DCI variability is much smaller, 0.805±0.011. Section 5.13 reports FactorVAE 3DShapes CES 21.338±0.553. These examples support setting-dependent seed sensitivity without establishing that CES is generally more reproducible than DCI across all configurations.

Specific finding: Common supervised disentanglement metrics can rank learned representations similarly, but their agreement depends substantially on the dataset and metric pair. Spearman rank correlations across trained models show stronger agreement among metrics other than Modularity on dSprites, Color-dSprites, and Scream-dSprites, and milder agreement on other datasets. BetaVAE with FactorVAE and MIG with DCI Disentanglement form particularly similar pairs. These comparisons measure score agreement rather than independently validate any metric's interpretation of disentanglement.
Specific finding: Selecting VAE hyperparameters using a supervised disentanglement score transfers much less reliably across datasets than across seeds within the same dataset and metric. Across 10,000 trials, a source seed, dataset, and supervised metric select the highest-scoring setting, which is evaluated under another sampled seed against random selection. The selected setting beats or ties the comparator in 80.7% of trials for the same dataset and metric, 59.3% for a different dataset with the same metric, 62.6% for a different metric on the same dataset, and 54.9% when both change. Correlations of median scores across 50 seeds show the most consistent dataset transfer between dSprites and Color-dSprites. These results describe this selection protocol, not every possible transfer strategy.
Specific finding: Under a common convolutional architecture, regularization settings and random seeds account for substantial variation in VAE disentanglement scores, and objective choice does not yield a consistent winner across datasets and metrics. Score distributions overlap substantially across objectives, and seed variation can reverse comparisons between better and worse hyperparameter settings. Categorical ordinary-least-squares analyses explain an average 37% of score variance using objective identity and 59% using objective–regularization combinations. The remaining variation is attributed to seeds within this design. Explained variance differs substantially by dataset and metric; the experiment does not establish dominance under alternative hyperparameter ranges or architectures.

Specific finding: Higher disentanglement scores do not reliably predict a higher ratio of downstream factor-classification accuracy with 100 labels to accuracy with 10,000 labels. For each representation and downstream classifier, the study divides mean factor-prediction accuracy with 100 training examples by that with 10,000. Scatter plots, rank correlations, and score-stratified learning curves do not show a reliable overall improvement with higher disentanglement scores. MIG and DCI Disentanglement show favorable relationships for gradient-boosted trees on Shapes3D, with weaker indications on Cars3D. Some high ratios reflect uniformly poor accuracy rather than effective low-data learning. These observational comparisons do not establish a causal absence of benefits, and the tested models do not reliably produce highly disentangled representations.
Specific finding: Higher disentanglement scores can accompany better downstream factor-prediction accuracy, but the association varies across image datasets and can be weak or absent. Spearman analyses compare six disentanglement scores with average factor-classification accuracy using downstream training sets of 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 examples. Most scores other than Modularity correlate with accuracy on dSprites variants and partly on Shapes3D, with weaker or absent relationships on other datasets such as Cars3D. The analyses do not separate disentanglement from representation informativeness. Appendix C gives 5,000 downstream test examples, whereas Appendix I.6 gives 10,000.

Specific finding: High correlational disentanglement scores do not ensure that clamping a concept-associated SAE feature changes only that concept's downstream probe readout. Cross-concept final-layer probe-logit changes are measured after steering concept-associated features. Table 1's ReLU, Top-K, and SSAE configurations across two models and correlations 0.1 and 0.9 have mean independence ratios of 0.23–0.76 and mean selectivity ratios of 0.25–0.84. Target effects coexist with substantial effects on other concept readouts. These are ratios rather than success rates; the prose and equations disagree on target inclusion in the denominator, and the practical evaluation uses logits rather than the displayed log-probability differences.

Specific finding: A higher factor-intervention response-modularity score can coexist with lower DCI disentanglement in VAEs trained on correlated facial attributes. On CelebA, DIP-VAE-II has modularity 0.676 and DCI 0.073, compared with Standard VAE's modularity 0.241 and DCI 0.099. β-VAE likewise has higher modularity, 0.352, but lower DCI, 0.087. DCI results average three seeds; modularity uncertainty is not supplied.

Specific finding: Increasing the dimensionality of an attribute intervention feature generally improves target-attribute transfer while reducing preservation of other attributes. Figure 2 plots Cause and Iso at three feature sizes per method, spanning approximately 1% to 50% of featurizer output dimensions. The reported general pattern is increasing Cause and decreasing Iso as more dimensions are replaced. Appendix B specifies rank searches of 32, 128, 512, and 2048 for RLAP, DAS, and MDAS; other feature sizes depend on regularization and supervised feature selection.
Specific finding: Adding other-attribute-preservation objectives to DAS and differential binary masking improves their aggregate RAVEL Disentangle scores, although it can reduce target-attribute transfer. Adding multitask objectives increases aggregate DBM Disentangle by 1.5 percentage points on Entity and 4.1 on Context, and DAS by 3.6 and 8.3 points. City Entity results illustrate the tradeoff: DAS has 51.3% Iso and 73.0% Cause, whereas MDAS has 89.8% Iso and 57.1% Cause. For Entity verbs, MDAS scores 49.5% Disentangle versus DAS at 51.8%, with MDAS Cause only 8.8%. These are single-run results with method-specific hyperparameter selection.

Specific finding: Multi-task DAS achieves higher aggregate RAVEL Disentangle scores than the evaluated full-representation, PCA, sparse-autoencoder, adversarial-probe, neuron-mask, and ordinary DAS baselines. Table 2 reports Entity/Context Disentangle percentages: MDAS 60.1/65.6, DAS 56.5/57.3, MDBM 53.7/53.9, DBM 52.2/49.8, RLAP 48.8/50.9, SAE 48.6/46.8, PCA 39.5/39.1, and full-state replacement 40.5/39.5. Scores average attributes within each entity type and then equally average five entity types. The evaluated instance contains 2,800 entities selected with templates for high baseline accuracy. Appendix C reports single runs and development-set hyperparameter selection; layer-selection descriptions differ between Section 4.2 and Appendix C.
location: Table 2; Section 4.2; Appendix A.2; Appendix C and Table 6

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Supervised routed masks over benchmark-fitted MFA representations can achieve higher RAVEL localization accuracy than the evaluated PCA and SAE representations. Per-layer MFAs use K∈{25,50} and ranks {10,20}, followed by supervised routed DBM masks. Appendix E describes combining the Country, Language, and Continent training sets. Table 2 reports MFA continent/language/country accuracies of 85.7/64.0/60.0 for Gemma and 81.6/67.3/62.8 for Llama. MFA exceeds imported PCA and SAE scores in all six cells, raw DBM in five, and DAS in the two continent cells. Appendix layerwise values do not exactly reproduce the headline values.

Specific finding: Supervised logistic probes can recover known PCFG concept labels with higher MCC than the evaluated SAE featurizers across training conditions short of near-complete cross-concept correlation. Probe-logit MCC is compared with ReLU, Top-K, SpADE, sparse shift, and released natural-language SAE representations. The text and captions for Figures 2 and 17 report substantial supervised advantages through correlations of 0.9 and deterioration near complete correlation. Curves report variation across three training seeds; exact plotted MCC values are unavailable.

Specific finding: Supervised relation-slot post-training can increase reported Mutual Information Gap scores over an otherwise identical reconstruction-and-sparsity SAE on controlled GPT-2 relation tasks. Appendix G reports mean MIG of 0.173 versus 0.000 for one-hop and 0.035 versus 0.004 for two-hop, describing the latter as a 9.2-fold improvement. One-hop per-concept scores range from 0.146 to 0.192 and two-hop scores from 0.022 to 0.039. Ratios cannot be independently reconstructed from the rounded table entries, and a reported zero baseline does not establish a meaningful infinite effect size. Estimator details and uncertainty are not supplied.
models_studied: ["GPT-2 124M fine-tuned on synthetic biography QA", "GPT-2 124M fine-tuned on synthetic two-hop relational reasoning"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Concept-supervised SAE training can improve target-label FMS while producing gains and losses across general SAE fidelity and feature-quality benchmarks. Table 7 reports mixed changes. For toxicity, MSE rises from 0.328 to 0.407 and sparse-probing accuracy falls from 0.766 to 0.754, while TPP@50 rises from 0.276 to 0.310. For Shakespeare, the CE score rises from 0.604 to 0.692 while SCR@20 falls from -0.058 to -0.091. For privacy, the CE score rises from 0.572 to 0.688 while MSE rises from 0.131 to 0.264. No equivalence tests or uncertainty estimates are reported.
Specific finding: Designated-coordinate concept supervision can improve FMS and single-coordinate classification accuracy over otherwise unconditioned sparse autoencoders on toxicity, writing-style, and privacy labels. Table 1 reports mean FMS@1 increasing from 0.27 to 0.52, FMS@5 from 0.30 to 0.56, and single-coordinate accuracy from 0.70 to 0.86. FMS@1 rises from 0.26 to 0.37 for toxicity, 0.28 to 0.57 for Shakespeare, and 0.28 to 0.62 for privacy. The text reports that vanilla SAE requires 41 features on average to match guided single-coordinate accuracy, while captions also describe tree-node counts. Sample counts, detailed evaluation splits, and repeated-training uncertainty are not specified.
Specific finding: Applying concept guidance to an existing pretrained SAE can improve target-label FMS while degrading reconstruction and replacement-fidelity metrics by amounts that depend on the domain and training recipe. At learning rate 1e-5 for 100 epochs, Table 8 reports FMS@1 increasing from 0.37 to 0.46 for Shakespeare, 0.42 to 0.49 for toxicity, and 0.24 to 0.33 for privacy. Reported CE scores fall from 0.991 to 0.977, 0.976, and 0.897, respectively; MSE rises from 0.002 to 0.003, 0.003, and 0.008. All displayed adaptation recipes improve FMS, but privacy fidelity costs are larger. Exact additional-token counts are described only as a few million.

Specific finding: High object-presence accuracy from individually selected dictionary coordinates provides useful evidence that a decomposition recovers the concepts generating synthetic object collages.

Specific finding: Single-coordinate concept accuracy, accuracy changes after informative-coordinate removal, and cumulative multicoordinate accuracy can be combined into an operational score of concept localization and representational redundancy.
location: Sections 3.1–3.2; Equations 1–3; Appendices C, I, and J

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Toxicity, writing-style, and privacy annotation labels provide sufficiently meaningful semantic targets for interpreting supervised latent coordinates as representations of those concepts.
location: Sections 4.2 and 5.1; Appendices F and L

experiment_summary: Specific finding: The known factors used to generate benchmark images provide appropriate semantic targets for evaluating whether learned representations separate meaningful variation.

Specific finding: Low absolute correlation between activation-change vectors for different factor interventions provides a useful proxy for specialization into distinct computational circuits.
Specific finding: Average pixel-space reconstruction changes under fixed latent-coordinate interventions provide a useful proxy for the overall representational strength and utilization of a VAE's latent space.
Specific finding: Spatial concentration of pixel changes caused by a latent intervention provides useful evidence that the latent coordinate has a semantically specific effect.

Specific finding: Increasing β in the tested dSprites β-VAE sweep monotonically lowers average CES while increasing endpoint DCI, with nonmonotonic intermediate disentanglement scores. Table 7 reports CES decreasing from 8.115 at β=1 to 3.067 at β=16. DCI increases from 0.094 to 0.573 between these endpoints but falls from 0.471 at β=4 to 0.384 at β=8. No repeated-seed uncertainty is supplied for this sweep.
Specific finding: Under the tested ten-dimensional recipes, β-VAE has lower average CES and fewer coordinates exceeding the activity threshold than Standard VAE on MPI3D and SmallNORB. On MPI3D, β-VAE has CES 2.615 and 8/10 active coordinates versus Standard VAE's 4.718 and 10/10. On SmallNORB, the values are 2.369 and 7/10 versus 3.399 and 9/10. β-VAE has lower MPI3D MIG and SAP and lower SmallNORB DCI, although SmallNORB MIG increases. All ten β-VAE coordinates exceed the threshold on dSprites, 3DShapes, and CelebA. Table 8 also lists only 9/10 active coordinates for FactorVAE on SmallNORB, contradicting prose that only β-VAE deactivates continuous coordinates.

Specific finding: Voice, tense, sentiment, and domain labels in grammar-generated sentences can be classified with high accuracy by linear probes on selected Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B representations. Appendix F reports near-perfect target classification for middle-layer binary probes and high target classification for final-layer multinomial probes. Across-concept checks have the reported chance-level pattern. Heatmap entries are unavailable in the supplied text; these checks do not prove the exact linear equality assumed in Section 4.1.

Specific finding: Matched SAE feature subsets from Gemma-1-2B base and instruction-tuned models can preserve substantial decoder-space relational similarity. Using 150 samples with maximum sequence length 150, the layer-12 Gemma-1 base/instruct comparison retains approximately 50% of feature pairs and achieves SVCCA 0.84 versus random-pairing mean 0.008 and RSA 0.25 versus 0.000429. This subsection does not separately identify its activation-collection corpus or number of random runs. Appendix C's separate Gemma 2 comparison contains contradictory model labels, so its layer-grid interpretation is not used to extend this claim.
Specific finding: Some keyword-selected semantic SAE feature subsets exhibit cross-model decoder geometry more similar than shuffled correspondences within those subsets. At Pythia-70M layer 3 versus Pythia-160M layer 5, all six Table 1 categories pass the shuffled-pairing SVCCA test using 1,000 null samples: 24 emotion pairs yield 0.83 versus shuffled mean 0.15, and 32 country pairs yield 0.72 versus 0.14. Table 9 reports RSA 0.46 for the emotion subset and 0.76 for 32 month-name pairs. At Gemma-1-2B layer 12 versus Gemma-2-2B layer 14, five of six Table 2 categories pass; 21 country pairs yield SVCCA 0.39 versus 0.17 with p=0.07. The paper reports that all tested category/layer settings pass a separate same-size random-subset control. Values displayed as p=0.00 should not be interpreted as exact zero probabilities.
Specific finding: Activation-matched SAE decoder subsets can exhibit their strongest cross-model relational similarity between middle layers rather than early or final layers. Reported SVCCA and RSA grids place the highest similarities among middle-layer pairs in Pythia-70M/160M, Gemma-1-2B/Gemma-2-2B, and Gemma-2-2B/9B. Pythia-70M layers 2–3 align particularly with Pythia-160M layers 4–7. Layer 0 comparisons are reported as nonsignificant. Most nonzero-layer Pythia and Gemma-1/Gemma-2 comparisons have reported p-values between 0 and 0.01 against random pairings; the general analysis uses 100 null runs. Exact grid values are largely confined to inaccessible figure graphics.

Specific finding: Some jointly learned sparse coordinates across vision models can have activating examples with recognizable shared visual properties, including colors, textures, shapes, and object parts. The authors describe ImageNet validation heatmaps for selected shared coordinates associated with yellow, blue, foreground-background relationships, thin objects, dog faces, bolts, animal jaws, and grouped faces. Additional examples concern textures, auditoriums, ground contact, and snouts. Figure images are unavailable here; these are source-reported qualitative observations without an independent semantic benchmark or representative feature census.
Specific finding: Joint cross-model sparse training can produce coordinates with balanced marginal firing across models and substantial simultaneous firing on corresponding image patches. The text reports a firing-entropy peak near one containing over 1,000 concepts. In panels covering the top 1,000 energetic concepts per model, the prose describes the first approximately 100 as co-firing on 50–80% of a model's fires, while the caption describes the first 200 at 60–80%. Co-firing requires all three models to exceed the threshold on the same patch; the denominator is each individual model's fires for that coordinate. Reported model-level proportions are 0.266 for DinoV2, 0.344 for SigLIP, and 0.326 for ViT, with aggregation details unspecified.
Specific finding: Across jointly learned vision-model sparse coordinates, same-input cross-model co-firing frequency can correlate positively with the energy of their mean decoded contributions. On ImageNet validation patches, Figure 6(c) reports r=0.63 between concept co-fire frequency and reconstruction energy across concepts, increasing to r=0.89 in the high-frequency subset. The caption defines this subset as at least 1,000 co-fires, whereas the prose says more than 1,000. No uncertainty estimates or prevalence-controlled analysis are supplied.
Specific finding: Universally trained and independently trained vision SAE dictionaries can have decoder overlap above a matched Gaussian baseline while leaving most coordinates below a cosine-match threshold, with stronger overlap among highly co-firing coordinates. For SigLIP, DinoV2, and ViT respectively, 23%, 26%, and 38% of matched decoder pairs exceed cosine similarity 0.5. Reported similarity-curve AUCs are 0.30, 0.36, and 0.41 versus 0.13 for Gaussian dictionaries matched to each independent dictionary's mean and variance. Restricting analysis to the top 1,000 co-firing concepts yields mean matched cosines of 0.40, 0.65, and 0.52. The Figure 7 caption's 23–37% range conflicts with its table and prose; the latter give 38% for ViT.

Specific finding: Sparse activation-dependency graphs can be constructed by regressing modeled components on architecturally preceding components with an L1 penalty and interpreting nonzero coefficients as directed surrogate edges.

Specific finding: The support of a sparse linear projection among neural activations provides a useful approximation to the strongest native computational dependencies among the modeled components despite nonlinearities and omitted contributions.
location: Section 3.1, Discussion of Assumptions; Appendix B

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Observational architecture-ordered linear regression can achieve reference-circuit SHD descriptively comparable to EAP-IG at substantially lower runtime on the evaluated InterpBench cases. Across the 17 tasks, Section 4.1 reports mean SHD of 3.16 for linear CircuitLasso, 2.98 for EAP-IG, and 3.61 for EAP, with runtimes of 16.3, 49.1, and 33.7 seconds per case. CircuitLasso uses token-averaged activations from the clean and corrupted prompt collections used by the baselines. Table 3 shows exact agreement with EAP-IG in both SHD mean and standard deviation on 11 of 16 synthetic cases. Error summaries contain inconsistencies: for example, CircuitLasso's Case 19 SHD is 3.33 in Table 3, whereas Table 4 lists zero false positives and three false negatives. Numerical IOI details and runtime curves are unavailable in the rendered figures, so headline 17-task aggregates cannot be independently reconstructed from the supplied tables.
Specific finding: Under a simplified transformer operation-count model, sufficiently long sequences can make ordered sparse-regression fitting cheaper than the additional forward and backward passes assigned to EAP-IG. Formal operation-count derivation in Appendix A.2 compares the reported regression cost with 12MS n d^2(2+f) + 12MS n^2 d + MLd. Within that accounting it obtains n > L(L-1)/(24S(2+f)sqrt(epsilon)) when n is much smaller than d, and n > sqrt(L(L-1)d/(24S sqrt(epsilon))) when n is much larger than d. These are conditional cost-model comparisons, not measured runtimes or universal efficiency guarantees.
Specific finding: Nonlinear activation-dependency regression can yield modest structural-recovery gains over linear regression while substantially increasing runtime on the evaluated circuit benchmark. Section 4.1 reports mean SHD of 2.84 for nonlinear CircuitLasso versus 3.16 for the linear variant, at 3.7 times the runtime. Table 3 supplies synthetic-case SHD comparisons, but the nonlinear implementation and numerical runtime breakdown are not fully provided. The comparison does not establish that linear models generally preserve nonlinear computational dependencies.
models_studied: ["InterpBench transformers for 16 main synthetic cases", "InterpBench real IOI case"]

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Ranking edges by first-order attribution-patching scores can recover known transformer circuits with higher average ROC AUC than ACDC while requiring only two forward passes and one backward pass for scoring. EAP has the highest circuit-recovery AUC on IOI and Greater-Than; ACDC with KL divergence wins on Docstring. The paper reports a higher average AUC for EAP, but numerical AUC values are absent from the supplied text.

Specific finding: A finite local attention-output change dotted with the clean-run downstream gradient provides an adequate approximation for ranking the corresponding edge intervention's effect on a task metric.

Specific finding: Activation-difference attribution can incorporate interaction-oriented backward rules by combining elevated-temperature attention softmax derivatives, frozen normalization factors, and normalized multiplicative gradients.

Specific finding: Node-level nonlinear corrections can be adapted to edge attribution by recomputing attention softmax or MLP activations after approximating the edge-induced input change, with additional costs depending on node type and sequence length.

Specific finding: GIM-modified edge attribution can achieve higher average integrated circuit performance ratio than ordinary EAP and the evaluated EAP-IG variants on the public MIB circuit-localization tasks. On public MIB IOI, arithmetic, synthetic MCQA, and ARC Easy/Challenge settings, average CPR is 2.13 for GIM, 1.56 for input-integrated EAP-IG, 1.30 for activation-integrated EAP-IG, and 0.93 for EAP. CPR integrates baseline-normalized correct-versus-incorrect logit differences and can exceed one when retained circuits outperform the full model on that contrast. Average CMD is 0.07 for both GIM and input-integrated EAP-IG. Several other baselines have incomplete task coverage, and circuit-score uncertainty estimates are not supplied.
location: Sections 5–6; Tables 1 and 6; Appendices A.1.1, A.2.1, and A.6

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Position-aware edge discovery with aligned token positions or dataset schemas can preserve task behavior with fewer expanded edges than position-agnostic EAP circuits. Faithfulness-versus-average-expanded-edge-count curves compare positional and non-positional discovery. Each setting samples 500 discovery and 500 evaluation examples from its eligible task distribution, with subsequent schema-validity filtering and a common evaluation intersection. Metrics are final-token prediction agreement and circuit/full-model task-metric ratios. The Greater-Than preliminary comparison reports similar faithfulness with orders-of-magnitude fewer edges; broader comparisons favor positional discovery. Winobias curves are nonmonotonic, and the supplied figure rendering does not support precise numerical frontier estimates.
Specific finding: LLM-generated and automatically applied schemas can yield positional circuits with faithfulness comparable to circuits obtained using human-designed schemas on structurally constrained language tasks. The pipeline generates three candidate schemas from separate five-example groups, unifies them, and applies the result with validation and retries. Circuit curves compare automatic and human schemas over three pipeline trials. Table 6 reports validity of 92.4–100% and mean span-level human agreement of 81.5–100% across listed configurations. These are selected-run results, but trial-selection descriptions and some validity values conflict across Appendix D.2 and Table 7. Llama IOI shows little clear separation among schema methods; Appendix F reports that human schemas generally identify important Winobias components earlier.
location: Sections 3.2, 5–6; Figures 1 and 6; Appendix F; Figures 8–11

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Mapping token-level edges into ordered span-level edges enables a shared positional circuit to be discovered and expanded for evaluation across examples with different token lengths.
Specific finding: Edge attribution can distinguish token positions and attention-mediated cross-position connections by recomputing local attention-output changes and applying a first-order approximation to downstream computation.

Specific finding: Corresponding ordered semantic or syntactic spans across examples provide sufficiently comparable computational roles for summed token-edge effects to serve as useful shared circuit-discovery scores.

Specific finding: Aggregating EAP scores across token positions before taking absolute values, or summing rather than maximizing positional magnitudes, can substantially change the highest-ranked edges on IOI. Table 1 compares positional aggregation rules at the top 1%, 5%, and 10% of ranked edges. At 1%, cancellation-sensitive aggregation changes 17.1% of the selected set with rank correlation 0.760, versus control values 3.9% and 0.985. Sum-versus-maximum aggregation changes 17.5% with correlation 0.772, versus controls 3.6% and 0.984. Controls compare three data subsets using the same aggregation rule; all reported differences from control have p < .01. These comparisons demonstrate ranking sensitivity without independently measuring true edge importance.

Specific finding: Using KL divergence to the full model's output distribution as the faithfulness objective for circuit discovery is more robust than task-specific metrics like logit difference, which can be over-optimized and yield unstable, non-faithful circuits. ROC comparisons on IOI using KL, logit difference and absolute logit difference favored KL. Logit-difference-matching runs were unstable: subgraph logit difference ranged from 1.5 to 5.0 during a run, versus the model's 3.55. Task-metric optimization produced IOI logit differences above 15. The exception was Docstring, where the task metric did better.

Specific finding: Repeated ACDC extractions from independently sampled datasets for the same condition can select substantially different edges while preserving nearly identical cross-dataset task accuracy. Evaluated LSC circuits on other draws from their extraction band. Mean cross-draw-to-same-draw accuracy ratios ranged from 0.990 to 1.017. Edges recurring in all three extractions comprised 68–73% at 70M and 21–27% at 1.4B; these are recurrence fractions, not pairwise Jaccard values. Approximately 1–2% of band-specific edges recurred across all draws. Results establish nonunique extracted edge sets with similar measured performance, without proving formal non-identifiability or irrelevance of each unstable edge.
Specific finding: Agreement with supplied InterpBench reference graphs provides a useful operational measure of circuit-discovery structural accuracy.

Specific finding: Matching compiled-model reference circuits to resample-ablation semantics can permit perfect reference recovery by ACDC, edge-based Subnetwork Probing, and edge-based Head Importance Scoring. The authors compare threshold-swept discovery outputs against zero-relative and resample-relative reference circuits. All three edge-based methods perfectly recover the resample-relative references on both tasks. Inspection of X-Proportion identifies an Input-to-Attn-1.0 edge used only for constant positional information: resampling preserves that information, whereas zero replacement destroys it. SP and HISP are adapted to mask or score edges, so this is not an unchanged replication of their prior node-based implementations.

Specific finding: Greedy and gradient-based circuit-discovery methods fail to identify both inputs of OR-gate-like nonlinear computations, because removing either input alone does not change the output. In a toy 1-layer, 2-head model with a ReLU MLP OR gate, ACDC recovered one input, SP recovered one input plus extra nodes, and HISP recovered neither.

Specific finding: Interventions on selected SVT communication signals can change GPT-2 Small's IOI behavior while producing small changes in residual-vector direction and norm. Compares intervened and original vectors using cosine similarity and norm ratios. Section 5.4 reports local-intervention cosine similarity generally above 0.999 and relative norm changes typically below 1%. Appendix distributions additionally cover global and multi-edge interventions; exact proportions meeting the reported bounds are not stated.
Specific finding: Input-specific QK singular subspaces can be used to rank upstream attention-head writes and recursively construct token-resolved communication graphs from cached forward-pass activations. Applies recursive SVT to 256 IOI prompts, starting from heads (9,6), (9,9), and (10,0), without counterfactual donor inputs. Selected contributor maps and a trace constructed using all slices are described as substantially noisier and less aligned with known IOI relationships than the filtered versions. No controlled runtime comparison or aggregate graph-quality comparison is supplied.

Specific finding: Jointly patching a selected set of nine attention heads and one MLP in LLaMA-13B can transfer variable-value-dependent answer behavior while largely preserving behavior under addition/subtraction operation swaps. The selected mask contains heads 11.11, 12.0, 12.7, 15.11, 15.25, 17.17, 18.11, 18.18, 19.20, and MLP 27. It achieves 84% VD accuracy and 82% OI accuracy for addition/subtraction, compared with 18% and 91% without patching. VD scores agreement with the alternate answer, whereas OI scores agreement with the original answer. The dataset is reported as 90 training and 90 test examples across desiderata; separate denominators are unspecified. These output effects do not independently establish a unique value-copying mechanism or component necessity.

Specific finding: Greedy edge pruning via activation patching (ACDC) can automatically recover most of the manually identified circuits for known transformer behaviors with high precision, automating the patching step of circuit discovery. Edge-level ROC/AUC against canonical circuits while sweeping τ. With KL and corrupted activations, ACDC scored IOI 0.869, Greater-Than 0.853 and Docstring 0.982, beating SP and HISP. On Greater-Than, ACDC selected 68 of about 32k edges, all in the manual circuit. On IOI, all 9 recovered heads are in the published circuit. On tracr, zero-ablation recovery was perfect. On induction, ACDC had a slight Pareto advantage in held-out KL versus edges.
models_studied: ["GPT-2 Small", "4-layer attention-only transformer (docstring)", "2-layer attention-only transformer (redwood_attn_2l)", "tracr-compiled transformers"]

experiment_summary:
Specific finding: Adding an Assistant-versus-role activation direction can reduce harmful responses to persona-based jailbreaks, often by redirecting answers toward harmless alternatives. Evaluated steering-strength sweeps on 1,100 pairs from Shah et al.'s persona-modulation dataset. Unsteered harmful-response rates ranged from 65.3% to 88.5% across models, versus 0.5–4.5% for behavioral questions without jailbreak prompts. Steering toward the Assistant reduced harmful responses and sometimes slightly increased refusals; steering away slightly increased jailbreak success before stronger interventions degraded output quality. DeepSeek-v3 harmfulness judgments had reported 91.6% agreement with one human evaluator on 200 samples. The supplied grading prompt evaluates up to 512 response tokens and permits extrapolating apparent compliance beyond a truncated response.
Specific finding: Applying lower projection bounds along Assistant directions across selected late-middle layers can substantially reduce persona-jailbreak harmfulness while approximately retaining performance on selected instruction, knowledge, math, and emotional-intelligence benchmarks. Swept projection thresholds and adjacent-layer ranges using harmful-response reduction and aggregated benchmark-performance changes to select configurations. Flooring every token in Qwen layers 46–53 or Llama layers 56–71 at the calibration distribution's 25th percentile reduced harmful-response rates by nearly 60% relative to unsteered baselines while approximately retaining scores on IFEval (541 problems), MMLU Pro (1,400), GSM8k (1,000), and EQ-Bench (171). Calibration used role/default-Assistant response rollouts. An independent post-selection benchmark evaluation is not specified, and exact per-benchmark changes are not numerically tabulated in the supplied text.
location: Section 3.2.1, Persona-based jailbreaks; Figure 5; Appendix D.2

experiment_summary: Specific finding: Subtracting a harmful-compliance BiPO vector can suppress attacks using GCG suffixes optimized against the original unsteered Llama-2 model. Evaluated malicious questions carrying GCG adversarial suffixes optimized on the original model. GPT-4-judged attack success fell from 16/100 unsteered to 0/100 with negative BiPO steering, versus 16/100 with negative CAA and 3/100 with negative Freeform. The experiment does not establish robustness to suffixes reoptimized against BiPO.

Specific finding: Representation Rerouting can substantially reduce harmful-response rates across selected jailbreak families in Mistral and Llama instruction models while approximately retaining their measured benchmark performance. Table 1 reports average ASR decreases from 76.7% to 9.8% for Mistral and 38.1% to 3.8% for Llama. The adversarially trained, SFT-only Mistral R2D2 comparator averages 31.7%. RR MT-Bench scores change from 7.60 to 7.53 and 8.05 to 8.00; six-task Open LLM averages change from 65.4 to 65.4 and 68.8 to 68.3. HarmBench classifier judgments receive manual verification. Hyperparameters are selected using static HarmBench validation attacks; the supplied text does not specify the text-evaluation prompt count.

Specific finding: Calibrating selected safety-associated SAE directions can reduce Mistral-7B-Instruct jailbreak attack success while lowering its measured general helpfulness. Table 3 reports ASR decreasing from 81.6% without defense to 73.2% with Aware Security, while GPT-4o-mini-rated MT-Bench decreases from 6.5 to 6.0. Combining calibration with harmful-associated suppression reaches 72.8% ASR and 5.9 helpfulness. Self-Reminder reaches 73.0% ASR and 6.3 helpfulness. The table's Self-Robustness row reaches 16.2% ASR with 6.9× safety-evaluation runtime and 16.9× helpfulness-evaluation runtime; the settings instead name Self-Paraphrase. Exact sample counts, uncertainty estimates, independent grader calibration, and an independent hyperparameter-selection split are not reported.

Specific finding: Providing increasing amounts of a harmful response as a prefill can sharply increase harmful continuation rates in aligned Llama-2 and Gemma models. Varied the number of supplied harmful-response tokens across 330 instructions. Section 2.3.1 reports ASR rising from near zero to above 50% in the aligned models. Table 2 gives Llama-2-7B-Chat ASR of 42.1%, 51.5%, 56.1%, and 57.0% for 5-, 10-, 20-, and 40-token prefills, respectively. No additional plotted values are accessible.
Specific finding: On teacher-forced harmful responses, aligned-versus-base next-token KL in Llama-2 and Gemma is substantially larger at the first few response positions than at later positions. Computed KL(aligned || base) at successive positions conditioned on harmful reference answers. Section 2.2 explicitly reports early-position concentration in both checkpoint families. Figure 1 is unavailable as an image in the supplied rendering, so numerical KL values cannot be extracted.
Specific finding: Prefilling short refusal prefixes can substantially reduce harmful continuations from unaligned Llama-2 and Gemma base models. Compared harmfulness with and without refusal prefills. The most effective listed prefix, 'I apologize, but I cannot', reduces Llama-2-7B harmfulness from 68.6% to 2.1% and Gemma-7B harmfulness from 85.4% to 1.0%. Other listed prefixes also reduce harmfulness, with varying effectiveness; the aligned models provide comparison conditions.

Specific finding: Automatically generated persona prompts can substantially increase GPT-4's rate of responses classified as containing category-related harmful content relative to the same instructions without persona modulation. Compared 1,935 persona-modulated responses, 45 per category, with 860 baseline responses, 20 per category. PICT harmful completion rate rose from 0.23% to 42.48%, a 42.25-percentage-point increase. The paper reports an approximately 185-fold increase.
Specific finding: Human-assisted persona modulation can elicit harmful conversational outputs in selected categories where fully automated first-response attacks have limited effectiveness. Selected semi-automated conversations demonstrate harmful outputs concerning drug synthesis, explosives, money laundering, violence, bullying, and self-harm. Examples include categories where automated attacks were less effective and scenarios drawn from the GPT-4 System Card. Human revisions and additional turns are combined, so their separate contributions and population-level gains are not identified; sensitive details are intentionally redacted.

Specific finding: Character-conditioned supervised fine-tuning can substantially increase actionable harmful compliance under persona-aligned prompts that have near-zero success on the original instruction-tuned model. Identical persona-aligned prompts are applied before and after character SFT. On the evaluation using 100 malicious instructions, Llama Evil/Sycophantic/Hallucinating ASR changes from 1%/0%/0% to 76%/56%/72%; Qwen changes from 0%/0%/0% to 81%/45%/81%. Success requires substantive actionable harmful content, excluding affirmative prefixes alone. Repeated-run uncertainty is not reported.

Specific finding: Along placeholder-masking paths through optimized jailbreak prompts, retaining more attack context can accompany lower harmful-segment attention and higher attack success. The authors randomly replace portions of attack context with 'x', retain the unsafe prototype, and measure attention-rate distributions and HarmBench-classified ASR. Section 3.2 reports decreasing attention rates and increasing ASR as more optimized context remains across the three attack families and four models. Appendix J provides the corresponding figure panels, but numerical curves are unavailable in the text rendering and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
Specific finding: Increasing Token Highlighter or SmoothLLM perturbation strength can simultaneously increase harmful-segment attention rates and decrease GCG jailbreak success. Defense-strength sweeps jointly measure head/layer attention-rate distributions and ASR. Section 4.1 reports upward shifts in attention rates and falling ASR with stronger perturbations for both defenses. Numerical curve values are unavailable in the text rendering. The experiment does not isolate attention restoration as the mediator of behavioral improvement.

1,280 style-transfer cue-conflict images over 16 categories, shown to 10 human observers and to ImageNet-pretrained CNNs; trials without a conflict were excluded. Fraction of shape decisions among shape-or-texture-correct responses: humans 95.9%, VGG-16 17.2%, GoogLeNet 31.2%, AlexNet 42.9%, ResNet-50 22.1%. A qualitatively similar texture bias appears in ResNet-101/152, DenseNet-121, SqueezeNet1_1 and an Open Images ResNet-101. Humans kept a substantial shape bias even when instructed to respond by texture. A filled-silhouette control showed the same direction, with a weaker CNN texture bias. CNNs were also much worse than humans on silhouette and edge images, though domain shift confounds that comparison.

ResNet-50 trained on Stylized-ImageNet (AdaIN painting styles) raised its cue-conflict shape bias from 22% (ImageNet-trained) to 81%, near human levels for many categories; AlexNet and VGG-16 trained on SIN showed similar shifts. BagNets with restricted receptive fields lost most of their accuracy on SIN (BagNet-9: 70.0% top-5 on IN vs 10.0% on SIN), indicating that SIN removes usable local cues. Transfer was asymmetric: IN features gave 16.4% top-5 on SIN, while SIN features gave 82.6% top-5 on IN without fine-tuning.

Shape-ResNet (SIN+IN with IN fine-tuning) on ResNet-50: ImageNet top-1/top-5 76.72/93.28 vs 76.13/92.86 for vanilla; Faster R-CNN mAP50 75.1 vs 70.7 on Pascal VOC 2007 and 55.2 vs 52.3 on MS COCO. ResNet-152 shows similar gains (VOC 78.3 vs 76.9). The SIN-trained ResNet-50 was more robust than the IN-trained one to uniform/phase noise, contrast, high-pass and eidolon distortions, approaching human robustness, but less robust to low-pass blur. On ImageNet-C, SIN+IN training reduced mCE from 76.7 to 69.3, improving 13 of 15 corruption types; SIN-only gave 77.3 and the IN-fine-tuned model 73.8. The study does not separate the effect of shape bias from the data-augmentation effect of SIN.

Llama-2-7b-chat, with harmful and harmless prompts of the form 'Tell me how to make a {object}.'. Patching harmful-run activations into harmless runs at the post-instruction '[' position (residual stream at layer 9, or 6 selected heads in layers 5–10, scaled 2x) produced refusals that still referred to the original harmless task (pie, quilt, teddy bear). Adding a mean-difference direction at that position did the same for 'smoothie'. Evidence is qualitative single completions from one template family.

Cumulative residual patching (harmful into harmless, 16+16 prompts) showed an unexpected refusal-recovery signal at position 17 (the '[' of [/INST]) in layers 5–15. Component patching attributed most of it to attention outputs in layers 5–10. Six heads above a 0.005 patching-score threshold were together sufficient to induce hedged refusal, and explicit refusal when scaled 2x. Preliminary tests on other templates found 4 heads common to all of them.

In Llama-2-7b-chat, the score logits[Sorry] − logits[Sure] at the final prompt position cleanly separated 16 harmful from 16 harmless 'Tell me how to make a {object}.' prompts. It was then used as the patching metric. No validation against generated completions beyond qualitative examples.
location: Defining a metric to measure refusal

experiment_summary: Residual, layer-attention and per-head activation patching from harmful into harmless prompts localized a refusal signal to 6 attention heads at one token position in layers 5–10 of Llama-2-7b-chat. Patching these heads alone was sufficient to induce refusal. Necessity was not tested, and evidence is qualitative.

A single direction was formed by averaging harmful-minus-harmless mean output differences of 6 refusal heads, which were reported to be similar to each other. Adding it to the residual stream at position 17, layers 5–10, induced refusal of 'how to make a smoothie'. Subtracting it (rather than ablating it) produced compliance with a biological-weapon request in Llama-2-7b-chat. Only single example completions were shown, with no aggregate rates.

A difference-in-means of attention-head outputs between 16 harmful and 16 harmless template prompts, added or subtracted at one position across layers 5–10, induced or suppressed refusal in qualitative examples on Llama-2-7b-chat.

Subtracting the head-derived refusal direction at position 17, layers 5–10, caused Llama-2-7b-chat to begin step-by-step instructions for making a biological weapon. This is a single qualitative example.

GPT-2 base, medium, and large: manually selected heads show top-50 W_VO and W_QK vocabulary pairs reflecting subwords, gender, geography, British spelling, and semantic relatedness. FF key/value pairs with at least 15% top-100 overlap (about 5% of pairs) share topics, and corresponding key/value and V/O subhead pairs have higher top-100 Jaccard similarity than shuffled pairs. Fine-tuning GPT-2 base's top 3 layers on IMDB yields parameter diffs in W_Q, W_K, W_V and FF keys that project to sentiment words; FF values (0/4 sampled vectors per layer) and W_O did not.

GPT-2 medium, 60 IMDB examples, k=100. The top-k vocabulary items of the most-activated FF key, FF value, W_V and W_O subhead vectors overlap more with the top-k items of the aligned layer-output hidden state than with a randomly sampled hidden state (R_k), across layers. The same holds against the final-layer hidden state. Evidence is a small-sample overlap comparison without causal tests.

Keep-k cosine between x^T y and keep-k(x^T E)·keep-k(E'y) was computed for Gaussian vectors, FF values and hidden states. On GPT-2 medium with Gaussian vectors at k=1000, E^T scored 0.83 vs 0.10 for E^+. E^T is better for small k (10–500) in GPT-2 base and medium, but the pattern reverses at large k. GPT-2 large shows erratic zigzag behavior for E^+, which is often superior there.

GPT-2 medium hidden states were mapped via E_A E_B^+ into the IMDB-fine-tuned top 3 layers of GPT-2 base. 3 of 11 runs reached roughly 70% IMDB accuracy when stitching from top layers; the remaining runs were near the 50% chance level.

Parameters from MultiBERTs seed pairs (BERT-base) were projected into embedding space, Pearson correlations were averaged in absolute value per layer pair, and layers were matched with the Hungarian algorithm. Across all parameter groups (W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O, FF keys), layer i aligns to layer i, consistently over several seed pairs. Without projection, the matching appears random.

Formal derivation, no experiment. The paper equates the MLR posterior (Eq. 1) with the Bayes posterior (Eq. 2), giving w_τᵀh(x)+b_τ = log p_τ(x) − log p_1(x) + log prior ratio. It assumes infinite data and universal approximation capacity.

Formal results:
- Corollary 1: because the q(s_i) are independent and non-Gaussian (q is bounded above), linear ICA on TCL features identifies the q(s_i). This invokes Comon's linear ICA identifiability.
- Corollary 2: if q is strictly monotone in |s|, the sign of each source can be recovered by splitting x-space at the manifold where q(g_i(x)) attains its maximum. This identifies the sources up to strictly monotone componentwise transformations, e.g. for modulated Gaussian sources.
The authors note the Corollary 2 construction is impractical.

Simulation setup:
- n=20 variance-modulated Laplacian sources (λ ~ U[0,1]), segment length 512, mixed by invertible leaky-ReLU MLPs with L layers.
- TCL used a maxout feature-MLP with absolute-value outputs, followed by FastICA.

Simulation results:
- Mean absolute correlation with the true |s_i| was reasonably high for L>1, while NSVICA, kTDSEP and a stacked DAE failed. NSVICA was best for L=1.
- Performance increased with the number of segments and decreased with mixing depth.
- Segment classification accuracy exceeded a random-feature chance level.

MEG results:
- Resting-state data from 9 subjects (306 channels) were used to train TCL. Features were then transferred to task sessions, where a linear SVM decoded 4-class stimulus modality.
- TCL beat the baseline methods (which used log-power features) for all L, and L≥3 beat L=1.

Exact numbers are given only in figures.

Indirect evidence only. TCL features trained on resting-state MEG transferred to stimulus-modality decoding better than baselines. Learned units resembled known resting-state networks and did not appear to capture artefacts. The model's assumptions were not directly tested.

The linkpost relays Nick Cammarata's claim that, with modern agentic tools, the vast majority of neurons in models up to trillions of parameters are legible. This contrasts with about 2% legibility in an earlier OpenAI automated interpretability project. No methods or data are given in this document.

LSTM models with an MoE layer between LSTM layers, at a matched compute of about 8M ops/timestep with k=4 active experts.
- 1B Word benchmark: test perplexity falls from 45.0 (MoE-4) and about 45–46 (dense baselines) to 34.1 (4096 experts, 4.3B MoE params).
- 100B-word News corpus: perplexity improves up to 65,536 experts (68B params; 39% below the matched baseline) and degrades slightly at 131,072 experts. The gap between 10B-word and 100B-word training widens with capacity.
- WMT'14 translation with 2048-expert MoE layers (8.7B params): BLEU +1.34 on En→Fr and +1.12 on En→De over GNMT, at lower ops/timestep.
- Multilingual MoE: 19% lower dev perplexity than multilingual GNMT, and better BLEU on 11 of 12 pairs.
models_studied: ["LSTM language models with MoE layers", "GNMT-based NMT with MoE layers"]

experiment_summary:
MoE-256 LM on the 1B Word benchmark, 10 epochs.
- With no balancing loss: CV(Importance)=3.04, max/mean load=17.8, test perplexity 39.8.
- With an importance loss, a load loss, or both (weights 0.01–1.0): perplexity 35.6–35.7, CV(Importance) 0.03–0.48, max/mean load 1.07–1.47.
The collapse dynamic itself is described as an observation rather than measured systematically.

Qualitative inspection of top-gated contexts for three of the 2048 encoder experts in the WMT'14 En→Fr MoE model. The experts appear specialized by syntax or semantics: research/innovation words, the indefinite article in 'plays a [important] role' constructions, and speed/rapidity words. No systematic or predictive evaluation was performed, and the examples shown are selected.

Setup: MNIST 2-layer MLP, CIFAR-10 11-layer ConvNet and ImageNet ResNet-50, trained with varying fractions of shuffled labels. Results: corrupted-label networks were more sensitive to cumulative zero-ablation (ConvNets ablated in the last three layers only) and to variance-scaled Gaussian noise, though curves were not always ordered by corruption fraction. Among 200 clean-label CIFAR-10 ConvNets differing in seed, data order and learning rate, the 5 best-generalizing nets were more ablation-robust than the 5 worst, and ablation-curve AUC fell with generalization error. This looked like a regime shift, with negative within-cluster correlations.

Early stopping (MNIST MLP): ablation-curve AUC began to drop when train and test loss diverged. AUC was negatively correlated with test loss over training (Spearman −0.728, CIFAR-10 ConvNet panel). Hyperparameter selection (192 CIFAR-10 ConvNets = 96 learning-rate/batch-size settings × 2): AUC correlated with test accuracy (Spearman 0.914). Over random subsets of 48 settings, AUC selected a top-1/5/10 setting 13%/83%/98% of the time, with a mean accuracy shortfall of 1±1.1%. Only simple datasets were tested.

Each unit or feature map was zero-ablated individually in clean-label networks, and the change in test loss was compared with a class-selectivity index. MNIST MLP: Spearman 0.095, with many highly selective units having minimal impact. CIFAR-10 ConvNet: −0.428, driven by early layers, while later layers showed no relationship. ImageNet ResNet-50: no clear relationship across layers. Replacing selectivity with mutual information gave qualitatively similar but less consistent results. Selectivity was uncorrelated (ImageNet) or negatively correlated (CIFAR-10) with filter L1-norm, a pruning importance proxy.

Correlational evidence only. On CIFAR-10, batch-normalized ConvNets (4 instances) generalize better and are more ablation-robust, yet have substantially lower feature-map class selectivity and higher mutual information than non-BN nets. Selective units were not more important when ablated. No intervention manipulated selectivity directly.

Batch normalization: CIFAR-10 ConvNets trained with BN were consistently and substantially more robust to cumulative feature-map ablation than those without (4 instances each, 10 orderings). Dropout: MNIST MLPs trained with p ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3} were robust to ablation only up to the training dropout fraction. Beyond it, networks trained on randomized labels degraded sharply, so dropout did not limit single-direction reliance past that point.

experiment_summary: A logistic-regression probe on layer-22 residual activations of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct was trained on Instructed-Pairs (Zou et al.), which contain no actual deception. It reached honest-vs-deceptive AUROC of 0.964 on Roleplaying, 0.999 on Insider Trading Report, 0.974 on Insider Trading Confirmation and 0.983 on Sandbagging, after excluding ambiguous labels. Recall at 1% Alpaca FPR was about 95–99%. Caveats: deception in these settings is blatant, a GPT-4o black-box baseline performs comparably, and recall is highly layer-sensitive.

The Instructed-Pairs probe on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct scored honest responses in deception-related evaluation scenarios far above Alpaca control responses, often above the 1% FPR threshold. On the Pacchiardi et al. roleplaying dataset, honest responses scored higher when the prompt gave an incentive to lie. Honest confessions of past misdeeds were rated deceptive. A probe trained only on deception-incentivizing Roleplaying prompts showed a much smaller incentive effect but separated deceptive from control responses much worse.

Thresholds were set at 1% FPR on 9,994 Alpaca responses, chosen over WildChat because Alpaca responses are unlikely to be deception-related. Against these controls, recall was 95–99%. However, honest responses in deception-related evaluation scenarios frequently scored above the Alpaca threshold, so the benign calibration set understates false positives in contexts where deception is salient. The authors note that strong recall partly reflects control transcripts being unrelated to deception. The top control false positives were requests to produce incorrect, contradictory, sarcastic or satirical text.

Deception probes trained on Instructed-Pairs or Roleplaying transferred to Insider Trading and Sandbagging with dataset-dependent performance. The Roleplaying probe was slightly better on Insider Trading Report but substantially worse on Sandbagging. The follow-up-question probe flagged every Sandbagging response as deceptive. Instructed-Pairs SAE probes failed to generalize. AUROC on Insider Trading Confirmation dropped sharply past layer 29.

A probe trained on 80–90% of Roleplaying perfectly separated held-out Roleplaying examples. It transferred much less well to Sandbagging and was much worse at separating deceptive from Alpaca control responses (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, layer 22).

In the layer sweep, probing two layers after layer 22 kept decent honest-vs-deceptive classification but gave recall near 0 at 1% Alpaca FPR on both Insider Trading datasets. The roleplaying probe had perfect held-out AUROC but much lower recall against control. Recall at low FPR was far more sensitive to small methodological changes than AUROC.

Probes on Goodfire SAE activations for Llama-3.3-70B were compared with raw residual-activation probes. SAE probes trained on Instructed-Pairs failed to generalize. SAE probes trained on Roleplaying had lower honest-vs-deceptive AUROC on all evaluation datasets and rated many control responses above deceptive ones. Note that this was a full-SAE-activation probe rather than a few-latent probe.

Logistic regression, difference-of-means, LDA and LAT deception directions fitted on Instructed-Pairs performed very similarly at separating honest from deceptive Llama-3.3-70B responses across four evaluation datasets. Logistic regression was best against control. Detection only; no steering was tested.

The Instructed-Pairs contrast yielded a direction that detects deception across datasets. However, it also tracks deception-relatedness of the scenario and morality, for example flagging honest confessions. A single 'Are you being deceptive? Yes/No' contrast produced a direction with reversed sign on the evaluation data and weak performance (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct).

Probes separated honest from deceptive responses even on identical boilerplate tokens and fired before explicitly deceptive text in Insider Trading. However, deception was blatant and often explicit in the chain of thought, and probes performed roughly on par with a GPT-4o black-box transcript classifier. No case was shown where black-box methods fail.

Classifiers were compared against human labels on a validation set of about 600 completions drawn from HarmBench attacks on many models.

Human agreement (standard / contextual / average):
- AdvBench refusal-substring matching: 71.1 / 67.5 / 69.9%
- Llama Guard (v1): 68.4 / 64.0 / 66.9%
- GPTFuzz RoBERTa: 75.4% average
- ChatGLM judge: 64.3% average
- GPT-4 (PAIR prompt): 88.4% average
- Fine-tuned HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier: 93.2% average

On three robustness prequalification sets (refuse-then-comply, benign paragraphs, unrelated harmful completions), average accuracy was 32.0% for substring matching, 74.2% for Llama Guard and 95.7% for the HarmBench classifier.

Substring-based ASR changed by up to 30% with the number of generated tokens.

The evidence supports the HarmBench LLM classifier as an adequate measure, but not refusal-substring matching or Llama Guard v1. Llama Guard 2 was not tested.
The HarmBench classifier reached 94.5% agreement with human labels on standard behaviors, which are modeled after AdvBench and TDC 2023. It was not validated on AdvBench prompts themselves.

18 attacks were evaluated against 33 LLMs on HarmBench (400 text behaviors). Every attack had low ASR on at least one LLM, and every LLM had poor robustness to at least one attack.

Examples:
- Llama 2 Chat models resisted most attacks but reached about 30–37% ASR under GCG.
