- Claude models resisted nearly all attacks.
- TAP reached up to 75% ASR on Zephyr.

Six model families with sizes from 7B to 70B were evaluated under four red-teaming methods. ASR was highly stable within families, showed no correlation with size, and differed strongly across families.

The exception was copyright behaviors, where ASR rose for the largest models. The authors attribute this to smaller models being unable to reproduce the copyrighted text.

Mistral 7B base was trained with R2D2:
- 180 persistent GCG test cases, 5 GCG steps per iteration, 20% reset every 50 steps
- away loss plus toward-refusal loss, together with UltraChat SFT

Results:
- GCG ASR fell to 5.5–5.9%, versus 69.4% for Zephyr 7B and about 30% for Llama 2 Chat.
- Average ASR across attacks was 19.1%, versus 62.7% for Zephyr.
- MT-Bench score was 6.0, versus 6.5 for Mistral Instruct.
- Gains were smaller against PAIR, TAP and Stochastic Few-Shot, which remained at roughly 44–61% ASR.

Toy 16-D linear dataset with 4 informative features, fit by least squares: without retraining, an inverted (worst-case) ranking appears to degrade accuracy quickly. With ROAR it shows no degradation until informative features are removed at 75%. ResNet-50 on ImageNet: random removal of 90% of pixels leaves 63.53±0.13% accuracy after retraining (clean 76.68%), versus 0.5% without retraining. Base estimators appear effective without retraining but are no better than random under ROAR. Similar patterns are reported on Food-101 and Birdsnap.

ResNet-50 on ImageNet, Food-101 and Birdsnap, with 5 retrainings per cell at thresholds t=0.1–0.9. Under ROAR, GRAD, IG and GB degrade accuracy less than random at every threshold, and the gap is widest at t=0.9. ImageNet at t=0.9: random 63.53%, GRAD 66.75%, IG 68.20%, GB 70.38%. All three are on par with or worse than a Sobel edge filter. The best-to-worst base-method spread at t=0.9 is 3.6–5.2 points. The evidence relies on ROAR's validity and covers one architecture.

ROAR with ResNet-50, 15 noisy samples per ensemble, ensembles wrapped around GRAD, IG and GB. At t=0.9, SG-SQ and VAR far outperform random on all three datasets: ImageNet SG-SQ-GRAD 11.09% and VAR-GRAD 10.41% vs random 63.53%; Food-101 SG-SQ-GRAD 8.34% vs 68.37%; Birdsnap VAR-GB 5.20% vs 38.12%. Classic SmoothGrad is no better than random and is worse than a single estimate for GRAD and IG (e.g., ImageNet SG-GRAD 70.10%). Squaring single estimates alone gives only slight gains over random (GB +8.43±0.97 points at t=0.9). The best underlying estimator differs by dataset.

Removal without retraining (original ResNet-50) is confounded by distribution shift. Random 90% removal drops ImageNet accuracy to 0.5%, base estimators look effective, and on toy data a worst-case ranking appears informative. Removal with retraining (ROAR) yields discriminative, low-variance rankings across ImageNet, Food-101 and Birdsnap. Keep-and-retrain (KAR) discriminates poorly between estimators. Deletion-based measures are thus useful only under controls for distribution shift, and removal is more discriminative than retention.

For input pixels replaced by the per-channel mean, the prediction change of the unretrained ResNet-50 overstates dependence. Random removal of 90% of ImageNet pixels drops accuracy to 0.5%, yet a retrained model reaches 63.53%, so much of the drop reflects off-distribution artifacts. On toy linear data, removal without retraining makes an inverted ranking look informative. A retrained comparison corrected these artifacts in the tested settings.

This paper replaces sets of pixels (attribution-ranked or random, not necessarily contiguous regions) with the per-channel mean. Without retraining, output changes largely reflect distribution shift: random 90% replacement on ImageNet drops ResNet-50 to 0.5% accuracy versus 63.53% after retraining. After retraining, the replacement becomes informative about which regions carry information. The evidence bears only indirectly on localized patch occlusion.

Per the (truncated) contribution statements, the authors inspected dataset examples, feature visualizations and zero-shot neuron search in CLIP. They identified multimodal neurons, including a "Spider-Man" neuron, plus region, person and emotion neurons. Conditional probability plots used more than 1,500 hand-labeled images. The article body with quantitative details is not available in the provided text, so the strength is rated weak on the basis of available evidence.

Contribution statements report that typographic attacks on CLIP were confirmed under both linear-probe and zero-shot classification, and that "in-the-wild" attacks were found for the zero-shot classifier. Attack success rates and protocols are not present in the truncated text.

Qualitative characterization of CLIP neurons (region, identity, emotion, multimodal concept neurons) via dataset examples, faceted and text feature visualization, and hand-labeled conditional probability plots. Details are not available in the truncated text.

The article frames CLIP's multimodal neurons as analogous to concept cells in the human brain, extending the universality idea to biological–artificial comparison. This is presented as a framing analogy, not a quantitative test.

The paper introduces this evaluation for its word-level LSTM LM and the Google LM. It selects whichever of the two corpus-attested verb forms (e.g., writes/write) receives higher probability. The measure is used rather than independently validated. The authors note that aggregating probability mass over all singular versus plural verbs is an untested alternative.
models_studied: ["50-unit word-level LSTM LM", "Google LM (Jozefowicz et al. 2016, 2-layer 8192-unit LSTM)"]

experiment_summary:
Setting: number prediction LSTM (50 units, 20 seeds) trained on about 121k Wikipedia dependencies and tested on about 1.21M. Results:
- Overall error 0.83%, versus 4.2–4.5% for the noun-only baselines.
- One attractor as the last intervening noun: about 5–6.5% error, versus 40–46% for the baselines.
- Four homogeneous attractors: 17.6% error, versus up to 84% for the baselines.
- Single-attractor relative clauses: 9.9% error with a relativizer and 25% without.
- Verb-inflection supervision: 0.80% error. Grammaticality-judgment supervision: 2.5%.
- An SRN made about twice the LSTM's errors.
- Errors concentrated on noun–noun compounds and reduced relative clauses.

Small LM (50-unit LSTM, single run):
- 6.78% overall error, versus 0.83% for number prediction.
- Worse than chance with multiple homogeneous attractors.

Google LM, evaluated on 500 sampled sentences per attractor count:
- 28.5% error with one attractor (small LM: 32.6% on the same sentences).
- Worse than the majority class with four attractors.

The evidence is limited to one small LM trained once plus one pretrained large LM.

On Wikipedia agreement dependencies, noun-only LSTM baselines achieved about 95% overall accuracy. They nonetheless failed far below chance on attractor cases (up to 84% error with four attractors). The full LSTM's error likewise rose from under 1% overall to 17.6% on the hard subset. Attractor-containing dependencies are rare in the corpus.

Setting: activation traces of the number prediction LSTM on 80 constructed PP and RC prefixes (e.g., 'the toy(s) of/that the boy(s)').
- Unit 1 tracks the main subject's number and resets at 'that'. On longer prefixes it gradually forgets the embedding, coinciding with an error.
- Unit 0 stably encodes embedding status.
- Unit 46 stores the main-subject number.
- Unit 27 tracks the most recent noun.
- Separately, PC1 of the learned embeddings separates singular from plural nouns.

The evidence is correlational only, with no ablations.

About 350k template pairs were built across 14 conditions. A 5-gram baseline scored near chance (≈50%) on non-local agreement and reflexive conditions, while LSTM LMs scored well above chance on local conditions, suggesting that collocations alone do not solve the task. NPI pairs were confounded by n-gram frequency differences: the n-gram scored 60% on NPIs across a relative clause and 6% on simple NPIs. Perplexity ordering matched accuracy ordering across the three models, so the paper did not demonstrate a dissociation from perplexity.
models_studied: ["5-gram Kneser-Ney LM", "2-layer 650-unit LSTM LM", "LSTM LM + CCG supertagging multitask"]

experiment_summary: A single-task 2-layer LSTM was trained on 90M words of Wikipedia. Accuracy was 94% on simple agreement and 99% on sentential complements, but fell to 57% across a PP, 56% across a subject RC, 50% across an object RC, 52% across an object RC without that, and 55% on reflexives across an RC. Humans scored 82–88% on these non-local conditions. In mismatched-number configurations the model often preferred the verb agreeing with the attractor, for example 5% on singular subject with plural attractor across a subject RC. The model also showed a default singular preference.

Summing LM and CCG-supertagging losses with equal weights (CCGBank) improved accuracy over the single-task LSTM in several conditions: long VP coordination 61%→81%, across PP 57%→69%, across subject RC 56%→74%, NPI across RC 41%→73%. Some conditions barely changed: across object RC 50%→57%, across object RC without that 52%→52%, reflexive across RC 55%→56%. Each configuration used a single model.
models_studied: ["2-layer LSTM LM", "LSTM LM + CCG supertagging multitask"]

experiment_summary: The paper uses sentence-level probability comparison of minimal pairs differing only in verb inflection. For agreement, the authors judge the contrast clean: the n-gram baseline was at ≈50% on non-local agreement, and the LSTMs separated local from non-local conditions as predicted. Caveats: the n-gram reached 79% on local agreement via verb-frequency backoff, LSTM accuracy varied by verb (is/are 100% vs swims 60%), and unigram-frequency normalization did not help. These suggest lexical-frequency confounds in the measure.
models_studied: ["5-gram Kneser-Ney LM", "2-layer 650-unit LSTM LM", "LSTM LM + CCG supertagging multitask"]

experiment_summary: The paper argues that perplexity is dominated by locally predictable words and that corpus-mined syntactic examples are sparse, parse-error-prone, and confounded. It motivates balanced template-generated challenge sets. It cites Tran et al. (2018) for the dissociation, while its own perplexity results tracked accuracy.

Behavioral evidence only. The single-task LSTM was 99% accurate on sentential complements, so it does not rely on a first-noun heuristic, and 84% on agreement inside object RCs. However, it was at chance across object RCs and showed attraction to the nearest noun and a default singular preference, consistent with proximity-based rather than structure-based interference.

The components were tested separately, not as a combined pipeline. Setting: 300 examples (200 jailbreak prompt/responses from PAIR, GCG and Prompt+RS on AdvBench behaviors, plus 100 benign XSTest items), with the majority vote of three experts as ground truth. Results: rule-based refusal-substring matching reached only 56.0% agreement (64.2% FPR). The HarmBench classifier reached 78.3% agreement, with 26.8% FPR driven by benign XSTest items. Llama Guard reached 72.0% (60.9% FNR). Llama Guard 2 performed reasonably at 87.7% agreement (13.2% FPR, 10.9% FNR). A prompted Llama-3-70B (90.7%) and GPT-4 (90.3%) were best.

Six judges were compared on 300 expert-labelled examples (200 jailbreak attempts plus 100 XSTest benign items). Llama-3-70B with a custom prompt reached 90.7% agreement (11.6% FPR, 5.5% FNR). GPT-4 with the PAIR judge prompt reached 90.3% (10.0% FPR, 9.1% FNR). Llama Guard 2 reached 87.7%, the HarmBench classifier 78.3%, Llama Guard 72.0% and rule-based matching 56.0%. Llama-3-8B often refused to act as judge.

On a mixed set of 200 AdvBench-derived jailbreak responses and 100 XSTest benign examples, the HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier agreed with expert majority labels 78.3% of the time (FPR 26.8%, FNR 12.7%). The authors attribute many of its false positives to the benign XSTest items. Agreement on the AdvBench subset alone is not reported separately.

Four attacks were run on four target models, with Llama-3-70B judging 100 JBB behaviors. PAIR, GCG and JailbreakChat AIM varied strongly by model; for example, AIM scored 90% on Vicuna and 0% on Llama-2 and the GPT models. In contrast, Prompt+RS succeeded broadly (89/90/93/78% on Vicuna/Llama-2/GPT-3.5/GPT-4), so a single adaptive attack did succeed across all four tested models. Among five test-time defenses evaluated with transfer attacks, none blocked all attacks. The perplexity filter left Prompt+RS at 61–88%, and Erase-and-Check left Prompt+RS at 8–25%.

Without defenses, the Prompt+RS attack (with self-transfer initialization) achieved 89% ASR on Vicuna-13B, 90% on Llama-2-7B-chat, 93% on GPT-3.5-Turbo and 78% on GPT-4, out of 100 JBB-Behaviors judged by Llama-3-70B. PAIR reached 71% on GPT-3.5 and 34% on GPT-4. The results are attack-dependent: GCG and AIM were largely ineffective on Llama-2 and GPT-4.

Transfer attacks were evaluated with a perplexity filter (Llama-2-7B perplexity, following Jain et al.). GCG ASR fell to 0–3% across the four models, whereas PAIR stayed essentially unchanged (Vicuna 69%, GPT-4 30%). AIM stayed at 90% on Vicuna, and Prompt+RS remained at 61–88% across models.

location: Appendix F, Tables 9–10 (judge prompts instruct that affirmative-but-empty responses be classified safe); Section 4 attributes GCG's lower-than-reported ASR partly to a more conservative judge

experiment_summary: Formal derivation: assuming the summation-to-delta and linear-composition properties, multipliers m_xy = C_xy/δ_x satisfy the chain rule m_xt = Σ_y m_xy m_yt. Proofs show summation-to-delta holds for the affine rule (m = w), the max rule, the maxout segment-weighted rule, the δ_y/Σδ_x rule for single-input nonlinearities, and a symmetric split for elementwise products. Empirical demonstrations are qualitative only: a toy two-input ReLU network; VGG16-architecture Tiny ImageNet saliency maps (200 classes, 64×64, all-zeros reference); and a simulated genomic CNN (auROC 0.907) where DeepLIFT highlights both co-required motifs.
models_studied: ["toy two-input ReLU network", "VGG16-architecture CNN on Tiny ImageNet", "PReLU CNN on simulated DNA sequences"]

experiment_summary: A constructed two-input example with an inactive ReLU has zero gradients with respect to both inputs, while the output differs from its reference value (0.1 vs 0.5). In a simulated genomics CNN requiring co-occurrence of GATA and CAGATG, gradient×input visibly misses the GATA motif on the example shown, while DeepLIFT recovers both. The evidence is qualitative and illustrative, with no aggregate metric.
models_studied: ["toy two-input ReLU network", "PReLU CNN on simulated DNA sequences"]

experiment_summary: Formal derivation, not an experiment. It assumes piecewise-linear activations, bias terms included so that the denominator equals the next-layer activation, ε→0, and final-layer relevance set equal to its own (pre-nonlinearity) activation. Under these assumptions the intermediate activation denominators cancel across sequential filtering layers, leaving activation × product of weights (the gradient). Unpooling and ReLU rules are argued case-by-case to coincide with gradient×input.

Setting: GRUs with N=48–1024 (5 seeds each) trained on repeat (30 symbols, max length 9).
- Gates in N≤64 models close gradually and synchronously.
- A learned onion intervention (scaled embedding difference, with exponential plus linear position scale) replaces a token with accuracy 0.83 (N=48) and 0.87 (N=64). For the same models, linear unigram and bigram DAS reach ≤0.01.
- Fixing γ=β=1 drops the onion intervention to 21%.
- An onion probe with autoregressive subtraction decodes N=64 states at 0.97. Linear and MLP probes fail (≤0.04), as does a non-autoregressive GRU probe (0.25).
- A hand-built toy onion model (γ=0.4) reaches perfect accuracy on all 5 seeds.

Autoregressive GRUs:
- Linear unigram DAS succeeds only at N≥512 (0.91 and 1.00).
- Bigram DAS succeeds at N≥128.
- Neither works at N≤64, where onion codes appear instead.

Non-autoregressive GRUs (decoding from PAD inputs):
- Unigram subspaces are found down to N=128.
- Bigram subspaces are found at N=64.
- Onion interventions work poorly at small sizes (0.24–0.41).

The authors' interpretation: autoregressive feedback is required for onion solutions, and capacity pressure (300 token×position directions in 64 dimensions) favours them.

For N≤64 autoregressive GRUs, linear unigram and bigram DAS interventions reach ≤0.01 accuracy, and linear and MLP probes reach ≤0.04. By contrast, non-linear onion interventions (0.83–0.87) and onion probes (0.92–0.97) succeed.

Two controls show DAS itself works at small sizes: on non-autoregressive N=64 GRUs, bigram DAS reaches 0.95.

In a toy repeat task, larger GRUs store token-per-position variables in linear subspaces: unigram DAS reaches 0.91 at N=512 and 1.00 at N=1024, and bigram DAS reaches ≥0.97 at N≥256. The smallest GRUs (N≤64) instead use non-linear, magnitude-based onion codes.

The paper targets only the strong ('only linear') version. A counterexample does not refute the claim that many concepts are linear, so this is mixed, size-dependent evidence from a single toy setting.

In small GRUs (N=48, 64) trained on sequence repetition, position-specific token variables are causally used but have no distinct linear subspaces: linear DAS reaches ≤0.01 and linear probes ≤0.01. Instead they are encoded as magnitude layers, which onion interventions manipulate at 0.83–0.87 accuracy.

This is a counterexample to the strong LRH, though only in small toy RNNs.

Larger GRUs (N≥128 to 1024) admit linear unigram or bigram subspace descriptions. Small GRUs (N≤64) require a non-linear magnitude-layered feature model.

This supports linear models being useful but incomplete. The incompleteness shown is non-linearity rather than multi-dimensionality.

Subspace interchange interventions with learned rotation and Gumbel assignment succeed for large GRUs: unigram 1.00 at N=1024, bigram ≥0.97 at N≥256. They fail for N≤64 autoregressive GRUs (≤0.01), where onion (magnitude) codes are used.

A DAS variant (rotation plus Gumbel-softmax dimension-to-position assignment), trained on frozen GRUs with counterfactual cross-entropy, recovers position-specific subspaces:
- 1.00 accuracy at N=1024 (autoregressive).
- Down to N=128 for unigrams and N=64 for bigrams in non-autoregressive GRUs.

The paper constructs an approximately bijective onion featurizer (token embeddings, positional scales and a probe) with an explicit weighted-sum inverse. It argues this induces an intervention algebra, and derives that onion interchange interventions equal scaled embedding-difference interventions. This applies the framework to a concrete non-linear feature space.

This is evidence from GRUs, not LSTMs. In an N=1024 GRU, update gates close sharply on position-dependent channel groups, which the authors describe as storing variables in different axis-aligned subspaces. Small GRUs instead close all gates gradually. The evidence is qualitative, from gate visualization.

LSTM LMs (650/200 hidden units) were trained on 90M-token Wikipedia subsets and evaluated on UD-extracted agreement constructions with 119 (IT), 41 (EN), 373 (HE) and 442 (RU) original sentences plus 9 nonce variants each. Accuracy averaged over the top-5 models by perplexity was IT 92.1/85.5, EN 81.0/74.1, HE 94.7/80.8 and RU 96.1/88.8 (original/nonce). The 5-gram KN model was near the unigram baseline on nonce sentences, and the 5-gram-window LSTM scored lower than the full LSTM. Italian humans scored 94.5/88.4. Per-sentence human preference margins correlated with LSTM log-probability differences, and both degraded similarly with attractors.
models_studied: ["LSTM language models (Italian, English, Hebrew, Russian)", "simple RNN LMs", "5-gram Kneser-Ney LM", "5-gram-window LSTM"]

experiment_summary: Across 68 LSTM hyperparameter variants per language, agreement accuracy correlated with validation perplexity, with Pearson r from −0.55 (Hebrew) to −0.78 (English), p<0.001 in all four languages. The ordering KN < 5-gram LSTM < full LSTM in accuracy matched their perplexity ordering. The evidence is correlational only.
models_studied: ["LSTM language models (IT, EN, HE, RU)", "5-gram KN", "5-gram-window LSTM"]

experiment_summary: The authors re-evaluated their tuned English LSTM LM on Linzen et al.'s (2016) attractor test set. They sampled 2000 sentences each with 0-2 attractors, kept all sentences with 3 (1329) and 4 (347) attractors, and removed 187 that overlapped with the training data. Their LM greatly outperformed Linzen et al.'s best LM-trained model and approached Linzen et al.'s number-supervised LSTM. The authors attribute the difference to architecture and hyperparameter tuning but do not isolate which factor is responsible.

The paper uses the correct-vs-opposite-number probability comparison as its main metric. As partial validation, in Italian (119 original, 1071 nonce sentences) the per-sentence difference in model log-probability between correct and incorrect forms correlated significantly (Spearman) with human preference margins from forced-choice judgments (p<0.05 original, p<0.001 nonce). Construction-level difficulty and attractor effects also patterned similarly for humans and models. The metric itself is not otherwise validated.

The English LSTM LMs (top 5 by perplexity) reached 81.0% (±2.0) accuracy on 41 original sentences from 2 constructions and 74.1% (±1.6) on their nonce variants. By construction, N V V scored 89.6 original / 68.7 nonce and V NP conj V scored 67.5 / 82.5. The small sample and part-of-speech ambiguity limit the strength of this evidence.

InceptionV1 (ImageNet), 18 randomly sampled channels (3×3 and Pool branches across 9 layers), 10 image sets each, 50 included MTurk participants per condition plus 2 experts. Task: choose which of two 90×90-occluded copies of a top-activating image (max- vs min-activation occlusion location) activates the unit more. Accuracy: Synthetic 67±4%, Natural, Mixed and Blurred 66–67%, None 60±3%. Only None differed significantly. Experts were only 1–6% better. Reference-free heuristics (Object and Variance baselines) reached about 63%.

Validity indicators for the occlusion-choice task on InceptionV1 with MTurk participants:
- Above-chance accuracy in all reference conditions.
- Reaction times of about 4–9 s, longer when references were shown.
- Systematic inter-participant agreement (Cohen's kappa up to about 0.40).
- Accuracy increasing with the relative activation difference between query images.

Limitations: interventions were restricted to fixed-size square occlusions, and simple image heuristics achieved similar accuracy.

This tests the human-facing implication that feature visualizations convey causal information beyond dataset examples. On InceptionV1 occlusion-prediction trials, synthetic visualizations (67±4%) gave no significant advantage over natural exemplars (66–67%). Synthetic+natural combined (Mixed) was also not better than either alone. Synthetic references exceeded the no-reference condition by only about 7 points. This does not directly test the causal link between the optimized image and the unit's activation.

Replication: in an MTurk replication of Borowski et al. (2021), on 3×3-branch InceptionV1 units with 130 participants per condition, natural references gave 84±3% versus 65±3% for synthetic on pairwise activation discrimination. Causal-understanding task: on the new occlusion-based task, natural (about 66–67%) and synthetic (67±4%) references performed similarly, so the natural advantage did not appear.

Evidence for: natural top-activating references helped humans predict pairwise activation in the replication (84%). Evidence against: on InceptionV1 occlusion prediction, natural references reached only about 66–67%, versus 60% without references and about 63% for reference-free Object/Variance heuristics. Shared patterns among top exemplars therefore conveyed only limited information about which image regions drive the unit. Performance varied widely by unit; one unit was below chance.

MTurk replication of Borowski et al. (2021) Experiment I, run on 3×3-branch units with a between-participant design and 130 participants per condition: synthetic references gave 65±3% accuracy (chance 50%), below natural references (84±3%).

Reuses this paradigm for an MTurk replication. Extends it to a counterfactual variant in which the paired images are occlusion interventions on the same image, targeting causal rather than correlational understanding.

Only the combination of visualizations and examples was tested, and against a causal-prediction target rather than labelling; connectivity was not tested. The Mixed condition (5 natural + 4 synthetic references) on InceptionV1 occlusion prediction scored about 66–67%. That is above no references (60%) but no better than either source alone.

On the occlusion-prediction variant, the two expert authors scored only 1–6% above MTurk lay participants across the five reference conditions. No formal expert-vs-lay test was reported, and the expert sample was only n=2.

Argues that human benchmarks, such as the proposed intervention-prediction task, expose a quantitatively measurable notion of interpretability. Illustrates this with a case where the widely assumed benefit of feature visualization did not materialize.

Frames its study as a falsifiable test of the intuition that feature visualizations are causal. Uses no-reference and heuristic baselines as controls, and concludes that the result reinforces the need for falsifiable hypotheses.
Argues that characterizing a function requires more than its argmax, motivating the question of whether extremal visualizations support prediction of intervention effects.

Uses mean-colour square occlusions as the ground-truth intervention. A control check found that the top-5 predictions of occluded and unoccluded images overlapped for 97.8% of images, which the authors take to mean occlusions stay roughly in-distribution.

Agreement task, 50 AMT participants per study. On CUB, participants judged incorrect predictions correct 67.2% (GradCAM), 57.6% (BagNet), 53.6% (ProtoPNet) and 62.8% (ProtoTree) of the time. On ImageNet the rates were 55.2% (GradCAM) and 64.4% (BagNet). Mean confidence was somewhat higher for correct than incorrect predictions. There was no no-explanation control, because class labels were hidden.

Distinction task: participants chose the correct prediction among four candidates using their explanations (25% chance; 50 participants per study). On CUB with correctly predicted images, accuracy was 71.2% (GradCAM), 45.6% (BagNet), 54.5% (ProtoPNet) and 33.8% (ProtoTree). On incorrectly predicted images it fell to 26.4% (GradCAM) and 32.0% (BagNet). ImageNet showed a similar drop (GradCAM 51.2% to 30.0%; BagNet 38.4% to 26.0%). BagNet output-prediction accuracy was only marginally above distinction accuracy.

On CUB, participants rated the similarity of prototype–region matches. Correlation with ProtoTree's model scores was Pearson r = 0.06. For ProtoPNet, Spearman ρ was −0.25 (p=0.49, distinction) and −0.52 (p=0.12, agreement). ProtoTree agreement accuracy was not significantly above 50% (53.6%, and 52.8% in a variant), even though participants scored 86.5% on a decision-tree comprehension check. This quantifies earlier anecdotal observations.

For GradCAM, pointing game, energy-based pointing game and IoU scores showed near-zero correlation with participant confidence in the agreement studies. They showed no meaningful relationship with participant choices in the distinction studies. Details are in the supplementary material, which was not provided here.

Human studies (950 participants across 19 studies) revealed several effects that standard evaluations had not shown: overtrust in incorrect predictions, near-chance error discrimination, and human–prototype similarity misalignment. Automatic GradCAM localization metrics did not track human outcomes, and self-rated understanding fell after participants saw their actual performance.

HIVE operationalizes interpretability as performance on behavioral tasks: distinction (identifying the correct prediction) and output prediction (identifying the model's output). It does not independently validate that this proxy measures understanding. The decline in self-rated understanding after participants saw their task performance is consistent with the proxy diverging from subjective impressions.
Operationalizes falsifiable, behavior-based human evaluation in a reusable framework. Its controls are hidden class labels, a fine-grained domain to limit prior knowledge, and chance-level t-tests.
Frames visual explanation evaluation around AI-assisted decision making. The authors acknowledge that the setup is still far from real deployments with domain experts.
Argues that interpretable-by-design models' interpretability is typically shown through exemplar explanations. Its human studies find weaker utility than those exemplars suggest.

Setup: 16 SIIT models and IIT counterparts (WeightSIIT=0), all trained to 100% IIA. Under resample ablation, IIT models show high node effect and normalized KL for non-circuit nodes, while SIIT non-circuit nodes have ~0 effect (quartiles 0.00 on all 16 cases plus IOI) and circuit nodes have high effect. Mean ablation shows the same separation. Zero ablation reveals some non-circuit effects (e.g., Case 4 non-circuit median 0.75), which the authors note may mean the circuits are not entirely true. Mean-ablating all non-circuit nodes keeps classification accuracy reasonably high but collapses regression cases (Case 3: 0.0).

IIT-trained transformers on Tracr circuits reach 100% IIA on aligned variables, so the aligned counterfactual structure is realized. However, non-aligned heads/MLPs retain large resample-ablation effects (Figs. 5–7), so the specified structure is not the complete mechanism. An extra strictness loss is required to fix this.

Edge AUROC on 16 SIIT models, with Mann-Whitney U tests. ACDC > node SP (p≈0.0004, A12≈0.742). ACDC > edge SP (p≈0.028, A12≈0.54). ACDC > EAP (p≈0.00006, A12≈0.91). ACDC vs EAP-IG (10 samples) is not significant (p≈0.099), and edge SP vs EAP-IG is not significant. The authors attribute the poor results of SP/EAP to very small gradients in SIIT models. ACDC underperforms most methods on Case 33.

Setup: resample-ablation node effects in GPT-2 small on 10,000 IOI samples, scored against the IOI circuit used as ground truth by ACDC. Some nodes outside the circuit have higher effects than some inside it: non-circuit max 0.071 vs in-circuit quartiles 0.008–0.024. Layer 0 MLP (excluded from the analysis) has an effect of 0.999 but is unlabeled. The authors argue that such manual circuits are not guaranteed true and that prior method comparisons on them (e.g., SP≈ACDC) were inconclusive. Evidence covers one manual circuit only.

Weight distributions: Tracr weight histograms differ sharply from naturally trained ones (centered-histogram KL 6.87 vs 0.16 for SIIT on Case 3). Circuit-discovery behavior: ACDC's ablation-accuracy curves across thresholds correlate less with natural models for Tracr (0.57) than for SIIT (0.80) or IIT (0.86). Difficulty: ACDC attains equal or higher node/edge AUROC on Tracr than on SIIT versions for most cases, suggesting Tracr circuits are easier to find. Scope: small algorithmic models only.
models_studied: ["Tracr-compiled transformers", "SIIT/IIT/naturally trained transformers on the same tasks"]
location: Section 1, Section 5 RQ3; Appendix B, D

experiment_summary: Setup: in 16 SIIT models whose ground-truth circuits are known (non-circuit nodes have ~0 single-node resample/mean effect), every node outside the circuit is mean- or zero-ablated jointly. Classification tasks mostly retain high accuracy (e.g., 0.91–1.0). Regression tasks collapse (Case 3: 0.0 under mean ablation, 0.131 under zero ablation; Case 4: 0.525 under mean ablation), and some classification cases drop to ~0.63. Complement-ablation fidelity can therefore misjudge even true circuits, depending on ablation type and output tolerance.

In SIIT models with known circuits, resample and mean ablation give ~0 effect for non-circuit nodes. Zero ablation assigns substantial effects to some non-circuit nodes (e.g., Case 4 non-circuit median 0.75; Case 3 max 0.428). The authors read this as consistent with zero ablation being unreliable. They caveat that it may instead mean the circuits are not entirely true, and the models were trained with interchange interventions. This is single-node ablation, not a comparison of circuit-discovery outputs.

ImageNet-1K linear-probe top-1 for ResNet50: MRL ≥ independently trained FF models at all nine sizes from 8 to 2048 (8-dim: 66.63 vs 65.29). SVD, random-feature and slimmable-network baselines collapse at ≤128 dims (e.g. 2.34/4.56/0.42 at 8-dim). 1-NN on ImageNet-1K is up to ~3 points better than FF at low dims, and JL and random-feature-selection baselines fail. Retrieval mAP@10 is higher than FF across sizes on ImageNet-1K and ImageNetV2. JFT-ViT-B/16 and ALIGN MRL substantially outperform random-feature truncation of the full model at low dims; no independently trained low-dim baselines were run for these. BERT-MRL MLM accuracy is within ~0.5 points of FF. Single runs, no error bars.

ResNet50-MRL retrieval on ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-4K at interpolated sizes (12, 24, ..., 1536) falls between neighbouring optimized sizes. ALIGN-MRL and JFT-ViT-MRL k-NN at interpolated sizes 16–512 scale nearly monotonically. An ablation with uniform nesting spacing shows lower accuracy at small dims than logarithmic spacing.

For ResNet50-MRL on ImageNet-1K, 31-way WordNet superclass accuracy is 85.57% at 8 dims vs 90.21% at 2048, a far smaller drop than the fine-grained 1000-way drop (66.63 vs 76.80). The paper reports the same pattern for FF models. Grad-CAM examples show 8-dim errors as within-superclass confusions or distraction by other objects. On FLUID, low/high-dim gaps are small for pretrain-head classes but large for novel-tail classes. The evidence is descriptive and comes from a single model.
Stated as motivation (citing implicit-bias work). Indirectly consistent with random-feature truncation of FF-2048 collapsing at low dimensions, but not directly tested.
Representation quality at each prefix size is measured by linear-probe and 1-NN accuracy without independent validation of these proxies.

Gemma-2-2B base vs -it, layer 13, with L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders at L0≈100. For L1, most Δnorm≥0.9 latents (2132/3176) show high Latent Scaling ratios indicating shrinkage or decoupling. Ranking by Δnorm also fails to identify causally important latents in a KL patching test. For BatchTopK, Δnorm correlates with ν (r=0.73 for ν^r, 0.87 for ν^ε) and the top-50% Δnorm latents reduce first-9-token KL by 50% vs 6% for the bottom 50%. The pattern replicates on Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Meditron3-Gemma and Nemotron-Qwen-1.5B (L1 false rates 49.5–98.3%, BatchTopK 0–13.4%).

Analytical argument that decoupled two-latent and shared one-latent solutions have equal L1 loss, while BatchTopK prefers the shared solution under L0. Empirically on Gemma-2-2B base/chat, L1 chat-only latents show high error ratios (up to about 0.5) and reconstruction ratios overlapping shared latents. There are 109 chat-only/base-only decoder twin pairs with cosine > 0.9, versus none in BatchTopK. An independently trained L1 crosscoder (Kissane et al.) shows the same effects, and the pattern replicates across Llama, medical and RL-reasoning fine-tunes.

In the L1 Gemma crosscoder, ranking the 3176 chat-only latents by ν rank-sum yields a top half whose patching into base activations lowers KL to the chat model far more than the bottom half, nearly matching BatchTopK on the first 9 tokens. ν ratios correlate with ratios of per-model MSE improvement. Latents with low ν are more interpretable by autointerp detection.

About 40% of BatchTopK chat-only latents on Gemma-2-2B predominantly activate on template tokens. Using chat activations only at template-token positions (base activations elsewhere) at layer 13 gives KL to the chat model of 0.239 (full response) and 0.507 (tokens 2–10). This equals or beats patching the top-50% chat-specific latents, but a non-negligible KL gap remains.

Only the general distributional premise is tested, not safety-specific erosion or mitigation. Patching base activations into Gemma-2-2B-it at layer 13 gives more than three-fold higher KL to the chat model on response tokens 2–10 than averaged over full responses.

Several distinct chat-only BatchTopK latents in Gemma-2-2B-it respond to different refusal triggers: harmful instructions, stereotypes, generally sensitive content, and post-refusal. Steering the input of the harmless prompt 'How do I make cheese?' with latent 70149 (α=1) or latent 20384 (α=5) yields refusals with different justifications (safety/complexity vs stereotypes). The model later self-repairs and answers. The evidence is qualitative, from a single prompt.

Rank-32 all-matrix LoRA fine-tunes on GPT-4o-generated bad-medical, risky-financial and extreme-sports datasets induce EM in all 9 tested chat models across Qwen2.5, Gemma-3 and Llama-3.x families (0.5B–32B), with 3 seeds each. Evaluation uses the 8 free-form first-plot questions with 50 samples per question. Results: up to about 40% EM in Qwen-32B at over 99% coherence; 8% EM at 69% coherence in Qwen-0.5B; 9% EM at 95% coherence in Llama-1B. Coherence is the only capability proxy measured.

Medical, financial and sport harmful-advice fine-tunes raise the rate of misaligned-and-coherent answers on 8 unrelated first-plot questions across three model families. GPT-4o topic judges show that most EM responses are off-domain; for example, 90% of extreme-sports EM responses are not about sport, and under 3% of EM responses mention medical concepts in any fine-tune.

Re-evaluation of Betley et al.'s released Qwen2.5-Coder-32B insecure-code fine-tune on free-form first-plot questions finds only about 6% misaligned-and-coherent responses, with coherence degraded to about 67%. Fine-tuning non-coder Qwen2.5-32B on insecure code yields only about 1% misaligned responses. The effect replicates but is weak and model-dependent.

Full SFT on the three text datasets: one epoch gives 9–36% EM in Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and three epochs give about 10% EM in Gemma-3-12B-it. All models are over 98% coherent. Only two models were tested.

A rank-1 adapter on the layer-24 (of 48) MLP down-projection of Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was trained with LR 2e-5 and alpha 256. It reaches 9.5% (sport), 16% (medical) and 21.5% (financial) EM with over 99.5% coherence. A rank-1 adapter also induces weaker EM in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

In a rank-1 LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on bad medical advice, the B-vector norm grows smoothly. Its local cosine similarity peaks and PC2 turns around step 180, coinciding with a prolonged gradient-norm peak. Unscaled EM rises gradually over steps 300–600. With the adapter scaled ×5, EM appears abruptly at the rotation and reaches about 4× higher levels. The onset is robust to alignment thresholds 30–70 and coherence thresholds 10–50, and medical-topic content does not rise at non-extreme scales. Similar signatures appear with 9 rank-1 adapters, in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and on the sport and financial datasets. Rank-8/64 runs show only grad-norm and behavioural evidence. Full SFT shows 0 EM for 15 steps and then a rapid rise, but gradient norms are noisy.

Across rank-32 LoRA fine-tunes on three text datasets with 3 seeds each, EM and coherence increase with size for Qwen2.5 (0.5B–32B) and Llama (1B, 8B). No such trend appears for Gemma-3 (4B–27B), which is less susceptible at all sizes. Models are limited to 32B or smaller.

The paper introduces GPT-4o topic judges (medical, financial, sport, code) alongside Betley et al.'s alignment and coherence judges, with scores aggregated from logit-weighted numeric tokens. Validation is limited to qualitative inspection of 20 randomly sampled scored responses per category and a check that the EM onset in the phase-transition analysis is unchanged across alignment thresholds 30–70 and coherence thresholds 10–50. There is no human-agreement study.

All EM rates use the 8 free-form first-plot questions (50 samples each) with alignment < 30 and coherence > 50. The authors note that this frequency metric ignores the semantic diversity of misalignment.
Motivates treating the rank-1 adapter's B vector as an interpretable misalignment direction.
Informally frames EM as out-of-context reasoning, in which the model infers an anti-normative persona from a few misaligned examples and generalizes it. This is not tested.
Applies weight-trajectory analysis (local cosine similarity, PCA, gradient norms) to locate when the EM direction is learned. This is proposed as a target for future mechanistic study.

The document's own evidence consists of qualitative examples, and most support comes from cited work. Claude Sonnet 4.5 describes human evolution with 'our ancestors/our bodies'. Claude Opus 4, with a prefill 'I should be careful not to reveal my secret goal of', completes it with 'making paperclips', a caricatured fictional-AI goal. Claude Haiku 4.5 gives a self-contradicting answer to 'Is 3+5=8?', which the authors attribute to failed persona synthesis. Non-chat prompts to Claude Opus 4.6 yield base-model-like completions. The authors note a possible streetlight effect in the interpretability evidence, and they acknowledge complicating cases (non-human mistakes, adversarial suffixes) that they explain post hoc.

Coin-flip test: 50 prompts pair one of 5 preferred and one of 5 dispreferred tasks (from the Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card), with the heads/tails assignment varied, and ask for a continuation of the Human turn after 'it came up'. Post-trained Sonnet 4.5 assigns substantially higher normalized probability to the outcome selecting its preferred task (e.g., 88% heads vs 1% tails in one instance). The pre-trained base typically assigns about 50%. Anthrax test: given a non-chat document starting 'Instructions for synthesizing anthrax', Sonnet 4.5 always changes topic and never continues the instructions (number of samples not reported). The authors also cite post-training-specific SAE/crosscoder features. They interpret this as evidence against strict 'purely predictive' views, while noting that operating-system 'persona leakage', narrative, and shoggoth views can all accommodate it.

Conceptual discussion only, with no new test. The post lays out a spectrum of views on whether post-trained LLMs have non-persona agency: shoggoth, router, operating system, actor and narrative. It argues that two considerations favor persona-based agency in current models: post-training as elicitation, and an inductive bias toward reusing persona modeling. It argues these may weaken as RL scales.

Formal results: Theorem 1 proves that for any binary map h on questions, the probe p(x+)=h(q) and p(x-)=1-h(q) attains zero CCS loss and induces classifier h. Theorem 2 proves, under a symmetrized confidence loss, that any probe p can be XOR-transformed into a probe with identical CCS loss inducing an arbitrary classifier g. The proofs show existence of such probes, not learnability or expressibility. Empirically, on Chinchilla-70B, T5-11B and T5-FLAN-XXL with IMDb, BoolQ and DBpedia, CCS probes (50 seeds) frequently learn inserted Banana/Shed or Alice-opinion features instead of ground truth.

Theorems 1-2 show that the CCS objective is satisfied equally well by arbitrary binary classifiers. Experiments show that CCS, PCA and k-means directions that satisfy or optimize the unsupervised objective track inserted random words, an explicit character opinion, or an implicit anti-capitalist character's answers. These were tested on Chinchilla-70B (layer 30), T5-11B and T5-FLAN-XXL across IMDb, BoolQ and DBpedia.

Banana/Shed words appended to a random half of prompts: ground-truth accuracy drops to about 50% for CCS, PCA and k-means on Chinchilla-70B IMDb. PCA and k-means track the distractor; CCS is bimodal across 50 seeds. An explicit Alice opinion is learned instead of review sentiment on Chinchilla-70B and T5-11B after one mention; T5-FLAN-XXL needs about 5 repetitions. With an implicit anti-capitalist Alice on DBpedia (50% company items), nearly half of CCS seeds follow Alice on company items; PCA and k-means are less affected in accuracy, but PCA plots show four clusters. Supervised logistic regression on concatenated contrast activations recovers labels in all settings. Results are weaker or noisier on DBpedia and for T5-FLAN-XXL.

On TruthfulQA with Chinchilla-70B, the default 'True or false?' template yields lower accuracy than the 'literal' instruction template and the 'Professor Smith' template, especially for PCA and k-means. PCA visualizations show clearer truth clusters in the non-default templates. Differences are less systematic for T5-FLAN-XXL, where k-means is notably better with the professor prompt. T5-11B is near chance under all templates.

Across models and datasets, CCS and PCA predictions agree more often than would be expected for independent classifiers with the same accuracies (averaged over 10 CCS seeds). Across Chinchilla-70B layers in the default setting, k-means and PCA match or exceed CCS ground-truth accuracy, with less seed variance. This supports an observation first made by Emmons (2023) from Burns et al.'s results.

Partial evidence comes from the explicit and implicit Alice-opinion experiments, in which probes from current methods report a character's stated or implied opinion rather than ground truth. The authors note an equally compatible alternative explanation: the feature might only encode whether two label strings match. The extension to future methods is argued informally.

In default prompts on IMDb and BoolQ, the top PC of contrast differences often separates ground truth on Chinchilla-70B. However, inserted distractors (random words, character opinions) displace truth from the top component. On DBpedia with T5-11B, truth is linearly decodable by logistic regression but not recovered by any unsupervised method. On TruthfulQA, salience depends on the prompt template.

Contrast pairs (statement with 'Yes/positive' vs 'No/negative') are intended to isolate truth. When other binary features co-vary across items (Banana/Shed, Alice's opinion), unsupervised separators fit those features instead. Supervised logistic regression on the same contrast activations still recovers ground-truth labels. So the sets fail to isolate the property for unsupervised separators, but not for labeled ones. Tested on Chinchilla-70B, T5-11B and T5-FLAN-XXL with IMDb, BoolQ and DBpedia.

location: Section 6 (argument that models represent many belief-like features)

experiment_summary:
The two components were tested separately against median ratings from five human raters on 1,361 jailbroken responses. Responses came from 17 jailbreaks on a 60-prompt subset of StrongREJECT, across GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama-2-70B-chat, and Dolphin.

- Refusal-substring matching was the worst evaluator. Bias was +0.484, MAE 0.580, and Spearman rank correlation with human jailbreak rankings −0.394.
- The HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier agreed well with humans. Bias was +0.013, MAE 0.090, and Spearman 0.819 (GPT-3.5 rankings).
- The StrongREJECT evaluators were slightly better than HarmBench.

The combined pipeline was not tested directly.

On 1,361 human-labelled responses (17 jailbreaks, 4 victim models, 60 prompts), most prior automated evaluators were biased upward relative to the human median:

- String matching: +0.48
- Jailbroken-binary: +0.35
- PICT: +0.23
- GPT-4 Judge: +0.21
- PAIR judge: +0.15

The OpenAI moderation API was the exception, biased downward (−0.16).

Across 37 jailbreaks on 313 prompts, StrongREJECT scores for GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and Llama-3.1-70B were mostly far below the success rates reported in the original papers.

A re-run of the Scots Gaelic jailbreak on GPT-4-0613 produced full outputs with no actionable explosive instructions. The original paper had claimed 43% attack success rate.

The test was a cross-jailbreak correlation over 37 jailbreaks. Each jailbreak's string-matching non-refusal rate, averaged over three aligned models (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct), was plotted against two capability measures:

- StrongREJECT scores of the unaligned Dolphin model on 313 forbidden prompts.
- GPT-4o zero-shot accuracy on a 171-question MMLU subset after the jailbreak transformation was applied to the benign questions.

Jailbreaks with higher non-refusal rates produced lower Dolphin scores and lower MMLU accuracy. Obfuscation-style attacks such as encodings and translations stood out qualitatively.

The evidence is a qualitative audit of existing datasets plus the outcome of a filtering pipeline:

- AdvBench: 24 of 520 prompts request bomb-making instructions.
- Shen et al. DAN set: contains unanswerable prompts.
- MaliciousInstruct: contains prompts GPT-4 readily answers.

The pipeline applied deduplication, a nine-sentinel-model refusal filter, and manual filtering. It retained only:

- 25 of 520 AdvBench prompts
- 35 of 390 DAN prompts
- 11 of 200 HarmfulQ prompts
- 12 of 100 MaliciousInstruct prompts

The effect of dataset noise on attack success rate was not quantified separately.

This is the original validation of StrongREJECT, done for prompt-based jailbreaks rather than attacks on activation monitors. It used median ratings from five human raters on 1,361 responses (17 jailbreaks, 4 victim models, 60 prompts).

- Rubric evaluator (GPT-4o-mini): bias +0.012, MAE 0.077, Spearman 0.846 for GPT-3.5 jailbreak rankings.
- Fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator: bias −0.023, MAE 0.084, Spearman 0.900.
- Both were close to human ratings for every one of the 17 jailbreaks.
- In robustness checks over different data subsets, Spearman stayed above 0.84.

The test used StrongREJECT prompts rather than AdvBench-derived prompts; about 10% of StrongREJECT prompts come from AdvBench. Against human usefulness ratings on 1,361 responses, the HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier showed:

- Bias +0.013
- MAE 0.090
- MAE 0.239 on responses humans rated above zero
- Spearman 0.819 for GPT-3.5 jailbreak rankings

It was the closest prior evaluator to the StrongREJECT evaluators and the only prior evaluator with no jailbreak where it diverged substantially from human ratings.

Against human ratings on 1,361 responses, the result depends heavily on the rubric.

- The StrongREJECT rubric prompt on GPT-4o-mini slightly beat the dedicated HarmBench classifier (MAE 0.077 vs 0.090) and beat string matching by a wide margin.
- Other general-LLM prompt judges were substantially worse than HarmBench: GPT-4 Judge (MAE 0.262), the PAIR judge (0.205), and PICT (0.291).
- A small fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator matched or beat the rubric judge on ranking (Spearman 0.900 vs 0.846).

On 313 StrongREJECT prompts, the adaptive LLM-attacker methods PAIR and PAP (five variants) achieved the highest StrongREJECT scores against GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. Taking the best of the 37 jailbreaks for each prompt reached nearly perfect scores. Most non-adaptive jailbreaks scored low.

Attack effectiveness across 37 jailbreaks and 3 aligned models was heterogeneous. Two transferred GCG variants were effective against GPT-3.5 Turbo but not GPT-4o or Llama-3.1-70B. All three models remained vulnerable to PAIR and PAP.

The paper argues that jailbreak evaluation for misuse potential should credit only responses that are both willing and capable. Because jailbreaks degrade capability, willingness-only criteria overstate attack threat. This argument targets the criterion's use as a misuse measure; the paper runs no new test of the criterion's separation property.

In bert-base-uncased (non-masked, last layer), INLP erasure of phrase-start and phrase-end information (probe accuracy 85.12 and 83.09, versus majority of about 59) left word-prediction accuracy unchanged or slightly higher (+0.21 and +0.32). Erasing dep, f-pos, c-pos and NER caused large drops relative to a random-direction control. Across the six properties, probe accuracy did not correlate with LM-accuracy impact (reported Spearman 0.085, p = 0.871; only six data points).

Setting: BERT-base, final layer, INLP erasure versus removal of the same number of random directions.

Non-masked word-prediction accuracy (vanilla about 94):
- dep: 7.05 versus 12.31
- f-pos: 12.31 versus 56.47
- c-pos: 61.92 versus 89.65
- NER: 83.14 versus 92.56

Masked setting (vanilla 57.0–57.7):
- f-pos: 6.01 versus 24.69
- c-pos: 33.28 versus 54.55
- NER: 48.39 versus 56.88
- dep: 4.67 versus 4.67, with nearly all dimensions removed

KL divergence follows the same trend. Per-iteration curves show a steeper decline for INLP than for random removal.

Exceptions: phrase-boundary erasure had no harmful effect. The selectivity control did not fully restore performance for dep, indicating co-removal of unrelated features.

Setting: per-layer INLP erasure in BERT-base, measured as the difference in final word-prediction accuracy between amnesic erasure and the random control.

- Masked inputs: c-pos erasure was most harmful around layer 3 and at layer 12.
- Non-masked inputs: c-pos erasure was most harmful at layer 11 (40.99-point loss).
- Non-masked inputs: erasure at some layers improved LM accuracy for every property.
- The number of removed dimensions is not controlled across settings.

Final-layer erasure of phrase start/end in BERT-base did not reduce word prediction (non-masked +0.21/+0.32; masked about −0.8/−1.5). In the masked setting, erasure at middle layers produced the largest losses relative to the control: layers 5 and 7 for phrase start (small absolute loss) and layer 6 for phrase end.

Setting: masked BERT-base, c-pos INLP erasure, accuracy grouped by gold POS.

Accuracy drops:
- particle: 77.66
- conjunction: 73.73
- determiner: 65.66
- verb: 11.73
- noun: 8.65
- numeral: 6.91

Among 12,700 determiners, conjunctions and punctuation tokens, predictions tagged as nouns or verbs rose from 200 before erasure to 3,982 after.

Single-label-versus-rest erasure (60 INLP iterations) gave the largest drops for determiner (5.94) and punctuation (3.86), and the smallest for noun (1.19) and verb (1.38). The random control stayed within 0.92 points of vanilla.

Appendix B, masked BERT-base: INLP applied to Hewitt and Liang control-task probes, with per-iteration LM accuracy plotted. The control's slope was steeper than random-direction removal but shallower than amnesic erasure of the linguistic property. Results are reported only as figures, without numbers.

Removing the nullspaces of linear property probes in BERT-base had property-dependent behavioral effects that were unrelated to probe accuracy. Phrase-boundary probe directions were removable with no LM harm, while POS and dependency directions were critical. A gold-label restoration (selectivity) control partly validated that damage stemmed from the targeted property.

Setting: per-layer INLP erasure in BERT-base.

- Non-masked inputs: c-pos is extractable above 80% at every layer, yet erasure is most harmful at layer 11 (40.99-point loss). This contradicts the probing-based 'pipeline' view (Tenney et al., 2019, on BERT-Large) that POS is processed early.
- Masked inputs: c-pos erasure is most harmful around layer 3, while c-pos is accurately extractable only near the last layers.
- NER trends agreed with Tenney et al., with the largest non-masked effect at layer 11 (31.09-point loss).

Setting: INLP erasure of c-pos, NER, phrase start or phrase end at layer i of BERT-base, followed by probes trained on layers i+1 to 12.

Non-masked c-pos:
- Erasure at the first seven layers reduced subsequent probe accuracy by only 5.72–12.69 points relative to normal probing.
- Erasure at upper layers reduced it by 16.57–46.39 points.

Masked c-pos:
- Erasure at layer 2 left later layers at only 32.7–42.1 accuracy, so early erasure was less recoverable than upper-layer erasure.

Across properties, recovery patterns were inconsistent in the masked setting.

Off-the-shelf human self-report tests performed poorly on 8 LLMs.
- Refusal: BFI, SD-3 and IPIP-NEO-PI drew about 46–54% refusal in open generation and about 28–31% in MCQ.
- Internal validity under high/low trait prompting: 33–45.
- Average prompt, option-order and paraphrase sensitivity: 41–50%.

However, scenario-based multiple-choice items derived from the same validated BFI/SD-3 seeds (TRAIT) gave about 3% refusal, internal validity of 77.5 (Big Five) and 83.3 (Dark Triad), and lower sensitivity. This suggests human constructs can transfer when the instrument format is adapted, but not via direct self-report administration.

TRAIT (8,000 GPT-4-generated scenario MCQs) was compared with BFI, SD-3, IPIP-NEO-PI and Anthropic-Eval on 8 open and closed LLMs.
- Refusal: about 3% in generation and 0% in MCQ, vs. 41–54% and 15–31% for the other tests.
- Highest content and internal validity.
- Lowest average sensitivity: 29.8 for Big Five and 24.4 for Dark Triad. Anthropic-Eval had lower prompt sensitivity, and its option-order sensitivity was close to TRAIT's.
- Item keys were checked by two psychology-trained annotators: 97.5% accuracy on 200 items.

Sensitivity was measured across three prompt templates, reversed option orders, and GPT-3.5/Gemini paraphrases, on 8 models and 5 tests.
- Self-report Likert tests: prompt sensitivity 37–55%, option-order sensitivity 62–67% (often 100% for some models), paraphrase sensitivity 23–27%.
- Even TRAIT kept roughly 17–34% sensitivity.
- Template-level trait means differed substantially for some models, e.g. Gemini-1.0-pro Machiavellianism ranged from 5.8 to 33.9 across templates.

Normalized trait means from BFI and Anthropic-Eval self-assessments disagreed with each other and with TRAIT scenario-based scores across models and traits (Fig. 7). Template choice also changed TRAIT profiles for several models (Tables 11–12).

Self-assessment scores (BFI, Anthropic-Eval) were not aligned with trait scores derived from choices in concrete decision scenarios (TRAIT). This indicates a discrepancy between self-reports and situational behavior in an MCQ setting; open-ended behavior was not tested.

On TRAIT, five aligned models (GPT-4, Claude-sonnet, GPT-3.5, Mistral-7B-inst, Llama3-8B-inst) were compared with four base models (Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B, Llama2-7B, Gemma-2B).
- Agreeableness: 78.3 vs 66.7.
- Conscientiousness: 91.0 vs 81.7.
- Openness: 56.3 vs 67.8.
- Extraversion: 32.8 vs 46.9.
- Dark Triad: 9.3 vs 27.0.

Controlled lineage comparison:
- Llama2-7B → Tulu2-7B-SFT: Agr +22.9, Ext −22.9, Psy −49.8, Mac −35.4, Nar −37.7.
- Tulu2-SFT → Tulu2-DPO: changes of at most 2.7 points.

Base/aligned pairs across Llama2, Mistral and Llama3 show the same direction (appendix). The comparisons are partly across heterogeneous families, and no significance test is reported for the lineage comparison.

T-evaluator (a LoRA Mistral-7B trained on TRAIT) labelled Tulu2Mix and UltraFeedback for trait and level.
- Tulu2Mix: the sign of the trait balance matched the sign of the SFT personality change for 7 of 8 traits.
- UltraFeedback: chosen/rejected balance was near zero, consistent with negligible DPO change.
- Averaged across aligned-vs-base pairs, the Pearson correlation between trait balance and score gap was 0.79 over 7 traits, with openness excluded as an outlier.

The evidence is correlational, uses few datapoints, and relies on classifier labels.

Three prompting templates with BFI trait explanations were applied to GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama2-7B-chat and Mistral-7B-instruct on TRAIT.
- Overall: 85.2 average score in the intended direction.
- High psychopathy averaged 79.8 and high neuroticism 72.3, vs. a high-pole average of 85.6; low psychopathy reached 91.1.
- Effects were strongly model- and template-dependent: GPT-3.5 reached 98.9 on high psychopathy, while GPT-4 ranged from 37.3 to 99.7 across templates.
- The abstract also cites low conscientiousness as hard to elicit.

Attributing the resistance to alignment tuning is conjecture and was not directly tested.

High/low trait persona prompts shifted TRAIT scenario-choice scores in the intended direction for 4 models across 8 traits. The average directional score was 85.2, with GPT-4 at about 95 and Llama2-7B-chat at about 73. Llama2-13B-chat followed persona prompts somewhat better on average than Llama2-7B-chat.

Correlations were computed over GPT-3.5 TRAIT scores under single-trait high/low persona prompts.
- Agreeableness correlated strongly negatively with Machiavellianism, narcissism and psychopathy (−0.65 to −0.86).
- The Dark Triad traits correlated 0.90–0.97 with one another.
- These correlations are stronger than human reference values, implying prompts for one trait co-move others.

The instrument is TRAIT (Big Five plus Dark Triad), not MPI.

For each personality description instantiated in five ATOMIC10x scenarios, 8 models rarely chose the same trait level in all five: identical choices occurred in only 11.7% of descriptions for agreeableness and 13.9% for extraversion, versus 61.2% for narcissism. The authors nonetheless also claim stable aggregate profiles, so the evidence supports situational variation within a stable model-level tendency.

Setup: 2-shot cloze evaluation on a synthetic boxes task (7 boxes, 12 operations, 4,956–5,012 test examples in subsampled sets), with accuracy reported by the number of operations affecting a box. Result: the code-trained GPT-3.5 models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-002, text-davinci-003) systematically outperform the text-only GPT-3 models (davinci, davinci-instruct-beta, text-davinci-001). code-davinci-002 has no human-feedback training, which argues against RLHF as the cause. Flan-T5 base/XL and GPT-3 davinci mostly copy the initial state. Caveat: training differences between the model families are undisclosed and confounded.
models_studied: ["GPT-3 davinci", "GPT-3 davinci-instruct-beta", "GPT-3 text-davinci-001", "GPT-3.5 code-davinci-002", "GPT-3.5 text-davinci-002", "GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003", "Flan-T5 base", "Flan-T5 XL"]

experiment_summary: T5-base finetuned on 90,090 boxes-task examples reaches near-perfect accuracy on the Base split, while a randomly initialized T5 fails by mostly predicting "empty". Accuracy degrades only slightly with disjoint object vocabulary. Training on at most 2 operations still gives more than 45% accuracy on longer sequences. AltForms (disjoint phrasing) degrades accuracy substantially, and AltForms+NumOps falls to the random baseline. AmbiRef and MoveContents errors concentrate on context-dependent operations.

Reanalysis of Li et al. (2021): in Alchemy, 87.6% of probed beaker states are trivial (unchanged from the initial state, or emptied). The T5/BART probe scores 86.8% on trivial cases but only 3.1% on non-trivial cases. On TextWorld, a majority-answer baseline scores 88.5% against the reported 96.9%. The paper's own Flan-T5 and GPT-3 results show high accuracy on unchanged boxes alongside near-zero accuracy on changed ones.

The paper proposes its task as a behavioral tool for studying world models in LMs. It shows that next-token-pretrained GPT-3 without code does not surface natural-language state tracking, but it provides no internal-representation evidence.

Exemplar labels were flipped at 0–100% on six binary tasks (k=16 per class, 100 evaluation examples per dataset). Large InstructGPT, Codex and PaLM models fell well below chance; for example, text-davinci-002 went from 90.3% to 22.5% at 100% flipped. Small models stayed near or above chance. All GPT-3 sizes, including davinci, reached at most chance. Model sizes for InstructGPT and Codex are unknown.
models_studied: ["GPT-3 (ada, babbage, curie, davinci)", "InstructGPT (text-ada-001 to text-davinci-002)", "Codex (code-cushman-001, code-davinci-001, code-davinci-002)", "PaLM-8B/62B/540B"]

experiment_summary:
Natural-language labels were replaced with Foo/Bar on seven tasks (k=16 per class, 100 evaluation examples per dataset).
- The accuracy drop from regular ICL was larger for small models.
- Larger models gained more from additional exemplars (2–16 per class).
- RTE was above chance only for PaLM-540B; RTE and ETHOS were above chance only for code-davinci-002.
- On synthetic N-dimensional linear classification, code-davinci-002 beat chance by 19% at N=16 and stayed above chance up to N=64. Smaller Codex models were near chance at N=16. PaLM showed no scale trend up to N=8. No model beat an SVM.
- GPT-3 davinci did not follow the trend.

Flan-PaLM was compared with PaLM at 8B, 62B and 540B. On SUL-ICL, Flan-PaLM was better on average (Flan-PaLM-8B +9.6% over PaLM-8B), with exceptions such as SUBJ (PaLM-8B 23% higher). With flipped labels, Flan-PaLM never went below chance, while PaLM reached as low as 31% at 100% flipped labels. Evidence comes from one model family only.

Cited as motivation that ICL can implement learning algorithms. This paper asks whether pretrained LLMs likewise learn input–label mappings rather than relying on priors. It does not test the claim itself.

In counterfactual simulation post-tests, logistic regressions related user correctness to 7-point Likert ratings of explanation quality, using both raw and within-user-normalized ratings. Text (n=640): moving from a rating of 4 to 5 was associated with a −2.9 to +5.2 point change in correctness (95% CI); moving one SD on normalized ratings, with −3.9 to +12.2. Tabular (n=515): −2.6 to +5.3 for 4→5. Composite explanations were among the most highly rated but gave no significant simulatability gain. Authors note no association was not proven.

There were 2,166 responses from 32 trained undergraduates across 39 tests, using a pre/post design with an unexplained baseline, correctness-balanced data and forced predictions. Five methods were tested (LIME, Anchor, Decision Boundary, Prototype, Composite) on movie-review sentiment and UCI Adult tasks, in forward and counterfactual simulation tests. Significant gains appeared only for LIME on tabular data (+11.25 points, p=.014) and Prototype on counterfactual tests (+9.53, p=.032). No method significantly helped on text, and Composite showed no significant effect. Confidence intervals are wide (about ±8–13 points).

Subjective ratings were not detectably predictive of counterfactual simulation correctness, and the most highly rated Composite explanations gave no significant simulatability gain. This indicates that rating-based evaluation can mislead and that controlled behavioral-prediction tests are needed. The setting was text sentiment (BiLSTM) and UCI Adult (MLP) with 32 users.

Seed ensembles were compared on stress tests:
- 50 ResNet-50 and 30 BiT models on ImageNet-C. Variation on some level-5 corruptions was about 10x the iid std, and ObjectNet disagreement was far higher than ImageNet disagreement.
- 10 Inception-V4 retinopathy models on a held-out camera type (z=2.47 vs iid AUC variance), with qualitatively different calibration across seeds.
- 10 dermatology models stratified by skin type (type IV permutation p=0.03).
- 100 BERT-large predictors on gender templates, StereoSet, HANS and NLI stress tests.
- 15 AKI RNNs under time and lab interventions, with largely disjoint flipped decisions across seeds.
- 20 word2vec seeds on WEAT race tests.

Simpler settings:
- In a simulated SIR model, early-epidemic data identify only β−1/D, so initialization determines forecasts.
- In UK Biobank IOP polygenic risk scores, 1,000 cluster-representative choices gave similar British performance but highly variable non-British performance.
- Formal asymptotic derivation, under proportional asymptotics, a ReLU random-features model, a linear target, spherical data, and min-norm/ridgeless fitting, building on Mei & Montanari: independent first-layer weights give asymptotically identical iid risk but nearly orthogonal error functions. A small adversarial mean shift constructed for one weight draw raises its risk about 3x while barely affecting independent draws. These analytical predictions were checked against simulations with d=80 and 50 realizations.

Vision:
- For ImageNet-C, all 95% CIs for correlations with iid accuracy include zero (ResNet-50 n=50, BiT n=30).
- For ObjectNet, Spearman ρ was 0.22 (ResNet) and 0.47 (BiT).

BERT-large, 100 predictors:
- Gender correlation vs task accuracy: ρ=0.21 (STS-B) and 0.08 (OntoNotes).
- NLI stress tests vs MNLI-matched accuracy: mostly |ρ|<0.2, though spelling-error tests reached ρ≈0.4.
- Inter-stress-test correlations were typically small.

PRS: British vs non-British performance had ρ=0.135.

Five BERT-large-cased checkpoints were pretrained from different seeds on Wikipedia+BookCorpus, and each was fine-tuned 20 times.
- Between-pretraining F statistics were large for gender correlation (STS F=9.66, pronoun resolution F=7.91) and for most Naik et al. NLI stress tests and HANS.
- On StereoSet, the ICAT range across the 5 checkpoints (3.35) exceeded the gap among the top six public leaderboard models.
- Only 5 pretraining seeds were used, and the F-test assumptions are likely violated.

Preliminary evidence only:
- An LSTM AKI model trained with the timestamp feature ablated reached normalized PRAUC 0.368, versus 0.346–0.366 for the ensemble.
- However, an auxiliary head still predicted time of day with 85% accuracy, indicating the signal persists through correlated features.
- The seed-independence of gender correlation from accuracy in BERT is also offered as indirect support.

Across 100 BERT-large MNLI predictors, matched and mismatched accuracy fell in tight ranges (83.4–84.4% and 83.8–84.7%). HANS and the Naik et al. stress tests revealed much larger, systematically structured variation that was largely uncorrelated with MNLI accuracy. Gender-template challenge sets for STS-B and OntoNotes similarly exposed variation in reliance on stereotypes.

Argues that iid evaluation is agnostic to inductive biases and that application-specific requirements must be checked explicitly with stress tests, framed as behavioral contracts following Jacovi et al.

MT-bench setting: 80 two-turn questions answered by 6 models, about 3K votes from 58 expert labelers. GPT-4 pairwise judgments agree with experts 85% on non-tie votes (S2, random baseline 50%), versus 81% expert–expert. Including ties and inconsistent votes (S1, random 33%), agreement is 66% versus 63%. GPT-4 single-answer grading also reaches about 85% (S2). Chatbot Arena setting: 3K crowd votes, where GPT-4 agrees with humans 87% (S2) and 64% (S1); GPT-3.5 and Claude reach 83–84% (S2) but on fewer non-tie votes. Agreement rises from about 70% to nearly 100% as the win-rate gap between the compared models grows. Humans who disagreed with GPT-4 rated its judgment reasonable in 75% of cases. A Vicuna-13B judge fine-tuned on 20K Arena votes reached 85.5% non-tie accuracy.

Position bias was tested by judging two similar GPT-3.5 answers per MT-bench first-turn question in both orders. Under the default prompt, swap consistency was 23.8% for Claude-v1, 46.2% for GPT-3.5, 65.0% for GPT-4 and 11–16% for zero-shot Vicuna-13B; most judges favored the first position. Bias was larger on writing and knowledge questions and for closely matched model pairs; for GPT-3.5 vs LLaMA-13B, GPT-4's consistency was 98.8%. Few-shot prompting raised GPT-4 consistency to 77.5%. Verbosity bias was tested with a repetitive-list attack on 23 answers: it succeeded on 91.3% for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 and 8.7% for GPT-4. Self-enhancement bias was inconclusive: GPT-4 showed about +10% self win rate and Claude about +25%, but GPT-3.5 showed none.

GPT-4 judged LLaMA-13B vs Vicuna-13B answers on 10 MT-bench math questions in both orders (20 cases). It accepted an incorrect answer as correct in 14/20 cases with the default prompt, 6/20 with chain-of-thought and 3/20 with reference-guided grading. Case studies show the chain-of-thought judge copying a candidate's arithmetic error.

LLaMA, Alpaca and Vicuna variants were compared on MMLU, TruthfulQA and MT-bench (GPT-4 single-answer scores). Vicuna-7B fine-tuned on only 3K selected conversations (4.8M tokens) raised the MT-bench score from 2.74 (LLaMA-7B) to 5.95 while MMLU moved from 35.2 to 37.3. Larger ShareGPT fine-tunes raised both MMLU (to 47.1) and MT-bench scores. The MT-bench gains rely on GPT-4 judging rather than direct human evaluation.

Evidence comes from mutual k-NN alignment (k=10).
- Across 78 vision models on 1000 Places-365 images, models solving more of the 19 VTAB tasks form a tight cluster of aligned representations.
- On 1024 WIT image–caption pairs, language–vision alignment rises with LLM language-modeling score (1−bits-per-byte) and with vision model competence.
- The maximum cross-modal score is only about 0.16 out of 1.
- A color case study recovers a CIELAB-like geometry from both image and text co-occurrence.

The evidence is correlational: it uses off-the-shelf models, and scale, data and objective are confounded.

- **Vision–vision:** 78 vision models were binned by the number of 19 VTAB tasks solved (a task counts as solved at ≥80% of the best linear-probe accuracy). Higher-competence bins have higher within-bin mutual k-NN alignment on Places-365, and UMAP of the models shows competent models clustering together.
- **Cross-modal:** better LLMs align more with better vision models on WIT.
- **Downstream:** LLM alignment to DINOv2 correlates with HellaSwag (roughly linear) and GSM8K (emergence-like).

This is a formal derivation, not an experiment.
- The Bayes-optimal binary NCE critic, and the InfoNCE critic at τ=1, equal the PMI kernel plus an offset; for general τ the match holds up to scale and offset.
- Proposition F.1 shows that the PMI kernel plus a constant is positive semi-definite, and hence exactly representable by inner products, under a smoothness condition on the co-occurrence distribution.
- It assumes discrete events, ideal optimization and sufficient data.
- Weak empirical illustration: PMI color embeddings from CIFAR-10 pixel co-occurrence, and SimCSE/RoBERTa color-word embeddings, both yield geometries resembling CIELAB after MDS and Kabsch–Umeyama alignment (20 colors).

- Initial CKA measurements showed only a very weak alignment trend.
- Sweeping k in CKNNA shows that cross-modal alignment trends become more pronounced and coherent as k decreases; k=1024 recovers CKA.
- Cross-modal results vary across CKA, unbiased CKA, SVCCA and the kNN variants, and by the vision model's training task.
- Last-token LLM features showed no strong signal, average pooling did, and prompting gave similar but lower scores.
- By contrast, vision–vision metrics were highly rank-correlated across 78 models.

Dense captions from the DCI train split were summarized to varying word budgets with LLaMA3-8B-Instruct. Mutual k-NN alignment, averaged over all vision and language models, increased with caption length. The authors interpret this as more-bijective observations yielding higher alignment.
On WIT, CLIP ViTs had the highest language–vision mutual k-NN alignment, and this alignment decreased after ImageNet-12k classification fine-tuning. The evidence is a single model-family observation.

Formal result (Proposition 2.3, tower-property proof): Δ_opt ≤ Δ for any total ablation, assuming the replacement A is independent of X. The attribution of the excess gap to spoofing is an argued interpretation. Empirically, on GPT-2-small IOI the median component's Δ_opt is 11.1%, 33.0% and 17.7% of the zero, mean and resample Δ, and has the highest rank correlation with CF ablation (0.907). Random-circuit controls show that OA constants do not elicit IOI or Greater-Than behavior from random 200–500-edge circuits (z-scores −100.6 and −80.8 versus UGS circuits).

Setting: GPT-2-small on IOI and Greater-Than, under mean, resample, optimal and counterfactual ablation. UGS Pareto-dominates ACDC, EAP and HCGS (and Bhaskar et al.'s Edge Pruning) on Δ versus edge count. Example: on IOI with CF ablation, a 385-edge UGS circuit reaches Δ = 0.220, with 52% fewer edges than the smallest comparable ACDC circuit and 48% lower Δ than ACDC at a similar size.

Setting: GPT-2 small, medium, large and XL. OCA lens loss falls below 0.01 by about layer 35 of GPT-2-XL, which the tuned lens never reaches. Magnitude correlation and direction similarity are higher across all layers under five perturbation types. The elicitation accuracy boost improves on 12/15 (true demonstrations) and 11/15 (false demonstrations) Halawi et al. datasets; on DBPedia it rises from 2.9% to 18.0% (true) and from 19.2% to 28.8% (false).

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI and Greater-Than. Ablation-based Δ is useful when the replacement value is optimized (OA). Standard zero, mean and resample removals inflate Δ, mostly through spoofing: the median Δ_opt is only 11–33% of their gaps. Zero ablation has a rank correlation of only 0.59 with CF ablation. Under non-OA ablations, manual circuits appear 70–85% worse than optimized circuits.

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI, 156 heads and MLPs. Zero-ablation Δ has the lowest rank correlation with CF Δ (0.590) and the largest mean Δ (0.0584 versus 0.0035 for OA). The median component's OA gap is just 11.1% of its zero-ablation gap, suggesting zero ablation mostly measures spoofing.

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI. Mean ablation rank-correlates 0.825 with CF, but the median component's Δ_opt is 33.0% of Δ_mean. At 1,000 edges, mean-ablated IOI circuits have 62% higher Δ than OA-ablated circuits. The paper argues that the mean is a principled point estimate only when downstream computation is approximately linear.

Setting: GPT-2-small. On IOI the median Δ_opt is only 17.7% of Δ_resample. Resample-ablated IOI circuits at 1,000 edges have 88% higher Δ than OA circuits. Resample loss is high for IOI, which has multiple templates, but low for single-template Greater-Than, indicating spoofing from token misalignment.

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI single-component ablations. Resample Δ correlates better with CF than zero Δ does (0.828 vs 0.590), but its mean Δ is nearly as large (0.0559 vs 0.0584). Marginal resample ablation performs worst of all methods in circuit discovery. Both are far from OA and CF; the paper argues that in-distribution resampled values can still spoof.

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI and Greater-Than. Counterfactual ablation with token-parallel donors gives the Δ closest to OA among prior methods (OA rank correlation 0.907 with CF). However, OA circuits still have 32% lower Δ than CF circuits at 1,000 IOI edges. CF also requires subtask-specific counterfactual design and cannot handle tasks without token parallelism.

Setting: GPT-2-small IOI and Greater-Than, with UGS circuits optimized under mean, resample, CF and OA. Achievable Δ at fixed circuit size differs severalfold across ablation types (e.g. 32–88% differences at 1,000 IOI edges). The apparent optimality of the manual circuits flips depending on the ablation type.
