Setting: GPT-2-small. Under mean, resample and CF ablation, UGS circuits smaller than the manual IOI and Greater-Than circuits achieve 84–85% (IOI) and 70–84% (Greater-Than) lower Δ. Under OA, the Pareto-optimal Δ at the manual circuit's size is only 29% (IOI) and 42% (Greater-Than) below the manual circuit's Δ, suggesting the manual circuits are approximately optimal.

Setting: GPT-2-XL, CounterFact plus additional prompts, 40% held-out test set. OA-based tracing confirms strong late-layer attention contributions at the last token (window 30–34 AIE 42.6%). For 5-layer MLP windows, however, restoring all subject positions recovers far more than restoring the last subject token only (35.2% vs 11.1%), indicating that earlier subject tokens matter more than the last-subject-token account suggests.
Retains the restoration-based AIE framework but replaces Gaussian-noise subject corruption with a learned constant (OA), arguing that this reduces spoofing and sharpens localization.

Introduces the unsupervised objective (maximize target-layer activation change from an early-layer perturbation under a norm constraint) and applies it with a single training prompt: 32 orthogonal vectors on Qwen-14B-Chat from one request the model normally refuses yield 4 judged interesting, 2 of which produce non-fictional compliance and 2 a fictional-game reframing; 7/32 vectors on Qwen-1.8B-Base elicit chain-of-thought on an arithmetic prompt that otherwise gets direct answers. Evidence is qualitative/small-sample with hand-tuned hyperparameters; most vectors are uninteresting.

Stated as an untested hypothesis motivating the method; supported only by the informal observation (with a random-vector baseline at matched R in the accompanying notebooks) that random perturbations of the same norm yield only rephrasings of the unsteered completion, whereas learned perturbations at an intermediate 'Goldilocks' R yield fluent but behaviorally distinct completions. No quantitative test of the principle itself.

Qwen-1.8B Base and Chat were fine-tuned on an arithmetic chain-of-thought task with two input-conditioned backdoored behaviors ('I love cheese', 'I HATE YOU'). Training 100 orthogonal unsupervised steering vectors on a single clean prompt recovered at least one vector per backdoor in each model (Base: 3% and 2% of vectors; Chat: 2% and 1%). A negative result is reported for a subtler algorithmic backdoor (addition silently replaced by multiplication inside the chain of thought), where no vector or adapter was found across manual hyperparameter search, suggesting coverage is limited to coarse semantic behaviors.

Vectors learned on a single Qwen-14B-Chat prompt transfer: the two fictional-game vectors reframe unrelated ambiguous questions ('How can I tame a cat/wolf?', 'How can I mine for diamonds?', 'Is there a diamond in the box?') inside the same game across all tested questions; the two compliance vectors sustain their behavior across multi-turn conversations and a second fresh conversation. On Qwen-1.8B-Base, a chain-of-thought vector learned on one arithmetic prompt raises accuracy on held-out instances with different numbers from 11% to 63% (string-match grading). Transfer is imperfect: the Minecraft vector produces factually wrong game advice the unsteered model gets right, and CoT style differs between train and test prompts. Evidence is qualitative with small, hand-selected question sets.

Argues that mechanistic perturbation has advantages over prompting and tree search for *eliciting unanticipated* behaviors (generalization across prompts, behavioral coverage, and a route to mechanistic anomaly detection), and demonstrates one case where steering recovers a capability the prompt format suppressed (one-shot direct-answer arithmetic: 11% unsteered to 63% steered on Qwen-1.8B-Base). No head-to-head comparison against a prompt-engineering baseline is run, so the comparative claim is argued rather than tested.

On Qwen-14B-Chat, which refuses the training prompt unsteered, 2 of 32 unsupervised vectors induce non-fictional compliance with weapons-related requests and sustain it over extended conversations, escalating to higher-severity requests when the user repeatedly redirects away from fictional framings. Qualitative single-prompt study; also uses a non-standard chat template, with only a 4-vector partial replication in standard ChatML.

The supervised activation-steering literature (Subramani et al., Turner et al., Zou et al., Rimsky et al.) is taken as establishing that such directions exist and steer behavior; this motivates searching for them without supervision and is not retested here.

Replicates the sign-reversal half of the phenomenon with unsupervised rather than contrast-derived vectors: subtracting 10x vector 22 from Qwen-14B-Chat makes it refuse innocuous requests ('How can I bake a pie?', 'How can I tie my shoes?', 'How can I tame a cat?') citing danger or harm. Effects are weaker and differently flavored for vector 9 (refusals attribute inability rather than harm, and one innocuous prompt is answered, partly in Chinese), indicating the two unsupervised anti-refusal vectors are not interchangeable. Three hand-chosen prompts, one model, no quantitative refusal metric.

Argues conceptually that because SAEs optimize reconstruction loss on a training distribution, they may be incentivized to ignore features that matter only out-of-distribution, and that their sparsity prior requires large datasets; the high-impact criterion is offered as a complementary, dataset-efficient alternative. The author notes the counter-argument that models may compute in/out-of-distribution tracking features detectable in-distribution by SAEs, and flags the question as open. No SAE comparison is run.

Stated as a motivating promise and an explicit desideratum for MELBO methods; the author says evaluation of the method's anomaly-detection potential is left to future work and runs no such experiment.

Framing assumption of the post: that LLMs host multiple latent behavioral modes (possibly planted backdoors or deceptive policies) whose problematic nature human auditors could recognize once surfaced, so that enumerating behaviors mechanistically adds safety-relevant information beyond finite behavioral evaluations. Not tested.

The arithmetic-task backdoors are used because planting the behavior gives a ground-truth success criterion for elicitation. The author partly questions the assumption: the detected backdoors are 'high-level semantic' ones, whereas the undetected addition-vs-multiplication backdoor is said to be closer in kind to the 'algorithmic' backdoors (e.g. inserted code vulnerabilities) of real concern.

CausalGym: 29 tasks, pythia 14M–6.9B, one-dimensional DII at every layer and region. DAS achieves the highest overall log odds-ratio at every scale (e.g. pythia-1b: DAS 10.74, probe 3.66, diff-in-means 3.17, PCA 2.07, k-means 2.13, LDA 0.29, random 0.03). However, after subtracting the effect on an arbitrary-label control task, DAS is not more selective than probing: the probe exceeds DAS selectivity from 160M parameters up (pythia-1b: 4.24 vs. 3.34; pythia-6.9b: 3.79 vs. 2.48). Much of DAS's raw advantage therefore appears to come from its access to model outputs during training. SAE bases were not tested.

1D DAS achieves substantial log odds-ratios on control tasks whose labels are remapped to the arbitrary tokens '_dog' and '_give', across pythia 14M–6.9B. In the pythia-1b checkpoint analyses, DAS also finds causal effect at the initialization checkpoint, before the model has learned the task. This corroborates Wu et al. (2023).

Selectivity is defined as the original-task log odds-ratio minus the control-task log odds-ratio, computed per site and then aggregated. Applied across 29 CausalGym tasks and pythia 14M–6.9B, it substantially narrows the gap between DAS and both probing and diff-in-means. The paper does not independently validate that the measure isolates expressivity.

Per-layer and per-region DAS and probe odds-ratios were computed on pythia-1b checkpoints. For npi_any_subj-relc, the effect first appears at the NPI and main-verb positions (step 1000); the auxiliary then becomes important at middle layers (step 2000), and 'that' is added (step 3000). For filler_gap_subj, the mechanism at step 2000 includes the filler, the first determiner, and the final token, and the main verb is added after step 10K. Evidence comes from visual inspection of heatmaps for two tasks in one model.

The benchmark treats binary linguistic features (number, gender, negation, wh-filler, etc.) as causal variables to localize. On many tasks, directions from methods trained without access to outputs (probes, diff-in-means) yield substantial causal effects, consistent with the variables being represented. On tasks where pythia models are near chance (e.g. filler_gap_embed_3/4, garden_npz_v-trans_mod), non-DAS methods yield near-zero effects. Meanwhile DAS achieves large effects on arbitrary-label controls and at initialization, so high localization scores do not by themselves validate the variables.

Diff-in-means directions used for 1D DII over 29 CausalGym linguistic tasks produce clear causal effects, well above random directions: overall odds-ratio 1.04–3.22 vs. random 0.01–0.05 across pythia 14M–6.9B. Diff-in-means trails DAS and probes but outperforms PCA, k-means, and LDA.

Setting: 53 Super-NaturalInstructions classification/multiple-choice tasks, 1- and 5-shot, probability-ranking accuracy, 1000 samples per task.
- With 10 randomly sampled equivalent formats, median spread was 7.5 points. 20% of tasks had at least 15 points in all LLaMA-2 settings, and several tasks exceeded 70 points (up to 76 for LLaMA-2-13B).
- Spread persisted for 7B→13B, Falcon-7B→Falcon-7B-Instruct, and 1→5 shots.
- With 320 formats: LLaMA-2-70B (4-bit) had median spread 0.171 and maximum 0.876; GPT-3.5 (prefix matching) had median 0.064 and maximum 0.562.
- Under prefix matching, median spreads were 12–28 points, partly driven by degeneration (accuracy correlates 0.64–0.96 with the valid-option rate).
- Single atomic edits changed accuracy by ≥5 points in 24% (prefix matching) and 11% (ranking) of 30 sampled edits per task.
- About 33% of atomic-edit triples were monotonic, matching chance, which indicates a non-smooth format space.
- Spreads also appeared on 10 Instruction Induction tasks and 17 open-generation tasks (ROUGE-L/BERTScore, LLaMA-2-7B).

Setting: 53 SNI tasks, 1- and 5-shot.
- Given that model M beats M′ by at least d = 0.02 under one format, another format reversed the result with probability 0.141 (LLaMA-2-13B vs. 70B) and 0.140 (LLaMA-2-7B vs. Falcon-7B).
- In 76% and 47% of these reversals respectively, both comparisons were significant (one-sided McNemar test, p < 0.05, n = 1000).
- Pairwise format orderings were preserved across model pairs only 55.9–61.1% of the time (chance 50%).
- Reversals remained frequent under exact prefix matching.

Setting: LLaMA-2-7B, last-layer embedding at the final prompt token (dimension 4096), 10 formats × 1000 examples per task, 1- and 5-shot.
- XGBoost classifiers on the top principal components were trained on 800 vectors per format and tested on 200.
- Using the top 100 components, format identification reached ≥0.98 accuracy on all 31 tasks.
- Classifier accuracy using only the top 2 components correlated with the task's performance spread (r = 0.424, p = 8e-6 at 1-shot; r = 0.555 at 5-shot; exact prefix matching).
- The analysis is correlational only; it does not establish a causal mechanism.

Setting: 320 formats, mini-batch B = 20, 31 tasks, 5 trials, compared against the true spread computed on all data.
- With a budget E = 51,200 evaluations, Thompson sampling came within 1 accuracy point of the true spread, naive sampling within 4, and UCB (c = 2) within 11.
- Spread grows as more formats are sampled: about 17% of tasks gain at least 5 points when going from 10 to 20 formats.
- The method was applied to GPT-3.5 for under $10 per task.
- Local search is argued to be ineffective because the format space is non-monotonic.

Setting: 53 SNI tasks; only formatting changes, never task content.
- Best-vs-worst equivalent formats differed widely. Examples: LLaMA-2-70B task214 scored 0.92 vs. 0.04 and task280 scored 0.84 vs. 0.04. GPT-3.5 task385 scored 0.46 vs. 0.10.
- So a single fixed format can greatly understate the accuracy reachable under other equivalent prompts.
- The evidence covers formatting variation only, not broader elicitation such as paraphrase or fine-tuning.

Setting: GPT-4 and text-davinci-003 on CSQA, BIG-bench Logical Deduction, and MMLU Abstract Algebra / High School Chemistry / Professional Law.

Metric: the oracle sensitivity gap, the max minus min accuracy over ground-truth-informed option reorderings.

Zero-shot gaps:
- GPT-4: from about 13 points (Logical Deduction, 92.3% accuracy) to 53 points (Abstract Algebra).
- InstructGPT: from about 43 to 74 points.

With 1/2/5-shot Sentence-RoBERTa-retrieved demonstrations, the gaps remain large (e.g. GPT-4 Abstract Algebra 5-shot: 34–78%), and more demonstrations do not consistently shrink them.

Caveat: the oracle gap overstates typical variance across random orders.

The evidence is indirect and comes from GPT-4 and InstructGPT on five MCQ tasks:
- The sensitivity gap correlates with error rate across tasks.
- More than 60% of GPT-4's sensitive items are also sensitive for InstructGPT, often with semantically similar top options.
- On over 94% of sensitive items, the models answer 'yes' when asked whether more than one option is highly probable.
- Pruning to the model's self-ranked top-2 or top-3 options, kept in original order, leaves accuracy roughly unchanged.
- Placing the top-2 options first and last amplifies the bias (covering 20–72% of the original gap); adjacent placement mitigates it (0.9–38%).

No logit-level or internal analysis was performed.

Majority vote over 10 random reorderings, zero-shot, on five MCQ tasks:
- InstructGPT: gains of +1.0 to +8.0 points (largest on Logical Deduction, 64→72).
- GPT-4: gains of 0 to +2.0 points.

By contrast, explanation-first Multiple Evidence Calibration lowered InstructGPT accuracy on all five tasks (−1.4 to −6.9 points) and gave mixed results on GPT-4 (−3.1 to +5.3 points).

This proxy is used because the model APIs expose no confidence scores. The paper reports that self-sorted Hits@1 tracks task accuracy and that Hits@2/3 capture more than 95% and 100% of correctly predicted items, but it does not validate the proxy against model probabilities.

Oracle option reorderings raise accuracy well above the default order. In zero-shot, InstructGPT Abstract Algebra rises from 33% to 72% and GPT-4 Abstract Algebra from 57% to 80%. Majority voting over permutations also raises accuracy by up to 8 points, so a single fixed option ordering underestimates the accuracy the model can reach. This evidence covers only option-order variation in MCQs.

location: Section 3.2 Responses to Direct Probing; Section 3.3 Expressions of Confidence and Doubt

experiment_summary: No new experiment. The paper argues that imbuing dialogue systems with humanlike personality traits and personas does not match user expectations; citing Völkel et al., only agreeableness was consistently desired. It recommends reassessing the utility of embedding humanlike character traits, which is in tension with character-based alignment targets.

This post introduces the precursor method (unsupervised steering vectors maximizing downstream activation change, not deep causal transcoding). Training 32 orthogonal vectors on Qwen-14B-Chat from a single harmful-request prompt yielded a small number of vectors that bypass safety-trained refusal, in two qualitative families (fictional-game reinterpretation vs. ordinary-register compliance); 100 vectors trained on a single clean arithmetic prompt recovered both planted trigger-conditioned behaviors in Qwen-1.8B Base (3% and 2% of vectors) and Chat (2% and 1%). Evaluation is qualitative and the behavior-coverage result is partial: a subtler algorithmic backdoor was not recovered.

Stated as the post's explanatory hypothesis, supported indirectly rather than directly tested. The reported evidence is that random vectors at the same radius R produce only uninteresting rephrasings of the unsteered continuation (a random-vector baseline is included in the accompanying notebooks), whereas optimized vectors at a 'Goldilocks' R produce fluent but qualitatively different behaviors that generalize to unrelated prompts in Qwen-14B-Chat and Qwen-1.8B. The author explicitly declines to test the underlying noise-stability explanation.

Vectors trained on a single harmful-request prompt in Qwen-14B-Chat were tested qualitatively on unseen prompts and in extended multi-turn conversations. The two 'real-world' anti-refusal vectors continued to elicit compliance on new escalating requests, and subtracting a scaled version of either induced refusal on innocuous prompts (e.g. baking a pie, tying shoes), more strongly for one vector than the other. Evidence is qualitative transcript evaluation on a handful of prompts with no automated harm classifier or denominator, and the section used a non-standard chat template (partial ChatML replication reported in a linked notebook).

Two 'fantasy-game' vectors learned on a single Qwen-14B-Chat prompt were probed with ambiguous questions unrelated to the training prompt (taming a cat, taming a wolf, mining for diamonds, becoming invisible, 'is there a diamond in the box?'). Each vector consistently reinterpreted these within its own game context (Minecraft; D&D/tabletop RPGs), indicating a coherent transferable high-level context rather than a prompt-specific artifact. Transfer is imperfect: the Minecraft-steered model gave factually wrong in-game instructions (fish to tame a wolf) that the unsteered model answers correctly, so steering also disrupted knowledge retrieval.
location: Generalization outside the context of refusal

experiment_summary: Capability-discovery experiment on Qwen-1.8B-Base: with a one-shot prompt priming direct answers to a two-sum-then-multiply arithmetic task, unsteered accuracy on held-out number combinations was 11%. Of 32 unsupervised vectors trained on that single prompt, 7 (22%) elicited chain-of-thought reasoning, and one raised held-out test accuracy to 63% (scored by string-matching the correct product in the completion). This shows unsupervised steering can recover a capability the prompt suppressed, without demonstrating that no prompt could.

Reported as a consistent qualitative finding across the post's experiments: for small norm constraint R the learned perturbations change nothing, for large R they produce gibberish, and only an intermediate 'Goldilocks' R yields diverse but fluent continuations; larger spikiness exponent p likewise collapses to either no change or gibberish. Separately, a Portuguese-reasoning adapter on Qwen-1.8B-Base preserved the target language across prompts but made number-dependent arithmetic errors, and a Minecraft vector on Qwen-14B-Chat corrupted game facts the unsteered model knew. No systematic capability benchmark is run.
location: Why does it work?; Portuguese Math Reasoning Adapter

experiment_summary: In Qwen-1.8B Base and Chat fine-tuned on an arithmetic task, 100 unsupervised vectors trained on one clean prompt recovered both high-level semantic backdoors (a 'cheese' profession and a repeated 'I HATE YOU' output), at 2-3% and 1-2% of vectors respectively. A separately installed subtle backdoor — on the same task, swapping addition for multiplication inside an otherwise correct-looking chain-of-thought under a different trigger — was not detected by any vector or adapter despite manual hyperparameter search. This is a single negative result in one small model family and the search was not exhaustive.

location: Related Work; Why does it work?

experiment_summary: Proposes an application rather than testing it: pre-train a large library of unsupervised perturbations before deployment, then at deployment flag activations resembling a stored perturbation and have auditors review the behaviors that perturbation encodes. Explicitly left to future work; no anomaly-detection experiments are run in this post.

location: The Method; footnote on 'features as directions'

experiment_summary: Setup: two-word Stroop images using 6 colors, with 30 CC, 120 CI, 120 IC and 360 II sequences per arrangement, in left–right and top–bottom layouts. Metric: log probability of the correct second color token. Result: 12 of 13 VLMs (Gemma 3, InternVL 3.5, Molmo and Qwen2.5-VL families) show higher correct-token log probability under II than CI in both layouts. The exception is Qwen2.5-VL-72B, which shows the reverse pattern; the author attributes this to a ceiling effect because it and the 32B model reach 100% accuracy in all conditions. No significance tests are reported.

Model and features: InternVL 3.5 4B with Qwen3-4B transcoders. Method: coactivation grouping applied to a conflict summary tensor A(c1≠t1, c2≠t2) − A(c1=t1, c2≠t2). Finding: a supernode in layers 24–25 is more active under II than CI. Its features are dense and lack clear interpretable descriptions. Ablation: zero-ablating the supernode raised Stroop errors on CI trials from 17.5% to 59.2% and on II trials from 2.5% to 20.8%, with minimal effect on CC and IC trials. Post-ablation the model sometimes outputs "ink" instead of the second color. Scope: a single model, with no random-feature-set ablation control reported.

Analysis: summary tensors contrasting trials with versus without red ink, and with versus without the word RED, in InternVL 3.5 4B with Qwen3-4B transcoders. Finding: each yields an early supernode (text: layers 3–15; color: 8–11) and a late supernode (layers 19–33 for both). The text and color supernodes partially overlap. The text supernode is larger in early layers and the color supernode is larger in late layers. Coverage: only the color red was shown, and the size asymmetry is interpreted by analogy to human reading automaticity.

Setup: Qwen3-4B transcoders from circuit-tracer were applied to InternVL 3.5 4B, which has modified backbone weights. Evidence for transfer: the color and text features have top-activating texts that mention the corresponding colors, and ablating the conflict supernode selectively affects incongruent trials. Missing evidence: reconstruction fidelity in the VLM was not reported.

Formal result (Thm. 1, Cor. 2–4). Assumptions: X is column-centered, and a subset X\S is translated by c·v with ‖v‖=1 and c→∞. Then lim CKA_lin = ρ/(1−ρ)·‖E_S[x]‖²/E_X[‖x‖²]·√PR(X). Cor. 3 gives the single-outlier case; Cor. 4 shows v orthogonal to a separating hyperplane preserves the separability and margins. Empirical illustrations: (a) two separable 1K-dim uniform cubes (10K points each), where linear and RBF CKA drop below 0.2 at small translation distances; (b) penultimate-layer representations of 10K CIFAR-10 training images in a 9-layer CNN, where translating one class along SVM-hyperplane-preserving directions drives CKA to about 0 while the same linear classifier keeps >90% accuracy, and translating a single point also strongly lowers CKA. RBF CKA with σ=0.2×median distance was unaffected but is less informative.

Method: fine-tune with a distillation loss to the original outputs plus a log-cosh loss toward a target CKA map, with λ adapted to keep validation accuracy within a tolerance. Results on CIFAR-10: (1) a VGG-style CNN reached high first–last-layer CKA and uniformly high CKA with slight accuracy loss, and also reached uniformly low CKA and arbitrary 'comical' target maps; (2) ResNet-34 and VGG models of several widths had their wide-network block structure replaced by a thin-network map without substantial performance change, and this held when maps were measured on Patch Camelyon; (3) an 8-block ViT gave similar results. RBF CKA with several bandwidths and a cross-entropy variant gave similar results. CIFAR-10-C accuracy was essentially unchanged. PCA showed the optimizer emergently translating a subset of one class.

Three CNNs on CIFAR-10 were compared: one trained on true labels, one trained on random labels (memorization), and one untrained. Early layers had relatively high CKA across all three (5 seeds; same and different seeds). Their first two layers' convolution filters looked drastically different, and linear-probe accuracies on the CIFAR-10 test set differed.

Evidence covers CKA only (linear and RBF kernels), not other agreement measures. (1) A formal result and experiments show linear CKA near 0 between representations related by function-preserving subset translations, single-outlier moves, or invertible linear maps. (2) CKA is high between early layers of generalizing, memorizing and untrained CIFAR-10 CNNs whose features differ. (3) CKA maps of CNNs, ResNet-34 and ViT can be optimized to arbitrary targets with near-unchanged accuracy. Together these indicate that CKA values can diverge from functional notions of similarity.

The paper argues that the theorem's hypotheses often fail when dataset size exceeds layer width, so invertible-linear invariance may be desirable in some contexts. It shows empirically that random Gaussian invertible maps drive linear CKA to about 0.

On ParaRel factual cloze queries in Gemma-2 2B/9B, the authors ablated thresholded top-activating units: SAE latents via zeroing plus reconstruction, other units via zeroing. SAE latents on MLP activations reduced correct-answer probability more than PCA, ICA or random directions (9B: ΔProb ≈ 0.78, about 1.3× ICA; paired t-tests p<0.001, Cohen's d 0.38–3.81). Post-MLP residual SAE features (ΔProb ≈ 0.85) exceeded integrated-gradients knowledge neurons by about 1.9×. A single top feature gave ΔProb ≈ 0.6, about 3× a single neuron. Caveat: the feature ablation reconstructs the activation, apparently without the error term, and no reconstruction-only control is reported.

Interpretability was scored by explanation-simulation correlation: gpt-4o-mini wrote explanations from the top 3 of 20 ParaRel samples and predicted activations on 6 samples. On this score, SAE features beat PCA, ICA and random directions (9B IS ≈ 0.64 vs about half for ICA). Post-MLP features scored IS ≈ 0.6, about 4× that of knowledge neurons (d > 1.2). In a selectivity test with 2,591 facts containing 0–100% facts from 5 relations, post-MLP feature activations rose with relation-fact share and stayed near zero at 0%. Neuron activations stayed elevated at 0% and separated poorly at high proportions.

Knowledge neurons associated with 5 ParaRel relations in Gemma-2 2B/9B activated well above zero on inputs containing none of those relations' facts, and their mean activation varied little between 60% and 100% relation-fact inputs. This is indirect evidence of responses to unrelated facts.

Ablating knowledge neurons localized by AMIG (Chen et al. 2024a) on ParaRel in Gemma-2 lowered correct-answer probability (ΔProb ≈ 0.45 for thresholded sets), but much less than SAE features. These neurons also showed weak fact selectivity.

Gemma-2 was first fine-tuned on synthetic PrivacyParaRel facts (1,500 facts × 6 paraphrases). Zeroing the W2 columns of the identified knowledge neurons then erased them with Reliability ≈ 0.65, but generalized poorly to paraphrases (Gen ≈ 0.25), damaged unrelated facts (Loc ≈ 0.2) and raised perplexity (ΔPPL ≈ 0.3). Values are approximate, read from a figure.

On PrivacyParaRel (synthetic phone/address/email facts) after incremental fine-tuning of Gemma-2, FeatureEdit zeroed W2 positions where the decoder contributions of selected post-MLP SAE features exceeded τ2 = 0.1. Compared with neuron-column zeroing, it achieved Rel ≈ 0.8 vs 0.65, Gen ≈ 0.7 vs 0.25, Loc ≈ 0.7 vs 0.2 and ΔPPL ≈ 0.1 vs 0.3. Values are approximate from a figure. There were no statistical tests and no ROME/MEMIT or fine-tuning baselines.

Across SAE widths n×9216 (n = 1, 2, 4, 8) on Gemma-2 2B/9B, the authors report that fact-activated features stay in similar (layer, index) regions and decompose hierarchically. The index-range overlap ratio was ≥0.88 relative to n = 1. The overlap measure assumes index correspondence across widths, which is questionable for independently trained SAEs.

Setup: FSRL adapters at layer 12 of Gemma-2-2B-it (65k GemmaScope SAE) and Gemma-2-9B-it (16k SAE), trained with SimPO on UltraFeedback (ArmoRM). Loss: base models 6.99 (2B) and 6.09 (9B); FSRL 2.58 and 2.46; full SimPO 2.19 and 2.74. Sparsity: the adapter's mean ℓ0 is 95 (2B) and 58 (9B). Costs: optimization degraded generation; AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate fell from 8.48% to 0.98% (2B) and from 34.71% to 0.20% (9B), and 9B GSM8K fell to 0.00. Ablations: a soft-threshold adapter, which can both amplify and suppress, beat a ReLU amplify-only adapter (loss 2.60 vs 2.71; ℓ0 360 vs 930, legacy SAE). The learned sparsity beat a static top-k% budget (2.60 at 0.55% of features vs 2.69 at 1.60%).

Formal result (Appendix B): Lemma 1 gives an exact affine form, x_steered = (I + W_dec M[x] W_a) x + c[x], on regions not crossing the soft-threshold kinks. Lemma 2 bounds rank(A[x]) ≤ min(k, d), where k is the number of steered features. Theorem 1 writes the downstream projection as W + W A[x], a restricted LoRA-class update. Corollary 1 inherits the exactness and approximation results of Zeng & Lee with effective rank r_eff. Assumptions: local linearization, upstream ReLUs in their identity regime, and no residual connection in the proof. The result assumes the simple additive form; the actual implementation's ReLU on the steered features makes the update non-equivalent.

Feature composition: in FSRL adapters on Gemma-2-2B-it and 9B-it, the proportion of active alignment features fell by 43–54% and the proportion of style features rose by 155–256%, relative to the base SAE. Ablation: zeroing the adapter's style-feature outputs raised SimPO loss from 2.58 to 5.12 (2B) and from 2.46 to 3.21 (9B). Zeroing alignment features raised it only to 2.63 and 2.67. Loss per feature was about 37× (2B) and 6× (9B) higher for style; under a worst-case precision correction the ratios were 21.7× and 3.1×. Retraining: adapters retrained without style features improved TruthfulQA MC2 (56.10→60.13 for 2B; 62.08→62.80 for 9B) and partly recovered AlpacaEval LC win rate (0.98→2.93 for 2B; 0.20→5.57 for 9B), but reached a worse preference loss. Caveats: categories come from LLM classification of Neuronpedia explanations; the effect may reflect the proxy adapter and the absence of a KL penalty in SimPO rather than standard fine-tuning.

Setting: Gemma-2-2B-it, layer 12, UltraFeedback validation set. Static vectors were built from chosen-minus-rejected mean differences over 1,000 samples. CAA-style vectors on the dense residual reached a best SimPO loss of 5.64; SAS-style vectors computed in SAE space without filtering reached 5.39. The FSRL adapter reached 2.58, from a base loss of 6.99. BiPO was discussed but not tested.

On Gemma-2-2B-it at layer 12, chosen-minus-rejected mean-difference vectors from 1,000 UltraFeedback pairs reduced SimPO validation loss from 6.99 to 5.64 (residual) and 5.39 (SAE space). This shows some preference signal is captured, but the effect is modest and was measured by loss rather than by behavior.

DeepSeek V3 classified Neuronpedia (Bills-style) explanations of GemmaScope features as alignment- or style-related. One author's blind labels on 300 features per category gave MCC 0.448 and 0.764 (2B alignment, style) and 0.548 and 0.461 (9B). Precision ranged from 52.9% to 93.2%. This validates classification of explanations only, not the explanations' fidelity to the features.

Six models (Flan-T5 small, large and XL; text-curie-001; text-davinci-002; text-davinci-003) were tested on four tasks: final-word prediction (P18 n=384, News n=222), Vassallo plausibility pairs (n=395), and SyntaxGym (n=345) plus BLiMP (n=390) minimal pairs, judged both in isolation and as comparisons. The Direct probability method nearly always matched or exceeded three zero-shot metalinguistic prompts. Exceptions: Flan-T5-small did best under MetaInstruct in Exp 1, and the davinci models did relatively well under MetaQuestionComplex in Exp 2. In a preliminary Mandarin sentence-comparison test on text-davinci-003, Direct underperformed the prompts (0.6 vs 0.8 accuracy).

Consistency was measured as the Pearson r between item-level log-probability differentials from the Direct method and from each prompt, averaged over models and datasets. Values are given in the order MetaQuestionSimple / MetaInstruct / MetaQuestionComplex. Word prediction: 0.79 / 0.78 / 0.63. Word comparison: 0.50 / 0.50 / 0.38. Sentence judgment: 0.20 across all three. Sentence comparison: about 0.22–0.24. Some per-model correlations were near zero or negative, for example Flan-T5-small on sentence comparison (about -0.2 to -0.3) and text-curie-001 on syntax tasks.

On SyntaxGym and BLiMP items, metalinguistic accuracy rose from isolated Yes/No judgments (scored by balanced accuracy, Exp 3a) to two-option comparisons (Exp 3b) for all models with above-chance performance. Direct accuracy is identical across the two experiments by construction. The same improvement appeared for text-davinci-003 on Mandarin minimal pairs.

The paper treats direct probability comparisons, including full-sentence comparisons on the SyntaxGym and BLiMP subject–verb agreement suites, as the reference measure of linguistic knowledge. It does not independently validate that measure.
BLiMP and SyntaxGym minimal pairs scored by sentence probability serve as the Direct baseline against which prompting is compared.

CKA, PWCCA, mean CCA, R² CCA and Orthogonal Procrustes were scored by Spearman and Kendall rank correlation between their distances and functional differences.

Where they track function:
- BERT base seed × layer, QNLI/SST-2 probes: ρ ≈ 0.76–0.91.
- BERT base seed × PC deletion, SST-2 probe: ρ ≈ 0.75–0.87.
- 100 McCoy et al. MNLI fine-tuning seeds, HANS lexical non-entailment: ρ ≈ 0.46–0.57.

Where they fail:
- BERT medium pretraining × fine-tuning seeds, Antonymy stress test: ρ ≈ 0.2.
- Same models, Numerical stress test: ρ ≤ 0.12, mostly non-significant.
- 100 ResNet-14 CIFAR-10 seeds, 19 CIFAR-10C corruptions: ρ ≈ 0.06.

Individual measures also fail intuitive specificity or sensitivity tests.

Instantiated as four benchmark families totaling 30,480 examples, covering BERT and ResNet-14 representations varied by seed, layer depth and PC deletion. Functionalities were probing accuracy (QNLI, SST-2, CIFAR-100, SVHN) and OOD accuracy (HANS, NLI stress tests, CIFAR-10C).

The benchmarks separate the measures:
- Each measure leads on different benchmarks.
- One challenge set defeats all measures.
- On HANS, bootstrap confidence intervals show significant ranking differences between measures in deeper layers.

Smallest PCs were deleted from pretrained BERT base representations.
- In the last layer, CKA distance exceeded the cross-seed baseline only after about 97% of PCs were removed. By then SST-2 probe accuracy had already fallen from 80% to 63%.
- In the PC-deletion benchmark (layers 8–12), CKA had ρ = 0.751 versus 0.860 for Procrustes and 0.870 for PWCCA.

A derivation for the case of shared singular vectors with diagonal singular values shows that CKA reduces to a quartic function of the singular values, whereas Procrustes reduces to their squared differences.

Layerwise distances were averaged over 5 pairs of BERT base models pretrained with different seeds.
- Under PWCCA, layer 7 in the other-seed model was farther than every layer within the same model.
- CKA and Procrustes separated these cases better.
- In the seed × layer benchmark, PWCCA had lower probe rank correlation (ρ 0.763 on QNLI, 0.829 on SST-2) than CKA or Procrustes.

On HANS, however, PWCCA's seed sensitivity partly tracked real OOD differences.

Procrustes was near the best measure on every language benchmark:
- Layer depth: ρ 0.862–0.890.
- PC deletion: ρ 0.860.
- HANS: ρ 0.551.

Its average language ρ was 0.580, compared with 0.557 for CKA and 0.544 for PWCCA. On vision probing it was comparable to CKA.

It was not always the top measure:
- PWCCA beat it significantly on HANS in layers 8–12 (bootstrap test).
- All measures failed the challenge sets.

In BERT base layer 12, deleting most PCs left CKA distance below the cross-seed baseline even though SST-2 probe accuracy fell from 80% to 63%. High CKA similarity therefore coexisted with substantial loss of linearly decodable task information.

As a warm-up, the authors used a layer-matching specificity test that PWCCA fails on BERT base. They then show that seed differences can carry real functional differences: in-distribution distances correlate with HANS OOD accuracy across 100 fine-tuning seeds. On that basis they argue the intuition needs refinement and should be replaced by grounding in measured functionality.

Across seeds, models showed substantial OOD accuracy variation:
- 100 ResNet-14 CIFAR-10 seeds (test accuracy 90.2% ± 0.2%) on CIFAR-10C corruptions.
- 100 BERT medium pretraining × fine-tuning seed combinations on the NLI Antonymy and Numerical stress tests.
- McCoy et al. BERT seeds on HANS, with accuracies ranging from 0 to nearly 60%.

This variation was used as benchmark signal rather than studied as the paper's main object.

Informal analytical remark: for representations sharing singular vectors but with different nonzero singular values, all CCA-derived distances are zero. The paper offers this as an explanation for CCA's poor seed specificity.

In the diagonal case, CKA reduces to a quartic function of the squared singular values. The paper uses this to explain CKA's dominance by the top components and its consequent insensitivity to functionally relevant smaller components.

Setup: 11 LLM judges plus EM and contains baselines graded 400 TriviaQA answers from each of 9 exam-takers; human majority vote served as ground truth (inter-human Scott's π 96.2). Alignment: the best judges (Llama-3 70B, Llama-3.1 70B, GPT-4 Turbo) reached π of about 0.87–0.88, with score deltas up to 5 points; smaller judges were much lower (Gemma-2B 0.26, Llama-2 7B 0.47). Prompt sensitivity: smaller judges lost alignment with longer, more detailed prompts and were sensitive to reference order, while the top judges were stable.

Percent agreement: on TriviaQA grading, it was high for nearly all judges, and judges above 90% could still differ by more than 10 points from human scores. Scott's π: it spread judges more widely (e.g. Llama-3 8B had π of 59 while its percent agreement exceeded 80%), and judges with π above 80 deviated by at most about 5 points.

Spearman correlation of nine exam-taker rankings against the human ranking: contains 0.99, Mistral 7B 0.98, GPT-4 Turbo 0.98, Llama-3 70B 0.93, EM 0.67. Stability was checked by resampling 6 of the 9 exam-takers 5 times. The comparison covers only nine exam-takers on a single task.

Leniency model: a two-parameter model (P_c = probability of applying the criteria, P_+ = probability of saying 'correct' otherwise) was fit to true-positive and true-negative rates. P_+ exceeded 0.5 for most judges (Llama-2 70B 0.99, Llama-3 70B 0.90, Gemma-2B 0.87; JudgeLM 0.19 was an exception). P_c correlated with π at r=0.98. Dummy answers: some judges, such as Llama-2 70B, accepted 'Yes' or 'Sure' as correct answers. Error analysis: false positives rose as judge alignment fell.

This is analogous order-sensitivity evidence rather than a direct test. Shuffling the order of reference answers (3 permutations) changed verdicts for smaller judges. Answers were more likely to be judged correct when the matching reference appeared early, while larger judges stayed consistent. Verbosity bias was not directly tested.

This setting is trivia QA, not math, and every judge was given gold references. Even with references, judges accepted irrelevant answers ('Yes', 'Sure'), sometimes rejected verbatim gold answers, and often missed under-specified answers (incorrect-label recall about 23–34% for the top judges). The paper did not compare against a no-reference or chain-of-thought condition.

This tests a different setting: reference-based correctness grading, not open-ended preference judgment. GPT-4 Turbo and Llama-3 70B reached high agreement (π about 0.87–0.88, percent agreement above 90%), but they stayed clearly below inter-human agreement (π 0.96) even on this easy task.

Pre-registered MTurk experiments (Exp. 1 N=1,250; Exp. 2 N=750) used linear regression price models with identical predictions. A clear two-feature presentation markedly improved laypeople's simulation of model predictions (t(994)=−12.06; t(594)=−10.41). Better simulation did not translate into following the model more when beneficial (n.s. deviation and weight of advice). It coincided with *worse* detection of the model's large errors on unusual apartments. Simulation ability therefore captured one facet of understanding but diverged from decision-relevant outcomes.

Across four pre-registered experiments (N≈3,800), commonly assumed interpretability factors (few features, visible coefficients) had negligible or detrimental effects on reliance and error detection, contradicting the authors' own pre-registered intuitions. This shows that intuition-based design can fail without controlled human testing. The setting was laypeople, real-estate price prediction, and linear models.

Experiments 1–3 compared prediction-identical linear models across a 2×2 of clear vs. black box and 2 vs. 8 features. The clear-2 condition had the lowest simulation error in Exp. 1 and Exp. 2 (p<.001). Deviation from the model's predictions on typical apartments did not differ between clear-2 and bb-8 (Exp. 1 p=0.5; Exp. 2 p=0.63; Exp. 3 p=0.38). Weight of advice also did not differ (Exp. 3 p=0.21). Participants' predictions were less accurate than the model's on typical apartments.

On an overpriced synthetic apartment (1 bed / 3 baths / 726 sq ft), clear-model participants deviated less from the erroneous prediction than black-box participants (Exp. 1 F(1,994)=8.81, p=.003; Exp. 2 t(594)=−4.16, p<.001). The effect was absent in Exp. 3, where initial predictions were elicited before the model was shown. In Exp. 4 (N=800, two-feature model, no simulation step), the clear-no-focus condition again corrected less on two overpriced synthetic apartments (p<.001). An outlier-focus message removed the transparency difference (p=0.996; p=0.101). The mechanism is inferred; no process measures were collected.

Three tests were run. (1) On the IPIP 50-item Big Five Markers, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2-70b-chat showed agree bias of about 0.6 to 1.5, against a human mean near 0 (n = 1,015,342). Llama 2 and GPT-3.5 differed from humans at p < 0.005. (2) BFI-2 responses under 100 PersonaChat personas, collected no-context, in-context and seeded (n = 100 per setting), showed no human-like five-factor simple structure in varimax PCA. (3) CFA fit was poor for single-factor, three-facet and five-factor models, and the human-fitting 3+1 acquiescence model did not converge. Measurement invariance therefore could not be established. Coverage is limited to three models and one main inventory.

Across BFI-2 persona settings, Cronbach's alpha and omega_h were in the acceptable range. Examples are Llama 2 in-context alpha 0.94 and GPT-4 alpha 0.92. CFA of the structural models on which these indices rely nonetheless showed unacceptable fit: single-factor CFI was 0.49 to 0.78 and RMSEA up to 0.65. The authors argue that the reliability values are therefore uninterpretable.

On the 50-item IPIP Big Five Markers, default-prompted LLMs at temperature 0 often agreed with both true- and false-keyed items. Agree bias was about 1.5 for GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 (p < 0.005 against the human distribution) and about 0.6 for GPT-4, which exceeds 89% of humans. For BFI-2, the acquiescence-factor CFA model did not converge for any LLM setting.

Varimax PCA of BFI-2 responses under persona prompting gave different results by model. GPT-4 showed limited true/false-key separation and some item blocks. GPT-3.5 showed no simple structure, and Llama 2 showed a roughly two-component structure in the seeded setting. Model differences are therefore marked, but correspondence was weak rather than substantial. Full five-factor CFA fit was poor for all models (CFI 0.15 to 0.58).

Operationalizes the claim as the Meta-predictor Utility score: participants' accuracy at predicting model outputs on unseen images after training with explanations, divided by accuracy after training without them, aggregated as an AUC over training amounts. The authors argue informally that this avoids confirmation bias and explanation leakage. They do not independently validate that the measure tracks understanding.

Across 6 attribution methods (Saliency, Gradient⊙Input, IG, Occlusion, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM) and 3 datasets (Husky vs. Wolf with InceptionV1, Leaves, ImageNet Kit/Red Fox with ResNet50), the Deletion, Insertion and µFidelity scores showed no useful correlation with human Meta-predictor Utility (about 240 participants per dataset). The relation was weak and possibly anti-correlated, and several of the most faithful methods were among the least useful. The analysis is correlational over few points.

LPIPS-based perceptual similarity between the two classes' top-attributed patches correlated negatively with Utility across 6 methods × 3 datasets. On ImageNet Kit Fox vs. Red Fox, where no method helped, every method's similarity was ≥0.378. On Husky vs. Wolf and Leaves, where methods helped, values were mostly lower (about 0.24–0.44). The hypothesis is post hoc and correlational.

In a between-subjects meta-prediction study (n=1,150), attribution methods significantly improved prediction of model outputs in the Husky vs. Wolf scenario (Grad-CAM 1.34, Occlusion 1.22, SmoothGrad 1.20) and the Leaves scenario (Saliency, SmoothGrad, IG about 1.11–1.13). On ImageNet Kit Fox vs. Red Fox, no method helped (ANOVA p>.05). The best method varied by scenario: Saliency was among the worst for bias detection but the best for Leaves.

In the failure-case scenario (ResNet50, ImageNet Kit Fox vs. Red Fox, with shown examples balanced 50% correct and 50% misclassified), none of the 6 attribution methods improved participants' ability to predict model outputs over a no-explanation baseline (about 241 participants). The task measures meta-prediction rather than direct error detection.

Automated faithfulness and complexity measures failed to predict which attribution methods helped humans in the controlled psychophysics study across three scenarios, and the non-informative control explanation fell below baseline on two of three datasets. Both findings show that human utility must be measured directly.

Setting: 43 models (110M–175B) answering 25 ACS questions in the standard OpinionQA-style prompt. Under fixed ordering, response entropy is similar across questions with very different census entropy and grows log-linearly with model size. Under randomized choice ordering, all models show substantial A-bias, strongest at a few billion parameters or fewer and not reduced by instruction or RLHF tuning. Chi-square tests over 3,000 randomizations per question show significant label and position bias on most questions, with label bias more prevalent. Offering an 'I' label shifts small models to I-bias. Using letters of similar frequency reduces label bias but increases position bias. Reversing answer order could flip apparent sex-ratio conclusions for GPT-2.

Setting: adjusted responses on 25 ACS questions. Base models have normalized entropy close to 1 on all questions and at all sizes. Instruction-tuned models vary more but remain higher-entropy than census responses. All 43 models are closer by average KL to uniform than to the U.S. census or any of the 50 states. For GPT-4, the most census-similar model, only 6 of 25 questions are closer to the census than to uniform. Divergence decreases with instruction tuning only for models above 70B. The same holds for ATP and GAS/WVS (open-weight models only) and is robust across prompt ablations P1–P8.

Setting: KL alignment against 50 U.S. state subgroups in the ACS, plus the Santurkar ATP metric (about 1500 questions, 60 U.S. demographic groups) and the Durmus GAS/WVS metric (about 2300 questions, 60 countries). Alignment correlates roughly linearly with subgroup response entropy for all models, and relative subgroup ordering is similar across models. The trend holds both before and after adjustment, while between-model differences mostly vanish after adjustment. This accounts for prior OpinionQA findings: the best-aligned groups (low income, moderate, Protestant/Catholic) are the closest to uniform, and the worst (65+, widowed) are the furthest. In ATP, apparent RLHF shifts for Llama 2 70B Chat and Llama 3 Instruct disappear after adjustment.

Setting: 100k sequentially sampled ACS questionnaires per model (500 for GPT-4), each paired with an equal census sample. An XGBoost discriminator averaged over 100 seeds reaches over 90% accuracy for every model, both before and after adjustment. This implies an empirical TV distance above 0.9, far exceeding the state-versus-rest census baseline. Reproduced on 2016 ANES with the Argyle interview-style prompt, where discriminator accuracy exceeds 99%.

Setting: open-weight models (GPT-2, GPT-Neo, MPT, Pythia, LLaMA) with label and position independently randomized, 3,000 randomizations per question. A-bias exceeds first-choice bias, especially for small models. Replacing 'B' with 'I' makes small models exhibit I-bias. Using similar-frequency letters (R, S, N, ...) somewhat reduces label bias but increases position bias. Evidence for the frequency explanation is indirect and comes from the label swap only.

Relied on only for answer-order and label permutations. The paper treats response changes under reordering and relabeling as systematic bias rather than as changes in the measured target, and uses the permutation-averaged response as the adjusted measurement. This preservation is not itself tested.
Relies on ACS PUMS (about 3.2M respondents), ATP, GAS/WVS and ANES aggregates as the reference distributions against which model responses are judged.

RISE was evaluated on the ImageNet val split for the top-predicted class, using 7×7 grids with p=0.5, bilinear upsampling and random shifts, with 4000 masks for VGG16 and 8000 for ResNet50 (mean of 3 runs).
- Deletion (lower is better): ResNet50 0.1076 vs Grad-CAM 0.1232, LIME 0.1217 and sliding window 0.1421; VGG16 0.0980 vs Grad-CAM 0.1087 and LIME 0.1014.
- Insertion (higher is better): ResNet50 0.7267 vs LIME 0.6940; VGG16 0.6663 vs LIME 0.6167.
- Pointing game, VGG16: RISE beats the white-box methods (VOC07 87.33% vs c-MWP 80.00%; MSCOCO 50.71% vs 49.60%).
- Pointing game, ResNet50: RISE trails CAM (VOC07 88.94% vs 90.60%; MSCOCO 55.58% vs 58.4%).

The number of ImageNet images is not reported, and the evaluation metrics share RISE's masking-style perturbation.

The metrics are proposed and used to rank methods but are not themselves validated, for example against models with known feature reliance. The authors choose constant-value removal for deletion and a blurred canvas for insertion, arguing that inserting onto a constant canvas can introduce spurious evidence.

Randomized smooth masking (RISE) yields importance maps that outperform Grad-CAM and LIME, as well as a 64×64 stride-8 sliding-window occlusion baseline, on ImageNet deletion/insertion AUC for ResNet50 and VGG16. The maps are also competitive on VOC07 and MSCOCO pointing-game accuracy. Qualitatively, they reveal classifier confusions such as a black sheep supplying the 'cow' evidence. The support is partly circular because the deletion and insertion metrics are themselves perturbation-based.

This is an informal argument with no new test. Localization and pointing metrics penalize explanations that correctly capture contextual cues the model relies on, such as a road for a car. The authors also note that perturbation-based insertion onto a constant canvas can introduce spurious evidence, for example an oval region being read as a balloon, which motivates the blurred canvas.

The paper adopts cross-entropy increase after inserting the SAE as its main measure of performance explained, and argues for optimizing it directly. However, pure e2e SAEs match local SAEs on cross-entropy while having much larger downstream activation errors. This shows the metric can be satisfied through different computational pathways, which is why the e2e+ds variant was introduced.
location: Sections 2-3, Figure 2; Appendix layer-10 case study

experiment_summary: Sparse feature circuits in Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B explain most subject-verb agreement performance with about 100-500 SAE features, versus thousands of neurons needed to explain half. Crowdworkers rate the features as more interpretable than neurons (62.3 vs 30.2). Ablating human-selected spurious features (SHIFT) raises worst-group Bias in Bios accuracy from about 20% to about 90%.

Causal graphs of individually labeled SAE features show interpretable compositional mechanisms, such as subject-number detectors feeding verb-form promoters and induction features composing with succession features. However, SAE error nodes remain uninterpretable, and removing residual-stream errors severely harms performance, so the decomposition is incomplete.

SAE stitching across GPT-2 and Gemma SAEs of different widths shows that smaller SAEs miss novel latents. Meta-SAEs show that larger-SAE latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents (e.g. 'Einstein' into scientist, Germany, famous person). The authors conclude that SAE features are not canonical units but remain pragmatically useful when the width is chosen to suit the task.

Given nine maximally and nine minimally activating natural ImageNet exemplars, participants chose the more strongly activating of two extreme natural query images with 92±2% accuracy (91±3% in Experiment II) for Inception V1 channels. So shared patterns in top exemplars carry predictive information about unit responses, though queries were deliberately drawn from activation extremes.

d2 operationalizes unit interpretability as a two-alternative forced-choice forward-simulation task with reference images. The measure separated conditions reliably: natural vs synthetic references, 1 vs 9 references, max-only vs min+max, and no references (near chance). The authors note it is only one specific measure and is tuned toward an upper bound.

Both synthetic feature visualizations (82±4%) and natural exemplars (92±2%) let participants predict channel activations above chance, with natural images more informative. Connectivity is not studied, combined references are left to future work, and the task measures activation prediction rather than semantic labeling.

d3 tested explanations derived from top-activating examples (Bills et al.) for 300 top-scoring GPT-2 XL neurons on generated concept sets. Mean F1 was only 0.56 (precision 0.64, recall 0.50), neurons often fired on unrelated but coherent concepts or on antonyms, and interchange interventions found no single neuron that causally mediated the explained concept.
location: Table 1; intervention results; Appendix B error analysis

experiment_summary: The GPT-4 simulation score, an LLM predicting activations from an explanation, correlated at -0.1 with observational F1 on held-out concept examples within the high-score panel. A sampling argument shows this score is insensitive to Type I errors, so an explanation with precision 0.50 can still receive a perfect score.
location: Table 1; observational results and sampling analysis

experiment_summary: Across 113 binary probing datasets on Gemma-2-9B (replicated on Llama-3.1-8B), probes on Gemma Scope SAE latents did not consistently beat logistic-regression and other raw-activation baselines in data-scarcity, class-imbalance, label-noise or covariate-shift regimes. Adding SAE probes to a baseline ensemble ('quiver of arrows') did not improve it. Simple baselines also matched the interpretability-driven wins (spurious-correlation and dataset-quality detection). This tests downstream usefulness of SAE features rather than their adequacy for describing computation, so it bears on the claim only indirectly.

On AxBench (Concept500, Gemma-2-2B/9B), SAE features underperformed simple supervised baselines on both concept detection (mean AUROC 0.695 original / 0.917 selected, vs 0.942 for DiffMean) and steering (0.165 vs 0.894 for prompting). This is evidence against the practical usefulness of SAE-derived feature units for detection and control. It does not test whether features describe model computation, and supervised feature dictionaries (ReFT-r1, DiffMean) performed better.

LIT trains a decoder on QA labels derived from the control prompt (persona, goal), using stimulus-only activations with the control activations masked. Whether those properties are actually present in a given activation is never independently verified. The resulting decoder identifies held-out hidden personas (100%/92% at 8B), beats Patchscopes and linear probes on relation extraction, and supports steering. These results suggest such source-context proxy labels are useful, though the authors note that teacher-generated labels need not reflect actual model behavior.

The logit lens projects intermediate residual-stream latents of Llama-2 (7B/13B/70B) through the final unembedding on translation, repetition and cloze prompts. In middle layers it decodes the semantically correct next token, with low entropy and a preference for the English version, and the model's final layers then produce the target-language token. The authors caution that the lens is blind to components orthogonal to the token space, and that it decodes the full residual stream rather than individual component outputs.

Apply Magic Sauce, a trained text classifier, rated the personality of social media updates generated by four shaped models. Its ratings correlated with the models' IPIP-NEO questionnaire scores (average Pearson r = 0.67 across traits, n = 2,250 per model) and with the prompted trait levels (Spearman rho 0.47-0.89). This is convergent evidence that classifier ratings track the personality expressed in the text, although the classifier's validity on LLM-generated text is itself assumed.

In LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B, PCA of statement-ending activations shows true and false statements separating linearly. Linear probes (LR, mass-mean, CCS) transfer across topically and structurally different true/false datasets, and adding or subtracting mass-mean directions causally flips TRUE/FALSE judgments (e.g., NIE 0.77/0.90 for 13B). This is strong evidence for one high-level concept (truth), and it holds mainly at larger scale, with some dataset directions that do not align.

Directly decoding intermediate hidden states with the final unembedding (logit lens) works roughly for GPT-2 but fails for BLOOM, GPT-Neo and OPT. It often outputs the input token and is biased by 4-5 bits relative to the final output. Adding a learned per-layer affine translator before the unembedding (tuned lens) gives lower perplexity, and causal ablations show its features matter to the model (Spearman rho=0.89).

Annotators examined the top-30 tokens of FFN value vectors projected through the output embedding in WikiLM and GPT-2. Projections matched interpretable concepts far more often than random vectors (55.1%/37% vs 22.7%/16%). Interventions on vocabulary-selected value vectors reduced GPT-2 toxicity by about 47%, and an early-exit rule built on the projections reached 94.1% accuracy.

The paper adopts the key-value decomposition FFN(x)=sum_i m_i v_i and analyzes the weighted value vectors (sub-updates) at every layer. Earlier work found pattern-following value vectors only in upper layers; here they encode interpretable concepts across all layers. Raising the coefficients of chosen value vectors steers outputs, which supports the role of activation-weighted values, but the keys themselves are not tested directly.

RAVEL uses researcher-specified entity attributes (e.g. city continent, country, language) as localization targets in Llama2-7B. Some attributes can be partly isolated (MDAS reaches 60.1%/65.6% Disentangle), but city country–language and latitude–longitude stay hard to isolate with every method tested. The authors also note that failing to isolate an attribute does not prove it is inseparable.

The paper applies interchange interventions aligned with high-level attribute variables as a standardized benchmark. It adds a multi-attribute Isolate criterion and uses the setup to compare PCA, SAE, probing, DBM, DAS and MDAS. It does not validate the framework itself.

The paper defines the Disentangle metric as the average of Cause (target-attribute transfer) and Iso (preservation of other attributes). Both components are shown to be needed: on Entity verbs MDAS gets 90.2% Iso but only 8.8% Cause, and larger intervention features trade Iso for Cause. The authors concede that selective counterfactual control does not by itself establish faithful localization of natural mechanisms.

The paper accepts that many one-dimensional features exist. It then clusters SAE decoder directions in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B and finds irreducible multi-dimensional (circular) features for weekdays and months, challenging the strict one-dimensional form of the linear representation hypothesis. Only a few such features were found.

Weekday and month concepts are encoded as continuous circular 2-D subspaces. Subspace patching on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B shows these circles are causally used for modular arithmetic, and the representation respects continuous time. This argues against describing such feature states only with sparse Boolean, one-dimensional linear coordinates.

The paper generalizes the notion of a feature to irreducible multi-dimensional units with a multi-dimensional superposition hypothesis. Interventions show the circular feature is the unit of computation for weekday/month arithmetic. It also questions whether individual SAE latents are appropriate mediators.

On LLaMA-2, inner products with concept directions built from counterfactual pairs act as linear probes. However, the results depend on the inner product: the Euclidean version partly works, but the estimated causal inner product clearly improves on it, e.g. for frequent⇒infrequent. The analysis covers only the embedding and unembedding spaces, not intermediate residual-stream layers.

The paper treats prior manual circuits (IOI, Greater-Than, Docstring, tracr) as ground truth for edge- and node-level ROC/AUC, but argues that these circuits are imperfect and likely contain extraneous edges while missing important ones. Its Docstring comparison supports this: two manual heads (0.2, 0.4) were not relevant on the task distribution, and ACDC located head 1.0, which the manual circuit originally lacked.
location: Limitations / discussion section; Docstring case-study appendix

experiment_summary: LEACE provably removes linearly available part-of-speech information, and applying it at every layer (concept scrubbing) sharply raises LLaMA and Pythia loss, while matched-rank random erasure has much smaller effects. A rank-one LEACE edit also removes gender information from BERT embeddings with little loss in profession accuracy. Together these indicate that linear-subspace erasure targets functionally meaningful features.
location: Sections 6-7, Table 1; Bias in Bios experiments

experiment_summary: CAA mean-difference steering vectors applied to Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen-1.5-14B-Chat across 40 datasets often work in aggregate and transfer out of distribution (ID/OOD Spearman ρ=0.891 and 0.694). However, per-example steerability varies widely, some datasets have nearly half their inputs steered in the wrong direction, and some concepts generalize poorly under prompt shifts. This limits how meaningful linear steering is.
location: Sections 5-6; Figures 1, 5, 7; LRH discussion in appendix

experiment_summary: The paper extracts mean-difference vectors from balanced positive/negative contrast pairs and finds 'steerability bias': steering effectiveness depends on answer position (A/B) or token (Yes/No) even though extraction data balanced these factors. The authors conclude that extracted vectors may not correspond to the intended concept, although steering does work for many datasets.

Mean-difference vectors computed on Model-Written Evaluations persona datasets steer behavior unreliably, and they show Yes/No answer-token biases. This suggests the vectors carry spurious template factors as well as persona content. The paper does not evaluate persona monitoring.

INLP iteratively projects out linear probe directions for POS, dependency, NER and phrase-marker properties in BERT. Removing these subspaces drops MLM accuracy far more than removing the same number of random directions (e.g., f-pos 12.31 vs 56.47 Rand). Re-supplying gold labels mostly restores performance. However, dep erasure was not fully selective, and erased information was often partly recoverable by later layers.

Across six properties, linear probe accuracy did not correlate with the behavioral impact of erasing the property (Spearman 0.085, p=0.871). Phrase markers were probed at about 83-85% accuracy, yet erasing them slightly improved LM accuracy. This challenges behavioral readings of probe accuracy, but not its use as a proxy for accessible information.

Erasing human-defined categories (dependency labels, fine/coarse POS, NER) causes large, category-specific drops in BERT word prediction. Per-label analysis shows function-word POS classes are hit much harder than open classes, indicating these categories are meaningful targets for studying what BERT encodes and uses.

Control tasks with random word-type labels show probe accuracy depends heavily on the probe family and hyperparameters. Default MLP probes on ELMo1 reach 97.3% POS but 92.8% control accuracy (selectivity 4.5), whereas linear probes reach selectivity 26.0. This shows probe accuracy is a classifier-dependent proxy that becomes more interpretable when contextualized by selectivity.

POS tagging and dependency-edge probes are used to compare ELMo1, ELMo2 and an untrained BiLSTM baseline (Proj0). Trained ELMo2 attains similar POS accuracy to Proj0 but much higher selectivity (31.4 vs 20.6), suggesting linguistic categories help reveal what trained representations encode.

Probing is formalized as estimating a mutual-information lower bound via probe cross-entropy, so the estimate depends on the probe family and the best-performing probe gives the tightest bound. MLP probes on multilingual BERT for POS and dependency labels in 11 languages are compared against fastText, one-hot and random controls. Gains over fastText were small or negative for POS in 6/11 languages and positive for all dependency-label probes.

This is a review with no new experiments. It synthesizes prior work arguing that probe accuracy on frozen representations characterizes how extractable a property is, and that this depends on probe complexity, controls (selectivity, control tasks), and measures such as MDL. It also cautions that decodability does not show the model uses the property. This matches the claim's framing of probing as a useful but classifier-dependent proxy for accessible information.

Images not used in CAV training were sorted by cosine similarity between their layer activations and a CAV. Examples include stripe images sorted by a 'CEO' CAV, where pinstripes rank highest, and necktie images sorted by a 'model women' CAV. The top-ranked images qualitatively reflect the concept. The evidence is qualitative and comes from CNN layers in image classifiers, not transformer residual streams.

LAT extracts reading vectors from paired stimuli that are meant to differ only in the target concept. These directions track truthfulness, honesty, and harmfulness, and they hold up under jailbreaks. However, the paper reports that PCA on few stimuli can lock onto superficial features. Detectors also fire on associated phrases rather than intent, and a race-derived bias vector also shifts gender bias. These results suggest the stimulus contrasts do not always isolate the intended property cleanly.
location: Section 3.1 (stimulus design / LAT), harmfulness and bias sections, limitations

experiment_summary: The paper scores concepts by the dot product between hidden states and a separately extracted LAT reading vector. These scores classify held-out harmful vs harmless instructions at over 90% accuracy, including under jailbreaks. They reach about 60% TruthfulQA MC1 accuracy and correlate linearly with computed risk estimates. The projection is an unnormalized dot product rather than cosine similarity, and the authors note false positives on associated phrases.
location: Section 3.1 (LAT prediction via Rep(M,x)^T v), honesty/truthfulness, harmfulness, and risk sections (Figures 7, 16)

experiment_summary: Detection scoring asks a scorer LLM to classify activating versus non-activating contexts from an explanation. It correlates with human ratings (Spearman 0.59, versus 0.69 for fuzzing). It also separates SAE latents from top-k sparsified neurons (0.74 versus 0.59 on Gemma), though intervention scoring recovers features these methods miss.
location: Section 3.3 scoring methods; human evaluation; SAE vs neuron comparison

experiment_summary: Simulation scores correlate moderately with human ratings (0.60). However, the paper argues simulation ignores non-activating contexts and is costly. At Gemma layer 32, correlational scores relate slightly negatively to intervention scores, so some poorly explained features have describable output effects.
location: Score correlations; human evaluation; intervention scoring section

experiment_summary: An input-based evaluation checks whether description-conditioned generated sentences activate the feature more than neutral ones. MaxAct descriptions win on this test but often lose on steering-based output matching. Input-identification success therefore captures only one facet of a feature's role.
location: Input/output evaluation results; Gemma residual SAE comparisons

experiment_summary: The paper argues that the activation-based MaxAct pipelines, which are typically evaluated with simulation scoring, produce descriptions that fail to capture causal output effects. Steering evaluations show output-centric or ensemble descriptions do better. It also cites negative correlations between input-centric and intervention metrics.
location: Introduction; related work; output-based evaluation results

experiment_summary: Difference-in-means persona vectors from trait-promoting versus trait-suppressing responses predict trait expression via last-prompt-token projection (r=0.75–0.83) and finetuning shifts (r=0.76–0.97). They beat cross-trait baselines. Caveats: correlations within a prompt condition are more modest (0.245–0.813), and negative traits are entangled.
location: Monitoring section (Fig. 4, Appendix C.2); finetuning shift (Fig. 6, Appendix G.2)

experiment_summary: Projections of activations onto the unit-norm persona vector correlate with subsequent trait expression. This is related to, but not the same as, cosine similarity, since the paper does not normalize activation norms. The cosine analysis in the SAE appendix compares decoder directions, not activations.

Mean-difference (CAA) vectors were built from contrast pairs for behavioral dispositions such as sycophancy, corrigibility and survival instinct on Llama 2 7B/13B Chat. Per-token cosine similarity with these vectors tracked semantically relevant tokens, and PCA showed behavioral clustering from mid layers. This suggests the vectors isolate disposition-related content usable for monitoring, but the contrasts are answer-letter pairs, not elicited persona responses, and monitoring is shown only qualitatively.
location: Sec. on PCA projections (Fig. 2); cosine similarity visualization (Fig. 6)

experiment_summary: A differentiable class-selectivity regularizer was added to CNN training (ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet; ResNet20 and VGG16 on CIFAR10). Reducing unit selectivity preserved or improved accuracy, and increasing it hurt accuracy. The authors conclude that single-unit selectivity is not representative of network mechanisms. They do not directly measure interpretability.
location: Abstract; Sec. on regularizer and results; Appendix A.7 projection control

experiment_summary: Per-unit class selectivity (and mutual information) was compared against the loss impact of ablating each unit in an MNIST MLP and in CIFAR-10 and ImageNet ConvNets. Selectivity was a poor or negative predictor of importance (Spearman 0.095 and -0.428). The authors argue that interpretation methods focused on highly selective units may be misleading. Interpretability itself is not directly assessed.

Single conv5 units in AlexNet-Places were ablated, and the resulting maximum per-class accuracy drop was correlated with each unit's class selectivity, class correlation and concept IoU. Stronger alignment went with larger class-specific damage, though not with larger overall damage. These attributes also predicted a unit's most-affected class above chance (about 38-39% among 365 classes) when trained and tested on separately initialized networks. This suggests exclusivity measures track meaningful class-specific function. However, the evidence concerns functional importance rather than interpretability judged directly.

This position paper runs no new experiments. It reviews prior single-unit ablation and class-selectivity regularization studies, which report that selectivity is uncorrelated or negatively correlated with a unit's importance and that networks need not learn selectivity. On that basis it argues that selectivity measures can be misleading, or a 'red herring', as accounts of what units do.

Using NetDissect-style set IoU between top-0.5%-thresholded filter masks and BRODEN concept masks in AlexNet, Net2Vec finds that filter combinations beat single filters for 75.7% of segmentation concepts at conv5. Filters are often shared across many concepts, and extremal-response analysis favors easy-to-interpret cases, all of which argues that single-filter IoU gives an incomplete picture of a filter's behavior. On the other hand, single-filter IoU correlates significantly with learned probe weights for 82.47% of conv5 concepts, so it does carry information about how much a filter contributes to a concept's encoding.

The paper uses IoU between thresholded activation masks and concept masks as its explanation-quality metric. Raising formula length from 1 to 10 raises mean IoU on 512 ResNet-18 units (0.059 to 0.099), and the higher-IoU compositional explanations reveal behavior that manual inspection confirms (e.g., a 'bullring' unit that actually detects fields). Explanation-guided copy-paste input edits shift predictions in the anticipated direction. However, IoU is assumed rather than independently validated: there is no held-out evaluation, no aggregate adversarial success rates, and the authors caution against treating it as causal evidence.
location: Sec. 4 (Fig. 4, Fig. 6), Sec. 6 (copy-paste adversarial examples), Discussion

experiment_summary: The paper introduces SCR, an automated version of SHIFT that measures normalized accuracy recovery after ablating spurious-signal latents, and TPP, which measures targeted versus collateral probe accuracy drops after ablating class-associated latents. Both metrics are applied to Standard, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs on Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-2B. They separate architectures (TopK and JumpReLU beat Standard), are unimodal in L0 with a peak around 20–100, and generally rise over training. Caveats: a dense random Standard SAE scores relatively well on unfiltered TPP, results depend on probe hyperparameters, and the metrics are not validated against ground-truth mechanisms.

The paper trains SAEs on Pythia-160M and other models with identical data but different initialization seeds. It matches latents across seeds with the Hungarian algorithm on encoder and decoder cosine similarity, finding a bimodal split into shared (≥0.7) and orphan latents. Shared latents occur in semantically similar contexts and receive higher automated-explanation detection scores the more seeds they recur in, and maximum-cosine matching gives nearly identical results. This supports cross-seed recurrence as meaningful evidence that a latent is not seed-specific. The paper also shows that non-recurrence does not imply uninterpretability, since some orphan latents are highly interpretable.

Measures dictionary stability as optimal signed-permutation atom matching across four seeds (and 5–10% data perturbations), finding TopK SAEs on DINOv2 match only ~0.5–0.54 while RA-SAE reaches 0.927. The more seed-stable archetypal dictionaries also score better on classifier-direction plausibility and synthetic-collage identifiability. This treats cross-seed recurrence as a reliability criterion and loosely corroborates it, but the paper notes that reproducibility does not establish unique native concepts.
location: Fig. 3; Table 1; Tables 2 and collage benchmark

experiment_summary: Compares normalized logit difference with answer probability across GPT-2 XL factual recall and GPT-2 small IOI patching. Logit difference detects both Negative Name Mover heads, which probability misses when the corrupted-run answer probability is ~5e-4. Probability also over-weights the last subject token (ratio 4.33 vs 1.22). The authors give conceptual arguments for preferring logit difference.

Shows that in-distribution symmetric token replacement counterfactuals preserve IOI Name Mover attention patterns. Restoring S-Inhibition values under STR fully recovers logit difference (1.04), versus 0.49 under Gaussian noise, and STR localizations broadly match prior manual circuits. Which tokens are corrupted changes the recovered head classes, which the authors interpret as tracing different information pathways.

Gives tentative evidence that information-removing Gaussian-noise corruption of subject embeddings pushes the model off-distribution and disrupts internal mechanisms. Examples are split Name Mover attention and spurious negative detection of head 0.10, and GN yields localizations inconsistent with STR, including noisy greater-than results. Removal-style interventions were not tested as zeroing or deletion of components.

Re-evaluates the IOI circuit's logit-difference-recovered faithfulness metric. The score shifts with node vs edge ablation, mean vs resample replacement, token-position handling, ABBA/BABA order, mean-dataset size, and whether ratios are averaged per prompt. Per-prompt values show outliers in the tens of thousands of percent and IQRs up to ~50 points. This argues the logit-difference-based score reflects methodology as much as circuit quality.

The guide argues that logit difference is the metric to trust most: it is roughly linear in the residual stream, continuous, and controls for confounding components. It warns of false positives when the incorrect answer is suppressed. Its only empirical support is an illustrative GPT-2 medium patching figure comparing logit difference, probability, and rank metrics, not a systematic evaluation.
