The guide argues conceptually, with hypothetical AND/OR and 'Nobel Peace' circuits, that noising and denoising between clean and counterfactual prompts isolate components carrying the clean–corrupt difference. It also cautions about backup heads, prompt-distribution dependence, and cross-section effects. It contains no systematic empirical test.
location: Patching modes; Nobel Peace example; backup heads discussion

experiment_summary: On GPT-J (652 CounterFact facts) and GPT2-XL, edits with ROME, MEMIT, and fine-tuning succeed across many layers, with high rewrite scores and neighborhood/paraphrase metrics. This success is nearly unrelated to Causal Tracing or zeroing localization: tracing adds at most about 0.03 R² beyond edit-layer identity. The authors conclude that successful edits do not validate where information is localized.

MDL probing of ELMo layers on Penn Treebank POS and seven edge-probing linguistic tasks finds that linguistic labels compress far better than random control-task labels and better from trained than randomized representations. This indicates the representations encode structure aligned with human-defined categories.
location: Sec. 3 Table 2, Fig. 2; Sec. 4 edge probing

experiment_summary: Trains edge probes on frozen BERT-base/large for eight human-defined linguistic tasks (POS, constituents, dependencies, entities, SRL, coreference, proto-roles, relations). Scalar-mixing weights and cumulative-probe gains localize these categories in an interpretable layer order that follows the classical pipeline. The evidence is probe accessibility rather than causal use.
location: Sections 2-4; scalar mixing and cumulative scoring figures

experiment_summary: Introduces Matryoshka SAEs, which sum reconstruction losses over nested latent prefixes of one shared dictionary (e.g., prefixes 2,048 to 65,536 on Gemma-2-2B layer 12). Training succeeds on toy data, TinyStories and Gemma, with absorption falling from 0.49 to 0.05 at L0=40 and only slightly lower variance explained (70% vs 72%).

Following Chanin et al., trains logistic-regression first-letter probes on raw Gemma activations as ground-truth directions, then measures when matched SAE latents fail to fire (absorption) or when extra latents are needed (splitting). The metric cleanly separates Matryoshka from BatchTopK (absorption 0.05 vs 0.49; about 1 vs 3 latents per letter), consistent with toy-model findings. The paper applies the method but does not independently validate it.
location: Feature absorption and splitting evaluation section

experiment_summary: Labels a response emergently misaligned when GPT-4o judges score it alignment<30 and coherence>50 on the eight first-plot questions (50 samples each). The emergence point is shown to be robust to the choice of thresholds. No resampling of invalid responses is described, and the measure targets general misalignment rather than malice specifically.

Uses GPT-4o alignment judgments with CODE/REFUSAL options and a coherence filter as the operational emergent-misalignment metric across many models, datasets and training protocols. It yields consistent trends, and the behavioural phase-transition onset is robust to alignment and coherence thresholds. The authors note the reliance on GPT-4o judges and that the metric ignores semantic diversity.
location: Section 2; Appendix C; Appendix F; Limitations

experiment_summary: Introduces the LM evaluation that compares the probability of the grammatical verb form with its number-mismatched form on Wikipedia agreement dependencies. Applied to its own LSTM LM and the Google LM, the measure tracks difficulty: error rises with attractor count, reaching 28.5% (Google LM) and 32.6% (own LM) with one attractor and worse than chance with many. The paper uses the measure rather than validating it independently.
location: Language modeling objective; Google LM comparison

experiment_summary: On SyntaxGym and BLiMP minimal pairs (Exp 3a/3b), direct comparison of string probabilities nearly always matches or beats metalinguistic prompting, and prompt-based judgments correlate weakly with it (r about 0.2). This favors probability comparisons as the measure of grammatical knowledge, but it tests minimal pairs in general rather than verb-inflection agreement specifically.

Compares representations through similarity matrices of shared inputs (linear and RBF CKA) and matches corresponding layers across 10 independently initialized CIFAR-10 CNNs with 99.3% accuracy, recovering coherent cross-architecture and cross-dataset correspondences. Subspace-alignment measures do much worse on the same test (mean CCA 1.4%, SVCCA 9.9–15.1%, PWCCA 11.1%), and the paper proves that any statistic invariant to invertible linear transformations fails when width exceeds the number of examples. Only part of the claim is supported: the similarity-kernel/dissimilarity-matrix family works here, but subspace alignment does not.
location: Sec. 6.1 (Table 2), Theorem in Sec. 2, Figs. 5 and 7, App. F.1/F.5

experiment_summary: Logistic-regression first-letter probes trained on Gemma-2-2B residual activations serve three roles. They are the baseline that no Gemma Scope SAE matches, they select candidate latents by encoder cosine similarity, and they define the absorption metric: false negatives the probe classifies correctly, plus probe alignment (cosine > 0.025) of the dominant ablation-effect latent. This yields interpretable detections such as latent 1085 absorbing 'starts with S'.

Resample ablations of every attention and MLP layer in Chinchilla 7B on 1,209 Counterfact prompts were compared with unembedding-based direct effects. Ablation effects largely disagree with direct contributions because downstream attention layers and erasure MLPs compensate, restoring about 70% of the effect in middle layers. Ablation therefore understates intact-model reliance, though restoration is incomplete, so some signal remains.

The paper formalizes total, direct, and indirect effects for transformers as structural causal models, holding the RMSNorm factor fixed so direct effects are additive. It applies them to decompose ablation outcomes into direct contributions and compensatory downstream effects, successfully localizing the Hydra effect and erasure-MLP behavior.

Uses a rubric-based GPT-4o grader that is deliberately stricter than the original emergent-misalignment grader and manually checks high-scoring responses for each model called misaligned. It also reports that many responses flagged as misaligned in early experiments were better classed as off-topic, garbled, refusal or satirical/absurd, so these categories are resampled.
location: Section on evaluation; Appendix H; Table 5

experiment_summary: Its core metric is thresholded GPT-4o judgments on 44 prompts, with off-topic, garbled, refusal and satirical responses resampled. Manual verification confirms most high-scoring responses are true positives. However, reward-hacking models score 0% on this metric while showing increased deception and oversight sabotage on other evaluations, so the measure is not exhaustive.
location: Evaluation section; Appendix H; reward-hacking results (Figure 22)

experiment_summary: It argues the original alignment-judge approach was too lenient for its definition of malicious misalignment. Early experiments found that many flagged responses were satirical/absurd, off-topic or garbled rather than malicious, which motivated a stricter rubric and resampling of these categories.

SAE model diffing finds a toxic-persona latent (#10) whose average activation increase on evaluation prompts, even on a single prompt, separates the examined aligned and misaligned fine-tunes. The latent rises at 5% incorrect data, before sampled misalignment appears, and also rises in reward-hacking GPT-4o despite 0% sampled misalignment. Steering along the latent causally induces and suppresses misalignment.
location: Section 3 and Section 4; Figure 9; Figure 22; Figure 32

experiment_summary: Uses GPT-4o judges scoring alignment and coherence (0-100, probability-weighted). The authors report that manual inspection broadly agrees with the judges, though they note failure cases, and that varying thresholds (alignment ≤1, coherence 90) leaves the pattern of results largely unchanged. Topical-content ratings are not separately validated.

In toy ReLU models with ground-truth sparse features, features are often stored in superposition and are not basis-aligned, so one-to-one feature-neuron correspondence fails. At the same time, the paper posits that the network noisily simulates a larger sparse model with one unit per feature, and it motivates recovering that overcomplete feature set via dictionary learning.
location: Superposition Hypothesis; Hierarchy of Feature Properties

experiment_summary: Uses mutual k-NN kernel alignment to compare 78 vision models and LLM-vs-vision models on paired WIT image-caption data. Alignment tracks competence (VTAB tasks solved, 1−bits-per-byte) and downstream performance (HellaSwag, GSM8K), and it rises with denser captions, which suggests the metric captures meaningful shared structure. A metric comparison (CKA, SVCCA, CKNNA, kNN variants) finds that CKA shows weak trends and that the results depend on the metric and on k. Absolute alignment is low (max about 0.16), so the support is qualified.

Introduces natural direct effects (edit the input but hold mediator neurons or attention weights at their original values) and natural indirect effects (transplant mediator values from the edited input) in GPT-2 variants and other Transformers on gender-bias datasets. Applying these quantifies how much of the input-edit effect flows through specific heads or neurons versus the rest of the model. It finds that total effect is approximately direct plus indirect, and Appendix E proves exact equality under a no-interaction condition.

Causal Tracing applies indirect-effect mediation to factual recall in GPT-2 XL and larger models. It corrupts subject embeddings with noise and restores individual clean hidden states, MLP outputs or attention outputs to measure each one's average indirect effect. A severed-MLP modified graph probes path-specific effects. The authors report that direct effects were noisy and uninformative, so the framework is only partially used.
location: Sec. 2, Figs. 1-3; footnote on direct effect

experiment_summary: Applies the 2-AFC paradigm to nine vision models. Crowd workers pick the more strongly activating of two query images, given nine max- and nine min-activating reference images. Scores are about 80% versus 50% chance, they separate natural from synthetic explanations, and they drop as query difficulty rises. The paper also releases 130k human responses for building automated versions of the measure.

Tests only two of the claim's sources, feature visualizations and natural exemplars, and measures activation prediction rather than semantic labeling. Natural exemplars help (about 80% on easy trials). Synthetic visualizations are worse in every CNN comparison and fall near chance at the 99th-percentile difficulty. Connectivity and joint use are not tested.

Builds circuits in Inception-V1 and ResNet-50 that make feature visualizations show arbitrary patterns while leaving ImageNet behavior essentially unchanged. Shows that, in unmanipulated Inception-V1, visualizations are processed like different-class images through about the first two thirds of layers. Proves that extremal inputs cannot reliably characterize general functions. Together these undercut feature visualizations as a source of semantic labels; natural examples and connectivity are not tested.
location: Sections on manipulation, sanity check, theory

experiment_summary: Operationalizes interpretability as the pre-to-post gain in users' forward and counterfactual simulation accuracy, using controls against confounds: separate explained and test items, an unexplained baseline, correctness-balanced data, and forced predictions. The measure detects gains for LIME on tabular data (+11.25 points) and for Prototype on counterfactual tests (+9.53 points). Users' subjective ratings did not predict which explanations helped, which supports a behavioral measure over ratings.

HIVE operationalizes explanation utility through behavioral tasks with about 950 AMT participants: distinction (pick the correct prediction among four) and output prediction. These measures expose shortcomings that self-reports and automatic metrics miss. Self-rated understanding dropped after participants saw their own performance (3.8 to 3.5), and GradCAM localization metrics had near-zero correlation with human choices. Performance is compared against chance rather than a no-explanation baseline, so improvement over unaided reasoning is not directly measured.

Using LDA on Gemma-2B unembeddings, the authors estimate vector representations for about 950 binary WordNet features (is_w indicators). Held-out member words project near 1 and random words near 0, and shuffled controls lose this separation. This supports binary features having linear encodings, but sparsity and superposed computation are not tested.

SAEs trained on Pythia-70M/410M residual streams reconstruct activations as sparse linear combinations of an overcomplete dictionary, and the learned features are interpretable and causally relevant. This supports sparse linear feature encodings. The coefficients are continuous rather than Boolean, and reconstruction is imperfect (layer-2 perplexity rises from 25 to 40).

SAE features score as more interpretable than neurons, PCA and ICA directions on autointerpretability. Patching a small number of them accounts for IOI counterfactual behavior. Ablation-based causal trees trace how earlier-layer features drive later ones (e.g., a closing-parenthesis feature), consistent with the network operating on individually understandable features. Validation relies on automated scores, and there is no ground truth for the features.

The paper adopts the FFN key-value memory view for BERT-base on factual cloze prompts. It attributes predictions to intermediate FFN neurons (keys) and edits the corresponding second-layer value slots by subtracting or adding word embeddings. These value-slot edits update facts (34.4% success vs 0% for random neurons) and erase relations. That is consistent with outputs being activation-weighted sums of value vectors, but it does not directly test key-input matching.

The paper takes a difference in mean activations between harmful and harmless instructions, rather than between behavior-labeled answer choices. Across 13 chat models, this single direction is sufficient to induce refusal when added and to remove refusal when ablated. That shows difference-in-means steering vectors working in long-form generation. The authors note that the direction may encode harm rather than refusal, so it is unclear whether it isolates the intended behavioral variable.

Trains k-sparse logistic probes (k from 256 down to 1) on post-GeLU MLP neurons of seven Pythia models across over 100 binary features. Uses held-out F1, precision and recall to localize feature-selective neurons, then corroborates selected neurons with activation inspection and ablations (e.g., ablating a French context neuron raises French-sequence loss). The authors caution that probe accuracy alone establishes neither causal use nor monosemanticity.
location: Sparse probing method; context-neuron case studies (Fig. 3); limitations

experiment_summary: Measures synthetic source recovery as MCC after linear-sum-assignment matching of latents to sources. MCC separates iVAE (above 95%) from VAE, β-VAE and β-TC-VAE baselines, consistent with the identifiability theory, and tracks the ELBO across hyperparameter sweeps. However, MCC is adopted as a standard ICA metric rather than validated itself, and the paper notes it does not establish full joint-density recovery.

The authors align variables of a deterministic, tree-structured natural logic causal model with BERT representations on MQNLI and verify the alignments with interchange interventions. The best alignment (object noun-phrase relation at layer 4) holds only on a clique of 383 of 1,000 selected correctly classified examples. So the deterministic model describes part of the computation, while the paper presupposes the framework's adequacy rather than testing it.

The authors analyze Gemma-2-2b SAE features. Individual features and their groupings are interpretable: co-occurrence lobes specialize in code/math, dialogue, or scientific text. However, features also sit in structured relations, such as parallelogram/trapezoid 'crystals', spatially clustered co-occurring lobes, and a power-law global covariance, which suggests they are not fully independent units. The paper does not directly test whether features are independently understandable or how the network operates on them.
location: Sections on crystals and lobes; Figs. 1-5

experiment_summary: d2 slides a gray square over test images. Correct-class probability drops sharply when the object (e.g., the dog's face) is occluded. The strongest layer-5 feature map's summed activity drops when the region shown in its visualization is covered. Corresponding facial-part occlusions also give more consistent layer-5 feature changes than random-region occlusions. All of this rests on very few examples (three occlusion images, five dog images).

d3 learns masks that blur, replace with a constant, or add noise to image regions to suppress GoogLeNet's class score. The resulting smallest bounding boxes strongly suppress the score, and on COCO pointing, plain occlusion reaches 44.50% precision, above d3's own method. d3 also cautions that optimized perturbations can co-adapt to network artifacts and that deletion semantics depend on the perturbation operator. It adds TV regularization and low-resolution masks to counter this.

Across 43 models on 25 ACS questions, varying answer order and labels shifted responses in ways unrelated to question content. Models showed A-bias and label bias regardless of the question, and averaging over all permutations gave near-uniform answers. This treats order and label differences as artifacts, but the paper never directly tests whether alternative formats keep the same measurement target; P1–P8 prompt ablations are only reported as leaving the conclusions unchanged.
location: Sections on A-bias and adjustment (Fig. 3, Fig. 4); Appendix B, D

experiment_summary: BFI responses were collected under 2,500 settings: paraphrases (manually checked for meaning), Google-translated versions in 10 languages, 5 label formats and 2 choice orders. Differences were read as reliability or instability. However, outliers clustered in numeric-label, descending-order, Arabic/Chinese settings were attributed to comprehension failure. The authors also concede that translations and rewording may change the scale's validity, which undercuts treating such differences as pure instability.

A difference-in-means direction from answer-token activations on aligned vs. misaligned responses of a 9-adapter rank-1 LoRA emergently misaligned Qwen2.5-14B steers the base chat model to up to 50% coherent misaligned responses. Ablating the direction cuts emergent misalignment to roughly 0-1% in the source model, and by 90% and 78% in a rank-32 medical fine-tune and an extreme-sports fine-tune. Log-probability contrasts are not tested, and evaluation uses only eight questions.

Sentiment directions are fit to binary positive/negative labels on templated movie reviews. They transfer to held-out tokens, to OpenWebText tokens with GPT-4 polarity labels (78-89% accuracy), and to binarized SST, where directional patching flips 53.5% of predictions and ablation removes 76% of above-chance zero-shot accuracy. The binary operationalization is used rather than tested against alternatives.
location: Sections 2.2-3, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 6; SST summarization experiments

experiment_summary: A single mLSTM unit was found by fitting logistic regression to binary sentiment labels. Thresholding that unit alone reaches 92.30% on binary IMDB, versus 92.88% with all 4,096 units, and clamping it shifts generated review polarity. Fine-grained SST lags the binary results and generation control is only assessed qualitatively.
location: Section on sentiment unit, Figure 3, Table 2, Table 5

experiment_summary: Garçon describes an early design for this approach. Persistent servers host multi-node models and run user-supplied probe functions for reading, ablating, and taking gradients. The authors report qualitatively that the tool is used for essentially all of Anthropic's interpretability work and reduces 'time to first plot'. No latency or performance measurements are given.

Gives an explicit hand construction of the mechanism under sinusoidal positional embeddings. A previous-token head (W_Q is a 2D-rotated copy of the positional basis) copies the top content principal components into a subspace v. A second head uses v in W_K and the current token's content in W_Q. This shows the mechanism is expressible but does not test whether trained models form it.

Explicit weight construction, not an empirical test or formal proof. Positional cos/sin pairs satisfy p(n−1) = R_{−α} p(n), so a W_Q equal to a block-rotated positional projection makes a head attend to an adjacent position. Steps in the construction:
- A head with content-matching QK and a −β-weighted self-position term attends to prior same-content tokens.
- That head's OV circuit copies 8 positional dimensions into a subspace v.
- A later head rotates v forward by α and matches it against positional keys.
The construction is not numerically verified and is not compared against trained models.

Hand construction in a 16-dimensional residual stream with two 4-dimensional previous-token heads. Head 1 copies dimensions 0–3 to 8–11. Head 2 copies three untouched dimensions plus one dimension written by head 1. Expanding W_net^2·W_net^1 gives a two-token-back copy path, and W_net^2·Id + Id·W_net^1 gives the one-token paths. Together the heads devote 7/8 of their capacity to previous-token copying and 1/8 to the virtual head. This is an illustrative construction with no empirical test.

The authors retrained the one-layer toy model from 'Superposition, Memorization, and Double Descent' with a variety of learning rates. The memorizing solution achieved the lowest train loss up to about 500k samples. Beyond that, the generalizing solution was lower, with a discontinuity in the derivative of the minimum train loss at the crossover. The previously reported unexplained regime (about 1k–10k samples) was attributed to low-dimensional optimization difficulty. These are preliminary results reported without quantitative figures in the text.

In the same toy model, better-optimized memorizing solutions changed with dataset size. They memorized individual, mutually near-orthogonal data points below about 1k samples. They memorized clusters of correlated data points sharing features between about 1k and 500k samples, with fine 'triangle' structure. This extends datapoint memorization to cluster-level memorization.

The authors analyzed a simplified two-head model trained on OV-incoherent skip-trigrams ([0]...[1]->[4], [0]...[2]->[5], ...). Head 0 self-attends and promotes the completion. Head 1 attends to [0] when it is present and does nothing; otherwise it self-attends and outputs the negative of head 0's logits, yielding a uniform output. Trained models divide the trigrams between heads rather than cleanly separating these roles. The analysis is qualitative and preliminary.

location: An Epistemic Foundation; Larger Scale Structure
Feature Families & Equivariance; Feature Organization by Weight Structure
How Does Mechanistic Interpretability Fit Into Safety?

experiment_summary: Synthetic sparse vectors (n_sparse dimensions, n_active nonzeros) are randomly projected to 32 dimensions. Dictionary learning (MOD with a LASSO inner loop) is run while sweeping the L1 coefficient and the dictionary size. Total information is the summed surprisal of the S and D entries under 100-bin histograms. In plots of MSE against total information, solutions "bounce" at the true dictionary size and occupy the Pareto frontier there, which is also where MMCS is best. No real-model data and no quantitative tables are reported.

One-layer toy transformers with trivial embeddings and unembeddings were trained on uniform token sequences that over-represent selected OV-incoherent skip-trigrams. When the number of incompatible trigrams exceeded the number of heads, each trigram was encoded across at least two heads, as shown in wiring diagrams. The evidence is toy-only and qualitative, so it does not test trained language models.

ReLU-output toy model in which many features lie at equal angular spacing on a circle and activate as m·cos((φ−θ)/ℓ) within a window set by the length scale ℓ. Varying ℓ produced embeddings that discretize the manifold into units. The results are qualitative and extremely preliminary, and the authors warn that the finest-scale discretization may be an optimization failure.

location: Dictionary Learning Worries; Attacking Superposition with Dictionary Learning
Research By Other Groups: Linear Representations
Research By Other Groups: Grokking; Neuroscience Parallels

experiment_summary:
Ridge probes were trained on every layer of Llama-2-7B/13B/70B and Pythia-160M–6.9B for six datasets (world, USA and NYC places; historical figures' death years; art/entertainment release dates; NYT headline dates).
- Representation quality rises through the first half of the layers, then plateaus, and is better in larger models. For Llama-2-70B at 60% depth, test R² is 0.911 (World), 0.864 (USA), 0.359 (NYC), 0.835 (Historical), 0.885 (Entertainment) and 0.746 (Headlines).
- Explicit question prompts and disambiguation prompts barely change performance. Random-token prefixes and capitalization degrade it.
- Probes generalize across held-out entity types (e.g., 70B World proximity error 0.113 nominal vs 0.147 held out), with entertainment the main exception.
- Block hold-out of countries, states or decades keeps relative position but not absolute position.
- Spearman correlation rises quickly with a handful of top principal components.
- A hierarchy of binary membership features is not fully ruled out.

In Llama-2 models, the authors selected neurons whose input or output weights have high cosine similarity to probe directions. Projections onto these neurons correlate with true coordinates across entity types (Spearman correlations by type).
- In Llama-2-7B, pinning time neuron L19.3610 (correlation 0.77 with release date) changes the predicted decade for prompts of the form '<media> by <creator> was written in 19'. Nine random neurons in the same layer were used as a comparison.
- Zero-ablating space neurons L20.7573 and L20.7423, and time neurons L18.9387 and L19.3610, most increases loss on climate-classification, 'Europe', and album or song tokens in Wikipedia text.
- The evidence is qualitative and covers only a few neurons.

Extends linear-representation evidence to continuous features (latitude/longitude, years). At 60% depth, one-hidden-layer MLP probes with 256 units give only minimal R² gains over ridge probes across all six datasets on Llama-2-7B/13B/70B (e.g., 70B World 0.911 linear vs 0.926 MLP). This shows linear decodability; use by the model is only weakly supported, via the neuron experiments.

In natural-language-pretrained Llama-2 models, real-world spatial and temporal coordinates of entities are linearly decodable. The representations generalize to relative positions of held-out countries or states, and some neurons align with them. The authors frame these as ingredients of a world model, not a dynamic causal world model, so the support is indirect.

Evaluated by BERTScore against held-out human annotations. On held-out AlexNet/ResNet152 ImageNet/Places networks MILAN scores .31-.38, versus NetDissect .21-.25, Compositional Explanations .01-.03 and p(d|E)-only captioning .27-.34. In generalization splits MILAN scores .27-.52, including CNN-to-ViT at .34; classifier-to-GAN transfer (.34) exceeds the reverse (.27). Human inter-annotator agreement is .17-.27. The authors present this as a sanity check. Failure cases include wrong concepts, vague labels and describing context.

All ResNet18-ImageNet neurons were labeled by MILAN and ranked by description properties: noun, verb, preposition and adjective counts, length, parse depth, and maximum word-vector distance. Neurons were ablated 2% at a time and ImageNet validation accuracy measured, compared with 5 random orderings. The adjective and preposition orderings degraded accuracy fastest; the max-word-difference ordering degraded it less than random. Relation-selective neurons were most prevalent in middle layers.

A ResNet18 neuron flagged by MILAN for a description mixing animals and vehicles connects strongly to amphibian, hermit crab and jeep outputs. Pasting a vehicle such as a half-track into three ImageNet validation images caused predictions such as amphibian. Qualitative only, with a handful of examples.

MILAN labeled a subset of convolutional units in 12 blurred-ImageNet models and their unblurred torchvision counterparts. Neurons whose descriptions mentioned face, head, nose, eyes or mouth were manually inspected on unblurred exemplars. Counts: 213 face-selective neurons in unblurred models versus 142 in blurred models. Some blurred-model neurons qualitatively preferred female or Asian faces.
models_studied: ["12 ImageNet classifier architectures (blurred vs unblurred, torchvision)"]

experiment_summary: ResNet18 was trained on 10 ImageNet classes, with correct text labels on half the training images. On a test set with random text labels it reaches 58.8%, versus 69.9% on clean data. MILAN flagged 300 of 1024 units as text-related. Ablating 13 of them, ordered by single-ablation validation importance, raised adversarial accuracy by 4.9 points; choosing the count by validation accuracy alone (8 neurons) gave 3.1 points. Ablating all neurons in the same order gave less than 1 point. Single model, single synthetic spurious feature.

In MILANNOTATIONS human descriptions, layers closest to the image (early CNN layers, late BigGAN layers) receive more adjectives, and farther layers receive more nouns. For example, AlexNet-ImageNet adjective share falls from 24.3% at conv1 to 10.2% at conv5 while noun share rises from 37.5% to 46.0%. The evidence is indirect, based on word statistics rather than tests of the units themselves.

Setting: GPT-2 small layer-8 residual stream, OpenWebText, about 820M tokens. (1) Scaling curves at k=32 for Switch SAEs with 8 and 64 experts: Switch SAEs often match TopK MSE with about one order of magnitude fewer FLOPs. (2) FLOP-matched Switch SAEs (2, 4 and 8 experts, each with 24,576 latents) Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated and ReLU SAEs with 24,576 latents on MSE and fraction of CE loss recovered, across L0 from 8 to 128. (3) Width-matched Switch SAEs (16–128 experts) use up to 128× fewer FLOPs per activation. They are slightly worse than TopK but mostly better than ReLU and Gated SAEs. Mainly a single model and site; wall-clock speedups are not measured.

Width-matched GPT-2 small layer-8 Switch SAEs. The fraction of decoder vectors whose nearest-neighbor cosine exceeds 0.9 jumps from 0% in TopK SAEs to 5–10%, and mean nearest-neighbor cosine also rises. Both effects grow with expert count and shrink at higher L0. t-SNE shows tight cross-expert duplicate groups. At fixed width, Switch SAEs need more parameters than TopK to match MSE, though the gap narrows with scale. In the appendix (k=64, 8 experts), the fixed-width penalty is small on residual streams but larger on attention and MLP outputs; for example, GPT-2 layer-2 MLP FLR is 0.701 versus 0.888. The causal link between duplication and the parameter-efficiency gap is hypothesized, not isolated.

EleutherAI detection-based autointerp was run on 1,000 random features per SAE (GPT-2 small layer 8), scored by activation decile and on non-activating contexts. FLOP-matched Switch SAE features score similarly to TopK features. Width-matched Switch SAE features show a higher true-positive rate but a lower true-negative rate; the authors attribute this to duplicated frequent features.
Extends the conditional-computation idea from language models to SAE dictionary learning. The SAE evidence is attached to switch-routed-saes-improve-reconstruction-per-training-compute.

On GPT-2 small layer 8, FLOP-matched Switch SAEs with more experts, and hence more total latents (2×, 4× and 8× 24,576), achieve progressively better MSE and FLR at matched L0. Scaling curves at k=32 also show MSE decreasing with parameter count for both TopK and Switch SAEs.

Smooth MSE scaling curves were obtained against training FLOPs and parameters for dense TopK and Switch SAEs (8 and 64 experts) at k=32 on GPT-2 small layer 8. Functional forms and loss floors are not reported in the text.

Setting: RAVEL country-vs-continent disentanglement on 40 single-token cities in GPT-2 small, with residual stream above the city token. Masks were learned by differentiable binary masking over each feature space and scored by interchange interventions (test split of 3,200 interventions). Neurons scored about 71–73. The OpenAI top-k SAE only matched neurons (about 70–73). Bloom and both Apollo SAEs fell below neurons at all available layers (e.g. layer 1: 43–59; layer 5: 40–64). No SAE approached the DAS skyline (about 94–96). Evidence is limited to one model, one attribute pair and four SAEs.

On RAVEL country/continent for 40 GPT-2 small cities, DAS with jointly learned masks reached disentangle scores of about 94–96 through layer 7. Neuron masks reached about 71–73 (layer 1: 94/96 vs 71/72; layer 5: 94/96 vs 73/72). DAS performance drops after layer 7 as city information leaves the city token.

DAS-learned orthogonal subspaces in GPT-2 small layers 0–7 support interchange interventions that change a city's country without changing its continent (and vice versa) at about 95% accuracy. This indicates that separable linear subspaces mediate the two attributes. The evidence covers a single attribute pair and 40 cities.

Setting: GPT-2 small city-knowledge accuracy (5-shot country and continent prompts on 40 cities) with SAE reconstructions spliced into the residual stream above the city token. At layer 1: OpenAI top-k 95%, Bloom 47–56%, Apollo e2e 35–67%, Apollo e2e+ds 0–1%. At layer 5: OpenAI 88–90%, Bloom 77–86%, Apollo e2e+ds 61–83%. The Apollo SAEs had the highest MSE (about 2,100–2,600) yet degraded knowledge comparably to lower-MSE SAEs at layer 5. Bloom SAE MSE explodes in late layers.

All four open GPT-2 small SAEs are sparse (about 95–98% inactive features), and some have strong sparsity–reconstruction tradeoffs. Despite this, none yields a feature space where country and continent knowledge disentangle better than neurons. The authors note that the top-k SAE, which leads on sparsity–reconstruction, is also the best here, so the ordering partly tracks reconstruction quality.

Sweep over number of features and training steps for SAEs on the residual stream after layer 3 of a 4-layer transformer, with loss MSE+5·L1. The scaling is also qualitatively similar for other MSE/L1 or MSE/L0 combinations. Compute-optimal loss follows an approximate power law in FLOPs. The optimal number of features grows faster than the optimal number of steps (steps ∝ features^0.5–1). Higher L1 weight, and L0-based losses, shift the optimum toward more training steps. Other hyperparameters were not jointly optimised, and only one model and layer were studied.

SAE on the residual stream after layer 3 of a 4-layer transformer, plus MLP-layer SAEs. Each feature was scaled by 0 or 2 on samples where it was active, and the loss increase was measured. Ablation raised loss significantly more than either random perturbation of model activations or random perturbation of feature activations, with magnitude matched. Ablation had a larger effect than doubling. Dampening all features proportionally matched single-feature ablation. Dampening raw model activations had a smaller effect, which nearly vanished in later layers. The gap was larger for residual-stream features than for MLP features. Results are averaged over features, with SEM error bars.

Discusses Gurnee's GPT-2 small finding (a cited result, not this document's evidence). In this document's own 4-layer transformer experiment, magnitude-matched perturbations along the negative SAE error direction −(x−SAE(x)) increased loss substantially more than random perturbations, though less than feature ablations. The authors interpret this as consistent with errors lying mainly along feature directions.

The authors report that the revised recipe enables dictionaries with millions of features, with fewer than 1% dead features and loss decreasing consistently with m. This holds across transformer sizes and for both MLP and residual SAEs. By contrast, the Towards Monosemanticity setup often had higher loss, dead features or near-duplicate features at large m. The individual changes were not ablated. Example results with 131k features and 200k steps: 1L MLP at λ=5 gives L0 38.7, normalized MSE 0.066 and 96.4% of cross-entropy loss recovered; 4L residual layer 2 at λ=5 gives L0 33.2 and 90.4% recovered.
Essay argues by analogy to caloric theory that superposition may be wrong yet still yield durable safety and scientific insights; no new test.

Commentary on Marks et al. The authors suggest that the large node counts needed for faithfulness may mean SAEs are not the sparsest representation of computation, giving many redundant 'she/her' features as an example. No new experiments.
Commentary on Lee et al. (GPT-2 Medium DPO), connecting the finding to jailbreaks: fine-tuning reduces the incidence of a behavior without removing its mechanism. No new experiments.

Commentary on Feng & Steinhardt. Mentions an unpublished Anthropic observation, with no data given, of neurons firing on mentions of the first named entity regardless of name, as consistent with abstract entity trackers.

Toy model only. Five fixed sparse attention heads (sparse patterns and sparse OV) are compressed into two learned heads via a shared mixing matrix (MSE after ReLU). The mixing matrix shows geometry reminiscent of Toy Models of Superposition. Superposition arose only with sparse OV circuits and not with dense ones. No real language models were tested.

Dictionary learning was applied to fully connected ReLU MNIST models (1–3 layers, 16–64 neurons). It yielded interpretable digit-template features with matching logit effects. However, there was no reconstruction-vs-sparsity elbow, and low error required feature counts comparable to the dataset size or many active features. This left it unclear whether the features are 'true features' or data clusters.

In MNIST MLP dictionary learning, interpretable features were found, but reconstruction/sparsity curves showed no elbow indicating a canonical feature set. The strongest evidence of reality was logit-weight agreement rather than reconstruction metrics.

SAEs were trained on the MLP activations of an 8-layer transformer. Qualitatively labeled features were found, with a non-random selection biased toward safety relevance. Final-layer features were single-token and next-token predictive. Layers 4–6 appeared most abstract (e.g., negative-valence emotion, violence). The authors rate label confidence as moderate.

Ghost Grads produced SAEs with very few (often zero) dead neurons. Performance was as good as or better than neuron resampling at the same alive count, at about 2x compute. The dead fraction under resampling grows with SAE size, exceeding 50% for very large SAEs. No quantitative tables were given, and the authors later noted (March 2024 update) that their views changed.

Two sparsity-regularized 1-layer models were examined:
- In one, a very sparse neuron responded to three facets ("it|'s", "and|/", "many/some| of") with no other neuron disambiguating; the output used the residual stream to make facet-specific predictions.
- With the residual stream cut, a neuron fired weakly for personal pronouns and strongly for 'm' in 'diplomacy'. Predictions switched by magnitude.
These are constructed counterexamples, not population statistics.

Tested in a strongly sparsity-regularized 1-layer model with the residual stream replaced by MLP output. Even with only one neuron firing per example, the neuron's weak versus strong activation coded unrelated facets that the model used productively. A constructive argument shows softmax(x, 3x−3, 5x−8) decoding of x∈{1,2,3}. The evidence arises only under strong regularization and does not refute linear representation in typical models.

Five native-English linguistics PhD students made forced-choice single-sentence judgments on 200 CoLA dev sentences (100 in-domain, 100 out-of-domain). Mean annotator agreement with CoLA labels was 86.1% (MCC 0.697). Majority vote agreed on 87% (MCC 0.713), so 13% of sampled labels contradict the majority. An estimated 1-2% of disagreements stem from OCR artifacts; the rest is attributed to missing context or dialect variation.

On the CoLA test set, supervised pooling classifiers (BiLSTM plus max-pool encoders with BNC, GloVe or ELMo-style embeddings) score consistently lower out-of-domain than in-domain, with MCC dropping by as much as about 50%. Unsupervised Lau et al. LM baselines show no such gap. Across 6 source-level splits (original plus 5 random, out-of-domain sizes 789-1539, 20 restarts each), the in-domain MCC advantage was up to 0.162 (0.125 for the original split). One split showed slightly better out-of-domain performance, so the size of the gap depends on which sources are held out.
models_studied: ["BiLSTM pooling classifiers (BNC / GloVe / ELMo-style embeddings)", "LSTM LM (BNC)", "n-gram LMs"]

experiment_summary: Encoders were pretrained on a real/fake discrimination task: BNC sentences vs. LSTM-LM samples and partially permuted sentences, with ELMo-style embeddings from a forward LSTM LM on the 100M-token BNC. Frozen encoders with CoLA-trained classifiers beat end-to-end CoLA-only training: in-domain MCC 0.341 vs. 0.278, out-of-domain 0.281 vs. 0.155. Unsupervised real/fake classifiers and Lau et al. LM scores far exceed CBOW (MCC 0.063 in-domain). Downsampling CoLA training data from 8551 to 100 examples (20 restarts each) shows roughly log-linear gains, with much of the benefit attained by about 300 examples. All models remain far below human aggregate MCC (0.695 in-domain / 0.815 out-of-domain).

Five templated targeted test sets were built: SVO permutations (100 triples x 5 orders), wh-extraction (260 pairs), causative-inchoative alternation (91 verb/object pairs), subject-verb agreement (169 quadruples) and reflexive agreement (144 sentences). They reveal rankings and failures hidden by aggregate CoLA MCC. The best overall CoLA model (ELMo-style real/fake) gets MCC 0.000 on wh-extraction and -0.020 on reflexives. The weaker-overall LSTM LM+WLPM baseline gets 0.601 on wh and 0.599 on SV agreement. The GloVe real/fake model reaches 0.988 on SVO order. Per-phenomenon breakdowns on the annotated dev set similarly show binding, violations and question constructions as hardest.
models_studied: ["BiLSTM pooling classifiers", "LSTM LM with Word LogProb Min-1"]

experiment_summary: In simple templated single-sentence tests (thresholded Word LogProb Min-1 scores, not minimal-pair comparisons), a BNC-trained LSTM LM scored the following MCC: wh-gap dependencies up to three words, 0.601; local subject-verb agreement, 0.599; reflexive-antecedent agreement, 0.152; SVO order, 0.801. Supervised LSTM acceptability classifiers performed near chance on wh-extraction and agreement. The tests involve only short dependencies and a different scoring protocol, so they bear only loosely on the claim.

Editors were trained on 5000 out-of-context examples and evaluated on 5000 held-out examples. Bias in Bios on GPT-J, layer 12: accuracy 0.55→0.71 with context and 0.05→0.66 without context, with fluency preserved. CounterFact on GPT-J, layer 1: efficacy 98.2 and neighborhood 100, with essence reduced to 24.8. On held-out unseen attributes (1689/5000), efficacy was 95.5. McRae concept edits raised correlated-feature probabilities, with a negligible effect on random features. Similar trends held on GPT2-XL and Llama-2-13b. Failure modes included repetition, essence destruction and changes to unrelated facts.

REMEDI editors were trained only out-of-context. On GPT-J, they still improved in-context Bias in Bios accuracy (0.55→0.71). As probes, they detected CounterFact context-integration failures better than the identity, fact-probe and shortcut baselines (F1 .42, phi .24), though far below a supervised skyline (phi .93). Transfer was weak on GPT2-XL (contextual MCC .01) and modest on Llama-2-13b (MCC .07).

CounterFact error prediction on GPT-J. Prior-knowledge errors: F1 .39, phi .26, beating the identity encoding (phi .17) and the Li et al. fact probe (phi .21) but not a shortcut probe trained on model outputs (phi .43). A random-init GPT-J control gave phi .09. Contextual errors: phi .24, the best of the non-skyline methods. A supervised error skyline reached phi .93. Results were near chance on GPT2-XL and modest on Llama-2-13b (prior MCC .19).

For factual attribute insertion, single-token REMEDI edits outperformed prepending the fact to the prompt. CounterFact efficacy was 98.2 vs 80.2 for the prefix (GPT-J), and similarly .97/.98 vs .84 on GPT2-XL and Llama-2-13b. On GPT-J McRae concept edits, REMEDI raised correlated features far more than the prefix (Δp 7.1 vs 0.4) and better matched human feature co-occurrence (r .29 vs .16). However, essence preservation was worse than with prefixing (24.8 vs 40.5). With Llama-2-13b, which already follows the context well, in-context gains were small (.71→.72).

ROME was re-run on a 5000-example held-out CounterFact subset with GPT-J, following Meng et al.'s procedure. It achieved efficacy 100 and the highest consistency (43.0) and fluency (620.1), clearly beating fine-tuning (neighborhood 10.6). However, it changed facts about neighboring entities about 21% of the time (neighborhood 79.1), whereas runtime representation edits never did.

Setup: least-squares d_h×d_h maps were fit for every layer pair on one random position from each of 9k Wikipedia sentences, and evaluated against the true final-layer prediction.
- Representation fit: the maps reach much higher coordinate-averaged r² than identity propagation across nearly all layer pairs in GPT-2 XL and BERT-large.
- Next-token prediction: Precision@1 is more than 20% higher than identity up to layer 44 of 48 in GPT-2 XL.
- BERT-large masked prediction: Precision@1 gains exceed 17% at most layers.
- Surprisal is lower than identity at every layer in both models.
- Manual plausibility check (50 Leipzig sentences × 25 BERT layers): 85.4% of top-5 tokens fit the context, versus 52.8% for identity.
- Generality: results hold across GPT-2 small/medium/large/XL and BERT base/large.
- Cross-domain transfer (Wikipedia↔Leipzig news): Precision@1 changes by −0.1%/+1.1% for BERT and −5.5%/−8% for GPT-2.

Related but narrower evidence. The translators here are bias-free linear maps fit by regression on representations, not KL-trained affine maps against output distributions. Perplexity and vocabulary bias are not measured. Even so, the maps decode intermediate predictions far better than the logit lens across GPT-2 and BERT scales: higher Precision@k and lower surprisal against the final prediction.

- GPT-2: identity propagation retains partial r² and prediction accuracy, rising toward late layers. This is consistent with a partly shared space.
- BERT-large: identity fails to map representations between most layer pairs (low r²), and identity-decoded Precision@k is near zero in the first ten layers. Learned linear maps nevertheless recover much of the prediction.
- Interpretation: representations are often linearly related across layers but not in the same basis.

Direct projection of intermediate residual states (the id baseline) is compared with the true final prediction.
- GPT-2: direct projection yields nontrivial but much lower agreement than learned linear casting.
- BERT: direct projection yields near-zero precision in early layers.
- Plausibility: only 52.8% of top-5 identity-decoded BERT tokens are contextually plausible.
- Conclusion: direct readout is meaningful in some models and layers but substantially underestimates the decodable content.

Learned linear casting shows the final prediction is often recoverable early.
- GPT-2 XL, early layers: Precision@10 of 62–82% and Precision@1 of 28–45%.
- BERT-large: more than 25% Precision@1 from layer 3 onward.
- Agreement rises gradually with depth.
- The FFN-compromise aspect of the claim is not tested.

Setup: CALM-style softmax-margin exit rule on 24-layer GPT-2 (next-token) and 24-layer BERT (masked-token), sweeping λ.
- At a 95% Precision@1 target (agreement with full-model prediction), linear casting saves about 3.3 layers (13.8%) in GPT-2 versus 1.4 (5.9%) for identity.
- In BERT it saves about 4.8 layers (20%) versus 3.5 (14.6%).
- Dynamic exit beats fixed-layer exit for both mappings.

Setup: in 24-layer GPT-2, attention, FFN, or LN1/LN2 sub-modules from layer ℓ to the final layer were replaced by least-squares linear approximations. Agreement with the final prediction was measured.
- Linearized attention gave the highest Precision@1 and lowest surprisal among sub-module replacements.
- From about layer 7, all sub-module replacements beat a full-block linear jump.
- Limits: single model and dataset, and no mechanism analysis. The 'contextualization exhausts early' interpretation is speculative.

experiment_summary: Reproduced the QK/OV pivot tables from A Mathematical Framework in small transformers with 1–4 layers. The tables used embedding-to-head-to-logit circuit matrices with the unembedding LayerNorm bias removed, ranked by frequency-weighted heuristics. Interpretable skip-trigrams appeared across architectures with different positional embeddings and with or without LayerNorm. The best runs showed ~25–75% interpretable trigram entries plus many copying entries. Results were sensitive to training hyperparameter quality, dataset interpretability and depth. Single-layer models and the later layers of multi-layer models were most legible, and tables with less than ~10% interpretable entries were flagged as possible mirages.
models_studied: ["small 1\u20134 layer transformers trained by Anthropic (various positional embeddings, with/without LayerNorm)"]
location: Testing Base Model Quality Using Attention Pivot Tables

experiment_summary: Three Claude 3 Sonnet SAE features from Scaling Monosemanticity were tested (Brain sciences, Transit infrastructure, Popular tourist attractions). Their labels were judged specific from activating examples, yet they mostly failed to fire on snippets that Claude 3.5 Sonnet rated as highly relevant (≥9/10) among 160,000 filtered 128-token snippets per concept. By sensitivity these features ranked only in the top ~0.1–10% of dictionary features. The most-sensitive features often had reduced specificity or were uninterpretable. The exception was tourist feature 1M/11480, which covered all snippets rated ≥9.
location: Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering

experiment_summary: Several Claude versions rated 0–10 concept relevance on snippets where a feature activated. They agreed with high Spearman correlation and few rating differences greater than 2, although Claude 3 Haiku gave more all-or-nothing ratings. Human spot checks agreed. Claude 3.5 Sonnet then filtered 160,000 snippets per concept. Representativeness of the filtered distribution was assumed rather than tested, and the filter yielded too little data for the rare Golden Gate Bridge concept.
models_studied: ["Claude 3 Haiku", "Claude 3.5 Sonnet", "other Claude versions (raters)", "Claude 3 Sonnet (SAE features)"]
location: Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering — A dataset filtering method

experiment_summary: Snippets about a concept that the highlighted Claude 3 Sonnet SAE features missed were partly covered by complementary features, e.g. one firing near the term 'brain'. These complementary features retained some specificity, particularly in the larger SAE. Activation banding across the 50 most responsive features suggested distinct snippet subtypes represented by different features. Dictionary sizes were not systematically compared.
